note: The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the Paraiyar woman and the Brahmin woman differ in flesh, skin, bone or pleasure. The Kural still allows distinction by deed; Sivavakkiyar's bodily test allows none.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar says there is no mark of caste on flesh, skin or bone. The Naladiyar replaces caste with merit; Sivavakkiyar removes it and puts nothing in its place.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after sleep, a cycle that resumes; Sivavakkiyar says the dead are not born, as milk does not return to the udder or the fallen fruit to the tree, and denies it four times. On the plain reading of 1011 the two make incompatible claims about what follows death; on tradition's softer reading (not born into this body again) the conflict dissolves.

The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Sivavakkiyar says blinking at a rosary and counting places are nothing beside looking at one's own mind. Both set the inner change above the outward mark of the devotee.

The Kural's life flies off like a bird leaving its shell; Sivavakkiyar's life slips out and the body lies there. Both make the parting sudden and the body the thing left behind; Sivavakkiyar adds that people have watched it and learned nothing.

The banyan and its seed: the Naladiyar's tiny seed grows a vast shade to show that a small virtue in worthy hands spreads wide; Sivavakkiyar's banyan is folded back into its seed to show that the whole is already within the self. The same tree, growing outward in one and inward in the other.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from deeds; Sivavakkiyar says the one origin became the differences of caste and every being. Both deny that caste is primordial, the Kural by pointing to work and Sivavakkiyar to the one source.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are only words, and austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar asks 'what good castes?' and demands to be told how the Brahmins came to be. Both empty the word; the Naladiyar refills it with conduct, Sivavakkiyar with blood.

The Kural says that giving up craving at once yields a nature that does not shift; Sivavakkiyar says that once the wanting is renounced the thing wanted is quickly seen. Both make the gain immediate on the dropping of the want, though the Kural's gain is a state and Sivavakkiyar's is a sight.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh, and hell will not release the eater; Sivavakkiyar says the Saiva who rejects flesh grew on milk made of blood and is flesh himself, so the rejection is folly. The conflict holds if 1112 is a defence of eating; the Kural's ground is the killed creature and Sivavakkiyar's is the eater's own body, so each leaves the other's reason unanswered.

Both are fables of creatures busy inside an enclosure while death waits: the Naladiyar's turtle plays in the pot with the fire lit beneath, Sivavakkiyar's cocks and chicks quarrel in the guarded coop until the old jackal gets in. The Naladiyar names its moral (Death waits his moment); Sivavakkiyar leaves the coop and jackal unexplained.

Kural 269 says leaping past Death becomes possible for those with the power of austerity (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). 1119 says Death who came hunting is bewildered and goes for those who can see within themselves (தேடிவந்த காலனும் திகைத்திருந்து போய்விடும்). Both make a discipline, not a god's favour, the thing that turns Death away; the Kural's is tapas, Sivavakkiyar's inward seeing.

Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). 1122 says the sacrifice the Brahmins perform is itself goat-flesh (ஆட்டிறைச்சி அல்லவோ யாகம்). The Kural compares merits and leaves the rite standing; Sivavakkiyar calls the rite killing and the priests' meat-rule a lie.

Kural 34 says that to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர). 1146 calls installed images, homa, Vedas and bound books fierce babbling (கடும்பிதற்று) that ended as nothing when the Lord was known. Both dismiss outward religion as noise; the Kural's standard is a clean mind, Sivavakkiyar's a knowing of the Lord.

Kural 1 makes the letter A the first of all letters as the Lord is the first of the world. 1152 begins with the one letter within which the whole world rose (ஓரெழுத்து உலகெலாம் உதித்த அட்சரம்). Both ground the world in a first letter; the Kural uses it as a comparison, Sivavakkiyar as the first rung of a mantra ladder that ends in his own refrain.

Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns. 1156 says the loincloth, thread and tuft did not come with birth, so they are not what a Brahmin is. Both deny that outward marks make the religious man; the Kural speaks of the ascetic's hair, Sivavakkiyar of the Brahmin's thread, and the Kural supplies a conduct test where Sivavakkiyar supplies none.

Both make the body a clay pot. The Naladiyar's pot seeps filth from nine openings and only a fool calls it a woman; Sivavakkiyar's false pot (பொய்க்குடம்) tosses on the water when it holds only the five, and sits content when it has scooped up Siva. The same vessel is a cause for disgust in one and, filled rightly, a seat of delight in the other.

Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which part is the woman. 1169 lists what ten months of the womb's impurity became, two hands, two feet, two eyes, a body of sound, taste and smell, and says the 'pure' body is that impurity. Both take the body apart to deny it worth; the Naladiyar's aim is desire for a woman, Sivavakkiyar's pride in one's own body and birth.

Kural 274 likens the man who hides in austerity and does what is not austerity to a hunter in a bush snaring birds. 1175 asks what the false guise (கள்ள வேடம்) and the shut eyes are for, and calls the mumblers fools and then gurus. Both treat religious show as a hunter's cover; the Kural says what the hunter takes, Sivavakkiyar only exposes the bush.

Kural 278 says many bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed, with impurity in their minds (மனத்தது மாசாக). 1177 addresses those who bathe daily to remove dirt whose dirt is never removed, and asks where the dirt was. Both say water misses the dirt that matters; the Kural reports it of hypocrites, Sivavakkiyar tells the bathers where to cut.

Kural 298 divides purity: outer purity comes by water, inner purity is seen through truth. 1177 says daily bathing leaves the dirt and asks where the dirt was, so that it can be cut there. Sivavakkiyar's 'where' is the Kural's 'inner'; the Kural grants water its outer purity, Sivavakkiyar grants it nothing.

Kural 357 says that if the mind ponders and knows with certainty what is, one need not think again of birth. 1178 tells those lost in recited books to ask for themselves what birth, death, thought and standing are (நீர் நினைந்து பாருமே). Both put the mind's own inquiry above learning as the way past birth; Sivavakkiyar names the books as the obstacle.

Naladiyar 195 says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them, and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage. 1179 says caste difference does not exist at all for those who have known the Lord within. Both empty the word of substance; the Naladiyar replaces birth with merit, Sivavakkiyar with knowledge, and only Sivavakkiyar says there is nothing there (இல்லையே).

Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in the body has no home of its own. 1183 asks where life was before it took up the body, what joins life and body, and tells the jnani who took a body to answer. Both treat the body as the soul's lodging and ask after the soul's own place; the Kural's question is about impermanence, Sivavakkiyar's about origin.

Both say that nothing one owns goes along with one and only the deed does. The Naladiyar says it of all deeds at death; Sivavakkiyar says it of gifts and dharma, which return like a bolted horse while elephants, armies and horses do not.

The Kural cuts off the pride that says 'I' and 'mine'; Pattirakiriyar, after thinking over everything he saw as his own, rests in what he takes as His. The Kural removes the claim, the pulambal transfers it.

The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes only from what one does; Sivavakkiyar mocks renouncers who claim to be Brahman yet keep caste distinctions. Both deny that caste marks anything real.

Both separate owning books from understanding them. The Naladiyar distinguishes scholars who keep books from those who understand and teach; Sivavakkiyar calls those who stack books and recite liars, and asks what fixity and knowledge they have.

The Kural says virtuous action is not killing, and killing brings every other evil deed; Sivavakkiyar says that even one who kills for food, lies and steals may, if he can lovingly join the Lord, know the gods within himself that day. The conflict holds if 1239 makes realisation override the moral law; if it means only that the sinner is not shut out from the Lord, the Kural's ranking of deeds is untouched.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar says those who draw pond water without a drop of moisture in the mind achieve nothing, and that cutting the mind's dirt makes the light, you and I one. Both make the inner state the whole of it.

The Kural speaks of those with impurity in their minds who bathe as if distinguished and go about concealed; Sivavakkiyar says those who dip in the tank do not cut the dirt of the mind. Both charge the bather with a dirty mind under clean water.

The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes only from the work they do; Pattirakiriyar asks to go about with no division of caste, as Kapila's agama says. Both deny caste by birth; the Kural keeps a distinction by deeds that the pulambal does not mention.
The Kural ranks one abstention from killing above a thousand oblation-pourings, leaving the rite its lesser merit; Sivavakkiyar takes the next step and asks what the fire pit is at all.

The Kural defines giving as giving to those who have nothing, making need the whole criterion; Sivavakkiyar makes the recipient's conquest of the senses the criterion and calls gifts to the unmastered a waste. If the Kural's definition is taken strictly, the two cannot both hold.

The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and only deeds distinguish; Sivavakkiyar grounds the same equality in the shared senses, the shared pain of birth and the shared food, sleep and pleasure.
The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them; Sivavakkiyar's 'caste, caste, caste, caste' is such a word, and the one who says it never sees the letter SA.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go; Pattirakiriyar rests on no object and keeps only the watch for grace. Both leave a single hold when every other is dropped.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births and the rest cannot; Pattirakiriyar asks to join the Lord without parting and so cut off birth. Both make attachment to the Lord the one means of ending rebirth.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar asks what the ash on the body is for and puts the cutting of impurity and desire in its place. Both put inner cleanness over the visible sign.

The Kural says cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; Sivavakkiyar asks what can hold on to the one that has no holding, and answers that learning cannot, only asking those who have reached. The paradox is the same; the Kural treats it as method, Sivavakkiyar as a question about who can teach it.

Both make learning worthless without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning has gained if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge, and Sivavakkiyar tells the book-reciting yogis that there is no knowledge other than the Lord who stands as knowledge.

The Kural's many who bathe like the distinguished with impurity in their minds are Sivavakkiyar's 'dumb ones' who fall into water over pollution; the Kural's point is hypocrisy, Sivavakkiyar's that bathing cannot reach where impurity began.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from what they do; Sivavakkiyar argues the same from breeding: a Brahmin and an outcaste woman produce a child with no mark of difference, unlike a buffalo and a cow.

The Naladiyar calls 'good caste' and 'bad caste' mere words, made real only by tapas, learning and effort; Sivavakkiyar denies caste a basis in the body itself. The Jain text keeps a replacement standard, the Siddhar offers none.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar tells those who prepare seats and smear ash to first know where knowledge of the Lord arises and subsides. Both put inner state before outward preparation, though the Kural's is moral and the Siddhar's is gnostic.

The Naladiyar separates those who collect books and fill the house from those who understand them; Sivavakkiyar's book-carriers babble lies and do not know where birth and death occur. Both make possessing books a different thing from knowing.

The Kural asks what an appearance high as the sky can do if the heart sinks into a known fault; Sivavakkiyar asks what reciting transcendent knowledge does while a thieving heart remains. Both make the inner fault cancel the outward height.

The Kural says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Sivavakkiyar reports the day he stood with 'I' destroyed in the ocean of silence. The Kural's is an ethic of renunciation, the Siddhar's an experience, but the thing removed is the same.

Both use the frog that stays slimy in water: the Naladiyar for readers of flawless books who never gain discernment, Sivavakkiyar for bathers who never scrape the dirt from the mind. The image makes the same point in two domains, that immersion does not clean.

Both use the ladle that cannot taste what it stirs: the Naladiyar for the fool who mocks teaching he cannot savour, Sivavakkiyar for the stone and pot that cannot know the Lord they are made to hold. The same kitchen image serves ethics in one and the critique of idols in the other.

The Naladiyar scorns those who see that life may leave in a blink and still do no good; Sivavakkiyar scorns those who know all that is born dies and still talk of 'our property and yours' as if deathless. Both treat denial of death as the root folly of householders.

The Kural says that as this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள்; Sivavakkiyar says that where there are hands and wealth and no அருள், there is no Supreme, only a waste hell. Both make compassion, not rite, the condition of the beyond, and both set it against பொருள்.

The Kural's woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the raft to cross it certainly does not; Pattirakiriyar means to cross the sea of desire and climb the shore by kindling the inner homa fire. The same காமக் கடல், the lover's with no way across, the ascetic's crossed by fire.

The Kural says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next will be a good guest to the gods; Sivavakkiyar says the guest who comes becomes the Lord and grants life. Both make hospitality a path to the divine, the Kural by reward, the Siddhar by identity.

The Kural says not killing one creature to eat is better than a thousand sacrifices with oblations; Sivavakkiyar says the goat and cock offered at the Pidari shrine do not cure, since the deity is not the cause. The Kural's ground is non-killing, the Siddhar's is futility, but both set aside blood sacrifice.

The Kural's hidden conduct is a hunter in a bush snaring birds under cover of austerity; Sivavakkiyar's pious thieves make puja and vows flourish while seizing others' property. Both describe religion used as a blind for predation.

The Kural's hypocrite is red as the kunri seed outside and black at the tip; Sivavakkiyar's is white with ash outside and a liar within, his ash the dust where a donkey rolled. Both are judgements of the outward sign by the inner fault.

The Naladiyar's sages who see the body as a bubble in rain and resolve to end their wandering are the model; Sivavakkiyar's drummers who preach that the body is a bubble and then rob their hearers are the parody. The same image is held sincerely in one text and sold in the other.

The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Sivavakkiyar's matted-haired, ochre-robed men have kept the hair and not given up the fault. Both deny the outward mark any weight.

The Kural says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth; Sivavakkiyar asks whether plunging the head in countless rivers makes a pure jnani and answers that devotion does. Both deny water the power to make the inner clean.

The Kural asks why one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு) does hurtful things to other lives (மன்னுயிர்க்கு); Pattiragiriyar uses the same two words and asks when he will stop killing and eating மன்னுயிர் and think of them தன்னுயிர்போல். The Kural's rule of compassion becomes a condition of finishing tapas.

The Kural begs all who beg not to beg of those who conceal; the Azhuganni, baring his teeth to the base for goods, asks the Mother for wealth so that he need not go to them. Both find the shame of begging in the giver as much as in the asking.

The Kural says not killing is the whole of virtue and that killing brings every other evil; Ramadevar's rite is a procedure meant to bring an enemy's death and calls its teaching a secret for being saved. On any reading of 1534 as a killing rite, the two are incompatible.

The Naladiyar sees the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts, and praises those who resolve to end their wandering; Kaduveli calls the body a bubble on water and asks the mind for a means to stay unattached. The Naladiyar's bubble argues for ending rebirth, Kaduveli's for a method of non-clinging in this life.

The Kural says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; Kaduveli tells the mind to subdue and kill the vile anger. Both make anger the fault to be destroyed outright rather than measured; Kaduveli adds a caste slur to name it, which the Kural does not.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they have done; Kaduveli says nothing comes along at all, and that bearing the body is itself the trouble. The Naladiyar's exception for deeds is what Kaduveli's own pallavi relies on, since Yama comes for sin, so his flat 'nothing' is rhetorical, not a denial of karma.

The Kural makes understanding an inner fortress that enemies cannot destroy; Kaduveli has a fourfold fort within that must be captured from the enemy before one can rule the land. The Kural's fort is a possession that protects; Kaduveli's is held by the enemy and must be stormed, so the same image runs in opposite directions.

The first letter as the First Being: the Kural has the world begin from the Primal Lord as letters begin from அ; Pattiragiriyar wants to know within himself the letter that stood as the first beginning. The link holds on the reading of அரி as that primal letter, which is one of two.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes only from the difference in what they do; Kaduveli tells the mind to know the many castes said to be unequal as one and declare it as kinship. Both deny difference by birth; the Kural keeps a difference by work, Kaduveli names none.

The Kural says many with impurity in their minds bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed; Kaduveli says not to put on a false guise or wet one's obligations in many Gangas. Both pair ritual bathing with concealment: the bath is the disguise.

The Kural makes giving up craving the cause of an unshifting nature; Kudhambai makes the end of desire the consequence of knowing oneself and joining the Lord. The Kural asks for the renunciation first, Kudhambai expects it to follow.

Both open with the letter A as first: the Kural makes the Primal Lord first of the world as A is first of the letters; this text goes further and makes the A itself the Lord's foot and the root of the body.

The Kural's invocation names one Primal Lord as the first of the world; the work that borrows Valluvar's name invokes Brahma, Vishnu, the sun-moon light, Agastya, the guru and Guha in the body's channels, which is one reason the attribution is not taken seriously.

The Naladiyar says good and bad caste are only words and that austerity and learning make a lineage; the Siddhar text makes knowledge of the cosmos in the body the thing that destroys the charge of low birth. Both answer caste with attainment, in the ethical and the yogic domains.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of any other plan; the text that borrows Valluvar's name says it burned the fate-deed that was there from the first. On the reading that 1635 claims karma itself destroyed, the two are incompatible; the Kural's own 620 (seeing fate's back by toil) is the nearer relative.
Kural 620 says the untiring will see fate's back; 1635 turns that into the Siddhar claim of burning fate-deed and the triple void outright by unpanicked effort.

The Kural says that even with the fivefold awareness there is no benefit for those who lack true perception; Agappei asks what use study or doing is, since all the told ways are only pointers. Both deny that acquired knowledge avails without the inner seeing, though the Kural keeps learning and Agappei discards it.

The Kural says those called freed are those freed of craving and no others; Agappei says begging does not end birth and the Lord is where desire has ceased. Both put freedom in the ending of desire rather than in the outward act of renunciation, and both deny the title to the one who has only given up possessions.

Both claim escape from death through practice: the Kural says leaping past death is possible for those who have gained the power of tapas; Idaikkadar asks whether Antaka can approach one who holds the ineffable Lord within night and day.

The same reversal of attachment: the Kural says cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go, and Idaikkadar says hold (பற்றி) with love the one who stands free of attachment (பற்றற்று) so that agitation flies off.

Both make the death of desire the decisive step: the Kural says giving up craving at once gives a nature that never shifts, and Idaikkadar says that when the cow called desire is slain one sees and knows the whole cosmos, where taming the mind and killing anger (1745, 1746) were not enough.
The body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings, which the fool mistakes for a beauty, and Idaikkadar's body-pot whose nature is a jar of excrement.

Idaikkadar, having ordered attachment cut (1751), keeps one small unwavering desire for Brahman; the Kural keeps one clinging, to the one without clinging, as the means of letting the rest go. Both admit a single desire as the lever against desire.

Both deny that wealth lasts; the Naladiyar argues it from the rich man who comes to beg gruel, Idaikkadar from a list of twenty possessions with the single verb 'they do not stand'. The Naladiyar's chapter draws the lesson of giving; Idaikkadar draws that of joining the Siva-way.

The two attachments Idaikkadar cuts are traditionally 'I' and 'mine', which the Kural says must be cut to enter a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar names what follows: the higher pleasure and union with the Supreme.

Both call a human being who lacks the essential thing a tree: the Kural those without courtesy, however sharp, and Idaikkadar those who do not reach Siva by their own minds. Idaikkadar's tree also puns on தானு, Sthanu, the fixed one they fail to reach.

Both promise a lasting gain from keeping the senses under: the Kural says that withdrawing the five like a tortoise gives protection through seven births, and Idaikkadar says karma wears away for those who do not let the grazing senses rise above them.

The Kural says a household life that keeps to virtue has more endurance than those who do penance; Idaikkadar says household life is affliction and the good dharma is renunciation. The conflict is direct on the ranking of the two dharmas, which the Kural's chapter on household life argues one way and this verse the other.

The Kural says the domain of the five must be crushed and all that one has wanted let go; Idaikkadar says those who let the senses loose like dogs are demons. Both make the restraint of the five the first condition, the Kural in the chapter on renunciation and the Siddhar in a herdsman's song.

The Kural says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is protection for seven; Idaikkadar says untied dogs are never fit for guarding. Both treat restraint of the senses as protection, the Kural from the side of the one restrained, the Siddhar from the side of what the senses are for.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar blows the flute so that neither 'mine' nor 'I' remains. The pair of words is the same; the Siddhar's means is to play the flute as the Lord's own.

The Naladiyar calls the body a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, admired only by a fool dazzled by its skin; Konganar says those who have seen find no filth in it and should look within it. The conflict holds on the plain reading: for the Naladiyar seeing the body truly is seeing its filth, for Konganar it is seeing past the filth to what it holds.

The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', for it is the companion that does not perish; Konganar says that if fortune has come, do charity quickly and finish temple work, and 1947 adds that those who finish it do not die. Both make haste the whole of the counsel; the Kural's reward is a companion at death, Konganar's a kind of deathlessness.

The Naladiyar tells the wealthy to give, since the span cannot be exceeded and tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; Konganar says the one who has must feed the one who has not and must not say 'tomorrow', and gives the four Vedas as authority. Both make the urgency of giving rest on the nearness of death.

The Naladiyar says cows differ in colour but their milk does not, so virtue is one though its ways are many; Konganar says the one milk became ghee, curd and buttermilk, so caste differences are products of one substance. The image runs the opposite way: in the Naladiyar many sources give one thing, in Konganar one source gives many.

The Kural's tortoise draws in its five in one birth and is protected for seven; Pattiragiriyar's tortoise draws in its five on seeing a man come (ஆள்கண்டு), and he asks when he will do likewise and subside as a mute. Pattiragiriyar adds the approaching danger and takes the withdrawal into silence rather than into future births.

The Naladiyar's kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas were carried off and spoken of as dead; Pambatti's elephants, armies, chariots and horses are no help when Yama comes. Both take the king's army as the strongest case of a protection that fails.

The Naladiyar's kin arrive unasked and leave wordlessly, leaving the body to its own people like a bird leaving its tree; Pambatti's kin simply do not die with the dying. Both state the limit of kinship as a fact of nature, without reproach.

The Naladiyar tells the lover not to desire the woman for her spear-like eyes, since she too will stoop over a staff; Pambatti says her beauty is turmeric fading in sunlight and the lover will flee when the body goes like the parrot from the silk-cotton pod. Both argue from the beauty's end to the desire's emptiness.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one' because its dark skin dazzles him; Pambatti's lovers call a skin that will shrivel a round breast like Meru and fall into the stinking well. Both oppose the flattering name to the anatomy, and both blame the eye that is dazzled.

The Naladiyar refuses the men who call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears, having seen the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit; Pambatti says those without strength of mind call an eye that oozes filth a sword. The same simile (the eye as a blade) is rejected by the same means, a look at the organ.

The Naladiyar's untaught men call smiles jasmine buds and pearls, and the poet answers with the teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground; Pambatti's owl-men call spittle nectar and a mucous nose a bud. Both reduce the praised mouth to its fluids and remains.

The Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; Pambatti's pot of pus, blood and fat breaks and dog, jackal, ghoul and vulture eat it as their own. The broken vehicle and its scavengers are the same lesson against praising the body.

The Naladiyar's firm-minded see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; Pambatti's body is a bubble rising on water that will surely depart, and the hearer is to hold the Creator. The image is the same; the Naladiyar draws renunciation from it and Pambatti devotion.

The Kural says outer purity comes through water and inner purity is seen through truth; Pambatti says the body's impurity does not leave by bathing in rivers. Pambatti goes further than the Kural, denying even the outer cleansing, since the stench is in the fish; but both locate real purity elsewhere than in water.

Valluvar asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Pambatti asks what all merits achieve if the heart does not think of the One's feet. The same 'what use' question, with merit and penance in place of learning.

The Naladiyar's wedding drums become funeral drums for the bridegroom on the same day; Pambatti's wedding finery becomes the corpse's finery. Both use the one body dressed for marriage and for burning, and both draw renunciation from it.

Valluvar tells the reader to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging; Pambatti ends his stanza with பற்றானைப் பற்றி, holding to the one who holds nothing. The same paradox, compressed into two words.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, and the fool who praises it is deceived by its skin; Sangili's nine-gated one 'takes on beauty' for those who know it. The same nine openings, loathed in the one text, are in the other the thing to be known; Sangili's 2125 then uses the Naladiyar's disgust too.
The Kural asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Sangili looks for a body that is his own and finds none. Both make the body a place one stays in without owning.

The Naladiyar's wedding drums sound the same day as funeral drums for the bridegroom; Sangili's wedding show (மணக்கோலம்) becomes the corpse show (பிணக்கோலம்). Both rest on a single word changing while the scene stays.

The Kural calls the lowest understanding the one that takes the impermanent for permanent; Sangili lists what perishes, what is born, what is kept, what is seen, and tells the listener to know it. The Kural judges the error, Sangili supplies the inventory.

The Kural's life leaves the body as a bird leaves its குடம்பை; Sangili's soul leaves the கூடு, the cage or nest, and goes. The same image of the body as a bird's left dwelling, used by the Kural for the thinness of the body-life bond and by Sangili for the unreality of all who remain.

The Kural says the domain of the five must be crushed and all one wanted let go at once; Sangili says to burn off desire and attachment and then do yoga and live in this world. The letting-go agrees; Sangili's yogi stays in the world where the Kural's chapter is on renunciation.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else noisy show; Sangili says forest wandering and ritual acts yield no supreme arising to one whose mind runs. Both locate the test in the mind and treat the visible acts as secondary.

The anril that never parts from its mate is the figure of fidelity in both: in the Naladiyar it is the courtesan's broken promise never to part; in Pattiragiriyar it is the soul that should cling to grace when its companion is parted. The bird is the same, the bond is a lover's in one and the Lord's in the other.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Thirikonar's guru cuts egoism (ஆணவம்) out by the root. The Siddhar makes the guru the cutter where the Kural leaves it to the renouncer.

The Kural says hiding in austerity and doing what is not austerity is a hunter snaring birds from a bush; Thirikonar's chariyai-men praise the awakened one in order to embrace her, outward service as a cover for desire. Both expose the garb of religion used for gain.

The Naladiyar separates those who fill a house with books from those who understand them; Thirikonar's book-ghosts are the first kind, possessed by books, and the awakened one is told not to want their company.

The Kural's bird leaves its egg or nest empty, an image of how slight the bond of body and life is; Punnakku's chick lies whole in the egg, an image of the life complete within the body-shirt. The same egg, used once for leaving and once for what is already inside.

The Naladiyar's drummers beat three times and the dying carry the dead; Punnakku's mourners beat drums and weep without counting their own days. Both use the funeral drum to show that those who mourn are on the same road.

The Kural asks whether the life lodging in a corner of the body has found no home of its own; Punnakku says the body and even the loincloth are on loan. Both make the body a lent or rented place, not the self's possession.

The Kural says that giving up insatiable craving at once gives a nature that never shifts; Kanjamalai says that when desire is thrown out root and bundle, the dissolution of mind joins of itself. Both make the positive state follow immediately and without further effort from the removal of craving.

The Kural says what is not yours will not stay however guarded and what is yours will not leave though thrown away; Kanjamalai says do not push away what has come and do not crave what has not. The Kural's chapter is on ஊழ், fate; Kanjamalai draws from the same fact the yogi's equanimity rather than a doctrine of fate.

The Kural says the moment attachment ends it cuts off births; Kanjamalai says give no room to desire, do not get bound in the body's pains, do not take birth again. Both make the end of craving and the end of birth one event; Kanjamalai adds the guru's feet as the thing to hold instead.

Nondi's wicked 'chandalas' are company he forgot in order to find the fit vessel and join the worthy; the word marks conduct, not birth. The Kural redefines birth by conduct in the same way: having conduct is noble birth, failing in it low birth. The agreement holds if சண்டாளர் is read morally, as the stanza's contrast with பாத்திரம் suggests.
Both say the ascetic's outward form without the inner strength is a disguise: the Kural's cow grazing in a tiger's skin, Kakapusundar's robed and staffed guru roaming like a dog.

The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kakapusundar mocks the ochre, the staff and the stoop as show. Both make the marks of renunciation worthless without the thing itself.

The Naladiyar says good caste and bad caste are empty words and lineage is made by tapas, learning and effort; Kakapusundar says caste is spoken only by the unseeing and all are born of the same seed. Both empty birth-caste, though the Naladiyar puts conduct in its place and Kakapusundar puts common origin.

Both make release a matter of the mind knowing with certainty: the Kural's mind that ponders and knows what is need not think of birth again; Agasthiyar's mind subdued by devotion, knowing the state in the whorl, has moksha itself. Agasthiyar adds the yogic place; the Kural does not.

The Kural sets truth spoken with the heart above austerity and giving; Agasthiyar makes truth the first requirement of being human and closes the run on it, while keeping rites and samadhi in their place below it.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and everything else is noisy show; Agasthiyar says a right mind is the whole of mantra and the breath practices are unnecessary. The same move, mind made the sole essential and outward means set aside, in ethics and in yoga.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Agasthiyar says the daily practitioner lives as long as the earth and is not caught in Death's hand. The conflict holds if Agasthiyar's claim is about the physical body, as the Siddhars' kaya-siddhi tradition takes it; if 'not caught by Death' means release from rebirth, the two need not clash.

The Kural says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back, taking rebirth as real and release from it as the goal; Agasthiyar lists 'there is birth' among the things scripture made up for a living. The conflict depends on reading 2425 as denying rebirth rather than as mocking its preachers.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them, and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Agasthiyar says caste was set up for livelihood. Both deny caste a real basis, the Naladiyar replacing it with merit and Agasthiyar with knowledge of pooranam.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, not even the body they adorned; Pattinathar says nothing was brought at birth and nothing is taken at death, and draws from it that the wealth held in between is Siva's and is to be given.

The Kural opens with 'a' as the first of letters and the Primal Lord as first of the world; Agasthiyar closes 2444 with the Supreme as the first letter. The image of God as the first letter is shared; the Kural uses it as a simile, Agasthiyar as an identity within the Omkara science of 2445.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Agasthiyar asks what the learners of the Agamas and many books know if they cannot tell the undying head and foot. Both measure learning by a knowledge it does not itself contain.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of anything else one devises; Romarishi says fates are only what one has thought, with the god concurring. On the reading that 2468 makes fate the product of thought and not its master, the two claims are incompatible.
The Kural's hunter hiding in a bush is Valmiki's fruit-eating mute who calls his wandering yoga: austerity worn as cover for what is not austerity.
The Kural's cow grazing in a tiger's skin; Valmiki's yogi in matted hair, tiger skin and ash who does not know the cause. The skin marks the pretence in both.

The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from work; Valmiki says caste was made by men to live by. Both refuse birth as a ground of rank, though the Kural keeps a ground in deeds that Valmiki does not mention.

The Kural makes understanding the seeing of the true substance of whatever is heard; Valmiki's seeing needs no witness, companion or hearsay. Both place knowledge in direct seeing rather than in report, and Valmiki goes further in dismissing report.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which part is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar says karma itself took the form of a woman, became the breasts and flesh men speak of, and threw him into the pit of filth and blood. Both dissolve the woman into her body; Pattinathar adds that he fell in.

The Kural says the greatness of those whose word is full is shown by their hidden words (மறைமொழி); Pattinathar says the graced may be known by their austerity, nature, grace and love and even by their obscure words (இருளுறு சொல்). Both make the dark saying a sign of the great rather than a defect.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot seeping filth from nine openings that only a fool calls beautiful; Valaisami's body is a vessel of filth too, but he names it only to ask what subtle thing enters it and where that comes from. The same image serves disgust in one and inquiry in the other.

Both say water takes the nature of the ground it lies in; the Kural applies it to understanding, which takes the nature of one's company, and Pattinathar to the Lord or the soul, which stands in each soul according to its ripeness. The image is the same, the domain different.

The Kural says the wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pattinathar likens the ungiving man to a fruitless tree, a dried tank and a cow without milk and asks why he was created. Both judge a life by what it yields to others.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after it; Pattiragiriyar asks to know the way (வகை) by which he died and came back alive, as darkness follows a lamp going out. Both treat death and the next birth as one continuous passage, and Pattiragiriyar wants the passage itself understood.

Valluvar says neither the shaven head nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Vaalaisami asks who will accept the beard, matted hair and sannyasi costume of one who runs about in base antics. Both strip renunciation of its outward marks and judge it by conduct.
The Kural calls hardest of heart those who live by deceit while seeming to have renounced; Valaisami's false gurus, who talk of the substance and take money, are that type in an alchemist's dress.

The Naladiyar says the bellies of the senseless are burning grounds for the beasts and birds they eat; Pattinathar's flesh-eaters feed the inert pot of the body with killed lives and are themselves bitten by Death. Both make the eater's body a place of the dead.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Pattinathar calls his own body a pot of rice and curry and the woman's body a pit of filth and blood. Both strip the body to a vessel of waste; the Naladiyar aims it at the lover's eye, Pattinathar at both bodies at once.

The Kural says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods anxiously and then say they have no support; Pattinathar asks what being on earth is worth for those who will not feed the guests who come yet live in prosperity. Both treat hospitality as the test of a household.

The Naladiyar ends its funeral-drum stanza with சாவார் சாப்பிணம் சுமப்பார், the dying carry the dead; Pattinathar's mourners are சாம்பிணம், corpses that will die, rolling and crying round the corpse that has gone. Both make the funeral a procession of corpses; Pattinathar adds that the dead man at least left his desires.

The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's 'wealth' is a life without partiality, hot anger, slipping from good or daily seeking. Both define the good by what it abstains from, and both place anger in the heart (நெஞ்சில் / உள்ளத்து) rather than in act.

The Kural asks where the life of the one who conceals hides when the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pattinathar asks for a wealth that never says 'there is nothing' to askers without even looking at them. Both treat refusal of the asker as a kind of killing.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and that hell does not open its mouth for the eater; Pattinathar heads his conditions for wealth with not killing and not eating what was killed. Both put killing and eating together and before the other faults.

The Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left; Pattinathar says crowned kings and all the rest burn to a fistful of ash, and that even seeing it people cling to life. The Naladiyar's lesson is impermanence; Pattinathar's is that seeing it does not teach.

The Kural says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like that crowd breaking up; Pattinathar asks where the kings' wealth and their hand-built theatre halls (நாடகசாலை) are once the Lord's mind turns. Both use the theatre for the vanishing of wealth; Pattinathar makes the Lord the one who empties it.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; Pattinathar names the Siva-bliss as what stands free of 'I' and 'mine' (எனதற நினைவற) along with the two deeds and the malas. Both make the end of the two possessives the threshold; the Kural's reward is a higher world, Pattinathar's is the Lord himself.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, called 'broad-shouldered one' by the fool; Pattinathar counts the openings one by one, rheum, wax, mucus, spit, wind and urine, and says the mind took this grass hut for firmer than stone. Both reduce the body to its leaks; the Naladiyar aims at the lover, Pattinathar at the mind's own trust in its body.

The Naladiyar's firm-minded see the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts; Pattinathar's catalogue includes the bubble on water (நீரிற் குமிழி) and then says the body is worse, a stain of maya. The Naladiyar makes the image the mark of understanding; Pattinathar treats it as too kind.

The Kural says the friendship of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its nest (குடம்பை) behind; Pattinathar names the body a hut (குரம்பை) from which the bird that is life flies off, in the middle of his catalogue. Both use the one bird and the left nest; Pattinathar makes it one name among forty for what he is laying down.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which of them is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar goes limb by limb and sets bone, sweat, mucus and wax against the flower and fruit each is called. Both dissolve the praised woman into her matter; Pattinathar does it against the poets' conventions by name.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any other plan. Pattinathar says rolling so that the devotees' feet touch one's head tears the leaf of fate. On the Kural's plain reading fate is unbeatable; on Pattinathar's, devotion beats it. The conflict depends on taking கிழிப்பது as cancelling fate rather than only ending its grip on the mind.

Both deny that the outward signs of the ascetic matter: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one quits what the world condemns, and Pattinathar says forest, air, rags and bowl are nothing without inner love. The Kural's test is conduct, Pattinathar's is love, but both move the mark inward.

Both make standing among people a function of money: the Naladiyar says a man with a few coins gains rank whatever he wears, while one with nothing is lower than a corpse though well born; Pattinathar says mother, wife, child and kin all become enemies once wealth is gone. The Naladiyar counsels on wealth, Pattinathar draws the conclusion that only the Lord's feet are free of the dependence.

Both make the fate of the body after the life leaves a matter of indifference: the Naladiyar asks what it matters whether the corpse is dragged with a rope, buried with care or thrown anywhere; Pattinathar lists forest, shore, city, house and porch as the places where the body may fall and gives the life a companion that does not depend on which.

Both describe the desired body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings and churns with slime, dazzling the fool with its dark skin; Pattinathar's pus-hole, pit of filth and hidden wound. The Naladiyar blames the fool's eye; Pattinathar asks for the state that leaves the pleasure behind.

The Kural curses the creator if even begging is needed to live: let the one who made the world wander and perish. Pattinathar lists loincloth, porch, leaves, water and the Lord's name as enough, and 345 adds that when hunger comes Siva gives. On the Kural's plain reading a life sustained by begging is an indictment of the world's order; on Pattinathar's, it is the life in which nothing is lacking. The conflict holds if both speak of the same begging; the Kural's chapter is about want forced on a man, Pattinathar's about want chosen.

The Kural says to do virtue without delay, since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar measures property to the house, wives to the street and children to the burning ground, and says what follows is the pair of deeds, merit and sin. The Kural names only the good companion; Pattinathar adds that sin follows just as faithfully.

The Kural says that removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where wealth should be stored; Pattinathar's teaching to his heart is to hold wealth as nothing and look at the face of the hungry (பசித்தோர் முகம் பார்). The Kural keeps wealth and redirects it; Pattinathar has already dismissed it and keeps only the looking.

Pattinathar calls the begging bowl, the loincloth and the verandah wealth without lack, proclaimed by the Veda; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is the worst of lives; for Pattinathar it is the chosen one. The conflict holds unless the Kural is read as about the poor who beg from need rather than the renunciant.

Pattinathar tells the heart that good and evil come only as Brahma wrote, so that even worship changes nothing and the right stance is not to waver; the Kural says those who toil without flagging will see fate's back. On Pattinathar's plain reading, no effort alters the outcome; the Kural claims effort can. The tension softens only if 365 is read as counsel for the mind's peace rather than a claim about causation.

Both set the household against its end: the Naladiyar's man sees the corpse carried and the kin wailing yet marries and believes there is joy here, and the funeral drum answers him; Pattinathar's wife, sons and house, real day by day, went away as a lie, an old tale and a dream. The Naladiyar's warning is before the fact, Pattinathar's report is after.

The Kural says the false embrace of women of wealth is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Pattinathar lists going to the harlots as the one act of a heart that refused self-knowledge and the guru. Both place the courtesan at the far end from knowing what is real.

The life as a bird: the Kural says body and life are friends only as a bird that flies off leaving its shell or nest; Pattinathar's mother dandled him so that the sky-bird would not fly away, that is, kept the life in the infant body. Pattinathar uses the Kural's figure for what the mother held back for a time.

The Kural says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today; Pattinathar says the same of his mother, enthroned, then in the street, then ash, and adds what the Kural does not, that the whole of it is Siva. The Kural's observation becomes a Saiva conclusion.

The body as a vessel with nine openings that seep filth: the Naladiyar's fool praises the pot that leaks from nine holes because its dark skin dazzles him; Pattinathar calls it a nine-mouthed wound and names the cure. The Naladiyar's image serves to shame desire, Pattinathar's to ask for medicine.

The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's list of what the mind will not give up has lying, flesh and anger beside not thinking of the Lord and not reciting the five letters. The Kural's ethical list is kept and the Saiva items added to it as the same kind of thing.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot seeping filth from nine openings, which the fool addresses in the words of love poetry; Pattiragiriyar's is a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow and spread. The Naladiyar uses the image against desire for another's body, Pattiragiriyar against attachment to his own, and sets the feet against it.

The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar says speak the Lord's name before Death, the dimming eye, the mourners and the pyre. Both make the time before death the only time, and differ in what is to be done in it, virtue in the Kural and the name in Pattinathar.

The Naladiyar says the body lasts like water on a grass tip, so do good right now, for people will say 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone'; Pattinathar's five 'befores' end at the same wailing kin and the pyre. Both reason from the suddenness of the end to an act now.

Pattinathar names taking alms and eating them among the four things that alone are happiness; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is a life not worth the world's making; for Pattinathar it is the whole of the good life. As at 357, the conflict holds unless the Kural is confined to the needy.

The Kural says not asking, even from those who give gladly, is worth ten million times more; Pattinathar goes beyond not asking: he will not go even when called with insistence, and eats only what is brought to where he sits, though the body waste. The Kural's restraint on asking becomes a refusal of the giver's house.

The Naladiyar's worthy man goes before no one except those who embrace him and say 'come in, eat'; Pattinathar will not go even to those, and accepts food only if it is carried to him with eagerness. The Naladiyar allows the welcoming host as the one exception; Pattinathar removes it.

The vultures at the stinking body: the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures crowd in and tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; Pattinathar's heart is asked whether it has not seen the vultures hop, strip the skin and eat. Both end the body's story at the birds and use the sight as the argument against loving it.

The Kural asks why one who knows what is hurtful to his own life does hurtful things to other beings; Pattinathar tells the heart not to intend harm to anyone, since the body one would protect by harming belongs already to the dogs and vultures. Both ground harmlessness in the self, the Kural in the self's own knowledge of hurt, Pattinathar in the self's having no body to defend.
The body as a bubble on water: the Naladiyar praises those firm enough to see it so and end their wandering; Pattinathar confesses that his thought takes the bubble for permanent.
The Kural calls taking what does not last for lasting the lowest understanding; Pattinathar confesses that very thought in himself, and adds that it is held fondly (ஆதரவாய்).
The Kural says cutting off the pride that says 'I' and 'mine' enters the highest world; Pattinathar's guru cuts the ego (ஆங்காரம்) at the root. Pattinathar adds that Om itself goes with it.

In the Kural the town, not knowing the woman's worth, makes the lover a present of gossip; Pattinathar's speaker, whose state is now visible, expects to be the country's song and the lookers' talk. The lover's gossip becomes the jnani's.

The Kural says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not returning, so that learning is the way to the real; Pattinathar says the cause is not learning and not hearing but what is shown by a hand. The conflict holds on the reading of கற்று as learning the true texts, which is how Parimelazhagar takes it; if the Kural means only 'having learned to see', the two agree.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging, in order to let clinging go; Pattinathar says he held her as the hold of those who hold to nothing. The Kural commands the soul to hold; Pattinathar has the Lord do the holding.

The Naladiyar says the scheming of women whose minds are with another man is plainly known and fools still do not grasp it; Pattiragiriyar takes a woman whose mind is elsewhere even in her husband's pleasure as the model for keeping the Lord's feet in his thought. The straying wife is the ethical poem's warning and the Siddhar's figure for devotion; the moral domain and the devotional one use her oppositely.

Both make the lowest understanding a mistake of perception: the Kural's paltry mind takes what does not last for what lasts; Pattinathar's shell-for-silver people cannot reach the Lord. The Kural's object is impermanence, Pattinathar's the Supreme.

The Kural makes the Primal Lord first of the world as the letter A is first of letters; Pattinathar says he is not born of letters and not held in a book. Not a conflict, since the Kural's letter is a simile, but Pattinathar refuses the medium the Kural uses.

The Kural says cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging, so as to let clinging go; Pattinathar names the same thing பற்றற்ற பற்று and adds that the Lord came to earth to show it. The Kural's paradox is made a person.

The Naladiyar's petty-minded say 'we are rich' and never think where they must go, and their wealth vanishes like lightning; Pattinathar's boast 'all this earth is our holding' is the same speech, confessed in the first person after the vanishing.

The Naladiyar's body is a bubble in pelting rain, forming and bursting again and again, and those who see it so resolve to end their wandering; Pattiragiriyar's life is a bubble on water (நீரில் குமிழி) to be left so that the flood of grace may rise. The bubble leads to a resolve in the Naladiyar and to a request for grace in Pattiragiriyar.

The Naladiyar asks what it matters whether the body is dragged with a rope or buried once the dancer has left it; Pattinathar's man who could not bear an ant on his body consents at death to its binding and burning. The body that was everything becomes a thing one lets others dispose of.

The Kural says that for those bent on ending births even the body is excess; Pattinathar says the body is one's own enemy and he died not knowing it. The Kural states the ascetic's view, Pattinathar the cost of not holding it.

The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; Pattinathar's heart, given a birth in which to share rice, thought gold, house and women permanent instead. Both make giving the lasting use of a passing thing.

The Naladiyar says share the food of blameless wealth from the day it comes, because it turns like a cart wheel; Pattinathar adds that it came by earlier deeds and was not got today, and that the destitute and the learned were owed a share.

The Naladiyar says those who live on earlier austerity and do none now will stand outside the house grieving; Pattinathar says gold and women come only from austerity done before, and the heart that does not hold to the guru now is blind. Both treat present fortune as spent merit.

The Kural pictures the body and life parting as a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; Pattinathar ends his list of everything that stays with கூடு, the cage or nest, left while 'you' went. The nest is the body in both.
The Naladiyar's firm see the body as a bubble in pelting rain; Pattinathar's heart trusted the water-bubble life as certain. Same image, opposite minds.

The Naladiyar says give at once what comes to hand, for those who gave first escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives; Pattinathar's heart gave not a nut's worth of rice and did not ask who would stand by it when Yama's messenger drags it. Giving is the only provision for that journey in both.

The Kural says the gambler's winnings are like the hook swallowed by a fish; Pattinathar is the kendai fish writhing on the hook of women's maya. The same hook, baited with winnings in one and with women in the other.

The Kural says that for those bent on ending births even the body is excess; Pattinathar says the escape he failed to make was to leave the country the five ruled, the body, as the Pandavas left their kingdom. Both make leaving the body itself the renunciation that counts.

The Naladiyar asks whether spices, flowers and finery can remove the body's foulness, which eating strengthens; Pattinathar's body stinks however it tries not to, a salt-pot leaking its ooze. Both say the stink is the body's nature, not a lapse.

The Kural says the friendship of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell; Pattinathar says he was bound by believing this body and life would be permanent. Both deny the bond between body and life any permanence; the Kural states it as a fact, Pattinathar as the error he lived by.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews, skin and flesh and asks which part is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar lists sinew, flesh, skin and bone and their stench and says that inside them he was deluded. Both make the inventory of tissues the cure for delusion about a body; the Naladiyar aims it at desire for another's body, Pattinathar at his own.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Pattinathar asks what it matters however much one has learned or gained if one does not know the Lord. The same question, learning weighed against knowing the Lord and found light; Pattinathar adds possessions to the scale.

The Kural says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not returning, making learning a route to the seeing; Pattinathar says those who say 'we shall know by learning' do not see the feet, and that without gaining it birth is not cut. Pattinathar does not deny the Kural's result but denies that learning as such produces the seeing; the Kural's கற்று is the condition he says is not enough.

The Naladiyar praises those firm in understanding who see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; Pattinathar confesses the opposite history, having taken the bubble for his support. The verdict on the body is the same and the Naladiyar's praised man is what the poet failed to be.

The Naladiyar says those who delighted in fleeting youth later rise painfully on a staff, and that the wise renounced knowing grey hair would come; Pattinathar's stanza is that sentence drawn out, from the praised youth of sixteen to the staff in the red hand. The Naladiyar draws the lesson of early renunciation that Pattinathar leaves to the reader.

The Kural's rule for a real field, manuring before ploughing and guarding after weeding, is the order Pattinathar's heart-farmer follows: he manures with truth before sowing and builds the fence of peace against the five cattle after pulling the weeds. The farming knowledge is the same; Pattinathar moves it to the mind.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one' because the dark skin dazzles him; Pattinathar lifts the skin and lists what is under it, hair, wound, blood, bone, marrow, slime, worms, excrement, nerves and disease, and asks which of them is 'I'. The Naladiyar aims at desire, Pattinathar at the self.

The Naladiyar ranks striving in austerity as the best way to live and dwelling with those one loves as the middle; Pattinathar says the austerities bring the ascetics no more than the man who dwelt with women and kin and kept the name on his lips. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's ranking is of the paths to the goal; if it ranks only the dignity of lives, Pattinathar is answering a different question.

The Kural says the field of the five senses must be crushed and all that was wanted let go at once; Pattirakiriyar watches the mind that roams by the five senses' paths fall burnt. Both make the senses' mind the thing to be killed, not trained.

The Kural condemns those who, unrenounced in heart, live by deceiving as though renounced; Pattinathar confesses to exactly that false outward service and asks whether the Lord will take it anyway. The confession turns the Kural's verdict into a plea, and it leaves the verdict standing.

The first sight of the woman in both: the Kural's man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a rare peahen or human; Pattinathar's hero sees the grace of a golden peacock and red-streaked eyes and love is born. Pattinathar states the effect (காதல் விளைத்தன) where the Kural leaves the man reeling.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods; here the 'I' (நான்) dies in the chain that ends in the state of release. Both place the death of the self before the gain.

Gossip as a gift to the lovers: the Kural's man says the town made him a present of gossip; Pattinathar's friend tells the hill lord that his partings spread the gossip (அலர) and that the field's vengai now bears his name. In both the rumour is turned toward the match rather than against it.

The woman's heart runs ahead of her to the absent man: the Kural's woman's heart climbs as she thinks of his return; Pattinathar's girl says her mind has run here and gone worshipping after the pitiless hill lord. Pattinathar adds the devotional verb தொழுது.

The same figure with the same claim: those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Pattinathar's Ekambar is the one who makes us cross the sea of birth (பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர்). The Kural names no god; Pattinathar names Ekambar of Kachi.

The Kural's king with all six, army, people, wealth, ministers, allies and fort, stands among kings as the male leads its herd; Pattinathar grants the same horses, elephants, infantry, chariots and parasol and says kingship and drum never shine without Kambar's ash on the brow. One condition is added that the Kural does not have.

Both deny that birth sets rank: the Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from what one does; Pattinathar says one born at the bottom of a killing, flesh-eating clan is best of all if he loves the Lord's anklets. The Kural's measure is work, Pattinathar's is devotion, and both set it against descent.

The bangles that slip from the wrist announce the man's parting in both: the Kural's woman asks whether her slipping bangles do not already say the lord of the shore has left; Pattinathar's mothers search the street for the white bangles that fell from the girls wasted by the begging Lord.

Both say Death can be leapt past: the Kural's one who has the power of austerity can; Pattinathar's Brahmin of Kadavur lived because the Lord crushed Death. The Kural credits tapas, Pattinathar the Lord's act for a devotee.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Pattinathar says the Lord crushed Death so that the Brahmin of Kadavur might live. The conflict holds if the Markandeya story is taken as a claim that one man did escape; if the Naladiyar speaks of ordinary men and the verse of a miracle, they need not clash.

Both speak to the heart as a separate party in a parting: the Kural's woman's heart climbs at the thought of the man's return; Pattinathar's mother asks her faltering poor heart where the eloped girl now walks on the stony path. The love is a lover's in one and a mother's in the other.

In both the bangles know before the woman is told: in the Kural they register the lord of the shore's parting before her mind does; here they tighten at the mere news of the chariot, so that the slipping bangle of separation runs in reverse.

Both refuse the deferral of 'today, that day, some day': the Naladiyar puts Death behind the one who asks when, Pattinathar puts the god's leaving behind the one who says 'we will serve tomorrow'. The Naladiyar asks for virtue as far as one can; this verse asks for service without a day's gap.

The same crystal that takes the colour of what lies against it: in the Kural it is the face showing what is strongest in the heart; in Pattinathar it is the god showing each sect its own belief. The figure explains an appearance by its neighbour in both, but the Kural reads a man and Pattinathar excuses a god.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Sivavakkiyar says the Sama and four Vedas and all the sastras, recited in safety, leave one not knowing Siva. Both deny learning any worth apart from the Lord, though Sivavakkiyar's route is inward perception, not bowing.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; Sivavakkiyar asks the builders of long houses with shut doors whether they mean to live, and shows them standing helpless when Death's sound comes. The Naladiyar draws the lesson of giving, Sivavakkiyar of holding to the feet.

Both say use the body while it lasts: the Naladiyar tells those with a sturdy body to take the fruit it can yield before it departs like mist; Sivavakkiyar says make yourself firm while the boat lasts, for when it breaks there is no one left in the open.

Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an afflicting spirit to those without discerning understanding. Thiruppugazh 10 shows that embrace from the inside: the kohl eyes, the smile, the net of talk, 'come in' (மனைக்கு எழுந்திரும்), the bed, and then the plea to be freed from the sorrow of these poisonous girls (நஞ்சன சிறுமிகள் துயரற). The song is the experience the Kural's verdict describes.

Kural 261 says bearing what pain comes and causing no pain to living beings is the form of tapas (அற்றே தவத்திற் குரு). Thiruppugazh 1000 calls singing Murugan's valour in the Valli story so that all the land knows, and seeking his feet, the rare tapas (அருந்தவம் வாய்ப்பதும் ஒருநாளே). On the reading that the Kural's definition is exhaustive, the two disagree about what tapas is.

Both stand the lover of pleasure beside the funeral: the Naladiyar's drum answers the man who sees the corpse carried yet thinks there is joy here, and 1001 asks at the drum and the burning ground whether that is sweet.

Kural 915 says those whose knowledge is refined by good intellect will not plunge into the base charms of women whose favours are common (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). Thiruppugazh 1003 confesses the converse: seeking the courtesans, he never learned or tried to follow the words of the great virtuous ones (பெரிய குணதரர் உரைசெய்த மொழிவகை ... பயிலவு முயலவு மறியாத). Both tie the plunge to want of the knowledge that teaching gives.

Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into taking a worthless woman's love as their own will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Thiruppugazh 1003 reports that outcome from inside: after seeking the courtesans, his kin and all people call him fool, witless and low-born (அசடன் அறிவிலி இழிகுலன் இவன் என இனமும் மனிதருள் அனைவரும் உரைசெய). The song gives the Naladiyar's public ridicule as the poet's own shame.

Kural 322 sets sharing one's food and sustaining many lives (பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல்) at the head of all the virtues the authors gathered. Thiruppugazh 1006 opens its long list of lacks with that one: not a millet-grain's thought of sharing (பகிர நினைவொரு தினையளவிலுமிலி), then without compassion. The self-accusation follows the Kural's order of virtues.

1008 likens women with spear eyes to நடுவன், Yama, who strikes young men without pause (இடைவிடாது எறு நடுவனும் என); Kural 1083's man says he never knew Death (கூற்று) before and now knows it in a woman's grace and warring eyes. Both name the beloved's look as Death itself; the Kural says it in wonder, the song in fear of capsizing in the sea of fate.

The Kural's woman says that when her lover is away evening comes like enemies to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்). For the love-sick hill girl of the song the gentle things turn hostile in the same way: the moon burns like the sun (இந்து வெயில்காய) and the soft breeze comes like fire (மிதவாடை வந்து தழல்போல), with gossiping women's blame added (வசைகூற).

Kural 1084 says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்); 1012 makes the same eyes the poison that rose when the gods churned the sea (இமையவர் பற்றிக் கடைந்த அன்றெழு நஞ்சுபோலே), stronger than Kama's five arrows. The song enlarges the Kural's life-eating look into the world-threatening halahala.

1013 shows women, once Kama stands before them, burned by the white crescent like the undersea fire (கொளுந்து வெண்பிறை வடவை எறிக்க), the bees' song and the Malaya breeze wounding the body; Naladiyar 392 hears the rain-clouds' thunder as a funeral drum for women without their companion. In both, the ordinary beauties of nature turn into instruments of pain for the lovesick woman.

Naladiyar 29 says the body lasts like water on a grass tip, so do virtuous deeds now before people say he was gone with his kin wailing (கேள் அலற); 1014 pictures the kin wailing, the palm-wood pyre and Death tying the life, and asks before then (உடன்றுபோமுன்) to learn in the discipline of those who think of Murugan as the giver of the goal. Both use the wailing at death to say 'act before'; the Naladiyar asks for அறவினை, the song for learning in the devotees' company.

Kural 1131's lover says that for one who suffers in love there is no safeguard but the palmyra horse (மடல்); 1017's praise has Murugan himself, bowing at the hunter girl's feet and wandering unseen in the millet field, resolve to mount the new madal (புதியமடல் ஏறவும் துணிந்த). The song gives the Kural's desperate lover's last resort to the god.

1018 describes women who show eyes, hair and arms, ask for coins through a broker and stand in the street like peacocks (தெருவினில் மயில்போலே நிற்பார்); Naladiyar 354 says the other kind, unlike household women, show off their charms themselves like a fresh flood (புதுப்பெருக்கம் போலத் தம் பெண்ணீர்மை காட்டி). Both mark the courtesan by self-display; the song adds the broker and the price.

Naladiyar 55 tells the heart that youth has passed to no purpose and disease and old age are coming now (கொன்னே கழிந்தன்று இளமையும்), so set out on the good path; 1019 traces the same life in stages, youth robbed by sly-eyed women, middle age bound by kin's rope, then coughing and losing breath to the pyre, and asks for the day he escapes this forest of a body (மெய்க்காட்டைத் தவிர்வதும் ஒருநாளே). The song spells out the wasted span the Naladiyar sums up in a line.

The Naladiyar says that to loveless women men without wealth are poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார்) is sugar. The song shows a man acting on that rule, going for wealth as far as Bengal and China (பொருள்தேடி வங்காளம் சோனம் சீனம் போய்) to join such women's shoulders, and asks whether he must suffer such hard pain (வன்பே துன்பப் படலாமோ).

1020 describes women who praise a man lavishly for money (பொருட்கு மிகத் துதித்து இளகி) before their elaborate lovemaking; Kural 911 warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. Both locate the danger in the flattery bought by money.

Kural 1085 asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ); 1023 has kohl eyes that surpass Yama in killing (யமனை அட மீறிச் சீறும் மைக்கண் விழிவலை). The song takes the Kural's riddle as settled and puts it to work in the courtesan's net.

1023 describes women who price their breasts and sell love's pleasure on camphor beds to the measure of the coins (முலையை விலை கூறிக் காசுக்கு அளவே); Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends with the oil (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both say the love is exactly as long as the money.
The Naladiyar's hoarder who neither enjoys nor gives dies mocked by his own wealth; 1028 adds that such men, who seek money and live without giving, go to Death's town.

1029 asks whether the girl should waste away under Kama's arrows, the roaring sea, the cuckoo and her own mother's harsh enmity (மாதாவின் வார்மைப் பகை); Kural 1147's woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (அன்னைசொல் நீராக). In both the mother's scolding feeds the love-sickness it means to check.

Both put a woman's eye to a doubting question with Death among the answers. The Kural asks whether it is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three; 103 lengthens the list to poison, fish, Kama's arrow and Yama's messengers, and turns the doubt into the poet's own confusion before he asks for Murugan's feet.

1030 confesses that while great craving remains he cannot speak truth (பேரவா அறா வாய்மை பேசற்கு அறியாமே); Kural 364 says purity is the absence of craving and it comes by wanting truth (அவாவின்மை ... வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்). Both bind craving and truthfulness together, the Kural as a rule, the song as self-accusation.

1030 regrets learning books whose noise never ends (ஆரவாரம் மாறாத நூல் கற்று); Naladiyar 256 says the learned hold back while others talk, as dry palm leaves rattle and the green leaf is silent. Both treat noisy learning as the mark of learning gone dry.

Kural 1110's lover says closeness to the woman is like knowledge, each union showing how little was known before (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால்), a delight that keeps renewing; 1031 confesses he is never sated (தணியாமல்) by lips that taste ever new (புதிதாய) like fresh cane juice and asks instead for the meaning no one can find. The same endless freshness of desire is joy in the Kural and the obstacle to the true meaning in the song.

Kural 340 asks whether the life, a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்), has no home of its own; 1034 calls the body a hut of skin, bone and flesh (குடிலூடே) where life dwells until the trident-bearer comes to seize it. Both picture the body as a temporary shelter the life must leave; the song asks for devotion before the eviction.

The song repeats the stock comparisons poets give patrons (வேளே போல்வாய், மாலே போல்வாய், காரே போல்வாய்) and regrets carrying them in vain (வீணே) to men who neither fit the praise nor give. Naladiyar 219 judges abuse better than praise of qualities a man does not have (இல்ல புகழ்தலின் வைதலே நன்று). The Naladiyar gives the moral rule; the song confesses breaking it.

Naladiyar 26 says that once the dancer has left the skin bag (தோற்பை), it does not matter what is done with the body. The song takes the body's end, the hut of sinew, skin and water (நாரால் தோல் நீரால்) becoming a place for dogs and ghouls, as a deadline and asks for the strength to sing the feet before then (நாய்பேய் சூழ்கைக்கு இடமாமுன் ... தாள் பாடு ஆண்மைத் திறல் தாராய்). The Naladiyar's indifference to the corpse becomes in the song a reason to act while the body still serves.

In Kural 1133 the lover says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse lovers ride (காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்). The song says women's eyes make even sleepless gods and Vedic ascetics free of infatuation resolve to mount it (துறவரான பேர் யாரும் மடலேறத் துணியுமாறு). The Kural's private loss of shame becomes in the song a power that undoes renunciation, and the poet asks for a way out.
