Thiruppugazh 105 asks for grace to leave the sea of births and reach the high good state (பிறவிக் கடல் விட்டு உயர் நற்கதியைப் பெறுதற்கு அருளைத் தரவேணும்). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song, beaten by Kama's arrows, asks for what the Kural names as the only crossing, and asks it of grace rather than of effort.

Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts (the Naladiyar's மொக்குள், 1054's குமிழி); the Naladiyar praises those who see it so and resolve to end birth, and 1054 confesses cherishing it anyway.

Naladiyar 35 says those who took the body's fruit early, as one takes jaggery from the cane, feel no distress when Death comes (கூற்றம் வருங்கால் பரிவதிலர்). The song asks for the flawless truth so that the mind may ripen and praise the feet (மதியும் மூத்து உனது அடிகள் ஏத்திட) before Death's men come to fight for the hut of bones and disease. Both make the use of the body before Death the answer to Death.

Naladiyar 91 says those who give gladly what they can even when they have little (இல்லா விடத்தும் இயைந்த அளவினால்) will not find the door of that world shut. The song confesses not giving even a handful of bran (தவிடின் ஆர்ப் பதம் எனினும்) to those who ask, and calls this dying without having lived. The measure is the same in both: giving is judged by what one could give, however little.

The song opens the funeral with drums sounding (படு பறைகள் ஆர்த்தெழ) and the household crying. Naladiyar 24 counts the drum beats, once, again, and at the third the corpse is covered and the fire lifted (முக்காலைக் கொட்டினுள்), the dying carrying the dead. The Naladiyar takes the drums as proof that no one escapes; the song uses the same scene to ask Murugan to turn Death back.

The song confesses the love poetry the poet made for courtesans: are their eyes sword or vel, their hair cloud or forest, their mouths milk or nectar (பாலோ தேனோ பாகோ வானோர் அமுதேயோ). Naladiyar 41 mocks the 'worthies' who cry 'O fair, lovely girl' (மாக்கேழ் மடநல்லாய் என்றரற்றும் சான்றவர்) without seeing that the body is a flimsy dwelling. The Naladiyar names the blindness the song confesses in its own praise-verses.

The song says lust, through women's eyes, drew the poet with delight into the rotting hut that runs with blood (குருதி ஒழுகி அழுகும் அவல குடிலை இனிது புகலாலே). Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen vultures tear at the stinking cart (முடைச்சாகாடு) once its axle breaks. Both set desire's delight against the body that rots.
Both say nothing goes with a person at death; the Naladiyar names deeds as the one thing that does, while 1066 lists wealth, servants and wife that do not and turns to praising the feet.

The song traces the body from the womb to a wheezing, pitiable old age (பழசாய் இரைப்பொடு ... விருத்த பரிதாபம்) and asks that before he dies (மடியாமுன்) he be given a life of saying 'Muruga'. Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth rise later leaning on a staff. Both turn the certainty of old age into a reason to act before it; the hymn's act is a name, the Naladiyar's renunciation.

The poet babbles the books of learning (கலைநூல் பிதற்றி) while his black hair turns white without understanding, and asks to be taught true knowledge. Naladiyar 52 says the best reflect on old age and death and do their real work, and none are more foolish than those who prattle (பிதற்றும்) on grammar and astrology. Both use the same verb for learning recited without the knowledge that matters, set against greying.

The poet trusted that the wife he joined and his sons would not falter (கலங்கிடார் என்று), took pleasure in the world, and fell into misery. Naladiyar 25 mocks the man who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried off and still marries, saying there is joy here (உண்டு உண்டு), and the funeral drum answers him. The hymn is the confession of the man the Naladiyar mocks.

The singer asks whether Kama's arrows may strike the young girl who lies with pallor (பசலையொடு அணையும்). Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in return (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The hymn sets the classical pallor of love inside a frame of praise, with Murugan as the absent lover.

The poet describes women adorned with civet, agil, sandal, pearls and gems, with blue-lily eyes and nectar speech, in whose beds he melts helplessly (அவர் வசம் உருகி அழியும்). Naladiyar 47 says the fool praises 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' to a pot seeping filth from nine openings because its covering of skin dazzles his eyes (கருந்தோலால் கண் விளக்கப்பட்டு). The Naladiyar names what the adornment the hymn lingers on covers.

The Naladiyar says those set on the right path will not embrace such women; 108 says their laughter makes even renouncers weaken. If 108's துறவினர் சோர is taken literally, it doubts the Naladiyar's confidence; it may be only the poet's hyperbole.

Thiruppugazh 108 spends its first half on the courtesan's toilet, turmeric bath, saris, combed hair, camphor dot, agil and musk paste on the breasts (அகில்புழுகு ஆரச் சேறு தனத்திட்டு), and asks for the feet to end the desire it rouses. Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands (படுசாந்தும் கோதையும்) have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks. The Naladiyar supplies the end of the body the song only adorns.

The poet speaks of eating women's spittle and throwing away the capital in his hand (கையில் முதலைக் களைந்து). Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure the courtesan's favour by what is in the hand; the hymn speaks from after the hand is empty.

Sunk in the sea of lust that grows from dark delusion (கருமயல்), the poet sought fish-eyed women as if they were the real thing, or wealth (பொருள் என நாடி), until the last day. Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes what is not the thing for the thing (பொருள் அல்லவற்றைப் பொருள் என்று). The hymn is a case of the error the Kural names, with Death's noose as its end.

The poet melts over doe-eyed women whose eyes are like strife-making swords with poison set in them (விடம் எலாம் வைத்த கலகவாள் ஒத்த விழி). Kural 1084 says the eyes of the artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). Both make the eye a killer; the Kural's lover admires it, while the poet asks to be saved from it by the wisdom of the feet.

After listing the women's lily-like kohl eyes (குவளையேர் மைக்கண்), ear-rings, gait, hair, breasts and speech, the poet asks, 'should I give my mind to these?' (சித்தம் விடலாமோ). Naladiyar 44 asks, 'shall I give way' (கவற்ற விடுவேனோ) when men call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears, and answers that an eye is like a scooped-out palm fruit. Both refuse the catalogue with the same kind of rhetorical question; the hymn answers it with a catalogue of the god's names.

In a mother's voice the singer lists what wastes her daughter: Kama's flower arrows, the bees' humming, the sea's waves and roar, and the moon that burns like the sun (கலைமதி அங்காயும் வெயில்). Kural 1228 says the herdsman's flute becomes a messenger of the burning evening (அழல்போலும் மாலை) and a weapon that kills. Both turn gentle sights and sounds into weapons against the separated lover, the stock torments of akam carried into the hymn.

The song sees the body as blood, water, skin, gut and bone (குருதி சலம் தோலும் குடலுடன் என்பாலும்) holding a life of delusion and lust until Death takes it. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin (குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும்) and asks which part is the garlanded woman. The same inventory serves the Naladiyar against desire and the hymn as a prelude to death.

Thiruppugazh 109 asks that, instead of thinking real (மெய் என மனம் நினைவது) the wife, kin, children, rich land and town, he be given the work of worship. Kural 345 says that for those set on ending births even the body is excess, so what of other ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). The song lets go of the household; the Kural extends the same letting go to the body itself.

The poet describes union with women in detail, then calls it the cruelty and deceit of women who give union (கலவி தரு மகளிர் கொடுமை எனும் உறு கபடம்) and asks not to lose his mind in it. Kural 913 says the false embrace of women who sell themselves (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both judge the embrace itself as a lie.

The Kural says not asking even from glad givers is ten million times better; 1092 shows the poet who begged from patrons who gave nothing, and seeks the end of that poverty not in better patrons but in the one Thing.
Both list the body's gut, fat, blood and flesh (குடர், கொழு, குருதி, தடி) to undo desire; the Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman, 1093 shows women perfuming and adorning that same body.

The women's eyes are made as if Death and Kama had joined to worship slaughter (வதை பழக மறலி விறல் மதனன் வழிபடுதும் என), to take young men's lives. Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both put Death in the woman's eye; the Kural's lover marvels, the poet calls himself the blind man it has caught.

The poet describes lovemaking at length and vows that even when lost in passion he will not forget Murugan's feet (அவசமுறுகினும் அடிகள் மறவேனே). Kural 1125 has the lover say he would recall her qualities if he forgot, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's inability to forget is moved from the beloved to the god's feet, and kept even inside another love.

The Thiruppugazh shows women who price their breasts (முலையைவிலை கூறிவிற்று), lead a man into a fine house and onto a flowered bed (வடிவதிக வீடுபுக்கு மலரணையின் மீதிருத்தி), melt his heart and seize what wealth there is. The Kural says the false embrace of women who sell themselves (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both say the paid embrace is empty; the song gives the setting the women stage, and the Kural replaces the bright room and flowered bed with a dark room and a corpse.

In the Thiruppugazh the women tell their lover that while body and life are one there is no yours and mine (உடலுயிரதாயிருக்க உனதெனதெனாமறிக்கை), and the poet calls this a deceit (தோதகம்) and asks for teaching to end it. The Kural's lover says sincerely that his bond with the girl is that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்னமற் றன்ன). The same figure of body and life is a vow of love in the Kural and a seller's line in the song.

The Thiruppugazh's women swear they cannot bear to be apart for a moment (ஒருபொழுதொணாது), and the poet names their union a deceit. The Naladiyar recalls the woman who said, like the anril birds, 'we will never part from you' (நித்தலும் நம்மைப் பிரியலம்) and then turned away like a ram's horn. Both treat the paid woman's vow of never parting as the snare itself.

Kural 329 says those whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are base in their work (புலைவினையர்) to those who discern. Thiruppugazh 11, asking Murugan to end his birth today, names himself small, base, a killer (சிறியன் புலையன் கொலையன்), setting புலையன் beside கொலையன் as the Kural joins them. The poet passes on himself the judgment the Kural passes on killers.

The Thiruppugazh speaks of women who seek only money (தனந்தனை நாடி), offer refuge with sweet words knowing their own deceit, and measure out their love falsely (நின்றளந்தும் சளங்கொண்டிடும்). The Kural describes women who weigh the gain and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்) and tells a man to weigh them in turn and keep away. The song's measuring and the Kural's weighing name the same calculation behind the sweet words.

The Thiruppugazh describes lovemaking as falling into a sea of pleasure (இன்பவாரியில் விழுஞ் சிந்தையேன்) and asks how such a mind will ever reach the shore (கரைசேர்வேன்). In the Kural the woman says the sea of love surely exists (காமக் கடல்மன்னும் உண்டே) but there is no safe raft to cross it (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). Both make desire a sea with no crossing; the Kural's lovesick woman wants to reach her lover, and the poet wants to get out of desire itself.

The Thiruppugazh pictures lovers entwined like anril birds until two hearts become one (அன்றில்போல் உளமிரண்டொன்றுமாய்), and asks to pass beyond the deeds those women bind him in. The Naladiyar quotes a paid woman who promised never to part, like the anril birds that never separate (புணர்பிரியா அன்றிலும்போல்), and then left. The anril, the bird of unbroken union, appears in both books inside the courtesan's embrace, and both poets look past it.

The Thiruppugazh lists the women's eyes as Kalakuta poison, cruel Death's form and Kama's arrows (கண் காளகூடம் கொடுங் கால்ருபம் பொரும் காமபாணம்), and asks whether his swinging senses will ever stop without saying 'Om namo Kanda'. The Kural's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both see death in a woman's eyes; the Kural says it in wonder, the song as a danger it wants a mantra against.

The Thiruppugazh asks not to be worn down by dog-like disputants (நாயொப்பவர்) who call good words evil (நற்சொலைத் தீதெனா) and argue against those who come to true austerity. The Naladiyar says that when the guileless explain virtue, the crooked do not hear it, just as the tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk-rice (குணுங்கர்நாய் பாற்சோற்றின் செவ்வி கொளல்தேற்றாது). Both use the dog for one who cannot receive good words.

The Thiruppugazh describes women whose sword eyes, sharper than the vel, make war on young men's lives (இளைஞராவியை வளைந்தமர்செய் வாள்விழியர்) while their hearts hold deceit. The Kural's man says he never knew what Death was until now: it is a woman's grace with large eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both see the woman's eyes as a battle that takes a man's life; the song adds that the eyes serve a deceit aimed at his wealth.

The Thiruppugazh calls the body a hut filled with disease and evil (நோய்தீமை இட்டகுடில்) whose binding will come undone when Death's messenger comes, and asks Murugan to think of him before life is lost. The Kural asks whether the life, lodging in the body as a temporary shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு), has found no home of its own. Both make the body a poor lodging for life; the Kural leaves the question open, the song answers it with praise of the Lord.

Both say the paid embrace is false. The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in the dark; 111 shows it from inside, the price bargained, the tight embrace and the man melting like wax, and calls it a madness from which only release frees him.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the dying man as a bird caught in the snare of the tattvas' workings, giving up its life (ஒட்டில்பட்ட குருகு சத்துவிட்டப்படி), and asks Murugan to come with his devotees at that hour. The Kural says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Both picture death through a bird; in the Kural the bird goes free of its shell, in the song it struggles in a trap and needs a rescuer.

The Thiruppugazh begins with the body of the five elements (பூதக்காயம்) and confesses that he wanders pretending like those who make a show of devotion (நிற்பாரைப்போல அப்பாவித்து), asking for knowledge beyond the bond. The Kural says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind. Both set the pretender's show against the five elements of his own body; the Kural has them mock him, and the song makes the same body the ground of his confession.

The Thiruppugazh confesses seeking wealth like a merchant, like one after honey (செட்டாகத் தேனைப்போல), and singing a few songs to men newly come into fortune. The Naladiyar says people cling to the wealthy and will not leave them though they give nothing, like ants circling a pot of ghee they cannot reach. Both show the seeker hovering round the rich for a sweetness he may never get.

The Thiruppugazh describes consorting with women whose devotion is for silk and palm-leaf earrings, and himself stumbling about in full view of foes and friends in the neighbourhood (ஒட்டார் நட்டார் வட்டாரத்தே ... தடுமாறும்). The Naladiyar says those fooled into taking a paid woman's love as theirs, who take wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both add public shame to the cost of such love.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the body as a torn, leaking hut (பைப்பீறற் கூரை) and himself running to every land seeking its food (இரைதேடி) until worn out. The Naladiyar says the foulness of the body is always strengthened by the work of eating (உண்டி வினையுள் உறைக்கும்), and finery cannot hide it. Both see the body as a thing endlessly fed and never made sound.

The Thiruppugazh confesses that for women who speak false talk of pleasure he went mad taking their lies for truth (பொய்க்கே மெய்க்கே பித்தாகி) and ran to every direction and island for money for their hands. The Naladiyar says some trust the words such women speak to be believed (தேறா மொழிந்த மொழிகேட்டுத் தேறி) and take them for their own, though they belong to no one. Both put the ruin in the man's taking false words as true.

The Thiruppugazh describes women who pass off false love as true and press for coins into their hand (காசுக்கே கைக்குத்திடு மாதர்). The Naladiyar says the friendship of harlots is like a lamp's light: as the light ends when the oil runs out, their love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure such love by the hand, the song by what it demands and the Naladiyar by when it stops.

The Thiruppugazh confesses that he sought food all over the earth and praised unkind, thieving men with words of desire (சோரர்க்கே வித்து ஆசைச் சொற்களை ஓதி), and asks for good words to sing Murugan's feet. The Naladiyar calls the lowest way of life following, out of desire for wealth (பொருள்நசையால்), people who do not recognise one's worth. The song confesses living that lowest way and asks to leave it.
The Naladiyar says even the starving should not tell their need to men without courtesy; 1125 confesses doing exactly that, going in verse to the cruel and loveless, and asks to be stopped.

1128 calls the courtesans' offer கூடா நட்பு, friendship that does not join, after which they bring ruin and leave (கேடா விட்டகல்). Kural 821, in the chapter titled கூடாநட்பு, says the friendship of those close without inner consent is an anvil to strike on once the chance comes. The song moves the Kural's false-friend pattern into the courtesan's trade, using its very name.

1128's courtesans name a price (விலைகூறி) and stay only if they get a share of the wealth (பொருள் கூறாகப் பெறில் நிற்கவும்), speaking false friendship. Kural 911 warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. The song shows the bargain the Kural names in one line.

Thiruppugazh 113 describes women who swear oaths, rouse desire and then make a man's wealth in hand run out (கைப்பொருள் மாள) before quarrelling and bewildering him. Naladiyar 377 says those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then turns away will be laughed at. Both name the same sequence, a show of love, the hand's wealth taken, then the turn.

1130's women bargain the price (விலைபேசி) and snatch whatever wealth comes (வருபொருள் கண்டு ஏற்கவே பறிக்கும்) while calling a man in with sweet looks. Kural 912 names women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own good nature (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்) and says to weigh them and keep away. The song is the scene; the Kural adds the advice the song turns into a plea.

Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot swim the great sea of birth (இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). 1132 narrows the sea to the eddying pool of coupling (சுழி மிதுன வாவியில் புகுந்து முழுகி) and asks for the good, imperishable feet (அழியா மன் நல் பதங்கள்) so as not to drown. The song applies the Kural's image to the poet's own drowning in lust.

Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth rise later leaning on a staff. 1133 is the life Naladiyar warns of told from inside: years spent on the burning belly, then grey hair (நரைகளும் பெரிதாயே), the name 'old man' (கிழவன் என்றொரு பேர்), faltering steps, and the question whether he will perish without reaching the Dancer's raised foot.

Kural 1085's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). 1136 opens with the same questioning list, vel or carp or sword or flower, a messenger sent by Yama, a deer or poison (எமன்விடு தூதோ மானோ விடமீதோ). The Kural's wonder becomes in the song the poet's record of the praise that ruined him.

Kural 173 says those who want the other joy will not do wrong out of desire for the small joy (சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி). 1137 grants that the pleasure of union is slight (சுகம் அற்பமாகினும்) and still says he cannot, cannot leave it (விடவோ இயலாது இயலாதே), so he asks for release as a gift. The song adds the condition the Kural leaves out: knowing the joy is small does not by itself free a man from it.

1139 counts among the base those who shout down rivals with many quarrelsome books and rise by winning (கலகக் கலை நூல் பல கொண்டு எதிர் கதறி ... வென்று உயர் கயவர்). Naladiyar 313 mocks men who itch to rise and debate on the strength of a word (சுனைத்தெழுதல் காமுறுவர்) without grasping the power of learning. Both treat learning used for contest as a failure of learning.

Both put the faithless woman beside liquor and make her the mark of lost fortune: the Kural's women, drink and dice are the company of those Fortune has left; 1141 calls the drinking courtesans themselves மூதேவிகள், Misfortune, who bring poverty.

1143 calls the body a raw clay pot with eight openings and one (எட்டுடன் ஒரு தொளை ... பசு மட்கலம்) soaked in deeds and disease; Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot (கும்பம்) seeping from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) that the fool praises for its skin. Naladiyar uses the pot to cure desire; the song uses it to ask for the knowledge beyond the tattvas.

1144's courtesans, once the wealth in his hand is gone, say 'no shame? go, go now, call the others' (வெட்கமிலை நட ஏகும் ஏகும் இனி மற்றவரை அழையும்). Naladiyar 373 says such women would bow and send away even red-eyed Mal if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). The song gives the dismissal in the women's own words.

Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in a corner of the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) has no home of its own. 1145 calls the body a hut (குரம்பை) worn out in the pit of union and asks when, leaving it (விட்டு அகன்று), he will reach Murugan's lotus feet. The song names the home the Kural's question leaves open.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums while the kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still believes in household joy; 115 adds the mourners washing and letting go of the bond, and asks Murugan to come before that day.

1150 counts among his faults that he took this passing life as lasting (மாதேச வாழ்வை நிலையென்றே). Kural 331 calls exactly this, taking what does not last as lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்), the lowest kind of understanding. The song lists the Kural's verdict as one item in a confession.

1151 confesses he sees no way to end his passion and no companion to help (ஒழிக்க ஓர் வகை காணேன் உறுந்துணை ஒன்று காணேன்). Kural 1164's woman says the sea of love is there but no raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்), which commentators read as having no helper. Both name the lack of a helper out of desire; the song then finds it in Murugan, who himself longed for Valli.
Both make the courtesan's love last as long as the man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out when the oil ends; in 1154 the wealth in his hand is gone and everyone drives him off with 'chi, chi'.

The Kural says smallness adorns itself in self-praise; 1155 gives the examples, the coward praising his valour and the miser calling himself Dharmaputra, and then applies the charge to the poet himself.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them; 1155 mocks men of base lineage (இழிகுலத்தர்) for claiming a high one, which treats birth-rank as real. The conflict holds if இழிகுலத்தர் is read literally as low caste rather than as a term of abuse for base men.

Both hear the funeral drum and see the corpse covered. The Naladiyar counts the beats with detachment and ends 'the dying carry the dead'; 1158 is the dead man's own view of his mourners, and turns the scene into a plea for the feet at that hour.

The Kural says that for those whose delusion is gone (மருள்நீங்கி) and whose sight is clear, darkness leaves (இருள்நீங்கி) and joy comes. 1159 asks that darkness not cover (இருள் மூடாவகை) a mind caught in delusion (மோகாதி) and the senses, and that knowledge rise like dawn (நிற்குண ஞானோதய). The song turns the Kural's statement into a plea, with delusion, darkness and clear knowledge in the same order.

In Thiruppugazh 116 the sounds of the night, the sea's drum, the flute and the bull's bell, pierce the lovesick girl's ears like an iron spike (வேயோசை ... இருசெவியின் நாராசம் உறுவதென). In Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is the burning evening's messenger and a weapon that kills. Both turn the pastoral flute, sweet in itself, into a weapon against the separated woman.

The Kural asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ), since it has all three. 1160 also measures women's eyes against three things: it says they beat the carp (சேலை அடர்த்து), have more of poison (ஆலம் மிகுத்து) and are fiercer than the deer (உழையைச் சீறு). The Kural's lover wonders at the look; the song makes the same comparison into arrows (விழிக் கணை) and asks to put that desire far away (ஆசையினைத் தூரவிடுத்து).

The Naladiyar's wife feels shy each time her husband embraces her and wonders how women who embrace many men for gain (பொருள்நசையால் பன்மார்பு சேர்ந்து) do it every day (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). 1164 describes those women from the cheated man's side: daily they make love (தினம் ... புணர்ந்திட்டு), daily they cheat and seize his goods as if collecting a debt (தினம் தெட்டிக் கடன்பற்றிக் கொளும் மாதர்). The wife cannot imagine that daily trade; the song says what it costs the man, and asks for the feet so that he may gain Sivam.

Both show an old man with failing speech or teeth and a staff whose eyes are still on desire. The Naladiyar says such a man has no way to safety; 1166 is the old man's own confession and still hopes his mind will turn to song.
Both put good deeds before the body fails: the Kural before the hiccup stops the tongue, 1167 before the day the wife spits and life slips away. 1167 joins dharma to bowing before Murugan.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) and those who do not cannot. 1168 pictures births rising like the seven seas (திரை ஏழே போல் எழு பிறவி மாக்கடல்) and asks Murugan to end his weariness in it, give him his feet to wear (உனது தாளே சூடி) and lift him into the assembly of devotees. The song keeps the Kural's sea and feet and adds the devotees' company (அடியார் வாழ் சபை) as the place reached.

Thiruppugazh 117 confesses that he praised as equal to the five heavenly trees men who never gave a single coin (ஒரு காசே கொடாதவரை ஐந்து தருவை நிகரே யாக) and begged daily in great Tamil without finding a footing. Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who hide what they have (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The song is the Kural's warning lived out: the poet begged of exactly those the Kural names, and found no footing.

The Naladiyar's paid women seem sweet while the man is fooled and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாமார்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்). 1173's women take the wealth of many and then pick a quarrel to drive them out (பலர் பொருள் கவர்ந்து இடை கலாமிட்டு ஓட்டிகள்), after weeping and rubbing their eyes as if in love (அன்புமுடையாரைப் போல் ... கண்பிசையும்). The song gives the same turn from feigned love to hostility and adds the false tears.

Both make the palmyra horse the end point of love's suffering. In the Kural it is the lover's only strength; in 1174 it is what a learned renouncer and yogi is reduced to, and he asks whether fate or grace brought him there.

The Kural's woman says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to cross it (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 1181 cannot cross the ocean called desire (ஆசை என்கிற பாராவாரம்) and sets beside it a second ocean, of tantra, ritual, Veda and Agama, whose shore he never sees. The song keeps the Kural's sea with no crossing and adds the sea of scripture, which does not save either; only the guru's grace is left.

The Naladiyar says men without money are poison to the paid women, while a man who has worked an oil press is sugar to them if he has wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம் அன்னார்). 1182 calls them dancing girls who soften at the sight of gold (பொன்கண்டு இளகு கூத்திகள்). Both make gold the only thing that moves them; the song adds the poet's own enslavement and asks to praise the hills instead.

Both describe women who take all the wealth from a man's hands while he believes in their love. The Naladiyar ends in the town's laughter at the fool; 1183 ends in a plea to be taken out of that union.

Both go through the woman part by part. 1185 lists waist, gait, feet, hair, earrings, breasts, lips, eyes, smile and forehead, each ending in -க்கே, and confesses a swoon at every limb (அவயவம் அனைத்தூடினும் அவசமுறு மயல்). The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman (எத்திறத்தாள்). The same catalogue serves the infatuation in the song and its cure in the Naladiyar.

The song says the poet has already reached desirelessness (வேண்டாமை ஒன்றை அடைந்து) and fallen melting at the feet. Kural 362 says that not-being-born comes when one wants not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). The Kural makes வேண்டாமை the means to release; the song treats it as the threshold already crossed, from which only grace remains to be asked.
The herdsman's flute as a weapon of evening: the Kural's woman calls it a messenger of the burning dusk that kills, and in 1189 the cowherd's flute is among the things wearing the girl down.

The Naladiyar sketches the old man whose speech fails and teeth fall but who still keeps his eyes on desire; 1194 lists every stage of that decay down to the stench of the sickbed and turns it into a plea for grace at the last moment.

1194 ends its catalogue of decay with 'now it is a matter of a moment' (நிமிஷம் இங்கினி ஆச்சு) and turns to Murugan. Naladiyar 55 says youth has passed for nothing and disease with old age is coming now (இன்னே பிணியொடு மூப்பும் வருமால்) and calls the heart to set out on the good path. Both make the arrival of old age the last call to turn, one as prayer and one as self-address.

The song asks on what day, before he becomes the work of Mugadi (முகடித் தொழில்), the goddess of misfortune, Murugan will grant him the work of his service (அடிமைத் தொழில்). Kural 617 says Mugadi (மாமுகடி) dwells in sloth and Lakshmi at the feet of the one without sloth. Both set Mugadi against a chosen labour, effort in the Kural and service to God in the song.

1205 asks Murugan to grant that he not be born again (இனிப் பிறவாது நீ அருள்புரிவாயே). Kural 362 says that if one must want, one should want non-birth, and it comes when one wants not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). The Kural adds the condition the song leaves to grace: freedom from desire is the way to non-birth.

1207 describes women who call young men and draw out a great deal of money (மிக்க காசு இழைத்து), until he is drained, tongue dry, living in fear and shame. Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்), as a lamp's light ends with the oil. The Naladiyar gives the rule; the song is the man inside it, emptied and still asking.

1208 speaks of breasts that rise and plot killing like Death (கூற்றெனக் கொலைசூழும்). In Kural 1083 the man says he never knew what Death (கூற்று) was and now knows it: a woman's grace with war-making eyes. Both name the woman's body as கூற்று, the Kural as a lover's discovery, the song as the wanderer's danger.

Thiruppugazh 121 describes courtesans who swear an oath (சூள் உரைத்து) that until the body's nest is left (உயிர்க்கூடு விடுமளவும்) they will never slacken in union, then wipe out a man's wealth and go to meet the next. Naladiyar 372 recalls a woman who swore she would leap with him from the high peak, then, since he had no gold, showed a pain in her feet and would not go. Both oaths are vows to the death, and both end where the money ends.

Both turn on a courtesan's vow never to part: the Naladiyar woman who promised to be like the gem on its thread turns like a ram's horn, and 121's women who swear union until death strip the man and go to meet the next. The Naladiyar asks the heart to leave; 121 asks Murugan to come.

1213 says the women lead a man by their foul-smelling passage (பீறற் சலத்து வழி நாற) and torment him with infatuation. Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot that seeps filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) and the fool dazzled by its skin. Both answer desire with the body's foulness; the Naladiyar argues it, while the song complains of still being led by it.
Both name the courtesan's want as money, not love: the Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth bring harm, and 1214 calls them women whose minds seek coins.

The song pictures the mantra as a sword (மந்த்ர வாளால்) that cuts down Yama's servants who come by fate's path for the life (விதிவழியின் உயிர்கவர வருகொடிய யமபடரை வெட்டித் துணித்து). Kural 269 says that for those who have gained the power of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Both hold that Death can be overcome by a discipline; the Kural names tapas, the song a mantra which, it says, sects and the sixty-four arts cannot reach.

The song tells of women who cling with love and then leave without attachment by deceit (அணைந்து பின் பற்றற்று அகல் மாயம்), leaving the heart sore and burning. Naladiyar 376 gives the same turn in one woman: she who promised never to part, like a gem on its thread or the anril birds, has turned away like a fighting ram's horn. The Naladiyar dramatises the promise and its breaking that the song names in a phrase.

Among the poet's faults the song names piling great wealth and eating it without sharing (ஈட்டு மாபொருள் பாத்து உணாது), ending in a body for crows, dogs and jackals. Kural 227 says the fiery disease of hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). The song uses the Kural's own word for sharing to name its absence as a sin that ends in a wasted death.

The poet asks whether he should go about without fear or shame (அச்சக் கூச்சமற்று), called a rake (தூர்த்தன்) by all who hear, infatuated and mad after wealth. Kural 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று). The Kural's judgement on the shameless is applied in the song as a confession by one who sees himself becoming that.

The song opens with drums beaten in a throng (கட்டக் கணப்பறைகள் கொட்ட) as the clan binds the body for the burning. Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded in the hall for a wedding may that same day sound as funeral drums (மணப்பறை ஆயின அன்றவர்க்கு ஆங்கே பிணப்பறையாய்). The funeral drum is the opening image of both; the Naladiyar sharpens it by setting it against the wedding drum.

The song opens on women who make men take up the begging bowl (கப்பரை கைக்கொள வைப்பவர்), catching young men with kohl and painted faces. Naladiyar 377 says the worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at. Both make the man's ruin the end of the courtesan's love; the song names its last stage, the bowl.

Thiruppugazh 123 confesses he never sought the rare life and asks whether, thinking to end birth, he will not give up the burden of desire (பிறவியற நினைகுவன் என் ஆசைப்பாடைத் தவிரேனோ). Kural 362 says that if one must want, want not to be born, and that comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). Both tie the end of birth to the end of desire.

Among those the poet lives with, the song names women who show their price (விலைகாட்டு ... அரிவைமார்) and liquor (கள்), and asks for the feet while life lasts in a wilting body. Kural 920 puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The pairing of priced women and drink is the same in both; the song's lines are hard to divide, so its full list is uncertain.

The Kural's women who weigh the profit before they speak match 1231's women who sell love after reckoning the coins in a man's hand (கைக்காசின் அளவறிந்து); 1231 adds the poets who sing such women's bodies.

The song asks for the day when, crossing the sea of birth with its deceitful fish and sharks in the boat of true speech (மெய்கள் தோணிப் பிறவி அலைவேலை), he will lay flowers on Murugan and recite his words. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). The song keeps the Kural's sea and adds a boat, truthful speech, and worship as the crossing.

The song asks that before the sorrow called death draws near (மரணம் என்ற துக்கம் அணுகாமுன்), while Death torments him with his deeds, he may stand with untroubled mind thinking of Murugan's feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல்வாராமுன்). Both set the deadline at the death-throe; the Kural asks for good deeds before it, the song for an untroubled thought of the feet.

The song tells of women who embrace a man close, take his money and then bite his lips again (ஆகம் உற அணைத்து காசை அபகரித்து மீள இதழ் கடிப்பது), and the poet drunk on the poison of desire. Kural 913 calls the false embrace of women who want wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both put the deceit in the embrace itself; the song shows the theft placed between the embraces.

The song calls Murugan the one who dwells in the bodies of devotees who conquered the five senses (ஐந்திந்த்ரியங்கள் வென்று ஒன்றும் அன்பர் அங்கம் பொருந்தும்). Kural 6 says those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) live long. In the Kural the god is the one who controlled the senses; in the song he lives in the devotee who has.

The song asks Murugan to clear away the pleasure of living with wife and children, praising them in the heart as 'my wealth' (எந்தன் தனங்கள் என்றென்று), and to give his feet. Kural 63 records that people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்பதம் மக்கள்) and gives the reason, in a chapter praising the getting of children. On the reading that the Kural approves the saying, the song treats as a bond to be cleared the very claim the Kural explains and accepts.

The song lists, among the attachments of a body of filth and blood, the study of many arts, suffering daily without meaning (கலைபல பிடித்து நித்தம் அலைபடும் அநர்த்தம்). Kural 400 calls learning the imperishable, excellent wealth, beside which other things are not wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி). On the reading that கலை is learning in general, the song counts as a bond what the Kural sets above all possessions; if கலை means only worldly arts the conflict narrows.

The song fears the wretchedness of being cast off after he served the women and then stopped giving the money they wanted (காசைக் கொடாத பின்பு சீரற்று). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover but, since he had no gold, pleaded aching feet and left (காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாதொழிந்தாளே). Both show the courtesan's love ending exactly where the money ends.

The song asks that before the failing time comes for wealth, servants, kin, sons and house (தப்பு நிலைமை அணுகைக்கு வர ... குறுகாமுன்) he be given the thought to melt in devotion and hold the feet daily. Kural 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, so while you have it do at once what stays (அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both make the passing of wealth a reason for haste; the Kural's lasting deed is in the song devotion to the feet.

1248 likens women's breasts to the tusks of a rutting elephant (கடாக் களிற்று உரகோடு), to peaks and to tender coconuts, and confesses wasting nights and days in their net. Kural 1087 says the cloth over a woman's firm breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). Both use the elephant in rut for the breast's force; in the Kural the cloth restrains it, in the song nothing does and the poet asks to be set to praise instead.

1250 calls the body a leather bag (தோற்பை) oozing the mire of desire, wrongly taken as oneself, and pictures its tearing by scavengers. Naladiyar 26, in nearly the words of Tirumanthiram 167, asks what it matters whether the body is dragged off with a rope, buried or reviled once the dancer within the skin bag (தோற்பையுள் நின்று) has gone. The ethical and the devotional books share the figure; the song turns it into a confession of still tending the bag.
The Naladiyar's wise see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; 1252 calls the poet's own life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word instead.

1256 confesses that his mind went to women and asks whether a day will come when, thinking of the Lord, the books he learned would rejoice (கற்ற நூல் உகக்க). Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). The song applies the Kural's verdict to the poet himself: his learning is shamed until it is turned to the Lord.

1257 describes women who enchant with poison eyes, speak many desires (இச்சை பல பேசி) and whose minds crave good wealth (நற்பொருள் அவா மனத்தர்), and asks not to waste away infatuated with them. Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the talk and the craving the Kural names, and the daily wasting (நித்தம் மெலியாதே) that is the harm.

1258 has the poet, shown women's bodies, ready to ride the madal (மடலூர) and falling on those who drag out his life, and asks for the lamp of Vedanta to end that darkness. Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard or strength but the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). The Kural's last resort of a lover becomes in the song a mark of the rogue's delusion (தூர்த்தன் மோகாந்தகாரம்), answered by a lamp rather than a public plea.

1259 melts like wax in fire (எரியுறு மெழுகென) before women whose carp-eyes fight like weapons (படைபொருவன விழிக் கயல்). Naladiyar 44 refuses to be troubled by men who call eyes lilies, fighting carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The same comparison that the Naladiyar dismantles is the one the song confesses to have yielded to, asking the Lord to end the suffering it brings.

The Kural cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe; 126 claims the eyes have beaten the deer into the forest and trampled Yama himself. The same comparisons, but the Kural's lover wonders and the poet of 126 fears to fall.

1261 asks for the word of wisdom, rising bliss without 'I' and self (யானொடு தானிலா), that ends his deeds and the beginningless bond. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. Both make the loss of 'I' the gate to release; the song asks for it as a gift of grace after confessing that he took women's deceit for teaching.

1262 tells how Murugan, seeking Valli, lost his shame (நாணம் அழிந்து), changed form and walked till his feet ached, struck by Kama's arrows. Kural 1133 has a lover say he once had shame and manliness and now has only the madal that lovers ride. The Kural's loss of shame in a man's love is told in the song of the god himself, set against the poet's own confession of desire.

The Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay, and with kin wailing he was gone' urges virtue now; 1265 extends the same list of verbs from birth to corpse (பிறந்தார் கிடந்தார் இருந்தார் தவழ்ந்தார் நடந்தார்) and turns it into a plea for the Lord's 'fear not'.

1266 asks, before Death throws his long rope and seizes his life (நெட்டைக் கயிற்றிட்டு வளையாமுன்), to melt with devotion and be given true words to speak of the feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both use the 'before' of death to make the present urgent; the Kural asks for good deeds, the song for words while the tongue still works.

1267 calls the grief for children, mothers, in-laws and wife an illusory grief deeper than the sea (மைத்த வேலைக்கு நெடிது உற்ற மாயத் துயரம்) and asks for the feet so his mind may be stilled. Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and leave wordlessly, as a bird leaves its nesting tree (சேக்கை மரன் ஒழியச் சேண்நீங்கு புள்போல). The Naladiyar shows why the song's grief for kin can be called illusory.

1269's praise says the Lord thinks daily of keeping those who never fail in sweet speech from coming again by the womb (இனிய சொல் மறாத சீலர் கருவழி வராமல்). Kural 98 says sweet speech free of pettiness gives joy in the next life and in this. The song carries the Kural's reward for sweet speech to release from birth.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks where the woman is among them; 1270 calls the body a cage of filth, skin, water and bone, but draws service to the Lord from it rather than disgust at women.

1271 confesses a mind that thinks a hundred crore sorrows in an instant (மனநூறு கோடி துன்பம் நொடிமீதிலே நினைந்து) and asks for release on the day the body falls. Kural 337 says those who cannot know they will live one moment more think thoughts in the many crores (கருதுப கோடியும் அல்ல பல). The same crores of thought against a moment's life serve the Kural as irony and the song as confession.

1273 likens pearl-hung breasts to an elephant with two tusks thrust forward (இருகோடு முற்பட்ட கரிபோலும்) and says the women's spear eyes cloud his mind. Kural 1087 likens the cloth over a woman's breasts to the face-cloth of a rutting elephant. Both see the breast as an elephant; the song makes it the cause of his whirling grief and asks to worship the feet with many words instead.

1279 calls the body the nest where life dwells (ஆவியுறை கூட்டில்) and asks that it be fed the scripture of knowledge instead of women and wealth. Kural 338 likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest (குடம்பை) empty. The Kural uses the nest to show the bird will leave it; the song asks what the bird should be fed while it is still there.

Thiruppugazh 128 says that even though (ஆகிலும்) he is anxious with infatuation for women, he will not forget (மறவேனே) Murugan's golden body, six faces, vel and lotus feet. Kural 1125 has the lover say he would recall her qualities if he forgot, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's vow of unforgetting is turned in the song to the Lord's form, set against the very desire the Kural's lover feels.
The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1289 dramatizes those words (laughing talk, soothing care) and ends with the plunder of wealth.

1289 describes women who laugh and talk, tend a man until his mind is soothed, and then plunder his wealth (தனத்தைச் சூறைகொள் மடவார்). Naladiyar 377 has the worthless woman lick like a wild cow, take the wealth from his hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balk like an ox. Both show the same sequence, tender care first and the seizure of wealth after.
Both name 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது) as what must be cut; the Kural promises a world above the gods to whoever cuts them, and 1292 asks the cutting itself as a gift of knowledge.

In both the town's gossip feeds the girl's love-sickness rather than ending it; the Kural makes it manure for the sickness, and 1297 sets the reproach of women beside Kama and the moon as what sinks her in sorrow.

1299 asks not to enter the river of births with its waves (பிறவியலை யாற்றினில் புகுதாதே) and to be given the vision of Murugan's feet. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The same pairing, births as water and the feet as the way across, appears in the Kural's opening chapter and in this late song.

Thiruppugazh 130 puts the lover's praise as questions: is the hair a black cloud or darkness, are the eyes arrows or a vel (மேகமதோ இருளோ ... கணைகொலோ அயில் வேலதுவோ), and seeks women like golden peacocks. Kural 1081 is the first such doubt: is she a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்). The Kural's bewildered question becomes in the song the infatuated man's whole way of seeing, which he then calls worthless (கசடன்).

1300 asks for the knowledge that cannot be completed by writing on the leaves of books (புத்தகத்து ஏட்டில் தீட்டி முடியாது), revealed by grace. Kural 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own true understanding prevails (உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both put the deciding knowledge outside book-learning; the Kural leaves its source unnamed, and the song names it as grace.

1301 speaks of public women who desire gold (பொன்னை விரும்பிய பொதுமாதர்) and asks Murugan to desire the poet so that the poet may desire him. Kural 911 sets women who desire wealth against those who desire with love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்). The song takes the Kural's contrast between desire for wealth and desire for the person and carries it over to grace.

1304 asks not to be born into the deceptive false hut (மாயத் தெற்றிப் பொய்க்குடில்) of the five elements. Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in a corner of the body (துச்சில்) has no home of its own. Both see the body as a poor lodging the life does not own; the Kural asks a question, while the song asks to be spared the hut.
The Kural opens with A as first of letters and God as first of the world; 1307 makes Murugan the letter A itself (அகரமுமாகி), and the one above the three gods.

The Naladiyar says a harlot's love is like a lamp's light: விளக்கொளியும் நெய்யற்ற கண்ணே அறுமே, அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும். The Thiruppugazh speaks from after that moment: நீடு பொருள் போன பின்பு பாதகனுமாகி நின்று, when the great wealth had gone he stood a sinner. The song takes the Naladiyar's warning past poverty to guilt, the loss the proverb does not count.
The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1317 names their lavish lying speech and love set at a price, and adds the brass polished to pass for gold.

The Thiruppugazh lists courtesans who நேசித்தாரையும் எத்தி வடிப்பவர், cheat and drain even those who love them. The Naladiyar's worthless woman ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு, licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands, then bolts like a buffalo. Both make the affection itself the means of draining the lover; the Naladiyar adds the ridicule that follows.

The Kural's lover says பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென்பதனை இனியறிந்தேன், he never knew Death before and now knows it, in a woman's battling eyes. The Thiruppugazh calls the women மாய நமனுக்கும் உறவாகி, kin even to Death. The Kural's lover is overwhelmed by desire; the song makes the same identity of woman and Death a warning.

The Kural says பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The Thiruppugazh lists every display of the courtesans with the refrain காட்டி, showing, and calls them those who உயிரை விலைகொளும், buy a man's life for a price. Both say the embrace is false and paid for; the song makes the price life itself, not wealth alone.

The Naladiyar sees the old man with failed speech, a staff and lost teeth still eyeing desire; 1321 gives the same old age in detail, adds the medicines, and draws the remedy not from renunciation but from song and the feet.

The Kural's lover says he would remember her if he forgot, but மறப்பறியேன், he does not know how to forget. The Thiruppugazh says that even while sunk in love-play, மகிழ்கினும் ... முடிவடிவொடு அங்கை வேலும் மறவேனே, he will not forget Murugan's crowned form and the vel in his hand. The same claim of never forgetting moves from the beloved to the god, and in the song it holds even in the middle of desire.

The Kural says கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி, learning is the imperishable wealth and nothing else is wealth. The Thiruppugazh confesses that after learning கலைபல நூல்கள் and singing many poems he ran through the streets after பொருளெனும் ஆசை, the desire called wealth. The song limits the Kural's claim: learning is wealth only if it is not spent hunting the other kind.

The Naladiyar sees people with aching hearts begging at the gates of great houses in sight of all (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) and calls it former deeds. 134 confesses the same daily standing at the gateways of those who give food (மனைகள் தலைவாசல் நின்று அநுதினமும் நாணமின்றி) as the end of a life of desire. The pairing shows the shame the Naladiyar observes in others spoken in the first person.

The Kural's lover cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). 135 lists the same kind of question about a woman's eyes, vel or carp (வாள்விழி வேலோ சேலோ), but as the trap of the eyes' maya (இருகண் மாயையில் மூழ்காதே). The doubting simile the Kural uses for wonder the song repeats in order to refuse it.

Both reject the poets' comparisons for a woman's eyes as carp, spear and the like: the Naladiyar ascetic answers them with the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit, 135 asks not to drown in their maya and turns to studying Murugan's poems.

The Kural says the sweet words of braceleted women who desire wealth, not love, bring disgrace (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). 136 names courtesans who speak ever so sweetly (கனியக் கனியவுமே மொழி பேசிய விலைமாதர்) and asks not to wander thinking their union sweet. Both locate the danger in the sweetness of the speech.

The Naladiyar says those who mean to reach the right path will not embrace the large breasts of women who go their own way (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென்பார் ... தடமுலை சேராரே). 140 describes women who seize a man's wealth (பொருள்பறி) and asks whether he will give up the pleasure of the base path (புலையவர் வழி இன்பைத் தவிர்வேனோ). Both set the courtesan's embrace against the path, as a rule in one and a confession in the other.

The Kural's பொதுநலத்தார், women whose favours are common to all, are 141's women who set a price so that all may take their pleasure; the Kural says the wise will not touch them, 141 confesses that he did.

The Naladiyar says men fooled into thinking a courtesan's love theirs, after she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). 142 confesses he is like a fool to be laughed at (இடக்கன் எனச் சிரிக்க) for his melting infatuation (அனற்குள் மெழுக்கென). The Naladiyar's ridicule from outside is what the poet fears for himself.

The Kural says good deeds must be done quickly, before the hiccup comes that stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 143 has the hiccup rise in the man wasted by women (விக்கலுமே எழுந்து) and asks whether, leaving that disease, he will yet praise Murugan. The same sign of the end of life makes the urgency of the Kural's counsel the poet's own late plea.
The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink; 144 confesses to desiring those golden shoulders and sinking low (தாழ்வடைந்து).

Both list the body's contents, guts, fat, blood, bone and flesh. The Naladiyar asks where among them the garlanded woman is; 145 applies the list to the body the poet himself lives in, and answers with the Lord's grace.

The Kural says the two kinds of deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who love the Lord's true praise (இருவினையும் சேரா). 147 plays on கழல: for those who bow at his anklets, deeds come loose (கழல் பணிய வினை கழல்). Both make worship the thing deeds cannot hold to.

The Kural says the heart melts at the thought of begging; 15 confesses the act, a poet praising patrons as Tamil's refuge 'with a wounded heart', and asks to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet.

The Kural's lover asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்). 151 strings the same doubting questions on each feature, hair darkness or cloud, brow bow or crescent (இருளோ புயலோ, சிலையோ பிறையோ). The Kural's figure of wonder becomes in the song the catalogue the poet sets against the feet he would rather think on.

The Kural likens the false embrace of women for wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று). 154 moves from the women's embrace (கொளுமாதர் சுகமுற்று) straight to the burning of his own body and asks whether he will become a corpse (சடமாமோ). The corpse the Kural sets inside the embrace the song sets at its end.

The Naladiyar says those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth yet keep their eyes on desire have no way to safety (சொல்தளர்ந்து கோல்ஊன்றி). 154 runs from the women's embrace to stammering speech and the staff (சொற் குளறிட்டுத் தடிதொட்டு), disease, the sickbed and the pyre. The song extends the Naladiyar's picture of desire outliving the body to its end in the burning ground.

The Naladiyar says courtesans would send away even Vishnu with joined hands if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன் றில்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). 155 describes priced women who snatch gold (பொன்பறி விலைமாதர்) and shut the front door when the man pleads (கெஞ்சிட முன்றலை வாயில் அடைத்து). Both show the welcome ending where the money ends.

Both hear the funeral drums and see the body covered and the fire taken up. The Naladiyar ends in irony, the dying carrying the dead; 157 asks for release before that hour comes, while the hut of the body still stands.

Both take the body apart into blood, bone, nerves, skin and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which part is the woman one desires; 158 turns the list on the poet's own body and confesses that, knowing this, he still desires women.

Naladiyar 44 refuses to be moved by blind, petty men (கண்ணில் புன்மாக்கள்) who call eyes lilies, carp and spears. Thiruppugazh 16 gives those men's praise in full, eyes like carp (கயல் ஒக்கும் பருத்தகண்), hair like darkness, breasts like golden pots, and says the young men worship the women (இளைஞோர்கள் துதித்து முன் கும்பிட்டு), then calls himself a madman caught by them. The Naladiyar's speaker stands outside the comparisons; the poet confesses being inside them.

The Kural's first line makes A the first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 163 borrows the words (அகர முதல்) and asks for the meaning that is first in that way, the secret that 173 says Murugan told Siva.

The Kural's woman says that with her lover away the evening comes like enemies to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்). 164 lines up Kama's bow, the roaring sea and the hour when the light fades (ஒளிமட்கு மிகைப் பொழுதாலே) as attackers through which the creeper-girl's life grows faint (உயிர் எய்த்த). The song carries the Kural's hostile evening into a plea to the god for his garland.

Thiruppugazh 17 speaks of women who take a man's wealth and pick a quarrel (பொருட்கவர்ந்து ஒன்றிய பிணக்கிடும் சண்டிகள்) and asks what he gains by wearing out his body after them. Naladiyar 372 shows the quarrel's pretext: the woman who swore to leap from the peak with him found, when he had no gold, a pain in her feet (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டி) and stayed behind. Both tie the courtesan's company to the money and her excuse to its running out.

The Kural says an unlearned man's standing wilts once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 171 says the court poets' learning, decked with titles and regalia, breaks and changes colour when tested (முடிவில் அவை ஒன்றும் அற்று வேறொரு நிறமாகி முறியும்). Both make the test of speech the place where false learning collapses.
The Kural warns of women who weigh the profit and then speak of their goodness; 172 describes the same pretence from inside, women who take every possession 'with great friendship'.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from men's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks. 172's women take every possession under the guise of friendship (பொருட்கள் யாவையும் மெத்தவும் நட்பொடு பறித்து) and invent new tricks daily. Both locate the fraud in affection used as the instrument of taking.

The Kural calls the man who parades useless words not a man but chaff among men (மக்கட் பதடி). 177 names himself chaff in understanding (அறிவிற் பதடி), a fool made helpless by daily embraces, and asks for one word of grace. The rare word பதடி carries the Kural's contempt into the poet's self-judgement.
Both make a man's welcome depend on what he brings: the Naladiyar's courtesans find a moneyed oil-presser sugar, and 178's women question at the door those who come with property and carry it off.

Both say the courtesan's sweet talk serves her wish for wealth, not love. The Kural states it as a warning; 180 shows the sequence, talk, trust, then the wealth snatched, and asks for the Lord's love in its place.

The Kural's lover says the girl's shoulders are made of nectar because each touch makes his life sprout anew (உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப ... அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்). 185 drinks the nectar of women's smiles (நகையமுதம்) and perishes by it (அழியும்), and asks to drink instead the nectar of the Lord's feet (இருதாளின் அமுது). On the plain reading the same nectar of love gives life in the Kural and death in the song.

The Naladiyar's renunciant refuses men who call eyes water-lilies, warring carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. 186 uses the same conceit of eyes outdoing deer, mango slice and carp (முதிய கயல்கள்) to describe the women whose eyes forced him into bondage. The figure the Naladiyar dismisses is the snare the song confesses.
Both describe women who want a man for his wealth and whose sweet invitations harm him; the Kural warns, 19 confesses to having trusted them.

Thiruppugazh 19 calls himself the small fool who trusted the false minds of the courtesans (கணிகையர் தமதுபொய் மனத்தை நம்பிய சிறியனை) while they seized his wealth. Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into thinking such a woman's love their own (ஏமாந்து எமதென்று இருந்தார்), while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many. The fault in both is the trust, not only the women's greed.

The Kural asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the beloved (மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்). 190 describes the same embrace and says that even sleeping on that bed (அமளி மலரணையின் மிசை துயிலுகினும்) he will not forget the lotus feet. The song keeps the Kural's sleep in love but refuses to let it displace the god.

The Naladiyar scorns blind, petty men who call women's eyes lilies, carp or spears. 191 confesses he was such a poet, describing hair as cloud, breasts as lotus buds, face as moon (உருவக உரைசெய்து), and melted like wax in a furnace in the union that followed. The song indicts its own craft in the terms the Naladiyar uses against the praisers.

The Naladiyar says bright-browed women hide harmful intent behind words spoken to be believed and belong to no one but their own bodies. 193 abuses women who talk of love without knowing friendship, never melt despite sweet words (இன்சொல் புரிந்து உருகாத) and attend only to the act of union. Both find the courtesan's speech a performance that hides an unmoved heart.

Thiruppugazh 197 opens by likening a woman's breasts to an elephant (வாரணந்தனை நேரான மாமுலை) and goes on to ask that he see her whole charm as great maya in form (மாமாயையே வடிவாக நின்றது). Kural 1087 has the lover compare the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேல் கட்படாம்). The same elephant figure is the Kural lover's wonder and, in the song, the first item of an inventory the poet asks to see through.
Both use the string-puppet for a life with no inner agency: in the Kural the man without shame only seems alive, in 207 the poet dances on the strings of his two deeds.

Thiruppugazh 208 sets life beside the wealth that misers gather without giving (இடாது பல தேடும் கிராதர் பொருள் போல்): neither stays. Naladiyar 10 says those who give nothing and hoard will lose it (கொடாஅது வைத்தீட்டினார் இழப்பர்), as the honey bee's store shows. The hoard that is lost is the Naladiyar's lesson about giving, and in the song it becomes a figure for life itself.

Thiruppugazh 209 asks whether he must suffer lodged in a body like a nest in a bush (செடிநேர் உடற் குடம்பை). Kural 338 likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The same word names the body: the Kural stresses how lightly life leaves it, the song how mean a lodging it is.

Thiruppugazh 21 gives the courtesans' own street talk: what you gave before is not enough, give today, come to my house (பண்டு தந்தது போதாதோ மேல் இன்று தந்து ... இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே வாரீர்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song stages exactly the இன்சொல் the Kural warns of, and lets the demand for money show through it.

Thiruppugazh 210 asks whether he must go night and day to the gates of powerful men who slip away once praised in song (நழுவிய ப்ரசண்டர் வாசல் இரவுபகல் சென்று வாடி). Naladiyar 107 says that people with aching hearts standing at the long gates of great houses (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) in everyone's sight are paying for former deeds. The same wilting figure at the rich man's gate is a plea for release in the song and an explanation by karma in the Naladiyar.

Thiruppugazh 213 describes women who seize their lovers' belongings (உடைமை மனமுடனே பறிப்பவர்கள்) and calls himself the fool who became their slave (அசடன்). Naladiyar 377 says those who take as their own the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks are laughed at by many. Both make the man who takes this for love the fool; the song confesses it in the first person.

Thiruppugazh 215 describes courtesans who embrace to snatch coins (காசு பறிக்க மறித்து முயக்கிகள்) and act out a learned art of deceit (தோதக வித்தை). Kural 913 says the false embrace of women who love wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both name the embrace itself as false because it is for money; the Kural adds the image of revulsion.

The Naladiyar gives one picture, a pot of filth leaking from nine openings under a dark skin; 217 takes the body apart organ by organ and disease by disease, and adds the hut of five elements taken up birth after birth.
The Kural finds the body's joy in touching one's children; 218 asks for that very joy with the Lord as the child on the lap, and puns the child's kiss (முத்தி) into release.

The Naladiyar's man of worth, even when fortune leaves him, will not stand with bowed neck behind fools who hoard wealth (அருத்தம் செறிக்கும் அறிவிலார் பின்சென்று எருத்திறைஞ்சி). 220 confesses doing exactly that: making envoy poems and verse garlands for patrons, walking to fools (மடையரிடமே நடந்து) and being tossed a coin with 'come another time'. The song turns the Naladiyar's rule into a poet's confession and a plea to sing for the Lord instead.

The Kural says no help exceeds good company and nothing brings more affliction than bad (நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 222 asks not to be worn out mingling at the doors of the wicked (நாசர் தம் கடையதனில் விரவி) and sinking, but to speak the words of those who praise Murugan. The song applies the Kural's choice of company to devotion.
Both call the courtesan's embrace false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், பொய்க்கலவி) because it is for wealth; the Kural likens it to a corpse in a dark room, 227 adds poison and wealth snatched.
The Kural makes sharing one's food the chief of all duties; 23 arrives at the same act, sharing even a millet grain, through fear of death rather than compassion.

Both hear the funeral drum over the corpse while kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still marries and seeks joy; 23 draws a different lesson, that one should share even a grain before the summons comes.

The Naladiyar says leprosy rots the fingers when the old deed (பழவினை) of breaking crabs' legs and eating them comes home. 232 calls its many diseases பாதகவியாதி, diseases of sin, and says through them he has drunk sin like liquor. Both read disease as the fruit of one's own fault, the Naladiyar of a past deed, the song of present lust.

The Naladiyar says those who, with failing speech, staff and fallen teeth, still stay at home with eyes set on desire (காம நெறிபடரும் கண்ணினார்க்கு) have no way to safety. 233 confesses growing old (வயதாகி) while wandering after kohl-eyed women and seeking wealth for their ornaments, and asks whether he must go on wandering. The song is the Naladiyar's old man speaking of himself.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then turns away, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at. 235's dancers draw a man close, dose him (மருத்திட்டு ஆட்டி) and snatch his wealth (சீர்பொருள் பறி), and the song asks whether a bond with these false dancers can be right. Both describe a seeming affection that ends in taking the man's wealth.

In the Naladiyar the jewelled woman who swore to leap from the peak together shows a pain in her feet at the brink because the man had no gold (காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாதொழிந்தாள்). 238's women agree to deceitful play once red gold is spread as the price (விலையாக மிக்க செம்பொன் வரவே பரப்பி) and quarrel after a few days. The two show the same bond from either side: it begins with gold and fails without it.

The Kural says one who neither gives nor enjoys has nothing however rich; 239 is the confession of such a man, who kept his wealth for his hands and youth and shared nothing with the hungry, and finds it at the funeral.

The Naladiyar tells the man of great wealth to give it away, since none escapes Death and tomorrow the funeral drum will sound (நாளைத் தழீஇம் தழீஇம் தண்ணம் படும்). 239 confesses refusing to share food with the hungry and keeping wealth for himself until kin surround him weeping and drums beat (தமர்சுற்றியழப் பறைகொட்டியிட) as Death takes the life. The song is the Naladiyar's warning spoken as regret.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness deepens; the Kural's woman says it bewilders the whole town, while in 24 a mother names the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird as what wears her daughter down.

The Kural likens death to falling asleep and birth to waking (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு ... விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு). 241 asks whether he must again gain this birth that slips past in a blink, lying down and rising (இமைப்பினிற் சடக்கெனப் படுத்தெழச் சறுக்கும் இப்பிறப்பு). The song takes the Kural's calm image of sleep and waking and makes it the speed with which a birth is lost.

The Naladiyar ranks as the lowest life following, for desire of wealth, people who do not recognise one's worth (பொருள்நசையால் தம்மை உணரார்பின் சென்று நிலை). 245 confesses exactly that life: seeking out who the rich were, singing them quick verses (ஆசு கவிபாடி), and walking back and forth until they said 'come tomorrow' and turned their faces (நாளை நடவுமென ... முகம்வேறாய்). The song gives the scene of humiliation that the Naladiyar's ranking only names.

The Kural says that grace is not killing and its absence is killing, and eating that flesh is not right (அவ்வூன் தினல் பொருளல்லது). 247 lists among the bonds that keep him from release the daily satisfying of hunger with killed flesh (கொலூனை நித்தம் பசியாறல்), set against mukti (முத்தம்) and bondage (பெத்தம்). The pairing shows the Kural's ethical rule placed by the song inside the Siddhanta scheme of bondage and release.

The Kural asks whether the life that lodges in the body as a temporary shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has found no home of its own. 248 calls the body a house (வீடு) of bones, blood, filth and worms, full of conspiring tattvas, and asks whether he must desire and carry that house and wander (வீடதை நத்தி எடுத்து இவண் உழல்வேனோ). Both use the image of the body as a dwelling the soul does not truly own; the song adds the disgust and the tenants.

Both take the body apart into bone, blood, fat and entrails to break desire. The Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman; 248 turns the inventory on the poet's own body, a house he still longs to carry.

The Naladiyar says that even the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain good sense day by day (கற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகின் நல்லறிவு நாளுந் தலைப்படுவர்), like water taking the scent of pathiri flowers. 249 asks to live among those who speak of Murugan daily through the Thiruppugazh (உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழி மேவி) and never to part from the knowledge they impart (உணர்த்திய போதந் தனைப் பிரியாது). The pairing shows the Naladiyar's rule of learning by company applied to the company of devotees.

The Naladiyar rebukes the heart that will not let go of the bond of home and pines for children (மனைப்பாசம் கைவிடாய் மக்கட்கென்று ஏங்கி), as though it would live for ages. 250 asks not to die with his mind clouded by thoughts of house, wife and children (மனைகள் பெண்டிர் மக்கள் தமை நினைந்து ... மடியாதே), and for release now. Both name house and children as the attachment that holds at the end; the Naladiyar's remedy is good deeds, the song's is Murugan's coming today.

Both put the courtesan's embrace for money in a dark room (இருட்டறை). The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse; 252 keeps the room and the seized wealth but not the corpse, and confesses the pull instead of warning.

The Naladiyar mocks those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), saying many will laugh at them. 253 describes women who take the wealth in a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கவர்தரு) and calls himself a slave of desire and a fool (அறிவிலி) for melting before them. The song speaks in the first person the folly the Naladiyar sees in others, with the same word for the taking.

Both call the body a pot to turn the mind from women. The Naladiyar's pot is the woman's body seeping filth; 258 turns the image on the poet's own body, a false pot of flesh, skin and semen, and asks not just to leave desire but to have that birth cut off.

The Naladiyar says that to women without their lover the clouds thundering in every direction sound like the funeral drum (நெய்தல் அறைந்தன்ன). 259 asks whether a girl should waste away under the roaring, swelling dark sea (கனைத்து அதிர்க்கும் இப் பொங்கு கார்க்கடல்) and a moon risen red as fire. In both the loud sound of nature, cloud or sea, becomes a torment for the one who is parted.

The Naladiyar says that to loveless courtesans a man without money is poison, while even an oil-press driver with earned wealth is sugar. 260 describes courtesans who embrace whoever gives the most as if he were an old friend (அதிகமா ஒரு பொருள்தருபவரொடு பழைய பேரென இதமுற அணைபவர்). Both make the same charge, that the courtesan's affection is ranked by payment, not by the man.

The Kural says that as water changes with the soil, a person's understanding takes the nature of their company (இனத்தியல்பதாகும் அறிவு). 261 confesses that, having joined liars, sense-followers, blind fools, thieves and sectarian disputants (செறிதலுற்று), he knows nothing at all (அறிவேதும் அறிதலற்று) and sinks in the sea of the womb. The song shows the Kural's rule at work in one life, and asks for the feet as the way out of bad company.

Both make the town's gossip feed love's sickness: the Kural's woman calls it the manure of her disease, and in 262 the women's talk is one of the torments, with cuckoo, moon and sea, that waste the girl's arm.

The Kural says those who do austerity do their own work, while the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 264 asks whether it is fit to be kin to the women who kindle infatuation and, feeding desire, destroy austerity (மயற் புகட்டி தவத்து அழிப்பவர்க்கு உறவாமோ). Both set தவம் against desire; the song names the women as the means by which desire undoes it.

The Naladiyar compares a courtesan's love to a lamp's light: the light ends when the oil runs out, the love when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 266 describes courtesans who speak desire for many days to get money and, when the money ends, leave the man groaning at the door (பொருள்தீரில் ஏங்கியிடக் கடையில் தளிவைப்பவர்). The song gives the scene that the Naladiyar's lamp image compresses.

The Kural's lover says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse (ஏமம் மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). 268 ends by making Murugan himself the lover who painted Valli's feet, arms, face and breasts on the madal (மடலிடை எழுதிய பெருமாளே). The Kural's last resort of a suffering man is, in the song, a mark of the god's love for Valli.

The Kural makes the rain cloud (மாரி) the figure of a giver who seeks no return: what does the world give back to it? 271 mocks poets who call a base patron the pouring cloud (சொரியு முகில்). The Kural's image of true giving is the stock flattery the song refuses to sing.

Thiruppugazh 28 asks that Death not call him while his mind fails, speech goes and eyes roll (அறிவழிய மயல்பெருக உரையும் அற விழிசுழல), and asks now for the boon of drawing near the feet. Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both fix the moment when speech is lost as the deadline; the Kural asks for good deeds before it, the song for the Lord's feet.

The Kural's lover says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும்). 283 makes women's eyes a sharpened sword that rushes to the ears, cuts and pierces (வடிகூர் வாள் போல ... வெட்டித் தொளைத்து), and the Lord a rescuer from the prison of women's eyes (மாதர்கள் கண் சிறை). The killing eye the Kural admires the song asks to be saved from.
The Kural makes the Lord's feet the way across the great sea of births; 284 makes them a raft (புணை) and adds two more seas to cross, desire for women and the arts of learning.

The Kural's lovesick woman says the sea of desire certainly exists and the safe raft to cross it does not (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 284 names the seas of desire, birth and learning (ப்ரியக்கடல், கருக்கடல், கலைக்கடல்) and asks for a raft, the anklet-bright feet (கழற்புணை).
