The song answers the Kural's despair with a raft, on condition it is the Lord's.

The Naladiyar says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) while the learner's days are few, so one must choose what is fitting, like the bird that leaves the water and drinks the milk. 284 puts the sea of the many arts (அநேகங் கலைக்கடல்) beside the seas of desire and birth as one more sea to whirl in. The Naladiyar's shoreless learning becomes in the song something to be crossed, not sifted.

The Kural's woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 285 shows a girl melted and helpless under Kama's arrows and asks that her chastity not perish (கற்பழியாதே) while she is given back her senses. The song prays for the girl to be spared what the Kural says desire does.

The Kural's woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure (ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக) and her mother's words as water. 286 lists among the things that have left the girl sleepless and helpless the women in the street who quarrel angrily over her (தெருவிற் பெண்கள் மிகக் கறுவிச் சண்டையிட), beside Kama's arrow, the south wind and the moon. Both count the town's talk as a cause of the love-sickness, not just a result.

The Kural warns against women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). 287 says the courtesans babble bird-call arts precisely so that the money in a man's hand passes to them (கைப்பொருள் புக்கிடவே தான் புட்குரல் விச்சை பிதற்றும்). Both see the sweet speech as calculated for gain.

The Kural asks what learning is for if one does not worship the good feet of the pure knower (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). 288 confesses he has not left the babble of books (புத்தகப் பிதற்றை விட்டு) to praise Murugan, nor learned to melt praising the golden feet. The song is the Kural's question answered in the first person.

The Naladiyar says that studying worldly books while leaving the books of wisdom is only clamour (கலகல கூஉந் துணை) and does not remove confusion. 288 calls book-learning babble (புத்தகப் பிதற்று) that keeps him from praise and from a mind free of trouble (கலக்கமற்று). Both name the noise of reading that does not end bewilderment.

The Kural's lover says that the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). 290 calls the drooping in union (கலவியில் துவள் பிணி) an incurable disease (பிணி தீரா) and asks instead for a place in the Lord's refuge. On the reading that the பிணி is union itself, the Kural makes union the remedy and the song makes it the illness.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first whatever other way one devises (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 291 asks for the one thing that comes to erase what Brahma wrote (விதித்தன் எழுத்தினை தரவரும் ஒருபொருள்). If Brahma's writing is read as fate, the song claims there is something stronger than fate, which the Kural denies.

The Kural's woman says the pleasure of love is a sea (இன்பம் கடல்) and its pain greater than the sea. 295 describes union's pleasure as waves on a shoreless sea (கலவி கரை அழி இன்ப அலை) and asks for the Lord's love so that the care of being tossed on it ends. Both make love's pleasure a sea; the song finds the trouble in the pleasure itself, the Kural in the pain that follows.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood, knowing grey hair will come; 296 is the prayer of one who did not, asking even when his hair is grey and his body ripens and falls to be taken into the supreme light.

The Kural's woman asks whether Kama, who works on one side only, does not see her misery and grief (பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்). 297 tells of Kama, firm in deceit, loosing his five arrows on a lonely girl and asks the Lord whether he will not think of her wasting loneliness (பொன்றும் தனிமையை நினையாயோ). Both turn the love-sickness into a question to one who should see it.

The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much, so why any further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). 298 lists wife, children, old mother, town, garden, house and wealth and asks that all become alien to him before Death's men come, so that he may reach release (முத்தி வீடு அணுக). The song turns the Kural's rule into a plea, naming the ties one by one.
The Kural makes women of divided heart the company of those whom Fortune has left; 299 lives the sequence, infatuation, all money given away, then hunger burning in the belly.
Both see the living body as a stinking corpse: the Naladiyar's cart torn by vultures once its axle breaks, and 30's body that already stinks, rots and rattles with worms and bones.

Thiruppugazh 300 lists the street women's carp eyes (சேல் உற்று எழு நேர்விழி) and cuckoo speech and says he who lacks ஞானமுடன் கல்வி will fade in மயல் and die. Naladiyar 44 is the knowledge he says he lacks at work: it refuses those who call eyes கயல் and வேல், having seen an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The pairing sets the poet's admitted want beside the renunciant's remedy.

Thiruppugazh 302 borrows the lovesick girl's afflictions, Kama's arrows, the moon, and the many women who learned slander (வசை கற்ற பல தத்தையர்), and asks for பத்தி and முத்தி as the cure. Kural 1147 has the girl say the town's gossip (ஊரவர் கெளவை) is manure and her mother's words water for this sickness. The song takes over the Kural's alar convention, where slander feeds the love it attacks, and turns the lover's sickness into the devotee's.

Kural 353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) heaven is nearer than earth. Thiruppugazh 303 asks Murugan to dwell in the heart with compassion so that troubles and doubts are scattered (இடர் சங்கைகள் கலங்க அருள்வாயே). The Kural makes the clearing of doubt the seeker's attainment; the song adds that it comes as grace from within the heart.

Kural 1183 has the woman say her lover took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும்) in exchange. Thiruppugazh 304 sets one such line inside a praise song: is it fitting that the girl who bows to Murugan's flower feet should droop with pallor and infatuation (பசலை மயல்கொடு தளர்வது அழகோ)? The akam complaint against the absent lover is addressed to the god.

The Kural begs those who beg not to beg of those who hide what they have; 306 confesses doing exactly that, praising misers as generous, and its answer is not to choose better patrons but to give patrons up for Murugan.

Thiruppugazh 307 calls the courtesans women who speak many flattering words (நிதமொழி பலகூறிகள்), sell their arts for a price (கலைபகர் விலைமாதர்கள்) and ruin the families of young men (இளைஞர்கள் குடிகேடிகள்). Kural 911 locates the harm in the same place: the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth, not love, bring disgrace. Both make the trade and the speech, not desire alone, the charge.

Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு) than begging, even water for a cow. Thiruppugazh 310 shows the poet's tongue in that disgrace: he learned the poetry owed to Murugan, then flattered patrons as the wishing tree and as Kumanan, blind with begging (இரவான குருடு), stealing every word (சத்தம் அனைத்தும் திருடி) to fit them. The song applies the Kural's verdict to a bard's trade, where the begging also misuses the words.

Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) has not found a home of its own (புக்கில்). Thiruppugazh 311 calls the body by that very word, a hollow dwelling the instruments move into (கரணாதி குடிபுகும் பொக்கப் புக்கில்). Where the Kural denies the life a புக்கில், the song grants the body the name only to call it hollow.

Thiruppugazh 311 builds the body from bones, blood and bound nerves (அத்தி ... இரத்தம் செறி நரம்பிட்டுக் கட்டிய சட்டம்), a prison of deeds and a raft in the sea of birth. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, linking sinews and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman. The same anatomical catalogue serves the Naladiyar against desire and the song against embodiment and birth.
Both see through the bubble: the Naladiyar's body is a bubble in the rain that forms and bursts, while 316 sees the whole world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) as a bubble, and asks for the ripeness to reach the Lord.

Kural 151 calls bearing with those who scorn you the highest thing, like the earth that holds up those who dig into it. Thiruppugazh 318 asks what words could match the forbearance (பொறை) by which Murugan bore the poet's faults (பிழையுடன் பட்டு) and set him among devotees. The virtue the Kural asks of a man is praised in the god, with the poet in the digger's place.

Both picture the old man with failing speech or senses, leaning on a stick, staggering, teeth gone; the Naladiyar's still has eyes for desire, while 319 adds the disgust of his kin and wife and asks for the feet before that day.

Thiruppugazh 32, after describing lovemaking with women scented with sandal and kumkum, asks about the முகடி, the goddess of ill fortune, of mingling with them (அரிவையருடன் கலந்திடு முகடியும் நலம்பிறந்திட அருள்வாயே). Kural 936 calls gambling a முகடி that covers those it swallows (சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார்). Both name a vice as the ill-fortune goddess herself; Kural 920 already sets women, liquor and dice together. The sense of the song's line is uncertain.

Kural 350 commands: cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), so as to let clinging go. Thiruppugazh 320 lists among the poet's faults that he has not the least bond (பற்றுச் சற்றும் இல்) to the one who holds all and stands free of clinging (பற்றற நிற்கும் பொருள்). The song names as its lack the very attachment the Kural prescribes.

Kural 338 likens the body-life bond to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழிய). Thiruppugazh 321 calls the body a great hut (பெருங்குடில்) and a rag given by father and mother, from which Death drives out the breath and drags it away alone (தனியில் இழுக்கப்படும்). Both picture death as the life leaving its shelter, the Kural with the body left alone and the song with the life taken alone.

Kural 236 says: if you are born, be born with renown (தோன்றின் புகழொடு தோன்றுக). Thiruppugazh 322 asks for just such a birth (சனனம் பெறாதோ) in which many poets honour him as a true poet, a master of the tattvas and a man of virtue, and the world calls him forbearing and a renunciate. The song turns the Kural's renown into a devotee's, asked as the road to the supreme.

The Thiruppugazh song lists the body by its parts, எலுப்பு, சுக்கிலம், அத்தம், தடி, தொக்கு (bone, semen, blood, fat, skin), and calls it a pot (கடம்) it does not want to wander tending. The Naladiyar verse runs the same kind of list, குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும் ... தோலும் ... தடியும், and asks which of these is the garlanded woman. The Naladiyar turns the catalogue on the desired woman's body, the song on the poet's own, both to undo the desire named beside it.

The Thiruppugazh song tells the funeral in quick verbs: the corpse is carried, the drums beat (எடுத்துக் கொட்டிட), it is laid on the logs and the fire set (கட்டைப்பட ... அனல் ... கொளுத்தி), and the kin let go and leave. The Naladiyar verse counts the funeral drum's beats (முக்காலைக் கொட்டினுள்) until the corpse is covered and the fire taken up, the dying carrying the dead. The song uses the scene as the deadline before which it asks to sing the feet in Tamil, the Naladiyar as a call to see that the bearers are next.

The Thiruppugazh song pictures women who bind young men by the neck and unite on gold-adorned beds, and asks to avoid such unions (புணர் மாதர் பொருத்தத்தைத் தவிர்த்து) and gain the golden feet. The Naladiyar verse says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்தும் என்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of such women. Both make giving up that embrace the condition of reaching the goal, the Naladiyar as a rule, the song as a plea.

The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; 329 asks for the clinging that does not suffer, set against the clinging to food and wealth, if its line is divided so.

Thiruppugazh 33 calls the courtesan's bed a one-sided union (ஒருதலை மருவு புணர்ச்சித் தூர்த்தர்கள்), where she melts a man only while his wealth lasts. Kural 1196, in a woman's voice, says love is painful on one side only and sweet on both, like the load of a carrying pole (ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம் காப்போல இருதலையானும் இனிது). The song takes the akam term for unreturned longing and turns it on paid love, where only the man loves.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as a man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and in 33 the woman who melted him while wealth lasted beats him from the door when it ends.

The short Thiruppugazh song praises the holy feet fit to be set on the round flower (வட்டப் புட்பத் தலம் மீதே வைக்கத் தக்க திருபாதா) and asks the Lord to take hold of one whirling through every birth. The Kural speaks of the great feet of the one who moved upon the flower (மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் மாணடி) and promises long life to those who reach them. The flower that bears the feet is shared; if it is the heart's lotus, as the song's nuance suggests, both place the feet there.

The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). The Thiruppugazh song shows the tongue already failing in old age, coughing and stammering (திக்கித் திக்கிக் குளறி), and asks to speak pure Tamil with conviction (சுத்தச் சித்தித் தமிழைத் திட்டத்துக்குப் புகல). It applies the Kural's deadline to speech itself: what must be done before the tongue fails is to praise.

The Thiruppugazh song calls the body a hollow bag of skin (பொக்குப் பை ... தொக்குப் பை), a false hut the poet keeps tending. The Naladiyar verse calls it a skin bag (தோற்பை) in which a dancer works until he leaves, after which it does not matter what is done with it. The same skin bag serves the Naladiyar to show the body's worthlessness once the life goes, and the song to show the folly of tending it while alive.

The Thiruppugazh song describes women's eyes as vel, fish and poison (அயில் அப்புக் கயல் ... நச்சுக் கண்) and confesses that the poet staggers, loses sleep and work, and whirls for them. The Naladiyar verse names the same figures, darting carp and spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), refuses to give way to them, and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The song is the man who gave way, the Naladiyar the one who will not.

Both turn desire away by showing the desired woman old. The Naladiyar gives one picture, the woman bent on her mother's staff; 34 takes each charm the songs praise, hair, eyes, breasts, and shows its ruin, then names a different remedy, service at the Lord's feet.
Both picture old age by teeth lost and a body bent on a stick. The Naladiyar uses it against the old man who still desires; 341 carries the picture on to the corpse burned and the kin going home.

The Thiruppugazh song gives the death as the kin's wailing heard: 'he is dead, I am ruined' (செத்தார் கெட்டேன் அஆ உஉ), then they burn and leave. The Naladiyar verse gives it as the people's quick report: he stood, sat, lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone (நின்றான் இருந்தான் கிடந்தான் தன் கேள் அலறச் சென்றான்). The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now, the song asks whether the bewilderment will not end.

The Thiruppugazh song, spoken for a lovesick girl, names the stained moon that the poisonous serpent seeks (நச்சரவம் ... நச்சுமிழ் களங்க மதி) among her torments. The Kural's woman says the gossip from one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்பு கொண்டற்று). Both akam voices use the eclipse: the Kural for scandal swallowing the lovers, the song for the moon itself as a wounded tormentor.
The Kural warns that women who desire a man for his wealth bring him harm; 345 tells the harm from inside, the wealth given away and a poverty that burns like the undersea fire.

The Naladiyar verse says a courtesan's love, like a lamp's flame, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The Thiruppugazh song tells the result from the man's side: he gave much real wealth to quick-talking women until his life withered (மெய்ப்பொருள் பல கொடுத்து அற உயிர் வாடா), and now lives in poverty that burns like the undersea fire (மிடியெனப் பெரு வடவை). The song is the Naladiyar's emptied hand, lived.

The Thiruppugazh song describes women who talk money, send go-betweens and want many men's leavings (பலர் எச்சிற்கு ஆசைக் காரிகள்), and asks whether such company befits him (சந்தமாமோ). The Kural says those of refined understanding will not plunge into the base charms of women whose goodness is common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம்). Both rest the refusal on the women being shared by many.

The Thiruppugazh song lists the woman's deer-like eyes and spear-like eyes (மறிபோலுகின்ற விழி, அயிலே நிகர்ந்த விழி) among what destroys the poet's understanding (அறிவே அழிந்து). The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ), finding all three in it. The doe's softness and the deadly weapon are joined in both; the Kural is wonder, the song a plea not to swoon.

The Thiruppugazh song names the women outright as priced (விலைமாதர்), cheats whose way of life brings sickness of mind and sores. The Naladiyar verse says such women find a moneyless man poison and even an oil-presser sugar if he has wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம்). Both make price the whole of the bond; the song adds what it costs the man in body and mind.

Thiruppugazh 35 speaks of women who talk tenderly, snatch coins and whose hearts are weighed exactly to the coin (உருக்கம் பேசிய நீலியர் ... காசளவே மனம் உறைக்கும் தூரிகள்). Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the gain and then speak of their goodness (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்). Both describe the same weighing, tender speech measured by the money.

The Kural warns that the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of bangled women who want wealth, not love, bring harm. Among the courtesans' arts 353 lists binding men with idle talk (வம்புரை கூறி வளைத்து இணக்கவும்) and taking their wealth without anyone blaming them (நிந்தை செய்யாது பொருட்பறிக்கவும்). The song shows the Kural's point at work: the talk is the tool and the wealth is the aim, and the harm goes unblamed.

The Kural says a head that does not bow at the feet of the Lord is as useless as a sense organ that cannot sense (கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே). 354 asks whether he must perish without having sung with love on his tongue (அன்புடன் நாவிற் பா) and without worship of the feet by his hand (பாதமும் அங்கையின் நானிற் பூசையும் அணியாமல்). Both measure the bodily organs by whether they serve the feet: the Kural names the head, the song the tongue and the hand.

In the Kural the lover says he once had shame and manliness, and now has only the palmyra horse that the lustful ride (காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்). 356 says the breasts of these women make even renouncers ride the madal of desire (துறவோரை ஆசைமடல் ஊர்வித்து ஆளும்). The song carries the Kural's figure past the lover to the ascetic: the madal now marks the fall of a renouncer, not only of a man's pride.
Both say the courtesan desires the wealth and not the man; 357 sharpens it into a measure, the desire acted exactly as far as the gold goes.

Thiruppugazh 36 calls himself, among other names, one who has not written a single leaf, wholly ignorant (ஏடெழுதா முழு ஏழையை), and asks Murugan not to scorn him but to give him his cool feet. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). The Kural makes the feet the end that learning serves; the song asks for the same feet without the learning. The reading of ஏடெழுதா as 'unlettered' is not certain.

The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is a deadly அணங்கு to those who lack discerning knowledge (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). 360 says the courtesans take as a sacrifice the lives of the lustful who do not know the higher path (பரநெறி உணரா அக்காமுகர் உயிர்பலி கொளும்). Both find the danger in the man's want of knowledge, and both make it a matter of life and death.
Both take the body apart into entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin. The Naladiyar asks which part is the desired woman; 362 makes the inventory the hut in which the poet's own senses run wild.

The Naladiyar says that even if he were Mal whom the gods worship, women tender as young shoots would send away a man with nothing in his hand, bowing with folded hands (விடுப்பர் தங்கையால் தொழுது). Among the courtesans' traits 366 lists that they gently put out those without money (காசற்றாரை இதத்தில் ஒழிச்சிகள்). Both stress that the dismissal is courteous: the politeness is part of the trade.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. 369 ends its chain of conditions with the casting off of the impurity called 'mine' (எனதெனும் மலம் அறில்), after which the reality without rising or death is easily gained in knowledge. Both make the end of 'mine' the condition of the highest state; the song calls it a மலம்.

Both use the Kural's word for courtesans (வரைவிலா, வரைவில்) and picture their pleasure as something a man sinks into: the Kural's mire (அளறு), 370's sea of pleasure, which 370 sets against a second sea, the bliss of Siva.

The Kural says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard or strength but the madal (ஏமம் மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). 371 ends with Murugan, mad with longing for the doe of the millet field, writing a lone madal (மயல்கொடு தனிமடல் எழுதிய). The lover's last resort in the Kural is given in the song to the god, who takes the desperate lover's part for Valli.
Both make the courtesan a woman who weighs: in the Kural she weighs the profit and speaks of her virtue to match, in 373 she measures her heart to the money (திரவியம் அளவளவு அளவியர்).

The Kural's lover discovers that Death has a woman's eyes, half in wonder; 374 extends the discovery to every charm, breasts as Yama and the pearls on them as Yama's rope, and turns it into a reason to turn away.

The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). 377 asks whether he will worship the two feet that are a raft for the life (உயிர்ப் புணை இணைத் தாள்). The song makes the feet themselves the float by which the Kural's sea is crossed.

In the Kural the woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக). 379, in a lovesick woman's voice, names the excess blame the women of the town speak (வருணமட மாதர் கற்ற வசையின் மிகை பேச) among the things, with moon and Kama's arrows, that wear her life away. The song keeps the akam rule that gossip feeds the sickness, now with the god as the absent lover.

Both follow the drums of a funeral to the moment the body is left: the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead; 38 ends with the mourners leaving it on the road, and calls the whole scene mithya, a false life to escape.
Both count the flute among the torments of the lovesick woman: the Kural's herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills, and 380's sweet lone flute is one of four things she asks to survive.

The Kural says good deeds must be hastened to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 382 asks whether, before he dies with his old deeds unshed (ஊழ்வினை விடாமல் சாவதன் முனே), Murugan will take him into service (ஏவற் கொண்டிடாயோ). Both set the deadline at death's approach; the Kural asks the man to act, the song asks the Lord to claim him.

The song's women are அமுதம் ஊறு சொல் ஆகிய தோகையர் who call பொருளுளாரை, men of wealth, with 'என் ஆணை உன் ஆணை, my house is near'; the Kural says the இன்சொல் of women who want பொருள், not love (அன்பின் விழையார்), brings harm. The pairing shows Arunagiri dramatising the Kural's 'sweet words' as an actual street invitation sealed with an oath.

The song calls the women கரவது ஆம் மன மாதர்கள், women whose hearts hide, and the poet a fool who fell into their நீள்வலை not knowing true love (நேசமது அறியாத). Naladiyar 379 says such women hide a harmful heart (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் உள்ளடக்கி) and that those who trust their words and call them 'ours' are deceived. Both put the danger in the concealed heart behind the speech.

Both give a woman's eyes the power to eat the life of those who look: the Kural's lover says it of one girl with wonder, 386 of women's eyes in general, likened to Siva's throat-poison and Murugan's vel.

The song says the women's eyes are the churning-poison itself, eye-nets that take lovers' lives as sacrifice (காமுகர் உயிர்பலி கவர்வுறு ... விழிவலை). The Kural's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both fuse the eye with a killer, the Kural in wonder, the song in alarm.

The song has Death coming by fate's way, saying today is the day to take the life (இன்று உயிர்கொளும் நெறி இன்று என), and asks to worship the feet before (வருமுன்) that tumult of weeping kin. Naladiyar 20 says merciless Death roams looking for his people (ஆட்பார்த்து உழலும் அருளில் கூற்று), so take provisions in good time. Both press for action before Death's appointed hour; the provision in the song is worship of the feet.

Thiruppugazh 39 asks to mix with loving devotees of good mind who sing the Lord's praise and so gain their nature (பண்புடைய சிந்தை அன்பர் தங்களினுடன் கலந்து பண்புபெற). Naladiyar 139 says even the unlearned gain good sense by keeping company with the learned, as a new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers (கற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகின் நல்லறிவு நாளும் தலைப்படுவர்). The same logic, that one takes on the nature of one's company, is applied in the Naladiyar to learning and in the song to devotion.

The song lists the moon, the small south wind that comes like fire (எரியென வரு சிறு தென்றல்) and Kama's arrows as attackers of the girl alone on her flower bed. The Kural's woman says evening comes like strangers to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல). Both turn the hours and breezes of love-poetry into armed assailants of the lone woman.

The song asks to enter the shade of the feet, which are a raft of lotus (சததள மலர் வார் புணை நின கழல்), out of a life worn down in the world by the body. The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). The song makes the Kural's feet into the raft (புணை) that does the swimming.

The song asks not to be born into the sea of misery by cultivating the friendship of the wicked (கருக்காரர் நட்பைப் பெருக்கு ஆசரித்துக் கலிச்சாகரத்தில் பிறவாதே). The Kural says nothing brings more affliction than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லல் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). The song stretches the Kural's affliction into the next birth.

The song follows a life spent on women's breasts until the body bends, he walks coughing, speech goes (உரைபோய்) and feeling ends, and asks for the feet to escape fire-mouthed hell. Naladiyar 13 describes men whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth (சொல்தளர்ந்து கோல்ஊன்றி), yet still keep their eyes on desire, and says they have no safe way. The song is the Naladiyar's old man speaking for himself and asking for that way.

The song fears falling, a mere bubble, into the whirlpool of the sea of birth (புற்புதமாய பிறவி வாராகரச் சுழி). Naladiyar 27 calls the body a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts again and again (படுமழை மொக்குளின் பல்காலும் தோன்றிக் கெடும்). The Naladiyar's bubble is the body; the song makes each whole birth the bubble.

The song's women bewitch anyone at all for the love of wealth (ஆசை பொருட்டு ஆரையும் எத்தாக மயக்கிடும்) and send go-betweens to snatch money. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser is sugar if he has wealth. Both make wealth the only thing the women see in a man.

The lovesick woman in the song says the small wind of the end (இறுதிச் சிறுகால்), the moon and the sea make her life droop (உயிர் துவள). The Kural's woman tells evening it is not evening but an hour that eats the life of the wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). Both make the natural hour a devourer of the separated woman's life.
Both make the town's talk feed the girl's love-sickness: in the Kural gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water, in 397 the town reproaches her alongside the north wind.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as the money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and 398's women of magic arts cling only as far as the wealth goes (பொருளது அளவும் மருவுறு).

Thiruppugazh 40 asks to reach a pure mind, learn virtue, wealth and pleasure fully, and having left them, know grace itself (அமலமாகிய சிந்தை அடைந்து ... அறம்பொருள் இன்பமும் அடைய ஓதி உணர்ந்து தணந்தபின் அருள்தானே அறியுமாறு). Kural 34 says spotlessness of mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). For the Kural the pure mind completes aram; for the song it is the first step, after which aram itself is learnt and passed beyond into grace, if தணந்த is read as leaving the three aims.

The song asks Murugan to appear so that the two deeds take fright and the dark disease fades (இருவினை அஞ்ச ... இருள்பிணி மங்க). The Kural says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who love the Lord's true praise (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா). Both pair darkness with the two deeds and make the Lord's presence or praise the release from both.

The song names the body, among other vessels, a குடம்பை and a hut (குரம்பை) that heart and life move out of (நெஞ்சொடு உயிர் குடிபோம்). The Kural says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The song uses the Kural's own word and gives the soul the same departure.

Both call the body a pot (கும்பம்) of filth: the Naladiyar's pot seeps through nine openings under its dark skin, 402's is a pot where stench and liquor pool. The Naladiyar turns the image on the desired woman; 402 turns it on the poet's own body.

The girl says the flute's music comes like the sun to take her life (இரவி எனது உயிர் கவர வரு குழல் இசை). The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). In both the flute, not the lover's absence alone, is the killer.

The voice asks whether the girl should suffer from the moon, the rumour spread by the blaming women (மலந்தைமார் சொல் வதந்தி) and the south wind. The Kural's woman says the town's gossip is the manure of her sickness and her mother's words its water. Both count other people's talk among the forces that feed the lovesick girl's pain.

The song lays out a woman's beauty from face to gait and ends by asking whether one should be kin to those who coax and snatch wealth (குனகி பொருள் பறிபவர்க்கு உறவாமோ). The Kural says to avoid women who weigh the profit and then speak of goodness (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The song's catalogue is the 'speaking of goodness' the Kural warns against, and the last line names the weighing.

Thiruppugazh 41's praise names Murugan as the one who gives the virtue of the head and of the hands, of the kadamba garland, of Siva and of austerity (சிரப்பண்பும் கரப்பண்பும் ... சிவப்பண்பும் தவப்பண்பும் தருவோனே). Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a sense that cannot sense (எண்குணத்தான் தாளை வணங்காத் தலை). The Kural judges the unbowed head; the song makes the bowing head a gift of the Lord. The division of the chiming line is uncertain.

The song lists what women's eyes do: they meet arrows, wage war on the young (இளையோர் முன் செருவை) and wring out men's lives. The Kural's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it as the eyes that make great war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both see the eye as a warrior that kills.

In the song the girl who is modesty itself (நாணான தோகை) wilts as the townsfolk revile her and slanders pile up (நாடோர்கள் ஏச ... நானா பவாதம்). The Kural's woman asks how she can be ashamed of gossip (அலர்நாண) now that he who said 'fear not' has left her. Both join the girl's shame to the town's talk; the Kural's woman has passed beyond the shame the song's girl still suffers.

Both show the old man with failing speech and a staff. The Naladiyar's still keeps his eyes on desire; 412 follows the man spent on courtesans to the end, deaf and on a mat, while his own wife, children and kin call him a curse.

The Kural's woman says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள் நெடிய கழியும் இரா). 413's girl, struck by Kama's five flower arrows on her bed, says one night has come on like an old aeon (பழைய பேருகம் விளைந்ததென ஓரிரவு). Both make the lengthened night, not the absent lover, the torment of separation.

The Naladiyar says those who think the love of a worthless woman their own, while she licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). 415 confesses the same end from inside: wealth, youth, learning and mind spent on such women (பொருள் இளமை கலை மனமும் ஏகப் போக்கிய), until the world reviles him as an outcast (புலையன் இவன் என உலகம் ஏச). The quatrain's warning is the song's confession.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate: devise another way and it is there first (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 417 names fate as a cause of its ruin, deeds of fate bent on harm (ஊழ்வினையினால் மிகுத்த கேடுறுகவே நினைக்கும் வினை), yet asks Murugan to come with the vel to rule him and grant release (வீடுதவி ஆள). On the reading that the plea expects grace to override what fate decreed, the song sets a limit to the Kural's 'no greater strength'.

Thiruppugazh 42 asks Murugan to break the prison of the body given by birth and give the joy of his feet (பிறப்பங்கம் சிறைப்பங்கம் சிதைத்து உன்றன் பதத்தின்பம் தருவாயே). Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body has not found a home of its own (புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு). The Kural calls the body a temporary lodging; the song goes further and calls it a prison to be broken, and names the feet as the home.

The Kural names quarrelling, making up and union as the fruits of those who love (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம் கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்). 420 tells exactly that course, the sulk (புலவி மிகுத்திட்டு), bowing at her flower feet until love returns (அநுராகம்), and union, then asks whether even in union he would forget the golden feet (புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ). The song keeps the Kural's sequence but holds the feet above its fruit.

Both show vultures tearing at the body. The Naladiyar's stinking cart is shown to men who praise sandal and garlands; 422 sees the poet's own body as the feast of dogs, jackals, vultures and worms, and turns from it to the company of devotees.

The Naladiyar mocks the untaught petty men who babble that smiles are jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகைமுறுவல் முத்தென்று இவைபிதற்றும் கல்லாப்புன் மாக்கள்), having seen the teeth in the burning ground. 424 quotes such flattery in its own mouth, teeth like rows of pearls (பந்தித் தரளம்), lips sweeter than fruit, and names the speaker a dull-witted fool (மந்தப் புந்திக் கசடன்). The quatrain's mocked praiser is the poet's self-portrait.

The Kural says neither the shaved head nor long matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 428 confesses to both marks, the shaved head and the grown locks, with the condemned conduct, the hunt for gold, kept underneath.
Both bring a corpse into the courtesan's bed: in the Kural the man embracing her is embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 43 it is she who would embrace even a corpse for money.

Thiruppugazh 43 describes courtesans who lead moneyless youths astray and leave them spent, and who melt in bed when they get great wealth (பொருளில் இளைஞரை ... தளர விடுபவர் ... பெருகு பொருள்பெறில் அமளியில் இதமொடு குழைவோடே). Naladiyar 374 says to such women men without money are poison, and even an oil-presser with earned wealth is sugar (காணமிலாதார் கடுவனையர் ... செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம் அன்னார்). Both set the moneyless man and the rich one side by side to show love following only the money.

The Kural's man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). 430's girl is burned by cool moonlight (சீதநிலா எறிக்கும் அனலாலே), and the cure asked is that the god come and embrace her. Both turn coolness and fire inside out in love-sickness, with nearness as the only cooling.

The Kural says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with the bar of shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 432's woman says the cuckoo's call destroys her modesty (நாணம் அழிய உரைக்குங் குயிலாலே) as she wastes in longing. Both make shame the last barrier that love-sickness breaks.

The Naladiyar calls the body a paltry lodging (நொய்யதோர் புக்கில்) whose covering of skin, if torn, brings the crows. 433 names it a hut bound by the noose, made of skin, wind and flesh and stained (தோலாலே காலாலே ஊனாலே சூழ் பாசக் குடில் மாசு). Both set the body as a frail dwelling of skin against the sweet speech of women.

The Kural commands: cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). 435, after heaping names on itself, does not ask that desire end but that he think of the feet daily with a longing not let go (நினது தாளை நாடோறு மனதில் ஆசை வீடாமல் நினையுமாறு). Both turn attachment toward the Lord instead of ending it.

The Naladiyar's renunciant will not be moved by petty men who call eyes water-lilies, darting carp or spears (தெண்ணீர்க் குவளை பொருகயல் வேலென்று), having seen an eye is a scooped palm fruit. 437 lists the same likenings, deer, poison, carp, arrow, vel, sword, blue lily (கயல் மீனை ... வடிவேலை ... உற்பலத்தினை), then names the body an oozing filth and a bloated corpse (ஊதும் பிணம்). The song confesses being caught by the comparisons the quatrain sees through, and asks that the delusion clear (இப்ரமை தெளியாதோ).

The Naladiyar likens a harlot's love to a lamp: the light ends when the oil runs out, and her love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 438 lists the courtesans who for love of coin sell their breasts to many (காசாசையில் முலை பலர்க்கும் விற்பவர்) and the low-priced (விலைச்சிறுக்கிகள்). Both make money the whole measure of the love.

The Kural warns that the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). 439 shows such women crying the price of their breasts in the street (முலை விலைகூறி), luring with deceitful play and snatching life (உயிரே பறிப்பவர்கள்), and asks whether they can be kin (உறவாமோ). The song's scene is the Kural's sale and harm made visible.

Thiruppugazh 44 describes women born to quote a price who join with seeming love, friendship and kindness (பிறந்து விலைகூறி ... அன்பு நண்பு பண்பு முடனாகப் புணர்ந்து). Kural 917 says those without a firm heart touch the shoulders of women who join while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்). The song names what the Kural leaves unspecified in பிற: the price, under the show of love.

In the Naladiyar, to women without their companion the thunder of rain sounds like the funeral drum beaten in every direction (நெய்தல் அறைந்தன்ன). In 440 the roaring sea that bends and cries out (வளைந்து அரற்று கடல்) and the moon rising with poison torment the separated girl. Both turn a sound of nature into the separated woman's affliction; 440 then asks for mukti as the end of it.

The Kural names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்). 442 gives the women a hundred thousand minds (நூறாயிர மனமுடை மாபாவிகள்) and calls itself the clown reviled by earth and sky who is wholly in their thrall. The Kural's two minds become the song's hundred thousand.
Both hear the funeral drum while kin wail over the corpse; the Naladiyar's drum mocks the living, while 444 notes that the kin weep each for their own share.

The Kural says what is called virtue is household life itself (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). The song confesses that very life, wearied in samsara, delighting in kin and cherishing the family (சமுசாரம், சுற்றத்தவரோடு இன்பத் தழைத்து, குடிபேணி), as what leads him straight to the grave pit, and asks for the roots of the world's maya to be dried. On the reading that the song counts householding itself, not its excess, as the fault, the two judge the same life oppositely.

Both end the cherished body as carrion: the Naladiyar's vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks, and 446 lays the householder in a pit for vultures and dogs. The Naladiyar's target is the praise of perfumes and garlands; 446's is family life.

Thiruppugazh 45 speaks of women who bargain so that a man's wealth runs out and make him trust them (நன்றுபொருள் தீர என்று விலைபேசி நம்பவிடு மாதர்), and of himself wasting like a frog that has eaten poison. Naladiyar 377 says those who trust as their own the love of the woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands and then turns away will be laughed at (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு ... எமது என்று இருந்தார்). Both make the man's trust the trap that lets the wealth be taken.

The song asks not to roam with the heart in the seven hells (எழுநரகில் உழலும் நெஞ்சு) and calls Murugan easy to reach for those who practise the path of compassion (கருணைநெறி புரியும் அன்பர்க்கு எளியோன்). The Kural says those whose hearts are joined with grace will not enter the dark world of pain (அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). Both make compassion, not worship alone, the way out of hell, the song adding that it also brings the god near.

The Kural says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை). The song pictures the man who did not: eyes and ears failing (கண் செவியும் சுகங்கள் திரும்பி), he asks whether he must lie with the wrongs he did before and die (முன்செய்த வஞ்சினங்களுடன் கிடந்து உடல் அழிவேனோ). The song is the deathbed the Kural's warning looks ahead to.

The Kural says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not the man bring harm (பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார் இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song shows those sweet words at work, the courtesan speaking as if she knew the man already (நீர் எந்த ஊர் அறிந்தவர் போல ... இன்சொல் கூறி) and joining whoever shows gold in his hand, and then the harm: sores, worms, colic and death. The song gives the scene and the consequence the Kural compresses into இழுக்கு.

The song says the poet has come again and again, sprouting from seed (வந்து வந்து வித்தூறி), his life worn in the forest of his own deceits (எந்தன் வஞ்சனைக் காடு). The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). Both see rebirth as a seed sprouting; the Kural names the seed as craving, the song lets it grow into a forest the Lord must scatter.

Both give the courtesan's course in one sequence: the Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands and then balks like an ox; 458's coaxes, takes gold until the wealth is gone, then drives him off with deceitful words.

The song describes women who snatch a man's wages in a moment and embrace him on soft beds, and asks whether such women can be kin (பஞ்சணை மீது அணை மாதர்கள் உறவாமோ). The Kural likens the false embrace of women of wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room (இருட்டறையில் ஏதில் பிணம் தழீஇ அற்று). Both deny that the bedroom embrace makes a relation: the song's உறவு and the Kural's ஏதில், 'a stranger', answer each other.

The song's courtesans set their terms as money in the hand in advance (முற்பணம் கைக்கொடும் தாரும்) and cling until the man's debts cover him. The Naladiyar says such women would send away even red-eyed Mal, worshipped by the gods, with joined hands if he had nothing in his hand to give (தம் கைக்குக் கொடுப்பது ஒன்று இல்லாரை). Both make the hand with gold in it the whole condition of the courtesan's welcome.

The song asks that, doubt cast off and understanding (விடுசங்கையற்று உணர்ந்து), the poet circle Murugan, praise him and receive his golden feet. The Kural says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. The song makes the Kural's step a plea within worship: the shedding of doubt is what lets the circling and the praise reach the feet.
The Kural makes the letter A first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 467 takes the letter itself as a name of the Goddess, calling Sivakami the அகரம் and the life of all.

Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts; the Naladiyar praises the firm who resolve from this to end their wandering, and 469 asks from it for the one release complete in wisdom, silence and bliss.

Thiruppugazh 47 asks Murugan gently to bring to shore one who drowns in a sea of pleasure among women, and to give his golden anklets (இன்பக் கடலூடே அமிழுவேனை மெத்தென ஒரு கரைசேர்த்து அம்பொற் றண்டைக் கழல்தாராய்). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் ... இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). The song turns the sea of births into the sea of pleasure, and like the Kural makes the feet the way across.

The song tastes the woman's lips like jackfruit segments (பலாசுளையின் சுவை கண்டு இதழ் உண்டு) and ends by asking whether he must fall like a dog with his body wasting. The Kural's lover finds the water at his beloved's teeth like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன் கலந்தற்றே). The same image of the mouth's sweetness is joy in the Kural's love and the prelude to ruin in the song.

The song lists learning (கல்வி) with father, mother, house, gold, silver and kin as a trouble (அல்லல்) to be shed before he can sing the Lord. The Kural calls learning the one imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி), other things not wealth. The conflict holds on the reading that the song counts learning itself as a bond; if அத்து பண்ணு கல்வி means only learning pursued for gain, it narrows to a qualification.
Both make poverty the end of the courtesan's love: the Naladiyar's flood ends when the income ends, and 477's women first show delusion and then show poverty.

The song says the women, after their show of beauty, plunder gold like skilled raiders (வல்லவர்கள் போல பொற்சூறை கொண்டார்கள்) and asks whether infatuation with them is fitting. The Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the man's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and turns away, and those who thought her love theirs are laughed at. Both name the taking of wealth as the purpose behind the display.

The song's women coax with feigned love and then pick a quarrel (பசப்பிப் பின் பிணக்கைக் கூறிய வீணிகள்) once the money is asked and given. The Naladiyar's women seem sweet while a man is infatuated and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாம் ஆர்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்), and those who would reach the right path avoid them. Both mark the same turn from coaxing to coldness; the Naladiyar ties it to the path, the song to the plea for the feet.

Both list the body's insides, guts, blood, bone, sinews and skin, almost word for word (குடர், குருதி, என்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்). The Naladiyar turns the list on the desired woman; 48 turns it on the poet's own body, which he still fondles.

The song makes the body a walled hut where the tricksters of the senses (பொறி விரகாளர்) dwell and where craving for women and land gathers (ஆசை பெணாசை மணாசைகள் தொக்கு), and asks for release. The Naladiyar names the five senses as five mouths of craving (ஐவாய வேட்கை அவா) and promises release to one who can guard them. The song confesses that it cannot do this guarding and asks the Lord for the release the Naladiyar ties to it.

The song calls the women's long eyes a net like the spears in the hands of Death's messengers (காலத் தூதர் கை வேலெனு நீள்விழி). The Kural's lover asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both draw the woman's look and Death together; in the Kural it is the lover's wonder, in the song a warning against the trade.

Both make the courtesan's only question whose money there is: the Naladiyar's women find even an oil-presser sweet if he has wealth, and 481's women, with hearts dry as cane waste, think only whose wealth it will be.

The song's praise shows Murugan walking through the hunters' forest for love of Valli until his fragrant feet reddened (வேடக் கானகத்து வாசத்தாள் சிவப்ப வருவோனே). The Naladiyar's mother asks whether her daughter's feet, which drew back even from red dye on soft cotton, have borne the stony forest path (பரற்கானம்) of her elopement. Both measure love by tender feet on the wild path; the song gives the god the part of the eloping lover.

The song's women pain the heart while seeming close and hide enmity within (உள்ள நோவைத்தே உறவாடியர் ... உள்விரோதக்காரிகள்). The Naladiyar's women keep a heart that does harm hidden inside (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் தம் உள்ளடக்கி) and speak words to be trusted, yet belong to no one but their bodies. Both locate the deceit in the concealed heart behind the closeness.

Sinking daily in the sea of lust the women give, the song asks for its remedy in company: to join the Lord's devotees, the silent jnanis (உனது அடியாராகிய மோன ஞானிகளுடனே சேரவும்). The Kural says there is no greater support than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more trouble than bad. The song applies the Kural's rule to the spiritual life, setting the devotees against the women.

The song calls itself the fool who, loving women for a price (விலைமாதர்), drowns in ruinous deeds and sinks into the seven hells (ஏழ்நரகு ஆழும் மூடனை). The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who set no limit the அளறு, hell and mire at once, in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). The shared verb ஆழ் shows the song taking the Kural's hell literally and multiplying it to seven.

Among the things that torment the lovesick girl the song names the bell of the bull coming home at evening (அடைந்திட்ட விடைமேவு மணியாலும). The Kural's woman calls the herdsman's flute a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the gentle pastoral sound of the herds' return into evening's weapon against the parted lover.

The song's women will not call a man back unless he pays the sum they name (பலஞ் செப்பித் தர மீள அழையாதவர்). The Naladiyar says that even if he were Mal whom the gods worship, they would dismiss with joined hands a man with nothing to give (கொடுப்பதொன்றில்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). Both make payment the only thing that keeps a man welcome; the Naladiyar's god makes the point by exaggeration.

The song's women talk with betel-red mouths, play at intimacy and state their wage (சம்பளம் ஈது என ஓதி) before the bed. The Kural says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the sweet talk ending in the named wage, the motive the Kural names.

The song names women cheats (எத்திகள்) in every part and act and asks, as a dog wandering with them, for the anklet of wondrous wisdom by the Lord's own act (உன் செயலால் அற்புத ஞானத்தின் கழல்). The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an அணங்கு to those without discerning understanding. The song accepts the Kural's diagnosis, lack of understanding, and asks for the wisdom from the Lord rather than from his own effort.

The Naladiyar says it matters nothing whether the body is dragged, buried or thrown away once its dweller has left; 493 lists the same receivers of the corpse, vultures, jackals, fire and earth, but as weary claimants, so that the repetition across countless births is itself the burden.

The song lays out a woman from head to foot, her smile nectar and gems (அமுர்த மாணிக்க நகை), and only at the end asks to be given another thought (வேறு சிந்தனையைத் தந்து ஆள்வாய்). Naladiyar 45 refuses exactly such talk of smiles as jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகை முறுவல் முத்து), because the speaker has seen the teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground. The pairing shows what the song's 'different thought' looks like in practice.

The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 497 asks to be spared ochre, matted hair, forest wandering and fasting and to be given instead the inner knowledge in which the self subsides. Both set the ascetic's outward marks aside, the Kural for conduct, 497 for grace and knowledge.

The song's women gather asking 'will money come?' (பொருள் வருமோ) and join with many at once. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார்) is sugar. Both make money the only question these women ask of a man.

The song's wealth is a procession of drums, veena and conch that vanishes in a moment. Kural 332 compares great wealth to the crowd gathering at a dance hall (கூத்தாட்டு அவைக் குழாத்து) and its going to that crowd dispersing. The Kural gives the reason the song's noisy show is the right image for wealth: it is a gathered audience.

The song pictures the pomp of wealth, a palanquin under umbrellas (குடை சூழ் சிவிகை) with armies (பலபடை) and music, and calls it a false show that vanishes in a moment (நொடி மறையும் பொய்ப் பவுஷு). Naladiyar 3 shows men who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies (குடைநிழற்கீழ்ச் சேனைத் தலைவராய்) fallen when their deeds run out. Same emblems, same verdict.

Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise. The song asks Murugan to come so that his servant's two deeds turn to ash (அடியன் இருவினை நீறுபட) while the gods sing of the wonder. The song turns the Kural's 'do not cling' into a burning away at the god's coming.

The song's women, once both have drowned in infatuation (மயல் மூழ்கிய பின்), pawn his jewels and loot what he has (ஆபரணம் வைத்து அடகு தேடு பொருள் சூறைகொளுவார்). Naladiyar 377 says such a woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand (கைப்பொருள் கொண்டு), then lies down like a balking ox. Both put the taking after the fondness.

The song's client ends coughing and hiccuping like a howling dog (ஊளை நாயென) while people say 'chi chi'. Naladiyar 375 calls the men who embrace women of double conduct dull-witted like beasts (விலங்கன்ன வெள்ளறிவினார்). Both turn the client, not the woman, into an animal.

The song cries 'will birth never end?' (பிறப்பு முடியாதோ) and asks for the unfading flower of the feet (வாடா மலர்ப்பதவி). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song is the Kural's claim spoken as a cry from inside the sea.

The song asks whether the poet must wander daily at the women's command (கட்டளையாக ... நித்தமும் உழல்வேனோ) instead of holding the feet with true knowledge. Kural 909 says virtue, wealth and other aims are absent in those who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்). The Kural speaks of the husband and the wife; the song moves the same servitude to the courtesan and its loss to release.

The song calls the body a vessel (பாத்ரம்) of flesh, blood, bile and urine and asks to be moved from this pot to that one (இக்கடத்தை நீக்கி அக்கடத்துள் ஆக்கி). Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot (கும்பம்) seeping filth from nine openings that the fool admires for its skin. Both make the body a filthy pot; the song alone asks for another pot.

Both picture the body as food for scavengers: Naladiyar 48 has vultures tearing the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 510 the ghoul, the dog and the fly. The Naladiyar uses it to shame those who praise the body; 510 asks to be taken out of it into release.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums (பறை), and both make the funeral a lesson: Naladiyar 24 notes that the dying carry the dead; 512 sets the funeral at the end of a life spent on courtesans.

Naladiyar 25 mocks the man who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground and still marries, believing there is joy here. The song shows the cost in full: the courtesans' trade (முலைவிலை உரைசெய்து) runs without pause through old age to the same funeral. The song extends the Naladiyar's warning from marriage to lust.

In Kural 1241 the woman asks her heart to think and tell her a medicine (நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ நெஞ்சே) for love's sickness. The song reverses the roles: the poet tells his mind what is good for it (மனமே உனக்கு உறுதி புகல்வேன்), to worship the god who cuts the root of impurity. The form of the love poem's talk with the heart is turned to worship.

Both speakers address their own mind (நெஞ்சே, மனமே) and urge it to set out with them on the good path. Naladiyar 55 gives the reason as youth wasted and old age coming; 513 gives only the Lord, who cuts the root of impurity.

The song's women carry crores of deceit gathered in their hearts (வஞ்சமே கோடி கோடிகள் நெஞ்சமே சேர) while they coo. Naladiyar 379 says such women hide a harmful heart (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் உள்ளடக்கி) behind words meant to be believed. Both place the danger in the concealed heart behind the sweet speech.

Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of யான் எனது, I and mine, enters a world higher than the gods'. Thiruppugazh 518 asks for நானென்பது அற்று, the 'I' gone, together with the flesh, and places the goal in the light of nada and Brahman where knowledge wells up as bliss. The song takes the Kural's renunciation of 'I' and names what lies past it in the language of union rather than of a higher world.

Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which worthless men sink (ஆழும்). Thiruppugazh 519 lists the laughter, stares, threats and acting of thieving women who gather a man's wealth, and asks whether he must fall (விழுவேனோ) into their deluding net. Both make the courtesan's embrace a place one falls into; the song gives the arts that set the trap, the Kural the verdict on who sinks.

Both name the Lord the eight-qualitied (எண்குணத்தான், எண்குணன்): the Kural makes the head that does not bow to his feet useless; in 52 the eight-qualitied Siva is himself the one who bows, worshipping Murugan.

Kural 1020 likens the movements of the shameless to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) that feigns life by its string (நாணால்). Thiruppugazh 520 makes the newborn body of nine gates a doll (பதுமையின் செயல் போலவே) dancing on a rope of breath (வளிகயிறினுடன் ஆடி). The Kural uses the puppet for a man without inner shame; the song extends it to every embodied life, whose string is the breath itself.

Naladiyar 377 says the worthless woman licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from a man's hands (நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), and those fooled (ஏமாந்து) into thinking her love theirs are laughed at. Thiruppugazh 522 has the courtesans deceive (எத்தி மழுப்பி), snatch goods (பொருட்பறித்து) and give kisses and embraces, and the poet fears perishing daily for them. Both tie the caress directly to the taking of wealth; the Naladiyar ends in ridicule, the song in daily ruin.

Kural 997 says those without human quality are like trees (மரம்போல்வர்) even if sharp as a file. Thiruppugazh 523 asks not to wander like a tree in the street (தெருவினில் மரமென) talking with everyone in idle work, but to see the six-faced Lord within. In both the tree is a person with an outward faculty, sharpness or speech, who lacks the inner one that makes it count.

Both look ahead to grey hair and the staff and draw the lesson that one should act before they come: the Naladiyar praises those who renounced in childhood, 524 asks to serve the Lord's servants before the body ripens.

527 asks not to die in women's union and fall into hell (நெறியில் மாண்டு இங்ஙனே நரகில் வீழ்ந்து அலையாமல்), hell coming after death. Kural 919 makes the women's soft shoulders themselves the அளறு, hell and mire, in which base men sink. The Kural puts in the present embrace the hell the song fears after it.

529 asks for the feet so that what is mine and what is theirs (எனதாம் தனதானவை) fall away along with the frenzy of lust. Kural 346 says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. The song places that 'mine' beneath its desire for women.

The Kural says that letting no day fall idle (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) by doing good blocks the road of further births; 53 asks to sing the நமோநம praise daily and worship so as not to waste days (வீணாள் படாது). Both make the unwasted day the unit of the good life; the Thiruppugazh fills it with worship where the Kural fills it with good deeds.

533 begins wilting before jasmine (முல்லை) and women's teeth (பல்லுக்கும் வாடி) and ends with the body burned in the brands and dropped in the pit. Naladiyar 45 refuses the men who call smiles jasmine buds and sets against them teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground (புறங்காட்டு உதிர்ந்துக்க பல்லென்பு). The same jasmine-teeth figure leads both to the cremation ground, in the Naladiyar as the cure for desire, in the song as its end.

Both see the body as a bag full of holes (Naladiyar தொளைபலவாய், 534 தொள்ளைப் புலாற்பை). The Naladiyar tells the lover to look at the desired body as a bag turned inside out; 534 turns the image on the poet's own body and asks to be rid of it.

537 praises Murugan as the poet who reached the shore of all learning (கல்விகரை கண்ட புலவோனே). Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) and a short life must choose what to learn. Read literally, the song claims for the god a shore the Naladiyar denies exists for the learner; the conflict holds only if the god is measured by the human limit.

538 took mother, wife, children, family and wealth as all that was needed (குலம்வாய்த்த நல்ல தனம்வாய்த்தது) until Yama comes and he is burned at the இடுகாடு. Naladiyar 25 has the man who sees corpses carried yet marries and says 'there is, there is' (உண்டு உண்டு உண்டு) answered by the funeral drum. Both set household gain against the burning ground.
The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, to be free of all other clinging; 54 asks, after confessing his infatuation, to attain clinging to Murugan (நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ).

540 opens with வரைவில் பொய் மங்கையர், false women without bounds, and describes their embrace. Kural 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line (வரைவிலா மாணிழையார்) the hell in which base men sink. The song's word is the Kural's chapter word, though the song names no price.

Both picture a man who clings to house and desire into a failing old age. The Naladiyar's old man, toothless on his staff, still has his eyes on desire and so has no path to safety; 541's clings to children and gold until he is grey and breathless, and asks for grace before Yama's rope catches him.

545 lists the woman part by part, hair, moon face, banyan-leaf navel, carp eyes, breasts, each with its comparison, and the poet wanders blind (அந்தனாகி மயல்). Naladiyar 46 lists the body's parts as entrails, fat, blood, bone and sinew and asks which of them is the garlanded woman. The same part-by-part method dissolves the figure the song is caught by.

546 opens with the lover's riddle about the eye, கோலோ வாளோ வேலோ சேலோ மீனோ மானோ. Naladiyar 44 refuses the eyeless men who call eyes lilies, carp and spears (குவளை பொருகயல் வேல்) and sees a scooped-out palm fruit. The song voices the very comparisons the Naladiyar rejects, and then confesses where they led.

The song's courtesans act out a false love and deal with a man only as far as his coins go (அன்பு போற் பொய் நடித்துக் காசளவு உறவாடி). The Kural describes women who weigh the gain first and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). Both put the measuring of money before the show of affection; the song adds that the show is a studied art (இன்ப சாஸ்த்ரம், பண்டு இராப்பகல் கற்று).

The Naladiyar says the body appears like mist on a hill and goes, so its owners should take the fruit it can yield while they have it (யாக்கையால் ஆய பயன்கொள்க). The song tells the mind not to trust the body, a string-worked contraption Brahma locked (நம் ஆக்கையை நம்பாதே), and names the use to make of it now: to belong to the vel-bearer under his deed of possession (இனிமேல் நாம் ... வேலவனார்க்கு இயல் அங்கு ஆகுவம்). The song fills in what the Naladiyar's 'fruit' should be.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift in hand. The Naladiyar's women would send away even Vishnu with folded hands if he brought nothing; 550's will not speak to a man on the day he brings no gold.

The Naladiyar's courtesan licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hand and turns away, and those who think her love theirs are laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). In the song the greed for money is presented by the woman's kin as affection (சுற்றம் பரிவென வைக்கும் பணவாசை), and the poet calls himself mocked and deluded (பகிடி மருட்கொண்டு). Both name a feigned tenderness that covers the taking of money, and the ridicule that follows the one who believes it.

The Kural says men without a firm heart embrace women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர்). The song spells this out as a division among many men: eyes to one, breasts to another, thoughts to a third (ஒருவரொடு சிந்தை ஒருவரொடு நிந்தை), and confesses the delusion that the love is real (அன்பு பெருகவுளதென்று மனநினையும் இந்த மருள்). The song's six-fold ஒருவரொடு is a list of what the Kural compresses into பிறநெஞ்சு.

Both picture the courtesan's double dealing as a body turned to more than one man at once: the Naladiyar's eel shows its head to the snake and its tail to the fish; 553 gives the eyes to one man, the breasts to another, the hands to a third.

The Naladiyar says to loveless women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with wealth is sugar (செக்கூர்ந்து கொண்டாரும் செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம்). The song's women demand money before the cloth is touched (உடைதொடாப் பணம்). Both make money the only test applied to the man.

The Kural names the courtesans women who draw no line (வரைவிலா மாணிழையார்), whose shoulders are the mire base men sink in. The song charges that they couple even with outcastes without refusing (புலையர் மாட்டும் மறாதே கூடிகள்) and fall on many (பலர் மேல் வீழ்). The song's charge is a concrete case of the Kural's வரைவிலா.

The Kural groups double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song calls the courtesans goddesses of misfortune who make men poor (மிடியர் ஆக்கு மூதேவிகள்) and drinkers of liquor (பேய்நீர் ஊணிகள்). Where the Kural says such company follows the loss of Fortune, the song makes the women themselves the bringers of misfortune.

The Kural warns of the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்). The song's whole charge is in its first words, women whose minds are set on seizing wealth (பொருள்கவர் சிந்தை அரிவையர்), and it asks to stop wandering in that passion and praise the feet with a melting heart. Both define the courtesan by where her desire is aimed.

The Naladiyar says a harlot's love is like a lamp's light: it ends when the hand is empty as the light ends when the oil runs out (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The song's women look with disgust on a man once the wealth is gone (விரவிய திரவியம் இலரானால் வெறுத்து நோக்கிகள்). The song sets against that love, which ends with the money, a vow that does not end: he will not forget the feet in dream or waking (கனவிலும் நனவிலும் மறவேனே).

The Kural likens the cloth on a girl's unfallen breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேல் கட்படாம்). The song's breasts chase off the elephant (களிற்றைத் துரத்தி) and make even ascetics faint (தவர் சோர). Both pair the breast with the must elephant as a dangerous force; the Kural's lover sees it held in by the cloth, while the song's confessing poet sees it overpower all.

The Kural's lover asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). The song's eyes rival the carp and match the doe (கயலைச் சருவிப் பிணையொத்து), and through them the poet has lost goodness, knowledge and feeling (நலமற்று அறிவற்று உணர்வற்றனன்). The song counts the cost of the கூற்றம் the Kural only glimpses in the look.

The Naladiyar calls the body a pot seeping filth from nine openings, which the fool praises as a woman because of its dark skin. The song calls the poet's own body a basket that knows no cleanness (சுத்தமறியாத பறி காயம்) and recoils from its smell (சீசி இது நாற உடல்) as he seeks women's houses. The Naladiyar turns the disgust on the desired body, the song on the desiring one's own.

Both list the conventional comparisons for a woman's eyes, the carp, the lily, the spear. The Naladiyar names them as the talk of blind petty men to be ignored; 57 piles them up as the delusion that holds the poet, then asks to be freed of it.
Both call the courtesan's body a mire (அளறு) into which men sink; the Kural's word also means hell, and 574 asks to be taken by the Lord so as not to sink there.

Both counter desire by naming the body's openings and their seepage: the Naladiyar's pot oozing filth from nine holes, 574's rotting, cloth-stopped hole. The Naladiyar calls the lover a fool; 574 asks for rescue.

576 asks to reach the feet before youth becomes age. The Naladiyar verse pictures the man who fails to: speech failing, leaning on a staff, teeth gone, still with eyes set on desire in the house, with no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The Naladiyar shows the end the song's urgency is meant to avoid: desire outliving youth with no way out.
Both make the woman's eye Death: the Kural's lover cannot tell if her look is Death, an eye or a doe, while 578 calls the eye-corners Yama's messengers in a confession it was saved from.

The Naladiyar says that to women with loveless hearts (ஆணமில் நெஞ்சத்து) a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with wealth is sugar. 58 names the same motive in the women it adorns with sandal and musk: great desire seeking money (மிக்காசை கொண்டு பொருள் தேடு மதி) with cruel, deceitful hearts, while their glance feigns longing.

Among its names for courtesans the Thiruppugazh song calls them women who quarrel bitterly when not given (ஈயாத போதில் அறப் பிணக்கிகள்) and who sell their breasts (விலைத் தனத்தியர்). The Naladiyar verse says their love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both make payment the condition of the courtesan's affection, and the song asks on that ground whether a bond (உறவு) with them is fitting.

The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; 589 shows that degradation in the poet himself, trembling and cringing as he sings for gifts, and asks whether such a tongue can gain love for the Lord.

The Kural says the ills perish when the names of desire, anger and delusion (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்) perish; 59 names the same triad in Sanskrit form, காம க்ரோத லோப, as what souls waste away in. The Thiruppugazh's third term is greed where the Kural's is delusion.

The song names the courtesan who shows her breasts to many (கொங்கை நோக்கப் பலர்க்குங் காட்டி) and calls her life a trade (தொழில் பண்டாட்டம்). The Kural says those of refined understanding will not plunge into the base charms of those whose goodness belongs to everyone (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). The Kural's பொதுநலம், beauty held in common, is what the song shows in action, and the song asks Murugan for the knowledge the Kural assumes the wise already have.

In its refrain the song lists what the courtesans show, among them false pity and agreement of heart (வஞ்சத் திரக்கங் காட்டுவர் நெஞ்சிற் பொருத்தங் காட்டுவர்). The Kural says the weak-hearted touch the shoulders of women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணிப் புணர்பவர்). Both locate the deceit in a heart that is shown as one thing and holds another; the song's காட்டுவர் makes the Kural's divided heart into a performance.

The song's clearest phrase is that, leaving the support of truth for the support of the false (மெய்ச்சார்வு அற்றே பொய்ச்சார்வு உற்றே), he cannot leave the sea of births. The Kural says a wretched birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருளான் ஆம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). Both make the mistaking of false for true the cause of birth, the song as a confession and the Kural as a general law.

The song pictures courtesans who call to anyone at all and dance along the street (யாவராயினும் நத்தி அழைப்பவர் தெருவூடே). The Naladiyar says such women, whatever believable words they speak, belong to no one but their own bodies (யார்க்கும் தமரல்லர் தம்உடம்பினார்). The two halves fit: those who call everyone are kin to no one, and the song adds that this drowns the man in maya and births of malam.

The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; 603 confesses exactly that folly, living as if a bubble-like life with wife, sons and house would stand for a crore of aeons.
Both see life as a bubble (புற்புதம்). The Naladiyar praises those who see it so and resolve to end their wandering; 603 confesses that he knows the image and still lives as if it lasted.

The song asks Murugan to come and watch the day when his stammering servant, who worships the two feet, fights with his grace and cruel Death and his army fall (கொடிய மறலியு மவனது கடகமு மடிய ... நினதருள் கொடுபொரு மமர்காண). The Kural says that for those who have gained the strength of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Both let a human being overcome Death; the Kural grants it to the strength of tapas, the song to the servant fighting with the Lord's grace.

The poet says he gave the jasmine-smiling women whatever they wanted and gave them gold, and they said there was nothing and went (இட்டு பொன்னை இல்லை யெனஏகி), leaving him to think of his own lack (இன்மை உள்ளி). The Naladiyar says the harlot's love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The song is the confession of a man who lived out the Naladiyar's comparison.
The Kural names double-hearted women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom fortune has left; 609 opens its list with gamblers and money-loving women side by side and adds disease.

614 quotes the women's own coaxing words (இங்கே வருக, இனிய இதழ் தந்தேன்) and says they then strip a man of wealth and life alike (பொருள் உயிர்கள் ... பறிகொளும்). Kural 911 puts the harm in the same place: the sweet speech (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்) of those who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்). The song dramatises the speech the couplet warns against.

619 counts wife and children (மனைவி மகவான கடலலை) with women and wealth as one sea in which he sinks and wanders. Naladiyar 130 tells the heart that will not let go of the home bond and pines for its children (மனைப்பாசம் கைவிடாய் மக்கட்கென்று ஏங்கி) that only good done goes with the soul. Both put family attachment, not only lust, among the bonds.

620 describes price-women (விலைமாதர்) who talk of kinship (முறை பேசி) while looking for prosperous houses (வாழ்ந்த மனை தேடி). Kural 912 names the same move: women who weigh the gain and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்), and tells the man to weigh them in return. The song's scene is the couplet's charge acted out.

624 calls the women's eyes Death coming with its fortress and pressing into battle (வருமறலி அரணமொடு முடுகு சமர் விழியிணைகள்). Kural 1083 has the man say he never knew what Death was until now: it is a woman's grace with great battling eyes (கூற்றென்பதனை ... பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Death, war and eyes join in both; the Kural's lover is astonished, while the song makes the image a confession.
Both give the courtesan's vow of oneness and show it false: the Naladiyar's woman swore never to part, like gem and thread, and turned away; 626's women swear 'you are me and I am you' without shame.

627 says desire for young women's carp eyes takes a man down the false great road that multiplies the tangle of birth (பிறவி தரும் சிக்கு அது பெருகும் பொய்ப் பெருவழி). Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்தும் என்பார்) will not embrace such women. Both frame lust as a road that leads away from the true one.

629 lists among what feeds his net of desire the moon that burns like sun, the flute and the blame of women (நார்மாதர் வசையாலும்). Kural 1147 says the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக). Both make blame and gossip feed the longing they mean to shame; 629 turns the convention into its own state.

631 says that after the women make him cringe like a dog, disease comes and mother, kin and clan all laugh as his body wastes (தாய் தமர் குலத்தர் யாவரும் நகைக்கவே). Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into taking such women's love as their own get laughter from many (பலரால் நகை). Both end the courtesan's story in public ridicule.

632 says that after losing his wealth to women he can no longer bear to plead poverty before base and cruel men (பதகர் கொடியவாளிடத்திலே மிக வறுமை புகல்வதே ... இனி முடியாதே). Naladiyar 78 says even when starving, do not tell your need to those without courtesy (பண்பிலார்க்கு அற்றம் அறிய உரையற்க). The song is the shame the quatrain forbids, felt from inside.
Both describe women who take the wealth from a man's hand once he is caught; the Naladiyar adds that he is laughed at, 633 that his very strength of mind is destroyed.
The Kural says only those who join the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; 634 asks in the same image whether he will swim the long wave of birth and reach the pure feet.

635 calls the body an illusion like lightning at night, and not even that (அல்லில் நேரும் மின் அதுதானும் அல்லதாகிய உடல்). Naladiyar 8 says the wealth of the petty appears like lightning from a black cloud at night (எல்லில் ... மின்னுப்போல்) and vanishes. The same night-lightning is used for wealth in one and the body in the other, and 635 ranks the body below it.

638 begins its list of wants with the body, cloth, food and medicine for its sickness (மெய் உறுநோயை ஒழிக்கப் பரிகாரம்), and ends whirling in the mountain of births (பவகிரிக்குள் சுழல்வேனை). The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much (உடம்பும் மிகை), so what other ties should they keep? The song shows how the body's needs multiply into a household, the case the Kural cuts off at the root.

The Naladiyar says those who mean to reach the right way (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of women who go their own way. 641 says such women bring under passion's power (ராகத்தின் வசமாக) even those already walking the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga (சரியைக்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு). Read together, the song limits the Naladiyar's confidence: being on the path does not by itself keep one away.

644, on one division, asks whether the lustful man caught in women will forget even the feet that made him forget desire (ஆசையை மறப்பித்த கால்கள்).
