The Kural tells the reader to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). Both make holding the Lord the means by which desire is undone; the song's fear is losing that hold. The division of the song's line is uncertain.

The Kural's woman hears the cowherd's flute as the herald of a burning evening and a weapon that kills; in 647 the cowherds' bamboo flute is one of the evening torments, with the sea and the moon, of a girl sick for Murugan.

656 asks that, with 'mine' gone (எனது அற), he gain the feet and be told the word that marks the bound of silence. The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. Both make the end of 'mine' the condition of the highest gain, the Kural as renunciation, the song as reaching the feet.

657 asks whether the golden feet can be gained other than by words that make all the world know Murugan's emblems (அகிலமும் உணர மொழிதரு மொழியின் அல்லது). The Kural says the two dark deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise (பொருள்சேர் புகழ் புரிந்தார்). Both make proclaiming the Lord the working means, not ornament; the song adds that his own teaching is beyond words (நிர்வசன ப்ரசங்க).

659 asks whether his heart will not learn, while life remains in the world (உலகுயிர் உள்ள பொழுதே), to say that Murugan is Uma's son. The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set the deadline at the end of life; for the song the deed to be done before it is speech itself, praise.

The Naladiyar likens the harlot's love to lamplight that goes out when the oil runs out, and her love when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 66 stages the same course with a real lamp: she takes him upstairs by lamplight (விளக்கெடுத்து), coaxes coins, strips his hands of jewels and drives him out exhausted (இளைக்க விட்டுத் துரத்துவார்).

660 tells how, putting wealth by the handful into a deceitful woman's hand (கள்ள முள்ள ... கையில் அள்ளி பொருள் ஈய), his gems, grain, silver, learning and wealthy kin all vanished. The Kural says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song is a narrative of the Kural's verdict, with learning and kin lost alongside wealth.

Both define the giver by his shame at the word 'none': the Kural's man of good family does not utter the misery of 'I have nothing' and gives without refusing, and 662 names those ashamed to say 'there is none', who do not refuse from what they have, using the same word for misery (எவ்வம்).
The Kural calls the palmyra horse the only defence of those who suffer in love; 664 has Murugan himself, infatuated in Valli's field, mount it, the god taking the lover's last resort.

665 fears that when its time of speed comes the life, like a fierce elephant (வெங்கனல் உயிர் வேழம்), will run loose along the paths of the senses. The Kural praises one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்), the goad implying the senses as elephants. The Kural answers with firmness; the song asks instead for the strength to recite 'Vel, Kanda'.

Both take the body apart into its stuff, skin, flesh, blood and bone: the Naladiyar to ask which part is the desired woman, 665 to show the hut the life lives in before it asks for the strength to praise.

The song's courtesans show delight when big givers come (அதிகராய்ப் பொருள் ஈவார் நேர்படில் ரசனை காட்டிகள்) and drive off those who give nothing even after union. The Kural's women weigh the gain first and only then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). Both say the warmth is measured to the gift; the Kural draws the rule (keep away), the song gives the scene.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift: the Naladiyar's women send away even Mal if his hand is empty, and 666's women show delight to the man who gives much and drive off one who does not.

The faithful wife of the Naladiyar wonders how women who embrace many men's chests for gain (பொருள்நசையால் பன்மார்பு சேர்ந்தொழுகுவார்) manage it every day. The song shows exactly how: one man on the bed, one circling the door, one rushing in the street, set against each other (ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை ... ஒருவரை), all thought fitting as a living (உயிர்பிழைப்பது). The song answers the wife's question with the courtesan's method and motive.

The Naladiyar says such women would bow and dismiss even red-eyed Mal if he came with nothing in his hand to give (விடுப்பர் தங்கையால் தொழுது). 67 gives the dismissal in the woman's own words once the man is spent: 'you are finished, go today' (அற்றனை என இன்று ஓட்டு).

The Kural says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an afflicting spirit (அணங்கு) to those without discerning understanding. The song's women are illusion-and-song charmers (மயமாயங் கீதவிநோதிகள்) who fall on deluded lovers (மருளாருங் காதலர் மேல்விழு) and feed them a ghoul's food (பேயமுது). Both name the deception and place the danger in the lover's lack of discernment, the song turning the Kural's spirit into a ghoulish meal.

The Kural compares the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழிய). The song calls the body a mean nest (புன்கூடு) where the life dwells, with fierce Death already packed inside it (பொங்காவெங் கூற்றம் பொதிதரு), and asks for the feet before that life is taken. The nest image is shared; the song adds that Death lives in the nest from the start.

The Kural asks whether the life, lodging in the body as in a shelter (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு), has found no home of its own (புக்கில்). The song pictures the body as a hut (குரம்பை) carried from town to town and asks to drive out the five senses and enter the house and rejoice (வீட்டிற் புகுந்திருந்து மகிழ்வேனோ), where வீடு is also release. The song names the home the Kural says the life has not yet found.

Both set vultures on the body to answer its admirers: the Naladiyar shows them tearing at the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 679 calls the living body the hut they will feed on and makes it the reason to stop carrying it from town to town.

Both picture old age with speech failing, teeth gone and a staff in hand. The Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire; in 68 the women laugh at him, and the poet turns the scene into a prayer for Murugan to come at the hour of death.

The Kural says craving is the seed that brings unceasing birth to all beings (அவாஎன்ப ... தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The song says that through the women's eyes, breasts and waist the poet, without support, takes body after body (அநேகம் காயம்) and asks when that time will end. The song applies the Kural's general rule to the poet's own desire for women.
Both warn that the courtesan's sweet words serve her wish for wealth; 683 shows the words in action, the talk of old intimacy leading to the house where the wealth is plundered.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the hand, then lies down like a balking ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). The song's women give their lips while they plunder the wealth (கனிவாய் அதரந்தரு நாளிலே பொருள் சூறைகள் கொண்டு), then fall silent and pick quarrels (மோனமாய் ... சண்டைகள்). Both give the same three-step cycle of sweetness, taking and turning away.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). The song asks not to fall into the women's snare (கண்ணியில் விழாமல்) but to be held within the snare of knowledge of the feet (பதஞான கண்ணியிலுளாக). Both answer a binding with a better binding rather than with none.

The Naladiyar says those who take a worthless woman's love as their own will be laughed at by many (பெறுபவே தாமாம் பலரால் நகை). The poet, sunk in love-making, asks for knowledge before the world mocks him every way (உலகோர்கள் ... நகைகள் கூறி) as a madman reciting Kama's arts. Both make public laughter the end of infatuation; the song turns it into the reason to seek knowledge now.

689 asks whether he too must die (மடிவேனோ), stopped by eyes that rise like spears (அயிலொத்தெழும் இருவிழி), nectar speech and mountain breasts. Naladiyar 44 refuses that very comparison, calling those who liken eyes to a spear (வேல்) blind, petty men, and sees the eye as a palm fruit scooped out once its water is drained (நுங்குசூன் றிட்டன்ன). On the literal reading they disagree about what a woman's eye is: a killing weapon to the poet, a hollow socket to the ascetic, who walks on where the poet is stopped.
The Kural holds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking; 69 confesses a tongue put to exactly that use, poems of praise carried from one patron's door to another.

692 asks whether he should follow the gait of the price-women (விலைமானார்) and fall dazed into the pit called desire (மோகம் என்ற படுகுழியிலே மயங்கி விழலாமோ). Kural 919 makes the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும்). Both picture the courtesan's trade as a hole a man sinks into; the Kural names the sinker base, the song asks it of the poet himself.

693, in a woman's voice, asks not to waste each night seeking the palmyra horse (வனிதை மடல் நாடி நித்த நலியாதே) but that Murugan come to her bed. Kural 1136 is the lover who even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) thinks of riding the madal. The pairing shows the Thiruppugazh giving the madal, a man's resort in the Kural, to a girl who longs for the god.

695 sets the poet's wandering with the worldly (உலகோரொடு திரிவேன்) against being joined to the devotees who worship (உன் அடியாராய் வழிபாடுறுவாரொடு), and asks for that day. Kural 460 says there is no greater help than good company and nothing brings more affliction than bad company (நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை). The song applies the Kural's rule on company to devotion, the good company being the devotees.

The Naladiyar says learning has no shore and the learner's days are few, so one should choose what is fit, like the bird drinking the milk from the water. 70 asks that before the body ages in seeking endless crores of books (நூல் அனந்த கோடி தேடி) he be given the books of knowledge in which the Lord is mingled (நீ கலந்துள ஞான நூல்). Both set limited life against unlimited books; 70 names the choice as the jnana books.

Both set marriage and the household inside the march to the burning ground: the Naladiyar mocks the man who sees the corpse carried yet marries and thinks there is joy here, and 700 lists embracing women and bearing the household's burden between crawling and burning.

700 runs a life in plural past verbs, பிறந்தனர் கிடந்தனர் இருந்தனர் தவழ்ந்தனர் நடந்தனர், on to இறந்தனர் and the burning. Naladiyar 29 compresses a death into the report நின்றான் இருந்தான் கிடந்தான் ... சென்றான். Both tell a life as a run of verbs of posture to show how fast it passes; the Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good at once (இன்னினியே), 700 asks to end the birth itself.

701 lists the price-women's charms one by one, among them the voice like the yazh (யாழ்தரு கீத மென்குரல்), and ends in their feigned feelings (விலைமாதர் பாவகங்கள்) in which he sinks. Kural 911 says the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth and not love bring harm. The song spreads into a catalogue the charm the Kural names in one item, and both rest on the pretence.

702 tells the courtesan's cycle: fixing the price, the bed, then snatching the wealth (உள பொருள் பறித்து), quarrelling and beating the man away (கலகமிட்டு அவர் அகல அடித்தபின்). Naladiyar 377 has the same turn: she licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from his hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks like a buffalo, and the man who thought her love his is laughed at. 702 adds what the Naladiyar leaves out, the new man taken up with new stories.

705 names among the girl's torments the flute with its seven-note holes (ஏழோசைத் தொளையாலே), beside Kama's fragrant arrows. Kural 1228 calls the herdsman's flute a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the flute's music into a weapon against the lovesick; in 705 the bamboo (வேய்) is named in a run of rhyming words that is hard to divide.

706 asks Murugan to come lest the girl perish from the sea's roar, the slander the women speak each day (நாளும் வஞ்சியர் உற்று உரைக்கும் வசை) and the moon that burns like poison. Kural 1147 says the town's gossip (ஊரவர் கௌவை) is the manure on which this sickness grows. Both make gossip feed the love-sickness rather than shame it away; the song can only ask the god to end it by coming.
The Kural says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; 707 lists those who forget the good done them among the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, giving that 'no escape' a place.
Both condemn the man who begrudges another's giving: the Kural says his kin will be left without food or clothing, and 707 puts him among those who fall into Yama's pit.

710 shows the whole performance of feigned infatuation (மாமயல் உடைத்தார் போலவும்): messengers by the hundred, the embrace, betel bitten halfway, all to snatch the man's wealth (நீள்பொருள் பறிப்பார்). Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்), like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The Kural judges the embrace; the song shows the staging that makes it false.

715 lists the gross body as skin, bone, pus, nerves, rheum and phlegm rolled into a lump (தோல் எலும்பு சீ நரம்பு பீளை ... கோழை), which the poet carries and wastes in. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews and skin (குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும்) and asks which of them is the woman. The same inventory of the body cures desire for another's body in the Naladiyar and turns the poet against his own body in 715.

Both make the Lord's feet the way across the sea of births: the Kural says only those who join his feet swim it, and 718 calls the twin lotus feet a raft (புணை) to be grasped instead of the leaking body.

718 calls the body a hut of the senses made of skin and holes from which blood drains (குருதி வடி தொளைத் தொக்கு இந்த்ரியக் குரம்பை) and asks not to take it as everything. Naladiyar 42 sees the same body as full of holes under a skin covering (தோல்போர்வை மேலும் தொளைபலவாய்) that hides its falsity. Both make skin and openings the body's truth; the Naladiyar asks for a changed view, the song for the feet as a raft away from it.

The Kural calls the petty knowledge that takes the impermanent for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்) the lowest. 72 opens with that error made personal, taking the impermanent thing for oneself (நிலையாப் பொருளை உடலாக் கருதி), and follows it with what results: wasted days, deafness, blindness and the bed of filth.

720 asks to leave house, sons, wealth and town together with the delusion of 'I and mine' (யானெனதென்று) and be taken into the expanse of silence. Kural 346 says one who cuts the pride of saying I and mine (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. The song uses the Kural's very pair and names what replaces it: மோன தடம்.

721 says the vel that crushed the demons was thrown so that the poet's two deeds might turn to dust (அடியேன் இருவினை தூள்பட அயில் ஏவிய). Kural 5 says both deeds (இருவினையும்) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise. The song turns the Kural's general promise into a weapon: the same இருவினை are not merely kept off but shattered by Murugan's vel.

722 begins by asking to stop babbling scriptures noisily (கலகலெனச் சில கலைகள் பிதற்றுவது) without saying even a little about Murugan. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the pure one's feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). Both judge learning by whether it turns to the Lord; the song makes it the first thing to renounce, before hell and rebirth.

Both see the courtesan's sweetness as aimed at a man's money: the Kural warns that such women's sweet words bring harm, and 723 shows the flattery on the bed with the hand already reaching for the purse.

723 counts among its sufferings that the world says 'chi, chi' (உலகத்தவர் சிச்சியெனத் திரி) at the man who trades in courtesans. Naladiyar 377 says those who think a courtesan's love their own, while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both name public contempt, not only lost money, as the price.

727 names the women as harlots trading love for money (வேசி என்பவர், காதலின் பொருள் மேவின) and asks instead to worship desiring the good path to Siva's bliss (சிவபோக நல் நூல் நெறி). Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென் பார்) do not embrace such women. Both set the courtesan's bed against the path, and the song names that path as Siva's bliss.

728 asks whether, though vowed as a hereditary servant, his life must swing like the beam of a balance (துலையலை மாறு போலுயிர் சுழல்வேனோ) between that vow and the women. Kural 118 praises the worthy for being like a balance that levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல்). The same instrument is the Kural's figure of steadiness and the song's figure of a soul that cannot settle.

729 says the women are as if Death himself had put on a woman's festive form to seize young men's lives (உயர் காலன் பெண் தனக்கு உள கோலாகலம்). In Kural 1083 the lover says he never knew Death before and now knows it, in a woman's grace and warring eyes (கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன் பெண்டகையால்). The Kural's lover's hyperbole becomes in the song a literal warning, with Death as the one in disguise.
The Kural calls the embrace of deceiving women an அணங்கு, a possessing spirit; 73 gives the deceit a literal form, the love-pellets and the charm hidden in the betel.

Both use the courtesan's being common to all as the charge: the Kural's women 'whose goodness belongs to everyone' (பொதுநலத்தார்) and 730's பொதுவிகள். The Kural says the wise don't plunge in; 730 is the confession of one who did.

730 calls the women plunderers who sing their love to the measure of the money (பொருளளவு ஆசைப் பாடிகள்) and belong to all. Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends with the oil (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure the love exactly by the coin; the Naladiyar adds the image of the lamp going out.
The Kural's women weigh the profit and then speak of virtue; 731's women have minds set on the coin and lying speech. Both make the calculation the mark of the courtesan.

In 732 the courtesan flatters the client that if one looks for his equal even Kadamban, Murugan, falls short (ஒப்பார் உனக்கீடு பார்க்கிற் கடம்பன் மட்டோ). Naladiyar 373 says such women would send away even the red-eyed Mal whom the gods worship if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன் றில்லாரை). The Naladiyar states the hidden condition of the flattery: the client is a god only while he pays.

733 lists the women's eyes as sharper than a spear (பார்வையாமிகு கூரயில்) among the parts that draw the poet into infatuation, and asks to be freed of it. Naladiyar 44 refuses those who call eyes lilies, carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேலென்று) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. The song keeps the poets' simile and prays against its pull; the Naladiyar dismantles the simile itself.

738 asks that, in the company of those who think of Murugan (உனை நினைபவர் துணைகொள), he not be lost in the sea of seven births (எழு பிறவியெனு உவரியினிடை கெடாது). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song keeps the sea and adds the devotees' company as the means of crossing.

In 739 the lover asks whether the night as long as an aeon (ஊழி இரவு) must be spent burned by the moon, Kama's bow and the beating sea. Kural 1169 says these long nights (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel man himself. Both make the lengthened night the separated lover's torment; the song addresses it to Murugan.

The Kural calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that true knowledge removes by seeing the true thing. 74 places the courtesans within that larger condition, the darkness of defiled birth and its bonds (பங்கமேவும் பிறப்பு அந்தகாரம் ... பந்தபாசம்), and asks for the feet as the way out.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any scheme to avert it; 742 cites the same elders' word and grants it (தகவாம் அது), yet asks for the Lord's grace to free him from what fate brings. Not a tension, since the poet does not deny the saying: grace is set beside fate as the one thing no human scheme is.

In 743 the speaker says that by the evening, Kama's arrows, the cuckoo and the fire-pouring moon her life grows faint (ஆவிதளர்வுற்று வாடும்). Kural 1221 tells the evening it is not evening but the hour that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). Both make the evening hour a threat to the lover's life itself.

745 asks Murugan to come and make the Upanishad clear before his heart's thought perishes (என்னெஞ்சு தான் நினைவு அழியாமுன்). Kural 335 says good deeds must be rushed to before the hiccup stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set a deadline at death's first sign: the Kural for good deeds, the song for receiving teaching.

745 lists the body as fat, blood, nerves, flesh, gut, bone and skin packed row on row (நிணமொடு குருதி நரம்பு ... தசைகுடல் ... எலும்பு தோல்). Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews and skin and asks which of these is the woman. The same anatomy serves the Naladiyar against desire and the song as the frame of the poet's confession.

Both see the body as a vessel of filth with nine openings; the Naladiyar uses it to mock the man who praises a woman's arms, 745 to confess the poet's own frame and ask, before thought fails, for teaching.

748 confesses that, not reckoning that life may end in a moment (மாத்திரை யாகிலும் ... வாழ்க்கையை நீடென மதியாமல்), he flattered fools as if each were Vishnu to get gold. Naladiyar 302 asks whether it is wrong to go hungry rather than eat by degrading deeds, since death and rebirth take only the instant of a blink (விழித்து இமைக்கும் மாத்திரை). Both set the brevity of life against self-abasement for a living; the song is the confession of the man the quatrain warns.

749 pictures the poet, after singing fine Tamil to unworthy patrons, lying on the fire of poverty and writhing like a long worm (வறுமையாகிய தீயின்மேல் கிடந்து நெளியும் நீள்புழு). Kural 1049 says one may even sleep in fire, but in poverty one cannot close the eyes at all (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள் யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). Both measure poverty against lying in fire; the couplet rates poverty the worse, and the song makes poverty itself the fire.
The Kural says nothing is more shameful to the tongue than begging; 749 confesses a tongue spent praising unworthy men and a life left in poverty.

750 dwells on the women's voices, like the yaazh, the parrot and the cuckoo, and calls them women with a price who strip wealth from those who kiss them (விலைமாதர் ... பொருள் பறிப்பார்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love bring a man harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The song lavishes on the sweetness of the voice what the couplet says is its danger.
Both tie the courtesan's favour to money: the Naladiyar says a rich oil-presser is sugar to her, 750 that she strips of wealth the men she kisses.
Both picture old age by faltering steps, the staff and fallen teeth; the Naladiyar faults the old man still clinging to desire, 752 asks to be freed from the birth that brings such an end.

752 ends its portrait of old age, staff in hand, with the old man left standing outside (வெளிநிற்கும் விதம்). Naladiyar 326 says one who did no good before old age will be told 'sit outside, go' in his own house even by the maidservant (புறத்திரு போகு என்னும் இன்னாச்சொல்). Both see old age as being put out of one's own house; the quatrain draws a lesson to do good early, while the song asks to be freed from the birth that leads there.
The Naladiyar says the harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; 757 shows the moment, the woman leaving the bed because the cash and cloth are not enough.

757 quotes the women's welcome and then shows them, just before bed, finding the cash and cloth not enough and going off in spite (காசு ஆடை வாவியும் போதாமை தீமை கொண்டே போம்). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover but, there being no gold, showed a pain in her feet and would not come on (காணம் இன்மையான் ... கால் கால்நோய் காட்டி). Both catch the moment when the money falls short and the promised love is withdrawn on a pretext.

758 describes women who melt the heart by arts of stealth, cruelly snatch what a man had saved (முன் கருதி வைத்த வைப்பவை ... தறுகணில் பறித்து) and then embrace him. Naladiyar 377 says the woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from his hand, and then lies down like a balking ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர் கைப்பொருள் கொண்டு). Both show tenderness used as the means of taking a man's money.

759 says the women's glance is spear, sword, Kama's arrows and the messenger Death sends (நமன் விடு தூதும்). Kural 1083 has the lover say he never knew what Death was and now knows it: a woman's large, warring eyes (பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென்பதனை இனி அறிந்தேன்). Both make the woman's eye Death; the couplet says it in wonder, the song in warning against women who want money.
The Kural names double-minded women with liquor and gambling as the company of those whom fortune has left; 761 calls the women குடிகேடிகள், ruiners of families.

761 calls the women changers who join men in many ways and snatch their money (பணம் எத்தப் பறிகாரிகள் மாறிகள் விதம் எத்தக் கொடு மேவிகள்). Naladiyar 375 likens them to the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish (மலங்கன்ன செய்கை மகளிர்), embraced by the dull-witted. Both charge the women with double dealing; the quatrain gives it an image, the song a list of names.
The Naladiyar says courtesans would bow to Mal himself yet send away a man with nothing in his hand; 763 shows them handing the ruined man a begging bowl and staff.

763 says the women, once the gold is gone, hand a man the begging bowl and staff, say 'go', and even give poison (கஞ்சுளியும் தடியும் ஈந்து போ என நஞ்சை இடும்). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and a rich oil-presser sugar (காணம் இலாதார் கடுவனையர் ... அக்காரம் அன்னார்). Poison belongs to the same reckoning in both: the moneyless man is poison to them in the quatrain, and in the song they give him poison.

The lovesick girl of 764 lists the evening's attackers, among them அசைவன விடைமணி, the swinging bells of the bulls coming home. Kural 1228 makes the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) the envoy of the burning evening and a killing weapon (கொல்லும் படை). In both a pastoral sound of homecoming cattle, harmless in itself, becomes an arm of the evening against the parted woman.

767 describes women who run many trades (பல வாணிபம்), will not give a moment without money (பணமே ஒரு காசு இடை செய்யார) and are deceivers (சற்பனை காரர்). Kural 913 calls the embrace of பொருட்பெண்டிர், women for wealth, a பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், a false embrace. Both make the courtesan's love a trade and its show a falsehood; the poet adds that he is the sinner caught in it and asks how to reach the shore.

The Kural names them பொருட்பெண்டிர், women of wealth, whose false embrace is like a hired man clasping a stranger's corpse in a dark room. 77 uses the same name, பொருளின் மகளிர், after a full description of the embrace, and asks whether he will not give up their 'love' (அன்புப் பண்பு); the description the Kural refuses, 77 gives in full before refusing it.

Kural 920 names double-minded women, drink and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்). 770 asks that the courtesans and the cruel poverty (கொடு மிடிமை) both leave him, poverty being what the women's thefts have left. The Kural puts loss of fortune before the company; the song shows the company producing the poverty.

In 770 the women flare up if no gold is given now (செம்பொன் இங்கினி இலையெனில் மிகுதியும் முனிவாகி) and quarrel that a month has passed without a gift. In Naladiyar 372 the woman who swore to leap from the peak with her lover holds back at the edge, showing a pain in her feet, because he has no money (காணம் இன்மையான்). Both show the courtesan's love ending at the empty purse, one in open anger, the other in a feigned excuse.

771 lists Murugan's grace, victory, குணம் and his love for Valli and closes with the vow மறவேனே, I will not forget. In Kural 1125 the lover says he would recall the woman's குணம் if he ever forgot, but he does not know how to forget (மறப்பறியேன்). The devotee's vow and the lover's boast use the same claim, unbroken remembrance of the beloved's qualities.

773 asks Murugan to see how he stands ashamed (வெட்கி நிற்பது) after singing rich verses to rubbish men, calling them wish-trees (கற்பதாரு) and suns of the three worlds. Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு) than asking, even water for a cow. The song shows the degradation the Kural names: the tongue's shame lies not only in asking but in the flattery the asking requires.

The Naladiyar's kings who rode elephants under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and spoken of as dead; 774 gives the same royal splendour, walls, singers and chowries, and asks only whether it ends as a handful of ash.

776 names the women for a price (விலைமாதர்) among other insults நரகச் சிற்சாடிப் பீடிகள், pits of hell. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு, hell or mire, in which worthless men sink. Both make the courtesan herself the hell, not merely a road to it.

Among the habits of the women in 778 is இருநிதி இலரைத் தூர நீக்கவும், sending far away those without wealth. Naladiyar 373 says such women would send away even red-eyed Mal, worshipped by the gods, if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). The same dismissal of the moneyless, which the Naladiyar sharpens by making the visitor a god.

Both make a woman's eyes a weapon: the Kural's eyes eat the life of those who see them and are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentleness; 78's eye-corners are whetted as weapon upon weapon (படையம் படையென அந்திக்கும் கண்கடை). The Kural's lover is held in wonder; 78 names the same look the source of his bewilderment (மறுகிடு மருளன்) and asks for grace.

In 781 the courtesans speak for themselves: வாரும் முற்பணம் தாரும் இட்டமென, come, give the money first, then as you please. Kural 912 describes women who weigh the gain first (பயன்தூக்கி) and then speak of their good nature, and tells the man to weigh them in turn. The song gives in their own words the order the Kural describes: payment first, pleasantness after.

The Naladiyar's vultures tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; 785 makes the fallen body a packed meal that vultures and crows greet as their food, the end that adorning it as if it were Kama ignores.

789 asks not to wander asking who on this earth gives generously (த்யாகம் ஈபவர் யாரென்று அலையாதே). Naladiyar 306 asks why anyone, with a mind racked by desire, should go begging of strangers (ஏதிலவரை இரவு) when poverty can be ended by asking of oneself. Both refuse the round of patrons; the Naladiyar's cure is inward consent to hardship, the song's is the feet.

791 sets two seas side by side: the life whirling in the waves of the sea (வாரிதி அலையூடே சுழலும் எனதுயிர்) and the ocean of silent supreme bliss (மவுன பரமசுக ... உததி) into which it asks to sink. Kural 10 has the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) that only those who reach the Lord's feet can swim. The Kural's way out of the sea is to cross it; the song's is to sink into another sea.

792 counts among its wasted years having learned useless arts without grasping a little of their meaning (சவலைக் கலை கற்று அதனிற் பொருள் சற்று அறியாதே). Naladiyar 135 gives the reason this is ruinous: learning has no shore and the learner's days are few (கல்வி கரையில கற்பவர் நாள்சில), so one must choose like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water. The quatrain supplies the rule whose breach 792 confesses.

796 confesses seeking many useless arts without grasping the one fruit (பலசவலைக் கலைதேடி ஒருபயனைத் தெளியாது) and asks, before death, to seek the lotus feet. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not worship the good feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both name the feet as the one fruit (பயன்) that learning exists for; the song is the Kural's question answered as a confession.
The Naladiyar's harlots' love ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends with the oil; 797 shows the same end acted out, the man twisted round, kicked and abused once his wealth is gone.

797 shows the courtesan coaxing with sweet words until the money reaches her, then, when the wealth ends, twisting round to kick and abuse (பொருள்தீரின் முறுக்கியே உதை கொடு வசை உரைதரு). Naladiyar 377 has her lick like a wild cow, take the wealth from his hands, then balk like a stubborn ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி ... சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). Both turn on the same reversal, fondness while the wealth is in hand and a physical turning away after it.

798, in a girl's voice, asks Murugan to send his kadamba garland so that the mother who raised her will not speak blame (வளர்த்த தாய் தமர் வசையது மொழியாதே) and the neighbours will not slander her (அயலவர் பழியாதே). Kural 1147 names the same two voices as what feeds the lovesickness: the town's gossip its manure and the mother's word its water (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The song asks the god to stop exactly what in the Kural makes the sickness grow.

799 heaps names on the courtesans, among them women with weeping hearts (அழு மனத்திகள்) and those who take young men's wealth (இளைஞர்கள் பொருள் பறித்த). Naladiyar 372 tells one such scene: the woman who vowed to leap from the peak with him, finding he had no gold, showed a pain in her feet and wept (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டிக் கலுழ்ந்து). The quatrain gives the story behind the poet's one-word epithet for tears used as a feint.

The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring ruin. 80 gives the sweet words, the cuckoo voice saying 'come home' (வாரும் வீடே), and their show of love on the bed, 'as if loving' (அன்புளார் போல்), and asks whether union with them is fitting.

807 describes women who play the loving true form to everyone (எவரையும் அன்புடை மெய்க் கோலராக) and take the coins the day is worth, and asks to sing Murugan and enter release instead of falling into their net. Kural 915 says those whose knowledge is refined will not touch the base charms of women whose goodness is common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). The song's 'with everyone' is the Kural's பொதுநலம, and both set understanding or devotion as what keeps a man out.

Both use kings to show impermanence: the Naladiyar's commanders on elephants under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn, and 812's lords of elephant armies and conquered directions end as a handful of ash; 812 adds that they never thought to worship.

814 asks whether, caught in the courtesans' net, he will fade like an elephant fallen into a pit (வலைபட்டு உழைத்து குழி உற்ற அத்தியென மங்குவேனா). Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). Both picture the man not as seduced but as sunk in a hole he cannot climb out of.

Both name the body's nine openings and the filth inside a skin covering: the Naladiyar's fool praises a pot that seeps from nine holes, and 815 calls the body a hut with nine gates, its filth sloshing under the skin.

816 asks whether it is right that the poet's days go in vain (நாயேன் வாணாள் வீணே போகத் தகுமோ) without singing the vel or falling at the feet. Kural 38 says that letting no day fall away unused (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) by doing good blocks the road of one's days (வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்). The song takes the Kural's measure of a life by its days and confesses the opposite case, with praise of Murugan as the good the days lacked.

817, in a lovesick girl's voice, says her mother has turned against her (மாதா மாறானாள்) and the town's slander is heard (கோளே கேள்), while the north wind cuts like a saw. Kural 1147 says this sickness grows with the town's talk as manure and the mother's word as water (ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). Both set the same pair, town gossip and the mother's anger, around the parted girl's longing; the Kural states plainly that they feed it.

The Kural says that one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான்) enters a world above the gods'. The song asks that the 'I' break (யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு) and gives a method for it, breath and gaze held and body, speech and heart made one (காயமும் நாவும் நெஞ்சும் ஓர்வழியாக), turning the Kural's renunciation into a yogic practice.

820 says the women's long, proud eyes (மதர்விழி) are nets, and that they come so that men's lifetimes end (மனிதர் வாணாள் அடங்க வருவார்). Kural 1083 says the man never knew what Death was and now knows it: a woman's grace with large, warring eyes (கூற்றென்பதனை இனியறிந்தேன் ... பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both make the woman's eye a form of Death; the Kural speaks in the lover's wonder, the song in the penitent's fear.

The Kural defines justice as investigating and showing favour to no one; the praise in 821 tells of the Chola king who heard the cow's bell and drove the chariot over his own son, the extreme case of 'no one' including one's own child.

822 questions a woman's speech, eyes and face in a string of alternatives (மொழி பாலோ தேனோ, விழி வேலோ கோலோ, முகம் பானோ நிலவோ). Kural 1081 has the lover ask whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman (அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ ... மாதர்கொல்), his heart reeling. The song uses the Kural's form of bewildered questions, then reuses the same form for the soul's questions about the inner light.

825 describes the price-women (விலைமகள்) who befriend a man struck speechless to seize all his wealth and think others' wealth their own. Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man, out of love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song acts out the Kural's distinction between love and wealth in a scene of seizure.

826's courtesans spread their hands and say 'put down everything in your hand' (கையில் உற்ற பொருட்கள் யாவையும் வை எனக் கை விரிக்கும்). Naladiyar 373 says that even Vishnu, if he had nothing in his hand to give (தம் கைக்குக் கொடுப்பது ஒன்றில்லாரை), would be sent away by them with folded hands. Both make the hand the measure of welcome: the song shows the open hand demanding, the Naladiyar the folded hand dismissing.

827 confesses flattering drunken misers to end the misery of poverty (என் பாடு கூறிடும் மிடி தீர) before clinging to Murugan's feet. Kural 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness that thinks to end poverty's misery by begging (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம் என்னும் வன்மை). The song is the Kural's case told from inside: the begging poem quoted, then repented.

The Kural begs every beggar not to beg from those who hide what they have; 827 is the confession of a poet who did just that, flattering misers to end his poverty, and turns to the Lord's feet instead.

829 says that even if he wanders thirsting for union with dancing women (கலவி தாகம் உண்டு உழல்கினும்) he will not forget the feet. Naladiyar 378 says those who mean to reach the right path will not embrace such women's breasts (தடமுலை சேராரே செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென் பார்). On the reading that 829 lets desire and devotion run together, the two disagree about whether the path survives the embrace.

831 asks whether, quarrelling and embracing women again and again, he will wander having given up penance (தவம் அற்க விடுத்து உழல்வேனோ). Kural 266 says those who do tavam do their own work and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). The song places the poet on the Kural's wrong side, with the doubled verbs (சருவிச் சருவித் தழுவித் தழுவி) showing the futile repetition.

832 says the poet grieves as his five senses run (ஓங்கும் ஐம்புலன் ஓட) after pleasure and asks Murugan to rule him by speaking Om. Kural 24 says one who guards the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the higher world. Where the Kural's goad is the man's own firmness, the song looks for it outside, in the guru's pranava.

833 says that craving union with women (கலவிக்குள் உளம் நச்சி) he lost his wealth and fell into poverty and ruin (வளமற்று மிடிபட்டு மடிபட்டு). Kural 920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those Fortune has left (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). The song tells as a sequence what the Kural states as a sign: desire first, then the loss of திரு.

834 questions the women's features in pairs of alternatives, among them whether their eyes are fish or vel (அக்கண் இணைக்கு இணை சேலோ வேலோ). Kural 1085 asks of a girl's look whether it is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both use the same questioning form for the eye, with a weapon among the answers; the song makes the questions part of the craving it asks to be freed from.

836 calls the price-women deceivers even while they lie on the bed (அணைமீதில் துயில் பொழுதே தெட்டிகள்). Kural 913 says the false embrace of women of wealth (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both locate the deceit in the embrace itself, the place where trust would be greatest; the Kural gives it its grim image.

838 calls the poet a fool who rejoices that house, wife, kin and abundant wealth are permanent (மனை துணைவியர் தமர் பொருள் பெருத்த வாழ்விது சதமென மகிழ்வுறும் அசட்டன்). Kural 331 calls the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for what lasts (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும் புல்லறிவாண்மை) the lowest. The song's அசட்டன் is the Kural's புல்லறிவு, named in household terms.

838 speaks of common women who, though the young man who joined them first is still there, go to another if they find more wealth (வேறொரு பெயர் தமதிடமது துவட்சியே பெறில் அவருடன் மருவிடு). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser with earned wealth is sugar. Both say the measure of such love is wealth alone; the song's reading of its opening lines is tentative.

Both picture the courtesan whose mind is with another man while she embraces this one; the Naladiyar marvels that men still don't see it, and 838 says she leaves the lover of many days as soon as another brings more wealth.

839 confesses not having thought of the Lord as a companion (துணை) in his karmic bond, disease and lust, and so wandering daily in griefs, and asks for thought of the red feet. Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety cannot be removed except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது). The song is the Kural's claim seen from the side of one who has not yet reached the feet.

841 asks whether, plunging into a sea of pleasure, giving up all conduct and losing the tapas that brings clarity (சீலம் அனைத்தும் ஒழிந்து ... தேறு தவத்தை இழந்து), he must wander. Naladiyar 57 calls blessed those who keep their vows (விரதங்கள்) and guard good conduct (நல்லொழுக்கம்) when unbearable troubles come to break them. The Naladiyar fears pain as what breaks vows; the song confesses that pleasure did it.

842 asks that before his body falls into Death's tongue like a frog into a snake's mouth (காலனது நா அரவ வாயிலிடு தேரையென) he be granted to say once 'Muruga Vel' among devotees. Kural 335 says good deeds must be done at once, before the hiccup comes and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both set a deadline at the tongue; the song's one good deed is a single utterance of the name.

843 has the soul enter and live in the body's house (வீடு புகுந்திட்டு அதில் மேவி) until it becomes a corpse. Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has not found a home of its own. Both make the body a house the soul only occupies; the Kural's question about a lasting home is the one the song's ending (சடமாமோ) leaves open.

844 asks whether Murugan will now give his holy feet so that the poet may cross the great sea of birth (கருப்பெருங் கடலது கடக்க உன் திருவடிகளைத் தரும்). Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்) and others cannot. The song's plea uses the Kural's image and its condition, the feet, almost word for word.

845 asks for grace so that the memory of a night of union (நினைவு நெஞ்சினின்று அற) and the longing to see those faces leave his heart. Kural 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because even remembering it (உள்ளினும்) gives a joy that does not end. On the reading that both speak of the same remembered union, the Kural prizes the memory as joy and the song asks for it to be erased as bondage.
The Naladiyar says the courtesan's love ends when the man's money ends; 846 goes further, that no amount, thousands of thousands of gold coins, ever satisfies her.

847 pictures the round of births as mothers multiplying: one mother, two mothers, many crores of them (ஒருதாய் இருதாய் பலகோடியதாய்), this one becoming that one. Naladiyar 15 has each mother leave to seek her own mother, so that the world goes on mother-seeking-mother (தாய்த்தாய்க்கொண்டு ஏகும்). Both make the chain of mothers the figure of endless birth; the Naladiyar reads it as pitiable impermanence, while the song asks to break it by saying 'Muruga' once.

848 confesses that, to end his poverty, he went to cruel men of the earth (கடுத்த துற்சன மகாதகர்) and set them in verse as a kalpaka king and an Arjuna, and now asks not to be worn out by that fancy. Naladiyar 301 asks whether men of clear understanding (தெருண்ட அறிவினவர்) would follow the self-deluded rich who think the poor live only through them. The song is the confession of one who did what the Naladiyar says the clear-minded will not do, and it adds the false praise as the price of following.

849 calls the poet a low man who will not hear the counsel told him (உரைத்த புத்திகள் கேளா நீசன்) and a fool who does not grasp the true thing in his own mind (உளத்தில் மெய்ப்பொருள் ஓரா மூடன்). Kural 848 describes the man who neither does what he is told nor understands for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான்), whose life is a disease until it departs. The song applies the Kural's double failure to itself, and asks for the feet so that the old sayings become felt knowledge.

The Kural's lover says blue lilies, if they could see, would hang their heads, saying they cannot match her eyes (குவளை கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்). The song's blazon uses the same conceit, eyes that cast shame on arrow, carp, bee and lotus (கணை அம் கயல் வண்டு புண்டரிகங்களையும் பழி சிந்து பார்வை), but the whole catalogue ends in the question whether to trust these deceivers (செயல் வஞ்சரை நம்புவேனோ): the Kural's praise is turned into evidence against the women.

850 says the street women's first thought is 'is there money?' (பணம் உண்டென தவலம்படு நினைவு), and that their sweet talk changes the minds and deeds of those who see them. Kural 912 tells the reader to weigh the women who weigh the profit and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்), and keep away. Both put the reckoning of gain before the sweet speech; the song adds that the women's maya is a sorrow only the Lord can end.

The Kural says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). The song calls the poet's own trade, begging by singing Tamil (இசைக்கும் செந்தமிழ்க் கொண்டு அங்கு இரக்கும் புன்தொழில்), base, and asks for its disgrace to end: the tongue that sings Tamil is the tongue the Kural says begging shames.

862 says the poet's life is caught in the net of a union he enjoys even in dreams (கனவிலும் நுகர்தரு கலவியின் வலையிடை) and is perishing there (உயிர் தட்டுப்பட்டு அழிகின்றதோ). Kural 1213 has the woman say her life lasts because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace when she is awake (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). The same dream-union that keeps the Kural's lover alive is, for the song, the net in which life is lost.

The Kural names God only as the one of eight qualities, whose feet the head must bow to; 863 takes the same epithet, எண்குணமுற்றோன், and places that Lord dancing in a hall within, to be seen in yogic vision.

866 reduces the dancing women to their soiled skin (பங்கமார் தொக்கு) and asks not to sink in it but to win the Lord's love through Tamil. Naladiyar 42 says the body is handsome only through the skin that covers its falsity (தோல்போர்வை ... பொய்ம்மறைக்கும்) and should be seen as a bag turned inside out. Both name the skin as the whole of the attraction; the Naladiyar argues it, the song states it in two words and turns to song.

868 pictures old age: black hair whitening, teeth falling, the back bent and a stick shaking in the hand (ஒர் தடி கை நடுங்கப் பிடித்திடும்), and asks when he will reach the feet. Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), renounced in childhood, while those who delighted in youth will rise painfully leaning on a staff (கோல் ஊன்றி). Both make the grey hair and the staff the end that should turn one early; the Naladiyar warns, the song speaks from inside that end.

Both picture old age with failing speech, lost teeth and a staff; the Naladiyar faults the old man who still stays in the house eyeing desire, while 868 adds the household's scorn and asks for the feet that end birth.

869 describes the body of phlegm, guts and rheum that falls to dust, and asks to be freed from cherishing it with earrings, ornaments and clothes (கடுக்கனும் சில பூடணம் ஆடைகள்). Naladiyar 43 asks whether chewing spices, filling the head with flowers and putting on a false finery (பொய்க்கோலம்) can remove the foulness the great saw and abandoned. Both set adornment against the body's filth as useless; the song asks for Sivayoga and jnana to end the cherishing.

The Kural counts the man who heaps up wealth and does not use it as already dead; 873 puts those who hoarded and buried without giving (ஈயாது தேடிப் புதைத்த) among the wicked bound for the lowest births. Both condemn wealth withheld, the Kural as a life wasted, 873 as a sin with a sequel.

873 ends its list of the wicked with those who hoard and bury wealth without giving (ஈயாது தேடிப் புதைத்த துட்டர்கள்) and says they will wander in the lowest births, like dogs (கடைப்பிறப்பினில் உழல்வாரே). Kural 1002 says the delusion of clinging without giving (ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்) brings an unworthy birth (மாணாப் பிறப்பு). Both name the same fault and the same punishment, a low next birth for the one who does not give.

875 praises Murugan as the hero who confounds and cuts down the fools who tell lies, heap up wealth and frighten simple people to make their living (அபகடம் உரைத்து அத்தம் மெத்தப் படைத்து உலகில் எளியரை மருட்டி). Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears (அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம்). The Kural states the law that such wealth departs; the song gives its enforcement to the Lord, who strikes the deceivers themselves.

The Kural's lover asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe, and finds it all three; 876 asks the same question through a dozen guesses, Death (மறலி) and the deer (மான்) among them. The Kural's doubt is a lover's wonder; in 876 it ends by calling such women demons to be avoided.

876 runs through the stock likenesses of a woman's eyes, the vel (வடிவேலோ), the red lily (செங்கழுநீரோ), the kayal and kendai fish, and asks whether kinship with women whose eyes plunder can be. Naladiyar 44 names the same set, lily, darting carp and spear (குவளை பொருகயல் வேல்), only to refuse them: an eye is a scooped-out palm fruit (நுங்கு சூன்றிட்டன்ன). Both reject the woman's eye; the Naladiyar strips the simile away, while 876 keeps every simile and reads each one as a weapon.

877 asks Murugan to be angry with him like a mother and speak one teaching (கோபித்துத் தாயென நீ ஒரு போதத்தைப் பேச) so that by that grace he gains the feet. Kural 795 tells one to seek the friendship of those who can speak till one weeps and rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து) and teach what is proper. The value the Kural places on a friend who rebukes is what the poet asks of his god: a grace that corrects rather than only comforts.

878 asks when his mind's attachment to the false union (பொய்க்கலவி) with women who seal and sell their breasts (முத்திரையிட்ட தனத்தை விற்பவர்) will end. Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) and likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The song's பொய்க்கலவி is the Kural's பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், and both tie the falsehood to the sale.
The Kural puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; 88 joins two of the three in one figure, the courtesan who herself drinks palm toddy.

The Naladiyar compares a harlot's love to lamp-light: as the light ends when the oil is gone, their love ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Among the song's charges is the same: the women coldly drop, with love gone, those who have no money (காசிலாதவர் தங்களை அன்பற ... நெகிழ்ந்த), so the song's catalogue contains the Naladiyar's whole verse as one item.

880 names women who quote a price (அரைப்பணம் கூறு விலையினர்), whose love falls short with anyone (குறைப்படுங் காதல் குனகிகள்) and who seek money every day (பொருட்டினந் தேடு கபடிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not from love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. The song lists in detail the trade the Kural defines in one line: love absent, money sought.

Both picture the old man walking unsteadily on a staff after a life of desire; the Naladiyar says those still set on desire then have no way to safety, while 881 asks the golden feet even so, even if he is born again.

889 describes sleeping in the beloved's embrace and vows that even so sleeping he will not forget Murugan's feet (துயில்கினும் உனதடி மறவேனே). Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep on the soft arms of the one you love (மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்). Both set the sleep of love beside the divine: the Kural lover weighs heaven against it, while the poet keeps the god's feet within it.

The Kural warns that the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth rather than love bring harm. The song shows the order exactly: on the bed they say 'first give the gold coins' (பொற்பணம் முதல் நீ தா), and once paid they speak as sweet as milk and honey (ஈந்தால் ... ஆன்பால் தேன் போல செப்பிடும்); the sweet speech is the receipt for the gold.

893 asks whether he will wander, sinking daily in the mud (சேறுதனில் நித்தம் மூழ்கி) of the price-women and pouring away his days. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (ஆழும்). The song takes the Kural's image of the mire, and adds the daily repetition and the wasted days.

894 calls the body a house Brahma built of blood, brain, flesh, skin and pus that stinks through nine gates (நவத்துவாரம் நாறும்), a puppet of disease to be eaten by foxes and dogs. Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot oozing filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்), which the fool addresses with love's epithets because of its dark skin. Both make the nine openings the proof of the body's foulness; the Naladiyar aims at desire, while 894 aims at the wish to carry the body in vain.

The Naladiyar's man sees kin wailing over a corpse carried to the burning ground and still marries believing there is joy here; 895 follows the mourners home from the pyre, where Kama soon sets them laughing again. Both find the same forgetting at the edge of the burning ground.

The Kural says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and delusion perish; 896 asks to remove the three faults (முக்குற்றம்) as the first step toward the shoreless sea of release. The link depends on reading முக்குற்றம் as the Kural's three.

Kural 37 says there is no need to state what virtue is: look at the palanquin's bearer and its rider (சிவிகை பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை), taking the rider's place as merit's fruit. 898 shows the rider in his palanquin (தண்டிகையில்) with chowries and horns, but opens with the body that flies, ants, foxes and crows will eat, and calls the pride arrogance like a rutting elephant's. Read together, the song limits the Kural's lesson: the rank may be the fruit of past virtue, but the one who rides is carrying a corpse to be.

Kural 335 says good deeds must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 899 pictures the same last stage, cough, swollen belly, sense fading, and asks Murugan to come on the peacock and give his feet before life goes (உயிர்போமுன்). Both fix the deadline at the body's last failing; the Kural puts the work on the person, the song puts it on the god.

The Naladiyar says household women cannot dress up their womanliness the way maids do, while the other kind, like a fresh flood, show their charms themselves (புதுப்பெருக்கம் போலத் தம் பெண்ணீர்மை காட்டி). The song is built on the same verb, காட்டி repeated for hair, brow, smile, eyes, breasts and hips, ending in women who show their practised arts (தொழில் அதிகம் காட்டு மடமாதர்): beauty as display is the shared mark of the women both texts set apart.

903 calls the courtesans இனிய நயமொழி பழகிகள், practised in sweet pleasing speech, who join fools to get their money (மடையர் பொருள்பெற மருவிகள்). Kural 911 says the இன்சொல் of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), brings harm. The Thiruppugazh's rhyming abuse makes the same charge: the sweet word is the instrument of the money-seeking.

905 calls the poet's sorrow ஒருநாள் பிரிவதும் அரிதாய்ச் சுழல்படும் ஒழியாத் துயர், a whirling grief in which even one day's parting is hard to bear. Kural 1269 says ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும் for those who wait for a distant lover's return. The Thiruppugazh borrows the parted lover's measure of a single day, but names it as the bondage to be escaped (தவிரேனோ).

908 begins its அலமல ('enough') list with the body of blood, worms and flesh, then sets aside wife, children, kin and every tie but those who think of the Lord. Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off birth உடம்பும் மிகை, even the body is excess, so why further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). Both reason from the body outward to every other bond.

909 confesses the friendship that grows with women he does not think enemies (பகையே என நினையாது உற நண்பு கூரும்). Kural 882 warns: do not fear foes like swords, fear கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு, ties with enemies who seem kin. The Thiruppugazh applies the Kural's statecraft warning about the enemy within to desire.

The Naladiyar says that those with aching hearts who stand begging at the gates of great houses (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) do so as the fruit of former deeds (முன்னை வினையாய் விடும்). The song confesses the same wandering at the doors of fools (முஞ்சர் மனை வாசல் தேடித் தேடி உழலாதே) and asks that the former deeds go (முந்தைவினை ஏவராமல் போக): what the Naladiyar states as fixed consequence, the song asks Murugan to remove.
The Kural says the good remember through seven births those who wiped away their distress; 911 makes the same vow, never to forget, toward the Lord who cut away the stain of desire and gave jnana.

912 thanks the lord who took him as his servant in a dream (கனவில் ஆள் சுவாமீ), so that he would not fall into the womb but sing and serve. Kural 1213 has the parted woman live because she sees in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்) the man who gives no grace awake. The dream in which the beloved comes becomes, in the Thiruppugazh, the place where the god's grace was given.

914 shows the courtesan swearing her price (விலை ஈதே கடிய சத்தியமாம்) and turning harsh (கடுகடுத்திடுவார்) when the money given runs out, and asks whether having joined them is not enough. Naladiyar 378 says such women are sweet while a man is deceived and become harsh as a ram's horn (தகர்கோடாம்) once they have had their fill, and those who seek the right way do not embrace them. Both mark the same turn from sweetness to harshness when the payment ends.

918 says the courtesans make the wealth in the lustful man's hand their kin (கைப்பொருள் உறவாகி) and put a price on anyone's heart (யாரையும் நெஞ்சை விலைப்படுத்திடு). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison, while even an oil-presser who has earned wealth is sugar (அக்காரம்). Both say the man himself does not count, only what he holds.

After its lovemaking scene, 924 says the Lord's lotus feet with anklets and his golden shoulders with vetchi flowers dance in the poet's eyes (என் நயனத்தில் உற்று நடமிடும்). Kural 1126 has the woman say her lover does not leave her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is not hurt when she blinks. The beloved living in the eyes is given in 924 to the god, in place of the women the song describes.

927 describes the tight embrace (கட்ட முயக்கு) with nail-marks on the neck in which words stop and life faints, and asks for a disciplined contemplation having left that experience. Kural 1108 says the embrace (முயக்கு) so close that no breeze can pass between is sweet to lovers. The same close embrace is the Kural's sweetness and the Thiruppugazh's thing to be left behind.

Both take kings riding elephants under the white umbrella as the case that proves death spares no one; the Naladiyar says they too were carried off, 928 that in their music and pride they never know the death Brahma has written.

929 vows never to forget, night and day (இராப்பகல் மறவேனே), the forms in which Murugan stands at Vayali and at Vanji. Kural 1207 has the parted woman ask what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's vow of unbroken memory becomes the devotee's vow toward a shrine form.

The Naladiyar pictures the old whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, and says that those who still turn to desire have no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The song gives the same decay, hearing gone, acts faltering, harsh voice (செவி கேட்பற்று ... செயல் தடுமாறி), and asks at that very stage for the golden feet and a little grace (சற்றருள்): it allows a way the Naladiyar closes, on condition of grace.

The song asks whether, instead of drowning in the sea of births made by the two deeds (இருவினைப் பிறவிக் கடல் மூழ்கி), the poet will reach the goal by grace. Kural 10 uses the same sea (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) and says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim it. The hymn's plea assumes the Kural's rule and asks grace to be on the right side of it.

The song lists what women's eyes do, among them putting Yama's soldiers to flight (எமபடர் படைகெட்டோட நாடுவ) and torturing life (உயிர்வதை நயனம்). Kural 1083 says the man never knew Death until now, and it is the woman's warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). The Kural makes the eyes Death; the song makes them stronger than Death's army, and turns the image toward a plea for the feet.

Both take the coming of grey hair as the reason to turn now: the Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood knowing old age will come, and 940 asks for service at the feet while youth lasts, before the hair whitens like a crane.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness is fullest: the Kural's woman says it buds in the morning and opens at evening; 948 gives that hour to the poet himself and arms it as Kama's army of breeze, moon, cuckoo and sea.
Both describe the courtesan's charm as calculated: the Kural's women weigh the profit before speaking of their virtue, and in 952 they name the price and learn their arts of deceit.

The song rests its plea on there being no other giver: if Murugan does not grant the boon, who else will (வரம் தராவிடில் பிறர் எவர் தருவாரே). Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்). The hymn's plea is the Kural's claim spoken by one in need of it.

Both picture the old man whose teeth are gone and whose body is scorned; the Naladiyar faults him for keeping his eyes on desire still, while 955 lists the decay and asks only for grace at the hour of death.

959 says the courtesans call men while weighing their property (அழைப்பர் ஆஸ்திகள் கருதுவர்), look only at money and drive a man off when he is finished. Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the profit and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The song shows the weighing in action, the festival calls and the potions; the Kural gives the rule that the man should weigh them in return.

Both make the courtesan's embrace an embrace of a corpse, but in opposite directions: in the Kural the man who embraces her holds a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 959 the women, looking only at money, will embrace even a corpse.

The Naladiyar says that one who sees kin wailing in crowds (சுற்றத்தார் கல்லென்று அலற) as a corpse is carried to the burning ground and still marries believing there is joy is answered by the funeral drum. The song gives the wife, sons and evening kin crowding and wailing (மண்டிக் கதறிடு) and the worm-body as food for the fire (புழுவுடல் அங்கிக்கு இரை), and asks for the feet on that day: the household is shown helpless at death in both.

962 traces the chase after women into roaming for money, hiding and becoming a thief, then a man of darkness (திருடனாகி ... திமிரனாகி), and asks instead for clear jnana (தெளியும் ஞானம்). Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure. The song places theft on the same scale of dark and clear knowing and shows desire as the road to it.

964 asks that, having crossed the sea of desire (ஆசைக் கடலேறி) and bathed in the sea of jnana, he be given the life of knowledge of the Lord (பதிஞான வாழ்வு). Kural 370 says that giving up craving, never filled by nature (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா), at once gives an unchanging nature (பேரா இயற்கை). The Kural states the exchange; the song names what the unchanging state is, a life in knowledge of Pati.

965 asks for kindness to living beings as a kind of understanding (பூதத் தயவான போதம்), with truth and discipline as its ground. Kural 249 says that virtue done without kindness is like a man without clarity seeing the truth (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால்). Both tie compassion to knowing: the Kural makes the lack of one like the lack of the other, and the song asks for them as one gift.

966 lists the courtesans who coax and speak as if on a man's side (குனகிகள் பக்ஷம் போல பேசிகள்) and hook men by desire of wealth (பொருளாசைக் கொளுவிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song's 'as if on your side' is the Kural's sweet word without love, named from the man's experience of it.
Both fault the courtesan's double dealing: the Naladiyar's eel shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish, and 966's women talk as if on a man's side while hooking him for his wealth.

The Naladiyar tells the heart that it will not let go of attachment to the house (மனைப்பாசம்) and pines for its children, and asks how many ages it expects to live. The song lists the crawling, crying child, the house of golden halls and the wife taken as refuge (தஞ்சம் என்று), then names the time when these fade (மங்கு காலம்) and asks for the feet instead: the same house and children, with the feet put where the Naladiyar puts good deeds.
Both tie the courtesan's company to money: the Naladiyar's love lasts as long as a lamp's oil, and 970 ends with the wealth sought now wasted and no goal left.

973 asks that he not, desiring women's shoulders (மடவார் தோள் விரும்பி), cross the bounds (வரம்பு கடந்து) and waste away. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) of women who keep no bounds (வரைவிலா) the mire where base men sink. The song turns the Kural's women without bounds into the man who crosses his own.

974, for a lovesick girl, says the evening and the north wind's thrown fire (வாடை எறிந்த அனல்) have worn her thin before her lover comes. Kural 1228 has the woman say the herdsman's flute is a messenger for the fire-like evening (அழல்போலும் மாலை) and a weapon that kills. Both make evening a burning, and give it a companion that carries the fire, the wind in the song and the flute in the Kural.

975 calls the courtesans those who raise a man up and let the ladder fall (ஏறிட்டிட்டு ஏணியை வீழ்விடு). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap with him from the peak and, at the peak, having no gold from him, showed a pain in her feet and would not come (மேற்காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாது ஒழிந்தாள்). Both picture the bargain as a climb that she abandons at the top when the money ends.

Both take the death of kings as the proof of impermanence: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas are carried off, and 978's sword-bearing kings reach the burning ground in a moment; 978 draws from it the renunciant's resolve to end birth.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). The song names the bond of desire for women and children (மடமாதர் மக ஆசை தொந்தம்) and asks not for release from it but for love of the two feet (இருதாளின் அன்பு தருவாயே): the Kural's principle in the form of a prayer.

980 says the courtesans demand the coins named and, when the money is not in hand, drive the man out midway (காசு கேட்டது கைப்பற்றா இடை காதி ஓட்டி). Naladiyar 373 says that even if he were Mal worshipped by the gods, they would send off a man with nothing in his hand to give (தங்கைக்கு கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை), bowing as they did it. Both make the empty hand the end of welcome; the Naladiyar adds the mock courtesy of the dismissal.
Both follow the corpse from the wailing and the drums to the fire; the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead, 981 with the ash and a prayer not to be born again.

983 runs through a life from youth, trade and price-women to wrinkled skin, grey hair and walking with a stick (தடியோடு திரி), then a list of diseases. Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood knowing grey hair comes (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), while those who delighted in youth will rise painfully leaning on a staff (கோல் ஊன்றி). The song fills in the life the Naladiyar warns of, stage by stage, down to the staff.

Both show the man whose speech fails and who walks with a staff; the Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire, while 983 traces the whole road from the price-women of youth to the staff and a catalogue of diseases.

984 asks whether honey or the syrup of cane can match union (தேனோ கருப்பிலெழு பாகோ இதற்கிணைகள் ஏதோ) and then calls its endless repetition a mud-bath of sorrow (சேறாடல் பெற்ற துயர்). Kural 1121 has the lover say her mouth's moisture is milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன் கலந்தற்றே). The song uses the same sweetness of love's poetry, and then judges it as mire.

Kural 71 says no bolt can shut in love, since the small tears of the loving (ஆர்வலர் புன்கணீர்) proclaim it. Thiruppugazh 986 turns the tears into the thing prayed for, eyes brimming (விழிபுனல் தேக்கிட) with love growing ever more (அன்பு மேன்மேல்). The Kural treats tears as the sign of love; the song asks for the sign as the gift.

The Kural's women weigh the profit before they speak of virtue; 987 makes the weighing literal, the courtesans assaying the gold they take and counting the hours before the quarrel that ends the bargain.

Thiruppugazh 987 describes courtesans who hug a man's neck, take the wealth from his hand (கைப்பொருள் கழற்றி), count the hours and pick a quarrel to drive him off (கணக்கிட்டுப் பொழுதேற்றி வைத்தொரு பிணக்கிட்டு). Naladiyar 377 gives the same sequence in animal images: the woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth in his hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), then balks like an ox. Both make the turn come exactly when the money has been taken.

Thiruppugazh 989 places Death hidden in the sky (விண்மேல் நமன் கரந்து) while the body wastes and the heirs quarrel. Naladiyar 20 warns that merciless Death roams looking for his men and bids the reader keep his stealth in mind (அதன் கள்ளம் கடைப்பிடித்தல் நன்று). Both picture Death as concealed and watching, the Naladiyar to urge provision in time, the song to ask Murugan to come before life goes.

Kural 1121 says the moisture at the white teeth of the soft-spoken girl (வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்) is like milk mixed with honey. Thiruppugazh 990 uses the same ஊறல் twice: the poet wanders in the ஊறல் of the sinful body, while Murugan drinks the ஊறல் of Valli's mouth (வாயில் ஊறல் குடித்து) to end her longing. The Kural's lover's praise is given to the god, while the same word in the plea names what the poet must escape.

Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் ... இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்). Thiruppugazh 992 fears that, not falling at the lotus feet (பாத வாரிஜத்தில் விழாதே), he will drown in the great ocean of seven births (மகோததி ஏழ்பிறப்பினில் மூழ்கா). It is the Kural's image and claim, stated as the poet's own danger, with the feet reached by the litany of praise.

Kural 266 says those who do tapas do their own work, and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Thiruppugazh 993 charges itself with exactly that pair: a demon of desire (ஆசாப சாசனை, ஆசாப ஈனனை) and a ruin who never sought the gain of tapas (ஊதியத் தவம் நாடாத கேடனை). The self-condemnation reads as the Kural's 'others' speaking of themselves.

Kural 1084 says the girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றத்தால்). Thiruppugazh 997 has the women's kayal eyes plunder life like a spear (ஆருயிர் சூறை கொண்டிடு வேல்போலே). The Kural's lover is overwhelmed by one girl's look; the song takes the same life-taking eye as a danger that sets fate's sorrow whirling.
Both invocations name God as the one who conquered the five: the Kural's one who quenched the five sense-gates, Tirumular's ஐந்து வென்றனன்.

Both invocations close on the number eight: the Kural's எண்குணத்தான், one of eight qualities, and Tirumular's உணர்ந்தெட்டே. Tradition reads both as the eight divine qualities, though Tirumular's eight may also be the eightfold form.

Both promise the end of sorrow to those who come to the Lord's feet; Tirumular reaches it through worship with lamps and offerings, the Kural through reaching the feet of the one without liking or aversion.
The Kural praises the path of the one who quenched the five senses; Tirumular says those who seek through the senses (பொறிவழி) only lament, and the Lord is found within.

1010 sets மருள் (delusion) and அறிவு side by side in one heart, like darkness and light, and says only those who have broken மருள் are knowers. Kural 351 names the same மருள் as taking what is not real for real, and says it produces birth without worth. The Kural gives what மருள் is and costs; Tirumular gives where it lives and who has left it.
Both say deeds cannot cling to the one turned to the Lord: the Kural through his true praise, Tirumular through seeing the fire rise within.

1035 says those who seek without attachment (பற்றற நாடி) and pass through the spreading light have joined the one who is the whole flame. Kural 350 says to cling to the one without clinging (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை) in order to let clinging go. Both make the end of attachment the condition for reaching the Lord, and Tirumular's பற்றற echoes the Kural's paradox.

105 says the Lord stands beyond the two kinds of deeds (இருவினைக்கு அப்புறம்). Kural 5 calls him the Lord to whom the two deeds of darkness do not cling (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா இறைவன்), and so they do not cling to those who praise him. Both define the Lord by his distance from the pair of deeds.

Kural 39 says only the joy that comes through virtue is joy: அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம். 1056 names Parashakti herself as புண்ணியம் ஆகிய போகம், the enjoyment that is merit. The Kural defines rightful pleasure by its source in virtue; the Tirumanthiram makes the Goddess that pleasure.

In 1058 the poet, using the love lyric's words, says he desired the coral-bodied maiden and placed her within himself: என் உள்ளே நயந்துவைத்தேனே. In Kural 1128 the woman keeps her lover in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவர்) and so fears hot food. The beloved lodged inside the self is the same figure, turned in 1058 on the Goddess.

The Kural calls a head that does not bow at the feet of the Lord of eight qualities as useless as a sense that cannot sense; Tirumular tells the head to wear the Goddess's feet and the mouth to praise her. The same claim for the head, turned to the Goddess.

The Kural traces joyless birth to the delusion (மருள்) that takes what is not real as real (பொருள்). Tirumular uses the same pair: the Goddess turns the deluded mind into one that has found the true thing, so grace is the remedy for the Kural's diagnosis.

1099 says that if one recites and realises (ஓதி உணரில்) Bhairavi, body and life become the Lord and births are destroyed. Kural 357 says that if the mind ponders and realises what is (உள்ளது உணரின்), one need not think again of birth. Both make realising, not the act alone, what ends birth; the Kural names truth as the object, the Tirumanthiram the goddess.

11 ends by calling great Nandi the rain-pouring cloud (பெயலும் மழைமுகில் பேர்நந்தி). Kural 11 says the world keeps going by the rain from the sky (வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்), so rain is amrita. The Kural's praise of rain as what sustains the world becomes in Tirumular a name of the Lord.
Both make reaching or bowing at the divine feet the end of births: the Kural's sea of births, Tirumular's cruel births. Tirumular gives it to the goddess, the Kural to the unnamed Lord.

Kural 367 says that if one cuts off craving thoroughly (அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின்), unfailing deeds come as one wishes. In 1108 craving is held down (அவாவை அடக்கிவைத்து) inside the whirl that lights the breath, and the goddess does it, saying 'fear not'. Set beside the Kural's self-effort, 1108 makes the subduing of craving the goddess's work, and it is held down rather than cut off.

1116 says foolish men (பேதை மனிதர்) babbled and passed away, while the first mother gives grace to those complete in effort (முயற்றியின் முற்றி). naladiyar:52 says the best do their own work, mindful of death, and none are more foolish (பேதையார்) than those who babble (பிதற்றும்) endless grammar and astrology. Both set useless talk against effort and call the talker a fool.
The Kural says the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise the Lord truly; 1122 praises her by name after name and ends that she drove out the poet's deeds.

The Kural's one who guards the five (ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டி) is a seed for heaven. 1127 has the same team, five elephants and the mahout with his goad (கும்பக் களிறுஐந்தும் கோலொடு பாகனும்), but they do not end under control: with the Lord and the lady they all merge and are lost in the union of love (அன்பிற் கலவியுள் ஆயொழிந்தாரே). The image is the same; the Kural ends in restraint, 1127 in absorption.
