Both set love (அன்பு) against bone (என்பு). For the Kural a body without love is bone wrapped in skin; Tirumular has the father reached through love and the mother present in the bone within bondage. The pairing depends on reading என்பிற் as 'in the bone'.

Both cut a pride (செருக்கு) voiced as possession: the Kural's 'I' and 'mine', Tirumular's 'my mother, my father' said of the divine parents. Tirumular extends the Kural's renunciation of ownership to the soul's claim on God.

114 says the Lord, once the tarnish was cut, set coral in crystal (பளிங்கிற் பவளம் பதித்தான்): the red Lord shows in the cleared soul. Kural 706 uses the same property of crystal, that it shows what is set beside it (அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்கு), for the face showing the heart. One image serves both a mystic claim and a courtier's rule for reading faces.

Both join penance, power and the defeat of death: the Kural says those who gain the power (ஆற்றல்) of austerity can leap past death; Tirumular's goddess of rare penance stands in his power (ஆற்றல்) and drives Death (கூற்றம்) away.

The Naladiyar calls the body a stinking cart that only the ignorant adorn and praise; Tirumular calls it the temple where the Lord dwells. The conflict holds if கோயில் is read as giving the body worth, not only as locating the Lord in it.

Both use the bird that drinks milk and leaves water. The Naladiyar makes it the wise learning only what is fitting; Tirumular makes it the parting that turns deeds into seeds that cannot sprout into births.

The Kural counts sloth and sleep among the pleasure-boats of those bound for ruin; Tirumular gives the same words (சோம்பு, தூக்கம்) to the freed resting in Sivam. The Kural's verdict is on worldly duty; Tirumular names a state beyond it.

Kural 339 says death is like sleep and birth like waking from it (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு). 129 says that sleeping (தூங்கி) the siddhas saw Sivaloka, Siva-yoga and Siva-bhoga within themselves, and 121 calls them dead with the body. Tirumular uses the Kural's sleep-as-death for a sleep from which no waking into birth follows.

Tirumular's third line nearly repeats the Kural's: ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ... ஐந்து அடக்கி. The Kural makes the restraint a protection through seven births (எழுமையும்); Tirumular's version ends instead with those who 'heard both' (இருமையும்) and stand flawless.
The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular makes the feet the refuge, the path and the goal itself.

The Naladiyar makes guarding the craving that enters through the five gates the effort that reaches release; Tirumular says the five come under control of themselves (தானே) once one has met the Lord. Restraint is a cause in one, a result in the other.

The Kural calls the wealth of the பேரறிவாளன், the man of great knowledge who acts for the world (உலகவாம்), a village tank (ஊருணி) full of water. 1419 gives the same title, பேரறிவாளன், to the Lord who makes town and world alike (ஊரும் உலகமும்). The word and the pairing of town and world move from the generous wise man to the Creator.

Both make learning the start of a way that ends in seeing the true: the Kural's learners who see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள்) take the road of no return; Tirumular's learn what is to be learned, then pass through yoga and knowledge to see the Supreme.

1421 says those who learn what is to be learned and go in due order (முறைமுறை) through yoga and knowledge reach the Supreme and are Siddhantins. Naladiyar 317 says books are easy for those who learn them in order (நெறிப்பட்டுக் கற்பவர்க்கு), but their meaning is hard for anyone to grasp. The Naladiyar warns that ordered learning does not by itself reach the meaning, which 1421 places only at the end of yoga and knowledge.

143 compares dying people to the unfired vessel that turns back to clay when rain falls (விண்ணின்று நீர்விழின் மீண்டுமண் ணானார்ப்போல்). Kural 660 compares wealth got by deceit to water poured into a pot of wet clay (பசுமண் கலத்துள்நீர்). The unfired pot that water destroys stands for the body in 143 and for ill-gotten wealth in the Kural.
Both make the feet the way: in the Kural reaching the Lord's feet takes one across the sea of births; in Tirumular going by the feet of the Supreme power one becomes Siva.

The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா). 1438 says the pure Saiva goes beyond outward garb (வேடம் கடந்து) and crushes the bonds of desire (ஆசாபாசம் செற்று). Both move the test from the ascetic's marks to what is given up, one in common ethics and one in Saiva doctrine.
Both cut the bonds of desire by turning to the Lord: the Kural by clinging to the one without clinging, Tirumular by going to Siva's side and crushing ஆசாபாசம்.
The Kural calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Tirumular says that when the body falls only vows and knowledge go on the road with the dead, not wife or children.

144 says nothing goes along the road with the dead but the vows they kept and the knowledge they gained (கொண்ட விரதமும் ஞானமும் அல்லது). Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they did (தாஞ்செய் வினையல்லால்), good or bad. Both strip away kin and body; Tirumular names only the good companions, the Naladiyar the deeds of either kind.
The Kural ends the pride of 'I' and 'mine' between a person and his goods; Tirumular ends the speech of 'I' and 'He' between the soul and the Lord. Both close with the 'I' given up.

The Kural says the senses must be crushed as part of renouncing; Tirumular says the five, hard to curb, subside once the truth beyond speech is attained. The same subduing is a task in one and a result in the other.
Both make the Lord's feet the only crossing of a sea: the Kural's great sea of births, Tirumular's leaping sea of deeds. Reaching the feet is the condition in both.

Tirumanthiram 1451 says that for one who takes the shade of the Pure One's feet as refuge (திருவடி நீழல் சரண்), the surging sea of deeds (தத்தும் வினைக்கடல்) will not reach him. Kural 7 says that only those who reach the feet of the incomparable one (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் தாள் சேர்ந்தார்க்கு) can remove the mind's anxiety. Both make reaching the feet the single way out; the Kural names inner care, Tirumular the force of karma.
Both set one abstention above a mass of offerings: the Kural puts not killing and eating above a thousand fire sacrifices, Tirumular puts giving up flesh above crores of sandal and flowers.

Tirumanthiram 1457 describes the yogi who holds himself still as a post and does not react to scratch or blow. Kural 126 speaks of drawing in the five senses like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) as a protection for seven births. The same withdrawal of the senses appears in the Kural as a moral discipline with a reward, and in Tirumular as the posture that makes union (கூடல்) possible.

The Kural says those who learn and know the truth here do not come back; Tirumular says letters, songs and the sixty-four arts do not remove birth, and only the yogic way does. The difference may lie in what each means by learning.

Tirumanthiram 1462 repeats that if one acts standing firm in longing (விரும்பி நின்றே செயின்), one becomes a true ascetic, true speech, true tapas, a dweller of heaven. Kural 666 says people gain what they resolved as they resolved it, if they are firm (திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). Both put the outcome in the steadiness of the will rather than the act; the Kural says it of worldly aims, Tirumular of the spiritual path.

Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings of just sceptre (ஒத்தசெங் கோலார்) and countless ascetics have fallen (வீழ்ந்தனர்). Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas on elephants were carried off as dead and no one has been left (எஞ்சினார் இவ்வுலகத்தில்). Both use the fall of kings as proof of impermanence; Tirumular adds ascetics to the fallen and sets against them those who come to the Lord in love.

The Kural asks what gain is greater than aram, which yields distinction and wealth; Tirumular says no path of aram is higher than jnana. They conflict only if the Kural's aram is meant to rank above liberating knowledge; Tirumular keeps aram but places it below jnana.

147 gives death's cause as the store of deeds running out (செய்வினை மூட்டிற்ற). Naladiyar 3 says even kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds are exhausted (வினைஉலப்ப வேறாகி வீழ்வர்). Both make the end come when the karma that held the life is spent.

Kural 123 says that restraint (அடங்க), recognised as knowledge (அறிவறிந்து), yields distinction. Tirumanthiram 1471 names knowledge, restraint and love (அறிவும் அடக்கமும் அன்பும்) as never parting from the city where the gracious Lord dwells. The Kural joins knowledge and restraint for worldly honour; Tirumular adds love and makes the three together the Lord's dwelling.
Both set the cutting off of 'I' and 'mine' at the summit: the Kural says whoever cuts that pride enters a world above the gods', Tirumular makes it jnana within jnana itself.
Both free the one who knows or praises the Lord from both kinds of deed: the Kural's twofold deeds of darkness do not cling to him, Tirumular's knower has passed beyond merit and sin alike.
Both promise victory over death to those of disciplined practice: the Kural to those who have gained the power of tapas, Tirumular to Siva-yoga siddhas who have put away anger.
The Kural says the world's 'greatness' is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Tirumular shows it in a single evening: a meal, a talk with his wife, a small ache, and he is gone.

Both tell a death as a short row of ordinary acts: the Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, he went', Tirumular's cooking, eating, talking and lying down. The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now; Tirumular draws none.

Both make clear knowledge of what is the condition of ending birth: the Kural's mind that has examined and known what is real need not think of another birth; Tirumular says those without clarity do not end their births.

Tirumanthiram 1489 says that for those without the joining path the fearful Lakshmi will not be in their house (வெருவுந் திருமகள் வீட்டில்லை). Kural 167 says the fair goddess (செய்யவள்), grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister. Both use the figure of Lakshmi leaving a house as the mark of failure, the Kural for envy, Tirumular for lacking the yogic path; 1489's reading is uncertain.

Both arm the mind against the five senses: the Kural's goad of firmness guards them like elephants, Tirumular's sharp sword of the mind cuts them down. The Kural guides the five; Tirumular strikes them.

Both make reaching the Lord's feet the crossing of a sea. The Kural names the great sea of births; Tirumular names only the shore, four times over, and makes it both the shade of the feet and the Lord's command.

The Kural calls a head that does not bow to the Lord's feet as useless as a sense that cannot sense; Tirumular says bowing and serving at Hara's feet is the very fruit of birth. One states the loss, the other the gain.

Tirumanthiram 1506 says that though people recite, worship and gather flowers, their mind is a stone fallen in a mossy pond (பாசிக் குளத்தில்வீழ் கல்), not knowing the love for the stainless light. Kural 278 says many bathe with impurity in their minds (மனத்தது மாசாக) and go about concealed. Both set outward observance against an untouched mind; Tirumular's stone sinks under the surface it disturbs.

Both make lesser things gain worth by nearness: in the Naladiyar the hare is worshipped with the moon, and the slight gain worth through friends steady as a hill; in Tirumular all that nears the golden mountain turns its colour, and the disciple takes the Lord's form.

Both use the lamp entering a dark room. The Naladiyar makes it austerity before which sin cannot stand, and warns the dark returns when the oil runs out; Tirumular makes it the Lord and the Mother entering delusion, with no warning that the light fails.

Both use the phrase சிறப்பொடு பூசனை: Kural 18 says festival and worship will cease, even for the gods, if the sky dries up; 1524 says the hill-girl, for those who stand doing worship with honour, cuts birth and sets them to worship (வழிபட வைக்கும்). Each makes worship depend on a giver outside the worshipper, rain in the Kural, grace in the Tirumanthiram.

Both treat good and bad deeds alike as what must be overcome, not good deeds as a ladder. The Kural says the two dark deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord truly; Tirumular says grace descends when the two stand in balance.

Both take a king to make the point: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and called dead, Tirumular's lord of the land rides a bier with the town behind and drums in front.

Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில்) has no home of its own; 1531 calls the body a hut full of holes (பொள்ளற் குரம்பை) which the Lord, a thief-chief, enters and leaves. Both see the body as a temporary shelter someone passes through; the Kural's lodger is the soul, Tirumular's is the hidden Lord, whom the sects fail to notice.

The Kural calls understanding seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever kind; Tirumular tells people to drop the claim that this or that sect is good and seek the God beyond the forms. Both look past the label to the thing.

1549 says the great austerity that goes the right way cuts the clinging of strong deeds and brings one before the Lord; Naladiyar 51 says sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness before a lamp, but evil rushes back when good deeds are exhausted, as darkness when the oil runs out. The Naladiyar adds the condition 1549 leaves out: austerity's power over deeds lasts only while its store lasts.

Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; 1550 says those who recite the shastras claim to understand, but the First Lord stands among those who know கமை, forbearance. Both deny that learning reaches the Lord; 1550, on the reading of கமை as kshama, names forbearance rather than worship as what does.

Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one; 1551 says those who bear the Lord's feet are without equal, while those who never think of release stay in the world grieving and weeping (ஏங்கி ... அழுவாரே). Both make the feet the only cure for a grief the Kural calls மனக்கவலை and Tirumular shows as weeping.

Naladiyar 25 says one who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground (கண்டும்) still marries and thinks there is joy here; 1554 says those who see the boat break up (கண்டும்) still do not cling to the feet. Both are about the sight of death failing to teach; the Naladiyar's failure is to keep seeking pleasure, Tirumular's is not to seek the Lord.

Both name the Lord as the one without equal and make reaching him the cure for the mind: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் removes the mind's anxiety, Tirumular's துணையிலி is reached by the mind that draws near.

156 says people, even seeing the dead man set down and left, think the wealth they seek will not leave them (அச்சகலாதென நாடும் அரும்பொருள்). Naladiyar 182 says fools think their household supports are secure and go heedless (பொச்சாந்து ஒழுகுவர் பேதையார்), though those supports only seem to stand. Both locate the folly in trusting what one has just seen fail.
Both make worship of the feet the fruit of knowing: the Kural asks what learning has achieved without it, Tirumular says his examining succeeded where the gods' failed because it ended in worship.

1578 says fools look at Siva come as guru and see only one of themselves (நமர்), while the meritorious say 'this is the Father'; Kural 1071 says the base look exactly like human beings (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்). Both turn on human likeness misleading the eye, in opposite directions: in the Kural the man-shape hides less than a man, in Tirumular it hides Siva. The pairing depends on reading பொய்த்தகு கண்ணான் நமர் as mistaking the guru for an ordinary man.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if it doesn't lead to the Lord's feet; Tirumular says even the knowledge of Vedanta cannot be known unless the Lord comes as guru. Learning is not enough in either, but for Tirumular the grace must come first.

1588: 'I have known and understood (அறிந்துணர்ந்தேன்) ... I was born and have ended this birth (பிறந்தொழிந்தேன்)'; Kural 356: those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). The Kural states as a rule what Tirumular claims in the first person: knowing here ends the return to birth.
Both say the two deeds, good and bad, cease for one devoted to the Lord: the Kural through praising him, Tirumular through holding his feet in the mind.
Both join the head to the Lord's feet: the Kural calls a head that does not bow to them useless, Tirumular says the old sages set the feet on their heads.

Kural 7 says that except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது); 1604 says the Lord's pair of feet is mantra, great medicine (மாமருந்து), tantra, gifts and the pure path. The Kural makes the feet the one remedy; Tirumular extends it so that every religious means is the feet.

1605 says that even if the bonds spread, once ego goes (ஆங்காரம் நீங்கி) and one stays in that state, the unfailing state of nectar is reached; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. Both make loss of the ego the condition of the highest state, and 1605 adds that it holds even while bonds still arise.

Both set a light against darkness in the soul. The Naladiyar's lamp is a person's own tapas, which drives out sin until its oil runs out; Tirumular's light is Siva's grace that comes to the renounced soul at its ripe time.

Kural 350 tells the renouncer to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging (பற்றற்றான்); 1616 names who that is: the righteous, unborn one with no one of his own (யாரும் இலாதான்), who lives in the burning ground and eats alms, himself a renouncer (துறவன்), and who cuts the births of those who renounce. Tirumular gives the Kural's 'one without attachment' Siva's face.

Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere (யாண்டும் இடும்பை இல); 1617 says the Lord made the path and the thorn, and the thorn pierces only those who slip from the path (நெறியில் வழுவின்). The Kural states that suffering is absent for those who hold to the Lord; 1617 gives the mechanism, that pain comes from straying, and leaves the maker, like the Kural's Lord, without will to hurt.

Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all wants let go at once (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை); in 1618 the five (ஐவர்) come like creditors demanding dues and the speaker says 'I owe them nothing' because his resolve is tapas to reach the feet. Both set the renouncer against the five; the Kural commands their defeat, 1618 shows it as refusal of a debt.

Kural 14: if the rains fail, ploughmen will not plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்); 1619: the sky gave rain (வானம் வழங்க) and a blue lily bloomed in the furrow, and yet the ploughman gave up ploughing (உழவொழிந்தான்). Tirumular's riddle inverts the Kural's farming fact: here the plough stops not because the rain failed but because it came and the field flowered, which supports reading the ploughman as a seeker whose effort ends at the vision.
Both put the full renouncer above the heavens: the Kural says he who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods', Tirumular that only he who renounces the earth reaches the Lord's state.
Both put the ascetic beyond death: the Kural says those who gain the power of tapas can leap past Death, Tirumular that for those who have withdrawn and let go, Yama is simply not there.
The Kural commends tapas because whatever one wants is gained as one wants it. Tirumular separates getting what one wants, which mere asking achieves, from tapas, whose greatness is ending birth.

Kural 25 makes Indra, lord of the wide heavens, witness to the strength of one who has quenched the five (ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் ... இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி); in 1627 Indra himself (இருந்திந்திரனே) comes to unsettle those who sit in tapas, and their minds stay set on Siva. In both Indra is the measure of the ascetic's power; 1627 places the ascetic's firmness in Siva rather than in his own strength.
Both define the ascetic by firmness under pressure: the Naladiyar's blessed push aside troubles that would break their vows, Tirumular's stay unblinking amid kings at war.

Both set inner work against learned talk: the Naladiyar calls those who prattle of grammar and astrology the greatest fools, Tirumular tells the reader to leave clever shastra-recitation for a moment's inward look.

The Kural asks for flawless learning followed by living by it; Tirumular says recitation (ஓதல்) is no longer needed once the Life of life is within. The two speak of different stages, so this limits learning rather than contradicting it.

1635 says those who know the outcome (விளைவறிவார்) do the true tapas of old and surpass those of heaven and earth. Kural 266 says those who do tapas do their own work (தங்கருமம் செய்வார்) and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile. Both treat tapas as the act of one who sees where deeds lead, the Kural naming the failure as அவம் and Tirumular the insight as விளைவு.

1637 says the worldly who listen to and serve the people of tapas (பணி கேட்கின்) may come face to face with Nandi. Kural 443 says the rarest of rare things is to cherish the great and make them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்). Tirumular carries the Kural's counsel on choosing great companions into the spiritual sphere, where service of the tapasvins becomes the way to the Lord.

1638 says to turn back the five so they do not stray into the field (புனத்திடை அஞ்சும் போகாமல் மறித்தால்), and then the light of the way becomes one's own. Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை) and all desires let go together. Both locate discipline in checking the five senses at their field; Tirumular adds the sword of understanding and the inner light that follows.

Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and causing no pain to others (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்). 1641 says that, truly seen, the tapas of those who take on hardship (இடரடை செய்தவர்) lies in a single mind holding the body (ஒருமனத் தாமே). Tirumular keeps the Kural's endurance but adds the condition that it counts as tapas only when the mind is one-pointed.
Both tie want to the lack of tapas: the Kural says the poor are many because few practise austerity, Tirumular pictures those without tapas or learning whirling around for rice.
Both picture those who do no tapas as shut out and reduced to want: in the Naladiyar they cling to the outer door of others' houses, in Tirumular they run from crocodile to bear in search of rice.

Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because what is wanted is gained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்). 1644 agrees that the fruit of tapas (செய்தவப் பேறு) is the mind becoming Siva, but says tapas is not needed (செய்தவம் வேண்டா) for one who has kinship with those already in Siva's bliss. It adds a second route to the fruit the Kural ties to tapas alone.

Both make அருள் the wealth above wealth. The Kural's அருள் is compassion toward living beings, and its chapter is named அருளுடைமை; Tirumular takes the same chapter name for the Lord's grace, the source of wealth, knowledge and divinity.

Both say that both kinds of deed, good as well as bad, must cease to cling, and both tie this to the Lord: the Kural to those who love his true praise, Tirumular to seeking his dwelling beyond the two.

Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்). 1649 says that by Siva's grace some become gods and some equal the deity (தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பர்). Both let a human be ranked with the divine; Tirumular puts the cause in grace, where the Kural puts it in the householder's right living.
The Kural says cling to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; Tirumular vows not to let go of Nandi until release, a clinging that is the way out.
Both condemn those who live by others while posing as renouncers: the Kural calls none more hard-eyed than they, Tirumular says the show of devotion they put on for food finds no feet of Siva.

1656 says that where men without knowledge wear the garb and live by begging, the land's honour decays and famine comes (வையகம் பஞ்சமாம்). Kural 559 says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Both tie a public calamity of want to wrong at the head of the land, the Kural's to the ruler, Tirumular's to false ascetics the ruler should remove.
Both put the world's welfare on the ruler's daily scrutiny (நாள்தோறும் நாடுக, நாடி நாடோறும): the Kural of those who do his work, Tirumular of all his people's conduct.

Kural 972 says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work one does (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை). 1658 sorts wearers of the garb by line, low (இழிகுலம்), right (வழிகுலம்), blamed and outcast (கழிகுலம்), and says the last are to be weeded out. The conflict holds only if 1658's குலம் words mean birth; if they name conduct, the verses agree.

166 says the time passed between with umbrella, horse and victorious sword (குடையும் குதிரையும் கொற்றவாளும்), and at death the life reaches its place, left or right. Naladiyar 3 has kings riding on elephants under the umbrella (குடைநிழற்கீழ்) who fall when their deeds run out. Both use the royal regalia to show that rank does not decide the end.

Both say austerity's garb belongs only to those who already have austerity, and set தவம் against அவம்: for the Kural taking it up without it is futile, for Tirumular those great in futility cannot carry it.
Both make the false ascetic a hunter: in the Kural one hiding in a bush to snare birds, in Tirumular a வேடர் who wears the garb to kill, punning on the word for garb-wearer.

Kural 133 says conduct is noble lineage (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை) and its lapse becomes low birth. 1667 says the ash of the sacred woods makes the form of those who have gained the stainless one's feet a high lineage (உயர்குலம் ஆமே). Both say high குலம் is made rather than born; the Kural makes it by conduct, Tirumular by ash and grace.
The same move in another field: the Naladiyar says the beauty of hair and garment is not beauty and learning's is; Tirumular says garb does not save and knowledge does.

167 calls the body a nest (இக்கூட்டையே) the dancer has left, so what is done to it no longer matters. Kural 338 likens body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Tirumular takes the Kural's empty nest and asks why anyone should care for it.

The two verses share most of their words: the dancer in the skin bag who worked it and has left, and the indifference of what is then done to the body. Tirumular lists crows, revilers, milk drops and praisers; the Naladiyar dragging, careful burial, casting out and revilers.

Kural 338 says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying from its nest (குடம்பை தனித்தொழிய). 1677 draws a consequence for garb: a garb begun on the body falls away when the body does (உடல்கழன்றால் வேடம் உடனே கழலும்), so it cannot serve the soul. Tirumular applies the Kural's parting of body and life to the ascetic's outward marks.
Both make self-control the handling of animals: the Kural's goad of firmness guards the five senses as elephants, Tirumular's firm reins hold the running horse.

Both say the ascetic's outward marks are not needed: the Kural, neither shaving nor long hair if one gives up what the world condemns; Tirumular, no garb if one reins in the running horse and seeks Nandi.

168 urges joining the Lord who is true wealth while life lasts, before favour, kingdom and wealth go to others (பிறர்கொள்ளப் போவதன் முன்னம்). Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts (அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both turn the impermanence of wealth into a call for immediate action; Tirumular names the lasting thing as the Lord.
Both condemn the split between word and deed: the Kural calls the bond with such people bitter even in a dream, Tirumular warns against saying one thing, thinking another and doing a third.
Both make the king's harsh punishment of the wicked a protection of the land: the Kural likens it to weeding the young crop, Tirumular says without it the earth falls to famine.

Kural 262 says tapas comes to those who have it, and for others taking it up is futile (அவம்). 1685 says all who stand in tapas without knowing that its karma rests in Siva gain only suffering in births (பவத்திடை நின்றதோர் பாடு). Both say tapas taken up without its inner ground is wasted; Tirumular names that ground as knowing Siva.

1688 says that to a deluded disciple who wavers and does not think through the tattvas the teaching is not to be given (பித்தான சீடனுக்கு ஈயப் பெறாதான்). Kural 720 says speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The same rule, that teaching is wasted on the unfit hearer, holds for the assembly and for initiation.

169 likens wealth to the moving moon that wanes greatly (இயக்குறு திங்கள் இரும்பிழப்பு ஒக்கும்). Naladiyar 125 likens the bond with the small to the full moon that wanes day by day (வைகலும் தேயுமே). The waning moon marks what is lost by its own nature, wealth in one and friendship in the other.

1690 says those who worship (தொழுதறிவாளர்) are the ones who know the flawless guru and the good way, while the rest know only ruin (அழிவறிவார்). Kural 2 asks what learning yields if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the pure knower (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both make worship the test of knowledge; Tirumular adds scripture as the eye (கருதி கண்ணாக) and the guru as the one to be known.

Kural 34 makes a spotless mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) the whole of virtue. 1695 takes the pure mind further: polished like a great gem by work (தொழிலார மாமணித் தூய்தான சிந்தை), it is where the Lord takes his place, and then deeds fall away and his feet are seen. The Kural's end becomes Tirumular's precondition for grace.

1696's true disciple thinks on the supreme tattva (பர தத்துவம் உன்னி) and fears the binding round of births (ஆர்த்த பிறவியின் அஞ்சி). Kural 358 calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that departs when one sees the true thing (செம்பொருள் காண்பது). Both tie the escape from birth to fixing the mind on the highest reality; Tirumular adds that the seeker must also keep to dharma (அறநெறி சாத்தவல்லான்).

Kural 351 says inglorious birth comes from taking what is not real as real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). 1697 makes the first mark of the true disciple that he considers how the real and the unreal stand (சத்தும் அசத்தும் எவ்வாறென), and then joins that discernment to devotion and grace. The Kural names the error; Tirumular builds the cure into the disciple's training.

170 calls fools those who say 'this wealth is mine' (என்னது மாடென்று இருப்பர்கள் ஏழைகள்) though even their shadow does not help them. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 170 shows the 'mine' in action that the Kural tells one to cut.

1700 tells the teacher to teach only those of ripe mind (மதிபக்குவர்க்கே உணர்த்தி). Kural 720 says that speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால்). Both hold that teaching is wasted on the unfit; Tirumular makes ripeness the measure where the Kural speaks of the hearers' group.
Both use the shadow that clings to the feet and never leaves: in the Kural it is the ruin that follows the evildoer, in Tirumular the true disciple's place at the guru's feet.

171 has the bees gather honey and store it, only for the strong to drive them off and take it (அதுவலியார் கொள). Kural 1009 says wealth amassed without love, comfort or virtue is taken by others (ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்). The bee image of 171 is the Kural's maxim made a scene.
Both use the honey bee whose stored honey others take. The Naladiyar spells out the lesson, that those who hoard without giving lose it all; Tirumular gives only the image.
Both use the phrase of leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்) as something attainable: the Kural through the power of austerity, Tirumular through letting go of wealth.

172 says give away your wealth and when Death comes you may even leap past him (கூற்றன் வருங்கால் குதிக்கலும் ஆமே). Naladiyar 5 says those who gave first will escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives (முன்னே கொடுத்தார் உயப்போவர்). Both promise escape from Death through giving, while Naladiyar 6, already linked, denies that anyone leapt Death.

Both tell the rich to give their wealth away in view of Death, but the Naladiyar says no one has ever leapt past Death and escaped, while Tirumular says one who sheds his wealth may leap past him. The conflict holds if Tirumular's leap means escaping death; if it means dying free of fear or bondage, the two agree.

1721 assigns the linga's material by birth: crystal for Brahmins, gold for kings, komalam for Vaishyas and the bana linga for Shudras (துறையடைச் சூத்திரர் தொல்வாண லிங்கமே). Kural 972 says birth is alike for all beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction comes only from the work they do. On the reading that 1721 fixes the form of worship by birth, the two conflict; 1721 does not say one worship is worth more, so the tension is over sorting by birth, not over rank.

On what the human body is: the Naladiyar breaks it into entrails, fat, blood, bone and sinew and asks which part is the beautiful woman; Tirumular says the body's very form is the Sivalinga, Chidambaram and Siva's dance. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for desire.

Both speak of the five senses as gates (வாயில்) to be mastered. The Kural praises the one who quenched the five sense-gates and the long life of those who follow him; Tirumular has Nandi enter the body by its gates and receive worship once the senses are put behind.
Both make wealth vanish without trace through a sudden image, the Naladiyar's lightning in a night cloud and Tirumular's capsizing boat; Tirumular adds a treasure in the body that does not sink.

174 says a helper who answers when called may come to those who share out the bright wealth that comes to them (விரிவுசெய் வார்கட்குக் கூவும் துணையொன்று கூடலுமாமே). Kural 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make giving the way to gain support.

Both start from the letter A. The Kural compares: as A comes first among letters, the Primal Lord comes first for the world; Tirumular makes the Lord himself the letter A, with Shakti as U, and the two become the earth and sound. The simile becomes an identity.

Both open with A as first: the Kural uses it as a simile, as A is first of letters so the Lord is first of the world. Tirumular takes the letter literally: A and U, known rightly, are themselves the lingam.

176 opens with the life leaving the body (உடம்போடு உயிரிடை விட்டோடும் போது), almost the Kural's words for the bond of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) in 338. The Kural ends on the bird gone; 176 adds that thinking of the Lord keeps Death's messengers from burning the life.
Both read the sun's daily course as a measure of passing life: the Naladiyar urges help to others before one's days run out, Tirumular faults those who see the sun set and do not understand.

Kural 6 promises long life to those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்). In 1775 the devotee worships the feet and the First Lord gives grace so that வென்றுஐம் புலமும் மிகக்கிடந்து, the five senses lie conquered. The Kural credits the Lord with the quenching and asks the devotee to follow; Tirumular has the Lord's grace do the quenching in the devotee.
Both call a failure of understanding ghostly: the Kural's man who denies what the world holds to be is counted a demon, Tirumular's who don't know how body, breath and soul join are like ghosts.
Both make true knowing the end of suffering: the Kural's one who knows the support and lives so that clinging ends is not touched by the pains, Tirumular's who have awareness have no suffering.

179 says that once youth has worn away and the strength for hard deeds is gone it is late, so hold to Nandi while life is still in you (உயிருள்ள போதே). Kural 335 sets the same deadline in the body, before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்), for doing good. The two set one urgency, worship in Tirumular and good deeds in the Kural, against the same failing of the body.

The Naladiyar says not to put off good deeds because one is young; Tirumular says to hold to Nandi while life lasts, since youth and strength wear away. The urgency is the same, the act urged differs.
The Naladiyar warns men not to desire a woman who will one day stoop over a staff; Tirumular turns the lesson on the man, who was cane to women and is now bitter fruit.

Kural 10 has a பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், a great sea of births, which only those who reach the Lord's feet can swim. 1801 has the Lord bathe him in அமுதப் பெருங்கடல், a great sea of nectar, and join him to his feet (அடிபுணைந்து, which can also read as the feet becoming a raft, புணை). The same great sea and the same feet appear, but in Tirumular the sea is nectar to bathe in, not births to cross.
Both name the Lord அறவாழி அந்தணன். In the Kural only those who reach his feet cross the other seas; in Tirumular he himself gives the way of no birth and comes into the heart as kin.

Kural 393 says only the learned have eyes (கண்ணுடையர்); the unlearned have two sores on their face. 1808 says only those with அருட்கண் (the eye of grace) see Hara, as the dark-eyed (இருட்கண்ணினோர்) cannot see even the sun. Both say having eyes is not the same as seeing: in the Kural the missing eye is learning, in Tirumular it is grace.

Tirumanthiram 1815 says great Nandi gave the way of no return (வாரா வழிதந்த மாநந்தி) and bade the poet bathe in the sea of grace. Kural 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Both name release by the same phrase; the Kural reaches it by learning and seeing, the Tirumanthiram receives it as a gift of the guru.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if it does not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge, so bowing is learning's fruit. Tirumular bows by leaving what he learned (கற்றன விட்டேன்): the feet are reached by setting learning down.
Both set a true lamp above ordinary lamps. For the Kural it is truthfulness; for Tirumular it is the lamp that lights the lamp, and its bearer becomes the lamp.

Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left confusion (மருள்நீங்கி), darkness leaves and joy comes (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும்). Tirumanthiram 1819 says light and darkness never end once and for all, and only when both light and darkness go (ஒளியிருள் நீங்க) does the soul become Siva. The Tirumanthiram limits the Kural's picture: release is not light winning over darkness but passing beyond the pair.

182 says that for those who rise each morning evening falls and the life span passes (மாலை படுவதும் வாணாள் கழிவதும்). Kural 334 says the thing that shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர் ஈரும் வாளது). Both make the ordinary day the measure of life lost; 182 adds that the Lord gives joy to those who think of him fittingly.

Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion (மருள்) that takes what is not the real thing (பொருளல்லவற்றை) for the real. Tirumanthiram 1821 names one refuge called the real thing (பொருளது என்ற புகலிடம்) and says that when the one who entered the mind to remove confusion (மருளது நீங்க) is grasped with clarity, the way to Siva follows. The Kural diagnoses the confusion; the Tirumanthiram names who removes it and where it leads.

The Naladiyar calls the body a pot seeping filth from nine openings, dressed in skin that fools the eye; Tirumular makes the same flesh body (ஊனுடம்பு) the Lord's shrine and the mouth its gate. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar is read as judging the body's worth itself, not only rebuking lust.

Kural 259 says not killing one creature to eat is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின்). Tirumanthiram 1824, playing on அவி, says we have nothing to show Nandi who eats the sacrificial oblation (வேட்டவி) and offer instead the song that cools the heart (பாட்டவி). Both take the word of the fire offering and put something else in its place, abstention in the Kural and sung praise in Tirumular.

The Kural says water gives outer purity and truth inner purity. Tirumular makes truthful speech and thought the condition without which the Lord is not seen, and only then counts flowers and water as praise.

183's riddle has five thick needles in one bag, and when frost falls on them the needle bag itself flies off (பருவூசிப் பையும் பறக்கின்ற வாறே). Kural 338 makes the bond of body and life a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே). Both picture death as a flight from a container; in the Kural the life flies and the nest stays, in 183 the bag of the body goes with it.

Tirumanthiram 1830 prays that, though the poet stays forgetful on this path (மறப்புற்று), he may worship without forgetting (மறப்பின்றி). Kural 537 says nothing is too hard if done with the tool of unforgetting care (பொச்சாவாக் கருவியால்). The Kural makes not forgetting the instrument of any achievement; the Tirumanthiram asks for it in worship as a gift, admitting he cannot keep it by himself.
Both make the sea of births what drowns those who do not turn to the Lord: the Kural's who do not reach his feet cannot swim it, Tirumular's who do not worship sink (அழுந்துகின்றார்) in it.

Kural 2 asks what fruit (பயன்) learning has if one does not bow at the good feet of the pure knower. Tirumanthiram 1836 says there is one knowledge of the fruit (பயனறிவு ஒன்றுண்டு): to those who strew flowers knowing the fruit, Hara keeps near so that they reach the three-eyed one's feet. The Kural makes reaching the feet the fruit of knowing; Tirumular makes knowing the fruit what turns flower-worship toward the feet.
In the Naladiyar Death uses the sun as a measure to eat one's days; in Tirumular the sun and moon measure out the world from within. Both make the heavenly lights the counters of a life.
The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show; Tirumular says daily adorning and praise do not bring knowledge of the Lord until the inner stain is gone.

186 repeats 'in the days you have' (எய்திய நாளில்) and urges praising the Lord in song so that youth does not pass in vain. Kural 38 says that if one does good so that no day falls away (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) it is a stone that blocks the road of one's days. Both count the days one by one; the Kural fills them with good deeds, 186 with sung praise.
Both set one simple act above a thousand great rites: the Kural puts not killing and eating above a thousand sacrifices, Tirumular puts one meal for a jnani above a thousand gifts to Brahmins.
The Kural sees householders as those who provide for renunciants, perhaps at the cost of their own austerity; Tirumular makes that provision the highest merit, above feeding Brahmins.

Kural 278 says many go about concealed, bathing as if great while their minds are defiled (மனத்தது மாசாக). Tirumanthiram 1865 says those who worship without the fitting disposition, matching only in outward face (முகமத்தோடு ஒத்து), stay deluded within (அகமத்தர்) age after age. Both set a correct outward rite against an inner state that does not match it; the Kural names the defiled mind, Tirumular the frenzy that passes for devotion.

Kural 263 asks whether others have forgotten tapas in order to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). Tirumanthiram 1867 says that charity done to those who never fall still and strive at rare austerity (அருந்தவம்) removes deep karma and becomes the golden world. The Kural observes that householders serve renunciants in place of their own tapas; Tirumular names what that service gains them.
The Kural makes giving and austerity depend on rain; Tirumular runs it the other way, making rain depend on the presence of one who seeks the Lord.

1868 says that where one person seeks the Lord in the fitting way, 'பார்மழை பெய்யும்', rain falls and the land lacks nothing. Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband commands the rain: 'பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை'. Both make one person's devotion, to the Lord in one case and to the husband in the other, the cause of rain for everyone.

187 says that all that grows on the branch with red shoots and cool flowers (செந்தளிர்த் தண்மலர்க் கொம்பில்) comes to die, yet people do not praise the Lord's feet. Naladiyar 17 says youth falls as fruit drops from every tree in the dewy grove (கனியுதிர்ந்து வீழ்ந்தற்று இளமை), so do not desire her spear eyes. One image of the tree shedding what grew on it serves two lessons: worship in Tirumular, turning from desire in the Naladiyar.

1884 says people in all eight directions welcome the Lord's devotees with prepared food, calling it nectar. Kural 263 asks whether the others have forgotten tapas 'துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி', in wanting to provide for renouncers. Both describe the householder's role as feeding those who have renounced; the Kural adds a note of irony that the Tirumanthiram lacks.

Both fault begging that comes from desire when the remedy lies within: the Naladiyar asks why one should beg of strangers when poverty can be ended by asking of oneself, Tirumular faults those who beg for their desires instead of reaping the field already ploughed.

Both put the world's creator beside begging. The Kural says that if the maker of the world decreed that people live by begging he should wander and perish; Tirumular says the maker of the seven worlds begged himself so that his devotees could reach him by begging. The conflict holds if the Kural is read as condemning all living by alms, not only the beggary of the poor.
The Kural says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion are gone; Tirumular says hunger, craving and anger do not stay in Siva's devotees, and adds that they pass beyond the heavens too.
The Kural says whatever else one fails to guard, one should guard the tongue; Tirumular says guarding the tongue alone only makes one mute, and silence is true only when the mind is still too.

1903 says a yogi who dies before completing samadhi goes to a world of refuge and returns to take up unbroken yoga again. Kural 398 says learning gained in one birth 'எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து', protects for seven. Both teach that inner gains outlast one life, the Kural for learning and the Tirumanthiram for yoga.

Both make release a matter of not coming back: the Kural's மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி and Tirumular's மீளார். Tirumular adds the setting of a silent samadhi at death; the Kural says only that seeing the true thing here leads there.

Both speak of what is done with a corpse once its life has left. The Naladiyar asks what it matters whether it is dragged off, buried or thrown anywhere; Tirumular says that burning or exposing a jnani's body ruins the land. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's indifference covers every body; if it speaks only of ordinary people, Tirumular's exception for the jnani escapes it.

Both tie the failure of rain to a wrong: in the Kural a king's crooked rule, in Tirumular the burning of a jnani's body. The same belief that the sky answers moral or sacred offence is applied to kingship and to the rites of the dead.

1912 says burying the jnani 'புண்ணியமாம்', is merit, while heaping fire on him ruins the land and letting him decay in the open disgraces him. Naladiyar 26 says that once the dancer has left the skin bag it does not matter whether the body is dragged off, 'நன்றாய்ந்து அடக்கிலென்', carefully buried, or thrown away. One makes the disposal of the body decisive and the other declares it meaningless.
Both take grey hair as the sign to heed: the Naladiyar's wise renounced in childhood knowing it would come, Tirumular faults those who see black hair turn white and still do not grasp it.

Both use dew on a grass blade. The Naladiyar makes it the body's brief life and urges good deeds now; Tirumular makes it the rare drop of bindu from which the body's strength grows, something to be kept rather than a reminder of loss.

Both start from the perishing body. The Naladiyar's wise see it as a bubble and resolve to end their births; Tirumular faults people for not guarding what keeps the body. The facts agree, the response differs.

Kural 148 calls not looking at another man's wife (பிறன்மனை நோக்காத) the great manliness of the worthy. 1937 asks the yogi to leave without looking at the women he sees (பார்க்கின்ற மாதரைப் பாராது அகன்று) and to lay waste the eye's desire. The Kural's rule of conduct about one class of women becomes in 1937 a discipline of the eye toward all, turned to the root centre.

Kural 360 says pain perishes when even the names of காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் perish. 1938 says one who harbours காமாதி (lust and its kin) lives in fear (உட்கும்), and that Siva-yoga does not stay without grace. Both name the same triad as the root of suffering; 1938 adds that removing it is grace's work before technique's.

195 says: considering how the earth must pass, do good (அறஞ்செய்மின்) and praise the Pure One. Kural 36 says do good without putting it off, for when you perish it is a companion that does not perish (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). Both ground the call to virtue in the certainty of passing.
Both see woman as கூற்று, Death. In the Kural the lover discovers it, struck by her eyes; Tirumular makes it a deliberate meditation that ends desire and with it death.

Kural 941 says the three humours the learned count, beginning with wind (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று), cause disease in excess or lack. 1955 names சீதம் and பித்தம் with waste as what must be removed before union. The same humoral medicine that the Kural applies to daily health Tirumular applies to conception.

Kural 350 says: cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு). 1956 says that if one holds without clinging (பற்றறப் பற்றினால்) the pride of delusion dies. Both turn the word பற்று against itself: a holding that frees from holding.

Kural 122 says to guard restraint as wealth, for life has no greater gain (ஆக்கம்) than அடக்கம். 1957 names among the things one must know about bindu அடக்கத்தில் ஆக்கமும், the increase that comes by restraint. The same pairing of restraint and gain, ethical in the Kural, is bodily in Tirumular.
The Kural says hunger never touches one used to sharing his food; Tirumular asks for a ladleful given before each good meal, the same habit in its smallest form.

Both make shared food the right use of plenty: the Naladiyar tells one who gains wealth to eat with many from that day, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; Tirumular asks for a ladleful before one eats.

The Naladiyar quells desire by taking the woman's body apart into entrails and blood. Tirumular does not reject union: kept with bindu unspent, it is Siva's own pleasure, and only the fool's infatuation is condemned.
Both rank not killing above ritual offering: the Kural above a thousand oblations of ghee, Tirumular as the brightest of the flowers of worship.

Both say killing is paid for after this life, but differently: the Kural through rebirth in a wretched, diseased body, Tirumular through hell; and Tirumular extends the guilt to those who only urged the killing.
Both send the flesh-eater to hell; the Kural says hell's mouth will not open to let him out, Tirumular describes his being flung into fire-mouthed hell.
Both make eating creatures a deed that returns on the eater; the Naladiyar's crab-eater gets a wasting disease in a later life, Tirumular's flesh-eater hell.

2001 says the darkness of bond and ignorance (அஞ்ஞானம்) vanished by the light of Siva that is knowledge, as dense darkness leaves at dawn; Kural 352 says true perception removes darkness (இருள்நீங்கி) and brings joy to those free of confusion (மருள்நீங்கி). Both make knowledge the light that ends inner darkness; the Tirumanthiram names that light as Siva's, the Kural leaves it as clear sight.

2009 makes the soul pure by the light 'as with the seed of the spreading banyan' (படர்கொண்ட ஆலதின் வித்து); Naladiyar 38 says a tiny banyan seed (ஆலம்வித்து) grows to shade so vast the sky seems small, and so does a small gift given to the worthy. Both use the banyan seed for something minute that holds a vast growth: in the Naladiyar the fruit of virtue, in the Tirumanthiram the soul (அணு) once its bonds are driven off.
Both argue from the wife already at home: the Naladiyar asks why a man with a loving wife looks at another's, Tirumular calls it leaving ripe jackfruit for a wild date.
Both end the adulterer with a lost leg: in the Naladiyar the leg is cut off as the king's punishment if he is caught, in Tirumular he breaks it falling from the sour mango he climbed.

Both judge outward ascetic marks worthless without inner change: the Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what is condemned (Parimelazhagar counts hair-plucking under shaving); Tirumular says hair-tearers do not know the impurities or grace.

Both picture the senses as five elephants to be controlled. The Kural says the one who guards them with the goad of firmness is a seed for release; Tirumular shows the mahout exhausted and confesses he does not know how to manage it. The goal agrees; the confidence that it can be done does not.

Both count five senses and the gates through which craving comes and goes, and make guarding them the way to release; the Naladiyar names the five gates, Tirumular adds the nine openings and a herdsman.
Two animal images for the same discipline: the Kural's tortoise draws its five limbs in; Tirumular's five lions go out to feed and must have claws and teeth cut. Withdrawal against disarming.

2029 bids one shut the pot of countless holes (எண்ணிலி இல்லி) in the dark room and not go along with it; Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot (கும்பம்) seeping through nine openings that the fool praises. If இல்லி is the perforated pot, both picture the body as a leaking vessel: the Naladiyar to cure desire for it, the Tirumanthiram to bid its openings closed. The reading of 2029 is uncertain.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate; Tirumular gives fate's great strength the earth but assigns heaven to praise and human life to the mind, so fate is one power among several. The tension depends on reading 2030's domains as limits.

2032 says he who sets about curbing the restless senses (இந்திரியம் அடக்கல்) is himself immortal (அமரன்); Kural 6 says those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five sense-doors (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) live long (நீடுவாழ்வார்). Both promise lasting life for sense-restraint; the Kural gives it to those who follow the restrained one, the Tirumanthiram to the one who restrains.

The Kural says the field of the five must be crushed (அடல்வேண்டும்); Tirumular calls those who say 'curb the five' ignorant and says full curbing makes one inert. The conflict holds if 2033 is read as rejecting suppression of the senses, as its wording says, rather than only a wrong method of it.

Both treat the five senses as elephants to be held, the Kural's guarded by the goad of firmness (on Parimelazhagar's reading), Tirumular's by a fort of knowledge. In the Kural the guard works; in Tirumular the elephants break out.
Both make mastery of the five a supreme power: the Kural calls Indra witness to it, Tirumular calls it the wide world, tapas and Hara's state.
Both say a woman's attractive surface hides what should repel: the Naladiyar the body's foulness under the skin, Tirumular poison under fair leaves and fruit.
Both count life away by its units of time, the Kural's day a saw cutting life, Tirumular's nazhigais and days already gone; Tirumular draws the lesson of conquering the senses now.

2043 says 'கைவிடலாவது ஒன்று இல்லை', there is nothing one must give up, if one reaches him in thought and sings; Kural 341 says from whatever one has left, from that one has no pain, making release from pain follow each thing renounced. On the reading that 2043 answers the call to renounce objects, the two disagree on whether giving things up is the way; if 2043 means only that renunciation is secondary to praise, they differ in emphasis.

2045 says false gurus have looked over mantra, tantra, yoga and jnana but do not reflect and do not make others clear (தெளிவியாது), teaching for food; Naladiyar 318 says some fill houses with books without grasping their meaning, and those who understand and make others understand (தேற்றும் புலவர்) are another kind. Both separate possessing the texts from understanding them well enough to make another clear.

2046 calls a false guru one not free of lust and the rest (காமாதி நீங்கா) who teaches the unreal to others; Kural 834 says no fool is greater than one who studies, understands and teaches others (பிறர்க்குரைத்தும்) but does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). Both condemn the teacher whose own passions are unrestrained; the Tirumanthiram adds that what such a teacher passes on is அசத்து, the unreal.

205 says the pleasure of the man who enters another's home seeps up like a dream and cannot be had as things are had awake (கனவது போலக் ... நனவது போலவும் நாடவொண்ணாதே). In Kural 1215 the woman sets waking and dream side by side and finds each sweet when seen (நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ... கனவுந்தான்). The same dream and waking pair, which the Kural uses to make the dream equal to waking, 205 uses to show the stolen pleasure is no more than a dream.
Both shrink the adulterer's pleasure: small against great fear in the Naladiyar, a dream and a whirlpool in Tirumular.

2055 says that when the guru's presence is revealed 'the self must win itself' (தானே தனைப்பெற வேண்டும்). The Kural praises one who has wholly gained his own self (தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப்பெற்றானை), whom all beings worship. Tirumular places the same self-gaining inside the guru's presence, as the fruit of initiation rather than of tapas alone.
Both describe a woman who promises closeness and then turns away; the Naladiyar's said she would never part, Tirumular's bids the man stay near and leaves talking to others.

Both deny that hidden wrong is hidden: in the Kural the five elements within laugh at the deceiver's concealed conduct, in Tirumular the Lord stands everywhere as overseer. The Kural's witness is in the body, Tirumular's is the Lord.

2068 opens 'he knows what was done' (செய்தான் அறியும்), which the nuance notes may also be 'the doer himself knows', and promises that those who speak truth will be worshipped by the gods. The Kural says not to lie about what one's own heart knows (தன்நெஞ்சு அறிவது), for the heart will burn the liar. On the second reading of செய்தான் அறியும், both ground truthfulness in the doer's own knowledge of the deed; on the first, Siva stands where the Kural puts the heart.

2069's riddle says those who pound and eat the seed-grain (வித்துக்குற்றுண்டு) and lay waste the field have no birth, read as destroying the seed of karma. The Kural names craving as the seed (வித்து) that produces unceasing birth. The Kural says what the seed is; Tirumular's madmen are those who destroy it.

Both use sugarcane to show sweetness changing over time: the Naladiyar's cane eaten from the tip grows sweeter like the friendship of the learned, Tirumular's cane juice in the hand turns to neem in the body.

2081 tells the reader to give up சிற்றின்பம், petty pleasure, for the sweetness of the Lord. The Kural says those who want the other joy do not do wrong out of desire for சிற்றின்பம். Both set the same word against a greater joy, though in the Kural the small joy is gain from coveting and in Tirumular it is sensual pleasure.

2084 mocks those who store seed, sow and plant out seedlings without knowing their lifespan is ending (அற்றதம் வாணாள் அறிகிலா). The Kural mocks those who cannot know they will live one moment yet think thoughts in crores. Both set long-range plans against a span no one can count on; Tirumular's example is the farming year.
Both ask what is gained by learning or argument that does not end in bowing at the Lord's feet; Tirumular names disputation (வாது) where the Kural names learning.

2086 describes those who tend the body as if it were life (உடம்பினை ஓம்பி உயிரா) and end on a pyre of rough logs. Naladiyar 37 says one should not live doing service only to the body (உடம்பிற்கே ஒப்புரவு செய்தொழுகாது) but act for the world above. Both fault spending a life on the body's upkeep; the Naladiyar adds what to do instead.
Both describe the poor man estranged from those closest to him; the Kural goes as far as his own mother.
Both say kin and dependants fall away from the poor: the Naladiyar's crows leave the carcass and no one asks 'are you well?', Tirumular's dependants turn unloving.
The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular laments those who, given a rare human birth, never cherish those feet and so lose what that birth was for.

2091 says that in boundless youth people stand in the work of lust, which soon runs out (தீர வருவதோர் காமத் தொழில்), and forget the great one's joy. Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit and the spear-eyed woman too will walk bent with a staff, so she should not be desired. Both tie lust to youth and argue against it from youth's passing.

2094 warns that one who does not worship daily becomes an elephant that has thrown off its fear (அஞ்சு அற்று விட்டதோர் ஆனை), with அஞ்சு also 'the five'. The Kural praises one who guards the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும்). Both picture the uncontrolled self as an elephant; Tirumular's goad is worship, the Kural's is firmness.

Naladiyar 10 says misers who hoard without giving lose it, as the honey bee's store shows (தேனீக் கரி). 2097 uses the bee's labour over honey too, but sets beside it a honey that comes to the mouth without toil. The Naladiyar's bee teaches loss; Tirumular's contrast points to a sweetness not gathered by effort.
Both press for action before death arrives: the Kural before the hiccup stops the tongue, Tirumular while the porridge still boils and death runs near.

2099 says death comes leaping and the allotted days have fallen away, so stir the porridge while it boils (கொதிக்கின்ற கூழில் துடுப்பிடலாமே). Naladiyar 20 says death roams looking for its people, so take provisions in good time. Both argue from death's nearness that the work must be done now.
Both say what can never be filled is ended not by filling it but by removing its cause: craving in the Kural, impurity in Tirumular. This depends on reading the pit as desire and not only the belly.

2100 warns that the days before grey hair (நரை) are few, with திரை (wave, wrinkle) for the coming of age. Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair (நரை) will come, renounced in childhood. Both use grey hair as the deadline for turning to austerity.

Both deny that birth ranks people: the Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Tirumular says kin is one and God is one. The Kural keeps a distinction by deeds that Tirumular does not mention.

2106 asks when this body came to be ours (எக்காலத்து இவ்வுடல் வந்து எமக்கு ஆனது) and bids one seek the way not to enter another body; Kural 340 asks whether the life, a lodger (துச்சில்) in the body, has no home of its own. The Kural's question about the soul's tenancy becomes in the Tirumanthiram a practice: reflecting on the body as not one's own is the way to grace and to ending further lodgings.
Both make reaching the Lord the end of births: the Kural's crossing of the sea of births, Tirumular's freedom from all birth for the soul that holds the Lord in mind at death.

2108 pictures the soul as 'the one that flies' (பறக்கின்ற ஒன்று), which reaches its goal if the Lord is thought of at death; Kural 338 likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள் பறந்தற்றே). The Kural uses the flight to show how slight the bond is; the Tirumanthiram asks where the flight ends, and makes its end depend on the last thought.

2110 says the one of unfailing fame (கேடில் புகழோன்), by whom strong deeds perish (கெடுகின்ற வல்வினை), places those who seek his feet among the celestials; Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise (பொருள்சேர் புகழ்). Both join the Lord's fame to the ending of deeds; the Tirumanthiram sets this at the moment of rising upward, which the Kural does not.

2113 says there is one true austerity (மெய்த்தவம்), one true foot and one true path to take up, for those who stand wishing to take them up (வேண்டி நின்றோர்க்கே); Kural 265 says austerity is striven for here because one obtains what one wants as one wants it (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). Both tie tapas to the seeker's wanting; the Kural to what it yields, the Tirumanthiram to who may take it up.

2114 says the fire-coloured one gives joy to those who come to him (சார்ந்தவர்க்கு இன்பம்) and painful birth to those who turn away (பேர்ந்தவர்க்கு இன்னாப் பிறவி); Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere (அடி சேர்ந்தார்க்கு யாண்டும் இடும்பை இல). The Tirumanthiram adds the other half the Kural leaves unstated, and its verb கொடுத்திடும் puts the painful birth in the Lord's giving, where the Kural's வேண்டாமை இலான் names no aversion at all.
Both treat ties as obstacles to ending births: the Kural asks why one bent on that would keep other ties when even the body is excess, Tirumular calls clinging kin worse than deeds.

Both list the body's stuffs, fat, blood, bone, flesh, skin. The Naladiyar asks which of these is the beloved, to cure desire; Tirumular names them as the gross adjunct beneath the subtle bodies, without disgust.
Both name the five senses as what must be overcome; the Kural says their domain must be crushed, Tirumular describes the suffering they cause until one turns to the Lord.

The Naladiyar says the great saw the body's foulness and abandoned it; Tirumular calls those who disregard the body as filth dull and finds the cosmos in it. The conflict holds if மலம் in 2137 is read as bodily filth, as here.
Tirumular praises the oblation as sustaining sky, earth and gods; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations. Read together, the rite keeps its worth but not the first place.

The Kural calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Tirumular says vows and gifts are no sure support for the perishing flesh. The two can agree if the Kural speaks of the person and Tirumular of the body; the verse does not settle which it means.
Tirumular takes the Kural's own phrase, உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு. The Kural says that bond ends as a bird leaves its shell; Tirumular faults people who never come to know it.
Both separate the life from the body it lives in: the Naladiyar's dancer leaves the skin bag, and Tirumular's fools cling to bodies without knowing the life inside.
If புறங்கொடுத்து உண்ணுவர means eating after giving, both describe the worthy as feeding others first and eating after.

Kural 27 says the world is within the grasp of one who discerns the five, taste, light, touch, sound and smell (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு). 2153 says that once the five senses, their five objects and the four inner instruments are understood together (ஒருங்கே உணர்ந்தபின்), he abides as the whole cosmos (அண்டமும் தானாய்), turning the Kural's mastery of the world into identity with it.

Kural 339 explains death by sleep: dying is like falling asleep (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு). 2155 describes deep sleep in the terms of death: self-regard gone, understanding gone, the body undone (மேனி அழிந்து), knowing nothing in the unmanifest. The same likeness is read from opposite ends.
Both use the tortoise drawing in for the five senses held in. In the Kural it is self-restraint that guards through seven births; in Tirumular it follows when the silent and spoken letters meet.

2161 says the soul reaches release directly through the knowledge it contemplates (எண்ணுறு ஞானத்தின் நேர்முத்தி எய்துமே). Kural 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not returning here; both make knowledge the direct way out of birth, though 2161 adds the Lord's grace (அண்ணல் அருள்).
Both treat birth as a waking from sleep. The Kural uses it to show how quickly birth and death alternate; Tirumular makes embodiment the Lord's waking of the soul from anava's deeper sleep.

2175 says what is to come comes and what is to go goes (போவன போவ புகுவ புகுவன). Kural 376 says what is not yours will not stay though guarded, and what is yours will not leave though thrown away (சொரியினும் போகா தம). Both teach that things run their appointed course; 2175 adds that Nandi showed it.
Both make the letter A stand for what is first: the Kural compares God's place in the world to A among letters, and Tirumular names the real tattva the letter A.

2192 makes the husk and bran on the grain (முளைக்குத் தவிடுஉமி) the malas round the soul, to be separated (பாசம் பிரித்தே). Naladiyar 221 uses the same husk (நெல்லுக்கு உமியுண்டு) for the faults a chosen friend is born with, which one should bear rather than cast off. The same image argues for removal in the one and for forbearance in the other.
Both trace a bad end to delusion: the Kural's confusion that takes the unreal as real yields a joyless birth, and in 2194 the soul whose delusion grows reaches the seven hells.

220 says those who know great wealth to be ruin (பெருஞ்செல்வம் கேடென்று) keep to the oblation as the rare wealth (அருஞ்செல்வத்து ஆகுதி). Kural 241 ranks the wealth of grace as the wealth among wealths (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), since goods are found even among the base. Both keep the word செல்வம் and move it from goods to something else: the fire rite in Tirumular, kindness in the Kural.

Both make release the end of an obscuring mixture: the Kural's stainless sight, freed from confusion, removes darkness and brings joy; Tirumular says Shakti, knowledge and Siva are hidden by mala and light appears when the mixture ends. Tirumular names what hides; the Kural names only confusion.

The Kural guards the five senses with the elephant goad of firmness; Tirumular ends his verse on standing in the true way before the mind scatters with a charging elephant. The pairing holds if 2215's elephant is the mastered senses or mind; if it is the strength one gains, the images only touch.

The Kural says that one who loves himself should go near no evil deed, however small (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்). 2228 states the ground of that advice: the self is its own friend and enemy and itself eats the fruit of the deeds it did (தானே தனக்குப் பகைவனும் நட்டானும்).

Both say a person is the maker of his own rise and fall: the Naladiyar names who sets a man up and casts him down and answers 'himself', Tirumular says he is his own enemy, friend, next world and master.

The Kural says stainless sight removes darkness and confusion and brings joy (இருள்நீங்கி ... மாசறு காட்சி). 2245 also has darkness end and purity come (மத்த இருள் ... சுத்தஆவார்கள்), but the light that ends it is Siva's ray, not the seer's own clear sight.

The Kural defines purity as the absence of craving, which comes by wanting truth (தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை). 2262 defines purity as non-birth (பிறவாமை சுத்தமே), reached when the two deeds balance, grace descends and the guru removes the great impurity. The verse puts purity's cause in grace, where the Kural puts it in the person's own ending of desire.
The Kural traces joyless birth to taking the unreal for the real; Tirumular's first error is the same kind, taking the body for the self, and it too ends in birth again.

Both use the figure of a child raised by a foster-mother (செவிலி / கைத்தாய்). In the Kural grace, born of love, is nursed by wealth; in 2268 the soul, born of mahamaya with Siva as father, is raised by maya. In both the nurse is a lower thing that serves a higher end.
Both play on பற்று: the Kural bids one cling to the one without clinging in order to let go, Tirumular says the Supreme is grasped as attachment ends.
Both define the Brahmin's state by regard for every living being: the Kural's அந்தணர் are clothed in kindness to all lives, Tirumular's Brahman includes knowing all lives as one's equal.
Both define the goal by the end of craving: the Kural says the freed are those freed of craving, Tirumular that Vedanta is the place where craving ends.

2293 says the five malas leave like evening darkness before a flame (சுடர்முனம் அந்தி இருள்போலும் ஐம்மலம் மாறுமே); Naladiyar 51 says sin cannot stand before austerity, as darkness dies when a lamp enters (விளக்குப் புக இருள் மாய்ந்தாங்கு). The same image does the work of grace in one verse and of tapas in the other, and the Naladiyar adds that darkness returns when the oil runs out.
Both deny that marks of the body make the holy man: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed, Tirumular that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair.
Both place the giving up of anger where one has the power to act on it: the Kural says restraint counts only where anger can take effect, Tirumular says let it go while you can still win.

Both use the tortoise drawing in its five. The Kural makes restraint of the senses in one birth a shelter through seven; Tirumular puts the tortoise in a silent well and promises it a thousand years if it withdraws into truth.

2305 says that for those who can run past the five elements and their gods, காலனும் இல்லை, there is no Death. Kural 269 says those who have gained the power of austerity can even leap past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Both make Death something a disciplined person passes beyond; the Kural names the means as tapas, the Tirumanthiram as passing through the elements.
Both make the Brahmin depend on conduct, not birth: the Kural says his birth is ruined when conduct declines, Tirumular denies the name to those without truth and knowledge.

2313 pictures the soul in its malam turning endlessly like waves on the sea (கடலில் திரை) through heaven, hell and earth, freed only by grace. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births. Both make release from the round of births depend on the Lord, and both use the sea for it.

2314 says that when the soul becomes Siva, malam, bonds and gunas fade like the moon before the sun. Naladiyar 51 says sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness dies when a lamp comes in, but darkness rushes back when the oil runs out. The Naladiyar's lamp limits the victory to the life of the merit that feeds it; the Tirumanthiram's sun is the Siva-state itself and has no oil to run out.

Both treat the five senses as elephants to be mastered (in the Kural through the goad of firmness, as Parimelazhagar reads it). The Kural's reward is the field of release; Tirumular adds a lamp of knowledge lit inside the body.
The Kural defines understanding as seeing the true thing in whatever thing appears; Tirumular narrows it to knowing oneself, and calls every other knowing a ghoul's.

2327 says there is no need to teach those already full of knowledge (அறிவிற் செறிவோர்); the wise teach only those who have learned and stand in unknowing. Kural 718 says speaking before those who understand (உணர்வது உடையார்) is like watering a crop that is already growing. On Parimelazhagar's reading, that such speech makes the growth greater, the two disagree on whether the knowing are worth addressing; on the plain reading that the watering is redundant, they agree.

Kural 370 says that giving up craving, never satisfied, at once gives a nature that never shifts (ஆரா இயற்கை அவாநீப்பின் ... பேரா இயற்கை தரும்). 2336 says the soul's desire is withered by knowledge and so reaches the high state, but adds that the same Shakti first fed that desire (உயிரிச்சை யூட்டி). The Kural states the result; the Tirumanthiram makes both the craving and its ending the work of one power.

2339 says the reformed leave hell, leave splendid heaven too (திருவார் சுவர்க்கம்), and become Siva. Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Both place the goal above heaven; the Tirumanthiram says outright that heaven must be left.
Tirumular's அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டு: both define the அந்தணர் by a coolness of heart they wear. Tirumular adds that the land where they live prospers.

Kural 400 calls learning the wealth that does not perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்). 2358 says knowledge has neither destruction nor making (அழிவில்லை ஆக்கமும் இல்லை) and rests on nothing but itself. Both praise what cannot be lost, but the Kural's learning is acquired while the Tirumanthiram's knowledge was never made.

The Kural sets understanding against the folly (பேதைமை) that is birth. Tirumular says the knowledge that frees lies beyond both the world's knowledge and its ignorance, so the line falls not between them but past them.
Both make understanding a kind of total possession: the Kural says those with it have everything, Tirumular that their heart is the wide world itself and the place where the first Lord stays.

Kural 299 says not all lamps are lamps; for the worthy only the unfailing lamp (பொய்யா விளக்கு) is a lamp. 2367 sets the lamp of maya that goes out and the lamp of the body that smoulders against the pure lamp that keeps its flame. Both rank lamps and keep one; the Kural's is truth, the Tirumanthiram's is pure knowledge, with a farther lamp still sought.

2369 says those who remove the great malam, know themselves and abide in their ancient Lord do not come to birth again (வாரா பிறப்பே). Kural 357 says one whose mind ponders and knows what is (உள்ளது உணரின்) need not think again of birth. Both make true knowing the end of rebirth; the Tirumanthiram adds the removal of malam and union with the Lord.
If the two attachments are 'I' and 'mine', both say cutting them raises one above the gods: the Kural to a world higher than theirs, Tirumular to an offering they receive.
Both say Death does not approach the good: the Kural that it does not advance on one who keeps from killing, Tirumular that it spares the good while the unlearned king kills.
Both tie the land's prosperity to the king's conduct: the Kural rain and harvest to just rule, Tirumular the land's decline to a king who neglects austerity.

The Tirumanthiram says that if the king does not look daily to the right way, 'நாள்தோறும் நாடு கெடும்', the land declines day by day; Kural 553 says the king who does not examine and do justice daily, 'நாடொறு நாடு கெடும்'.
