The two share the same closing phrase almost word for word; Tirumular makes the daily duty a matter of தவநெறி, the way of austerity, where the Kural makes it முறை, justice.

2390 says that though souls do not think of the One, of themselves, their two deeds or the two mayas, the One stands within and feeds them (உள் உணர்ந்து நின்று ஊட்டி). The Kural says that even those who amass millions can enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால்). 2390 names who the apportioner is and makes the feeding inward.
Both call what true knowledge reaches செம்பொருள், the perfect thing, and tie it to release. The Kural leaves it unnamed; Tirumular says Siddhanta and Vedanta are that perfect meaning and show Siva.
Both condemn holy garb worn without the life it stands for; Tirumular adds that the king should force such men to live by it.

2401 ends with the soul become Hara as water becomes milk (நீர் பாலாதல்). Naladiyar 177 says water mixed with milk becomes milk and no longer shows its own colour (பாலோடு அளாயநீர் பாலாகும்), of small men joined to the great. The same image of losing one's colour in a greater body is used of company in the Naladiyar and of the soul's union with Siva in 2401.

The Tirumanthiram has the king test, through the wise, those who wear matted hair, tuft and thread (சடை சிகை நூல்) while lacking knowledge, and bring them to knowledge; Kural 280 says shaving or long hair is not needed at all if one gives up what the world condemns. Both make the marks worthless without the inner substance, but the Kural drops the marks while Tirumular keeps them and has the king correct those who wear them.
The Kural asks for cutting the pride that says 'I' and 'mine'; Tirumular names that 'I'-saying as anava, the root bond itself, and adds that grace is the means of its removal.
Both join the Lord's feet to the head. The Kural calls a head that does not bow to them useless; in Tirumular the feet come down onto the head, as grace given rather than worship offered.
Both say the king who fails to guard harms cows and the virtuous; the Kural gives the cost to the land (less milk, forgotten books), Tirumular the cost to the king (hell).

2434 says the Lord, like a parent who has seen his sons' faults, deals with each soul by its nature (உயிரது பான்மைக்கு) and without anger (செற்றமிலா). Kural 561 says a king is one who examines fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது). The same logic of weighing the case and answering it in measure appears for the Lord's dealing with souls and for a king's justice.

2435 says those who leave the three faults are freed and those who do not are caught in the three and perish (மூன்றினுள் பட்டு முடிகின்றவாறே). Kural 360 says that when even the names of the three, desire, anger and confusion, perish, pain perishes. The link holds if 2435's unnamed three are the ones 2436 names next (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்), as the chapter suggests.

Tirumular takes the Kural's three, காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம், word for word. The Kural says that when their very names perish, suffering perishes; Tirumular says that with them driven out he reached the abode within Om.

The Tirumanthiram says that one who wants release and wealth (முத்தியும் செல்வமும்) must keep to the path of dharma without lapse; Kural 31 says virtue yields distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்) and asks what gain is greater. Both make virtue the single source of both worldly and higher goods; Tirumular names the higher good as முத்தி.

Both use the cow and her calf. In the Naladiyar the calf finds its mother among many cows as an old deed finds its doer; in Tirumular the mother rises at the thought of her calf, as the Lord comes to the soul. One image carries karma, the other grace.

Both turn on பற்று: the Kural bids one cling to the one without clinging in order to let go of clinging; Tirumular repeats 'clinging so that clinging ends' in every line and makes it the way to the supreme beyond the supreme.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says one who comes to seize the world, for others or himself, has the evil nature of a pouncing tiger (பாய்ந்த புலியன்ன); Kural 552 says a king's demand is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over'. Both picture the grasping ruler as a predator, the Kural as a highway robber, Tirumular as a tiger.
Both use the crystal that shows what is near it. The Kural makes it the face showing the mind; Tirumular makes it the soul taking the colour of the Supreme it comes within.
Both make punishing wrongdoers a king's proper work, not a stain on him; Tirumular sets it beside punishment in the next world.
Both name the goal செம்பொருள். For the Kural, seeing it is the work of knowledge that ends birth; for Tirumular, Nandi as the true reality takes him and gives it by grace.
Both trace birth to not knowing what truly is: the Kural to the delusion that takes the unreal as real, Tirumular to souls that do not know what is. Tirumular adds that those who know come to grace.
Both call rain nectar (அமிழ்தம், அமுது): the Kural because the world is sustained by it, Tirumular because it makes the trees flow with nectar.
Both name a set of three whose ending ends the trouble: the Kural desire, anger and delusion, whose very names must perish; Tirumular the impurities and qualities, whose dying lets Siva appear.
Both use the crow that calls its flock before eating: the Kural for the wealth that comes to those who keep kin close, Tirumular as a lesson in giving.
Both say to share food with all before eating, friend or not; the Naladiyar warns that the door of the other world is shut on those who shut their door and eat.

Kural 24 says that one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness is a seed (வித்து) for the highest ground. 2506 says the seed of power is one's own stilling (தனது உபசாந்தம்). Both make self-restraint the seed of something higher; the Kural places the fruit in the world above, 2506 in the soul's own power and release.

2506 is built on வித்து: the seed of release is the Lord's knowledge, of devotion bowing and clinging, of attainment becoming Siva, of power one's own stillness. Kural 361 says craving is the seed (வித்து) that produces unceasing birth for all beings. Set together, the Kural names the seed of birth and Tirumular names the seeds of release, with stillness as the opposite of craving.
Both speak of a sea to be crossed. The Kural's sea is births, swum only by those at the Lord's feet; Tirumular's knower has already seen the shore, the waves of the soul settled to clear water.
The Kural defines folly as the conceit 'we are wise'; Tirumular's heartless men say 'we know fully' while blind to the Lord, as futile as cutting the hare from the moon.

2512 likens those who claim full knowledge without seeing Siva to men taking up a sword to strike the hare in the crescent moon (பிறையுள் கிடந்த முயலை). Naladiyar 176 says the hare in the bright moon is worshipped along with it (முயலும் தொழப்படுஉம்), as the lowly gain worth from friends like hills. Both use the hare in the moon, the Naladiyar for borrowed worth and Tirumular for an idle reach at what cannot be touched.

Kural 331 calls it petty knowledge (புல்லறி வாண்மை) to take what does not last for what lasts. 2514 uses the same word for standing at the womb's gate (கருவாயில்) and fighting so that foes may die. 2514 applies the Kural's term to hostile striving bound to birth, where the Kural applies it to mistaking the transient.
Both make mastering the five senses the condition of reaching the Lord: the Kural's one who quenched the five senses, Tirumular's one who conquers them and knows him as one.

Both set the bar for giving so low no one can refuse it: the Naladiyar asks for even a fragment of a rice grain daily before eating, Tirumular a handful before eating, with a leaf for God and a kind word added.

Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge (வாலறிவன்). 2520 says the Lord is good within the learning of those whose minds are not soured (கன்றா மனத்தார்தம் கல்வியுள் நல்லவன்). Both tie learning's worth to the Lord; 2520 adds the condition that the learner's mind be unsoured.

Both name the pride of 'I' and 'mine' as what must be cut. The Kural promises a world beyond the gods' to the one who cuts it; Tirumular makes cutting it, with the lesser releases set aside, the mark of the Siva-siddha.

The Tirumanthiram compares the merit of feeding the destitute to a well or tank (கூவல் குளம்) that people come to and drink from; Kural 215 says the wealth of the wise man who serves the world is like a full village drinking tank (ஊருணி). Both use the public water tank as the figure of wealth that belongs to everyone who needs it.
Both make feeding those who have nothing the very form of virtue; the Kural calls it where the wealthy store their wealth, Tirumular says the learned call such food virtue itself.
Both press good deeds by picturing the deathbed: the Kural's hiccup that stops the tongue, Tirumular's fever and eyes that no longer open.

2541: saying 'my Lord' within night and day, the poet found the Lord cut away strong karma (வல்வினை). Kural 5: the two deeds born of darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not cling to those who hold to the Lord's true praise. Both make constant turning to the Lord the thing that frees one from deeds; Tirumular puts it as the Lord's act, the Kural as a fact about the devotee.

The Tirumanthiram says to do austerity in its right way before Death comes, Death that takes no account of whether one is young (இளையர் என்று ஓராது); Kural 36 says do virtue without saying 'later' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது), since it is the companion that does not perish when one perishes. Both answer the excuse of delay with the coming of death; Tirumular names youth as the false comfort.
Both reject youth as a reason to put off virtue: the Naladiyar's storm drops unripe fruit, Tirumular's Death does not ask whether one is young.

Both say people do not know what the body is. For the Naladiyar its truth is the stinking cart the vultures tear when life leaves it; for Tirumular it holds Nandi, fragrant within. The tension holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a judgement of the body itself, not only of vanity about adorning it.

2551: the ignorant cry 'impurity, impurity' (ஆசூசம்) but do not know where impurity lies. Kural 278: many with impurity in their minds (மனத்தது மாசாக) bathe as if distinguished and go about concealed. Both move impurity from the rites people observe to the mind, and the Kural names the place 2551 says no one knows.

The Kural sets outer purity by water against inner purity by truthfulness; Tirumular also moves purity inward but keeps ritual among its sources: discipline, worship, the fire rite and knowledge free one from ritual impurity.
Both set the Real (பொருள்) against delusion (மருள்): the Kural makes taking the unreal for the real the cause of base births; Tirumular leaves all but the Lord's devotees whirling in delusion.

2558: those who say there is no higher state (பரகதி இல்லை) go the way of hell, as the world knows. Kural 850: one who says 'it is not' to what the world says is (உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) is set down on earth as a demon. Both condemn the denier and both appeal to the world's agreement (ஞாலம் அறியும், உலகத்தார்); the Kural places the penalty in this life, Tirumular in the next.

2562: the wretched (கலதிகள்), shown the way to see (காண்வழி காட்ட), cannot see (கண் காணா). Kural 849: one who shows the unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான்) himself does not see, and the unseeing sees only as he already saw. Both use showing and not seeing for the fool beyond teaching; the Kural adds that the shower is the one shamed.

2567: when the aimed arrow struck, the five killing elephants (கொல்லுங் களிறு ஐந்தும்) fell. Kural 24: one who guards the five (ஓரைந்தும்) with the goad (தோட்டி) of firmness is a seed for heaven. Both treat the five senses as elephants; the Kural controls them with a goad, Tirumular's aimed arrow fells them.
Both picture a great sea to be crossed. In the Kural it is the sea of births, swum by reaching the Lord's feet; Tirumular makes it the sea of deeds, crossed in the boat of austerity and virtue.
Both see the body as a bubble. The Naladiyar's wise draw from it the resolve to end their births; Tirumular sets the bubble beside camphor in fire and has the body go into the Supreme.

The Tirumanthiram calls the Lord 'the support that stands as support' (பற்றது வாய்நின்ற பற்று) and ties his teaching to the path of virtue and giving; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). Both play on பற்று to make the Lord the one attachment worth holding.

2595 says the teachings of grace, held through the fire, are like gold refined of its flaw in fire (குற்றம் அறுத்த பொன் போலும் கனலிடை), and one becomes a bright flame (செழுஞ்சுடர்). Kural 267 says those who endure pain shine like gold that brightens the more it is burned (சுடச்சுடரும் பொன்போல்). Both use firing of gold for purification; the Kural's fire is ascetic suffering, Tirumular's is holding to the guru's teaching.

Both deny that knowledge profits by itself: the Kural asks what learning gains without worship of the one of pure knowledge, Tirumular says knowing all things gains nothing apart from the all-knowing.
The Kural says knowledge from the five senses is no gain without true perception; Tirumular says knowing everything is no gain apart from the knowledge that knows everything.

2599 says grace comes to those who, with minds free of darkness (இருளற்ற சிந்தை), change their deluded mind (மருளுற்ற சிந்தையை மாற்றி) and praise the feet. Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight, free of confusion (மருள்நீங்கி), darkness goes and joy comes (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம்). Both pair the clearing of இருள் and மருள் as the condition of the good that follows; Tirumular names it grace, the Kural joy.

Both compare unshared wealth to the fruit of the poisonous etti. In the Kural it ripens in the middle of town where no one can use it; in Tirumular it ripens and falls, and the usurer buries his store in the ground.

The Kural says one who is not false in his heart dwells in the hearts of all people; Tirumular says the Lord dwells with those mingled in truth and does not enter before the false. Truthfulness opens the heart in both: to others in the Kural, to the Lord in Tirumular.

2606 says the Lord sits in the midst of those who shine without any falsehood (பொய்யொன்றுமின்றிப் புறம்பொலிவார்). Kural 299 says that for the worthy the only lamp is the lamp of not lying (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). Both picture truthfulness as a light; Tirumular adds that the Lord is found among such people.

Both make the way out of bondage a following: the Kural says cling to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go, Tirumular says cut the senses' bond and follow the one who cut away confusion.
The Kural praises those who keep to the path of the one who quenched the five senses; Tirumular tells the seeker to cut the five senses' bond and follow the one who has done so.
Both fault the person who watches beauty, youth and bodies pass and still does no good thing.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than what is apportioned, which arrives before any scheme to avoid it. Tirumular grants that former karma must be lived out, but adds that the jnani can stop karma not yet made, which the Kural's verse does not address.
Both have the wise meet arriving karma calmly: the Naladiyar's wise take it as old debt and are freed of confusion, Tirumular's jnanis live it out and are rid of it.
Both free the Lord's own from the hold of deeds: in the Kural the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise him, in Tirumular the jnani unties former karma by Siva's grace.
Both make cutting desire the one test that counts: the Kural says only those free of desire are truly free, Tirumular says yogic talk of breath is useless until desire and attachment are cut.

2614 says the Lord is not in the temple or in the ascetic's garb (வேடத்துளான் அலன) but in the heart of those who have given up longing. Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா). Both set the ascetic's outward marks aside for the inner giving up.

The Kural tells the renouncer to cling to the one free of clinging as the means of letting go; Tirumular tells him to cut desire even for the Lord. It depends on reading ஈசனோடாயினும் as desire directed at the Lord himself.
Both say desire is the source of sorrow and its ending brings unbroken joy: the Kural calls desire the sorrow of sorrows, Tirumular says bliss grows as desire is let go.

2616 says to fling away attachment (பற்றற வீசி) that makes the path of suffering, and that letting go of longing is true knowledge. Kural 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) births are cut off. Both make the ending of பற்று the decisive act; the Kural names birth as what ends, Tirumular suffering.
Both tie release to mastering the longing (வேட்கை) that works through the five: the Naladiyar has it guarded at the five gates of the senses, Tirumular has it flung away with the five elements.

2617 says the gods slept caught in one sea and earth's people sank in the sea of desire (அவாக்கடல் உட்பட்டு அழுந்தினர்), while the Lord holds the sea that never fails. Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). Both picture bondage as a sea, the Kural's of births, Tirumular's of desire, with the Lord as what stands above it.
Both set அவா (desire) beside தவா (unfailing): the Kural calls desire the seed of unfailing births, Tirumular has humans sunk in the sea of desire while the Lord holds the unfailing sea.

The Tirumanthiram says those who do not know virtue (அறம்அறியார்) do not know how to think of the Lord's feet (அண்ணல் பாதம் நினையுந் திறம்); Kural 8 calls the Lord a sea of virtue (அறவாழி) and says only those who reach his feet cross the other seas. The Kural joins virtue and the feet in the Lord; Tirumular makes knowing virtue the condition of approaching those feet.

2627 has the poet call like a calf for his Lord, and the Lord come seeking him like the cow. Naladiyar 101 says a calf among many cows finds its own mother, and an old deed likewise seeks out its doer (தாய்நாடிக் கோடலை). The calf-and-mother search is in one the Lord seeking the soul, in the other karma seeking the man.
The Kural says the fiery disease of hunger will not touch one who shares his food; Tirumular extends the promise to cough, fever and tumour, taking literally what the Kural keeps to hunger.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says those who stray from the path go back into the womb (கருப்பு ஆரும்) while those who keep it drive off the stain of deeds (வினை மாசு); Kural 38 says doing good every day is a stone that blocks the road of births (வழியடைக்கும் கல்). Both make steady right conduct what closes rebirth, and both use the figure of the road (வழி).

The Kural calls a head that does not bow to the Lord's feet as useless as a sense that cannot perceive; Tirumular says the same from the other side, that his head, mouth, eyes and mind were given to him for Nandi.

2666 says that by cutting the many bonds and contemplating beyond thought one reaches the Lord of the tattvas, and he himself is dharma (தருமமும் தானே). Kural 8 calls the Lord whose feet one must reach a sea of dharma (அறவாழி அந்தணன்), without whom the other seas are hard to swim. Both make the Lord himself the dharma one reaches, not a giver of rules; the Tirumanthiram names bond-cutting as the way, the Kural reaching the feet.

The Kural makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; Tirumular names another measure, the mind that reaches the Lord, by which even the smallest become high. The two need not conflict, but the test differs.

Both make the small great by what they cling to: in the Naladiyar the hare is worshipped with the moon it lives in, so the slight gain worth by friendship with steady men; in Tirumular those as small as a split millet seed become high by reaching the Lord with a firm mind.
Both read present fortune as the fruit of past virtue: the Kural points to the palanquin's bearer and rider, Tirumular to joy and sorrow settled by former deeds.

2674 ends with Tirumular saying that, his mind made clear by Nandi's grace, he will bow to gods no more and has become what others go to worship (போய்வணங்கும் பொருளாயிருந்தோமே). Kural 268 says all other lives bow to the one who has wholly won his own self (தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை ஏனைய மன்னுயிர் எல்லாந் தொழும்). Both make the one who is inwardly won the object of others' worship; the Kural gives the cause as tapas, the Tirumanthiram as the guru's grace.
Both refuse gain got by leaving fairness: the Kural says to give it up the same day, Tirumular that the Lord will not let pleasure sought that way stand.

2686 lists the lights and says that, by pure words recited daily, the light matches the way one has contemplated it (உன்னியவாறு ஒளி ஒத்தது). Kural 666 says people obtain what they have thought of as they thought of it, if they are firm (எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப). The same logic, that the result takes the shape of the steady thought behind it, governs the yogi's inner light in one and worldly undertakings in the other.

2688 says it is the intent of Isan to take as nectar the poison that came from the salt sea (அளங்கொளி ஆரமுதாக நஞ்சாரும்). Kural 580 says those who want a refinement worth loving drink poison though they see it poured (பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண்டு அமைவர்). Both make knowingly swallowing poison the mark of a larger nature, in the god's cosmic act and in the courtesy of a cultivated man.

2693 says that saying 'it is' and 'it is not' (உண்டில்லை என்னும்) is the way of this world, and asks after a supreme goal of which 'it was not before' cannot be said. Kural 336 says this world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). On the reading that 2693's 'is and is not' is the world's transience, the Kural gives the plain fact and the Tirumanthiram sets against it the light within that has no gap.

2694 says Isan is the sun of a spreading vision (படருறு காட்சிப் பகலவன்), and that the dense darkness of maya (மாயையின் ஆரிருள்) is cast off by renouncing the world that clings to the body. Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left confusion, it removes darkness and brings joy (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும் மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு). Both tie the ending of darkness to a clear seeing; the Tirumanthiram names that seeing as the Lord himself and adds renunciation as its condition.

Both use light driving out darkness: in the Naladiyar austerity drives out sin as a lamp does darkness, and evil returns when good deeds run out like a lamp's oil; in Tirumular the Lord's light casts off maya's darkness through renunciation, with no word of its return.

Both begin from the letter A as the first of all letters. The Kural uses it as a simile for the Lord as first of the world; Tirumular traces the letters from A through Om to Na, the first letter of Nandi's name, so the alphabet itself leads to the Lord.

Both correct what 'the ignorant' (அறியார், அறிவிலார்) say about love: the Kural that love serves not only virtue but also against wrong, Tirumular that love is not a second thing beside Siva. Each widens love past a limit set on it.

Both free a person from deeds through the Lord's name: the Kural says the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who love his true praise, Tirumular that saying Siva Siva makes evil deeds die. Tirumular adds the converse, that evil-doers do not say it.

Both join bones, burning and love. In the Kural virtue scorches the loveless as the sun a boneless worm; in Tirumular a man burns his own bones and flesh, and without love it still does not reach God.

Both picture release as crossing to a shore: the Kural's great sea of births is crossed only by those who reach the Lord's feet, and in 2720 the one who masters the Lord's letter is a vessel that has reached the farther shore.

Both answer endless learning with a choice: the Naladiyar says learning has no shore and life is short, so take only what is fitting, as the swan takes milk from water; Tirumular names the one thing to take, the Lord's letter, and makes it the vessel that does reach the shore.

The Kural calls letters and numbers the two eyes of the living; 2721 calls those who boast of knowing letters fools, because they don't know the letter that masters letters. The difference rests on எழுத்து meaning script in the Kural and the mantra in Tirumular, so it qualifies rather than contradicts.

The Tirumanthiram says those with longing (ஆர்வம் உடையவர்) see Hara and those with tenderness (ஈரம்) see his feet; Kural 74 says love begets longing (அன்பு ஈனும் ஆர்வம் உடைமை), which begets friendship. The Kural's chain from love to longing to friendship among people is carried by Tirumular to longing that ends in seeing the Lord.

The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular uses the same 'reaching the feet' to define the devotee, and makes the feet those of the dancer seen in the golden hall.

2745 says that to see the drama of the dance, seeking ends, the senses stop running and desire ends (ஆசை அறும்), and the gaze of bliss is held; Kural 370 says that if one gives up craving, never filled by nature (அவாநீப்பின்), that very state gives a nature that does not shift. The Kural makes the end of desire the gate of a lasting state; 2745 sets that end of desire inside the vision of the dance, beside the stilled breath and gaze.

Kural 332 likens great wealth to the crowd gathering at a dance hall (கூத்தாட்டு அவைக் குழாத்து), and its loss to that crowd breaking up; 2746, after the mythic dances, ends with the Lord who dances in the hall for all days (நாளுற அம்பலத்தே ஆடும்). The Kural's dance hall is the figure of what disperses; Tirumular's is the one whose dance does not end.

Both put a dancer inside the body. The Naladiyar's dancer is the soul in its skin bag, and once it leaves, the body does not matter; Tirumular's dancers in every embodied life are Siva and Shakti themselves.

Both use liquor to measure an intoxication that comes without drinking. The Kural says brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, while love delights those who merely see; Tirumular says the frenzy of Siva's bliss comes to those who saw the dance and even to those who only heard of it.

On one reading the Tirumanthiram speaks of the Lord who made daily sleep and birth (நித்தலும் துஞ்சும் பிறப்பு); Kural 339 says death is like sleep and birth like waking. The Kural's figure of sleep as a small death helps read 278's compressed phrase as the order of sleep and birth that men know yet ignore.

Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities (எண்குணத்தான் தாளை வணங்காத் தலை) is useless; 2785 calls the Lord's flower feet the great jewel on the crowns of the crowned gods (வானவர் தம்முடி மேலுறை மாமணி) and the jewel rising in loving hearts. The Kural's head bowed to the feet becomes in 2785 a head the feet adorn.

2796 says that once the great dance of bliss is known, the place where the self comes to an end is bliss (தான் அந்தம் அற்றிடம் ஆனந்தம்); Kural 346 says one who cuts the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான்) enters a world above the gods'. Both put the highest state where the self ends; 2796 names that end bliss and reaches it through the dance.

28 makes the Lord the companion on the way (வழித்துணை) for those who bow. Kural 36 gives that role to virtue: do it now, for when you perish it is a companion that does not perish (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). The same office of the one companion for the journey is filled by the Lord in one and by dharma in the other.

The Tirumanthiram asks the hearer to be free of the tangle of the five sorrowful snares (துன்புறு கண்ணி ஐந்து) and seek the mind friendly to the Lord; Kural 343 says the domain of the five (ஐந்தன் புலம்) must be crushed and all desires let go. Both name the five senses as what binds; Tirumular sets the freed mind on the Lord.

Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 2820 goes past cutting pride: after the gift that 'I' and 'He' are not two, even the 'I' that said 'I' ceases to think (நான்என்ற நானும் நினைப்பு ஒழிந்தேனே). The Kural's renunciation of the ego is carried to its disappearance in knowledge.

Kural 396 says understanding wells up as far as one has learned (கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு), as water does in a sand well as far as it is dug. 2830 uses the same measure, நினையும் அளவில் (as far as one thinks), but ends that Nandi, joining his grace, made him think as far as he thinks (நினைப்பித்தனனே). The Kural puts the measure in one's effort; the Tirumanthiram says even that measure is given.

Kural 3 says those who reach the feet of the one who walked on the flower will live long on earth (நிலமிசை நீடுவாழ்வார்); 2841 says those who think on his form see the aeons (ஊழியும் காண்பர்) and become celestials (உம்பரும் ஆவர்). Both promise lasting life to those who hold the Lord in mind; 2841 makes the means meditation on his form (உருவம் நினைப்பவர்).

Both ground equanimity in fate: the Kural asks why those who accept good fortune grieve at bad; Tirumular's knowers are unchanged whether anointed with sandal or struck with a chisel, since all comes by Nandi's decree.

The Kural says one enjoys only as the apportioner (வகுத்தான்) apportioned; Tirumular says nothing is laid by from heaven except by the decree one has made oneself, placing the apportioning in one's own former deeds.
Both make fate one's own past deeds: the Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Tirumular's decree is the one 'one made oneself before'.

Kural 621 tells one to laugh when trouble comes, since nothing presses back on it as well. 2850 lists thunder, the surging sea, forest fire burning the body and fierce wind (என் ... என்) and answers that, at one with him, he will seek the Lord (நான்ஒன்றி நாதனை நாடுவன்). The same steadiness before calamity appears as worldly resilience in the Kural and as union with the Lord in the Tirumanthiram.

Kural 1031 says that though it is toilsome, ploughing is foremost (உழந்தும் உழவே தலை), since the world follows the plough. 2851 keeps to the ploughing of knowledge (ஞானத்து உழவினை நான் உழுவேனே) though elephant, arrow and tiger threaten. The Kural's ploughing that holds through hardship becomes the jnani's practice that holds through danger.
Both picture the body as a bird's nest or shell the life leaves; the Kural uses it to show how slight the bond of body and life is, Tirumular to say the Lord will build another nest.

The Kural asks whether the life lodging in the body has found no home of its own; Tirumular accepts the body as a passing house and draws comfort from it: losing one is like entering another, for those who know Nandi.
If 2854's 'no going, no coming' is read of the knower, both say that examining and grasping what truly is ends birth: the Kural's mind that ponders and knows what is need not think of birth again.
The Kural names sulking and union as what lovers gain from love; Tirumular, using the same pair (புலவி, புணர்வு), says the Lord is both, carrying love's moments over to the soul and God.

Both make the one without attachment the only thing to cling to: the Kural bids one hold to his hold to let go of holding, Tirumular says the unattached hold to the Supreme and the kinless find him their kin.

935 says those who clung in pride to the dice (கவறும் கழகமும் கையும்) came to nothing. 2866 takes the same dice (கவறு ஐந்து) and makes the body the board and the Lord the player (பெருமான் இருந்து பொருகின்ற மாயக் கவறு), whose secret the poet cannot read. The pairing shows the gambler's vice of the Kural turned into an image of the Lord's hidden play in the body.

Naladiyar 38 says a banyan seed, tiny as it is, casts vast shade, and so small virtue in worthy hands covers the sky. 2870 has an elephant grown from the seed called ஐ (ஐஎன்னும் வித்தினில் ஆனை விளைப்பது) in a field entered by the Lord's favour. The same logic of a minute seed and a huge yield works in ethics in one and in the mantra-field in the other.
The Kural guards the five with the goad of firmness and calls that man a seed for release; Tirumular herds them and they yield milk. Both make the senses useful once controlled.

The Kural says the field of the five must be destroyed (அடல், which Parimelazhagar glosses as கெடுத்தல்); Tirumular wants the five herded so they give milk. If அடல் means only 'conquer', the two agree; on the stronger reading they differ on whether the senses are ended or tamed.

118 praises the balance that first sets itself level and then weighs (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்) as the ornament of the worthy. 2890 sets a balance in the field of the even mind (ஒத்த மனக்கொல்லை உள்ளே சமன்கட்டி) and weighs in the net of devotion. The same levelled scale is the image of fairness in the Kural and of the steadied mind in 2890.

126 says that if one draws in the five like a tortoise in one birth it guards for seven births. 2893 says that once the five horses have entered the nest (கூடுபுக்கு ஆனது ஐந்து குதிரையும்) those who have gone in will no longer see the womb-space (கருவெளி). Both tie drawing in the five senses to freedom from birth; 2893 makes it an end of birth, not a protection.

919 says the soft shoulders of women of fine jewels (மாணிழையார்) are the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (ஆழும்). 2894 says those who set their eyes on clothing, food, oil, ornaments, marriage thread and bangles sink into a pit (ஆறைக் குழியில் அழுந்துகின்றார்). Both picture desire for adorned things as sinking in mud; the Kural's object is the courtesan, 2894's the goods of household life.

29 says the Lord has settled as the linchpin (ஆணியன் ஆகி) in the minds of devotees whose nature does not bend. Kural 667 says not to scorn people for their looks, since a great rolling chariot has its linchpin (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி). The small pin that holds the great moving thing is a person of worth in the Kural and the Lord in the devotee's mind in Tirumular.
The Kural uses the ripe fruit left for the raw one for harsh speech when sweet words are at hand; Tirumular sets the sweet beside the poisonous etti, and his riddle leaves the referent open.

380 asks what is stronger than fate (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள), which comes first whatever one devises. 2909 sets drum, marriage thread and crowbar against each other and says the Lord's grace and love is strongest of all (இட்டம் வலிதென்பர் ஈசன் அருளே). If ஊழ் and grace are taken as rival answers to what is strongest, the two claims conflict; 2909 does not name fate, so the tension depends on that reading.
Both give the learned eyes. The Kural says the unlearned have two sores for eyes; Tirumular places an eye in the thought of the learned.

490 says to fold up like a heron when the time calls and strike like it when the moment comes (கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து). 2911 says the Lord rests in the pond not as a heron lies in wait. The Kural takes the heron's waiting-to-strike as a model of timing; 2911 uses the same image to mark what the Lord's stillness is not.

619 says that even if fate denies the end, effort pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 2913 says that when ploughing and sowing are done the rain does not fall and the earth, though she works, yields nothing (தான்பய வாது). On the reading that 2913 shows labour without grace bearing no fruit at all, it denies the wage the Kural promises.
The Kural says birth is cut only when attachment is cut; Tirumular says the bud's flowering is seen only by those who have let the bond go.

The Tirumanthiram tells the hearer to learn to serve the feet of the Steady One (நிலையுடையான் கழல் கற்கின்ற செய்மின்) while still alive; Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்). Both make worship of the feet the purpose of learning; Tirumular makes them a single act.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while young, since grown hard it destroys the cutter's hand. 2922 says the thorny soorai is thought stronger than the banana, yet when both are cut to pieces the banana takes the place and lives. Both turn on the strength of the thorn plant; the Kural fears it, while 2922 shows the fruitful plant outlasting it once both are cut.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says the learned pass away (கல்வியுடையார் கழிந்தோடிப் போகின்றார்) but praising the Lord night and morning makes the body lasting; Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and learners have few days, so they should learn only what is fitting. Both start from the shortness of the learner's life; the Naladiyar's answer is choosing what to learn, Tirumular's is worship.

In 1329 the lover wishes the night would last so he may go on pleading (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). 2934 borrows the same love-poetry frame, the man with the woman for whom dawn never breaks (புலர்ந்திலை போதே), but turns the endless night into a fault. The pairing shows Tirumular reversing the Kural's wish.

The Naladiyar verse says that joining those with understanding (உணர்வுடையாரை) brings joy, while company with the undiscerning brings pain that ends only on parting. 2938 repeats உணர்வுடையார் in every line and says such people themselves have no sorrow (உறுதுயர் இல்லை). The pairing moves the same word from the benefit of good company to the state of the one who has the awareness.
Both make learning something that goes with a person: the Kural through seven births, Tirumular as a companion, without saying how far.

Kural 4 names the Lord by an absence, the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்), and promises no suffering to those who reach his feet. 2941 builds a whole verse of such absences in -இலி, ending in மருவிலி, the one who clings to nothing, who then enters the speaker's mind. Both describe the Lord by what he lacks and make that the ground of the devotee's good.

Kural 1108 calls sweet the lovers' embrace that not even a breeze can part (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). 2943 says the Lord, beyond every grade of his being, stands mingled without imagining, like the desire of lovers in their enjoyment (அனுபோகக் காமம்போல் கற்பனை இன்றிக் கலந்து). The Tirumanthiram borrows the union with no gap between that the Kural praises in love and uses it for the soul's union with Siva.

2946 says the nux vomica fruit is lovely to look at but its taste is known only to those who eat it (தின்றார்க்கு அறியலாம்), and only the husband knows a young wife's qualities. Kural 1090 says brewed liquor delights only those who drink it (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறா), unlike love, which delights even onlookers. Both rest on the point that some things are known only by taking them in; the Kural marks love as the exception, the Tirumanthiram applies the rule to the bliss of samadhi.

Kural 1090 says love, unlike liquor, gives delight even to those who only see it (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல்). 2950 says desire shows itself suddenly (பொதுக்கென) even on hearing the words of two lovers, and that the Lord gives his wealth just as fast to those who have made themselves ready. Both note that desire is kindled without contact, and the Tirumanthiram uses that quickness for the speed of grace.

The Kural promises a world above the gods to one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine'; Tirumular describes the cutting from inside, the self, wealth, body and mind undone until even the 'I' that would notice is gone.

Kural 357 says that if the mind ponders and knows with certainty what is, one need not think again of birth (பேர்த்துள்ள வேண்டா பிறப்பு). 2956 says that when the mind's maya dies nothing dies after (பினைமாய்வது இல்லை) and that to remain having examined oneself (தனைஆய்ந்து இருப்பது) is the truth. Both make inner examination the end of further births.

Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is too much, so why any further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). 2958 names kinship itself a bond (உறவென்னும் பாசம்), says the speaker has left birth and it, and has become one with God. The Kural states the renouncer's aim; 2958 speaks as one who has reached it, naming the ties the Kural leaves general.

The Tirumanthiram says that to those who search (ஆய்ந்துகொள்வார்க்கு) Hara appears, and that learning becomes a thread ladder (நூலேணி) for the ready mind; Kural 2 says learning is fruitless if it does not end at the Lord's feet. Tirumular gives the positive side of the Kural's warning: learning rightly used is the ladder up to him.
Both say death can be beaten by those who have the power of tapas: the Kural speaks of leaping past Yama, Tirumular of striking him with the sword of knowledge in a mind where tapas has come.

Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள) and says it gets there before any scheme to avoid it. 2973 says the Lord broke up the fate written on the speaker's head (தலைவிதி பின்னம்செய்து) once his heart joined the Lord's feet. The Kural makes ஊழ் unbeatable by human contriving; the Tirumanthiram makes it breakable by the Lord, so the conflict holds only if the Kural's 'nothing' is taken to include grace.
Both turn attachment toward the Lord: the Kural says cling to the one free of clinging in order to let go, Tirumular says if you would cling, cling to the Supreme.

Naladiyar 150 says the well-born help even when they have nothing, as a dried river yields clear water at once when its bed is dug (அகழ்ந்தக்கால் தெற்றெனத் தெண்ணீர் படும்). 2991 has the Lord scoop the inner pond and make clear water (தெண்ணீர்ப் படுத்த). The same act, digging or scooping until clear water comes, figures hidden worth in a family and the Lord's clearing of a muddied mind.
The Kural says the two kinds of deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; Tirumular says the lord whom the worshipper keeps in mind cuts away deeds and the planets' sway.

300 lists many hearings, of virtue, of the andhanar's words, of the gods' mantras, and ends that hearing the Lord's ways (ஈசன் திறங்கேட்டும்) gains the Siva-state (பெற்ற சிவகதி). Kural 411 ranks the wealth of the ear first among all wealth (செவிச்செல்வம் ... செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). Tirumular keeps the Kural's ranking of listening and names the hearing that ranks first and what it yields.

301 sets an order: once you know him, recite, listen and realise (ஓதுமின் கேள்மின் உணர்மின்), and those who recited and realised stood exalted. Kural 391 has learning followed by standing in keeping with it (கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). Both make learning a first step that must be completed by something else; for the Kural it is conduct, for Tirumular realisation (உணர்தல்).

If அள்ளற் கடல் is the sea of births, the two verses agree: the Kural's sea of births is crossed by those who reach the Lord's feet, and Tirumular's sea of mire is cut for those who proclaim his bounty.

Kural 346 says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. 3016 names the 'I' a thief-chief (நானெனும் கள்ளத் தலைவன்) within the heart and outside, and has the Lord cut through the sea of mire for those who proclaim his bounty. On the reading of நானெனும் கள்ளத் தலைவன் as the ego, 3016 makes the 'I' that the Kural tells one to cut a hidden thief, and gives the cutting to grace.
Both raise listeners to the gods: the Kural's listeners, though on earth, equal the gods fed by oblation; Tirumular's hearers of Siva's word become gods.

3020 says as many as are the virtues, so much is the joy (அறம்பல எவ்வண்ணம் அவ்வண்ணம் இன்பம்), and though people see many outward things (புறம்பல) they do not praise him. Kural 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்), and all else is outside (புறத்த) and without praise. Both bind joy to அறம், and both set it against what is புறம்.

303 says the holy people who keep saying of him 'this is the Lord' will later become gods too (பின்னைத் தேவரும் ஆவர்). Kural 50 says the one who lives the household life as it should be lived is placed among the gods in heaven (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்). The same promise, an earthly person counted among the gods, is attached in the Kural to right household living and in Tirumular to speaking of the Lord.
The Kural calls number and letter (எண், எழுத்து) the eyes of living beings; Tirumular makes the Supreme their maker and goes on to the eye that takes things in. Learning's two eyes become his gift.
Both name the Lord as ஆதி, the first: the Kural makes the world have Adi Bhagavan as its first, as letters have அ; Tirumular calls Sankara 'the first, our first', present with all the world yet one.

Both honour the feet of the Lord named by his knowledge: the Kural's வாலறிவன் (one of pure knowledge), whose feet give learning its point, and Tirumular's மெய்ஞ்ஞானத்தவன் (one of true knowledge) and மலமிலான் (the one without impurity).
Both picture the moral life as walking on slippery ground. The Kural gives the words of the virtuous as a staff there; Tirumular asks the mind not to slip from listening and conduct.

306 mocks those who think the experience of the Real comes by mere closeness (செறிவால் அனுபோகம்), like children belching over rice made of sand (மணற்சோற்றில் தேக்கிடுமாபோல்). Naladiyar 321 says the fool scorns the teaching of virtue as the ladle cannot taste the milk-rice it stirs (பாற்கூழை முழை சுவையுணராது). Both use food that is handled but not tasted for people near the truth who do not receive it; the pairing depends on reading செறிவு as closeness.
Both call listening a துணை, a support. The Kural makes it a staff in faltering; Tirumular places it between the body and the mind on Siva's feet in a ladder of supports.
An image without life: the Kural likens the unlearned man's good looks to a clay doll; Tirumular makes the Lord a stone cow, giving no milk, to those who neither recite nor realise him.

The Kural makes learning the eyes and gives the unlearned two sores; 310, if read as it seems, gives sight to the unlearned who have the grace-eye and denies the learned their joy. The contrast depends on reading கல்லாதவர் as the book-unlearned.

310 says the unlearned (கல்லாதவர்), if they have the vision that knows the meaning, hold to the truth, and even the learned cannot see their joy (கற்றோரும் கல்லாதார் இன்பம் காணுகிலாரே). Kural 410 says others stand to those learned in the shining books as beasts to men (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). If 310's கல்லாதவர் are the literally unschooled, Tirumular grants them what the Kural denies; on a reading that limits 310 to the unschooled who have the inner vision, it is a condition rather than a conflict.

312 addresses those who feel the perishing hut of the body is lasting (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்). Kural 340 asks whether the soul, lodging in a corner of the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்), has no home of its own. Both make the body a temporary shelter, a hut or a borrowed corner, and the mistake is to take it for a dwelling.

314 says the able, thinking that life does not stay (நில்லாது சீவன் நிலையன்று), have entered virtue and tapas, while the unlearned live out the suffering of evil deeds. Kural 335 says good deeds must be done at once, before the hiccup stills the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both draw the same practical conclusion from the shortness of life: turn to good deeds now.
The Kural finds the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Tirumular will not even look at or listen to unlearned fools, though he too grants that the merely unlearned are good.

Both deny learning its fruit without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning gains if one does not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge, Tirumular calls the learned without Siva-knowledge wretches and fools.

The Kural says the world won't count as ruin the low estate of one who stays fair; Tirumular promises those who stand in the middle knowledge, no hell and godhood. The same virtue, given rewards beyond this world.

Kural 118 makes fairness the balance that first levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை). 323 says those who stand in the middle (நடுவாகிநின்றார்) are those who always hold the Lord's two feet and cling to his name. The same word for steadiness is used for leaning to no side in the Kural and for being fixed on one support in Tirumular.
The Kural simply says do not drink. Tirumular agrees, but keeps the vocabulary of drink: the clear toddy (தேறல்) he commends is Siva's bliss. Abstinence becomes a substitution.

326 says lust and liquor belong to the wretched (காமமும் கள்ளும் கலதிகட்கேயாகும்). Kural 920 says double-hearted women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom fortune has left (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both pair desire and drink as the marks of the luckless; Tirumular sets against them the nectar of bliss at the feet.

328 says those who drink do not ponder the inner truth, know pasu and pasam, or reach Siva-yoga: they do not know the meaning (கள்ளுண்ணும் மாந்தர் கருத்தறியாரே). Kural 929 says giving reasons to the drunk is like searching with a torch for a man sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Tirumular lists what the drinker cannot know; the Kural says he cannot be taught it.

329 says fools who drink deluding liquor do not discern maya, and to feel clear inside delusion is itself delusion (மயக்கில் தெளியின் மயக்குறும்). Kural 928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk (களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக), since what is hidden grows. Both distrust the drinker's own sense of being clear; Tirumular extends it from liquor to the delusion of maya. The 329 line is uncertain.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if it does not bow at God's feet; Tirumular turns the test on the worshippers, saying that even those who can recite many hymns lack understanding. Bowing is necessary in one, not enough in the other.

330 says liquor bewilders and destroys truthfulness (கள் வாய்மை அழிக்கும்) and leaves the drinker in the pleasure of women. Naladiyar 157 lists among the marks of the faultless that they do not drink (கள்ளுண்ணார) and never lie even by a slip (வாயில்பொய் கூறார்). Both join abstaining from liquor with keeping one's word true.

Both find the fault of drinking in self-forgetting: the Kural's drinker pays to buy self-oblivion (மெய்யறியாமை), Tirumular's sectarians lose the power they sought because they forget themselves (தம்மை மறத்தல்).
The Kural's fair man is a balance whose beam leans to no side; Tirumular's world, leaning to one side, is set level by Agastya. One image of rightness as balance, moral in one, cosmic in the other.

35 says praise the Lord who is the way when nothing else avails (ஆற்றுகிலா வழியாகும் இறைவன்), and he will change you (மாற்றுவன்). Kural 7 says that except for those who reach the incomparable one's feet, it is hard to change the mind's distress (மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது). The Kural says the change is hard without him; Tirumular promises that he makes it.

359 says gods who did tapas and whisper mantras in the ear, laying out the oblation with mantras while looking to their own gain (தாமுற நோக்கும்), make a cruel thing (கொடியது). Kural 276 says none are harder of heart than those who live by deceit, renouncing in appearance and not in heart (வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). Both judge religious form used for self-interest as cruel, not merely false.

Both turn to skulls. The Naladiyar's skulls in the burning ground grin at the living as proof of what the body comes to; Tirumular's are borne by Siva, and his bearing them is what keeps them from becoming dust. One image teaches the body's end, the other the Lord's hold even over what is dead.

The Kural defines folly as the pride that says 'we are bright'; Tirumular shows it at the top of the cosmos, Brahma and Vishnu each saying 'I am the Lord' through folly (பேதைமை), and failing before the fire.

392 calls the Lord one whose kindness is easy to reach (நயன் எளிதாகிய நம்பன்) and repeats எளிது. The Kural says the land of the king who is காட்சிக்கு எளியன், easy to see, is praised above others. Easy access, a virtue of a good king, is here a mark of the Lord.

4 ends with the poet standing free of darkness (இருள் நீங்கி நின்றேனே) through bowing and praising day and night. Kural 352 promises the same removal of darkness (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும்) to those of stainless sight who have left confusion. The same phrase is reached by worship in one and by true seeing in the other.

The Kural says the world has the Primal Lord as its first, as letters have 'a'; Tirumular says one alone creates, protects and removes the worlds. The Kural names only primacy; Tirumular spells it out as the three acts.

Both speak of the one who made the world. The Kural, conditionally, curses him if he meant some to live by begging; Tirumular praises him without reserve. Because the Kural's curse is conditional, this is a difference of attitude, not a contradiction.

The Kural says the world keeps going (உலகம் வழங்கி வருதல்) through rain, so rain is amrita. 413, in the chapter on protection (காத்தல்), has the Lord stand as the ocean, the dark cloud and the sky that pours rain. The Kural's rain that keeps the world becomes one of the Lord's forms of keeping it.

The Kural says it is rain that ruins and rain again that lifts the ruined (கெடுப்பதூஉம் ... எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை). 415 has the Lord stand at one time as a fierce gale (சண்ட மாருதம்) and at another as cool rain (தண்மழை). Both make one power the source of both harm and care.

Both put the world in the pot on the fire (உலை). The Naladiyar's turtle plays in the water not knowing it is being cooked, as men revel while Death waits; Tirumular sees the whole world softened and burnt like rice, a cosmic act he says he has come to know, not a warning to the heedless.

Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling (இருவினையும் சேரா) to those who praise the Lord. 430 says there is one strong Lord who made the deeds that cling (சேரும் வினை) to evildoers perish (மாயவைத்தான்). On the reading of மாயவைத்தான் as 'made to perish', 430 makes the Lord the agent of what Kural 5 states as a result, and extends it to the evildoers themselves.

441 calls the bag that binds the five elements the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை என்னுமிக் காயப்பை). Kural 80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை), and without it a body is bone wrapped in skin. The Kural adds a condition 441 does not state: the elemental bag alone is not yet what it calls உயிர்நிலை.

Kural 269 says even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is possible for those who attain the power of austerity. 442 names a particular discipline that has that effect: taking joy in the nada at the crown (உச்சியில் ... நாதத்தை நச்சியே இன்பங்கொள் வார்க்கு நமன்இல்லை).

Naladiyar 6 says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped (கூற்றம் குதித்துய்ந்தார் ஈங்கில்லை). 442 says there is no Yama (நமன்இல்லை) for those who long for the shining nada at the crown. If நமன் இல்லை means escape from death itself, the two conflict; if it means freedom from death's fear or from rebirth, they do not.

Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், possessor of eight qualities, without naming him; Tirumular gives the eight qualities to the matted-haired Siva who keeps the world and stays near the mind.

45 says this world runs only by ordinance (விதிவழி அல்லது இவ்வேலை உலகம்), yet by the way of praise the Lord of light becomes the sun showing the way to him. Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள), which gets there first whatever one devises. 45 grants fate's rule over the world and adds praise as a way it does not close.

Both use milk mixed in water. The Naladiyar's swan separates them, as the wise sort what is worth learning; Tirumular's milk stays in the water, the Lord present throughout the body and seen only by steady sight.

Both see the body as a pot. In the Naladiyar it is a woman's body, a pot oozing filth that fools admire for its skin; in Tirumular it is the vessel in which the Lord's form stands like milk in water, so to see within it is bliss.

Tirumanthiram 453 says that at the moment the two join (இன்புறு காலத்து) the Lord fixes 'பண்புறு காலமும் பார்மிசை வாழ்க்கையும்', the child's span and its life on earth. Kural 377 says no one, though he gathers crores, enjoys more than 'வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை', the share the ordainer allotted. The Kural names an allotting agent without saying when the allotment is made; the Tirumanthiram makes the Lord that agent and places the allotment at conception.

46 ends with the Lord whose form is the intellect entering our mind (புந்தி வண்ணன் எம் மனம் புகுந்தான்). Kural 3 names God மலர்மிசை ஏகினான், the one who went upon the flower, which the commentators, as Pope's rendering shows, read as the flower of the mind. On that reading both place the Lord walking into the devotee's heart.

Tirumanthiram 461 describes the body as a house the Lord built from bone (என்பு), nerve and red flesh, in which he set 'உயிர்நிலை', the seat of life, 'இன்பால்', sweetly. Kural 80 says 'அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை', the seat of life follows love, and that without it the body is 'என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு', bone wrapped in skin. Both set உயிர்நிலை against a frame of bone; the Kural makes love what keeps it alive, the Tirumanthiram makes the Lord who placed it there the one to seek.
Both list the body as bone, sinew and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which of these parts is the woman a man desires; Tirumular sees in the same parts a house built by the Lord and seeks its builder.
Both rank the householder with or above the ascetic: the Kural's virtuous household life endures more than those who do penance, Tirumular's householders are equal to great ascetics.

The Naladiyar's wise, seeing the pain in pleasure, keep off the household way; Tirumular says those who stay in the household equal great ascetics. The conflict holds if 47's first line is a general claim about householders, not only those who keep the Lord in mind.

Both describe the body by its nine openings. The Naladiyar makes it a pot seeping filth and calls the man who admires it a fool; Tirumular makes the nine gates sluices set by the Lord, who dwells at its crown and is met there. The conflict is over the body's worth and depends on reading 470 as valuing the body, not only describing how it was made.

48 holds to the Lord as a lamp that never dawns away (விடியா விளக்கு). Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off darkness, but when the oil runs out darkness rushes back (விளக்குநெய் தேய்விடத்துச் சென்றிருள் பாய்ந்தாங்கு). The Naladiyar's lamp of merit fails as merit is spent; Tirumular's lamp is the one that does not.

Tirumanthiram 488 says that when a cuckoo's egg is put in a crow's nest the crow raises it 'மயக்கத்தால்', out of delusion, taking the stranger for its own. Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked into the home and leave silently, like a bird 'சேக்கை மரன் ஒழியச் சேண் நீங்கு புள்', that leaves its nesting tree and flies far. Both figure the members of a household as birds that are not truly the nest's own; the Naladiyar dwells on their leaving, the Tirumanthiram on the parents' delusion in raising them.

Both picture salvation as swimming a sea: the Kural's sea of births, crossed by reaching the Lord's feet, and Tirumular's sea of sin, crossed by thinking of the Lord and reaching the shore beyond pasu and pasam.

5 says that search as you may there is no god equal to Siva and no one like him (சிவனொடு ஒக்கும் தெய்வம் தேடினும் இல்லை). Kural 7 names God by the same claim, தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான், the one with no likeness. Tirumular makes the Kural's title the outcome of a search and gives it a name.

Both say which gift truly counts. The Kural makes the recipient's need the test, calling all other giving a measured loan; Tirumular makes it the recipient's knowledge of Siva, and says gifts to fools bear no fruit however large. The conflict depends on taking மூடர் as the spiritually ignorant whatever their need.
Both say a small gift in worthy hands grows beyond its size: the Naladiyar's banyan seed shades the sky, Tirumular's sesame of gold yields release and siddhi.

Kural 269 says 'கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்', even leaping over Death becomes possible for those who have the strength of tapas. Tirumanthiram 502 says some went and came to know the Lord who masters Death ('காலனை'), and 'தேவருமாமே', became even gods. The Kural gives the escape from Death to tapas; the Tirumanthiram gives it to knowing the Lord who is Death's master.

Tirumanthiram 504 says 'ஆவன ஆவ அழிவ அழிவன, போவன போவ புகுவ புகுவன', what is to become becomes and what is to go goes, as Nandi showed. Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay however one cherishes it, and what is one's own will not go however one throws it away. Both state that what is allotted comes and goes regardless of effort; the Tirumanthiram makes it the teaching of the guru, which the disciple then follows.

The converse case: the Naladiyar's small gift that reaches the hands of the worthy grows like a banyan seed until the sky looks small; Tirumular's gift to the undisciplined is a crop sown after its season. Both make the recipient's worth decide the gift's fruit.

The Kural defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, all else being a loan expecting return; Tirumular judges the recipient by discipline and love, not by need. The conflict holds on the reading of 506 as about material giving.
The Kural's many who bathe with an air of distinction while their minds are stained, and Tirumular's deceitful who tramp from water to water: both deny that outer washing reaches the stain within.

Kural 298 says 'புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும்', outer purity comes by water, and inner purity is seen by truthfulness. Tirumanthiram 509 says there are many holy waters 'உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளே', within the heart, and that those of deceitful mind who do not bathe there wander over hollow and height. Both deny that outer water cleans the inner person; the Tirumanthiram keeps the figure of bathing and moves the water inside.

Tirumular finds all dharma within the Veda; the Kural makes the king's just sceptre the ஆதி of both the Brahmins' books and dharma. If ஆதி is read as support they agree that the Veda needs a guardian; if read as origin, the Kural places dharma's source in rule, not in scripture.

Kural 294 says that one who does not lie 'உள்ளத்தால்', in his heart, dwells 'உள்ளத்துள் எல்லாம்', in the hearts of all the world. Tirumanthiram 511 says that the One felt 'உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளே', within the heart, is known by none of the 'கள்ளத்தினார்', the deceitful. Both make the heart the place of presence and make truth or deceit of heart the condition; the Kural speaks of a man's place among people, the Tirumanthiram of the Lord's place in a man.

The same link between rain and worship, run in opposite directions: in the Kural, if the sky dries up, festival and worship cease even for the gods; in Tirumular, if the pujas lapse, the earth has no rain.

Kural 559 says that if the king bends justice ('முறைகோடி'), the sky withholds its rain. Tirumanthiram 517 says that if the pujas in the temples of the one who kicked Death lapse, the earth has no rain ('அவனி மழையின்றி') and kings lose their strength. The same pattern, a failure at the centre followed by drought, appears in two domains: the Kural places it in the king's justice, the Tirumanthiram in the temple's worship, and makes the king suffer it too.

Both list what declines when a guardian fails: in the Kural, if the king does not guard, cows give less and Brahmins forget their books; in Tirumular, if the temple pujas stop, kings come to harm and theft grows. The king is the cause in one and the casualty in the other.

52 opens 'the one who spoke the Veda is not a வேதியன்' (வேதம் உரைத்தானும் வேதியன் ஆகிலன்); read as a general claim, uttering the Veda does not make one a Vedic man. Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, for their cool kindness to every life. On that second reading both deny that the priestly name comes from recitation; on the main reading, that the Lord spoke the Veda, the link does not hold.

Kural 295 ranks one who speaks truth with the whole mind above those who do tapas and give gifts. Tirumanthiram 522 says the Lord knows the men who praise with lies, and that 'மெய்யே உரைக்கில்', if they spoke truth, he would make the gods worship them. Both set truthful speech above the acts usually praised; the Tirumanthiram makes truth the price of the highest honour and false praise of the Lord its failure.

529 says even Vedic Brahmins (வேதியராயும்) lost in pleasure and women's sulking abandon thought of the Lord; Kural 134 says a forgotten Veda can be learned again but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails (பிறப்பொழுக்கம் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both deny that Vedic standing protects one whose conduct has gone.
Both start from not honouring the great (பேணாது, பேணார்); the Kural warns of ills that do not leave, Tirumular calls those who do it base.

531 says those who speak to wound the teacher of the one syllable die as worms on the earth (மாய்வர் மண்ணிலே); Kural 898 says if the hill-like great are slighted, those who seemed to stand forever vanish from the earth with their line (மாய்வர் நிலத்து). The Tirumanthiram applies the Kural's warning about the great to the guru, with the same closing verb.

532 says those who trouble the minds of a chaste wife, devotees and knowers lose wealth and life within a year (அத்தமும் ஆவியும் ஆண்டொன்றில் மாண்டிடும்); Kural 900 says even those with overwhelming support do not survive if those of great distinction are angered (உய்யார் ... சீரார் செறின்). Both make offence against the inviolable fatal whatever one's means; 532 widens the class to the chaste wife.

Commentators read the Kural's வேந்தன் as Indra, who falls midway if those of exalted vows are angered; Tirumular names Indra's throne (வாசவன் பீடம்) and great kings' thrones as ruined when devotees are troubled.

535 traces famine to falsehood in the presence of the true guru; Kural 559 traces failed rain to a king who bends justice (முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் ... ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). The same logic, a fault at the centre spoiling the land's harvest, runs in the guru's presence and in the king's rule.

536 likens the ritualist beside the knower to one who eats bitter things while ghee, milk and curd stand at hand (கைப்பட்ட நெய்பால் தயிர்நிற்க); Kural 100 likens harsh speech, when sweet words are there, to grabbing raw fruit while ripe fruit is at hand (கனியிருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). The same figure of choosing the worse food beside the better serves speech in the Kural and the path of knowledge in the Tirumanthiram.

Kural 5 says the two kinds of deed (இருவினையும்) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 538 says the jnani's good and cruel deeds (நல்வினையான கொடுவினை) are taken off by those who worship and those who revile him, and Siva's bliss enters once he is in the Lord's keeping. 538 gives a means by which both deeds leave, on the traditional reading of how they are divided.

The Kural asks for bearing wrongs done to one and then forgetting them; Tirumular places forbearance inward, as checking the creature of craving that grips the senses. Both call it forbearance, but the Kural's is toward others and Tirumular's toward oneself.

545 says joining the great ones who stand in the path (பெரியார் உடன்கூடல்) is supreme bliss, and that only a few gain it; Kural 443 says cherishing the great and making them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்) is the rarest of rare things. The two chapters share a title, and 545 names as bliss what the Kural names as rare.

The Naladiyar's drain water that joins a great river becomes holy water, and the lowborn who join the good stand like a hill; Tirumular says joining the great is supreme bliss. Both make the company one joins transform the joiner.

548 says the one great in skill swims the whirlpool of births (பிறவிச்சுழி நீந்தும்); Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). 548 keeps the swimming figure but sets it in the company of the holy, where the Kural sets it at the Lord's feet.
The Kural calls cherishing the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things; Tirumular's verse begins with அருமை and ends with 'I have joined those strong in holiness'.

Both separate holding the Veda from living by it. The Kural says the Veda can be relearned but lost conduct ruins a Brahmin; Tirumular complains that reciters keep the six-limbed Veda but practise none of its qualities.
Both name sharing one's food (பகுத்துண்டு, பகுந்துண்பான்) among the chief virtues; the Kural sets it beside protecting all life, Tirumular makes it part of the yogi's yama.
The Kural puts not killing first and not lying right behind it; Tirumular's list of yama opens in the same order, கொல்லான் then பொய் கூறான்.

556 lists purity and truthfulness (தூய்மை ... வாய்மை) among the ten rules of niyama; Kural 298 joins the two, saying outer purity comes by water but inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). The Kural shows how two items on 556's list depend on each other.

564 says the horse of the breath gives a hold to the true but leaps and throws the false (துள்ளி விழுத்திடும்); Kural 814 says better solitude than friends like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா). The thrown rider figures false friendship in the Kural and unfit practice in the Tirumanthiram.

566 says the controlled breath gives elation without toddy (கள்ளுண்ண வேண்டா ... களிதரும்); Kural 1090 says brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights by a look (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறா). The same comparison, a joy that surpasses liquor because it needs no drinking, is made of love in the Kural and of breath in the Tirumanthiram.
Both say a discipline can overcome Death (கூற்று): the Kural credits the power of tapas with leaping past Death, Tirumular the measure of the held breath with kicking him.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says purified breath turns the hair black. Read literally, they disagree about whether ageing can be undone; read symbolically, 575 is not about hair, and the tension dissolves.

The Kural asks one to draw in the five senses like a tortoise for protection through seven births; Tirumular's withdrawal goes on past restraint to what is found inside: the one the Veda searched for.

59 says the learned are those who know the intent (கருத்தறிவார்) of what the seers of the eighteen languages say, whatever the language. Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது) in whatever is heard, from whoever's mouth (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). Both place learning in grasping meaning regardless of the source's tongue or speaker.
Both use the heron that waits motionless: in the Kural it is the king biding his time before striking, in Tirumular the yogi who holds still in breath and mind.
Both say no one who came before has escaped death: the Naladiyar shows it in kings under their umbrellas, Tirumular in all who came before.

Kural 27 says the world lies with the one who discerns the kinds of the five, taste, light, touch, sound and smell (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு). 599 places within the gathering of eye, tongue, nose and ear one ancient being who tunes them (பண்ணாக்கி நின்ற பழம்பொருள்). The Kural credits the person who masters the senses; Tirumular credits a presence within them that saves by breaking the self (புண்ணாக்கி நம்மைப் பிழைப்பித்த).

6 knows no way to enter the city apart from him (அவனன்றி ஊர்புகுமாறு அறியேனே). Kural 8 says that except for those who reach the feet of the sea of virtue, the other seas are hard to swim (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது). Both state the goal as reachable only through him, one as entering a city, the other as crossing a sea.

Both face writing beyond counting. The Naladiyar's answer is to choose what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water; Tirumular's is that the countless Agamas are hard even for the gods and their count is writing on water.

Kural 299 says not all lamps are lamps; for the worthy the lamp that does not fail, truthfulness, is the lamp (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). 602 sets lamps against each other: light the mind's lamp, smother the lamp of anger (சினத்து விளக்கு), and the mind's lamp becomes one that does not die (மாயா விளக்கு). Both rank lamps and keep one as the true one, the Kural an ethical virtue, Tirumular the mind made steady by meditation once anger is put out.
The Kural says those who have won the power of austerity can even leap past Death; Tirumular names a yogic means, the upper door seen open, for the same escape.

The Naladiyar says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give your wealth now; Tirumular says the yogi who sees the upper door will not hear Death even in dreams. The conflict holds on the literal reading of 622, that the yogi escapes death; if it means only freedom from fear of death, it dissolves.

Both speak of the one who goes upon the flower and of those who reach his feet. The Kural promises they live long upon the earth (or, as Parimelazhagar takes it, in the world of release); Tirumular promises Amaravati, then in the following verses the Siva-state.

Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the pure knower (வாலறிவன் நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). 633 joins the two: those who hold his feet with love and learn the Supreme's praise (பதத்தன்பு வைத்துப் பரன்புகழ் கற்றிருந்து) reach the Siva-state. The Kural makes worship the fruit of learning; 633 makes learning his praise part of the devotion that reaches him.

Kural 25 says Indra, lord of the wide heavens, is witness enough to the strength of one who quenched the five senses (ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல்). 634 says those who worshipped and did austerity become king of the gods (வானவர் கோவாய்), hailed as lord of Amaravati. Both measure the ascetic by Indra; the Kural puts him above Indra as witness, while 634 gives him Indra's throne, which 635 then goes beyond.

Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்). 637 says householders of unshrinking giving (இல்வழியாளர் சுருங்காப் பெருங்கொடை) may reach the gods' many ways, yet it becomes the way of the earth (பார்வழி யாகுமே). On the reading that the heavens lead back to earth, the household's highest reward in the Kural is in 637 short of release; on the reading 'a way for the world' there is no conflict.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if one does not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Tirumular says crores of Agamas are writing on water without the knowledge the Lord declared. Both measure scripture by what it leads to.

The Naladiyar says worldly books without the books of wisdom are only clamour that never removes confusion; Tirumular says even the Agamas, if their knowledge is missed, are writing on water. Both deny that bulk of learning is the point.

644 says twenty thousand eight hundred kinds of karma, mantra and yoga only tire the body (காய உழைப்பாகும்), and for siddhi they come down to four. Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short, so learn what is fitting, like the bird that leaves the water and drinks the milk. Both answer a boundless stock of means with the same move, reducing it to the few that serve the end.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says that by the eighth stage of practice grey hair and wrinkles do not appear. The conflict depends on reading 647 literally, as a claim about the body, and not as a figure for inner freshness.

653 says the nine airs are in accord (ஒத்த) with dhananjaya above them, and while it stays in accord body and life stay together; 654 and 655 list the swellings that follow when it does not. Kural 941 says the three humours beginning with wind (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று) cause disease whether in excess or deficiency. Yogic and medical texts share one logic: health is the balance of the body's airs or humours, disease their disorder.

658 places in the body of nine gates (ஒன்பது வாசல்) a place of nine channels, and those who still them gain visions. Naladiyar 47 calls the body a pot that seeps filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) to shame the lover. The same nine openings are a cause for disgust in the Naladiyar and a site of practice in Tirumular.

674 says that if the times of dying stay in one's own control (சாகின்ற காலங்கள் தன்வழி நின்றிடின்), great lightness comes in five years. Naladiyar 6 says the appointed days cannot be exceeded and no one has leapt clear of Death. The conflict holds if 674 means control over the hour of one's own death, as its wording suggests.

677 says that after seeing the breath's light, the passing times do not pass (போகின்ற காலங்கள் போவது மில்லையாம்), playing on கால் as breath and time. Kural 334 says the day is a blade that saws through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாளது) for those who see it. The conflict holds if 677 means that the master of breath is no longer worn down by time; on a reading where it describes only an inner experience, the claims do not meet.

Both say not every lamp is the lamp: the Kural's one true lamp is truthfulness, Tirumular's is the higher inner light that makes release easy. The image is shared, the light is moral in one and yogic in the other.

Both make God the one with no likeness: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான், Tirumular's தன்னைஒப்பாய் ஒன்றும் இல்லாத் தலைமகன். The Kural adds that only reaching his feet ends the mind's anxiety; Tirumular adds that he becomes father to whoever calls him so.
Both say a discipline can carry one past Death: the Kural's power gained through tapas leaps over Yama (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்); Tirumular's yogis of the brow and staff have no Yama (நமனில்லை).

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Tirumular says those who know the yogic way have no Yama. The conflict holds if நமனில்லை means escape from bodily death; if it means freedom from Yama's judgement after death, the two need not clash.

Both value the body for what it yields, but the Naladiyar has the body thrown away like crushed cane once its juice is taken, while Tirumular says the body must be nurtured because life and true knowledge perish with it.

On what the body is worth: the Naladiyar calls it a pot seeping filth from nine openings, attractive only through its skin, and the man who praises it a fool; Tirumular says he once held the body base (இழுக்கு) but found the Lord had made it his temple, and so cherishes it. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for lust.

Both rest on the three humours of the medical writers, wind among them: the Kural says excess or lack of them brings disease, Tirumular names the time of day at which practice removes each, and promises the end of age as well.
