734 says that those who embrace the blue-hued lady will, as the world sees, lose grey hair and wrinkles (நரைதிரை மாறிடும்) and become young. Naladiyar 11 takes grey hair as certain (நரைவரும் என்றெண்ணி), so the wise renounce in childhood and the rest end leaning on a staff. On the plain reading the two disagree over whether age can be undone; the Naladiyar answers it by renunciation, Tirumular by yogic union.
The Kural says that eating in measure is how one who has a body keeps it long; Tirumular counts the reduction of food among the means of perfecting the body.

736 promises that the yogic practice makes a fine body (நற்காயம்) that women with flower-decked hair look at with desire (கண்டிச்சிக்கும்). Naladiyar 41 mocks those who praise a girl's beauty without seeing the body's paltry dwelling: tear a fly's wing of skin and a stick is needed to drive off the crows. On the reading that 736 offers outward attractiveness as a good, the two make opposite claims about the body's beauty.
Both claim that Death can be overcome: the Kural by the power gained through austerity, Tirumular by seeing the Lord's feet in the inner fire before Death strikes.
Both make time the quiet cutter of life: the Kural's day is a saw for those who understand it, Tirumular's naazhigai run out while people know everything else.

748 tells the practitioner to complete the practice humbly without beating a drum about it (பறையறையாது). Kural 1076 calls the base beaten drums (அறைபறை) because they carry and proclaim any secret they hear. Both use the beaten drum for publishing what should be kept; 748 turns it on one's own practice.
Both say that discipline can carry a person past death: the Kural credits the power of austerity, Tirumular the ability to seek the Siva-state within.

Kural 337 says people do not know whether they will live even one moment (ஒருபொழுதும் வாழ்வது அறியார்); 786 agrees that no one knows the breath that measures life or the thing that perishes (ஆருமறியார்), then adds அறிவறிந்தேனே, 'I have known'. Tirumular grants the Kural's common ignorance but makes the measuring of life knowable to the yogi.

Both make the body a temporary dwelling: the Kural's life has only borrowed shelter in it, Tirumular's body is a fair hut the Lord has shaped. The Kural laments the lack of a home; Tirumular looks to loosening the bond of the old dwelling.

The Naladiyar counts those who prattle astrology among the greatest fools, beside those who neglect their real task; Tirumular sets weekday omens inside a yoga tantra. Whether this is a true conflict depends on whether the Naladiyar's சோதிடம் includes such day lore or means endless study that displaces the work of release.

The Kural says those who have gained the power of austerity can even leap past Death; Tirumular says Yama has no hold on the yogi who seals the body. Both make death conquerable, the Kural by austerity in general, Tirumular by a named technique.

80 offers staying in this body (இருந்தேன் இக்காயத்தே) for countless crores as attainment. Naladiyar 27 praises those who see the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts (மொக்குளின் ... கெடும் இதோர் யாக்கை) and resolve to end their wandering. On the literal reading of 80's long bodily stay, the two set opposite values on the body's duration.

Kural 339 makes sleep the figure of death (உறங்குவது போலுஞ் சாக்காடு); 801 says those who drive out sleep (உறக்கத்தை நீக்கி) and stay aware need not die (இறக்கவும் வேண்டாம்). The yogi takes the Kural's likeness literally and reverses it: removing sleep removes death.

The Kural says tapas should be striven for here, since it gains what one wishes; Tirumular asks why be born again when people do not strive at tapas beforehand. Both use முயல் and place the effort now.

The Kural asks what worth is if one does not do sweet things even to those who harm one. Tirumular's inward yogis are good even to the hostile, but worse than fire to doers of evil, so their goodness has a limit the Kural's does not state.

Both call the body a bag (பை). The Naladiyar says it should be looked at as a bag turned inside out, a covered foulness to be shunned; Tirumular says that inside the same bag a light shines and it becomes a temple. The conflict holds if 820's பை is read as the body, as tradition takes it.

Kural 6 praises the one who quenched the five senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்); 829 says the practitioner becomes lord when knowledge, enjoyment and the five go his way (தன்வழி அஞ்சே). Both make mastery of the five the mark of the lord, but 829 has them go his way within போகம், not quenched.

Both make union life-giving. In the Kural the lover feels his life put out shoots at each touch, as if her shoulders were ambrosia; in Tirumular union practised as yoga lets one live on earth for many ages. Love's hyperbole in one is a technique in the other.

The Naladiyar treats grey hair as certain to come, so the wise renounce in childhood; Tirumular says that for those who drink this water grey hair and wrinkles change and Yama is absent. The conflict holds if 848 is read literally of the body, not as a figure for spiritual youth.

The Kural's learned love learning more when they see the world delighting in what delights them; Tirumular wishes the bliss he gained on the whole world. Both make a private good complete only when it is shared.

850 names the Siva-water the hero's, the gods' and the primal medicine (ஆதி மருந்து) and says this medicine of light cannot be told. Naladiyar 132 says that in no world is there a medicine like learning for cutting away delusion (கல்விபோல் மம்மர் அறுக்கும் மருந்து). Both claim a matchless medicine, one for the body's decay, the other for the mind's confusion.
Both use the moon's two fortnights: the Kural for friendship with the good that fills and with fools that wanes, Tirumular for the inner moon whose growing and shrinking the yogi must learn.

863 says the base see the sixteen kalas in the body and do not think of it, until harsh Death sets them where he intends (கன்றிய காலன் கருத்துழி வைத்தபின்) and they fall. Naladiyar 331 compares those who revel in the world while great Death waits to seize them (கொலைவல் பெருங்கூற்றம் கோள்பார்ப்ப) to a turtle playing in a pot over the fire. Both make the fault not seeing what is plain while Death prepares; Tirumular names the unheeded thing as the inner kalas.

870 calls those who recite yet know nothing mutes (ஓதியும் ஏதும் அறியாத ஊமர்கள்), and says the Lord appears only to those who can join beginning and end. Kural 834 says there is no greater fool than one who studies, understands and teaches but does not restrain himself (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்கா). Both judge recitation empty without an inner act; the Kural names it self-restraint, Tirumular an inner yogic joining.

Both use the eclipse serpent that seizes the moon: the Naladiyar's spares the young crescent, as the worthy spare a fallen enemy; Tirumular's enmity of serpent and moon is ended and the two held together, an inner joining.

872 says not to sleep until what was eaten has settled (அயின்றது வீழ்வளவும் துயிலின்றி). Kural 942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats only after what was eaten is digested (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்). Both time the next act by the settling of the last meal; the Kural applies it to eating, the Tirumanthiram to sleep, within its moon regimen.

Kural 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade that saws through life (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்). 874 says yogis who stay through the aeon measure Yama by the nazhigai (நாழிகையாக நமனை அளப்பர்). On the reading that they count Death's span as a mere nazhigai, the yogi measures time rather than being cut by it, against the Kural's claim that time cuts every life.

880 says the mind joined with the breath binds the five senses (ஐம்புலன் கட்டுண்ணும்) and that is release (வீடு). Naladiyar 59 says one who can guard, without wavering, the craving that enters through the five gates of body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears will surely reach release (வீடு பெறும்). Both make holding the five senses the way to வீடு; 880 does it by breath and inner sound, the Naladiyar by firm guarding.

The Kural says that as A is first of all letters, the Primal Lord is first of the world (அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம் ... முதற்றே உலகு). 885 says that by one letter he became the whole world (ஓரெழுத்தாலே உலகெங்கும் தானாகி), and goes on to two, three and the great letter. Where the Kural uses the letter as a likeness for the Lord's priority, 885 makes the letter the means by which he becomes the world.

The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; 905 promises no further birth to whoever chants the five letters, and 898 has already made the Lord's feet the letters. The means is narrowed from the feet to the mantra that is the feet.

Both free a person from deeds through the Lord's name: the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who delight in his true praise (Kural), and subtle karma is destroyed by chanting the subtle mantra (909). Tirumular adds a count and a technique.

Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). 916 names a means for the same end: merely saying அரகர cuts off birth (அறும்பிறப்பு), yet people don't know to say it. The Kural leaves the way of reaching unstated; the Tirumanthiram makes it the spoken name.
Both define the Brahmin by something other than birth, if 940 is read that way: the Kural by kindness to all life, Tirumular by the five syllables dwelling in him.
Both say deeds lose their hold on one devoted to the Lord: the Kural through his true praise, Tirumular through his name kept up without tiring, with the Lord coming to remove the grief of deeds.
Both use the letter A to point beyond itself. The Kural makes A, first of letters, the image of the Primal Lord first in the world; Tirumular makes A the soul and gives the Supreme to U.
Both put a goad over 'the five'. In the Kural it is firmness of mind (உரன்) that guards the five; in Tirumular the five elephants in the forest are goaded by the five syllables.
Both make control of the five senses the way in: the Naladiyar's one who steers the craving of the five gates reaches release, Tirumular's one who holds the five together lets the First enter.

Konganar's Vaalaik Kummi counts going to foreign lands (தேசாந்திரங்களும் செல்லாதே) among things to avoid, with facing a tiger in the forest and courtesans' ways; Civakan calls those who never leave home fish in a well and sets out, and the god's road then holds elephant forests and ghoul-women.
teaches: On the same question, whether to go to other lands, the Siddhar's caution and the hero's resolve give opposite advice, and the epic's road is made of exactly the dangers the Siddhar lists, so the epic treats them as the hero's schooling rather than a reason to stay; the conflict holds only if the kummi's line is read as general advice and not as a rule for the adept alone.

note: The Caranas at Aranapatham wash away their own karma (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்) by renouncing rule; Tirumanthiram 2422 says the soul is cleaned of its dirt as cloth by a washer, and everything that comes to it is the bond of grace.
teaches: Both use the image of washing a stain from the self, but in the Jain epic the ascetic is the washer and the dirt is his karma, while in Tirumular the washer is grace and even the soul's bonds are its soap; the shared image exposes the rival accounts of who does the cleansing.

note: Tirumular calls flesh-eaters புலையர and sends them to hell; Civakan says the hunters were born low because of former killing and eating.
teaches: Tirumular makes baseness a name earned by what one eats now, whatever one's birth, while the epic makes the low birth itself the fruit of past eating, so the two texts tie the same stigma to flesh-eating from opposite ends of the karmic chain.

note: The Cintamani's god is worshipped as the one who cut away his own ghati karmas; Tirumular's grace-power comes as guru and removes the soul's bonds.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina is honoured for destroying his own karmas, the two texts disagree about what a god does with karma: the Jain god is the one who freed himself and is a model to circle, whereas Tirumular's Lord is the agent who frees the bound soul, so the worshipper's release comes from his own effort in one and from descending grace in the other.

note: Tirumular says the three cities Siva destroyed are the work of the three malas; the Jain hymn gives the destroyer of three guarded forts to the Jina, who rose to the world's summit.
teaches: Both a Saiva and a Jain poet read the three-city myth as the destruction of inner bonds, but they give it to different destroyers, so the pair shows the myth as ground the schools contested and allegorised in rival directions.

note: Tirumular has grace-power come as guru and end the malas when one's own agency ceases; the Jain hymn praises the Jina who ended karma that cannot be ended and taught the path of no return.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina ended his own karma and teaches others to end theirs, the two verses give opposite answers to who removes karma: in the Saiva verse one's own doing must stop and grace acts, in the Jain verse the liberated one is the one whose own effort ended it.

note: Tirumular lists removing poison among the powers that yoga brings; Civakan removes the venom by a spell he learned, after seven thousand Brahmins with mantras have failed.
teaches: Where the Tirumanthiram makes curing poison a sign of the yogi's attainment, the Cintamani gives it to a young layman as a learned art and lets the ritual mantra-masters fail, so the same power is moved from spiritual rank to skill and from priest to hero.

note: Tirumular's single five-hooded serpent lives in the anthill of enjoyment and, its hoods drawn into one, makes the body its fit home; the epic's snake of desire lives in the anthill of the body ruled by the five senses and bites again.
teaches: Both poets house a serpent of the five senses in the body's anthill, but Tirumular's can be stilled by discipline into one hood while the epic's strikes the moment a spell has cured the real snake, showing that a remedy for poison is no remedy for the senses.

note: Tirumanthiram 518 says that if pujas in the First One's temple stop, kings suffer, the rains' bounty falls and theft spreads; the epic says the Jina's shrines everywhere keep the city's wealth from failing.
teaches: A Saiva manual and a Jain epic share the belief that shrines keep a land prosperous, but the Saiva verse ties it to rites that must not lapse while the Jain verse credits only the shrines' presence.

note: Pattinathar calls vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, offerings, mantras and pujas all pretence; Civakan mocks standing in the five fires and eating grass, but goes on to urge austerity in the Jina's form (1435).
teaches: Both reject the Vedic ascetic's fire and diet, but the Siddhar rejects observance as such, while the Jain hero rejects one school's austerities only to set up his own, so the pairing separates a critique of ritual from a rivalry of disciplines.

note: Civakan says that if plunging in water won release the bear would gain it; Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so their deeds perish wander the land.
teaches: Both deny that outer bathing destroys deeds, but Tirumular keeps the bath and moves it inward, while the Jain hero drops it and replaces it with knowledge, vision and conduct, so the two show different ways out of the same criticism.

note: Pattinathar asks what forest life, eating wind, rags and the bowl avail without inner love, and says the Lord's true lovers reach release even living at home beside their women; Civakan says sin born of desire for women cannot be removed by union with women.
teaches: The two agree that going to the forest is nothing in itself, but they part on the household: the Saiva poet lets love free one beside one's wife, while the Jain hero makes leaving the wife a condition, so the shared attack on outward renunciation hides opposite views of the married life.

note: In Tirumanthiram 1775 worship of the Lord's feet brings grace by which the worshipper's own five senses are conquered; in 1468 the Jina conquered his own senses, and the worshipper's singing earns heaven, not sense-conquest.
teaches: Both tie the five senses to praise of holy feet, but the conquest is done by different hands: Saiva grace subdues the devotee's senses for him, while in the Jain hymn the conquest belongs to the Jina alone and remains the worshipper's own task.

note: Tirumanthiram 444 gives the eight qualities (குணம் எண்குணம்) to matted-haired Siva who keeps the world; 1469 has them seized from souls by the robber deeds.
teaches: On my reading of 1469, the two texts disagree about whose the eight qualities are: for Tirumular they are the attributes of a God who protects, for the Jain hymn they are the soul's own and are lost to karma, with no protector named who restores them.

note: Both warn men against women's smiles.
teaches: Tirumular's etti fruit says only that the smile is poison under a fair surface; the Jain sermon says what the poison does, endless rebirth in states of sorrow, and in 1555 offers heaven to those who refuse it.

note: Tirumular's dead man has his nine gates shut while the loving ones weep and leave; the Cintamani's dying lover has his eyes closed by the beloved and goes.
teaches: The epic turns Tirumular's unnamed mourners into the very women of the man's pleasures, so the lovers who melt in his arms are those who close his eyes, which joins the critique of desire to the meditation on death.

note: Arunagirinathar calls the nine-gated body a house Brahma built; the Cintamani's hut of flesh is built by a carpenter that 1578 names as the deed (வினை).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the same anatomy of the body serves opposite accounts of its maker, a god in the Thiruppugazh and one's own deeds in the Jain epic, and that the disgust can be shared while the theology differs; the contrast rests on reading 1577's builder through 1578.

note: Siddhar 301 also strips the body to wind, bile and phlegm and foul matter, but the poet confesses he still runs after women and begs the Lord's grace to free him; Civakan recites the catalogue and simply refuses.
teaches: The same catalogue that the Saiva poet finds powerless without grace is, in the Jain epic, enough by itself to master desire, which shows the two traditions disagreeing about whether self-knowledge alone can free a man from lust.

note: Siddhar 696 says the poet wandered over every forest and hill until his legs ached without seeing the Lord who moved within his body; 1603 shows crowds climbing a hill to shed their sins.
teaches: Within the Saiva tradition itself the climb that the epic describes approvingly is mocked as wasted walking, so the pairing shows the Siddhars turning against a practice that Jains and Saivas otherwise held in common.

note: Siddhar 910 calls the mountain of Ekambar the one that removes the hard deeds of those who bow (பணிவாரருவினை தீர்க்கும்); in 1603 women climb a hill so that their accumulated evil deeds may leave them (நிரைத்த தீவினை நீங்க).
teaches: A Jain epic and a Saiva poet share the belief that a sacred hill wears away karma, which shows a common practice of pilgrimage beneath the doctrinal quarrel over how deeds are destroyed.

note: The Jain hymn calls the Jina the one who scorched Kama; Tirumular makes the destruction of Kama's work Siva's yoga at Korukkai.
teaches: The pair shows two traditions claiming the same feat for their own lord and reading it the same inward way, as desire overcome in austerity, so the rivalry is over who did it, not over what it means; the tension holds only if the epithet is read as a title one lord alone may bear.

note: The epic praises the city's women for drawing back even minds bent on release; the Siddhar reproaches his heart for sinking into lust for women after keeping the company of ascetics.
teaches: The same lapse, a seeker of release pulled back by women, is the epic's yardstick of beauty and the Siddhar's confession of madness, so what one poet spends as a compliment is the very failure the other's renunciation is built to fight.

note: Pattinattar lists the body as a feast thrown to the pyre's fire (ஈமக் கனல்) and a leaf scorched in the fire of desire (காமக் கனல்); Civakan's body, called a pyre (ஈமம்), burns in desire's fever (காமக் கடுநோய்க் கனல்).
teaches: The same pairing of pyre and desire's fire is a reason to renounce the body in Pattinattar and a lover's complaint in the epic, so the image does not carry its lesson with it: the hero who will one day renounce here uses it only to say how much he burns.

note: Both name bathing at Kumari to be rid of a bodily affliction; the Thiruppugazh poet asks not to go there and be laughed at by many as a diseased wretch, and the epic's old brahmin goes there and is laughed at (பெரிது நக்கு, 2021).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the afflicted pilgrim to Kumari was a stock figure of ridicule, and that Civakan chooses that figure as a disguise precisely because a man so laughable is trusted inside a guarded house.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks whether a planted stone will speak; in 2058 a worshipper hears the shrine speak, and the narrator says the voice was a man's trick.
teaches: The Siddhar's scorn assumes the stone is silent; the epic shows a voice supplied to it by a hidden man, so the credulity he mocks can be steered by whoever stands behind the image.

note: Rudradattan counts the konrai-wearing god's taking the mountain-daughter as his half as a stain and a great blame; Tirumanthiram 16 names the same god by that half-woman form as the one the gods delight in.
teaches: The same mark of Siva, his body shared with Uma, is a counsellor's example of lust's disgrace in a Jain epic and a title of praise in Tirumular's invocation, so the image itself is where the schools part.

note: Both use the wood-apple swallowed by the elephant, whole in shell and emptied within: the Cintamani for a king whom Fortune has left, Tirumular for Siva swallowing soul, states and world.
teaches: The same figure of a shell kept whole while its substance is taken means ruin for a king and consummation for a soul, so Tirumular turns a stock image of loss into one of absorption in Siva.

note: In 2366 a god crowns Civakan with gold and sea-water; Tirumanthiram 1601 says that those who rule the three worlds wear crowns, but the bliss of the kings of the Lord's feet has no measure.
teaches: The Cintamani lets the crowning be the height of splendour, while the Saiva verse ranks the same crowned kings below those who serve at the feet, so what counts as the highest state is exactly what the two texts divide on.

note: The narrator says her adorned beauty would bewilder even the steady; the Tirumanthiram tells the heart to turn from women who smile and show their breasts, as the etti tree's fruit is good to look at and not to eat.
teaches: The narrator and the Saiva teacher agree that adorned beauty overcomes the heart, but the narrator offers it as wonder and the teacher as a poison to resist.

note: The wedding verses lay out darbha, sticks and ghee for the fire with care; siddhar 372 lists observances, vows, the Vedas, fire rites and water offerings as among the outward forms the Siddhar puts aside.
teaches: A Jain poem makes the fire rite the centre of a happy wedding while the Siddhar counts the same fire rite among forms to be left behind, so what counts as a sacred act depends on whether the aim is a household or release.

note: 2466 reports the fire rising right as an omen of fortune; Tirumanthiram 551 says the way of sacrifice has no way through while the eight-limbed yoga path leads to samadhi.
teaches: The epic reads the fire as a sign of worldly fortune, while Tirumular reads the same fire path as a dead end for release, so the same rite is a good for the household and no good for release.

note: Civakan says he will not be born again, having found the unborn one; Tirumular says that after he renounced and saw the light the lord of the gods set him here so that he would not die and be born again.
teaches: Both end births by reaching a lord who is not born, but the Saiva verse makes the lord the one who sets the seeker free while the epic verse puts the claim in the worshipper's mouth and does not say the Jina acts.

note: Tirumanthiram 207 says that union with young women is sweet cane juice in the hand and turns bitter neem in the body; 2598 sets the same pleasure as a sweet harvest of love enjoyed in peace.
teaches: Set against the Saiva warning, the epic's closing image of the king resting in love reads as a stage in a life the epic itself will end in renunciation, not a conclusion.

note: Tirumular says one who comes to seize the world for others or himself has the nature of a pouncing tiger; 262 shows Kattiyangaran's seizure: kin chained, wealth given to those who submit, one umbrella over the land.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the usurper's nature, and the Cintamani shows his method, buying loyalty and chaining kin, and calls the result a lamp of infamy.

note: Vijayai says the body is a fire of disease with life as ghee, and urges giving and good before Death leaves; Tirumular says give out the rice before the pot burns near, since the days slip away.
teaches: Both turn the household fire and the measure of rice into a warning that gifts must go out now; the epic frames it as the end of a king's pleasure, the Saiva verse as ordinary housekeeping.

note: 2628 has the matrons go in palanquins to their renunciation; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the town mount for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground.
teaches: One kind of vehicle is shown going two ways: a rich woman's palanquin carries her to a life given up while still alive, and the lord's palanquin carries him to the burning ground whether he chooses or not.

note: 2635 has the women fling off garlands and ornaments and sow thorns on Kama's road; Siddhar 19 asks when the singer shall leave silk clothes, gold ornaments, pretence and evil deeds and desire the Lord's feet.
teaches: Both strip off ornament, but one is done as a rite with no god in it and the other is a longing aimed at a god's feet.

note: The king is set above the love-god among women; Tirumantiram 203 says even those who hold knowledge are infatuated with women who bewilder and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The epic's compliment to the king and the Saiva verse's warning describe one hold, and the reader learns the praise is also a statement of how firm that hold is.

note: The Siddhar says weeping and worship are useless because good and evil come as the lotus-born god wrote; the king says birth and death come from the fruit of one's own deeds.
teaches: The two give the same counsel against grief for opposite reasons: the Siddhar's outcome is written by a creator, the Cintamani's by the sufferer's own deeds, with no god in the account.

note: Pattinathar asks how many mothers, wives, children and births he has had and has yet to have, and cries to the lord of Ekambam; Saccandan reckons births past the sands of the shore and tells his wife kinship lasts two days.
teaches: The same reckoning of countless births and passing kin brings the Siddhar to despair and a cry for Siva's help, and brings the Jain king to composure with no god, so the argument's outcome turns on where release is placed.

note: The mate asks who would take bitter neem after mountain honey; Tirumanthiram 207 says the sweet of young women turns to neem within the body.
teaches: The same pair of sweet and bitter serves a wife's refusal and a sage's warning, showing the image works both for pride and for renunciation.

note: Tirumanthiram 114 has Nandi cut away the tarnish and open the eye of grace so that a light shows that nothing can darken; 2745 asks a Jain ascetic's grace to clear the darkness of karma.
teaches: Both ask a teacher's grace to clear a stain, but Nandi gives it as a lord who acts on the soul, while the Jain sage is only asked and is a teacher, not a god.

note: Tirumanthiram 307 calls life and body a close support and the mind on Siva's feet the firm support that ends birth; 2748 lists the body hard to gain and its destruction among the sermon's topics, with release.
teaches: Both begin from the body, which the Saiva verse treats as a support to be used, while the Jain sage announces it as a thing that is rare and must end.

note: Tirumular says the subtle body eats the fruit in heaven and hell and then takes another body with the old deeds following; 2762 says the evildoer eats the harvest of deeds sown in the soul.
teaches: Both let the deeds ripen as an experience of hell, but the Saiva verse carries the sufferer on into a new birth by a subtle body, which the Jain verse does not say here.

note: Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind and drive the killers into fire-mouthed hell; in 2764 the hell-beings rise and fall on the blades with no jailer named.
teaches: The Saiva verse puts Yama's servants in charge, while the Jain verse leaves the pain to the deeds and the place, so the two show different views of who runs hell.

note: Siddhar 16 hopes to avoid being called a sinner and falling into the barren hell, by knowing the breath-thread; 2766 shows what that fall would be, the stake and the fire.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to avoid hell gains a picture of what he flees, and the epic's picture of hell gets a way out the Siddhar names, knowledge of the breath rather than the Jain sermon's virtue.

note: 2774 gives hell's tortures by molten copper and the oil-press without a cause; Tirumanthiram 198 binds those who urged 'kill, stab' and sets them in fire-mouthed hell.
teaches: Together they show hell as the fruit of a named sin and as a daily mechanical punishment, which neither shows alone.

note: 2791 shows the body as a skin of filth swarming with worms; Siddhar 41 calls it a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow.
teaches: Both teach disgust at the body, one to warn of birth, the other to leave the body for the feet of Siva.

note: 2797 says the body is a grove burned by the fire of disease; Siddhar 63 says this life has no standing, like a bubble on water.
teaches: Jain teacher and Siddhar agree that the body does not stand, but one asks escape from disease and the other from rebirth by grace.

note: The epic gods, with fifteen days left, blink and see their garlands fade and grieve like those who ate poisoned nectar; the Saiva verse says countless gods have died while the one with the forehead eye stays.
teaches: The two texts share the mortality of gods but part on the cure: the Jain verse leaves no god to rest on and moves the hearer to release, the Saiva verse moves him to the one undying Lord.

note: The epic says every being from Indra to a monkey eats the fruit of its own deeds, with release by understanding; the Saiva verse says the Lord stands beyond the two deeds and is the seed of the world.
teaches: The two give opposite places to the divine in karma: for the Jain verse no one, however high, stands outside deeds, for the Saiva verse the Lord alone does.

note: 2824 has the ascetic wither the five senses and so subdue them by effort; Tirumanthiram 140 says the senses come under control of themselves once the Lord is met.
teaches: One text holds that the senses are conquered by the ascetic's own labour, the other that they are conquered by meeting the Lord, so the two disagree on who does the work.

note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only in the sun's presence, as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun.
teaches: Both burn the impurity by fire, but one fire is the seeker's own three virtues and the other needs the Lord's sun.

note: 2868 teaches against killing as a cause of suffering ripening from deeds; Tirumanthiram 200 names killing, theft, lust and lying as sins great as mountains whose giving up reaches Siva's feet.
teaches: The same sins are shunned in both, but one pays out as karma and the other as arrival at a god's feet.

note: 2876 gives the old deed as a thread that cannot be torn away and burns the soul; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn like cotton only when the sunstone meets the sun's presence, and not before.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves the deed unbroken and the Saiva verse says what ends it, so the Saiva verse limits the Jain one's permanence.

note: 2885 has the prince reason that there is no kin and cut the bond of love; Siddhar 55 wishes to put kin away, like a lotus leaf on water, with the mind far off.
teaches: The Siddhar states a wish for detachment and the prince acts on an argument, so together they show the wish and its grounds.

note: 2886 compares the body to a doll that falls apart joint by joint when its pins are loosed; Siddhar 42 asks when the puppet taken up to match the two karmas will be thrown down.
teaches: The epic shows the doll's falling as a mechanism and the Siddhar wants to throw it down, so one explains how the body fails and the other why it is to be cast off.

note: Pattinathar asks what breasts, union with women and gathered wealth can do against the coming struggle, and says the god put an eyeless needle in his hand; Civakan stops wanting women's pleasure because he has tasted a greater sweetness.
teaches: Both rich men turn from women and wealth, but the Siddhar's ground is their uselessness before death and a sign from Siva, while the epic's is a higher bliss already tasted, so the same turn can be told as a loss seen through or as a lesser pleasure outgrown.

note: 2902 has Nandan turn away from release to worship a brother's feet; Tirumanthiram 284 has devotees who bow in devotion given release in return.
teaches: One text makes devotion the door to release, the other makes devotion a choice that outweighs release.

note: 2904 has Civakan act on the body's hollowness by handing on the realm; Siddhar 642 warns the heart that Yama takes the body from a golden throne and the gold stays behind.
teaches: The Siddhar only warns that the throne cannot be carried away, while the epic king acts on the warning and descends from it.

note: 2934 follows the embryo through the channel and into muddy water where it falls weeping without provision for the road; Tirumanthiram 451 has the Lord stay within the womb and form the embryo.
teaches: One text lets the body come into the world helpless and left to its deeds, the other has a Lord who forms it, so the same birth is read without and with a maker.

note: 2940 shows the body's colour, breasts and eyes fading with age as the women watch; Siddhar 23 asks when the speaker will see the bones within as white bones and see himself lowered like a cast-off corpse.
teaches: The epic shows the body's fading from the lover's side, the Siddhar from the renouncer's, so one is a loss and the other is a practice.

note: 2965 shows the wives stripping bangles and weeping at the king's going, while Tirumanthiram 157 has the wives and kin who wailed turn back at the town's edge.
teaches: The epic shows grieving women at a living man's leaving, where the Tirumanthiram shows the same women turning back at a dead man's bier.

note: 2984 sets wealth against the funeral rice and the wife's tears at the burning ground; Tirumanthiram 149 gives the man's public mansion, palanquin and three crores and then his silent going.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram shows a life of building and giving with no look back; the epic shows what the household is left with, so together they give the whole before and after.

note: 2985 calls the fruit of good deeds poison and says only crossing the flood of deeds gives bliss; Tirumanthiram 258 makes penance and virtue the boat that carries one across the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both see deeds as a sea to cross, but one holds virtue's fruit to be poison and the other makes virtue the boat, so the two disagree on whether good deeds help or only bind.

note: 2988 has the wives cross old deeds by leaving the household and gives no god; Tirumanthiram 219 has the worshipped fire rise and burn the diseases of deeds.
teaches: One text frees from old deeds by the renouncer's own crossing, the other by a fire that burns them when worshipped, which is the split between Jain effort and Saiva rite.

note: 2992 has the wives lay aside their ornaments like a vine shedding flowers; Siddhar 19 asks when the speaker will leave silk and gold ornaments and desire the feet.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to leave ornaments is shown done by women who give them up, but without the god's feet as its aim.

note: In 2998 the king mounts a palanquin that the gods carry; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the land mount the burning ground's palanquin for the last time.
teaches: The same royal vehicle is a bier in one and a god-borne chair to release in the other, so the reader sees how renunciation and death can wear the same procession.

note: 3020 praises the Jina as the master whose spoken word frees those who repeat it from suffering; Tirumanthiram 105 has the Lord stand beyond the two kinds of deed.
teaches: Jain release comes by hearing and keeping the word of one who went before, while the Saiva text puts the Lord beyond deeds so that deeds cannot reach him, and the two disagree on whether a liberated one also helps.

note: In 3033 the bees mourn the cast-off hair and garland; Siddhar 329 lists a loincloth, a porch and leaves to eat as all one needs once ornament is gone.
teaches: The Jain epic gives the loss of ornament a lament by those who lived on it, while the Siddhar counts it as pure gain.

note: 3039 has the freed ascetic reach it by wholly dropping attachment and hatred; Tirumanthiram 497 has the siddhas free of the bonds by becoming Siva and destroying the five malas.
teaches: The Jain epic makes release the result of the ascetic's own dropping of passions; the Saiva text has it come by becoming Siva.

note: 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas by the strength of his own mind; Tirumanthiram 120 has deeds made into seeds that have touched fire and will not sprout, by the one who parts milk from water, the Lord or guru.
teaches: The seeds will not sprout in both, but one makes the ascetic himself the burner and the other leaves the burner a god or teacher.

note: 3072 has Civakan spend four cold months in the open field, using the body up for release; Tirumanthiram 724 says if the body perishes the life perishes, so the body is nurtured to win knowledge.
teaches: One text treats the body as the means to be spent, the other as the means that must be kept alive, so they disagree on what a body is for.

note: 3081 fires the arrow of pure meditation like a roaring fire to destroy the foes; Tirumanthiram 219 has deeds burnt by the fire that is worshipped and fed with ghee.
teaches: One text burns deeds by an inner meditation like fire, the other by an outer fire kindled in worship, so the two disagree on where the fire is.

note: 3082 has Civakan win omniscience by his own war on the karmas; Tirumanthiram 113 has the Lord come down in a body, set his feet on the devotee's head and cut away the stain.
teaches: One text has the soul win release by its own battle, the other has it given from above, so the two disagree on whose act cuts the deeds.

note: 3101 has worship of the feet cut karma like a weapon; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages.
teaches: Both promise that worship removes karma, but one gives the cutting to an enlightened teacher's feet and the other to a worshipped fire.

note: 3117 pictures omniscience as a maiden embraced by the king at the top of the worlds, the self still distinct; Tirumanthiram 134 says those who feel the teacher's word become the reality, like ghee mixed in milk.
teaches: Both end in bliss, but the Cintamani keeps lover and beloved two, while the Tirumanthiram dissolves the self into what it meets.

note: Both build a field guarded by a fence against stray beasts: Cintamani 379's crop is life from infancy to old age, its beasts diseases and its fence the vows (சீல வேலி); Pattinattar's field is the heart, its cattle the five senses, its fence calm (சாந்த வேலி), and its fruit Siva's form.
teaches: The shared Tamil figure of the fenced crop carries opposite ends: the Jain teacher fences a life to be kept from harm by vowed discipline, while the Saiva poet fences a devotion that ripens into the god, so the doctrine lies in what each names as fence and fruit.

note: Tirumanthiram 1527: when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru, and when one's own agency ends the impurities go; Cintamani 380: a past good deed drives Civakan and his own understanding reaches out, and he takes refuge in the Arhat.
teaches: Both put a teacher at the turn toward release, but for Tirumular the teacher is grace descending once deeds cancel and one's agency ends, while for the Jain epic it is the push of a good deed and the youth's own understanding that bring him to the teacher's Lord.

note: Tirumular has grace come as the guru and end the soul's own doing; in the Cintamani the guru is himself a karma-bound ascetic who goes off to wear down his old deeds by his own penance.
teaches: The two texts set the guru on opposite sides of karma: for Tirumular the guru is the descent of grace that ends one's deeds, while the Cintamani's teacher, having formed his pupil, must still work off his own past by effort.

note: Bhadragiriyar asks when he will cut the sunken root of desire at its base; the epic says Accanandi cut the root of desire (ஆர்வ வேர் அரிந்து) and went on to austerity and release.
teaches: The same image of desire as a root to be cut is a lament of 'when?' in the Siddhar and a finished first step in the Jain epic, where it is only the start of a path that still needs austerity before release.

note: Tirumular threatens unending hell to a king who fails to guard cows, women, the virtuous and the holy; Civakan, not a king, binds himself to the same guard on pain of a eunuch's shame.
teaches: Read together, the duty to guard cows, women and the holy passes from the failed king to a private man, and its sanction moves from hell after death to dishonour in this life.

note: 496 has the merchant hold that effort alone can bring a flood of wealth in a day; Siddhar 641 tells the heart that the wealth it has came by the order of deeds done in earlier lives and was not got today.
teaches: The two disagree about where wealth comes from, today's effort or earlier lives, and the epic lets its merchant hold the first view only until the storm turns him to the second.

note: Tirumanthiram 724 nurtures the body because without it true knowledge cannot be gained; 605 bids all strive at hard penance while still in the body.
teaches: Both make the living body the only place where release can be worked for, but the proclamation spends the body in austerity while Tirumular guards it as the means of knowledge, so the same premise yields discipline in one and care in the other.

note: At Krishna's flute in the Thiruppugazh dry trees in the forest sprout and birds come down to the ground; at Gandharvadattai's yazh the trees of the grove put out shoots and the birds forget themselves and fall.
teaches: The same marvel of music that moves trees and birds is a god's sign in the hymn and a contest's evidence in the epic, where 659 adds the reverse, birds fleeing bad music, so the image becomes a measure as well as a wonder.

note: The spectators of 682 waste away like a butter doll in the sun of desire; in Thiruppugazh 142 the poet, melting like wax in fire for women, asks whether he must stay bound to that shame.
teaches: The same melting is in the epic the measure of a dancer's art and in the hymn a bondage to be prayed away, so the image shows how one bodily figure serves praise and penitence.

note: Tirumanthiram 346 reads Siva's burning of Kama as the yoga that destroys desire's work; the Cintamani says Civakan is as if the burnt Kama had risen again on earth.
teaches: Set beside the Saiva reading, the Jain poet's simile shows the burning of Kama handled as a story whose victim returns, so the myth becomes a measure of a hero's beauty instead of a victory over desire.

note: Tirumanthiram 2133 has the subtle body, its old deeds following, take up a new body; 799's arrows warn the slain against evil in the body they will take next.
teaches: Held together, the epic's warning to the dying presupposes the passage Tirumular describes, and Tirumular's mechanism is given a moral use: deeds follow, so the dead are urged to change their conduct across the change of body.

note: Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart and that those who wander the land without bathing in them do not destroy their deeds; Civakan takes the water of a jewelled conch at the Tirthan's feet as part of putting away his sin.
teaches: Read as part of the sin-clearing rite, the conch water is the outward tirtham Tirumular says cannot destroy deeds, so the pair sets an epic's confidence in rite against a Saiva yogi's insistence on the inward bath.

note: The Cintamani calls the Jina the lord of faultless kevala; Tirumular calls kevala the soul's sleep of utter stupor under anava, from which karma drives it out.
teaches: The same word for the soul's state 'alone' is the summit of release for the Jain poet and the lowest darkness of the bound soul for the Saiva, so the two traditions disagree on whether the soul left to itself is free or blind.

note: Tirumanthiram 533 says those who grieve the ascetics who teach the mantra are born as dogs; in 945 a dog dying with no merit hears a mantra and is born a god.
teaches: Both texts tie the mantra to rebirth as a dog, but run the scale in opposite directions: Tirumular uses the dog's birth as the punishment for wronging the mantra's teachers, the Jain epic uses the mantra to lift a dog out of that birth even without merit.

note: Tirumanthiram 905 promises that chanting சிவாயநம ends birth, by grace; in 946 the Lord's five padas, taken at death, bring the dog a good state (நற்கதி), a better birth.
teaches: Both are five-part formulas given at the decisive moment, but the Saiva five letters promise an end to birth through grace, while the Jain five padas here promise a better birth by the dog's own letting go of attachment and fear.

note: Both make a recited formula the agent of a change of state: Tirumular's சிவாயநம is an alchemist's pill that turns the body's cage to gold; the Cintamani's five padas are water that washes off black karma and bring a new god's body after death.
teaches: Set side by side, the two mantras do different work: the Saiva syllables transmute the body the devotee already has through the Lord's act, while the Jain padas clear karma so that a better body follows in the next birth, with no Lord who acts.

note: Both use iron turned to gold for a change of being: Tirumular says gold once made never turns back to iron, so one who has the guru's grace is not born again; the Cintamani's iron-to-gold is a dog reborn as a god.
teaches: The same alchemy marks a final release in Tirumular and only a rise within the round of births in the Cintamani, so the image's 'no return' belongs to the Saiva claim, not to the figure itself.

note: Tirumular says those who grieve the ascetics who taught the mantra are born as dogs (சுணங்கன்); the Cintamani's dog (சுணங்கன்) is raised to a god's birth by the mantra heard from Civakan.
teaches: Read together, the teacher's mantra decides birth in both directions: offending its teachers sinks a man to a dog, and receiving it lifts a dog to a god, so the same word names the bottom of the scale in both books.

note: In 962 the practiser yokes the plough, tills his own body and guards it with the senses' fence until release ripens; in Tirumular 1875 the first Lord has taken the poet's soul as his field to plough, and praise and blame fall away.
teaches: The two pictures of the tilled self disagree on who holds the plough: in the Jain allegory release is the crop of one's own labour, in Tirumular the Lord does the tilling, so the shared farm figure carries the dispute between release by effort and release by grace.

note: Pattinathar's verse has fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog each say of the body 'it is mine'; Kundalakesi 14 says worms feed and live in the body while one still calls it 'mine'.
teaches: The fragment finds the rival owners already at work in the living body, while Pattinathar lines them up at the corpse; held together, the claim 'mine' is false both before death and after it.

note: Pattinathar asks what use weeping is, since good and evil will not come otherwise than as the lotus-born god wrote; Kundalakesi 19 has a man stay unmoved by pardon and death because all that befalls is the fruit of deeds.
teaches: Both counsel the same steadiness, but the Siddhar grounds it in what a god wrote and the fragment in one's own deeds, so the same calm rests on incompatible accounts of who decides what comes.

note: Tirumanthiram 1662 makes wearing holy ash the first of the emblems of the flawless Siva-yogi; Kundalakesi 4 puts smearing the body with ash among the practices it calls mere words.
teaches: The same act, ash on the body, is for Tirumular the first sign of the true yogi and for the Kundalakesi a hollow show, so the two traditions disagree on whether an outward mark can belong to tapas at all; the tension depends on reading பொடி பூசல் as ash-smearing.

note: Tirumular bids the seeker hold to the Lord's feet, by whom strong deeds perish, and says the Lord will set him among the gods; Aravanan calls the Buddha's footprints on the hill the feet that destroy faults, and the next unit says the sisters who worshipped there were reborn beside Lakshmi.
teaches: Both give the feet power over past deeds, but the Saiva feet belong to a Lord who acts now and places the soul, while the Buddhist feet are the trace of a teacher who left long ago, and their fruit comes from the worshippers' own act ripening in the next birth.

note: Tirumular says joy and sorrow are settled by former deeds and that those who see their joy and still do not give know no dharma; Manimekalai sees the prosperous enjoying the fruit of dharma sown (108-109) while the hungry stand ragged at their gates.
teaches: A Saiva and a Buddhist text agree that karma explaining who is fed does not excuse withholding, and the epic adds that the giver's own gift is the deed that will return as a means of giving.

note: Tirumular bids refuge in the shade of the feet of the one God present in all ten directions, so that the sea of deeds will not reach; Aravanar goes to worship the footprints of the First Lord on one hill because they wash away hard deeds.
teaches: Both texts make worship of feet dissolve karma, but the Saiva feet are everywhere because their Lord is, while the Buddhist feet are a print left on a particular hill by a teacher of the past, so the shared gesture rests on opposite accounts of where the cleansing power lies.

note: The Siddhar says he has resolved to beg from any caste and lacks nothing; Aputtiran, driven from caste with stones in his bowl, begs from every house to feed the helpless and eats what is left.
teaches: Begging across caste lines is the Siddhar's chosen freedom and his sufficiency, while for Aputtiran it is what is left after caste expels him, and he turns it outward to feed others, so the same act carries renunciation in one and charity in the other.

note: Saathuvan argues that the departing life enters the body its deeds put on, as a reason for the Nagas to do good; Tirumular bids the reader seek the way by which, leaving this body, one does not enter another.
teaches: The same passage of the life into a new body is good news in the epic, a reason to act well for a better world, and the thing to be escaped in Tirumular, so the pair shows that a merchant's ethics of rebirth stops short of the release both traditions put beyond it.

note: Sivavakkiyar's man, having taken a woman for her form, would cut down any rival who desires her, though his own body will stink and be handed to the cremation keeper; Kanchanan cuts down the prince over a form that is not even his wife's, whose body is already gone.
teaches: The epic gives the Siddhar's jealous husband a case where the form (வடிவு) he guards belongs to another woman and his wife's body has already perished, so the jealousy is shown wrong both about whose body it is and about its lasting.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the planted stone called a god and asks whether it will speak while the Lord is within; the pillar deity grants that stone and wood do not speak but says deities the wise install in them stay and speak to men.
teaches: Both start from the same premise, that the stone itself is mute; they part over whether a power can be lodged in it, the epic answering yes for guardian deities of a city and the Siddhar answering that the Lord is found only within.

note: Tirumular's grace-power descends as the guru when good and bad deeds are balanced and the soul becomes Siva; the epic's Manimekalai, after births of compassion, becomes a disciple and is saved by cutting dependence herself (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி).
teaches: Both put a teacher at the threshold of release, but in Tirumular the teacher is grace that ends the soul's own agency, while in the epic the great one only gives dharma and the disciple does the cutting, so they disagree over who acts in release.

note: Tirumular calls killing, theft, lust and lying sins as great as mountains, whose giving up leads to Siva's feet; the ascetic names toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust as the five to be shunned and threatens hell to those who keep lust.
teaches: Two traditions share nearly the same list of sins but use it differently: Tirumular makes their giving up a path to Siva's feet, while the ascetic names no god, singles out lust as the one that contains the rest, and uses the list to warn a king of hell.

note: Tirumular describes the whole town wailing, renaming the dead man a corpse, burning him and bathing to forget; Manimekalai asks the queen whether she weeps for the body, since mourners themselves cast it into the burning ground, or for the life, whose next dwelling is set by deeds.
teaches: Tirumular's observation that mourners burn and forget the body they weep for becomes in the epic the first horn of a dilemma whose second horn turns grief for one life into pity for all lives.

note: Tirumular nurtures the body because its perishing ends the life before true knowledge is won; when the queen wishes Aravanar's aged body long life, he answers that ageing and death are the nature of the born and turns to teaching.
teaches: The pair sets the Saiva siddha's body kept alive for knowledge against the Buddhist teacher's body let go because knowledge has been reached and must be passed on, so the worth of a long life depends on whether knowledge is still to be won.

note: Tirumular says those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet and its bliss; Aravanar counts the same sins among ten and says that leaving them, with precept and giving, wins only birth as god, human or Brahma.
teaches: The same abstentions are release in the Saiva verse and only a better birth in the Buddhist sermon, which places release in knowing the twelve links rather than in conduct; the pair shows that the two schools agree on the list and disagree on what it buys.

note: Pathirakiriyar asks when he will see the bones within as white bones and himself lowered like a cast-off corpse; the king digs up his own former body, bones held together as if coated in white lime, and is bewildered.
teaches: The epic grants literally the sight the Siddhar longs for, one's own body as white bones, and shows that the sight alone does not free: the king is bewildered until Manimekalai tells him what it is for.

note: The Ajivika holds the elemental atoms to be without beginning; Sivavakkiyar says the elements and senses, and even the soul, are not beginningless, and only the truth mingled with them is.
teaches: The question of what is beginningless divides the two: for the Ajivika matter itself is eternal, for the Siddhar matter and soul are both made, and only the one truth is without beginning.

note: Both end with the two deeds turned back; the Jain does it by blocking new deeds and exhausting old ones, Tirumular by keeping the Lord's feet in mind.
teaches: The pair shows Jain and Saiva agreeing that release needs both good and bad deeds stopped, and parting over whether the stopping is one's own labour or follows from holding the Lord.

note: The Sankhya speaker has space, wind, fire, water and earth unfold from intellect; Tirumular gives the same chain from மான் (mahat), in his chapter on creation.
teaches: The same sequence of elements serves the Sankhya as nature unfolding by itself and Tirumular as part of the Lord's creating, so the cosmology was shared while its cause was disputed.

note: The Sankhya speaker counts twenty-five principles with no maker; Tirumular says the Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb.
teaches: Tirumular keeps the Sankhya count and adds a maker who shapes the twenty-five for each embryo, which is the step the Sankhya account leaves out.

note: The materialist makes awareness a product of the combined elements; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the dancing self is the five elements and answers with release into open space.
teaches: The tension depends on reading Sivavakkiyar's questions as rhetorical denials: the self that sees the house of release is not the elements, against the materialist for whom nothing survives their parting.

note: Manimekalai learns the five kinds of religion on her way to the Buddha's truth; Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him.
teaches: Both texts make a survey of the sects a stage to pass through, but Manimekalai's ends in reasoned teaching and Tirumular's in clarity about a Lord the sects miss.

note: The Saiva debater defines God as the eight forms; Pattinathar reads the eight forms and Siva's other emblems as teachings, and mocks those who whirl in word and meaning.
teaches: Set beside the debate hall, Pattinathar's verse shows the Saiva poets turning the same eight-form creed from a debating thesis into a teaching the arguers fail to grasp.

note: Brahma-vadin, Vaishnava and Saiva each name a different maker or keeper; Tirumular says the three gods are one in continuity and that those who divide them quarrel.
teaches: Manimekalai rejects the theistic schools for disagreeing with truth, while Tirumular faults only their division, so the same sectarian quarrel is read as error by the Buddhist and as a misunderstanding by the Saiva.

note: Both hold that heaven belongs to the round of deeds; Tirumular frees the soul from heaven, hell and earth by grace, while the seers have Kovalan freed by hearing the Buddha's dharma after he has eaten his deed.
teaches: The two agree that heaven is no escape from karma and part exactly on the way out: Saiva release is given by grace, while the Buddhist release comes after the deed is spent and the teaching heard, with no giver.

note: Arunagirinathar lumps Buddhists with the followers of Kapila and Kanada as clamouring disputants whose books cannot give the teaching; here a Buddhist teacher takes apart arguments of the Sankhya and the Vaisheshika by formal logic.
teaches: The pair shows the same quarrel from inside and outside: what the devotee hears as noise of books, the epic presents as a disciplined refutation, and it is the Buddhist the devotee counts first among the noisy.

note: Both turn from the noise of the schools to a teacher; Arunagiri asks Murugan for an upadesam and a vision past the logicians' quarrel, while Manimekalai's teacher answers with the rules of valid argument.
teaches: The pair shows two answers to the same fatigue with the schools: the Buddhist epic trains the hearer to argue rightly, the Saiva hymn asks to be lifted beyond argument by grace, and the tension holds as long as the logic is read as a path and not only as a tool.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Aravanar, who folds scripture into inference, ends his teaching of dharma with the rules of disputation.
teaches: The two give opposite answers to whether argument leads toward release: for Tirumular it is what the wise leave behind, for the Buddhist teacher it is the discipline that sorts true from false before doctrine is heard.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and debate (தர்க்க வாதம்), recited the Veda and gained release; the Buddhist teacher folds scripture into inference and makes logic the first part of the true doctrine.
teaches: The two disagree on the same question, whether scripture stands as its own source of truth above argument, and the Buddhist answer explains why the epic's road to release passes through debate rules that the Saiva verse tells the wise to leave behind.

note: Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the suffering of the bond; Aravanar says the born meet growing suffering, the unborn great bliss, and suffering comes from attachment.
teaches: Both trace suffering to a binding, attachment or the bond, but they disagree about birth itself: for the Buddhist teacher birth is the suffering and not being born is bliss, while for Tirumular birth was made for joy and the bond was laid on it by the same Lord; the conflict holds on reading இன்பப் பிறவி as birth made for joy.

note: The teacher says bondage and release have their own causes and no one exists to grant them; Tirumular says grace put the soul into bonds and grace gives release.
teaches: The two name the same pair, bondage and release, and give opposite answers to who brings them about: the epic denies any giver, and Tirumular makes one grace the giver of both, so the Buddhist and Saiva accounts of release divide exactly at line 251.

note: The teacher's ten bad deeds include killing, theft, lust and lying, as Tirumular's yama does, but the epic sorts them by body, speech and mind and counts coveting, anger and wrong view as deeds, while Tirumular adds sharing food and shunning drink.
teaches: Set side by side, the two lists of ten show the same core abstentions serving different ends: for the epic they decide the next birth, for Tirumular they are the first step of yoga toward Siva, and only the epic counts states of mind as deeds.

note: The drunk calls toddy-drinking a yoga whose fruit the ascetic should taste; Tirumanthiram 566 says breath-control gives the intoxication of toddy without drinking it.
teaches: The equation of drink and yogic ecstasy runs in opposite directions: the Tirumanthiram borrows toddy's joy as an image for breath-discipline, while the epic's drunk borrows yoga's name to sell toddy, so the pair shows the figure was common enough to be turned either way.

note: Pattinattar calls the body the enjoyment of deeds, gone the moment deeds end, and sends the mind to Siva's feet; Sudhamathi calls it born of deeds and the field where they ripen, and asks only that it be known and turned from.
teaches: The two share the premise that the body exists to eat karma but part on the remedy: the Saiva poet needs Siva's feet, while the epic's speaker names no god and puts release in seeing the body truly.

note: The epic calls the teacher whose seat this is the physician of the disease of birth (பிறவிப் பிணி மருத்துவன்); Arunagirinathar calls Murugan of Thiruttani the physician of the disease of becoming (பவரோக வயித்திய நாத) and asks his grace to cut birth's root.
teaches: The same title names two cures: in the Buddhist epic the physician heals by teaching dharma to those who have cleansed their minds, and his seat alone is left to be worshipped; in the Saiva hymn he heals by grace given to one who calls his name.

note: The patikam states as a thesis that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the Tirumanthiram says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling (வினை சேரகிலாமை).
teaches: If the patikam's line is read as admitting no release, the two give incompatible accounts of whether a past deed must be eaten, and the epic offers no grace that could stop it, since even the gods appear only to honour Kannaki after the deed has run its course; the Tirumanthiram puts grace before the fruit.

note: The Charana says the strong deed cannot be put off once it clings and that release from births comes through the Jina's spoken teaching; Tirumular says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling at all.
teaches: The two give incompatible accounts of whether a ripening deed can be stopped: for the Charana only the cycle of births can be ended, by teaching, while the deed must still be eaten; for Tirumular grace prevents the deed from clinging.

note: The brahmin tells the traveller to recite the mantras of five and eight letters and bathe in the pool he wants, though better to fix the heart on the god's feet; the Siddhar asks those seeking a holy water where the bathing is, and says the holy water is the five letters within.
teaches: Both move from outer water toward an inner formula, but the brahmin keeps the pool and makes the letters its key while the Siddhar dissolves the pool into the letters, so the pair shows two stages of one turn from pilgrimage to recitation.

note: Tirumular makes knowledge of the First, the meaning of the Veda, together with Parashakti abiding in his half, the mark of the one in niyama; the vari makes the hunters' war goddess the woman's form in the half of the forehead-eyed god, praised by the Veda, while carrying Vishnu's conch and discus.
teaches: The half-woman form that Tirumular holds as an object of contemplative knowledge is, in the hunters' song, a goddess with Vishnu's weapons on a fighting mount, so the pair shows the same Saiva image serving yogic discipline in one text and a war cult that will not keep her to one god in the other.

note: The hunters owe the goddess a bali as a debt; Tirumular, having nothing to show the god who eats oblations, offers a song as his food offering.
teaches: The vari is itself a song sung over the bali, so the hunters give both the blood and the song that Tirumular offers in its place, which shows the song offering was a companion of the blood rite before it was a substitute for it.

note: Tirumular praises the lord who swallowed the poison and shares half his body with the lady; the hunters give the poison-swallowing to the goddess herself.
teaches: The hymn moves Siva's defining act of grace to his consort through the shared body Tirumular names, and makes it the ground on which a goddess who eats the pitiless hunters' offerings still grants grace.

note: Tirumular lists the goddess's names (Tripurai, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani and others) and says by them the great one stands as many; the vari lists Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli and others for the hunters' goddess of the stag.
teaches: Both pile names on one goddess, but the hunters' names come from her weapons, mounts, hides and battle with the asura and end in a rite where a girl wears them, while Tirumular's end in the doctrine that one power stands as many, so the pair shows the same device of the name-chain serving a public rite of costume and possession in one text and an inner theology of a single Shakti in the other.

note: Tirumular says merit and sin both come with one into birth and both must be cut at the root to reach the Lord; the Jain tale shows merit carrying a monkey to a human birth and then to a god's body that keeps the monkey's hand.
teaches: The god who still bears a monkey's hand makes visible Tirumular's point that merit, too, works by giving births: the reward of the gift is another body marked by the last one, which is why the Saiva verse ranks merit as a bond to be uprooted rather than a road to the Lord.

note: The venba says both deeds will reach their doer and bids men turn to good dharma; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and frees the soul from them.
teaches: The venba's remedy for the two deeds is to do more good, which on its wording still returns to the doer, while Tirumular's is grace that comes when good and evil are balanced and ends them, so the pair sets merit-making against release by grace; the conflict holds if நல்லறம் is read as producing good fruit.

note: Tirumular says the king whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy goes to endless hell if he fails them; in the burning Madurai the cows and the virtuous are protected not by the king, who is dead, but by the fire itself.
teaches: The two list the same protected beings, but the Saiva verse punishes the failing king after death while the epic transfers his duty of protection, in this life, to the wronged wife's fire.

note: Tirumular says a land where Brahmins make the oblation dusk and dawn does not decline and its king prospers; here the Brahmin bhuta of the unfailing three-fire life leaves Madurai because its king erred.
teaches: Tirumular makes the Brahmins' rites the protection of king and land, while the epic makes the king's justice the condition of the guardian of those rites staying, so the two run the dependence in opposite directions.

note: The kuravai girls call Murugan's kurava wife their own clan's daughter; Thiruppugazh 1000 tells Valli guarding the hunters' millet from her platform and Murugan entering the field.
teaches: The epic's hill women claim Valli as kin and pray to Murugan as an in-law of the clan, while the later devotional song keeps the millet field and the hunter girl but makes the story a model of the god's grace to the devotee, so the kin claim comes first and the theology after.

note: Pattinathar's verse begins its list of the world's reversals with the born dying and the dead being born and turns from them to Siva, who frees from coming and going; Maadalan says the born die and the dead are born and calls it nothing new, the ancient way of life.
teaches: The same saying about the born and the dead serves the epic as a reassurance that the order of deeds holds and the Siddhar as a reason to loathe that order and seek Siva, so the line itself carries no verdict and its meaning depends on whether release or a good rebirth is the goal.

note: The epic tells Siva's burning of the three cities as an event (the gods asked, the fiery arrow obeyed) and the origin of a dance staged at a city festival; Tirumular calls those who say Siva burned the three cities fools and makes the cities the three impurities.
teaches: The same myth stands in one text as a literal victory reenacted by a courtesan for a crowd and in the other as an inner allegory whose literal telling is folly; the conflict depends on reading the epic's account as a statement of event.

note: Both speak of a handful or mouthful of food set aside as a gift; Tirumular says anyone can give it, the Valayapathi says no gift equals it.
teaches: The same small gift is easy in the Tirumanthiram and supreme in the fragment, and held together they say that the gift no one can excuse himself from is also the one no greater gift surpasses.

note: The Valayapathi says hard penance fit for grace leads to the dark-free state of no return; Tirumular says even burning one's bones and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without love that melts.
teaches: The two disagree on whether one's own austerity reaches the goal: the fragment's release needs no god and comes by penance, while the Tirumanthiram makes the most extreme penance worthless without love for the Lord; the conflict holds if the fragment's தவம் is read as sufficient by itself.

note: Both use the blind guiding the blind for a false teacher of release: the Valayapathi's அந்தகன் அந்தகற்கு ஆறு சொலல், Tirumular's குருடர்க்குக் கோல்காட்டிச் செல்லும் குருடர்.
teaches: Tirumular's blind guide fails for want of a true guru's sight, while the fragment names the missing thing as full knowledge in one who promises to clear past faults, so one proverb serves both a guru-centred and a knowledge-centred account of release.

note: Both start from crowned kings brought to nothing and rebuke those who see it unchanged: Pattinathar's கண்டு பின்னும், the Valayapathi's கண்டால் மயங்காதே. Pattinathar's way out is reaching the feet of the Lord of the golden hall; the Valayapathi's is standing in the highest path and striving.
teaches: From the same sight the two draw opposed remedies, refuge at a god's feet for the Saiva poet and one's own steady effort for the fragment, which names no god; the tension holds on the reading that the fragment's ஊக்கம் is sufficient by itself.

note: The hymn says the soul is not from anything other than itself; the Neelakesi's sage asks whether a child is the body, made of the parents' blood, or the soul, which came to a human birth by its own former deed.
teaches: The Neelakesi spells out what the Cintamani's brief formula denies: the soul is not produced by the parents or the elements but brings itself into each birth by its own deeds.

note: The Neelakesi praises those who leave home for forest and hill and strive with knowledge to wear away their deeds; Civakan says leaving the house of women for the forest does not wear away old sin carried within.
teaches: Read together, the two Jain epics place the cause of release not in the forest but in the knowledge the Neelakesi names (ஞானமொடு), which the Cintamani's ascetics lack until Civakan supplies it in 1436.

note: Neelakesi argues in debate that trees live, as their change with the seasons shows; the Cintamani's narrator says the same from their flowering at a woman's glance.
teaches: The Jain thesis that plants live appears both as a debater's proof and as a narrator's aside in a love scene, showing the doctrine was common enough to be argued from a poetic convention.

note: In Neelakesi 370 the Buddhist Mokkalan likens those who give trees life to men in madness; the Cintamani calls those who deny it madmen or ghouls.
teaches: The same charge of madness is thrown from both sides of the dispute over plant life, so the insult marks a live sectarian quarrel and not a settled view.

note: Dharmadattan sends the one who kills and eats flesh to hell; Neelakesi 97 shows hell's tormentors burning beings while naming the sins of killing and eating flesh.
teaches: Dharmadattan files regicide in one list with killing and flesh-eating, the very sins Neelakesi's tormentors name as they burn the damned, so a political crime is set inside the minor epic's catalogue of injuries to life.

note: Both apologies use the moon's spot for the poet's flaw: the Neelakesi's poet will own a fault since even the moon is not spotless; the Cintamani's asks the learned to wash the spot away with their wit.
teaches: The two Jain poets put the same flaw in different hands: the Neelakesi's poet takes it on himself, while the Cintamani's poet makes cleaning it the learned reader's task.

note: Both poets apologise for faults in their work: the Kundalakesi poet says faults in praise of the faultless one are not faults; the Neelakesi poet says the moon itself has a spot and he will own any fault.
teaches: The two rival works answer the same assembly in opposite ways, the Buddhist denying that his slips count and the Jain conceding them, so the debate between the books begins in how each poet stands toward his own fault.

note: The Udayana Kumara Kaviyam tells how Yugi, feigning madness and sense by turns, passed along the great streets with crowds about him to the prison where the Vatsa king was held; the Manimekalai likens the crowd's pity for Manimekalai with her bowl in the great street to the pity felt for Yugi's feigned sickness when he freed the Vatsa king.
teaches: The simile reads the nun's garb as a disguise like Yugi's, pitied by onlookers yet hiding a purpose of release, and the later Jain epic's street scene shows the crowd and the prison that the Manimekalai's one-line allusion assumes its hearers know.

note: The materialist's awareness arising from the elements like intoxication from mixed ingredients appears in the Neelakesi's materialist as well.
teaches: Buddhist and Jain polemic both put the liquor simile in the materialist's mouth, which suggests it was the standard Tamil way to state his theory of mind.

note: Here the materialist explains away dream and possession as the mind changed; the Neelakesi's Jain asks him how his elements account for dreams, mantras and omens.
teaches: The two epics use dream against the materialist in opposite directions: Manimekalai's opponent uses it to dismiss rebirth, Neelakesi uses it as evidence his elements cannot explain.

note: The Valayapathi argues against flesh-eating in a sermon with no opponent; the Neelakesi announces the view that accepts flesh (ஊன்கொண்ட காட்சி) as the first matter its heroine will debate.
teaches: Among the Jain-tradition epics the same ethic appears in two forms, as a plain moral exhortation in the fragment and as a doctrine to be defended against a named view in the Neelakesi, which shows meat-eating treated as a dividing line between schools and not only as a private fault.

note: The epic arms the wall with self-acting engines and names no defender; the Kural says every excellence of a fort is nothing without men excellent in action.
teaches: The epic's picture of a wall that fights by its own machinery is exactly the kind of fort the couplet calls empty, so the Kural supplies the missing term by which this lavish security can fail.

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; Civakan tells his sulking wife they are one life in two bodies.
teaches: Spoken with another woman's portrait still in his arms, the claim of a single life becomes an appeasing formula, so the Cintamani shows the Kural's declaration of union put to use in a marriage that is about to take a second wife.

note: The Kural's wife takes offence even at his adoring gaze, asking whom he is thinking of; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes at a portrait of another woman painted by her husband.
teaches: The Kural's comedy of jealousy depends on the husband's innocence, and the epic removes it: here the suspected other woman is real and painted by his own hand, so the sulk is no longer love's game but a just grievance.

note: The Kural ranks highest the woman who suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; the parrot says maidens hide their love-sickness from even their nearest, out of shame.
teaches: The silence the couplet praises has a working cost the couplet does not show: because the girl will not speak even to her confidante, the knowledge of her illness has to travel by a go-between who asks the man to diagnose it.

note: The Cintamani's wall is armed by Yavana engines that throw molten metal, arrows and stones outward; Kural 747 names three ways a fort is taken, the third (அறைப்படுத்தல்) by working on those inside.
teaches: Read together, the two show that the epic's elaborate machinery answers only the outward assaults of the couplet's list, leaving the inside danger by which this city is in fact lost to its own minister.

note: The Kural says penance is striven for because it gains what one wants as one wants it; Gunamalai says that if Civakan refuses she will win him even by penance.
