teaches: The girl takes the couplet's motive for தவம் at its word and aims it at a husband, which exposes how far the Kural's argument for penance rests on desire rather than release.

note: The Kural's man says the woman who causes his love-sickness is its only cure; Civakan writes that the little parrot she sent has cured his swelling sickness.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's rule that only the beloved herself can heal, the letter shows the cure passing to her token: a sent message relieves the sickness before any meeting, so the remedy can be borne by a proxy.

note: Kural 54 says nothing is greater than a woman who has the firmness called karpu; Gunamalai shows such firmness before marriage, against her own parents, for a man she has only chosen.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's firmness moves from a wife's fidelity back to a maiden's choice, where it shows itself as resisting her parents with death or renunciation rather than as serving a husband.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a full village tank everyone draws from; verse 106 has the inner city's families bring wealth from overseas islands and feed many (பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி).
teaches: The couplet says shared wealth is like a common tank but not where it comes from; the epic supplies the source in perilous sea trade and makes feeding many the mark that justifies calling the city heavenly.

note: Both use வரைவு for the courtesans: the epic says they sell beauty வரைவின்றி, the Kural calls such women வரைவிலா and their arms a mire for base men.
teaches: The same word that the Kural uses to condemn the courtesan becomes in the Jain epic an item in a city's praise, so the reader sees that a heaven-like city could include the trade the ethical book calls a hell.

note: In Kural 1316 the woman turns the man's 'I thought of you' into proof that he had forgotten her; in 1070 Gunamalai turns his praise of a powder into proof that he forgot her and keeps another in his heart (மறந்தீர், மனத்துள் உறைகின்றாள்).
teaches: The couplet's sulking logic, that any word of the lover proves his neglect, becomes in the epic a weapon aimed at a named rival's beauty, so feigned jealousy is how the epic's wife claims the hero among his many loves.

note: Kural 1109 names sulking, making up and union as love's rewards; verses 1071, 1072 and 1074 enact the three in order, sulk, appeasement at her feet, embrace.
teaches: The epic plays out the couplet's triad in full and then cuts it off with the king's runners, so love's three rewards are set as the calm the hero's karma-laden story breaks.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment past all bounds file down a king's conquering strength; in 1079 the king, raging over a sulking elephant, orders the hero seized and his strength rooted out.
teaches: The epic shows where such excess comes from: a usurper's envy of a subject's fame finds a trivial cause, and the order that follows is the first stroke of the file that will bring his own fall.

note: Kural 895 says those who draw a mighty king's anger will survive nowhere; Kantukkatan reasons that to contend with the king is the work of the doomed (விளிகுற்றார்) and sends his son bound.
teaches: The merchant applies the couplet's prudence to a king who is a usurper and his son's true father's killer, showing that the rule of not provoking the strong counsels submission even to injustice, a cost the couplet does not weigh.

note: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Civakan uses the waking from heavy sleep for the soul's appearing in the states of birth, adds release as a third motion, and draws from it a refusal to grieve at his own arrest.
teaches: The Kural's calm figure of sleep and waking only describes the cycle, while the Cintamani makes it an argument for conduct, so understanding birth as waking becomes the ground for refusing grief, and the cycle gains an exit the couplet never names.

note: Both measure a small but fatal thing as a split sesame seed: the Kural an inner enmity that holds ruin, Civakan the least attachment, which he calls a fault.
teaches: The sesame measure moves from a king's household enemy to the attachment inside the self, so the danger the Kural locates in a court the Jain hero locates in the heart that clings.

note: The Kural says the many lack because few do penance; the city women say they lose Civakan because they did no penance.
teaches: The couplet's account of why most people lack is turned into a mourner's self-blame, so lack of penance explains not poverty but the loss of a beloved, and the women accuse themselves while blaming the king and the father in the same verse.

note: The Kural says the weak who harm the strong beckon Death with their hand; the city women say the king who seizes Civakan has clapped his hands at Death and will perish with his line.
teaches: The women apply the couplet against the one who holds power, so the 'weak' party is the reigning king and the 'strong' is the bound merchant's son, which makes strength a matter of worth rather than of office.

note: The Kural tells those who serve hot-tempered kings to be like those warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Kantukkatan judges the king's anger a fire that burns all who come near and sends gold to quench it.
teaches: The Kural's fire teaches distance, while the merchant adds a remedy, gold poured like rain, so the pair shows a courtier's caution and a merchant's purchase as two answers to the same burning king.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's putting killers to death to weeding a crop; here the king sentences the youth who stopped the royal elephant from killing a girl.
teaches: The couplet's justice assumes that the king punishes the killer; the epic shows a king whose own beast is the killer punishing the rescuer, so the weeding image fails when the king himself decides what the weed is.

note: Kural 269 says that those who attain the power of austerity can even leap past death; here the ascetic's words, remembered, keep the stricken merchant alive.
teaches: The Kural places the power of tapas in the ascetic's own victory over death, while the epic shows it working on householders, through a foretelling whose remembered word revives a father who stood as if dead.

note: In Kural 1164 the woman parted from her lover says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; here Gunamalai, parted from Civakan and near death, crosses the sea of grief on the raft of the ascetic's words.
teaches: The Kural's parted woman has no raft because no one sends word; the epic gives its parted woman a raft from outside love altogether, an ascetic's prophecy, so the same plight is solved by religious authority rather than by the lover.

note: Kural 903 says stooping before one's wife brings a man shame among the good; Gandharvadattai, able to free Civakan, holds back because being saved by his wife would shame his strength and learning.
teaches: The couplet's shame is a man's fear of his wife's power, but here the wife herself fears it on his behalf and keeps her power idle, so the rule's cost falls on the woman who could act.

note: Kural 967 holds it better to be called ruined than to live following those who scorn one; Civakan says he does not want to live if he is set free by his wife's spells.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's preference for ruin over dishonour onto rescue by a wife, so honour can refuse even a loving help, and the story then lets a male friend's help pass as honourable.

note: Kural 107 says people remember through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow; Civakan, facing death, counts on the friend whose death-sorrow he eased in another body.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seven births literal: a dog that became a god still keeps the debt, and the debtor runs to the man who wiped his tears.

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; Madanan's men, fearing the king, kill a stranger and pass him off as Civakan to save themselves.
teaches: The story shows the exact deed the couplet forbids and shows its source in the tyrant's terror, so the rule against killing is seen giving way first where the sceptre is bent.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who take good fortune as good should grieve when it turns; Civakan, freed after imprisonment, neither grieves nor rejoices and ascribes both to former deeds.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's question with a stricter ideal: not only bearing ill as one bears good, but declining joy at good fortune too, since rescue is as much karma's working as captivity.

note: Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discerning sense; in 1183 the god warns of ghoul-women who come as pining lovers and, embracing, wring out a man's life.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's metaphor into a literal creature of its geography: the deceiving lover really is a life-drinking demon, and what saves the hero is the god's forewarning, standing in for the 'discerning sense' the couplet demands.

note: Kural 916 scorns women who spread a base goodness (புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார்) to all; in 1200 the river, sharing its own goodness to feed the world (தன்னுடைய நலம் பகிர்ந்து உலகம் ஊட்டலின்), is called a courtesan with approval.
teaches: The same act, a நலம் given to everyone, is a mark of baseness in the Kural and of bounty in the epic's simile, which shows that the Kural's contempt lies in the sale of a person and not in the sharing itself.

note: Kural 329 says those whose work is killing are base in the eyes of the discerning; 1205 calls the forest bowmen who kill travellers embodiments of sin (பாவ மூர்த்தியர்).
teaches: The couplet judges a deed, killing, while the epic fixes the same judgment on a forest people as a class, so the pair shows how the ethics of not-killing could harden into a picture of hunters as sin incarnate.

note: Kural 974 says greatness exists only for one who holds himself as single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) do; 1208 likens a straight unforking road to the minds of chaste women (கற்புடை மாதரார் மனம்).
teaches: Both texts use the chaste woman's mind as the model of an undivided line, for a man's greatness in one and for a road in the other, showing that karpu was read as singleness of direction rather than as purity alone.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can have grace; the hunter says he needs meat merely to keep his body alive.
teaches: The couplet's eater fattens himself by choice, while the hunter claims he must eat flesh to survive at all; the epic thus raises the case the couplet passes over and answers it not with grace but with the threat of hell and the promise of heaven.

note: The Kural says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; Civakan sets hell for the meat-eater against a god's birth for one who abstains and makes the hunter choose.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's one-sided warning into a two-way choice with a reward on the other side and has the eater himself pronounce the verdict, so the Kural's rule becomes a conversion by question and answer.

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Civakan's hymn worships the Jina's lotus feet from within that sea and asks that attachment's bonds be untied.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the hymn names what reaching the feet is supposed to do in a Jain frame: not a crossing given from outside but the loosening of attachment (பசை), so the same image of feet and sea carries a doctrine of release by unbinding.

note: The Naladiyar says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; the Cintamani's dancer calls the saying that chastity breaks for gold a lie and vows herself to one man.
teaches: The dancer answers the very proverb the Naladiyar states, in her own voice, so the pair shows the epic giving the woman of the stage a reply that the didactic tradition never lets her make.

note: The Kural says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease when they exceed or fall short; one healer blames out-of-balance wind, bile and phlegm for the girl's state.
teaches: The humoral theory the Kural states as the general cause of disease is here invoked for a snakebite and fails, so the epic marks a limit the couplet does not: a correct doctrine of illness misleads when the cause is a poison from outside.

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; in the epic the astrologer's verdict of death fails while a bird omen of rescue comes true.
teaches: The Jain epic does not dismiss divination wholesale as the quatrain does: it splits it, letting the star-reader's verdict be overturned while an omen pointing to a rescuer is fulfilled, so the scorn of the quatrain falls on fatalistic forecasting rather than on every sign.

note: The Kural orders the healer to find the disease, its cause and the means that subdue it, then act; Civakan names the causes and kinds of bite and the snake's type before he recites the cure.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's order as a contest: a crowd of healers who act first and diagnose in contradiction all fail, and the one who examines cause and kind before acting succeeds, so the rule is shown by the cost of breaking it.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan's lore sorts even snakes into four varnas known by the smell of their bite.
teaches: Read with பிறப்பொக்கும் as denying rank by birth, the couplet stands against a lore that fixes varna in nature down to snakes; the pairing shows that the Cintamani's hero carries birth-rank as plain knowledge even where the Kural, speaking of all living beings, had set it aside.

note: The Kural's man says she will not look at him directly but smiles as if narrowing one eye; the epic says Padumai bound Civakan with a look that looked as if it did not look.
teaches: The averted look that the Kural treats as a sign the man must decode becomes in the epic an act with an effect: the same not-quite-glance does not hint at love, it ties the hero fast, so the convention moves from evidence to force.

note: The Kural says penance is striven for here because what is desired is obtained as desired; the onlookers say only women who did rare penance before could be born to sleep on Civakan's chest.
teaches: The onlookers take the couplet's promise at its word and fill 'whatever is desired' with a husband's embrace, showing how the motive the Kural offers for penance could be heard as making penance the price of pleasure in the next birth.

note: The Acharakkovai sets out the mouth-rinsing the great have seen as the way: three sips, wiping, and touching the face's parts with the fingers; Civakan sips three times, wipes three times and touches his face with his fingers.
teaches: The rule book's after-meal rinse appears in the epic, step for step, as a mark of the hero's breeding, performed under the eyes of a king who will next examine him, so the code of conduct works in the story as a credential.

note: The Acharakkovai lists what one does not do in a great man's house: spit, climb a high seat, chew areca, speak out of turn, lie down; in the king's house Civakan sits on a high flower seat, chews areca and lies on a couch.
teaches: Civakan does three of the five things forbidden in a great man's house, and does them at the king's command, so the pair shows that the rule binds the dependent and the visitor and is suspended for an honoured guest whom the host himself seats, serves and beds.

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe and answers that it has all three; Civakan asks whether it is her bow, her eyes, her speech or her look and says he cannot tell.
teaches: Both men ask the same 'is it this or that' of a woman who wounds them, but the Kural settles the question in her look, while Civakan gives it up and lays the cause on his own desire, so the epic turns the couplet's question about her into an admission about himself.

note: Kural 81 says all of a household's keeping of goods is for caring for guests; the epic lists eating with guests as one item among the city's perfumes, gold and beds.
teaches: Where the Kural makes hospitality the purpose that justifies household wealth, the epic sets it inside a catalogue of pleasure, so the duty becomes one ornament of a city that will soon fall.

note: The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; Padumai finds the bull's bell, the moon, the anril and the evening burning like smokeless fire.
teaches: The evening's pastoral sounds that burn the parted wife of the Kural are given to a girl who has not yet been joined or parted, showing that the epic transfers the whole thurai of evening grief to the first night after first sight.

note: The Kural's woman asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave the unending sickness; the epic says Padumai lay sick with the love her own eyes had given her.
teaches: The couplet's blame of the eyes is spoken long after, by a woman left alone; the epic places the same diagnosis on the very first night, so the eyes are blamed before the love has any history.

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and his doubt whether she is a goddess.
teaches: The couplet leaves the heart reeling in doubt, while the epic expands the doubt into a list of named goddesses and settles it in the next verse, so the Kural's moment becomes the first stage of a scene that ends in union.

note: Both say the woman who causes the lover's sickness is its only cure.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as a lover's hope, but the epic puts it after the union and makes the remedy bodily, the sandal on her breasts, so the cure is something already taken.

note: Both compare a woman and her lover's view of her with the moon and its mark.
teaches: The Kural uses the moon's mark as the flaw her face does not have, while Civakan uses it as the figure of a bond that cannot be parted, so one image carries opposite values according to whether the lover is praising her face or swearing to their union.

note: The Kural's lover says anicham and swan's down are like nerunji to her feet; the epic has a whole city's women whose feet shiver on flowering cotton while they wear anicham.
teaches: A lover's private hyperbole about one woman's feet becomes in the epic a stock trait of a whole class of wealthy women, showing how the Kural's love conceits turned into description.

note: The couplet says all five senses find their objects in one bright-bangled woman; the epic names the same five, smell, taste, music, the sight of dance and her touch, as the round of the hero's pleasure.
teaches: Where the couplet gathers all five senses into one woman, the epic spreads them over perfumes, food, string music and dance with only touch left to her, showing a prince's pleasure as a court of arts rather than the single person the couplet praises.

note: The couplet says the bond between the lover and the girl is that between body and life; the epic has the husband leave his sleeping wife as a good life leaves the body.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a promise that the two cannot part; the epic takes the same simile literally, so the husband's going is a death for the wife, which is the cost the couplet's image leaves unstated.

note: The couplet likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; the epic has the abandoned wife as a body searching for its departed life and as a bird searching the nest for its mate.
teaches: In the couplet the forsaken body is an empty shell that feels nothing, which is its lesson on impermanence; the epic gives the left-behind body and nest a longing of their own, turning the image of death's indifference into one of grief.

note: In the Kural the bangles slip from the wasting wrist and so announce the parting; Padumai pulls her bracelets off herself, blaming them for having come between her and his embrace.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's involuntary sign into a deliberate act: the bangle no longer reports the grief but is punished as one of its causes.

note: The Kural's woman says her eyes do not sleep whether he is away or near; Padumai told her eyes not to sleep so she could keep sight of him, and they slept, and he went.
teaches: The couplet's sleepless eyes are the lover's watch against loss; the epic shows the watch failing once, so the eyes are blamed not for their suffering but for the one night they rested.

note: The Kural's man finds one pain inside the sulk, the worry that union may be delayed; Padumai says that if a husband leaves even in the sweet hour of the sulk, the wife's life leaves her.
teaches: The game of sulking assumes the lover stays to be won back; the epic names the case the couplet only worries about, where the partner leaves during the sulk and the delay becomes loss.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring words of one who was gracious can be at fault if he leaves; Padumai calls Civakan one who walks by grace and speaks dharma, and asks why he shows her no grace.
teaches: The couplet sets the fault on the gap between the lover's word and deed; the epic sharpens it by making the deserter a man praised for grace and dharma, so his own virtue becomes the charge against him.

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth; the friend's tree has ignorance as its seed and desire as its root.
teaches: Put beside the couplet, the verse shows a different order of causes: craving is not the first cause but what anchors the tree once ignorance has sown it, so cutting desire alone would not uproot it.

note: The Kural promises distinction to one who takes what hurts as pleasure; the friend says that bearing sorrow as joy is harder than weeping or dying.
teaches: The couplet's discipline for a man in adversity becomes, in a deserted bride's chamber, the hardest thing in the world, set above death itself in difficulty, so the epic measures the cost the couplet only rewards.

note: Naladiyar 23 has wedding drums turn into funeral drums in the same hall the same day; the friend sees parting within union, age within youth and sickness within health.
teaches: The quatrain shows one reversal as an event; the verse turns it into a rule that every good state already holds its opposite, and uses that rule to forbid even a blink of grief.

note: The Kural weighs help given at the moment of need as greater than the world; Civakan's gift comes at a dying dog's last moment and is repaid by a god at his own.
teaches: The Kural measures timely help by its worth to the one helped, while the Cintamani shows it returned across species and births, so the couplet's weight becomes a debt that the receiver carries into a new life.

note: The Kural bids one cling to the one free of clinging in order to let clinging go; the Cintamani's hymn says love wears the karmas away and yet, being love, cannot end them.
teaches: The couplet makes attachment to the unattached the way out of attachment, while the Jain hymn admits that very attachment and counts it still a bond, so the two disagree on whether devotion can itself be the final cause of freedom, on the reading of காதல் as love of the Jina.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Civakan says matted hair, robes and the skull bowl are seeds of a mean birth.
teaches: Where the couplet sets the marks aside as unnecessary, the epic counts them as harmful, sowing rebirth, so the pair shows two degrees of the same critique of outward signs.

note: Civakan says the body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; the Naladiyar warns that a harsh wind can drop the green fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
teaches: The epic's ripe fruit makes death a ripening that comes in order, but the quatrain's fallen green fruit warns that it need not wait for age, and the two urgings to act now rest on different pictures of when the body falls.

note: The Kural says one whose mind ponders and knows what is with certainty need not think again of birth; Civakan says knowledge, right vision and right conduct must all three be full before both kinds of deed pass.
teaches: Where the couplet lets true knowing alone end rebirth, the Jain formula makes knowing only one of three and insists on vision and conduct of non-harm as well, so the pair shows the Kural's chapter on true knowledge as a narrower account of release.

note: The couplet praises the host who tends the departing guest and watches for the guest to come; Subhadran feeds a thousand and eight guests a day for twelve years watching for one guest who will be his son-in-law.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's watching for the coming guest literally and turns it to a private end, so hospitality becomes a search, rewarded with a husband in this life rather than with welcome among the gods.

note: Kural 901 says men set on their wives miss the fine fruit and men of action do not want that desire; the epic shows a king whose rule is given up for it.
teaches: The Kural's flat warning becomes in the epic a seductive scene, so the reader is drawn into the very desire the couplet tells the man of action to refuse.

note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face; Subhadran, who has kept a great guest-feeding for years (1451, 1453), receives a guest he calls திருமகள் கணவன்.
teaches: The Kural's promise that fortune lives in the hospitable house is made literal: the guest the merchant takes in is the lord of fortune himself and becomes the son of the house.

note: Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot cross the sea of births; 1467 says those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and tongue do not reach the world of release.
teaches: The Kural leaves the Lord unnamed and the means as reaching his feet; the Jain hymn names him by the pindi tree and the triple umbrella and makes the condition a concrete act of worship, so the same exclusion becomes sectarian and ritual.

note: Kural 6 praises the one who quenched the five gates of sense (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep his path; 1468 calls the Jina lord of those who slew the five senses (ஐம்பொறியும் அட்டு) and promises heaven to those who sing his feet.
teaches: The Kural's sense-quencher is a teacher whose path is followed; in the hymn he is the head of a class of victors, and the reward moves from long life on earth to the world of the gods.

note: Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், the one of eight qualities, and calls a head that does not bow useless; in 1469 those who do not praise the Jina have the eight qualities taken from their souls by their deeds.
teaches: The eight qualities that the Kural gives to the one worshipped are, in the Jain hymn, the soul's own, lost to karma by those who will not praise, so the failure to worship costs the self what the god possesses.

note: Kural 1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame; in 1472 Kemasari's inner restraint and modesty (உண்ணிறை நாணும்) break together at the first sight of Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's woman says this in separation as a confession of defeat; the epic makes the same breaking happen at first sight and treats it as the sign that the destined man has come, turning a lament into an omen.

note: Kural 1082 says her returned look is like a striking goddess (தாக்கணங்கு) bringing an army; in 1473 Kemasari's look becomes an afflicting goddess (நோக்கணங்கு) and Civakan wonders whether she is a தாக்கணங்கு or a mortal.
teaches: The Kural settles that the woman is human and keeps the goddess as a figure for her look; the epic stops at the doubt and stacks அணங்கு on lute, look and woman, so the hero's own art is made one of the goddesses that strike him.

note: Kural 1086 says her eyes would not cause him trembling pain if her curved brows would straighten and screen them; in 1482 her brow is a strong bow bent at the middle that beats him.
teaches: In the Kural the brows could be the eyes' restraint if only they were straight; in the epic the bent brow is itself a weapon in league with eye, hair and breast, so the hope of a screen is gone.

note: Kural 1087 likens the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes; in 1483 her breasts are bound by a bodice as cruel things must be bound.
teaches: Both treat the covering of the breasts as a restraint put on something dangerous; the epic adds that the binding fails, since the bound breasts still wreck her waist and him, while the Kural's cloth only warns.

note: The Kural's man asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the epic answers by likening the lovers to those beyond birth and death.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's open question, the Jain epic lends sexual bliss the very vocabulary of release, then ends that bliss within the chapter by the hero's leaving.

note: The Kural's lover says the beloved is life when present and death when she leaves; Civakan offers to live serving her or leave his body, then is himself the one who leaves.
teaches: The couplet assumes the woman is the one who departs and the man the one who dies of it; the epic reverses the roles, so the parting the man dreads is the parting he chooses.

note: Naladiyar makes the sun Death's daily measure of one's days; the epic tells one day's sun as a whole life from infant to desireless old man, and the lovers go to bed.
teaches: The epic uses the Naladiyar's moral image of the sun as a life measured out, but withholds its moral, letting the lovers' indifference to the dying sun foreshadow the night that ends their union.

note: The Kural's woman demands to be told whether her man will go; Civakan leaves while Kemasari sleeps, so that she cannot ask.
teaches: The secret night departure is the hero's way of avoiding exactly the plea the couplet voices, and the couplet names what Kemasari is denied: the chance to speak before the going.

note: Both are a deserted woman weighing the assurance of the man who left.
teaches: The couplet asks whether those who trusted an assurance are at fault, and the epic heroine answers both ways at once, calling his word a lie and naming herself the one of evil deeds.

note: Both make the woman's shoulders the record of union and parting.
teaches: In the couplet the shoulders betray the parting to onlookers, while the epic woman questions her shoulders as witnesses of where he went, so the body that tells the secret becomes a confidant.

note: Both put the parted woman at night with no companion but herself.
teaches: The couplet's woman mocks the night for having only her as companion, and the epic's woman, as alone, makes her own reflection the companion and consoles it, so the loneliness turns inward on the self.

note: Both use the water bubble for what forms and bursts.
teaches: The impermanence figure that in the quatrain moves the wise to end their wandering is used by the epic's mother to keep a bride steady in the household until her husband returns.

note: The couplet calls children a man's wealth; the riddle says children of the body are others' and only merit is one's own son.
teaches: On the reading that line 4 denies ordinary children are one's own, the Jain riddle answers the Kural's householder by taking the very word மக்கள் and giving it to merit.

note: Both speak of householders who provide for renouncers.
teaches: The couplet chides those who give to renouncers in place of doing austerity themselves; the epic's householder does both, counting the gift to renouncers and his own fasts as two of four equal duties.

note: Both define tavam.
teaches: The Kural defines austerity as enduring pain and harming none, with no rite named, while the epic's lay teacher defines it as fasting on fixed moon days: the pair shows the same word as an ethic and as a calendar.

note: Both say deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord.
teaches: The Kural's unnamed Lord, to whose devotees the two deeds do not cling, is given a Jain identity in the epic, the Great One under the asoka and triple umbrella, so the couplet's claim is read as one about the Jina.

note: Both bid people take provisions for the journey because Death is coming.
teaches: The quatrain's bundle carried on the shoulder stays a figure; the epic sets it against the food anyone packs for a visit to kin, and says it to a man actually on the road, so the figure is pinned to an everyday act and to the hearer's own journey.

note: Both turn on eating flesh to swell one's own flesh.
teaches: The couplet asks how the flesh-eater can have compassion; the epic adds the end of the fattened body, carried only to feed vultures, so the cruelty is shown to profit no one but the birds.

note: Both list the body as a thing of filth with nine openings that dazzles the deluded; Naladiyar's fool is the lover, Civakan uses the inventory to refuse a woman.
teaches: The epic shows the Naladiyar's anatomy of the body being used by a man at the very moment of seduction, as a defence rather than a sermon, and by a hero who will still take wives, so the disgust is a tool of restraint, not a rule for life.

note: The couplet holds that one's own understanding prevails however many subtle books one learns; the epic says the deed blinds those who have swum through learning.
teaches: The epic gives the limit of learning that the couplet states a cause and a scene, the deed covering one's eyes at the moment of desire, so the 'own understanding' that overrides books becomes the karma that defeats even the learned.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews, skin, flesh and grease and asks which part is the garlanded woman; 1583 gives nearly the same list (குடர்கள், வழும்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்) but starts from the adorned hair and adds the three humours.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant catalogue is put in the mouth of a hero who is not renouncing, as a weapon against another man's wife, so the meditation on the foul body becomes a householder's defence against adultery rather than a step out of the world.

note: Naladiyar 41 says that if skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from the body a stick is needed to drive off crows; 1584 opens the body and sets crows at the eyes.
teaches: Both poets end the lover's gaze with crows at the body, but the epic uses the image on the living woman standing before the hero, turning a general memento into a refusal spoken to her face.

note: Naladiyar 44 refuses the petty men who call eyes water-lilies, carp and spears; 1585 blames the poets of kavya by name for painting brows, eyes and nose on a bag of skin.
teaches: Where the Naladiyar's opponents are anonymous fools, the epic names its own craft as the source of the illusion, so the critique of the simile becomes a self-critique of the epic genre.

note: Kural 414 says listening to the learned is a support in one's faltering (ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை); 1595 says learning is a companion to the heart in its weakness (மெலிவிற்கோர் துணை) and asks the learned Pavadattan why he grieves.
teaches: The epic applies the Kural's promise to a man of many treatises and shows it failing: his learning does not console him, and he is comforted only when a mantra returns his wife.

note: Kural 57 says the guard of confinement is useless and the best guard is the one women's own நிறை keeps; 1597 says women do not hold their restraint within (உண்ணிறை யுடைய வல்ல) and yield to pressing.
teaches: The Kural trusts the guard inside a woman, the epic's hero denies most women have it, and the story of this chapter is offered as his proof, so the two texts disagree on whether a woman's restraint can be relied on at all.

note: Kural 55 promises that the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; 1598 describes chaste wives who live worshipping their husband's hands (கணவற்கை தொழுது வாழ்வார்) as a few against the many of 1597.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's figure of the husband-worshipping wife but makes her a rare exception within women's general frailty, and drops the rain, so her power shrinks to ending her husband's distress.

note: The Kural's man laments that his might, feared by enemies in battle, broke before her bright forehead; 161 shows a king whose spear killed kings at the height of his fame just before he meets Vijayai.
teaches: Read with the story that follows, the couplet's lover's hyperbole becomes literal history: the warrior whose strength breaks before a woman is a king, and what breaks is his kingdom.

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies fall when their deeds turn, and enemies take their wives; 161 shows Saccandan at the full of his fame, the starting point of such a fall.
teaches: The quatrain gives the general fall of the umbrella king; the epic fills in one fall step by step, with the king's own infatuation as the turn and his queen driven out, so impermanence works through character and not only fortune.

note: The couplet names quarrel, reconciliation and union as love's rewards; the epic stages that sequence in the swans and has the hero watch it.
teaches: The couplet lists oodal, understanding and union as what lovers gain, and the epic shows that sequence complete in birds before a man who is parted, so the reward the couplet promises becomes, for the onlooker who lacks it, the cause of pain.

note: Both are a man describing the girl's averted gaze: when he looks she looks down.
teaches: The couplet catches the girl's averted look in the present as a sign of love, and the epic hero recalls the same look from the past while parted from her, so the gesture that once told him she loved him is what memory hands back in separation.

note: The couplet calls the bond with the girl that of body and life; the epic draws an inference from it during separation.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's simile into a test a separated lover can run, that one life cannot end while the other goes on, and so shows the image used as reassurance rather than praise.

note: The couplet allows a falsehood that yields faultless good; the narrator excuses the hero's false name in similar terms.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's exception a concrete case, a fugitive prince hiding his name from a usurper, and shows a narrator reaching for the exception to keep his hero truthful.

note: The couplet tells courtiers to keep near a king like men warming at a fire; the epic gives the same fire conduct to pupils with their teacher.
teaches: The epic moves the rule from court to schoolroom, and since the teacher is a hidden king, the princes unknowingly keep the courtier's rule toward a real king.

note: The Kural's lover says he once had modesty and manliness and now has only the palmyra horse; the epic's maxim says restraint is the beauty of manliness when love fails.
teaches: Against the Kural's man who says love has taken his manliness, the epic defines manliness as the restraint that remains when love is denied, so the same word marks opposite outcomes of desire.

note: The Kural condemns those who clung to dice (கவறு) and the gaming hall (கழகம); the epic makes the woman's body a board, dice and gaming hall for love.
teaches: Borrowing the Kural's own words for ruinous gambling, the epic frames love as a game one should give up for penance when it cannot be won, so the condemned dice become a figure for the pleasure renunciation replaces.

note: Evening as what eats the lives of the separated: the couplet's woman says it is not evening but the hour that devours; Kanakamalai sees it as a demon gaping to swallow her.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's figure of devouring evening into a visible monster, the moon its tooth and the red sky its mouth, showing how a Kural conceit was expanded into scenery.

note: The Kural's woman says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; Kanakamalai finds her raft in the garland Civakan made.
teaches: The pair shows that the raft the couplet denies can be supplied by a token of the beloved, but only as a raft through the night, not a way out of the sea.

note: Both women swim love's flood alone in the night watches (யாமம்).
teaches: Where the couplet's woman sees no shore and is simply alone, the epic adds the watchers who laugh at her, so the solitude of the night becomes public shame by day.

note: The Kural's lover says love's flood carries off the raft of modesty and manliness; Kanakamalai says she sold her modesty to buy a garland.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's loss into a trade: modesty is not swept away but given in exchange, and what it bought, the garland, becomes the new raft of 1663 and 1674.

note: The Kural's man sees two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that cures it; the epic says her eyes are poison and nectar at once.
teaches: The couplet's private double look of lover's sickness and cure becomes, in an epic, a public force that maddens sages and later unseats a king.

note: The king says such excellence belongs only to a king or a twice-born; the couplet says the learned low-born outrank the unlearned high-born.
teaches: Read together they show the epic using learning as a sign that betrays hidden royal birth, the reverse of the Kural's use of learning to override birth rank; the conflict holds on reading the king's line as a general rule rather than a compliment.

note: Both speak of a help weighed against earth and heaven: the couplet says they cannot repay it; the king says the help itself gave him earth and heaven, and finds no requital.
teaches: The pair shows a king accepting the couplet's verdict that such a debt is unpayable and answering it with a daughter, so the unpayable gift becomes a bond of marriage instead of a repayment.

note: Both have the bangles slip as the sign of the man's leaving, and both use the verb துற for his going.
teaches: Where the Kural's bangles announce that he has left, the epic's refrain makes the bangles leave as he left, so the body imitates the desertion it reports.

note: The Kural praises the manhood that does not look at another's wife; Nandattan, who must meet and speak to his brother's wife, keeps his eyes on her anklet.
teaches: The couplet forbids the look outright, and the scene shows how the rule is kept when a man must face and address the woman: the gaze goes to her feet, where looking becomes reverence.

note: Thirikadugam lists a husbandless woman's adornment among things unfit; Nandattan argues from the same norm that a wife still adorned has a living husband.
teaches: The ethical list states the rule as unfitness, while the epic turns that rule into a piece of inference, showing the norm was strong enough to serve as proof of a fact.

note: The couplet defines a king as one who weighs a case before punishing; Devadattan asks the same of companions planning to punish a king.
teaches: The pair shows the rule of inquiry before penalty binding not only the ruler but those who would avenge themselves on him, and its first question is not guilt but whether the wrong has happened at all.

note: The couplet says giving and sweet speech gather kin around a man; Civakan says friends and wives can be gained but a brother cannot be made.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's way of winning kin by gifts and kind words, Civakan's saying separates the circle that can be won from the brother who can only be born, so not all kin answer to the Kural's means.

note: The couplet says nothing that can be gained equals wise children; Civakan counts children among the gainable and sets a brother beyond gain.
teaches: Civakan's list puts children with wealth and wives among the things a man can acquire, and names the brother as the one bond that cannot be got at all, a value the Kural's ranking of gains has no place for.

note: The couplet makes the parted woman's pallor spread the moment the man goes; the friends treat its absence as proof of deceit.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's sign of parting into a test applied by men to a wife, and shows the test failing, since a wife who knows her husband is safe does not pale.

note: The couplet promises that those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere; Vijayai worships at the Jina's feet and in the next verse weeps for her son.
teaches: Placed beside the couplet, the scene shows worship at the passionless one's feet asked to remove a fault while the grief of attachment to a child runs on, so the promised freedom from suffering is a goal still far off, not a present state.

note: Verse 179 praises Vijayai's soles as if made without bone or sinew (என்பொடு நரம்பு இன்றி); Naladiyar 46 lists bone (என்பு) and sinew (நரம்பு) among the parts of the body and asks which of them is the garlanded woman.
teaches: Two Jain works use the same two words to opposite ends: the epic's praise must imagine the beloved's body without bone and sinew, while the quatrain dissolves her into them, so the courtly portrait depends on the very forgetting the ascetic verse is written to undo.

note: The proverb says one's suffering is one's own old deed and the foe only the sent servant; the friends see the usurper's deed ripen and the heir become its agent of Death.
teaches: Read together, the two show the sent-servant idea from both ends: the proverb tells the sufferer not to rage at the agent, while the epic shows men rejoicing to become the agent of another's ripened deed.

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and both reach for அணங்கு; the Kural's lover wavers among goddess, peahen and woman, while Sachchandan, on the likelier reading, takes her for an அணங்கு without doubt (ஐயுறான்).
teaches: The Kural's perplexity at first sight is a lover's healthy doubt; the epic gives a king who does not doubt, and his certainty that she is more than human is the first step of the absorption that later costs him his kingdom.

note: The Kural forbids trusting anyone unexamined but bids trust after examination; Vijayai bids the friends trust no one at all with the secret except Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's two-step rule of trust assumes time to examine people, and the epic shows a mother hiding an heir from a usurper dropping the second step altogether, so that danger turns examined trust into blanket silence.

note: The Naladiyar's eel-like doubleness belongs to women who sell intimacy; Vijayai, the faithful queen, puts the hearts of girdled women in general among things that do not go straight.
teaches: The quatrain confines double dealing to a class of women and blames the men who embrace them, whereas the epic's chaste widow extends the suspicion to all women when a secret is at stake, so the pair shows the charge widening from a trade to a sex.

note: The Kural praises those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses; the epic gives Vijayai that sense-restraint (பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று) in the verse that sends an army out at her word.
teaches: The couplet makes quenching the senses the way to a long, settled life, while the epic shows the same restraint in a widow who still commands a war of revenge, so ascetic control of the senses is shown sitting with, not ending, worldly purpose.

note: The Kural says to think before resolving, since rethinking after resolving is a fault; Buddhisenan says that once the raid is made, turning back brings blame, so weigh it first.
teaches: Buddhisenan supplies the reason the Kural leaves unstated: in war, the deed once begun shuts off retreat through blame, which is why the thinking must come before the resolve.

note: The Kural trusts the concurring word of three spies who do not know one another; the friends' three spies come back together (ஒன்றி) with one report.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's number three but drops its safeguard of mutual ignorance, showing a band of friends using the statecraft rule loosely, with trust in place of cross-checking.

note: The Kural's huge tusked elephant fears the tiger's attack; Civakan comes at the elephant like a lion (1833), but it ends not in fear but in one mind with him.
teaches: Against the Kural's picture of the strong beast cowed by a fiercer one, the epic's elephant is won into agreement, so mastery here is shown as concord after force, not fear alone.

note: The Kural's spy goes in the guise of renunciants (துறந்தார் படிவத்தர்) and gives nothing away; Padumukan's spies (படிவ ஒற்றாளர்) have found Civakan in disguise and are rewarded on their report.
teaches: The Kural writes spying as a king's instrument against enemies, while the epic turns the same disguised spy to a band of friends searching for their lost lord, which shows the technique is a means that serves loyalty as well as statecraft.

note: The couplet asks a wife to guard the good name of the house; Gandharvadattai guards her husband's name among her people by sending a false message.
teaches: Together they show the wife's duty of guarding the good name pulling against truthfulness: Gandharvadattai keeps the couplet's charge by deceiving her own father's envoy, and names the couplet's duty as her reason.

note: The couplet makes one day pass like seven for those waiting for a return; the epic's girl, told 'tomorrow', asks her parrot whether tomorrow is near or far.
teaches: The pair shows that a promised day of return does not shorten the wait but makes it measurable, and the epic turns the couplet's arithmetic into a question the waiting woman cannot answer.

note: The couplet's lover says he would recall her if he forgot, but he knows no forgetting; Gandharvadattai says she need not recall her husband, since he never leaves her heart.
teaches: The conceit that one who never forgets has nothing to remember becomes, in the abandoned wife's letter, a reproach: the same words that pledge constancy remind the new bridegroom that she has not moved and he has.

note: The couplet puts the lotus goddess in the effort of the unslothful; the verse says she will not embrace those who slip.
teaches: Where the Kural earns fortune by effort, the epic loses it by a lapse, so prosperity is shown as something kept by conduct and not only won by work.

note: The verse takes up the couplet's hands joined in worship and weeping tears that hide a weapon, adds hair and jewel caskets, and ends with those who trusted being dead.
teaches: The couplet names where a weapon hides; the epic turns it into a bodyguard's order and adds the outcome, showing the rule read as a practical protocol against poisoning.

note: The couplet says to cut a thorn tree while young; the verse says no enemy, however soft and small, should be called small, using the snake that kills an elephant.
teaches: The couplet's remedy is to strike early, while the epic's is to guard always, so the same fear of a small foe yields attack in one and vigilance in the other.

note: Verse 192 praises Vijayai's red-cornered eyes as fighting carp (களிக் கயல் பொருவ); Naladiyar 44's renunciant refuses men who call eyes பொருகயல் and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant names the epic's own stock of praise as the temptation he walks past, and the epic shows that praise doing its work on a king who does not walk past it.

note: Kural 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account; 1922 says wealth makes the diminished into mountains, and 1924 names the speaker and her son as those diminished in lineage and treasure.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet, often read as a dry observation about upstarts, onto a fallen royal house, for whom wealth is the way back to the standing birth once gave.

note: Kural 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth the other two aims, virtue and pleasure, come together; 1923 makes gold yield army, army land, land wealth, and wealth everything.
teaches: Where the couplet makes wealth the way to virtue and pleasure, the mother's chain loops wealth back into power and more wealth, and only her own first condition in 1920, wealth got by justice, ties it to அறம்.

note: Kural 445 says a king walks with his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them with care; 1921 has Vijayai give the same rule, and at 1924 she says there are no learned counsellors here.
teaches: The couplet assumes a court to choose counsellors from; the exiled prince has none, so the rule becomes a measure of what he lacks and throws the choice back on his own resolve.

note: Kural 497 says no ally is needed but fearlessness, provided one thinks everything through and acts by the place; at 1925 Civakan claims no strategy or allies are needed because he is strong.
teaches: Civakan keeps the couplet's conclusion and drops its condition, and the mother's next verses restore exactly the weighing of place that the couplet made the price of going alone.

note: Kural 481 says the crow beats the owl by day and that kings need the right time; 1927 tells of one crow that went among the owls in their own place and killed a thousand crore.
teaches: The couplet's even match, decided by the hour, becomes in the epic one against countless decided by time, place and cunning together, so judgment is shown to multiply strength and not merely to time it.

note: Kural 500 has the jackal kill the fearless elephant once its feet sink in the mire; 1928 has the roaring lion caught in the hunters' net in the forest.
teaches: Both reverse the strong beast by its setting, but the epic puts the reversal in a mother's answer to a son who has just called himself the lion, so the maxim is aimed at a person and not at kings in general.

note: The Kural's lover says all five senses find their objects in one woman; verse 194 gathers sound, scent, sight and touch in Vijayai and calls the joy inexhaustible.
teaches: What the Kural states as the joy of union, with no cost named, the epic puts in a king, and four verses later shows the cost: a man whose senses are all fed from one source slips from guarding the land (198).

note: Kural 1081's man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; here the women cannot tell whether the man is Murugan or Kama.
teaches: The epic gives the first-sight bewilderment of the Kural's lover to a crowd of women looking at a man, and narrows the choice to two gods, so the doubt is no longer whether the beloved is mortal but which divine lover he is.

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; 196 measures the king's wedded intimacy as greater than the sea, and the story goes on to make that desire lose him his realm.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on following the wife assumes a fault in the yielding; the epic gives a blameless, chaste queen (verse 7, வீடாத கற்பின்) and lawful marriage, and still the husband's boundless absorption alone ruins him, so the rule holds without any fault in the woman.

note: Vimalai calls desire the one sickness with no medicine; Kural 1102 says the woman who causes the sickness is herself its cure.
teaches: Read together they show the two sides of one sickness: to the sufferer who cannot speak of it, it has no cure, while the couplet, spoken from the side of union, finds the cure in the beloved, which the story will supply by marriage.

note: Kural 1180: the town reads the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. Vimalai: her pallor beats out her desire like a drum (பறையாய் அறையும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The drum that proclaims a hidden love sits in the eyes in the couplet and in the skin's pallor in the epic, so the pairing shows the body as a whole betraying what restraint tries to keep.

note: Kural 1091: her eyes have two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure. Civakan, shot by her brows, asks what medicine there is for the wound and looks back at her.
teaches: The couplet's two looks are both hers; the epic gives the second look to him, so the exchange of glances, not one woman's eyes, carries both the wound and the hope of a cure.

note: Kural 1083: the man never knew Death and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes. Civakan: those who named her called her woman; had they called her Death, men would flee the city.
teaches: The pair shows two steps of one discovery: the couplet's man learns that Death has a woman's form, and the epic adds that the name 'woman' hides it, so no one is warned in time.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the maiden's look is Death, an eye or a doe; Civakan asks whether her eyes are swords, mango slices, lilies, lotus, spears, arrows, carp, eyes, or Death come to kill.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's three-way doubt, the epic's ten guesses show the question turned into a catalogue that closes by choosing Death, where the couplet leaves the look holding all three at once.

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; the narrator says Civakan and Vimalai became one life in two bodies because they never parted.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's body-and-life bond conditional on never parting, and then has the husband part at the next dawn, which tests the image the couplet offers as a pledge.

note: The narrator reports that the pleasure of Vimalai's breasts is worth the three worlds; the Naladiyar, a Jain didactic work, lists entrails, blood and bone and asks where among them the garlanded woman is.
teaches: The epic gives full voice to the valuation that the Jain didactic tradition exists to unmask, and hedges it as hearsay, so the praise stands as the worldly view that Civakan's later renunciation will have to undo.

note: The Kural's woman (or her friend) refuses a promise of speedy return: tell it to those who will still be alive. Civakan makes exactly that promise, quicker than an arrow, and Vimalai answers only with tears.
teaches: The epic stages the very speech the couplet refuses to accept, and the bride's silent tears in 1994 are the wordless form of the couplet's retort.

note: Naladiyar 13 condemns the old who lean on a staff, toothless and tottering, yet keep their eyes on desire; Civakan, young, puts on that very figure with staff and white hair for love of a woman's beauty.
teaches: The quatrain's figure of shame, the old man still ruled by desire, becomes in the epic a costume a young lover wears to reach a woman, so the image meant to turn men from desire is used as an instrument of it.

note: Kural 586 sends the spy into closed places in the guise of renunciants, undiscovered whatever is done to him; Civakan enters a house closed to men in the guise of an old Brahmin and holds his part under the women's threats (2014-2015).
teaches: The statecraft couplet's method, borrowing a status no one guards against, is shown working in love, and its clause 'whatever is done to him' is tested when armed women surround the disguised man and he keeps silent.

note: The Naladiyar warns that grey hair will come and youth will not return; Suramanjari scoffs that those who think a dead tree revives by rain are mad.
teaches: The Naladiyar's truth that age is irreversible becomes, in the epic, the very certainty a schemer relies on: because everyone knows the old cannot become young, no one looks for the young man inside the old one.

note: The Kural says the fruit of tending a guest has no fixed measure but is as great as the guest's worth; Suramanjari feeds a guest she takes for a poor old brahmin.
teaches: The couplet assumes the host's offering and its fruit are reckoned by the guest's true worth; the epic shows a host who cannot see that worth, so the fruit she reaps, the end of her vow, is far beyond what she thought she was giving.

note: Kural 509 bids a ruler trust no one unexamined; the king vouches for Kattiyankaran by love and past victories and forbids further words.
teaches: Loyalty and battle service, the very grounds the king gives, are not the examination the couplet asks for, so the scene shows how trust can feel tested while skipping the test of fitness for power.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's sweet flute is evening's envoy and a killing weapon to the woman whose lover is away; 2050 is a sweet vina-song whose evening enters like a spear into a wound.
teaches: In the Kural sweet music wounds a woman because her lover is absent, while in the epic the lover himself plays the music to a woman who has no lover yet, so the evening-song creates the sickness it laments.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the learned forget their books; Civakan's oath calls such a guardian's fate down on himself if he fails her.
teaches: The bent sceptre that the Kural treats as a public disaster becomes, in a lover's oath, the worst private penalty a man can name, which shows how deep the guardian's duty sat as a measure of shame.

note: Kural 270 says the destitute are many because few do penance; the rich merchant says he and his daughter have done none.
teaches: The couplet ties lack to the absence of penance; the epic puts the same reasoning in a rich man's mouth, so the want that penance would have prevented is a want of good fortune in a child, not of wealth.

note: Kural 1251 makes restraint a door bolted by shame, broken by desire's axe; Suramanjari drives off the bee of shame and waves the garland of chastity.
teaches: In the couplet restraint stands only while shame bars it; the epic has a woman put shame away in order to keep her chastity, so the two virtues the couplet binds together are parted and ranked.

note: In Kural 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; Suramanjari refuses a chest many embrace like the Ganges.
teaches: The Kural's sulking pretext is that other women merely look at him, but in a polygamous epic where the hero has already married several wives the same refusal names a fact.

note: In Kural 1320 she is angry even at his gaze, asking whom he thinks of; here she is angry at his gaze on a painted figure, and he claims he took the picture for her.
teaches: The epic supplies the object the couplet leaves imagined, a painted woman on the wall, and turns the lover's defence round: his gaze was faithful because he mistook the picture for her.

note: The Kural says the loser of a lovers' quarrel is the winner, as union shows; Civakan casts himself as the small one who erred, yields, and wins her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's paradox a plot: a woman who swore to see the man defeated gets his surrender, and his surrender is exactly what wins him her.

note: Naladiyar 77 says the great bear faults hard to bear, which is why their friendship is sought; Civakan uses the same maxim to plead with a sulking wife after denying any fault.
teaches: A maxim about the forbearance of the great in friendship turns, in a lover's mouth, into flattery that makes the angry woman the great one and so obliges her to forgive.

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven to those waiting for the absent one's return; Civakan tells Gunamalai the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
teaches: The epic moves the measure of absence from the waiting woman to the returned man and inflates it from seven days to an aeon, said only once the parting is over and as a gift of words.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; 2107 takes the same unstable world and fame that stands, and uses the fame-seeker's wealth as a figure of what vanishes fast.
teaches: The pair shows the price side of the Kural's maxim: the fame that alone stands is bought with wealth that goes as fast as a desert crossed in a day, so lasting renown and fleeting riches are one transaction.

note: Kural 29 speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of virtue, held even for a moment; 2107 counts the anger of the holy among things that do not stay.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's crux over whether such anger lasts only a moment or is unbearable for a moment is settled one way in the epic, which takes its brevity as proverbial enough to serve as a simile of speed.

note: Rudradattan argues that lust's blame cannot be hidden and is drummed through the world; Naladiyar 89 says lust burns the mind itself, worse than fire or sun.
teaches: The counsellor argues from public disgrace and the quatrain from inward burning, so a reader sees that the ethics of desire had two separate arguments and that the epic, speaking to a king, chose reputation.

note: Kural 448 says a king without rebukers perishes even with no enemy; the king hears Rudradattan's rebuke, rejects it, and the counsellor withdraws.
teaches: The epic shows the middle case the couplet skips, a king who has a rebuker and sends him away, and its ruin comes through the trusted man, so the danger lies in refusing rebuke as much as in lacking it.

note: Kural 377 says even the rich enjoy only as the apportioner has apportioned; the king says his pleasures and life-days are measured by past penance and so refuses counsel.
teaches: The couplet's limit on enjoyment becomes, in a king's mouth, a licence to stop listening, which shows that a doctrine of allotted fruit can be turned against the duty to act on advice.

note: The Kural warns that honouring one's own spy openly lets out the secret; Govindan honours Civakan's companions exactly as his own men so that the enemy's spies cannot pick them out.
teaches: The couplet's insight that visible honour leaks a secret works in reverse too: honour spread evenly conceals, so a king can hide his guests by treating them like everyone else.

note: Kural 827 says the humble words of an enemy are like a bending bow; Kattiyankaran's letter bows, offers his life and calls Govindan lord.
teaches: The letter shows the bowed bow of the couplet in a full text, and Govindan's laughter (2148) shows the reader the couplet applied: the humbler the words, the plainer the threat.

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; the narrator says the king followed his heart to the queen because a past destiny sprouted.
teaches: The couplet treats being led by desire for one's wife as a fault to be avoided, while the epic adds a ripening past deed as its cause, which raises the question the couplet does not face: whether such a man could have chosen otherwise.

note: Kural 830 counsels befriending a feigned friend with the face while letting go in the heart; Govindan proclaims through the city that he has become one with Kattiyankaran while mustering his army.
teaches: The couplet speaks of an individual's face and heart; the epic turns the face into a public proclamation and the hidden heart into a state secret guarded by threat, so the mask needs the silence of a whole city.

note: Kural 882 bids one fear the bond with enemies who are like kin more than enemies like swords; the usurper delights in the kinsman-like gifts of the king who means to kill him.
teaches: The couplet's warning is spoken to the potential victim, and the epic shows that victim praising the gift that should have frightened him, while placing the kin-like enemy on the side the story favours.

note: Kural 830 counsels that when a foe must be treated as a friend, one should befriend with the face and drop friendship within; the Videha king makes himself one with the usurper so as to kill him by the sword of love.
teaches: The couplet's face-friendship is a defensive mask with an exit, while the epic turns it into the method of a killing and calls it வஞ்சம் even on the hero's side, so the pair shows how far the Kural's permission can be stretched once the foe is a usurper.

note: The Kural calls not looking at another's wife the great manhood; the epic's simile grants that the heart goes out to her and places virtue in the wise man's recalling it.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's ideal of never looking, the simile shows a working form of the virtue the Kural allows only as perfection: the desire arises and understanding turns it back.

note: The Kural says austerity is practised because it brings what is wanted as it is wanted; the narrator explains the kings' six days of failure by their ignorance of the greatness of ripened austerity.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's promise worked out as a plot: what the kings want, they cannot get by wanting, and the one who wins does so by merit of austerity, so tapas becomes the hidden cause of a marriage.

note: The epic likens the hero's arrows to the straight minds of the refined; the couplet holds that the straight arrow is cruel and that form proves nothing about worth.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the simile shows the epic choosing the arrow's straightness as a sign of virtue at the very moment the arrow starts a war of slaughter, which the Kural warns is the arrow's real nature.

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god; Vijayai rises, worships the god's feet, and then goes to her lord's feet.
teaches: A Jain epic keeps the wife's devotion to her husband but sets worship of the god first, so the couplet's exclusive ranking is answered with an order of two duties rather than a choice between them.

note: The epic gives the usurper the larger host, and the couplet says that many steadfast men make no army without leaders.
teaches: The counts set Kattiyangaran's bigger force against Civakan's smaller one, so the coming defeat of the larger host turns the couplet's rule about leadership over numbers into a plot.

note: Kural 780 calls a death that fills the eyes of one's patron with tears worth begging for; 2240's warriors have paid their debt of the red rice, and the only ones who cry over them are jackals.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's logic of a death owed to the lord but removes the weeping patron who gave that death its worth, leaving the debt paid with no one to mourn it.

note: Naladiyar 48 asks those who praise sandal and garlands whether they have not seen vultures tear the body once it breaks; 2244 sets the sandal-smeared chest that women embraced in the blood, embraced now by the sword.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ruined body to turn a man from desire, but the epic shows the same ruin of the beloved body in battle and draws no lesson from it, keeping beauty and slaughter in one image without preaching.

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; Ulokapalan plucks the arrow from his forehead and the gushing blood is likened to the dawn sun's first ray.
teaches: Together they show the wound pulled from the body as a fixed sign of the hero, and that the epic turns the Kural's psychological shock, a laugh, into visual glory, so the same act is valued as composure in the one and as splendour in the other.

note: The Kural says help to a foe in misfortune is the cutting edge of valour; Nabulan, seeing the Magadha king flinch, holds his blow, reassures him and goes elsewhere.
teaches: The couplet calls kindness to a stricken foe valour's sharpest point, and the epic shows what drives it in the moment: shame in the stronger man (நாணி), so that sparing is felt as a duty to one's own honour rather than as pity.

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; Vipulan will not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction.
teaches: The Kural ranks quarry by size and danger and puts the elephant at the top; the epic's warrior ranks by kind and puts every beast below a man, so the two measures of a worthy target diverge exactly at the elephant.

note: The Kural says one who tends his guests becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Vipulan calls his challenger a guest and gives him the first blow, and it is the guest, killed, who goes to heaven.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the duel inverts its exchange: in the Kural the host earns heaven by feeding the guest, while on the battlefield the host's hospitality is the first stroke, and heaven goes to the guest he kills.

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; the epic's thrower would not cast except at a young elephant, and spends that spear on one warrior.
teaches: The couplet ranks targets; the epic shows the ranking used as a courtesy between enemies, a man of the elephant-only code paying a foot soldier the honour of the elephant's spear.

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; the epic's youth plucks out the spear that fed on his flesh and laughs (பறித்து நக்கான்).
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's laugh a cause the couplet leaves open: the spear had been thrown by a man who kept his spear for elephants, so the wound is an honour and the laugh is the pride of having been judged worth it.

note: The Kural calls it flight when a fierce man blinks at a flung spear; the epic's warrior does not blink at all (இமைத்திலன்) as the spear comes, and takes it on his chest.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse shows where its standard leads: the unblinking eye is kept to the end, and the warrior who will not blink is the one the spear kills, so the code costs the life it measures.

note: Kural 780 says a death that fills with tears the eyes of those who sustained one is worth begging for; Ariccandan's speech promises rewards to men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them (தற்புறந் தந்து வைத்த தலைமகற்கு).
teaches: Together they show the couplet's patron-bond being used as a battlefield appeal, and that it can be spent on a bad master: the leader these men are asked to die for is the usurper, and the speech wins only their deaths.

note: Kural 380 holds nothing is stronger than fate, which forestalls any scheme; Kattiyangaran says the wise do not think of killing or being killed because deeds decide.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's fatalism to a schemer whose own plot made the war, so the reader sees how the doctrine that fate outruns all devices can also serve to excuse the devices one has already used.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain says that as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in when good deeds are spent; Kattiyangaran says that as a lamp dwindles when ghee and wick are gone, wealth perishes when the two kinds of deed wear away.
teaches: Both make karma the lamp's fuel, but the quatrain teaches renewing merit by austerity while the epic's usurper uses the image to explain the loss of a throne, so the lamp shows its political use: a fall can be read as fuel run out instead of a wrong repaid.

note: Kural 775 counts it flight for the fierce to blink when a spear is thrown; Kattiyangaran says that if he blinks when a spear comes, Civakan may laugh.
teaches: The king splits outcome from courage: he grants victory to fate yet stakes his honour on the couplet's unblinking eye, so the pair shows the unblinking gaze as the one part of valour fate cannot take.

note: Kural 904 says the man who fears his wife gains no distinction from his deeds; Kattiyangaran's self-curse is that if he loses in valour he may become a base man who fears his wife (இல்லாளை அஞ்சி) and slights a guest.
teaches: The vow ranks fear of one's wife as a disgrace equal to defeat in battle, which shows the couplet's household fault serving as a warrior's measure of shame, the worst a king can wish on himself.

note: The Kural binds the one at the king's side to speak what is good even to a king who destroys counsel; in the Cintamani the counsel comes from Wisdom as minister, after the realm is already given away.
teaches: With the minister's office handed to the usurper, the duty the Kural lays on the counsellor falls to the king's own wisdom, and it speaks only when advice can no longer save the realm.

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode in state fall when their deeds give out and their foes take the wives they married; the Cintamani's victors break into the fallen king's palace and drive his women out.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's fall of a king but changes its last turn: the victors expel the dead king's wives rather than take them.

note: The Kural says the tears of those who cannot bear oppression wear away the oppressor's wealth; when the usurper falls, the tears in the story are those of his own women.
teaches: The ruin that the tears of the oppressed bring on a bent sceptre falls in the story on the oppressor's women, who now weep in their turn.

note: Naladiyar 3 says that even kings who rode in state under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 2371 seats the victor on the lion throne in the full pomp of such a king, after the usurper's fall.
teaches: The throne scene stands on the ground the quatrain describes: the pomp the winner now enjoys is what the usurper lost, so the crowning is shown as one turn of a wheel, not a rest.

note: Kural 390 names giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people as the four that make a king a light; the proclamation of 2375 turns them into acts: remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.
teaches: The couplet's four virtues become a single proclamation with named relief, which shows what giving and care of the people cost a treasury and who is to benefit.

note: Kural 557 says a king's lack of grace is for those who live what the lack of rain is for the earth; 2376 has the king's wealth go as grace to the blind, the sick and the wives abandoned.
teaches: The couplet states the cost of a king's lack of grace in the language of rain, while the epic names those who would be left dry, showing who counts as the people the sceptre owes.

note: Naladiyar says a wife married on a fixed day, with the drum beaten that many may know, is the wife a man should keep to; the epic shows that drum beaten from an elephant and the day set by an astrologer.
teaches: The Naladiyar's drum and fixed day are the public face of a marriage, which the epic acts out as a city-wide command.

note: The Naladiyar says the same wedding drums that sound in the hall may be funeral drums that very day; here a wedding drum thunders for seven days and the city is told to live.
teaches: The Cintamani's wedding drum is heard here only as joy, while the Naladiyar hears in the same sound the fragility of the groom's life, so the two give opposing readings of the same instrument.

note: The wedding instruments sound and the carp-eyed women go to the bath; the Naladiyar quatrain says the drums that sounded as wedding drums may sound that day in that place as funeral drums for the bridegroom.
teaches: The epic gives the drums only their joyful sound, and the quatrain reminds the reader that a hero's wedding festival is not yet a safe ground for pride, which matters in a poem that ends with its hero leaving the throne.

note: Kural 906 says the man who fears his wife's shoulders is worthless though he live like the gods; Dharmadattan says the king valued a woman's pleasure above heaven and nectar.
teaches: The Kural weighs the wife-ruled man against the gods' life and finds him worthless, while the epic's king makes the same comparison in reverse, and the cost falls not on his worth but on the whole realm.

note: The dresser draws the creeper of desire in sandal paste on the bride's breasts; the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the body when the axle of its cart breaks.
teaches: The painted creeper is told as a high art at its best, so the Naladiyar's corpse image is shown to answer not coarse adornment but the finest.
