note: The bangled women stand desiring the bride's eyes, breasts, hips and hair; the Naladiyar tells the reader not to desire a woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
teaches: The gaze that the epic lingers on is the one the Naladiyar answers with the staff of old age, giving the scene's longing a time it will pass through.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Dharmadattan warns that Fortune will leave the man who seizes the king who made him, and that loyalty secures his line.
teaches: The Kural's 'no escape' for ingratitude is turned into a political forecast, the loss of fortune and lineage, and offered to a would-be usurper as prudence rather than only as virtue.

note: Kural 1083 has a man say he never knew Death and now does, it being a woman's grace and large war-eyes; 2451 says Death has come in a king's daughter's form and her own jewels bid the onlookers flee.
teaches: The couplet turns Death into one man's private discovery, while the epic makes it a public warning given by the jewels, so a figure of suffering becomes a danger announced to a crowd.

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says gossip spread like the serpent seizing the moon after one sight of him; in 2461 the shy bride's hidden face is the moon in the serpent's grasp.
teaches: The same moon-and-serpent figure stands for exposure in the Kural and for modest hiding in the epic, so the figure is a flexible one for a face that is partly seen.

note: In 2467 drums, conches and kings roar as the bridegroom takes the water; Naladiyar 23 says the same wedding drums can sound as funeral drums that very day.
teaches: The roar of the wedding drums sets Naladiyar's warning on how soon joy turns, and the epic's later turn to renunciation is its own answer.

note: Kural 388 calls the ruler who does justice and protects இறை; Dharmadattan calls the king a great deity because his favour makes and his anger burns.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's divinity a reward for just rule, while Dharmadattan makes it a matter of the king's power, which lets him use it to protect even a king who has abandoned rule.

note: Kural 1251 says desire's axe breaks the door of restraint barred with shame; 2477 shows the bride's shame giving way within a sanctioned marriage.
teaches: The Kural treats the fall of shame as a defeat, while the epic shows it fall inside a rite-bound marriage, so shame is given up here without the loss the Kural fears.

note: Kural 547 says the ruler guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter; 248 says the king's splendour guards the world even as he sleeps.
teaches: The Cintamani's king, who sleeps in pleasure and loses everything, illustrates the Kural's condition by its breach: majesty without unfaltering justice guards nothing.

note: The bride's ornaments protest that the 'king of kings' turned cruel-sceptred will not look into or hear their clamour (ஆய்ந்து கேட்டு மருளான்); the couplet says the ruler who does not examine daily and do justice loses his land.
teaches: The poet borrows the courtroom picture of the deaf king who spurns a plaint to make a lovers' jest, which shows how familiar the Kural's failed-hearing image was as a figure.

note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to keep to them as men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; 250 says the king's fire burns those who touch it along with their kin and can be nectar or poison.
teaches: The Kural's fire is a rule of prudent distance for courtiers, while Dharmadattan extends it to the minister who would seize the fire, and to his whole family.

note: The wedding dresses the bride in a necklace that seems to own her body; the quatrain says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, and the body they guarded and adorned is no use when Death seizes it.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain's warning, the wedding's lavish adornment of a body reads as the thing the Jain moral is aimed at, which the festive verse itself does not say.

note: Kural 1320 has the sulking woman accuse a man who only sits gazing at her of thinking of someone else; here Civakan's unblinking gaze and watering eyes make Ilakkanai say he weeps thinking of others.
teaches: The epic shows that the suspicion in the couplet can grow from the very rapture of the gaze, so the quarrel is a love's misreading and not a sign of a wandering heart.

note: Kural 1329 has the man wish the sulk would go on and the night lengthen so he might keep pleading; Civakan, pleading through the bees, calls her anger the fruit of his own past sin.
teaches: Where the couplet relishes the plea as part of love's game, the epic lets the husband feel the quarrel as an undeserved punishment, so the same scene reads as pleasure or as pain by the speaker's mood.

note: Kural 1327 says the one who yields in a lovers' quarrel wins; Civakan yields first, but the quarrel ends when the parrot threatens to hang itself.
teaches: Yielding does not by itself end the sulk in the epic; it takes the comic shock from a third party to break it, which limits the couplet's rule that the loser wins.

note: Naladiyar 384 praises a wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly; Ilakkanai relents only when the birds' scene makes her laugh, and gives the smile as her reward.
teaches: The quatrain's wife relents of her own judgment, while the epic's wife is brought round by a joke at her own expense, so the ideal is softened by what the story shows of how quarrels actually end.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a benefit; 253 names a minister who kills the king who raised him among those who sink into hell and leprosy.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's abstract unforgivable sin a concrete political form, the minister's regicide, and spells out where 'no escape' leads.

note: The verse measures a breast's shrinking against a king who will not hear justice; Kural 553 says such a king loses his land day by day.
teaches: The poet treats the sceptre's decline as a stock yardstick to measure the shape of a body, so the epic's court ethic works as common knowledge rather than argument.

note: The verse says the people honour only the rich and the poor have no kin, using it as a simile; Kural 752 states that everyone scorns the poor and honours the rich.
teaches: The Kural states the world's partiality as a fact and the epic applies it as a simile, showing the poet treats it as shared knowledge and as a cost on the neglected waist.

note: The women speak a desire and beg with their eyes, while Kural 1100 says that when two pairs of eyes agree, mouth-words are of no use.
teaches: The Kural's silent agreement of two pairs of eyes needs the other side's glance; the women here ask in words and eyes for what he has not yet answered.

note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky will not rain; 255 extends the effects to the planets, the hours, harvest, hunger, women's chastity and dharma.
teaches: The Cintamani turns the Kural's warning to an unjust king into an argument against a minister seizing power, treating usurpation itself as the bending of the sceptre.

note: Thirikadugam 50 names three separate 'planets' that cut off rain: a greedy king, deceitful men and a woman who crosses her bounds; 255 makes the bent sceptre the one cause from which failed rain and broken chastity both follow.
teaches: Where the Thirikadugam gives the king, the liar and the unchaste woman equal blame for drought, the Cintamani makes women's lapse a symptom of the king's fault.

note: The people see the hero's birth in the burning ground, rearing as a merchant's son and the kings' worship and ask why one should not do tapas; the quatrain has the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength because none lasts.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues renunciation from the failing of goods in general, and the epic argues it from one life in which a single man has held every state, so the argument rests on a case the hearers have seen.

note: Wealth does not come across seas and mountains without fortune, and may come home to those who go not a cubit; the couplet says what is not one's own will not stay and what is will not leave.
teaches: The epic draws the practical conclusion the couplet leaves unsaid: if wealth is the share fortune gives, the effort spent seeking it is better spent on tapas.

note: Poison, hiding and the elephant's tusks are the dangers the strong in tapas escape; the couplet says austerity's power lets one even leap past Death.
teaches: The Kural states the power of tapas at its limit and the epic lists the particular harms it turns aside, and adds that when tapas is spent no flight saves.

note: Civakan lays his endowment at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus; the Kural's opening couplets name the one who walked on the flower and promise long life to those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic names the lotus and puts a temple and a gift at the feet, filling in the figure the couplet leaves open, so it shows one tradition's reading of the lotus-walker as the Jina's temple god.

note: The world asks 'what penance must he have done' and the king repays the one who reared him with a queen's title; the couplet makes that very kind of question the repayment a son owes his father.
teaches: The couplet's repayment is a sentence the world speaks; the epic adds a repayment made in rank and land and paid to the nurse, so the debt to one who raised a child need not stay in words and is not only the father's.

note: Civakan raises a golden image and a dance to the friend who wiped away his trouble, and that friend was once a dog who changed birth; the couplet says the friendship of those who wiped away sorrow is remembered for seven births.
teaches: The Kural's memory across births becomes a literal chain from dog to god, and the epic makes the memory public and material in image and dance where the couplet leaves it in the heart.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre by its nature; 2583 says that under Civakan killing and miserliness are banished and the land becomes like Uttarakuru, with fish leaping into the fishers' yards.
teaches: The couplet's rule is carried to its extreme here, where just rule ends killing and scarcity as well as drought, but the epic offers it only as praise, so the couplet's causal claim remains unproved.

note: Naladiyar 371 says the friendship of harlots ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends when the oil runs out; in 2588 Anangamalai, a woman of the stage, is jailed and released and keeps worshipping a painted image of Civakan with no payment.
teaches: The quatrain's rule is a claim about women of her station, and her story tests it, which shows the epic treating constancy as the person's, not the profession's.

note: Vijayai says that no return can match those who ended her distress and gives them every delight; the Kural says that help given when none was given before cannot be paid back even by earth and sky.
teaches: The Kural states that such help is beyond repayment, and the epic shows what a queen does about it: she gives all she has and still says the debt remains.

note: Vijayai says no one knows how many days are given and that the dead cannot be recalled; the Kural says good must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue.
teaches: The Kural's urgency is made a mother's plea to a king at the height of pleasure, showing the rule's cost: it must be heard just when it is least welcome.

note: Vijayai says deed's force scatters us like clouds and there is no lasting fellowship; the Naladiyar says kin arrive unasked and leave wordless, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest.
teaches: The Naladiyar says parting happens at death; Vijayai says it is the working of deeds even in life, which is why she can ask her son to loosen his own attachments now.

note: Vijayai urges penance and giving before black hair turns white; the Naladiyar says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come, and the youth-lovers later lean on a staff.
teaches: The pairing shows that the call to act before age is made both to a king in his prime by his mother and as a general rule, so the epic's mother is speaking the Naladiyar's counsel in her own household.

note: Vijayai tells diners to think of austerity, not riches, as they eat milk-rice from gold bowls; the Naladiyar says the fool who hoards his wealth and dies is laughed at by the wealth itself.
teaches: The epic says wealth is not a thing to rely on at the table; the Naladiyar says what wealth does to the hoarder, and together they show that gifts and penance are what the dying keep.

note: Naladiyar 1 shows men who ate six-flavoured meals served by a willing wife and then beg gruel here and there; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now holds out a wide bowl for alms.
teaches: The Naladiyar's quatrain draws the rule that wealth cannot be counted on, and the Cintamani turns the same beggar's fall into a sight the preacher points to while urging the hearers to turn to dharma.

note: Naladiyar 13 shows those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire; 2626 shows a youth in a garland and spear who comes to lean on a staff and drool.
teaches: The sermon shows the young man whose decline the Naladiyar describes only from its end, and so makes the same warning about desire outliving the body's strength.

note: Kural 47 puts the householder who lives the household life rightly first among all who strive; 2632 has the nun say that penance is hard and that a gift sown with virtue yields fame and then the pleasures of the gods.
teaches: The Jain nun grades the gift of the householder as a fruit of fame and heaven and keeps the harder penance above it, so the Kural's 'first among strivers' is put against a ladder of fruits.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 2637 has the matrons pluck out their own dark hair and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the Lord's book.
teaches: The Jain rite of plucking the hair is joined to inward thought in the verse, which is the answer to the Kural's doubt whether the shorn head means anything without giving up.

note: The queen puts away pleasure for austerity; Naladiyar 53 says the best of people consider slowly and give up home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's counsel taken by a woman at the court while her husband is still held by pleasure, which makes giving up one's own household look like a path that is left open and not forced.

note: The king wins the love-god's war in play, with garlands and streams; Naladiyar 17 says youth drops like fruit and the woman desired for her spear-like eyes will walk with a staff.
teaches: The epic's delight at its brightest is the thing the quatrain tells the hearer not to desire, so the water-sport is set to be read against the old age it will bring.

note: The women dress, steam and garland themselves after the play; Naladiyar 16 likens the joy of youth to a lamb nibbling at the garland held out before the slaughter.
teaches: The same garland that is the sign of pleasure in the Cintamani is the bait of the sacrifice in the quatrain, and the reader sees both uses of one object.

note: The couch scene rubs off the sandal and tears at the garlands; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing the body they decorate.
teaches: Both pass through sandal, garland and body, one to delight in them and one to say the body is the cart that vultures will tear at.

note: The husband tells his wife the moon pales before her face and thereby ends her sulk; Kural 1118 tells the moon it would be loved if it shone like her face.
teaches: The face-and-moon compliment is shown at work in a quarrel as a way to end a sulk, not only as praise.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at the start neither shrinks nor grows, so why grieve in ruin; 269 says birth and death come from one's own deeds and grief is want of understanding.
teaches: Both forbid grief by appeal to a fixed outcome, but the king speaks while his own fault caused the ruin, so in his mouth deed-fruit is also a confession, which the Naladiyar's impersonal fixed mark is not.

note: The Naladiyar's best of men renounce house, youth, wealth and strength because they see these do not last; Civakan renounces in full possession of all of them.
teaches: The quatrain grounds renunciation in seeing that goods pass away, while the epic's king renounces while every good still stands and gives fear of kingship, roused by the dharma, as his motive, so impermanence is not the only road to leaving.

note: The women of the verse are worn and pale from love itself; Naladiyar 17 tells a man not to crave a woman's spear-like eyes, since age will bend her.
teaches: The Naladiyar waits for age to wear a woman's beauty, but the epic shows love's own use wearing it at the bed, long before old age.

note: The sons learn arts, weapons and horse-riding at five; Kural 61 prizes children who come to know what should be known.
teaches: The couplet names knowing as the child's worth, while the epic's lesson is the skills of a warrior's house, so what is 'known' differs.

note: The mate refuses a chest that has lain with courtesans; Kural 1311 has a woman refuse a husband's chest, calling him a philanderer.
teaches: The Kural's refusal rests on a seen glance, while the monkey's rests on a proved infidelity, so the sulk is shown with a real cause.

note: The Kural warns one who is about to oppress the weak to think how he stands before the stronger; Civakan sees that the strong seize the weak's wealth and draws not a rule for the strong but a reason to leave.
teaches: The warning that assumes a ruler who will listen is answered by a ruler who, having seen the same fact, withdraws from rule altogether.

note: Naladiyar 130 tells the heart that attachment to home and children is idle since nothing but good done goes with it; 2728 names the family itself as the fruit of that good and says it will be lost.
teaches: The quatrain makes the family a hindrance beside merit, while the verse makes the family a result of merit, so the reader sees that giving up the fruit and keeping the merit are different acts.

note: Kural 10 says that those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 2741 praises the Lord who crossed the sea of karma and makes his praisers lords of the wheel under the three umbrellas.
teaches: The couplet promises crossing the sea of births, while the verse promises kingship to the worshippers of a crosser, so the two disagree about what a follower gains.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness dies when a lamp comes, and returns when the oil runs out; 2745 asks for grace as a flame that will clear the darkness of the evil deed.
teaches: The quatrain gives the lamp's work a limit, since the dark returns, which raises the question whether the grace Civakan asks is a lasting cure.

note: Kural 543 makes the king's sceptre the origin of the books of the learned and of virtue; 2746 gives the ascetic the duty of telling the king dharma and leaves the king with the sceptre.
teaches: Where the couplet makes dharma depend on the king, the verse has the king come to the ascetic to hear it, so the two disagree about which gives the other its authority.

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one who has this rare body to take its full fruit, as juice from cane; 2749 gives the odds that make the body rare, the pole in the yoke-hole.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to use the body gets a reason in the epic's image of how improbable it is, and the epic's image gets a use to put it to.

note: Kural 338 says body and life part like a bird leaving its nest; 2754 says the life may be lost even before it leaves the womb, as a bubble bursts.
teaches: The Kural's picture begins at the nest-leaving; the epic starts earlier, with the embryo itself already at risk, so the loss is not only a late one.

note: Naladiyar 25 says the man who sees kin wailing at a corpse and yet marries and expects joy is answered by the funeral drum; 2758 shows men in the heart of pleasure cut off by Death while the living beat their faces.
teaches: The quatrain shows the lesson refused, the epic shows the death that teaches it, and together the reader sees that pleasure and mourning are the same scene seen at different times.

note: Naladiyar 33 sets the fool who sighs when the fruit of past deeds arrives against the wise who accept it; 2762 says the evildoer sows deeds in the soul and eats their harvest.
teaches: The quatrain names the response to the fruit, the epic names how the fruit is formed, so karma is shown as both cause and the way to meet it.

note: Naladiyar 84 asks the adulterer what pleasure he had, since the act brings disgrace, a cut leg and long hell; 2769 sets the adulterer in hell with a glowing copper woman in his arms.
teaches: The quatrain names the price of the act and the epic shows the price paid, so the pleasure is seen turning into the pain it earned.

note: Kural 255 says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; 2770 shows the killers of beasts and fish thrown daily into a seething pit.
teaches: The couplet says that hell waits, and the epic shows what its mouth holds, so the reader sees the rule enforced by the pain of the killer, not by a judge's word.

note: 2776 sends those bent on killing into hell on the cars of their sins; Kural 321 says killing brings all other evil deeds with it.
teaches: The couplet states killing as the root of other wrongs, and the epic adds the journey to hell as its end.

note: 2780 attacks the sacrifice of a lamb for the gods' pleasure with the recompense in Yama's world; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing and eating one creature.
teaches: The epic condemns the sacrificer by his punishment while the Kural condemns by comparison of worth, so the reader sees two ways to refuse sacrifice.

note: 2781 asks whose eyes would look on the creature cut apart and wailing; Kural 257 says flesh would not be eaten by those who saw it as another's wound.
teaches: The epic stages the very seeing that the couplet only wishes for, and shows it fails when appetite rules.

note: 2794 says the householders' wealth is a yoke of toil and pain; Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside the household life if it is lived by dharma.
teaches: Whether household life is a yoke or the best path depends on the claim of 2794, and the two works cannot both hold it.

note: The epic lists unmet wishes, parting, lost youth and old age as suffering; the quatrain lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as things that do not last and the best therefore renounce at once.
teaches: The epic names the pain of loss where the quatrain names its passing, and the quatrain supplies the action, renouncing without delay, that the epic verse leaves unsaid.

note: The Kural asks what one who keeps household life in dharma could gain by going the outer way; in the Cintamani the whole household, brother, friends and wives, goes that way and reaches a higher state.
teaches: The Kural's question assumes a householder could gain nothing more by leaving, but the epic answers it by having a just king's whole household leave together and arrive at the state that is ever new.

note: The epic teacher says all who have a body suffer, even gods bowing to higher gods; the quatrain says parting, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body and bids the heart cling to the wise.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to cling to the wise is shown to need the epic's wider claim, that no heaven escapes the suffering it names, before it becomes more than comfort.

note: The Kural's one who walked on the flower and his noble feet and the epic's wheel-king who walked on the open lotus and his feet which the virtuous praise; both give the lotus walker as the object of devotion.
teaches: The epic names what is learned at those feet, five, six and nine, where the couplet names only the reward of long life on earth.

note: The epic uses the same compound அறவாழி for the lord of dharma ('wheel of dharma' with வேந்தன், king, set against the Kural's reading of the Lord as a sea of virtue).
teaches: The epic's use of ஆழி with a king points to the wheel of dharma rather than the sea as the compound's meaning, which the couplet's other seas set against it leaves open.

note: The couplet says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who praise the Lord; the epic says that those who have understood both deeds and the Lord's scripture neither exult nor scorn, because every being eats its fruit.
teaches: The epic sets the escape in understanding, in a world where even Indra eats his deeds, while the couplet sets it in devotion, so the two give different accounts of how the deeds stop clinging.

note: The epic says those who eat the wounds of other creatures and honey with worms destroy their inner knowledge and are beasts; the couplet says that if men saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it.
teaches: Both call flesh another creature's wound, but the epic adds the charge that eating it destroys the eater's discernment, so the loss is the eater's own.

note: The epic defines sila as giving up what the great condemn, and the couplet says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns.
teaches: The two agree that sila is the giving up of what is condemned, but the epic's ascetics keep the plucked hair as discipline (2820) where the couplet makes the mark unnecessary.

note: The epic compares gifts to seed in good and poor soil; the quatrain compares even a small virtuous deed that reaches worthy hands to a banyan seed whose shade makes the sky seem small.
teaches: Both make the recipient decide the harvest, but the epic adds the poor-soil case, where the gift is lost, which the quatrain's banyan does not show.

note: 2824 names what the ascetics do to quench the five senses (wither them, keep from four sins); Kural 25 says only that the strength of one who has quenched them is witnessed by Indra.
teaches: The Kural gives the strength of one who has quenched the senses without the practice, and the verse gives the practice without the strength, so the two together show both sides.

note: 2841 says the middle sort of gift is paid by whatever one wishes in the land of enjoyment; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Cintamani ties each gift to its reward, while the Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical.

note: 2842 ranks gifts by the receiver, with a debased birth for a gift to the unrestrained; Kural 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving.
teaches: The Kural names the needy as the only true recipient, but the Cintamani's sage names the restrained, so who deserves a gift is answered in opposite ways.

note: 2845 defines release's path as knowledge, faith and conduct together; Kural 356 says those who learned here and saw the real thing reach the path of not coming back.
teaches: The Kural pairs learning and seeing, and the Jain verse adds the third (holding it in conduct), so the two give different recipes for the same release.

note: 2847 names what the freed soul has (endless knowledge, seeing, power and joy); Kural 362 says to want, want not to be born.
teaches: The Kural describes release as an absence of birth and desire, and the Cintamani's sage describes it as a fullness, so one calls release emptying and the other filling.

note: 2868 says killing a life brings great suffering; Kural 321 says not killing is virtuous action and killing brings all other evil.
teaches: One tells the rule and the other the fruit, so together the rule has a reason.

note: 2869 says the true word lifts to the towers of the upper world and the lie to hell; Kural 293 says that after lying your own heart burns you.
teaches: The Kural puts the punishment of a lie within and the verse sets it in the next world, so the two give two places for the same cost.

note: 2870 says theft is punished by kings and drops the thief into a fallen birth; Kural 290 says the thief loses his footing and the one who does not steal does not lose the world of the gods.
teaches: The verse spells the two punishments the Kural gives in one line, in this world and in the next.

note: 2870 teaches the giving up of theft and gambling to the prince; Naladiyar 157 says those of faultless vision do not steal, drink, scorn others or lie.
teaches: Both put the vows in a list for a lay hearer, so the list of vows seems a common teaching form.

note: 2871 puts another's wife as a sword over the neck and heavy suffering; Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses another's threshold.
teaches: The Kural lists four worldly costs and the verse gives one inward one, so the verse adds fear and the Kural adds blame.

note: 2871 says the one who goes to another's wife is like a bright sword over his own neck and falls into heavy suffering; Naladiyar 84 says if caught the leg is cut, the family shamed and hell follows.
teaches: Both put the cost of adultery in a worldly punishment and a future one, with the same image of a blade.

note: 2873 tells the prince to abandon wealth got with lies, deceit and dice; Kural 283 says gain got by stealth seems to grow and then perishes.
teaches: The Kural says the ill-gotten gain will not last and the verse adds that the greed behind it is itself what to drop.

note: 2875 sets caged birds crying for their kin and warns the captors that they will be parted from theirs; Naladiyar 122 says those who cage partridges and quails will go as slaves to strangers in irons.
teaches: Together they show the same crime repaid in two forms, loss of kin and loss of freedom, which neither names alone.

note: 2876 says the deed clings to the soul like a thread in a lotus stalk and follows it into each body; Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds done.
teaches: One gives the thread image of how a deed follows, the other the fact that only deeds follow, so each answers what the other leaves open.

note: 2883 has the father tell the youth who wants to renounce to rule and pass on the kingdom first; Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural leaves open what counts as time, and the father fixes it as the time after the duties of a king are done.

note: 2883 tells the youth to rule first and give the kingdom to a son before renouncing; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair will come.
teaches: One praises renouncing at the earliest, the other puts duty before the vow, so they mark two views of when the right time begins.

note: 2885 says kin were strangers in past births and will be strangers in births to come; Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go wordlessly, leaving the body like a bird its nesting tree.
teaches: The quatrain holds within one life and the verse extends the same estrangement across births, which turns a sad fact into a ground for cutting the bond.

note: 2887 shows a clinging that holds like the monitor's grip broken by a single word; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go.
teaches: The Kural names the means as a right object of clinging and the verse names a single word, so the means can be a sentence from a teacher.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world can be sweeter than sleep in the beloved's soft arms; Civakan, having tasted a nectar-like bliss, no longer wants the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
teaches: The lover ranks the beloved's arms above heaven, while the epic's hero, having tasted a higher bliss, finds women's embrace unwanted, so the two verses make opposite rankings of the same two goods.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not attend and judge perishes by himself; Saccandan, who gave up rule for pleasure, perishes, but by a minister's treachery, and is mourned as just.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single cause: neglect opens the door and another's crime walks through, so the ruin is self-made in the Kural's sense yet not self-inflicted.

note: 2904 calls the handsome body hollow and moves at once to choose an heir; Naladiyar 42 asks the viewer to look at a body whose skin hides its openings as a bag turned inside out.
teaches: The quatrain teaches the contemplation and the verse shows it driving an abdication.

note: 2906 tells the heir to guard the earth with the sceptre unbent and calls the guarding of dharma a king's highest joy; Kural 546 says the unbent sceptre, not the spear, wins victory.
teaches: The Kural says the straight sceptre wins, and the epic gives the heir a motive beyond winning, that it is the best joy a king can have.

note: 2907 says a king who takes revenue in measure keeps the treasure flowing; Kural 552 says a sceptred king's asking is like a robber's demand at spear-point.
teaches: The Kural condemns heavy taking as robbery, and the epic gives a prudent reason for lightness: the field that is grazed bare yields nothing.

note: 2910 says learned kings put away anger with mercy and keep what they desire hidden; Kural 590 says a king who honours a spy openly lets out his own secret.
teaches: The Kural treats concealment as a rule of spycraft, and the epic treats it as a trained temper in which anger is put away and wishes are kept back.

note: 2911 forbids a king even one false syllable for fear of losing fame; Kural 292 allows falsehood to stand as truth if it yields good free of fault.
teaches: One text bars all falsehood from the king, the other lets a blameless good justify it.

note: 2923 has the women wither like garlands on a burning vine when they read the king's intent; Naladiyar 392 has women without their companions hear the rain's thunder as a funeral drum.
teaches: The Naladiyar's grief comes after the absence, while the epic's grief comes before it, from the husband's choice.

note: 2927 makes food to the hungry a well in heaven and guarding life a title to earth and sky; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic gives the reward of heaven for giving, while the Kural says giving is right even with no reward, so the two differ on whether the gift needs a world to come.

note: 2929 says the beggar stands begging because he never gave; Naladiyar 107 says those who stand begging at great gates are living out their former deeds without saying which.
teaches: The epic names the former deed behind the begging, a life of not giving, where the quatrain leaves the cause as deeds in general.

note: 2938 strips the body of its sandal and flower to fat, blood, pus and soiled skin; Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which part is the woman.
teaches: Both teach desire away by breaking the body into its parts, and the epic does it to the very women who are the audience.

note: 2941's speaker, who ate rich ghee-scented food, fears the begging that renunciation brings; Naladiyar 1 says those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife may end up begging for gruel, so wealth is no support.
teaches: The quatrain uses the fall to beggary as the argument for renouncing, while the epic's speaker uses the same fall as the reason to fear renouncing.

note: 2960 asks whether renouncing wives can be worthy, while Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The Naladiyar's praise of the best renouncers leaves out the people left behind, whom the wives put forward as the cost.

note: 2962 asks whether a husband may give up the wife he took, while Naladiyar 56 says a husband cannot easily put away a wife even if she lacks good qualities.
teaches: The wife's plea is that the bond cannot be cast off, which the Naladiyar says too but only to praise those who avoid marriage.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and enemies take their wives; here the usurper mounts the elephant to proclaim himself and takes Fortune.
teaches: The quatrain names only the fallen king, but the epic shows the other half of the turn: the enemy who rises on the same elephant, a figure the poem's logic marks for the next fall.

note: 2977 compares the vanished smoke of incense and garlands to the fame of misers who gave nothing; Naladiyar 9 says the miser who guards his wealth is already counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Together they show the miser losing twice, his goods in the Naladiyar and his name in the epic, so hoarding gets a fate in memory as well as in wealth.

note: Kural 333 tells the possessor of wealth to do at once what stays because wealth does not; 2983 adds that Fortune stays with the one who is not attached and never clings to the one who is.
teaches: The Kural treats wealth's going as a fact to act on, while the epic makes clinging the cause of its going, so a reader sees what each assumes about why wealth leaves.

note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; 2988 calls the wives to cross old deeds and reach bliss at the top of the world above.
teaches: The Kural names the pride to be cut and the height, the epic names the deeds to be crossed and the place, so each gives what the other leaves open.

note: Kural 221 says giving to the destitute is true giving and the rest a loan with return; 2995 has the king give to those who ask in great want on the eve of leaving.
teaches: The king giving just before he leaves the world where any return could come is the case the couplet's test points to, so the epic shows the rule in its purest form.

note: Kural 342 says renounce while there is something to renounce, and many things come after; 3016 has the Jina tell a king, who has the most to give up, that renunciation is the excellent course.
teaches: The Kural counsels renunciation in general and never says who it is hardest for, and the verse sets it before a crowned king as the hardest case.

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births and others cannot; 3019 says those who do not reach the lord are kicked by their deeds into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread on a shuttle.
teaches: The Kural states the crossing and the failure to cross but gives no cause or picture for the failure, and the verse supplies deeds that beat the swimmer down and a turning that never ends.

note: 3022 has the king bow to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees; Kural 3 praises those who reach the feet of the one who walked on the flower.
teaches: Both place the object of worship on the lotus, the Kural without a name and the epic with a figure the king can bow to, so the stock image is shown being used as a scene.

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a dead sense; 3022 has the king bow with his gem crown, ear-rings and bands shining on the ground.
teaches: The Kural gives the cost of a head that does not bow, and the epic shows the most ornamented head in the book putting its crown to use by bowing.

note: Kural 8 says other seas are hard to swim except for those who reach the feet of the one called அறவாழி; 3023 uses அறவாழி for the wheel of dharma and also calls him a sea of virtues.
teaches: The Kural's single word அறவாழி can be a sea or a wheel, and the epic shows the lord named as both in one verse.

note: 3027 has the king take off jewels and garlands because the world is a drop of milk; Kural 345 says that for those cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The epic stages the stripping as a royal act step by step, while the Kural makes the body itself the last thing to be let go.

note: Kural 37 bids the reader look at palanquin-bearer and rider instead of being told what virtue is; 303 offers the queen alone among skulls as sight for those who know sin only by report.
teaches: Both turn visible fortune into evidence for unseen merit, but the epic applies it to one life reversed from palace to burning ground, and the proof falls on a sufferer the poet does not blame.

note: 3030 has Civakan pluck his hair like a lion shedding its mane; Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, wealth and strength at once because none lasts.
teaches: The epic does what the quatrain counsels with the same word for leaving, but shows a king with all of them to give up.

note: 3039 has the ascetics shed the milk of kindness on every life; Kural 30 names the virtuous, clothed in cool kindness to every being, as the true brahmins.
teaches: Both define the ascetic by his kindness to all lives, not by any robe or rite.

note: Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives sin out like a lamp but that sin returns when the oil of merit runs out; 3064 has the eight karmas cut to pieces by one firm mind.
teaches: The quatrain's lamp-and-oil picture makes the effect of austerity last as long as its merit; the epic claims a final cutting, so the two differ on whether it can return.

note: Kural 267 says austerity burns pain as fire burns gold so that it shines; 3070 has the sun's own fire ring burn on Civakan for four months while he stands on the elephant of knowledge.
teaches: The couplet gives the gold-and-fire image of austerity in general; the verse sets it in a particular season of heat and ties the shining to knowledge, not to appearance.

note: Kural 261 defines austerity as bearing the pain that comes and causing none to living beings; 3072 has Civakan live four months in the cold open field and guard sweet life.
teaches: The couplet joins the endurance and the harmlessness in one definition, and the verse shows them in one season, if the 'guarded life' is the lives of creatures.

note: Kural 360 names three roots of pain, desire, anger and confusion; 3080 names four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors who must be slain.
teaches: The Jain list of four widens the Kural's three, showing that one counts the roots of pain differently depending on the school.

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 3091 prays 'let our birth end' to the Lord who destroyed Desire and Death.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry across, and the verse names who the Lord has beaten (Desire and Death) and why they should be prayed to.

note: Kural 9 praises the one of eight qualities; 3092 praises the one who has cut four deeds together and knows the three times.
teaches: One text counts a Lord by eight qualities and the other by four deeds cut, so the reader sees two different measures of the same worshipped figure.

note: 3101 has the Lord's feet cut through the hard-gathered karma like a blade; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The verse gives the means by which the deeds are removed and the Kural gives the assurance that they will not cling.

note: 3105 pictures desire as grass that lures souls into the four-state pen and says reaching the pure one's feet lets one go to release; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
teaches: The verse supplies the trap that the Kural's sea leaves unnamed, and the Kural supplies the crossing the verse only names as going.

note: 3107 says that guarding all lives as one's own brings a high birth; Kural 327 says not to kill even if one's own life is the price.
teaches: The verse makes non-injury pay in a later birth, and the Kural cuts the rule loose from payment even at the price of one's life.

note: 3108 has the one who harms for food thrown by two deeds into burning flame; Kural 320 says pains rest on those who caused pain.
teaches: The verse names the form the returning pain takes, a hell of fire, which the Kural's general law does not.

note: Kural 10: only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births. Vijayai asks that the Jina's dharma and her newborn son be her raft across a sea of sorrow.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's sea and crossing but moves the sea from rebirth to present grief and doubles the raft, placing a mother's hope in a child beside the lord's dharma.

note: 3116 has the pyre burn the Lord's jewel-bright body with gods circling and rejoicing; Naladiyar 24 has the drums beat three times and the corpse be covered and the fire taken up.
teaches: The same flame ends an ordinary corpse in grief and a Lord's body in festival, so the pyre's meaning depends on who is burning.

note: 3118 has the king live with a woman who has no old age or death; Naladiyar 14 has the once-desired woman bent over a staff and a torment.
teaches: One text shows what the loved woman will become, and the other the woman who never becomes it.

note: 3120 has the women see the dirt on their adorned bodies and think of ending woman-birth; Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone and asks which part she is.
teaches: The quatrain gives the analysis of the body's parts and the verse shows women applying a like seeing to themselves.

note: 3121 sends the women who gave up desire to heaven as Indras; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
teaches: The verse ends in the gods' world and the Kural says release lies above it, so the same renunciation is given two different ends.

note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off dark, but only while the good deeds last.
teaches: The story shows the ascetics' fast washing deeds away, and the quatrain adds that the lamp burns only while its oil of good deeds holds.

note: 3134 has the penance end in birth as gods; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of I and mine goes to a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic's ascetics end among the gods, but the couplet puts above the gods a world reached only by cutting off the self, so heaven is not the last goal.

note: 3145 ends on the Lord's feet as the way over the sea of deeds; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births.
teaches: Both place the Lord's feet beyond a sea, but the Cintamani names the water as deeds and the Kural as births, so the epic fixes on karma as the thing to be crossed.

note: The Naladiyar sets the fool who sighs and breaks when deeds ripen against the wise who say 'it is old desert' and go free; Vijayai says exactly that her deeds are to blame, yet sobs (விம்மா) as she says it.
teaches: The quatrain makes knowing one's karma the cure for grief, but the queen shows that naming one's own deeds as the cause can be itself a form of grieving.

note: Kural 17 states that the sea itself depends on the cloud returning what it took; verses 32 to 38 narrate that loop, from clouds grazing the sea to the flood reaching the sea again.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's abstract dependence becomes a full itinerary, and the epic's long description gains its shape: it is a circuit of giving back, not a string of pictures.

note: In the Kural the woman's automatic blessing at her lover's sneeze is withdrawn the next moment in jealousy; in the epic the blessing at the infant's sneeze comes from a mother who cannot show herself, and sticks as his name.
teaches: The everyday sneeze-blessing, which the Kural shows can be taken back, here becomes the one bond between the hidden mother and her child that cannot be undone.

note: The Kural pictures the life leaving the body as a bird flying from a nest left empty; the epic pictures ascetics leaving the body as an exchange for an imperishable golden one, and uses it for the merchant leaving his dead son for a living child.
teaches: Leaving the body is loss in the Kural's figure and gain in the epic's, and the difference is the penance done beforehand.

note: Naladiyar 51 uses lamp and darkness to state that sin cannot stand before austerity and returns when good deeds are spent; 343 makes the departure of darkness at sunrise a figure for evil deeds' suffering leaving when old merit comes forward, on the road to a hermitage.
teaches: The quatrain's doctrine becomes the epic's narrative weather: the dawn that ends Vijayai's flight is the merit-and-darkness image itself, placed just before she enters the very austerity the quatrain says sin cannot face.

note: Kural 378 says drily that the destitute would renounce if only fate let what they must suffer pass them by; 347 has a queen stripped of everything reach the ascetics' grove because a former-birth deed made her suffer.
teaches: The epic takes up the case the couplet treats as hypothetical: the destitute queen does renounce, and the following verses show the couplet's point surviving the renunciation, since her fated grief for her son goes on inside the hermitage.

note: Kural 341 holds that from whatever one has let go one suffers no pain; Vijayai lets go her ornaments one by one (349 to 353) but ends with a vow for her son, whom she does not let go and for whom she grieves in 355 and 359.
teaches: The piecemeal renunciation the couplet describes is acted out jewel by jewel, and the pain the couplet promises to remove returns exactly at the one tie the queen keeps, which shows the couplet's claim from its other side.

note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; the Cintamani likens the river's flood to the hand of a generous man carrying wealth to those who have nothing.
teaches: The tradition's image ran both ways, wealth explained by water and water by giving, and the epic adds movement and direction toward the needy, where the Kural's tank waits to be drawn from.

note: Kural 6 says that those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses live long; Cintamani 375 sets those who reach the path that wears away hard deeds in a sea of bliss and those burnt by the five-mouthed snake of the senses in a sea of pain.
teaches: Where the couplet promises long life on the path of one who quenched the senses, the Jain teacher makes the reward the wearing away of karma and the penalty a sea of suffering, turning a blessing of the householder into a choice between release and pain.

note: Kural 348 says that those who have wholly renounced have reached the head and all others are caught in the net; Cintamani 376 names the net as Death's and austerity (நோற்று) as the way out of it.
teaches: The couplet divides men into renouncers and the netted, while the epic shows the netted as knowing their state, so renunciation is not only clear seeing but a doing that knowledge alone does not bring.

note: Naladiyar 331 shows people revelling in the world's net while Death waits to seize them, like a turtle sporting in the pot over the fire; Cintamani 376 makes Death the one who laid the net and the revellers people who know it is there.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the epic's step is to take away the excuse of ignorance: the turtle does not know its state, but the teacher's 'we' know Death's net and still turn to pleasure, so folly becomes a failure of will.

note: Kural 335 bids good deeds be rushed before the hiccup stops the tongue; Cintamani 377 asks whether anything intended can be done when the fire takes the body, after the teaching that ends birth has been rarely won.
teaches: The couplet's urgency rests on how near death may be; the epic adds that the means of release is already in hand and wasted by pampering the senses, so delay is the squandering of a rare gain and not only a race with death.

note: Kural 49 calls the householder's life itself what is named virtue; in Cintamani 382 the teacher, once Civakan has taken the Jain refuge, teaches him the householder's dharma alongside the errors of false paths.
teaches: The Jain teacher does not set renunciation against the household here but gives the new convert the householder's dharma as his first instruction, so the epic holds the Kural's household virtue as a stage inside the path to release rather than its rival.

note: The couplet bids one forget anger at anyone at all; the teacher asks Civakan to hold his anger against one man for one year only.
teaches: Against the couplet's unlimited forgetting of anger, the epic's ascetic sets a term to restraint, so a teacher who renounced anger for himself still leaves a prince's just anger intact for its time.

note: The couplet defines penance as bearing the pain that comes; the ascetic's penance gives way under the hunger-fire and he goes to the city to eat.
teaches: The epic marks a limit to the couplet's definition: there are pains, sent by past deeds, that a penitent cannot bear, and his penance has to be suspended and later resumed.

note: The Kural uses the spot on the moon to say a fault in the well-born is seen from far; the Cintamani uses it for a fault in a moon-full work and asks readers to wash it, not to see it.
teaches: The Kural's moon makes height expose a fault, but the Cintamani turns the same image into a reader's duty of charity, so the exposure the Kural warns of becomes something the audience may decline.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who relieve hunger above that of those who endure it; the ascetic's endurance fails and a child's feeding saves him.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's ranking as one scene: the ascetic's strength to bear hunger breaks, and the boy's strength to relieve it restores him and gives Civakan his teacher.

note: The couplet says the fruit of hospitality is as great as the guest's worth; the merchant's house that fed a hungry stranger gained a Vidyadhara king as the teacher of its son.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's measure working through time: the guest's worth was hidden when he came hungry to the door, and the fruit appeared only as the education of the boy who fed him.

note: The couplet asks what one gains by leaving a household life lived in dharma; the epic holds that once a man resolves to leave home for penance, the wise speak of no other dharma.
teaches: The two meet on a condition the couplet leaves out: the Kural weighs the householder's path before the choice, while the epic speaks of one who has already resolved, for whom the household dharma is no longer an option.

note: The Kural calls those free of craving the freed (அற்றவர்); the epic has Accanandi cut desire's root and then perform austerities before he leaves the body.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse separates what the Kural joins: being free of craving comes first, but release from the body comes only after austerity at the Jina's feet.

note: Both use the rain bubble (மாரி மொக்குளின், படுமழை மொக்குளின்): the Naladiyar for the body that keeps forming and bursting, the epic for the moment the released teacher's form ends.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the bubble used for opposite ends: in the quatrain its bursting is why the wise resolve to end their wandering, and in the epic the bursting is that resolve completed, the last end of a body that will not form again.

note: The Kural says the cows' yield fails when the guardian does not guard; the epic shows the king's herd driven off while the king sits fanned on his throne, and 437-438 his army breaks.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's cows into the actual herd of the realm: the raid becomes the first public proof that the usurper cannot guard, and clears the place for Civakan, who will.

note: The hunters restate the couplet's crocodile, strong in deep water, and apply it to themselves in their forest.
teaches: The couplet's rule of ground is here voiced by the losing side, so the pair shows the rule cannot by itself predict a fight and must be weighed against the enemy's strength.

note: Kural 1033 says the ploughman alone lives on his own, while all others bow (தொழுது) to eat; in the Cintamani the sower himself bows (தொழுது) to the seed as he sows.
teaches: The ploughman whom the Kural sets above all bowing still bows, to the crop on which his independence rests, so his self-sufficiency is itself a dependence.

note: Kural 265 says penance (செய்தவம்) is undertaken because what one wants is got as one wants it; the city women say Civakan's mother must have done penance (செய்தவம் உடையள்) and ask on which mountain to do it so that they too may attain.
teaches: The couplet's frank promise that penance gets what one wants is taken literally by lovesick townswomen, who plan austerity on a mountain to win a man, showing how the Kural's motive can be bent toward the very desire the next couplet condemns.

note: In Kural 1214 the woman finds pleasure in dreams because they bring the man who gives no grace when she is awake (நல்காரை); the women of 466 ask Civakan to grace them (அருளி) by coming in a dream tomorrow.
teaches: The Kural's dream comforts a woman for a lover who once was hers and now withholds himself, but the Cintamani's crowd asks the dream for a man they have only seen pass, so the convention turns from consolation for loss into the only union a stranger can hope for.

note: The Naladiyar says that when a banyan is eaten hollow its aerial roots hold it up, as a son covers a weakened father; Nandagon's banyan seed is the hope that a son of the fallen king lives.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the herdsman's seed image takes on the son's work of propping a fallen house, which the epic will make a war for a kingdom rather than a household's shame.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan holds that birth decides which wife a man may take first.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's levelling of birth stopping at the threshold of marriage in the epic, where rank of birth remains a rule of conduct even for a hero honoured for his deeds.

note: The couplet says the pleasure of love is a sea but its pain, when it strikes, is greater; 491 gives the bridegroom the sea of pleasure that cannot be contained, and no pain.
teaches: The epic uses the couplet's measure of pleasure as a sea but leaves out the greater sea of pain that the woman in the Kural speaks from, because the wedding has no separation in it.

note: 496 holds that a resolute man's effort can bring a flood of wealth in a day and that nothing fails to yield to it; Kural 620 holds that tireless effort sees even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts the Kural's boldest claim for effort in the mouth of a man whose voyage ends in shipwreck, so the claim is made to depend on the life-span and deeds he later invokes.

note: 497 restates Kural 759 (make wealth; no steel is sharper against foes) and joins to it the claims of 760 and 751 as a merchant's motto, a few verses before the sea swallows the wealth.
teaches: Put in the mouth of a man about to lose everything at sea, the Kural's praise of wealth as the sharpest steel is shown to say nothing about wealth's own exposure to loss.

note: 498 gives the merchant's reason for the voyage: men born into a weakening lineage must hold it up. Kural 1026 defines good manliness as making oneself able to rule the house one was born into.
teaches: The Kural's manliness of the house is the motive that sends a merchant onto the sea, and the verse adds a division the couplet lacks: restoring the line is the men's part, guarding against shame the women's.

note: Both prize what brackish ground or brine produces: the Naladiyar's salt above rice from good fields, the Cintamani's coral, conch and pearl though they taste of the sea.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues that a person's low origin does not lower his learning, and the Cintamani applies the same reasoning to a poem's faulty diction, so the brine image carries one argument about worth and origin from persons to texts.

note: 509 opens as Kural 621 opens and turns the couplet's laughter into a steel that cuts trouble, spoken by a captain to his crew in a storm that drowns them all but him.
teaches: The couplet's laugh in trouble becomes a leader's duty to others, and the scene shows its limit: composure saves the one who keeps it but cannot save the ship.

note: 513 shows the wealth Sitattan guarded and gathered (ஓம்பிப் படைத்த பொருள்) swallowed by the sea while he stands unhurried; Naladiyar 93 holds that wealth, however tightly held, leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: Read with the quatrain, the wreck becomes the ending of a merit that had held the wealth, and the merchant's calm becomes the right response to a loss that no grip could prevent.

note: Kural 292 lets a falsehood stand as truth when it yields good free of fault; Dharan's wreck and his 'no deceit' promise are falsehoods serving his king's purpose of bringing a guardian for the princess.
teaches: The pair tests the couplet's limit: the epic's lie does produce good, but at the cost of a man's real grief for friends he believed drowned, so whether its good is 'free of fault' becomes the question.

note: Kural 978 opposes greatness that bows to smallness that admires itself; the paddy simile sets the base man's erect wealth and the learned man's bow in one stalk at two ages.
teaches: The pair shows that the bow and the raised head can be stages of one thing rather than two kinds of people: what stands erect is empty, and the same stalk bows once it is full.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however guarded and what is one's portion will not leave; the king, told his daughter's portion lies in Rajamapuram, neither gives her to the gift-bearing kings nor tells them so, but keeps them waiting with his intent hidden.
teaches: The pair shows that knowing one's portion in advance does not end action: the king turns the couplet's resignation into policy, managing powerful suitors while waiting for fate to arrive.

note: The Kural says one remembers for seven births the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow; the Vidyadhara king says his people and the merchant's have held friendship for seven generations, bound by fate.
teaches: Side by side, the seven-fold span of friendship rests on two different grounds: in the couplet on gratitude for a single act of rescue, in the epic on an inherited tie that fate fixes and no deed has to earn.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on a beloved's arms; the Vidyadhara king says even the endless pleasures of the Jain land of enjoyment are misery alone, and sleep in a lover's lap is the gods' own state.
teaches: The couplet leaves its comparison with heaven as a question, and the epic answers it outright, turning a lover's boast into a father's argument for giving his daughter in marriage.

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of every contrivance; the king says that when the destined time comes no one can stop it, and so refuses every royal suitor.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the king's appeal to fate is not a surrender but a policy: he uses fate's strength as the reason to refuse every suitor and leave the choice to a contest, where the Kural sees fate only as defeating a plan.

note: The Naladiyar likens a miser's hoard, enjoyed by a stranger, to a lovely daughter of the house who goes to an outsider in due season; the king says daughters are like the conch's pearls, which profit others and never the conch.
teaches: The same commonplace, that a daughter is raised to go to another, serves the quatrain as an image of loss through folly and serves the epic as a father's consolation, so the pair shows the saying could carry blame or comfort.

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; the epic has a king act on an astrologer's word, which proves true.
teaches: Two Jain-tradition texts judge the astrologer oppositely: the quatrain dismisses his lore beside the duty death makes urgent, while the epic makes his reading the hinge of its plot. The tension holds only if the quatrain is read as denying astrology's truth, not just its worth.

note: The Naladiyar says friends who share joys but not sorrows do nothing for each other; Dharan inflicts sorrow on his king's friend to give him joy.
teaches: The quatrain's test assumes sorrow comes from outside and asks who will share it, while the epic's friend authors the sorrow himself and stands apart from it, a case the rule of sharing does not cover.

note: Kural 55 makes the chaste wife command the rain; the benediction of 604 asks for rain and for women's unswerving chastity side by side as goods of the realm.
teaches: The pair shows two ways of joining chastity and rain: the couplet gives one wife's karpu power over the sky, while the city's blessing wishes for both as gifts and gives women's chastity no power at all.

note: Kural 263 asks whether others, wanting to provide for renouncers, have forgotten their own penance; the proclamation in 605 bids people give to ascetics and also strive at hard penance themselves.
teaches: The epic's decree answers the couplet's chiding question by refusing the division of labour it criticises: giving to ascetics and doing penance are both laid on every listener.

note: The attendants call the princess's eyes not carp but blue lilies sheltering in the moon and line them with kohl; the Naladiyar's renunciant scorns those who call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The comparisons the Jain quatrain names as the talk of the blind are exactly the ones a Jain epic's attendants weigh and choose between, so the pair shows the same tradition keeping the lover's rhetoric in its epic and rejecting it in its ascetic verse.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the Cintamani's narrator says those who saw the princess would not look upon the world of release.
teaches: Both weigh a woman's beauty against a world beyond this one, but the Jain epic raises the Kural's god's heaven to release from births and gives the preference to dazzled onlookers rather than a lover, which makes it a danger to be overcome rather than a joy to be asked about.

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death and knows it now in a woman's eyes; the onlookers tell the suitors that her girdle and breasts are Death and bid them flee, 'we have told you'.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the onlookers' warning puts the suitors in the state the Kural's man has left behind, knowing Death only by report, and shows that being told does not save anyone, since the crowd stays.

note: The couplet says tavam is striven for because it gets whatever one wants as one wants it; the kings vow that if they lose her they will fight, or else do great penance.
teaches: The kings take penance on the couplet's own motive, as a way to the thing desired, and so show the weakness the couplet's next verse attacks: penance offered as the consolation of a failed suitor stays bound to the desire it should end.

note: The Kural's lover cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Cintamani's kings ask how she is not Rambha and then notice that her eyes blink (இமைக்குங்கண் இவையோ).
teaches: The pair shows the lover's doubt can be settled by a sign: where the couplet leaves the heart reeling among three guesses, the epic supplies the blink that separates a mortal from the unblinking gods and ends the doubt.

note: The Kural likens the cloth over a woman's breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant; Vinapati jests that the gods hid her breasts altogether because her eyes already killed.
teaches: The two take opposite sides of one premise, that a woman's breasts are a danger to be covered, and the pedi's jest pushes it to the end by having the gods remove what the cloth only veils, with the eyes left as the whole of the threat.

note: The Kural calls those lands whose riches need no seeking; the Cintamani's pools are strewn with gold beads from broken girdles that no one troubles to gather.
teaches: Set beside the reapers and threshers of 55 to 59, the gold no one picks up shows the epic taking unsought wealth to mean surplus beyond need after labour, not riches without work.

note: Kural 1115 jokes that her waist will snap if she wears anicham with its stems; the spectators of 679 say the dancer avoids flowers lest her small waist break, and lament that sandal and pearls were hung on her.
teaches: The couplet's lover's joke is turned into a crowd's mock indignation at those who dressed the girl, so the hyperbole of the slender waist becomes a charge against the adorner.

note: Kural 1081: the man seeing her first cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the crowd at the dance names her peacock, swan, golden creeper, lotus goddess or daughter of the gods.
teaches: The couplet's one man's bewilderment becomes a whole audience's at a staged dance, so the doubt about her nature is produced by art and costume, not by a chance meeting.

note: Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is; the crowd of 680 calls the sandalled, garlanded dancer a goddess or a daughter of the immortals.
teaches: The epic stages exactly the admiration the Naladiyar scorns and gives it to the whole city without rebuke, so the two works disagree on whether adorned beauty is a fit object of wonder.

note: Kural 1100: once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are useless; Anangamaalai sends her love to Civakan by a 'letter' of her eyes carried by her smile, in the middle of a public dance.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's wordless eye-language but makes it one-sided and public, a message sent across a crowd, and shows its cost when the king's enmity follows from it.

note: Kural 701 makes one who knows a mind before it speaks an ornament to the world; Kattiyankaran, once the minister, reads from the dancer's signs that she loves Civakan and turns the knowledge into grudge and seizure.
teaches: The pair shows that reading an unspoken mind is praised in the Kural for a use the couplet assumes, and in a jealous ruler the same skill feeds only his grudge and his violence.

note: Kural 226 says that ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; the usurper's soldiers recall that Civakan fed them in a thousand pots when they were faint, and the telling makes the king fear him.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's store paying out in loyalty: feeding hungry men lays up for Civakan the hearts of the usurper's own army, which is exactly why the giving is felt as a threat.

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for because whatever is wanted comes as it is wanted; the city's women say the princess must have done penance (நோற்றனள்) to enjoy Civakan's beauty.
teaches: The women apply the couplet's promise to a marriage, so the pair shows penance taken in common talk as the merit behind erotic good fortune, the very use the Kural's next verse warns against.

note: The Kural's lover says the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; the epic's princess has a sea of desire that overruns the fence of shame round her nirai.
teaches: Shame is a raft for the Kural's man and a fence round a prison for the epic's woman, so the same flood threatens a man's means of crossing but a woman's enclosure.

note: The Kural's woman says desire's axe breaks the door of nirai bolted with shame; the princess says the youth has opened the door of her hard nirai and entered her heart's guarded chamber.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the Kural's door of nirai but changes the breaker from desire to the man and the outcome from lament to a vow of marriage, so the breach of self-containment can be the start of a lawful bond.

note: In both the sulking woman's charge turns on eyes: in the Kural all women feast on the man with theirs, in the Cintamani the women say his loves are in his eyes, and refuse him.
teaches: The Kural keeps the eye-charge inside the couple's quarrel, while the epic lets the same charge end in snapped girdles and spilled gold, so the sulk becomes a sign of the city's wealth rather than a turn in a love.

note: The Kural says tapas is striven for here because one gets what one wants as one wants it; the bride's falling garland is read as a call to all the world to do tapas.
teaches: The Cintamani takes the Kural's frankly worldly motive for tapas and fixes it on a bridal union, showing how far that motive reaches in a work whose hero will at last renounce such joys.

note: The Kural asks what a sword is to those without courage and what learning is to those who fear the assembly; Padumukan mocks kings who lost at the art and turn to the sword.
teaches: The Kural tests the sword and learning separately, each by its own courage, but Padumukan adds that one who has failed the test of art cannot seek the same prize by the sword, so the second arena only confirms the first defeat.

note: The Kural counts dividing others among a minister's skills; Padumukan exposes the minister-turned-king's plan to divide the kings so they perish fighting each other.
teaches: The craft of division that the Kural lists without moral comment as a minister's skill is shown here in the hands of a minister who betrayed his king, and the epic names its result as a world made cruel.

note: The Kural defines a land as where unfailing yield, the worthy (தக்கார்) and the undiminished wealthy gather; the Cintamani's closing verse on Hemangadam makes it a place for those who do penance and those who make wealth, after ten verses of harvest.
teaches: The epic fills the couplet's three-part definition with a whole country, and reads its worthy ones as those who do penance, so the Kural's land is given room for renunciants beside the wealthy.

note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses capital for the sake of gain; the kings tell Civakan, as a merchant's son, that a true trader would save his capital and flee, leaving the girl.
teaches: The couplet's prudence is turned into a class insult, and the battle that follows shows that the rule cannot say what counts as capital: for the kings it is life and goods, for Civakan it is his name and the bride.

note: Both picture the bought embrace through a body: the Kural's woman of wealth embraces a stranger's corpse (பிணந்தழீஇ); the epic's net-woman embraces the flesh of wealth (தசை தழீஇ) and throws the body away.
teaches: Set beside the epic's hunter who keeps the meat of wealth and drops the carcass, the couplet's corpse reads naturally as the client handled by the woman, so the disgust in Kural 913 belongs to the trade itself rather than only to the man.

note: Kural 776 counts as wasted the days without a noble wound; 782 has the companions offer their chests to the tusk so the scar may lie beautiful.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps a sober ledger of wounded days, the epic turns the wound into ornament, so the same ethic moves from a reckoning of duty to an aesthetic of the body.

note: Kural 773 calls help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; 783 has the companions cripple a chariot and then bid its charioteer yoke fresh horses.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's ஊராண்மை into a battlefield move: the generosity is not mercy that ends the fight but an invitation to go on fighting on equal terms.

note: Naladiyar 3 has kings who rode under the umbrella fall when their deeds give out; 797 shows the kings' white umbrellas overturned by Civakan's arrows.
teaches: The quatrain names only spent deeds as the cause of a king's fall, while the epic shows the immediate cause, an archer and the kings' own desire, and in 799 sorts the fallen by their minds, so karma and the battle are both given as cause.

note: Kural 202 says evil is to be feared more than fire because evil yields evil; in 799 burning arrows kill the mean-minded kings and warn them off evil even in their next body.
teaches: The epic makes the fire itself the preacher: the burning arrow that kills is only the lesser fire, and its warning points to the evil that will follow the dead into the next birth.

note: The Kural says a jackal can kill a war elephant when its feet sink in mud, so ground decides; the epic says a single lion kills a herd of elephants, so the nature of the fighter decides.
teaches: Both answer how the few beat the many, but the couplet credits the place of battle and the epic the strength of the one who fights, two incompatible accounts of the same reversal if each is taken as the cause.

note: The Kural says it is not the spear but the ruler's unbent sceptre that gives victory; the epic says victory goes to the virtuous mind, and a betel leaf thrown by such a man becomes a spear.
teaches: The couplet ties victory to the justice of a king's rule, while the epic moves it into each fighter's heart and applies it to a war over a woman, where no sceptre is in question.

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; the epic says the Tirthan's feet remove all the sins done, and has Civakan worship there after killing in battle.
teaches: The couplet's claim covers both good and bad deeds and asks only praise, while the epic narrows it to sins and stages it as a rite after a specific act of killing, showing how a general promise was put to work as expiation.

note: Kural 216 likens wealth in a man of goodwill to a fruit tree ripening in the town's midst; 828 likens the crowd at the hero's house to birds on a tree heavy with fruit.
teaches: The couplet's tree is a figure for wealth that others may share, and the epic shows who actually comes to such a tree: a crowd that gives as well as takes, as 829 and 831 go on to say.

note: Kural 265 says tavam is striven for because what is wanted comes as wanted; in 829 the crowd sees the hero's wedding wealth as the fruit of his tavam and wishes it would come to them.
teaches: The onlookers accept the couplet's premise that tavam yields what one wants, yet only wish for its fruit instead of doing it, which is the very shortcut the couplet rules out.

note: Kural 1103 has the lover ask whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; 836 says even Indra, lord of the gods, could not have had this wedding.
teaches: Both set a human union above a god's world, but the Kural's lover measures it by private sweetness while the epic narrator measures it by public splendour, so the same boast ranks feeling in one and rank and wealth in the other.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay however guarded and what is one's own will not leave though thrown away; 848 says what is to come comes and what is to go goes, as the sea and river receive unasked.
teaches: The Kural states the rule of fate about possessions, and the letter applies it to a dispossessed heir in the same breath as an offer of arms, showing fate being cited to back an effort rather than to forbid one.

note: Naladiyar 103 says each one's enjoyments are measured by their own course, as no one rounded the vilam fruit; 848 says the sea need not fetch water nor the river beg rain.
teaches: Both argue from unmade nature, but the quatrain's fruit shows a lot fixed in advance while the letter's sea and river show a lot that flows in, so the same proof from nature can counsel content or confidence.
