note: The women treat the powder contest as a wager (வெல்வது சூது); the Kural says not to want gambling even when one can win, since the winnings are the hook the fish swallows.
teaches: The epic shows a wager whose real stake is not wealth but pride, and whose cost falls in a vow of seclusion on the loser, so the Kural's warning about winnings is widened to what a wager does to the one who loses face.

note: The maid cites the praise of the whole city, the merchant included, against Civakan's verdict; the Kural says understanding is seeing the true substance whoever's mouth one hears a thing from.
teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's rule tested where it is hardest, against unanimous acclaim, and shows that the epic does not let the lone judge rest on his authority either but makes him prove the truth by a test both sides accept.

note: The maid argues that moisture makes the bad good and drying makes the good bad; the Kural bids one examine qualities and faults, see which prevail, and take that.
teaches: The maid's argument exposes what the couplet assumes, that qualities hold still to be weighed; if condition changes them, weighing by inspection cannot settle a dispute, which is why the epic turns to the bees.

note: Civakan proves the powder by what the bees do with it; the Kural says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness.
teaches: Both put the proof in what a thing does rather than in what is said of it, but the epic adds that a touchstone convinces only when both parties accepted it beforehand, as the maid did in 890 and 891.

note: Shamed by the verdict, Suramanjari withdraws under a vow; the Kural says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic offers a third path to the couplet's choice between life and honour: a withdrawal from the world that keeps the wound open and names the act that will restore her honour.

note: The Kural says a king with no one to rebuke him perishes though he has no enemy; Saccandan had counsel (சொல்லாறு) and would not hear it.
teaches: The Cintamani's king shows that having rebuking counsellors is not enough, since desire can make a king deaf to them, so the Kural's safeguard fails at the point of hearing rather than of supply.

note: The Kural says those who set their desire on the home do not reach the fine fruit; the Cintamani's whole frame begins with a king whose desire for his queen grew thick and cost him his throne.
teaches: Held against the Kural's warning about desire fixed on the wife, the patikam locates the whole fault in the husband's excess while calling the queen's chastity unfailing (வீடாத கற்பு), and gives the couplet's lost 'fine fruit' a political price, the kingdom itself.

note: Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain within each pleasure and do not cling; in 909 Gunamalai, after the game that cost her a friend, sees that play meant for joy became the cause of sorrow.
teaches: The quatrain's discipline of seeing pain inside pleasure appears in the epic first as a girl's tears over a garden game, an early lesson in a story that ends in renunciation.

note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; 913 pictures giving to suppliants as damming the sea called அவா, with தவாவினை at its shore.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's pair of craving and unfailing deed and makes festival giving the practical means of checking craving, where the couplet names only the cutting itself.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are so because they bear cool kindness to every living being; in 934-936 the men skilled in the four Vedas, with minds of fire, beat a dog to death over a heap of rice.
teaches: The epic stages the Kural's definition as a test the Brahmins fail, and gives the cool kindness the Kural requires to the hero instead, so the name and the conduct come apart exactly as the couplet's reasoning allows.

note: Naladiyar 322 says those not disposed to virtue cannot take it in, as a tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk rice; in 944 a dog pricks its ears, weeps and takes in the teaching.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dog as the type of the creature who cannot receive dharma; the epic answers with a dog that hears and consents, so receptivity is made a matter of the moment of hearing, not of the hearer's kind.

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities (எண்குணத்தான்) is useless; 961 vows to bow the head to no one but the one who removes the eight karmas (எண்வினை) and gives bliss, and sets aside the gods of desire.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's positive command into an exclusion and fills its unexplained 'eight' with a count of karmas destroyed, so the Kural's open epithet is given a Jain content it does not itself state.

note: Kural 24: one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground; 962 builds the whole farm, with zeal as the plough, the body as the field, vows as seed, conduct as water and the five senses as the fence.
teaches: The couplet's one image of the guarded self as seed is spelled out as a season of tillage, and its unnamed 'finest ground' gets two harvests, heaven first and release after.

note: Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak that will not live without its hair; 978 has Civakan reckon death better than life when a stranger woman's life is in danger.
teaches: The epic moves the Kural's honour-death from guarding one's own standing to rescuing another, so that honour is measured by whose danger a man will not stand by and watch.

note: Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go silently, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest-tree; 993 says Gunamalai spurns her kin's talk like those who know their births.
teaches: The epic borrows the renouncer's detachment from kin, which the Naladiyar grounds in kin's passing, to picture a girl whose turning from family is love for one man, so the same outward withdrawal is shown to have opposite causes.

note: Kural 270 says the have-nots are many because few do penance; 997 has Gunamalai ask whether, like the small folk who did no penance, she has any door to escape her longing.
teaches: The couplet's explanation of want by the lack of past tapas is taken up by a lover as an account of why the man she wants is out of reach, showing the doctrine at work in ordinary speech about desire.

note: The Kural praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; Gunamalai, with longing like the sea, considers riding it.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's praised restraint from inside, as a near thing: the heroine reaches the very thought of the madal before turning to a go-between, so the Kural's 'does not ride' names a line held under pressure, not an absence of the wish.

note: Kural 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life; Kundalakesi 10 says each day's step takes us to lay our heads at the edge of Death's sword.
teaches: The couplet makes the day itself the blade; the fragment makes the day a step toward a blade held by Death and adds the condemned man's walk, so time becomes not only the cutting but the procession to execution with no reprieve.

note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart of the body; Kundalakesi 12 asks what delight is left in shoulders praised as Mandara when vultures and dogs pluck at them.
teaches: The Naladiyar turns the contemplation of carrion on a body adorned for love, usually the woman's; the fragment turns the same contemplation on a man's heroic shoulders, so the discipline is shown to apply to desire for either sex.

note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Kundalakesi 14 asks whether a body of deeds, fed on by worms, can be called 'I' and 'mine'.
teaches: The couplet gives the reward for cutting 'I' and 'mine' but not the argument; the fragment gives the argument from the body's foulness and tenants but promises no higher world, so together they separate the case against 'mine' from the hope it is made for.

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Kundalakesi 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth, as the stain on the god's throat is still a stain.
teaches: The couplet says height makes a fault more visible; the fragment adds that height does not change its nature, and carries the rule up from the well-born to the gods.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who welcome good when it comes should grieve when it does not; Kundalakesi 18 says those who know that what is due will come neither grieve nor exult.
teaches: The couplet only rebukes grief and leaves joy at good fortune untouched; the fragment strikes out elation too, so its equanimity is stricter than the Kural's.

note: Verse 2 praises the one who cut off the three faults without naming them; Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish for pain to end.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's unnamed three faults take on a Tamil list already current, and the couplet's goal of ending the three is shown as the very mark by which a Buddhist poet recognises his lord.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kundalakesi 4 dismisses a longer list, nakedness, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair, as words, and calls tapas a subdued life.
teaches: The couplet sets aside only the hair, and tests the renouncer by the world's blame; the fragment sets aside the whole repertoire of bodily austerity and puts the test in inner restraint, so the two differ on where the renouncer's proof lies.

note: Kural 1148 says thinking gossip can put out love is like thinking ghee can put out fire; Kundalakesi 5 asks whether a fire-pit can be put out with ghee, of those who would end desire by enjoying it.
teaches: The same proverb of ghee on fire serves the lover, for whom nothing will quench love and that is its strength, and the ascetic, for whom indulgence only feeds desire and that is its danger.

note: Naladiyar 24 ends with the dying carrying the dead; Kundalakesi 9 says the foetus, child, youth and young adult have each died in us and we die daily.
teaches: The quatrain makes the mourners already dying in the moment of a funeral; the fragment moves death inside each life, as a series of deaths of one's own former selves, so the bearer is also already a corpse many times over.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who bear hunger below the strength of those who remove it; in the patikam the renunciant who begs with a bowl is the one who ends Kayachandigai's hunger-fire.
teaches: The Kural sets the one who endures hunger and the one who relieves it as two kinds of strength in rank, while the epic gives both to one person, a begging ascetic whose bowl feeds others, so its Buddhist renunciation removes the Kural's ranking rather than falling under it.

note: Kural 362: if one must desire, desire not to be born, and that comes by desiring not to desire; the patikam closes with Manimekalai, having heard the dharma, vowing that becoming be cut off (பவத் திறம் அறுக என ... நோற்றதும்).
teaches: The Kural allows one desire, for birthlessness, and reaches it by turning desire on itself; the epic makes that one desire a vow kept with austerity after hearing a teacher, so the end the Kural states as inner paradox is reached in the epic through instruction and practice.

note: The quatrain says a small act of virtue that reaches worthy hands spreads like a banyan from a tiny seed; the goddess says Lakshmi's meal to a sage will not go to waste but will cut off her births, and also that the giver herself, as a seed of dharma, could be lost on barren ground.
teaches: The epic agrees that a gift to the worthy grows, but changes its harvest from a covering shade of merit to the end of rebirth, and adds that the giver's own attachments can still waste what the gift has sown.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of enduring hunger below the strength of removing others' hunger; the goddess gives Manimekalai the first strength by mantra, and the patikam (manimekalai:0:51-68) says the bowl for feeding others comes next.
teaches: The epic follows the couplet's order of rank but removes the effort from the lower strength: enduring hunger is granted as a gift, so the renouncer is freed for the higher task the couplet values, feeding others.

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Deepathilakai calls the feet of the Lord of dharma on Samantam the ship of dharma that frees from the great sea called birth (23-25).
teaches: The Buddhist epic takes the Kural's unnamed Lord and his feet as the Buddha's footprint on a named peak and turns swimming into being carried by a ship, so the couplet's open theism becomes a pilgrimage relic served by the gods.

note: The Naladiyar's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) is filled slowly at door after door by householders' small gifts; Manimekalai's bowl, held by a renunciant, never fails and only the takers' hands tire.
teaches: Set together, the two bowls reverse the flow between householder and ascetic: the quatrain's begging bowl is the image of a giver's merit filling, while the epic's is an ascetic's vessel that gives without end.

note: Kural 1042 calls poverty 'a sinner' (இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி) that comes with this world and the next both lost; Deepathilakai calls hunger 'the sinner' (பசிப் பிணி என்னும் பாவி, 80) that destroys birth, learning, modesty and beauty.
teaches: The Kural speaks to the poor man about what poverty takes from him, even merit for the next world; the epic speaks to the one who can cure it, so the merit the poor man loses becomes the giver's highest dharma.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger, read by its commentators as ascetics, below that of those who remove it; here a goddess tells a girl who has just renounced that removing hunger is beyond praise and the true way of the world.
teaches: The epic dissolves the couplet's ranking of giver over ascetic by putting the bowl in a renunciant's hand, so the one who endures hunger becomes the one who ends it.

note: The Naladiyar calls liberality milk a cow yields gladly to its calf, against the base who yield only when squeezed; Manimekalai wants the bowl to flow at the hungry's faces as a mother's breast flows at her newborn's (114-118), and Deepathilakai says it flows only for those who feed from compassion (120-121).
teaches: The epic turns the quatrain's distinction between glad and forced giving into a property of the vessel itself, which will not yield to a giver whose gift is not compassion.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who end others' hunger; an ascetic here names ending hunger as the one dharma equal for men and gods and calls it the dharma of tapas.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's ranking by giving the higher strength to a renunciant: with the bowl, the one who has left the household can feed others instead of only enduring hunger, and feeding becomes the ascetic's own discipline.

note: The quatrain says that knowing people still do blameworthy things because of deeds done before; the epic calls Virai's drunken death and Tarai's fall the ripening of a cruel deed.
teaches: The epic applies the quatrain's explanation to a death and then, at 46 to 48, names the drink and the leap, so a past deed is the cause behind the act while the act itself stays on the record.

note: The couplet asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve when it turns; Aravanar tells a king who has lost both queens not to grieve, since it is the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The couplet grounds equanimity in consistency toward one's own fortune; the epic's monk grounds it in karma and speaks it to a mourner, showing the same counsel turned from self-discipline into consolation for another's loss.

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the great sea of births; Aravanar says those who hear the Buddha's dharma pass beyond painful birth and vows to praise the Bodhi Lord's feet in every birth.
teaches: The epic names the couplet's unnamed feet as the Buddha's but moves the crossing onto hearing his teaching, and its worshipper expects many more births before that hearing, so the feet become a lifelong devotion rather than the crossing itself.

note: The couplet ranks not taking one creature's life above a thousand oblations; the boy takes the cow from a sacrifice and is caught, beaten and called a thief.
teaches: The couplet weighs abstention against sacrifice as a private choice of merit, while the epic shows what acting on it costs inside a sacrificing community: the rescuer is branded a thief and expelled from his caste.

note: The quatrain calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage depend on austerity, learning and effort; Aputtiran cites the brahmins' own seers born of cow, deer, tiger and jackal.
teaches: The quatrain denies birth rank from outside by naming what truly makes a line, while Aputtiran denies it from inside the brahmins' tradition, so the critique becomes a charge of inconsistency rather than a rival standard.

note: The couplet says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails; the brahmin witness declares the boy an outcaste because his mother confessed she acted unlike a brahmin wife.
teaches: The couplet lets a man's own conduct unmake his birth, and the witness stretches this into a son's birth unmade by his mother's conduct, a step the couplet does not take and one Aputtiran then turns back on the Vedic seers' own mothers.

note: The couplet says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; Aputtiran, the cow's son, begs from house to house to feed the blind, the deaf and the lame.
teaches: The couplet holds that even the worthiest cause cannot make asking honourable, while the epic makes begging on others' behalf its hero's virtue and the ground of the divine bowl; the conflict depends on reading the couplet's cow example as covering begging for another's need, which it seems to.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength to bear hunger below the strength to remove it; Aputhiran, who lives on begged food, grieves not at his own hunger but at finding no means to remove the travellers', and it is then that the goddess gives him the bowl.
teaches: Together they show the couplet's higher strength given to a man with no wealth at all: the epic makes the power to end others' hunger a gift answering grief, not a store of means, which the couplet's comparison of two strengths leaves unexamined.

note: Kural 25 makes Indra the witness to the power of one who has quenched the five senses; in the epic Indra's throne trembles at a beggar's feeding of all creatures, and he comes in person to reward it.
teaches: The epic moves the test that brings Indra down from the ascetic's restraint to a giver's feeding, and then shows the witness turning rival, since the god's reward will undo the giving it acknowledges.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; offered heaven's reward, Aputhiran laughs that heaven is a place where no one does dharma or gives, and asks what its king could give him.
teaches: The couplet's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, becomes in Aputhiran's mouth a judgment that heaven is worse than earth for a giver, because there is no hunger there for giving to meet.

note: Kural 19 says that if the sky gives no rain, neither giving nor austerity will last; Indra's abundant rain leaves Aputhiran's bowl idle for want of takers, and the hall of giving becomes a gambling den.
teaches: Rain is the condition of giving in the couplet, but the epic shows that rain in full measure can end giving too, since giving needs someone in want, so plenty sustains the giver's means and destroys his occasion.

note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even death is sweet when giving is out of reach; alone on an uninhabited island with no one to feed, Aputhiran will not keep his own life with the bowl, gives it away and starves himself to death.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's hyperbole literally: a giver cut off from anyone to give to chooses death, and refuses even the means of life that giving had put in his hands.

note: The couplet calls relieving the destitute's ruinous hunger the place where a man of wealth should store it; Aravanar likens laying aside the hunger-ending bowl to the gods keeping back their leftover nectar, and calls it unfit.
teaches: The couplet keeps a giver's profit in view by making charity a kind of saving, while the epic's bowl has no owner to profit and treats any keeping back as the gods' hoard, so feeding the hungry is pressed past prudence into a duty with no return.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven or the just-sceptred king has failed, and says want has come though the Kaveri flows. The link holds on the reading that the questions at 46-47 clear both.
teaches: The epic grants the Kural's premise that a just king brings plenty and still finds hunger in his land, so hunger becomes a want no sceptre cures and the place where the renouncer's bowl, not the king, must act.

note: The couplet says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; Manimekalai enters the street with a begging bowl and, at 71-74, calls receiving a chaste wife's alms a thing of great worth, while the crowd grieves at the sight.
teaches: The town's grief voices the Kural's shame of asking, and the nun's claim answers it with a begging that asks nothing for herself and seeks the worthiest giver, so the two disagree about whether all asking shames the asker.

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; Kayasandigai praises Athirai as standing alone among the house-dwelling wives of rain-giving chastity (வான் தருகற்பின் மனை உறை மகளிரின்) and so the right giver of the bowl's first alms.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's rain-giving wife as a known type and makes it a rank, one supreme among many, and a qualification for feeding a Buddhist bowl, so domestic chastity is set to work for the renouncer's charity.

note: Saathuvan is ruined by a courtesan and by dice and cast off penniless; among the Nagas he refuses the woman and liquor offered him, and comes home with treasure.
teaches: The couplet names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left, and the story runs the rule both ways: two of the three strip Saathuvan of wealth, and his refusal of a woman and liquor on the island is what brings fortune back.

note: The Kural argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; Saathuvan, told the Nagas cannot live without meat, lets them keep only the flesh of beasts that die of age and bids them harm no living thing.
teaches: The couplet treats the eater as the cause of all killing, while Saathuvan finds the one flesh no killing supplies and so gives people who cannot give up meat a way to keep the Kural's end without its whole demand.

note: The Kural says the evil disease called hunger will not touch one used to sharing his food; Aathirai fills the inexhaustible bowl saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth'.
teaches: The couplet promises that sharing guards the sharer from the disease of hunger, while Aathirai's gift, poured into a bowl that never empties, aims to cure the disease for everyone, so the pair moves from the giver's safety to a cure for the world.

note: The couplet's highest wife commands the rain; here the chaste wives who bring down the rain themselves worship Aathirai, whom fire would not burn.
teaches: The epic places a rank above the Kural's summit of wifely power, and grounds it not in daily worship of the husband but in a wife's readiness to die for a husband who had deserted her for a courtesan.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the dying of the born and the birth of the dead are like sleeping and waking, the simile of Kural 339 in other words, and draws from it that good deeds lead to a good world and ill to hell.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a calm statement of impermanence, but Saathuvan turns it into the premise of an argument against liquor and killing, showing that the image of sleep and waking implies a self that wakes again and must answer for its acts.

note: The couplet says the fire-disease of hunger seldom touches one who habitually shares food (பாத்தூண்); the unit opens on a bowl first filled with a chaste wife's share (பாத்தூண், 1) and on a woman with the elephant-fire disease whose hunger came from old deeds.
teaches: The couplet's protection covers only the sharer's own body, while the epic shows a fire-hunger that no habit of one's own sharing could have kept off because a former deed sent it, so the cure has to come from someone else's share.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who remove it; Viruchikan eats once in twelve years, and when his fruit is crushed his fasting power becomes a curse of hunger on another, which Manimekalai's bowl removes.
teaches: The story stages the couplet's ranking and adds a reason for it: the endurer's power, once offended, can itself manufacture hunger in others, so only the giver's power ends suffering rather than moving it about.

note: The quatrain says the best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their real work; Manimekalai says she understood the body's birth, ageing, disease and death and chose dharma.
teaches: The same reflection that the quatrain treats as a private discipline of the wise is here a defence a woman must speak aloud to a man pursuing her, and she doubts he will listen.

note: The quatrain says a harlot's love goes out like a lamp when the money is gone; Chithirapathi says courtesans leave a drained flower like bees and leave men like Fortune when their merit ends.
teaches: The moralist's charge against the courtesan is spoken in the epic by a courtesan as her house's rule, and she uses it to forbid her daughter's grief and renunciation, so the faithlessness the quatrain condemns turns out to be enforced on the women themselves.

note: The couplet honours the wife who worships her husband and no god; Chithirapathi describes the families whose women worship no god but the man who took them, to say Manimekalai is not of them.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's ideal working as a boundary of birth: women outside the families it describes are declared fair game, so praise of the chaste wife becomes an argument for coercing a woman who has chosen celibacy.

note: The couplet warns men off women who weigh the gain and speak of virtue; Chithirapathi describes dancers who take many gains with sweet speech and leave like bees, and tells the prince to bind such a woman.
teaches: The couplet's advice is to avoid the profit-weighing woman, while the courtesan who describes the same woman advises the prince to seize her, so a portrait meant to protect men becomes a licence to coerce a girl who has left that life.

note: The quatrain's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) fills slowly by alms at door after door; the guard reports a begging bowl (ஐயப் பாத்திரம்) that, taken into the prison, makes food flow for a crowd.
teaches: The quatrain uses the begging bowl as the image of slow accumulation in the giver, and the epic reverses its direction, making the ascetic's bowl the source that pours out, so in the Buddhist epic the mendicant is the giver and the city the receiver.

note: The couplet likens a king's punishing the cruel to weeding a crop; the Chola king, at a beggar's request, empties his prison and makes it a house of dharma.
teaches: Held against the couplet, the epic's king does not deny that the cruel must be punished but turns the instrument of punishment itself into an instrument of charity, so the sceptre is shown by feeding rather than weeding.

note: The couplet calls taking bad even if it were a good path and giving good even without heaven; Manimekalai cites the learned that for an alms-seeker both taking and giving are duty, and going to give is better still.
teaches: The couplet's flat ranking of giving over taking leaves no place for the mendicant, while the epic makes taking a duty when it serves giving, so the beggar's bowl is let in under the couplet's rule rather than condemned by it.

note: The Kural states that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the drummer's blessing wishes three rains and an unswerving king in the same sentence, as things the festival must secure.
teaches: The Kural makes rain follow from the king's justice alone, while the festival treats both rain and just rule as gifts to be prayed for from the gods, so the epic's city does not leave the causal chain to the king.

note: The Kural defines a land as one that goes on without crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the drummer ends the proclamation by wishing that hunger, disease and enmity leave the city.
teaches: What the Kural states as the mark of a true land, the epic's city asks for once a year as a festival blessing, showing that the freedom from the three ills was felt as a gift to be renewed by rite, not a settled condition.

note: The Kural advises not to do harm in hostility even when others act against you; the drummer bids the schools' debaters part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not accept their view (பற்றாமாக்கள்).
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's rule of non-retaliation from private enmity into public doctrinal debate, making civility between rival schools a law of the city's festival.

note: The couplet says the ruin of evil-doers stays at their feet like a shadow; the pillar tells Kanchanan his cruel deed will not leave him, even though the prince died by his own former deed.
teaches: The couplet considers only the doer, while the epic adds that being the instrument of another's ripened karma does not lift the deed from the one who kills, so karma explains the victim's death without excusing the killer.

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the pillar says the prince's ripened deed came here and took his life, and that Kanchanan's deed will reach him too.
teaches: The epic shows the old deed finding its doer across a change of birth and through a stranger's hand, which gives the quatrain's search image a path: the deed reaches the prince by way of another man's mistake.

note: The quatrain warns men not to desire the spear-eyed woman because she too will stoop and walk with a staff; Manimekalai, the woman desired, points her pursuer to an old woman and shows him eyes and face already changed.
teaches: The quatrain's warning against desire is spoken by a man to men about a woman, while the epic puts it in the mouth of the desired woman as her own defence, turning the lesson on aging into a refusal.

note: The quatrain asks whether spices, flowers in the hair and false finery can remove a foulness the great saw and gave up; Manimekalai says the flowers, paste, cloth and jewels that hide the flesh are a deceit 'those of old' devised.
teaches: The quatrain credits the great of the past with seeing through the body's adornment, while the epic blames those of old for building it, so the same disguise is a personal vanity in one and an inherited social custom in the other.

note: The quatrain's renunciant refuses talk of teeth like jasmine buds and pearls because he has seen fallen teeth and bones in the burning ground; Manimekalai shows teeth once like a row of pearls now loosened in a living mouth.
teaches: The quatrain needs the cremation ground to refute the pearl simile, while the epic finds the refutation in a living old woman, so the argument against the body moves from death to aging that every lover can see in the street.

note: The couplet says unguarded anger kills the one who has it; Kanchanan's anger, kindled by misread signs, kills the prince, and the pillar then tells him the deed will cling to him.
teaches: The epic traces how anger turns on its owner: it begins in a misreading of another's signs, kills someone else first, and returns as a deed that will not leave the angry man, which the couplet states as a single blow.

note: The couplet says that if the sky fails, hunger stays and torments the wide world; the deity foretells the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world.
teaches: Where the couplet treats hunger after drought as beyond remedy, the epic answers it with organized charity, the begging bowl standing in for the failed rain.

note: The couplet says harm done to others comes back on the doer of itself; the deity applies this to a killing done in zeal to serve a holy man and denies that the service exempts it.
teaches: The couplet does not ask whether a good motive changes the return of harm; the epic answers that it does not, and names the excuse it rejects, that the master served will protect his servant.

note: The Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the deity says the cook's killing came 'here' to strike the man reborn as the prince.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that seeks out its doer becomes in the epic a deed that crosses a death and a new body, so the 'doer' it finds is a person with another name who does not remember the act.

note: The couplet says women who obtain their husbands win great distinction in the world of the gods; the brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter it.
teaches: Taken together, the couplet and the brahmin's maxim make the wife and husband each the other's way to heaven, but the epic gives the maxim to a man urging a sixty-year-old to marry and then has Visakai deny it, so the reciprocal rule is shown as a pressure rather than a truth.

note: The couplet calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Visakai calls great virtue the true companion (விழுத் துணை) in place of youth, body, wealth and sons.
teaches: Visakai uses the couplet's idea of virtue as companion to replace the wife-companion the brahmin demanded, so a teaching about virtue outlasting death becomes an answer to the claim that a man needs marriage for heaven.

note: The couplet says evils will not touch a man for seven births if he has children of good character; Visakai says sons do not give heaven.
teaches: On the reading that the seven births are the parent's own, the couplet credits good children with protecting the parent beyond this life, which Visakai flatly denies, so the pair marks a point where the epic's teacher rejects a household hope the Kural endorses.

note: The quatrain says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounce in childhood; Visakai points to Dharmadattan's grey hair and turns him not to renunciation but to giving.
teaches: The quatrain offers only two paths, early renunciation or clinging to youth; Visakai, who has kept a vow of chastity since youth, shows a third for the grey-haired householder: shared charity without marriage.

note: The prince follows Manimekalai like a shadow (நிழல் போல், 185); the couplet says ruin stays at the evildoer's feet like his shadow.
teaches: The epic inverts the couplet's shadow: the prince makes himself Manimekalai's shadow, but his own evil deed is the shadow at his own feet, and it catches him in the hall where he followed her.

note: The couplet says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave the man who crosses into another's home; the ascetic says such men die when their evil deed ripens, and adds those who set their hearts on women ascetics.
teaches: The couplet's offence is entering a married woman's home; the epic extends it to desire for a renunciant woman, who has no husband's home to violate, and makes death, not lasting disgrace, the outcome.

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the brahmins forget their books; the king says that without the guardian's guarding there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity.
teaches: The king adapts the couplet's list of what fails without a guardian to ascetics' vows and women's chastity, the two things his son violated, so the general rule becomes the reason he must count his own son's death as just.

note: The Bhuta quotes the couplet to Maruthi and explains her lost power by her worship of gods, festivals and talk.
teaches: The couplet states the wife's power as a fact; the epic uses it as a test a chaste woman fails, reads தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally as a ban on worshipping gods, and adds festivals and gossip, so the couplet becomes a rule with conditions that can be broken.

note: Kural 284 says that a love grown in stealth yields at harvest a sorrow that does not die; Manimekalai tells the queen not to think that the harsh suffering of those who live by stealth is for thieves alone, since these ways bring sorrow to all who live in the world.
teaches: The couplet assigns undying sorrow to the thief; the epic refuses to let a listener file that sorrow under a class of criminals and extends it to a queen whose fault was deceit, making the rule about theft a rule about all concealment.

note: Kural 2 asks what learning is worth if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Manimekalai says learning that is merely learned is not learning, and names the learned as those who curb hatred, end hunger and love all creatures.
teaches: Both refuse learning its own worth, but the couplet completes it in worship while the epic completes it in compassion and the ending of others' hunger, so the pair shows two answers to the same question of what learning is for.

note: Kural 351 says a base birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal as real; Aravanar puts ignorance first in the chain of birth and defines it as trusting hearsay that a hare has horns.
teaches: The couplet names unreal things taken as real without saying which; the epic gives the error a mechanism, hearsay preferred to what is seen, and a place, the first of twelve links, so the couplet's one step to birth becomes a chain.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre; the ascetic credits Nagapuram's unfailing rain to Punniyarajan's birth, before any rule.
teaches: Where the couplet makes a land's rain the fruit of a king's just rule, the epic makes it the fruit of his former birth's charity, moving the cause of plenty from the sceptre to karma.

note: Kural 920 groups double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of men Fortune has left; the queen turns the charge on the courtesan house itself, a life built on drink, lies, lust and deceit, and from which a courtesan's own daughter flees in fear.
teaches: The couplet sees the courtesan only as a danger to the man, while the epic shows the same house as a danger to the women born in it, so that renunciation is a courtesan's escape, not only a patron's.

note: Kural 244 says one who sustains lives (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி) and holds to grace need fear no deed for his own life; the minister says the Buddha's dharma is not to pity one's own life and to protect other lives (பிற உயிர் ஓம்பும், 116), and charges the king with seeking a higher world for himself.
teaches: The couplet promises the protector of lives safety for his own; the minister makes indifference to one's own life the protector's mark, so a king's wish for his own release counts against his grace.

note: Kural 327 says not to take another's life even at the cost of one's own; the island goddess tells Aputhiran that by starving he killed his own life and that the merchants who came back and died where he lay died for his sake, so that he is a killer.
teaches: The couplet treats giving up one's own life as a price that may be paid to avoid killing; the epic counts giving up one's own life as itself a killing, and one that draws others to die.

note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; the sage of Kayankarai urges dharma before death that cannot be turned back (49 to 50), but adds that good deeds win only better births and that none escape birth except those who hear the coming Buddha.
teaches: The sermon separates what the couplet joins: haste in good deeds before death decides the next birth, but release waits on a teacher not yet come, so urgency to do good is not urgency to be free.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the minister says rain returned to Savakam after twelve years when the king was born, before he wielded any sceptre.
teaches: The epic moves the cause of a land's plenty from the king's rule to his birth, that is, to merit carried from a former life of giving, so a king can bring rain before he governs at all.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its own mother among many cows; Mathurapathi's word traces a killing done as Bharatan in Kalinga to Kovalan's death in Madurai, and says the former deed does not fail to come.
teaches: The pair shows how far the calf can walk: the quatrain gives the deed a homing instinct, and the epic gives it a road across a birth, a kingdom and a change of name, with a widow's curse as the means by which it finds Kovalan.

note: The couplet says anger left unguarded kills the one who holds it; Kannaki says her anger at Madurai, though it followed a just grievance, is a sin that will reach her after her heavenly merit ends.
teaches: Kannaki is the hardest case for the couplet, a woman whose anger an earlier epic praised as just, and the Manimekalai applies the rule to her anyway while stretching its reach across births: the self that anger kills is a future self, after heaven.

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Kannaki, though a goddess in heaven, says she must swim the hard sea of births (40) until she hears the Buddha's dharma and leaves birth.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic shows that even a deified woman is still in the sea, and it names the means of crossing as hearing a teacher's dharma, which the couplet's 'Lord' leaves unnamed and which here replaces devotion with understanding.

note: The Ajivika says everything a life meets is fixed at conception by prior fate; the Kural says those who strive without flagging see fate's back.
teaches: Against the Ajivika's fixed course, the couplet's claim that effort can rout fate stands out as a deliberate limit on oozh, which the Kural elsewhere (380) calls the strongest power.

note: The Kural says the fivefold sense-knowledge is fruitless without true understanding; Manimekalai tells the materialist, who trusts the senses alone, that true things are hard to know without true understanding.
teaches: The couplet's general claim becomes a debating move: the heroine uses its contrast between sense-knowledge and true understanding to show that a perception-only rule cannot reach even one's parentage.

note: The couplet says that without rain neither giving nor austerity lasts; the ascetic reports that Kanchi's ascetics, finding no almsgivers in the drought, have left for Vanji.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's rule as a chain: the drought ends giving first, and austerity, which lives on gifts, then has to leave the land.

note: The couplet gives the chaste wife power to bid rain fall; the king asks whether failed chastity among women withheld it.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's power run in reverse: if a wife's chastity can command rain, the community's women can be suspected when it fails, and the epic records the suspicion without confirming it.

note: The couplet says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; the Kanchi king names the bent sceptre as only one of three possible causes and cannot tell which holds.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's law into a king's anxious self-examination, and then sets it aside: the deity names no fault and sends a renunciant's bowl instead of a reform of rule.

note: The couplet asks whether the host who feeds guests need even sow his field; the epic likens the bowl's plenty to alms in ascetics' hands and to seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools.
teaches: Both make feeding others a kind of sowing, but the couplet promises the giver's field yields unsown, while the epic makes the yield depend on conditions, the worth of the receiver among them.

note: The quatrain has the best of people renounce home and wealth after slow reflection on impermanence; the ascetic renounces when the news of his son's death by evil deeds reaches him.
teaches: The pairing shows impermanence learned two ways: the quatrain's sage reasons his way to it, while the epic's merchant has it forced on him by bereavement and only then states it as the doctrine.

note: The quatrain mocks debaters who do not know how to make what they learned reach the hearer; the teacher's false theses are exactly theses that cannot reach the hearer, because he does not grant their terms or already holds the conclusion.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's complaint a precise form: an argument fails not only by poor delivery but when its subject or conclusion is foreign or already granted to the one it is aimed at.

note: The Kural promises the sky to those who have left doubt and become clear; the teacher describes two sound-looking proofs of opposite theses that together leave only doubt (சங்கயம்).
teaches: The epic shows a doubt that more argument cannot remove, since each side's reasoning holds, so the clarity the couplet praises cannot come from matching proofs alone.

note: The Kural calls taking what does not last for what lasts the lowest understanding; Aravanar's model rule is 'whatever is made is impermanent', valid only in that direction.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the textbook rule shows impermanence as something proved from being made, with the warning that the converse fails, so knowing the passing is a matter of inference as well as of seeing.

note: The couplet bids one see the true thing whatever nature (தன்மை) a thing appears to have; the Buddhist teacher strips perception of name, class, quality and action and assigns them to inference.
teaches: On the Buddhist account the 'nature' the couplet looks past is largely the mind's own labelling, so seeing the true thing becomes a matter of separating bare perception from what inference adds.

note: The couplet makes understanding the power to find the true substance in whatever one hears from anyone; Manimekalai has heard every school and judged them wanting, but asks a teacher for the true doctrine.
teaches: The epic shows the limit of the couplet's test: a hearer can reject what she hears from many mouths and still lack the means to find the truth, so the teacher gives her a method of knowing rather than an answer.

note: The Kural says that a mind which examines (ஓர்த்து) and knows what is with certainty (ஒருதலையா) need not think of birth again; Aravanar closes with examine (ஆய்ந்து) and know without doubt (ஐயம் இன்றி).
teaches: The couplet names examination and certainty as the way out of birth but gives no procedure; the epic supplies one, and its technical word for certainty, ஏகாந்தம், is the couplet's ஒருதலை in Sanskrit dress.

note: The couplet says that taking what is not a thing for a thing breeds an unworthy birth; the teacher gives a test for absence, that a thing which exists appears like a gooseberry in the hand, and the hare's horn does not.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's warning into a procedure: what would appear if it were there and does not appear may be judged absent, which gives the confusion the couplet fears a check in method.

note: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life rather than shame for life; Madhavi says that by staying alive after hearing of her lover's suffering she gave up her shame.
teaches: Read against the couplet, Madhavi's confession places her among those who kept life at the cost of shame, so the shame the town sees in her tapas already lay in her survival, and her renunciation becomes the answer of one who has failed the rule rather than a new disgrace.

note: Kural 349 says that when attachment ends it cuts off births; Aravanar says suffering comes from attachment, bliss to those free of it, and that birth itself brings growing suffering.
teaches: The couplet ties the end of attachment to the end of rebirth but sets no value on birth; Aravanar's lines add that birth is itself suffering and offer a bereaved lay woman five precepts as the way in, not the renouncer's clean cut.

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that gives unceasing births to all beings; in the chain craving (வேட்கை) gives clinging, karma and birth, but itself arises from feeling and contact and ceases only when ignorance ceases.
teaches: Both make craving the seed of birth, but the chain gives the seed its own seed: craving depends on feeling and, eleven steps back, on ignorance, so the Buddhist cure begins with knowledge where the Kural's chapter begins with cutting craving.

note: The Kural says griefs keep hold of those who keep hold of attachment; the teacher's truths say sorrow is caused by birth and clinging, and release, which is joy, by not clinging.
teaches: The Kural's one-verb picture of grip and grief becomes the second truth, and the epic adds its mirror, release as joy caused by not clinging, so the couplet's warning is shown to be half of a four-part formula.

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and delusion perish; the teacher names the same three, in the same order, as the cause of all he has taught and gives a separate remedy for each.
teaches: The Kural names the three roots and promises the end of pain but gives no method; the epic, using the same three words, assigns each root its own discipline, contemplation of impermanence for desire, friendliness for anger, hearing and reflection for delusion.

note: The Kural says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real as real; the teacher names ignorance first of twelve links that end in birth and defines it as holding hearsay clear, as that a hare has horns.
teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's மருள் can be given a precise epistemic fault, trusting report over what has been established, and that for the Buddhist teacher this confusion reaches birth only through ten links between, which the couplet's direct cause compresses.

note: Naladiyar says craving enters by five gates, body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears, and whoever guards them reaches release; the teacher counts six gates, with the mind among them, and places craving three links after the gates.
teaches: The pairing shows two models of the senses: the quatrain makes the five gates the entry of craving and guarding them the path, while the chain adds the mind as a sixth gate and puts contact and feeling between gate and craving, so guarding the gates is not where the chain is cut.

note: Kural 34 makes a spotless mind the whole of virtue; the Uvavanam seat shows that a flower laid without intention goes nowhere, as proof that a deed without intention bears no fruit.
teaches: The couplet puts the mind first in judging virtue; the seat pushes that principle to the disputed case of the unintended act and makes it a point on which schools divided, which the couplet never has to face.

note: Kural 929 says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with fire under water; here the drunk reasons with a sober ascetic, arguing that toddy kills nothing.
teaches: The epic reverses the couplet's direction, letting the drunk be the one who argues, and his argument from non-harm shows that the drunkard's reasons can borrow the ascetic's own principle and still be worthless.

note: The quatrain mocks the fool who calls a body of nine oozing openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Sudhamathi answers the prince's love-poetry questions about Manimekalai with the same inside-out view of the body.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's cure as speech to a lover just after he has used the love-poem epithets, and then shows it failing: the sight of the girl reaches him before the words do.

note: The proverb verse tells of the young Chola who tied on grey hair and judged a case (உரைமுடிவு) to prove that a family's craft comes half-known; Sudhamathi names the same act (உரை முடிவு காட்டிய உரவோன்) to shame his heir.
teaches: The proverb says the line's judgment is inborn, and the epic turns the same story against the line's heir, who must be lectured by a woman, so the inherited craft is invoked because it is missing.

note: The couplet says crushing foes comes through tapas if the ascetic so intends; Sudhamathi warns the prince that Manimekalai's fated austerity carries a curse for an arrow.
teaches: The couplet's power of tapas is invoked here as a shield for a girl who has barely begun austerity, and the prince's shrug at line 21 shows the threat carrying no weight until it is backed by practice.

note: The couplet is a woman's admission that the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint; the prince asks whether any restraint exists once desire takes hold.
teaches: The same claim that in the Kural is a woman's confession of her own defeat becomes, in a prince's mouth, a licence to press on a woman who refuses him, so the epic shows how the love-book's lament can serve as an excuse.

note: The couplet says the அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they wear cool kindness toward every life; Sudhamathi's Brahmin father, turned off by Brahmins and Jain monks alike, cries for any அறவோர் and is answered by a Buddhist monk, called மறையோன் at 68.
teaches: The epic tells the couplet's redefinition as a story: those who hold the title by birth or by vows fail the dying man, and the title of one who knows the sacred lore passes to the stranger who shows kindness to him.

note: The couplet says those sick with love cannot know the dignity of not going after one who has turned hostile; Manimekalai says her heart went after the stranger who had scorned her, and asks if this is the nature of desire.
teaches: The couplet's lovesick woman knows her loss of dignity and keeps loving, while Manimekalai, meeting the same fact in herself on a single sight, answers it with a curse on desire (91), the renunciant's reply the love chapter never gives.

note: The couplet says none but those who reach the feet of the அறவாழி அந்தணன் can cross the other seas; the goddess praises the Buddha's feet marked with the thousand-spoked wheel (ஆயிர ஆரத்து ஆழி), whom Sudhamathi has just called the one who turned the wheel of dharma (அறக் கதிர் ஆழி, 76).
teaches: The same words, அறம், ஆழி and the lord's feet, name the Buddha's wheel of dharma in the epic, which shows that ஆழி in the couplet's epithet could be heard as wheel as well as sea, and that a Buddhist hearer would find the Buddha in a verse that names no one.

note: The couplet says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; the epic's moonrise says the moon's spot shows like a fault in the worthy.
teaches: The epic can use the couplet's moral as the familiar term of a comparison for the sky, which shows the saying was common enough to be turned round.

note: The quatrain's speaker, having seen teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground, will not listen to talk of teeth like pearls; the demon woman eats the eyes without asking 'tooth or pearl', and Sarngalan, seeing it, dies of fright.
teaches: The sight of the burning ground that steadies the Naladiyar's renouncer kills an unready boy, so the contemplation of the dead body is shown to need a prepared mind and not merely a sight.

note: The quatrain warns that merciless Death stalks and takes even the child while its mother wails; Gotami wails over her son and asks whether a spirit took him, and Champapathi answers that no spirit takes a life, only the boy's former deed.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's wailing mother a voice and an answer, and the answer removes the stalking agent the quatrain imagines: what takes the child is his own deed, with fright as its occasion.

note: The couplet sets not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; Champapathi calls 'killing is dharma' a false word and counts a mother's offer of her own life for her son's under it.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet's rule against killing to giving one's own life in exchange for another's, which the couplet, concerned with animals and sacrifice, does not consider.

note: The couplet says that for those who have gained the power of tapas even leaping past Death becomes possible; Champapathi, the old ascetic goddess, shows her power by proving that no god can give back a life.
teaches: The power over death that tapas earns, in the epic, stops at the one who earned it: even the oldest ascetic goddess and all the gods cannot pass it to the dead.

note: The couplet says that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the goddess gives the same chain with the planets inserted between sceptre and rain, and aims it at the heir's desire for a nun.
teaches: The pair shows the rule's reach being widened: what the Kural ties to judging wrongly the epic applies to a prince's private lust, so the sceptre is bent by desire, not only by a verdict.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Manimekalai says the cruel deed ripened so that her father went to a foreign land and died by the sword, and that it casts 'us' into misery.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that hunts down its own doer explains how karma found Kovalan far from home, yet the daughter's 'us' lets the same ripening fall on her too, which the one-doer rule does not allow, so the pair opens the question whether a deed's fruit can be shared by kin.

note: Kural 350 bids one cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go; the two Naga kings, unable to let go of their great attachment to the seat each calls 'ours', stop their war when the great sage calls it 'ours' and preaches from it.
teaches: The couplet's paradox, giving up attachment by attaching to the unattached one, is staged as a scene: the sage does not tell the kings to own nothing but sets his own claim, 'this is ours', in place of theirs, and their war ends because a claim of the one without clinging displaces a claim of clinging.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine (ஓரா) and do justice falls by himself; the patikam has the Pandya fail to examine (தேரானாகி) and fall, but says he failed because the time of the deed's ripening had come.
teaches: The couplet treats the failure to examine as the king's own fault and the ruin as its consequence, and the epic keeps the consequence but places the failure itself inside a karmic order, which raises the question the couplet does not face of how a fated lapse can still be the king's guilt.

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god commands the rain; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and brought down its king.
teaches: The power the couplet gives the devoted wife is a blessing on the world through rain, and the epic turns the same power into fire against a city once her husband is wronged, so the pair shows the chaste wife's word as a force that can destroy as well as nourish.

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the patikam has a deed of a former birth in Singapuram find Kovalan in Madurai, and says it has run its course for both of them (நுங்கட்கு).
teaches: The quatrain's deed seeks the one who did it, but the epic's curse reaches across a birth and a country through the word of the victim's widow and falls on the doer's wife as well, so the pair shows the epic widening the quatrain's single doer into a household.

note: The couplet says nothing is stronger than ஊழ், which arrives first even when one devises (சூழினும்) another way; the patikam says the ஊழ்வினை comes in wrath and makes one eat it, through the finely made (சூழ்வினை) anklet.
teaches: The couplet's fate outruns any plan, and the epic gives the plan a body: the anklet Kovalan meant to sell to start life again becomes the instrument of the fate it was meant to escape, and the epic adds that fate comes in anger and feeds its fruit, which the couplet does not say.

note: The couplet says fate outruns any other plan; the narrator puts ஊழ்வினை behind a journey Kovalan plans, by his own word at line 51, to win back wealth.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's claim working from inside a person's own scheme: the plan to recover wealth is not overtaken by fate but is the road fate travels.

note: The couplet says all living beings join hands to the one who does not kill and refuses flesh; the epic shows lay votaries worshipping the stone seat set for the flesh-renouncing Charanas even when none is there.
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole of universal worship becomes an institution in the epic: a built seat honoured in the ascetics' absence, which then becomes the place where a Charana actually appears at line 161.

note: The quatrain says not even ascetics (உறுவர்) can remove what must befall; the epic shows an ascetic who sees the couple's coming fate by his inner lamp and tells them the deed cannot be put off.
teaches: The pair shows the quatrain's limit on ascetic power from the ascetic's side: the Charana knows, does not grieve, and states the rule himself instead of trying to avert the fate.

note: The couplet calls a head that does not bow to the eight-qualitied one as useless as a sense organ without sense; Kavunthi vows each organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head and mind, to the Arhat alone.
teaches: The couplet's single comparison between the bowing head and a dead sense is worked out by the nun into a vow for every sense in turn, and the eight-qualitied one is named in the preceding sermon as the Jain Lord (எண்குணன், line 188).

note: The couplet ranks those who fast below those who bear the harsh words of others; Kavunthi, whom the mockers address by her fasting body, curses them, and it is the insulted couple who ask that the words be taken as ignorance.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's two figures between two people: the faster answers insult with a curse, and the forbearance the couplet ranks higher comes from the young couple who were insulted.

note: The couplet says that crushing foes and raising those one loves come by tapas if one so intends; Kavunthi's penance gives her curse its hold and her word of release its power.
teaches: The epic shows both halves of the couplet in one act of one ascetic: the same tapas that turns the mockers into jackals sets the day they become human again.

note: The couplet defines the good path (நல்லாறு, நெறி) as the way that keeps not killing anything in view; Kavunthi's road counsel makes that literal, warning that a careless step on the shore may harm the crab and the snail.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's path metaphor turns into an actual walk where every footfall must be watched, and the nun counts harm to a snail as a grief equal to the dangers to the traveller herself.

note: The brahmin hails a Pandya who, when the thundering clouds withheld rain, bound them and made the harvest unfailing (மழைபிணித் தாண்ட மன்னவன்); the couplet says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The couplet makes rain the natural consequence of just rule, while the epic's praise makes the king compel the clouds, so the same belief appears once as a law and once as a dynastic feat that this epic will test when the Pandya's sceptre bends.

note: Kavunthi asks whether anything rare is out of reach for those who never swerve from truth and protect living beings, against the brahmin's pool that grants every wish; the couplet says austerity is pursued because it gains whatever is wished as it is wished.
teaches: Kavunthi uses the Kural's promise that discipline gains every wish against a pool that also grants every wish, and grounds that discipline in truth and non-harm, so the couplet's motive of attainment becomes an argument for ethics over pilgrimage.

note: The brahmin likens the summer that turns mullai and kurinji into paalai to a wide land that has lost its royal order when its king bent with his officers (கொற்றவன் கோடி); the couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky will not pour rain.
teaches: The couplet states that a bent king dries the sky, and the brahmin's simile reads a drought landscape as the look of a misruled kingdom, so the waste Kovalan crosses already pictures the bent sceptre waiting in Madurai.

note: The hunters pay for victory with blood at the goddess's feet; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations.
teaches: The conflict is about what an offering is worth: the hymn makes killing itself the price that buys the goddess's favour, while the couplet holds that no offering outweighs one life spared; it holds if the throat-blood of line 144 is a slain creature's.

note: The Kural says wealth that comes without grace and love should be let go; the hunters name themselves graceless takers of wealth by wounding and ask the gracious goddess to eat their due.
teaches: Where the couplet tells the getter to let graceless wealth roll away, the hymn shows a community whose living is exactly such wealth offering a share of it to a goddess of grace, who is asked not to refuse it; the tension rests on reading the due as paid from the plunder.

note: The couplet says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the difference in deeds; the vari credits a girl's penance with her glory and then declares her birth-clan, the bow-wielding hunters, the clan among clans.
teaches: The song agrees that distinction comes from a deed, the girl's penance, but hands that distinction straight back to the birth-group, the move the couplet's rule forbids, so the pair shows how a low-ranked clan claims rank through one daughter's merit rather than by denying that birth confers it.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the epic's fame says that in the just Pandya's land even beasts, serpents and thunder spare those who depend on it.
teaches: Held together, the two show the claim that nature answers a just sceptre turning, in the epic, into a traveller's reason to trust a stranger king, a reputation the story then puts to the test with the travellers' own lives.

note: The couplet likens a king's lack of kindness to the world's lack of rain; the epic likens travellers waiting out the scorching sun to subjects waiting for a cruel king to set.
teaches: The Kural pictures the bad king through the weather and the epic pictures the weather through the bad king, so the pair shows the image of misrule running both ways, and the epic placing it, unprompted, at the first step into the Pandya's land.

note: The couplet says the sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth and not his love bring him harm; here a courtesan writes to a man who has lost his wealth, asking only what her fault was, and he judges her blameless and himself at fault.
teaches: The pair sets the Kural's rule that a courtesan's sweet words are for wealth against a courtesan's letter written after the wealth is gone, so the epic tests the rule on the one case it cannot explain and has the man himself withdraw the charge.

note: The couplet says those whose knowledge is refined by good sense do not sink into the common charms of women who are everyone's; the epic says that in the net of the dancers' glances even ascetics' hard-won wisdom turns to something else.
teaches: The Kural makes refined knowledge a protection against the courtesan, and the epic's street denies the guarantee by naming ascetics among those caught, so the pair shows the rule holding only for the wise who stay away, not for any wisdom that walks into the street.

note: The couplet asks why those who take good fortune as good grieve when ill fortune comes; Kavunthi says the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed ripens.
teaches: The couplet's argument for calm rests on consistency between good and bad fortune, while the nun rests it on learning and adds a cause, desire for women and food, so the pair shows the Kural's equanimity before fate being turned into a renouncer's diagnosis of where suffering comes from.

note: The quatrain says that because a wife cannot be put away even if she lacks virtue and bears no child, the learned called marriage கடி; Kavunthi says the pains of parting and union belong only to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone.
teaches: Both make marriage a source of suffering from which the solitary are free, but the Naladiyar argues it to recommend renunciation while Kavunthi states it to a married man and then sends him on with his wife, so the pair shows the renouncer's diagnosis offered without its prescription.

note: The couplet says a wife who worships her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall; Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity fairer than any she has seen and quotes a saying that where chaste wives live the sky never fails and kings' victory never decays.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps the wife below the gods yet gives her command of the rain, Kavunthi makes the chaste wife herself the deity and extends her power from rain to the king's victory, which is the very extension the epic will turn against the Pandya when that power destroys his city.

note: The couplet holds that giving is good even if there were no higher world; the charana proves the worth of a gift by showing the god it produced, with the monkey's hand still on him.
teaches: The Kural deliberately cuts giving loose from any reward in a higher world, while the Jain tale makes a visible heavenly body the evidence for the gift's worth, so the pair separates two defences of giving, one that needs no world beyond and one that rests on it.

note: The couplet calls a fort that which cannot be taken by siege, storm or work on those inside; Madurai's gate is lined with every engine against attack as Kannaki passes through it.
teaches: The epic fills Madurai's walls with the defences the Kural's fort requires at the very moment it lets in the woman whose wrong will burn the city from within, so the pair shows a danger the couplet's three threats do not name: an injustice of the king's own that no engine on the wall can repel.

note: The quatrain says that when people who know what should be known still do blameworthy things, it comes from their own former deeds; the epic says the king inquired into nothing because it was the time for a deed to ripen.
teaches: The quatrain traces the knowing man's wrong to his own deeds, while the epic leaves open whose deed ripens, the king's or Kovalan's caught in its net, so one man's karma may be what makes another man err.

note: The couplet calls stealth a dark knowledge (காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure; the goldsmith, the real thief, lectures the guards on the eight arts of thieves as an unmatched skill.
teaches: The Kural grants that stealth is a kind of knowledge, and the epic shows that knowledge turned from taking goods to taking a life, as the thief's expertise in theft persuades the guards to kill an innocent man.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kovalan's former deed reaches him through a goldsmith's lie, a king's hasty word and a drunken guard's sword.
teaches: The quatrain's deed finds its doer by itself, while the epic shows it arriving through other people's free and blameworthy acts, so karma here does not excuse the hands it works through.

note: The couplet makes the householder the support of renouncers, the needy and the dead; Kannaki says that without her husband she lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the householder as one person, while Kannaki shows that a wife alone could not keep those duties, so the householder's dharma the Kural assigns depends on the pair being together.

note: The couplet says one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve later over his own fault (தன்பிழை); Kovalan, now in Madurai, grieves that he grew heedless (பொச்சாப் புண்டு) and failed his parents and his wife.
teaches: The couplet makes late regret the heedless man's whole penalty and puts the fault in him alone, while the epic has the heedless man grieve and still lose his life, and lets him ask in the same breath whether karma rather than his own lapse has brought him here.

note: The couplet defines the woman who guards herself, tends her husband, keeps their good name and does not flag; Kannaki hid her grief before his parents and followed him without gainsaying him though his conduct was unworthy.
teaches: The couplet does not say what such a wife owes a husband who wrongs her; Kannaki's answer is to name his fault and follow him all the same, so the epic shows the couplet's tireless wife carried into the ruin her husband makes.

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-qualitied one is as useless as a sense organ without its power; the kuravai asks what ear it is that has not heard Thirumaal's praise, and goes on to the eye and the tongue.
teaches: The couplet's simile, an organ without its function, becomes in the kuravai a definition carried through ear, eye and tongue, so the claim that the body's parts exist for worship is spelled out organ by organ and bound to one named god.

note: The city sees Kannaki weeping beyond bearing (அல்லலுற் றாற்றா தழுவாளை), the very condition the couplet names as the force that wears away a king's wealth.
teaches: The couplet's tears work slowly as an abrasive on wealth, but the epic makes one woman's tears the moment the people themselves declare the sceptre bent, the first step to the city's burning.

note: The quatrain's old deed seeks out its own doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kannaki laments a deed to be eaten that reached her husband through the king's fault.
teaches: Where the quatrain sends the deed straight back to the one who did it, the epic interposes a guilty king between deed and fruit, so karma and the ruler's fault both stand as causes of one death.

note: The benediction likens the Chola's bounty to the rain pouring from above; the couplet makes rain itself depend on the king's not bending justice.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the opening simile of rain and royal grace is not mere flattery but the old belief that the sky's giving follows the king's justice, which the epic will put to the test when a Pandya's crooked verdict brings fire rather than rain on his city.

note: Both see the king's white umbrella as the moon; the benediction praises the moon for resembling the Chola's sheltering umbrella, the quatrain says every king under such an umbrella has been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same moon-umbrella serves the epic's opening as a sign of rule that shelters the world and serves the Naladiyar as proof that such rule ends, so the pair shows the epic beginning in the confidence the ethics book was written to undercut.

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

note: The couplet makes inquiry (தேர்ந்துசெய்) part of what justice is; Kannaki's first words to the king name him as the one who did not inquire.
teaches: The couplet treats inquiry as within the ruler's power, while the epic shows a ruler failing it in an hour the narrator calls karma's ripening, and still holds him answerable for it.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the venba says dharma is death to the wrongdoer, but the speaker, who did no wrong, calls herself one of harsh deeds and the wrongdoer's queen suffers too.
teaches: The epic agrees that harm returns to the one who did it, but shows it spreading to the innocent queen and to the victim who names her own karma, so the couplet's neat return of pain to its doer becomes a wider ruin.

note: Kannaki states the forenoon-afternoon law of returning harm, in other words than the couplet's, as her warning to the Pandya's house.
teaches: The couplet's தாமே says the harm returns of itself with no agent, but the epic puts the law in the mouth of the woman who will herself bring the harm back that same day, so the impersonal return of a deed is shown working through a wronged person's act.

note: The couplet's wife commands the rain; Kannaki commands the fire god, who waits on her word.
teaches: Where the couplet's wife who worships no god has the rain at her word, the epic shows a god coming in person to take her orders, and the power that brings rain turned to burning a city, so the same claim for the chaste wife's word is shown in its most destructive extent.

note: The couplet says the king who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, having failed to examine, dies by his own sentence.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literally, as a king's own verdict on himself, and adds what the couplet does not allow for: that the ruin can be read as redeeming the rule it ends.

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; in burning Madurai the Vedic chant and the fire offering cease.
teaches: The couplet's warning that Vedic learning lapses under an unguarding king is shown happening in a single night, and with the cows spared, so the epic keeps one half of the couplet's penalty and lets the other fall.

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding a crop; the royal bhuta's office is to put down cruel deeds (கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து), and the Pandya killed Kovalan as a thief under that office.
teaches: Held together, the two show the licence to kill wrongdoers, which the Pandya invoked, being the very office whose guardian spirit now abandons his city, so the Kural's weeding image is shown to depend on the king knowing which are the weeds.

note: The couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the bhutas say that on the day the king errs in the order of rule the city is eaten by fire.
