teaches: Both bind nature's order to the king's justice, but the epic replaces the slow withdrawal of rain with an immediate fire on the city and gives the city's own guardian spirits the knowledge of the rule, so the couplet's consequence becomes a sentence carried out the same night.

note: The quatrain says sin cannot stand before austerity while merit lasts; the goddess says that when a former deed rises in wrath penance does not help those not upright.
teaches: Both limit what austerity can do, but the quatrain makes merit run out with time, while the goddess makes the bar moral: penance fails against a ripened deed for those who lack uprightness.

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god can command the rain; the venba takes its words and says the gods themselves worship such a wife.
teaches: The epic reads Kural 55 through Kannaki's end: the wife's power over nature becomes a claim on the gods, who now worship her, and the reward follows the burning of a city rather than a gift of rain.

note: The couplet says those born of good family do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct; the goddess says those born in the Pandya line joined to conduct (ஒழுக்கொடு) suffer no fault (இழுக்கம்) even in untamed youth.
teaches: The couplet's rule about good birth is spoken by the dynasty's own goddess while she excuses its present king, so the epic shows the rule used as a family's defence at the moment its member has failed.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than oozh, which arrives before any device; Kannaki blames the strong deed that pressed on her but also names herself the woman of cruel deeds.
teaches: Kannaki grants karma the force the couplet gives oozh yet keeps the burning of Madurai as her own act, so the epic holds fate and the agent's deed together where the couplet speaks only of fate's priority.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; here the pathini, who held to her husband alone, has become the god whom chaste wives worship, and the hill women ask her to keep their hill fruitful.
teaches: The couplet's power of the chaste wife's word passes, after her death, into a cult in which other chaste wives worship her, so the woman the couplet exempts from worshipping a god is herself made one.

note: The Kural warns that honouring a spy openly lets out the king's secret; Azhumbil Vel counts on the enemy's spies at Vanchi's gate to carry the proclamation.
teaches: The couplet treats exposure to spies as a leak to be prevented, while the epic court makes the leak its instrument, so the pairing shows intelligence used as a channel of open threat.

note: The Kural says the king who does justice and protects is set apart as இறை for the people; Senguttuvan says birth into a line that guards the people is suffering and nothing to be revered.
teaches: Read with தொழுதக as 'worthy of reverence', the two judge the same office oppositely: the couplet awards the protector divine standing, while the epic king, speaking after a just king's fall, denies that the office deserves reverence at all.

note: The couplet's spy goes in the guise of renouncers to get in and see; the defeated northern kings put on the guise of ascetics and performers to get away.
teaches: The couplet treats the renouncer's dress as a tool of the king's intelligence, and the epic shows the same dress used by kings themselves to escape a lost battle, so the guise that hides a spy's purpose also hides a king's shame, and it works because no one strikes a man who looks like a renouncer.

note: The couplet says the six-duty men forget their books if the guardian does not guard; the sages charge the Chera to guard the Veda-keepers of the Himalaya, which lies outside his kingdom.
teaches: The couplet ties the Brahmins' learning to their own king's protection, and the epic stretches that duty across the border, so that a king marching to punish northern kings is made guardian of the northern Brahmins, and he keeps the charge in victory (lines 248-250).

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding the crop; the new Pandya kills a thousand goldsmiths in one day as an offering of lives to the pathini.
teaches: The couplet's punishment by death is of the cruel, one by one, as care for the crop, while the epic's new king kills a whole craft for one goldsmith's lie and calls it an offering, so the pair shows royal punishment sliding from justice into collective sacrifice to restore a king's standing.

note: The quatrain says the best renounce home and wealth after slowly seeing that nothing lasts; here Kannaki's father and Madhavi renounce on hearing of deaths, and the two mothers simply die of the same news.
teaches: The quatrain's renunciation comes from calm reflection on impermanence, while in the epic it comes from the shock of bereavement and is only one of two outcomes of the same grief, so the pair shows the distance between the ethics book's ideal path to renunciation and the way the story's people actually reach it.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature to eat above a thousand oblations; Maadalan ranks the sacrifice of dharma above the war-sacrifice in which the king has killed for fifty years.
teaches: Read together they make a three-step ranking that neither states: the Kural puts abstaining from killing above the Vedic rite, while the epic's brahmin puts the Vedic rite above the killing of war and offers it as the remedy for that killing.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain calls the life a dancer (கூத்தன்) who leaves the skin bag, after which the body's fate does not matter; Maadalan's soul is like dancers who do not stay in one costume but go by their deeds into the bodies of gods, men, beasts or hell-beings.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dancer to make the abandoned body worthless, while the epic follows the dancer to its next costume, which its deeds choose, so the same figure moves from indifference to the corpse to anxiety about the next birth.

note: The couplet says do aram without saying 'later'; Maadalan says if the king says 'we will do aram tomorrow', life may leave today, and the aram he means is the Vedic royal sacrifice.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's urgency but narrows aram from the whole of virtue to one rite performed by priests for a king, showing how the ethical maxim could be recruited for a particular religious practice.

note: The couplet gives the wife who worships her husband power over the rain on her own; the ancients' saying quoted here makes the glory of famous women's chastity depend on kings doing justice.
teaches: The couplet's chastity commands nature unaided, but the epic's closing saying makes its public glory wait on the king's justice being tested, so the pathini's power is tied to a failure of the sceptre.

note: The couplet asks what learning is worth to those who do not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்) of the one of pure knowledge; the close says kings who do not bow at the good feet (நல் தாள் தொழார்) of Poraiyan find it hard to live, and Kannaki too praises Senguttuvan.
teaches: The close moves the Kural's phrase for bowing to the god's feet onto a living Chera king and makes the penalty for not bowing the loss of life rather than of learning's fruit, while the deified Kannaki joins the praise, so the epic ends by turning a devotional formula into a political one.

note: The quatrain says the best renounce without delay after slowly considering that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last; Maasaathuvan gives his wealth away and renounces only when the news of his son's death makes life seem death.
teaches: The pair separates renunciation reached by reflection from renunciation forced by bereavement: the epic's fathers come to the quatrain's act by the road the quatrain hopes to spare, after the loss has already happened.

note: The couplet says a ruler endures by just rule and without it his lustre does not endure; the Vanchi women sing that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends, and praise the Pandya for that.
teaches: The epic grants the couplet's link between a bent sceptre and the king's end but reverses its outcome for fame: the Pandya's dying of his own injustice is exactly what makes his line's glory endure and be sung by a rival kingdom.

note: The couplet asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; the epic likens the newly married couple to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity.
teaches: Both weigh a couple's joy against a heavenly world, but the couplet ranks love above heaven while the epic makes the couple's joy itself a heaven earned by past austerity, and so something that can be used up, which is how the epic prepares its turn from pleasure to karma.

note: The couplet says the woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems will hear no good drums for her waist; Kovalan asks why her attendants loaded her with garland, musk and pearls, making her small waist suffer.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's single joke of a waist too fine to bear flowers and spreads it over a whole toilette, moving the lover's praise from the secret meeting into the marriage chamber, where it is the husband who speaks it and the maids who are blamed.

note: The couplet says all of keeping a house is for tending guests and doing good; the epic's household is set up so that its charity and hospitality may be seen, and the story later takes both away.
teaches: The epic founds Kannaki's household on exactly the couplet's purpose, then lets a husband's absence and exile empty it, showing that the householder's dharma the couplet assigns to the house depends on the pair staying in it.

note: The quatrain mocks one who sees a corpse carried to the burning ground yet marries and thinks there is joy here; the venba says the newly married couple enjoyed every pleasure like people who had seen the world's impermanence.
teaches: The same knowledge that nothing on earth lasts is, for the Naladiyar, a reason to give up marriage and its joys and, in the epic's venba, a reason to take them while they last, so the pair sets out the two lessons impermanence can teach.

note: The couplet says griefs that never let go hold those who hold attachment and do not let go; Maadalan says those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads, and the mothers, held by love for Kannaki, are reborn near her temple.
teaches: The epic agrees with the couplet that attachment binds one to birth, but shows what the couplet does not: a bond of love that leads to a new birth beside the one loved, told without blame, so attachment's hold is the cost the mothers pay for staying near the pathini rather than only a grief.

note: The couplet bids one do virtue without putting it off, because when one perishes it is the companion that does not perish; the epic bids its hearers not wait on their remaining days but seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's உறுதுணை is aram, the Kural's undying companion, and the epic adds that the companion must be sought before youth, wealth and body fail, after a story in which the dead carried only their deeds and loves into their next births.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain, in its chapter on youth not lasting, says that since merciless Death roams looking for his people one should take provisions for the journey in good time; the epic's last lines say youth, wealth and body do not last and bid the hearers seek a true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: The epic folds the Naladiyar's three opening themes, wealth, youth and body not lasting, into one line and draws the same conclusion of provision for the journey, but sets it after a list of concrete deeds, so the provision is named as truthfulness, not killing, giving and the rest rather than left as a figure.

note: The couplet warns that the sweet words of bangled women who want wealth and not love bring harm; in the epic the garland priced at the king's reward is sent into the street by the doe-eyed woman, Madhavi speaks no word, and Kovalan buys it of his own infatuation.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single figure into a household that sets the price in the king's own coin and a dancer who is silent, so the harm the couplet lays on the woman's sweet speech here comes from a public custom and from the buyer's own desire.

note: The Kural's woman hears the herdsman's flute as evening's envoy and a killing weapon; the epic sets the herdsmen's music and the humming bee over an evening that grieves the parted and delights the joined.
teaches: Heard together, the two show that the flute's cruelty lies in the listener's separation, not in the sound, since the same pastoral music opens a night of delight for others in the epic.

note: The Kural's woman says the whole town reels in sorrow when evening spreads; the venba says the same moonlit night is cool to Madhavi with her lover and hot to Kannaki without him.
teaches: The parted woman's sense that the whole town suffers with her is set against a city where one night divides two women of the same house's story, which shows her claim is the projection of grief.

note: The spirit's first victims are those who hide behind penance (தவம்மறைந்து ஒழுகும்); Kural 274 likens hiding in penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds.
teaches: The Kural shows why the false ascetic's concealment is dangerous, that it lets him prey on others, but names no penalty; the epic imagines a city where the concealment is publicly broken and punished with death, setting a sanction beside the couplet's diagnosis.

note: Kural 559: if the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the epic's image weeps when either the king's sceptre or the judge's reading bends.
teaches: Both make a mute power answer a bent justice, but the Kural's answer punishes the whole land through the rain while the epic's image only grieves, and the epic adds a second culprit, the judge who twists the law-book, which the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 1083's lover learns that Death has a woman's form; the epic says Death took a woman's form because the king's just sceptre forbade its killing.
teaches: The Kural's conceit of the deadly beauty is a lover's discovery, while the epic gives it a political cause, the sceptre that holds Death in check, so a love-figure is turned into praise of the king.

note: The couplet's man says sulking is love's sweetness and the embrace after it sulking's sweetness; the epic says Madhavi gave Kovalan both union and sulking, after he had sat in a sulk.
teaches: In the epic the two halves of the couplet's cycle are things a trained woman gives, so ūdal becomes an art supplied to a lover rather than only a mood that lovers fall into.

note: The quatrain says the harlot's love is like a lamp that dies when its oil is spent; here Madhavi, a courtesan, gives Kovalan union and sulking and herself asks for the outing, and in the story it is Kovalan, not she, who breaks off (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The epic's courtesan breaks the quatrain's rule from the other side: the love ends, but by the man's suspicion on the shore, not by her turning away when his wealth runs out.

note: The couplet calls those whose work is killing base in the eyes of the discerning; the vari tells the fisher girl that her elders live by killing lives in the sea and she by killing lives in men's bodies.
teaches: The ethics book brands killing for a living as base, while the coastal song takes the fishers' killing as the plain inheritance of a family and makes it a compliment, so the pair shows a whole people's livelihood that the Kural's judgment would fall on and that the poetry of the shore never questions.

note: The couplet says her eyes would not make him tremble if her bent brows would straighten and screen them; the song says she takes lives with her bending brows, as her brothers take lives with boats.
teaches: In the Kural the curved brow is the eyes' failed guard, which could save him by straightening, while the song makes the curve itself the killer and the killing a family trade, so the pair shows the same conceit shifted from a hope of rescue to a charge of hereditary guilt.

note: The couplet says it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives a king victory; Madhavi's paired stanzas say the Kaveri's grace shows first her husband's unbending sceptre, then the strength of his spear.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear and removes the spear as a cause, while Madhavi's song sets them side by side as equal signs of one prosperous river, so the pair shows the court song keeping the force the ethical couplet sets aside.

note: The couplet's woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting and even remembering burns; Madhavi's woman says to the adumbu and the swans, let him go, we will not forget those who forgot us.
teaches: In the Kural not forgetting is a helpless bind, since memory both burns and keeps her alive, whereas in the song it is announced as a choice with an audience, a reproach to the forgetter, so the pair shows the same refusal to forget used as a lament and as a charge.

note: The couplet's woman lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Madhavi's woman, whose eyes cannot sleep in the evening, asks the sleeping neythal whether it sees the cruel man coming in its dreams.
teaches: The Kural's comfort depends on sleep, and the song removes it: the sleepless woman is shut out of the dream that keeps the couplet's speaker alive and can only ask a flower for it, so the pair shows the dream-comfort as a privilege of those who can sleep.

note: The Kural's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its mate is as hard as hers; Madhavi's heroine asks whether this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) exists in the land of the man who left.
teaches: Both put to evening a question that is really about the absent man's hardness, and the epic sets that question in a performance before a lover who is present, showing how the convention can be heard as a personal charge.

note: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute evening's envoy and killing weapon; Madhavi's heroine says evening has struck the fishers' palai and bids it, if so skilled in melody, take her life.
teaches: In both the music of dusk is the instrument that kills the parted woman, but in the epic the song is sung on a yazh by a musician, so the deadly melody of evening is the singer's own art turned on herself.

note: The Kural says that when evening comes the whole town reels and suffers; Madhavi's heroine says the world shuts its eyes and, if evening and her husband are such, the world has become poor.
teaches: Both widen one woman's evening grief to the whole settlement, and the epic adds the lover himself to the cause, so the poverty of the world is laid as much on the husband's nature as on the hour.

note: The couplet says a fate of loss makes a man foolish; the epic shows Kovalan, his deed ripening, take a sung convention for a confession and leave.
teaches: The epic supplies the mechanism the couplet only asserts: ripening fate does its work by making a man misread what is in front of him, here a song in an assumed voice, so the folly is the means of the loss.

note: The couplet makes sulking love's salt, good in right measure and spoiling only when overdone; the stanza calls not sulking at all, even at the husband's other union, a woman's great chastity.
teaches: Where the Kural sets a measure for oodal, the epic song sets it at nothing and names that karpu, so together they show the measure of sulking turning from a matter of love's taste into a test of a wife's virtue.

note: The couplet says this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; the vari asks whether the sickness her face and eyes gave can be cured only by her breasts.
teaches: The song splits the couplet's paradox across the body, the eyes and face causing the sickness and the breasts curing it, which shows how a later lyric turned the Kural's single riddle into a scene of parts.

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes; the vari's man says he did not know Death lived in the shore grove, and had he known he would not have come.
teaches: Both men learn Death in a woman's eyes, but the Kural's man ends in recognition while the song's ends in the wish never to have come, so the pair separates knowing love's danger from wanting to have avoided it.

note: The couplet asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three in it; the vari asks whether her eyes are fierce Death and answers that Death has become an innocent girl.
teaches: Where the Kural holds Death and the doe's innocence side by side in one look, the song makes one the form of the other, so the innocent girl is Death in disguise, a step from mixture to transformation.

note: The couplet says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is to come together and embrace; the venba has the cuckoo proclaim love's command to all who have sulked (ஊடினீர்) to unite (கூடுமின்), and chides the one who spurned the letter.
teaches: The couplet's pleasure rests on a condition, that union follows, and the venba shows that condition failing even under love's own command, so the sulk the Kural treats as seasoning becomes the start of a separation.

note: The couplet says sulking is like salt, and drawing it out a little too long is like a little too much; Kovalan's sulk, begun at the shore, is here drawn out into a refusal of her letter.
teaches: Past the couplet's 'little too much' the quarrel stops being a spoiled sweetness and becomes a verdict on the beloved's whole nature, which is how a lovers' sulk turns into the epic's break.

note: Saathan's rule that gods grant no boon without tapas uses the couplet's own word செய்தவம், and then he grants Maalathi a child she has not earned.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the tale shows that the rule linking tapas to its reward is the god's to state and also the god's to override, so grace in the epic stands beside the merit rule rather than inside it.

note: Devanthi, whose husband is a god, keeps worship at his shrine to have him back; the couplet sets worship of a god against worship of a husband.
teaches: Devanthi's case dissolves the couplet's either-or, since her god is her husband, and so throws Kannaki's refusal of the shrine in the next unit into relief as a choice the couplet's terms describe exactly.

note: Offered bathing and Kama's shrine as a way to keep her husband, Kannaki says it is not worthy; the couplet praises the wife who worships her husband rather than a god.
teaches: The scene shows the couplet's wife as one who refuses a rite offered for her own good, at the cost of the remedy, and that the refusal is framed as dignity (பீடு), not as doubt about the gods.

note: Kovalan devises a remedy for his ruin, to trade with the anklets in Madurai, and in the same line the narrator says the deed was driving him; the couplet says fate gets there first even when one plans another way.
teaches: The pairing shows fate overtaking a plan by using the plan itself: Kovalan's scheme to recover is the very road by which the deed reaches him, a case the couplet's bare 'it gets there first' does not picture.

note: Kovalan blames a deceitful woman for the poverty that shames him; the couplet ranks double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of those Fortune has left.
teaches: Kovalan speaks the couplet's judgment of himself, but the closing venba and the narrator put his ruin down to the old deed, so the epic lets the Kural's verdict on courtesans stand as a ruined man's account rather than as the cause.

note: The venba says the old deed drove Kovalan out of Puhar before dawn; the quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: In the quatrain the deed seeks the doer; in the venba the doer is moved toward the deed, so together they show karma working from both ends, the deed seeking and the doer being sent.

note: The couplet says that if the ruler bends justice the sky, bending its rain, will not pour; the summary credits the Pandya land, whose king bent justice in this book, with a sky that never fails to pour new rain.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the summary's line of unfailing rain claims for the Pandya land the very sign the Kural withdraws from a bent sceptre, so the epic's punishment for the bent sceptre falls on the king's own life and the city by fire rather than on the rain, and its stock praise of the land survives the verdict intact.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules with the sceptre as it should be; the summary lists the Chola line's righteousness beside the unfailing sky and abundant food, and the Madurai summary gives the same lines to the Pandya line.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the summaries' line of unfailing rain reads as the Kural's sign of just rule, yet the epic grants it equally to the line whose king it shows killing an innocent man, so the pair shows the epic keeping the sign as ceremony while placing the real test of the sceptre in a single verdict.

note: Both call the human body rare (அரிய, அரும்பெறல் யாக்கை); the Valayapathi derives the rarity from karma's long series of bodies, the Naladiyar draws the duty of pressing virtue from it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's command to use the rare body gains its urgency from the fragment's account of how many karma-driven bodies come before a human one, and the fragment's second rarity, wealth to enjoy, is what the quatrain says to turn into virtue instead.

note: Both put not killing above ritual merit; the Kural says abstaining from one killing is better than a thousand oblations, the Valayapathi refuses any dharma that comes with killing.
teaches: The Kural weighs non-killing against sacrifice and finds it heavier, while the fragment denies that a killing rite is dharma at all, so the pair shows the step from ranking merits to disqualifying a kind of virtue.

note: Both set the wealth of grace (அருள்) above wealth of goods; the Kural argues from distribution (goods are found even among the base), the Valayapathi commands that grace be made the wealth and ties it to escape from darkness hereafter.
teaches: The Kural gives the reason grace outranks goods, and the fragment gives the practice and its fruit, turning a valuation into a command with an afterlife reward the couplet does not mention.

note: Both trace meat back to a price: the Kural says no one would sell flesh if no one killed for eating, the Valayapathi says the eater's craving sets a price at which the trapper kills and sells.
teaches: The Kural makes the buyer answerable for the seller's killing; the fragment adds the trapper's own interest in more deaths, so the guilt runs both ways through the one price.

note: The Naladiyar makes the flesh-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Valayapathi, through rebirth, makes the beasts eaten the eater's own kin.
teaches: Put together, the eater's belly becomes a burning ground for his own relatives: the fragment supplies the kinship the quatrain's image lacks, and the quatrain supplies the funeral the fragment's argument implies.

note: Both tell of a man whom desire strips of shame and standing; the Kural's lover says it in his own voice as a loss of shame and manliness, the Valayapathi condemns it from outside as blame and stained fame.
teaches: The same loss is a lover's plea in the Kural and a moralist's charge in the fragment, so the pair shows the madal lover judged two ways: as one whose suffering should move his beloved, and as one whose reputation is ruined.

note: Kural 297 says unbroken truthfulness makes all other virtues unnecessary; verse 28 pairs giving up falsehood with practising dharma and promises a painless world for both.
teaches: Truth can be held as the whole of virtue or as one ornament worn with the rest; the fragment takes the second view and pays for it with a promise of the next world that the Kural does not make.

note: Both say rain falls at the chaste wife's word; the Kural makes it her one power, the Valayapathi sets it in a list of honours with the praise of country and town and credits it to what the learned of Koodal say.
teaches: Read beside the fragment, the Kural's single astonishing claim becomes an item of public reputation, cited on authority, so the rain is treated as the community's recognition of the wife rather than her private power.

note: Both rest on what the knowing say (என்ப; கூறினர் அறிந்தார்): Kural 330 reasons from a wretched life back to killing; verse 30 names the four states of birth as killing's issue.
teaches: The fragment supplies the cosmology, the Jain four states of birth, that the couplet's backward inference from suffering to killing needs but never states.

note: Both start from wealth that will not stay; Naladiyar 2 says share it at once, since it turns like a wheel, while verse 34 praises those who never wanted it.
teaches: The fleetingness of wealth supports two conclusions, the householder's 'give it while you have it' and the renouncer's 'never take it up', and the fragment chooses the more radical one.

note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; verse 35 grants that without wealth there is no living but adds that with it base men kill, and that it fails both this world and the next.
teaches: The fragment accepts the Kural's premise and then denies it its consolation: wealth is needed for life and still ruins it, so neither world is secured by it.

note: Both have grey hair as the sign and the staff as age's companion; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in infancy foreseeing grey, verse 36's speaker resolves only after forty, when grey has come.
teaches: The two measure renunciation by when it comes: the quatrain prizes foresight in childhood, while the fragment shows the ordinary case, a man who turns only when desire has already left him.

note: Naladiyar 183 bids one sow seed for the next life without confusion; verse 37 makes it a farmer's whole round, ploughing, sowing and watering, always and always.
teaches: Seed for the next life is not one act of sowing but a continuing labour, and the fragment spells out the farming year the quatrain compresses into a word.

note: Verse 38 repeats Kural 345 nearly word for word and adds two lines: while the body and ties remain, clinging karma drives the soul through many wombs.
teaches: The couplet's paradox, that even the body is too much for one who would end birth, gets its reason in the fragment: the body is where karma takes hold.

note: Kural 350 commands clinging to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; verse 39 says removing sin while still in attachment is washing blood with blood.
teaches: If the Kural's holding to the attachment-free one is itself an attachment, the fragment's simile denies that any attachment can cure another, so a release by devotion and a release by pure letting-go part here; the conflict depends on reading the Kural's பற்று as a real attachment.

note: Both use the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல், வெள்ளம் புதியது) for women's love; in the Naladiyar it is the courtesan's love that dries when the money stops, in the Valayapathi it is the new water the fish leave the old pond for.
teaches: The image changes its target: the Naladiyar confines the fickle flood to women whose love is bought, while the fragment turns it on any woman, even one with a perfect lover, so the charge moves from the market to the marriage.

note: Kural 377 says even hoarders of millions enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned; verse 42 says that without the seed of austerity the toil for wealth and pleasure bears nothing.
teaches: Both deny that effort alone secures enjoyment, but the Kural names an apportioning agent while the fragment puts the cause in one's own past austerity, a karma without a giver.

note: Kural 796 finds one benefit in ruin, that it measures one's kin; verse 45 shows that measure taken, the kin speaking as they please and standing out of reach.
teaches: The Kural turns desertion into knowledge for later choices, while the fragment gives the desertion without consolation, so the 'benefit' appears as what it costs.

note: Both deny that women can be kept by outward guarding; the Kural moves the guard inside the woman (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு), the Valayapathi says the learned found no guard at all.
teaches: The two share a premise, that confinement fails, and part on the conclusion: the Kural trusts the woman's own steadiness, the fragment trusts nothing, which shows that the Kural's inner guard is a choice and not the only way to read the failure of walls.

note: Both compare a courtesan's love to a river that fails with the rain; the Naladiyar's மாரி அறவே அறுமே and வாரி அறவே அறும் lie close to the Valayapathi's lines 3 and 1.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives only the ending, love cut off when income ends, while the fragment makes வாரி mean both flood and income and adds the rise, so the love is shown swelling with the wealth as precisely as it dries.

note: The Naladiyar's wife sets her ever-renewed shyness against women who join many chests for wealth; the Valayapathi says those women serve their payers like பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்.
teaches: Together they put the difference between wife and courtesan not in the service given, which the fragment says can look the same, but in what the Naladiyar's wife names: a shyness that never wears off and a bond that wealth did not buy.

note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; Valayapathi 61 calls begetting children and keeping household dharma the chief virtue, and a life with deceitful women barren.
teaches: The fragment turns the Kural's praise of children into an argument against the courtesan: her union is measured by the household's fruit, children, and found to yield nothing.

note: Kural 1047: one whose poverty has no virtue is looked on as a stranger even by his mother; Valayapathi 63: without wealth, a man's women disregard him, his kin shrink, and his own children will not cling.
teaches: The Kural limits its harsh rule to poverty without அறம் and names only the mother, while the fragment drops the limit and extends the desertion to wife, kin and children, which shows how far the claim reaches once its moral condition is removed.

note: Both say the poor man's well-founded words fail: the Kural's சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும், the Valayapathi's learning that goes புல்லென்று.
teaches: The Kural says only that the poor man's meaning goes slack; the fragment names who lets it, the discerning assembly of the good, and carries the loss from his speech to the learning he teaches.

note: The Naladiyar's bees do not go to the hill when the kanthal is not in flower; the Valayapathi's birds circle a fruiting tree and leave it when it falls.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows only the loss, that the poor have no kin, while the fragment adds the converse, a servant with food surrounded and a noble without it deserted, so the pair shows wealth outranking birth in both directions.

note: Kural 160 ranks those who fast below those who bear harsh words; Valayapathi 66 calls a vow (நோன்பு) without forbearance (பொறைமை) darkness.
teaches: The Kural only ranks fasting below forbearance, but the fragment makes forbearance the condition without which a vow is worthless, a stronger claim that turns a ranking into a dependence.

note: Kural 249 likens virtue done without அருள் to a confused man seeing the truth; Valayapathi 66 lists அருள்இல் அறன் among four goods it calls darkness put inside darkness.
teaches: The Kural makes graceless virtue a single paradox, while the fragment sets it in a series with a vow without forbearance, a lineage without wealth and a kingdom without ministers, so grace appears as one of several enabling conditions without which a good is void.

note: Both make women's faultless time short; the Naladiyar says even under a guard of swords, the Valayapathi says only while the man who cherishes them is watching.
teaches: On whether watching helps, the two disagree: for the fragment, the provider's gaze buys a brief steadiness, while for the quatrain even armed guard does not, so the fragment's distrust is milder in what it allows surveillance to achieve.

note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the corpse; Valayapathi 70 says the heart, though it sees the adorned hair burn, is still bewildered.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats delight in adornment as ignorance that the sight of the corpse would cure, while the fragment's heart has already seen the burning and is bewildered still, so the pair separates not knowing the body's end from knowing it to no effect.

note: Both prize children; the Kural ranks children who come to understanding above all gains, the Valayapathi makes a child the thing without which wealth is like a garland without scent.
teaches: The pairing shows two grounds for the same praise: the Kural values the child for its own understanding, the fragment for completing a householder's estate, so the fragment's child is an ornament of wealth and the Kural's a good in itself.

note: Both single out the tongue as what must be guarded above all; the Kural's tongue is speech, the Valayapathi counts it among the five senses and makes it lead to hell.
teaches: Placing the tongue among the senses lets the fragment's warning cover taste as well as speech, so the Kural's rule about words is widened into a rule about appetite, which the fragments' verses on flesh then fill.

note: In Akananuru 369 the foster mother laments that her girl refused the rich wedding her kin had prepared and went off across the waste with a youth; Gunamalai, told by her nurse of a match with a rich cousin, names death or penance as her only alternatives.
teaches: Beside the Akam girl who answers an unwanted family wedding by elopement, Gunamalai answers by a vow spoken to her nurse, keeping the refusal inside the house where it can move her parents instead of leaving them.

note: Kalittokai 11 gives the three tender creatures of the burning waste: the tusker who lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate with its wings, the stag that gives its shadow to the shadeless doe; 1187-1188 give the elephant shielding its calf, the cock bird sheltering the hen with its wings, and the stag shading the doe with its body.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the palai triad but changes its use: in the Kalittokai the creatures' care is the heroine's ground for hoping the man will return, while here it only measures the heat for a lone traveller with no beloved at home, so the akam sign of love becomes a road-guide's warning.

note: In both the man asks bees to judge whether any flower matches the woman, and both name her teeth and hair.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kuruntokai's appeal to the bee as the expert in flowers but asks about her teeth against the mullai, and its bees already live in her hair, so the witness the Sangam poem sends out to the flowers has been drawn inside the woman's own beauty.

note: In the Kuruntokai poem the woman prays that even when this life turns into the next he may be her husband; the epic's narrator calls the couple's love one joined through seven births.
teaches: What the akam speaker can only pray for, the epic narrator states as fact, yet ten verses later the hero leaves this bride in the night, so the seven-birth bond in the epic marks the depth of love without securing its continuance.

note: Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves her for wealth across the waste, then wealth alone is wealth and grace exists nowhere; Civakan's saying makes leaving for deeds and wealth a man's duty and staying a woman's.
teaches: The Sangam woman's voice hears the man's going for wealth as the end of grace, while the epic puts the same convention in the hero's mouth as a duty, and uses it, untruly, to cover a departure that is neither for work nor for wealth.

note: In both a hen swan is misled by a reflection in the water.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the hen swan runs to the moon's reflection thinking it her mate and is shamed when he appears, an image of a wife who welcomes a straying husband; in the epic the hen takes her own reflection for a rival and sulks, so the same mistake that there yields shame here yields jealousy of herself.

note: Both console a waiting woman by saying the flowers have been fooled by a false rain; in the epic the thunder is an elephant's trumpet and the song is overheard by warriors.
teaches: The akam friend's denial that the season has come is lifted whole into the epic and read by men as an omen that their lord lives, so a love convention becomes a sign in a war story.

note: In Akananuru 289 a wife waiting for her husband prays at each chirp of the lizard; here Vijayai reads the lizard's call, a dream and a throbbing eye as signs of her son.
teaches: The lizard omen of the akam wife waiting for her lover is given to a widowed mother in an ascetic's robe, showing that the epic carries the akam signs of reunion over to a son.

note: Kuruntokai 40's lover marvels that strangers' hearts mingled like rain and red earth; Civakan asks whether the woman who took his heart with one look knew him in a former birth.
teaches: Facing the same mystery of a stranger's sudden hold, the Sangam lover lets the merging stand without cause, while the Jain epic's hero reaches for a past birth, so the pair shows rebirth entering the love lyric as an explanation.

note: In Kuruntokai 333 the friend asks what harm there would be in revealing their secret; in the epic the girl discloses it to her friend, who carries it to the foster mother, then the mother, then the father.
teaches: The Sangam friend only proposes disclosure; the epic plays out the whole chain of telling through friend, foster mother and mother to the father, which ends in marriage the same day.

note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of rice, sand, lamps, water poured with petals and paddy by four mothers, and the kin giving the bride; the epic father gives his daughter before the fire with a dowry he announces.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam wedding, which names no fire and no dowry, the epic's gift before the flame with women, gold and villages shows the giving of a bride recast as a fire rite with property declared.

note: The Akananuru man remembers a wedding of sand spread under a pandal, lamps and garlands at an auspicious dawn; the Cintamani's order has plantain and areca, aloe pots, lute and dance and golden flags across the city.
teaches: The same wedding adornments grow from a household's sand pandal to a king's command that the whole city be decked, and so show how rank changes the scale and not the parts.

note: In the Kalittokai the herd girl is cried as the prize of whoever takes the fighting bull, and the taker himself has her; here the herd chief's daughter is the prize for recovering the herd, and the winner passes her to a friend.
teaches: The epic keeps the mullai custom of a herd girl won by a public feat, but moves the feat from the herders' bull-pen to a prince's war and lets the prize be transferred, which the bull-catch, where the girl goes to the man who wrestled, does not allow.

note: In Akananuru 18 the friend tells the lover that if her friend suffers harm for a single day she will not live after; in 976 Gunamalai's companion, facing the elephant, resolves that it should kill her together with her mistress.
teaches: The akam friend's stock claim that her life hangs on the heroine's is put to the test in the epic by a real beast, and the companion keeps it, so the convention is shown as a loyalty that can be acted on.

note: In Kalittokai 103 a herdsman wrenching a charging bull by the ear is likened to Mayon tearing the horse's jaw, and the herd girls will embrace only one who falls between the killer bull's horns; in 984 Civakan facing the elephant is likened to the gem-coloured lord facing the elephant sent to kill him, and Gunamalai's love follows.
teaches: Both poems make the man who masters a charging beast a Krishna figure whom a girl then loves, but the herders' bull-catch is a set contest whose price the community names, while the epic's rescue is unplanned and the girl chooses for herself.

note: The akam heroine asks that, when this life turns into the next, the same man be her husband and she the one close to his heart; the goddess tells Manimekalai that exactly this has come about, her heart still bound to her former husband, and calls it seed falling on scorched saline ground.
teaches: The bond across births that the akam poem asks for as the highest pledge of love is, in the Buddhist epic, the very danger to the merit that would end births, so the same wish is fulfilled and judged a loss.

note: The Akananuru remembers Cheralathan who carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped tribute at Maanthai; the epic's Chera of the carved bow feeds Buddhist sages in a Vanji grove. The Tamil shares only the epithet of the carved bow and the Chera line, not a name.
teaches: Holding them together shows the epic borrowing a Sangam conqueror's epithet to give Vanji's Buddhism a royal founder, turning the king remembered for hoarded tribute into a king remembered for a gift to monks.

note: The Ainkurunuru friend asks whether it is a kindness if the old velan of an unerring tradition casts his beads and says the girl's sickness is Murugu; the epic's old wise woman of the clan's ancient duty, possessed, declares Kannaki divine and Kannaki calls it confusion.
teaches: In the akam convention the possessed diviner of an old line is the one who gets it wrong, mistaking love for a god's seizure, while in the epic the possessed old woman's word is the true one and the hearer's doubt is the mistake, so the pairing shows the epic reversing the Sangam irony about divination to make it carry prophecy.

note: The Kalittokai's herders open their bull-catch by praising the Pandya who removed the tiger and the bow and set his fish in their place; the epic's herders open their kuravai on the Pandya whose fish is inscribed on the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow.
teaches: The same herders' praise of the Pandya emblem is kept in the epic but with the boast of conquest removed, so a work that follows all three kingdoms keeps the mullai custom of beginning with the king while setting the three emblems side by side.

note: Kalittokai 104 ends its herders' kuravai by praising the god of the ancient bright discus and wishing that the world take the one word of the Pandya with the thunder-loud drum; the epic's kuravai to the discus-holder (கதிர்திகிரி, line 99) ends in the same wish for the Pandya's drum.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam mullai close, god first and then the Pandya's drum, but moves the kuravai from the joy after the bull-catch to a rite against ill omens, so the inherited blessing now carries dread rather than celebration.

note: Both pledge a herd girl to the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, takes it (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான்); in the Kalittokai her kin give her to the catcher, in the epic no bull is penned.
teaches: The epic keeps the bull-catch pledge word for word but drops the contest, so a herders' marriage custom survives as the names of dance roles in a rite against ill omen.

note: Both tell of the husband of Karikal's line seized by the Kaveri flood at a festival; the akam poem leaves him taken, the epic has the sea bring him back to the wife who followed.
teaches: The Sangam memory of a lover lost to the river, which an akam courtesan uses as an image of a man taken away for good, is completed in the epic with a restoration won by the wife's steadfastness, turning a story of loss into an exemplum of chastity's power.

note: Akananuru 127 credits Cheralathan with driving off the sea-foe, cutting the kadamba and carving his bow on the Himalaya; the kuravai's closing blessing hails the king of the Kudavar who ruled Kolli and the Himalaya where the bow was carved.
teaches: A deed the akam poem ties to one named Chera becomes, in the epic's blessing, an epithet of the reigning king of the Kudavar without a name, which shows a Sangam memory turned into a dynastic title; the Tamil does not say the two kings are one.

note: In Kuruntokai 111 the mother takes the velan's word that Neduvel caused the girl's sickness, and the friend wants the lover to come so the household may see a great laugh (பெருநகை); here the friend's refrain is இதுநகையாகின்றே over the same mistake.
teaches: The laugh at the mother's misreading, a friend's private aside in the short poem, becomes the sung refrain of a public round dance, which shows the old akam situation turned into communal performance.

note: Natrinai 34's friend tells Murugan that, knowing the sickness is not his seizure, he came to the veri house at the velan's call, and so, though a god, he is truly foolish (மடவை மன்ற); the kuravai ranks the god as more foolish than the velan if he comes.
teaches: The single daring address to the god in the Sangam poem becomes a graded series (the velan foolish, the god more so) sung inside a hymn to the same god's spear, so the mockery of his coming to the rite sits beside praise of his power without contradiction.

note: Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that the one who afflicted the girl is not Vel, lord of their valli forest; the friend here tells the lover that he comes with kadamba and spear but has no six faces, no peacock and no kurava bride.
teaches: The Sangam friend's bare denial that the god caused the sickness is worked out here as a point-by-point comparison of the man with the god's attributes, which shows the denial leaning on an iconography of Murugan already settled.

note: Both have women parted from their lovers at evening (காதலر்ப் பிரிந்த, nearly the same half-line), and both liken their breath to air blown in a smith's furnace.
teaches: The epic takes a Sangam paalai heroine's evening lament nearly verbatim and turns it from one woman's crisis into a class of Puhar's women, one entry in a survey of the city's nights.

note: Both use the phrase of Karikal 'taking the cool water' (தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் / தண்பதம் கொண்டு): in the Akananuru a courtesan recalls how at Karikal's water festival at Kazhar the Kaveri carried off the dancer Atthi, and likens her lover's loss to it; the epic likens the joyful crowd on the shore to the first day of that festival.
teaches: The festival the epic uses as a simile of joy is, in the Sangam poem, the scene of a dancer lost and a courtesan abandoned, which is what this shore day will become for Madhavi.

note: In the Ainkurunuru the wife begins to push away her husband's chest, broad as the Kaveri's full flood, in sulking; in the vari the Kaveri herself is the wife who never sulks at the Chola's other unions.
teaches: The Sangam marutham gives the Kaveri's flood to the straying husband and lets the wife sulk at it, while the epic song makes the river the wife and her not sulking the highest chastity, so the same river image moves from licensing the wife's oodal to forbidding it.

note: In the Ainkurunuru the friend says the girl's sickness is not the ford-spirit's doing but the man's oath; Madhavi's heroine asks the sea god not to punish the false oath sworn in the grove.
teaches: Both rest on the belief that a water deity punishes a false love-oath, but where the Sangam friend turns that belief against the man, the epic's heroine asks the god to spare him, so the same belief serves blame in one and loyal forgiveness in the other.

note: The Akananuru friend asks the lord of the shore whether the oath he swore when his chariot crushed the girls' sand dolls was false too, with the sea as witness; the vari asks how simple girls could know that the man who swore by the sea god would break it.
teaches: The pair shows the epic lifting the neithal friend's charge, an oath with the sea as witness and the girls' sand-play spoiled, out of the courtship plot where it pressed for marriage and into a sung entertainment, where the charge of broken faith is performed by the man who will himself walk out at the song's end.

note: In the akam poem the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for her husband because he is a deceiving philanderer (மாயப் பரத்தன்); here the man refuses the go-between sent by the courtesan because her love is a dancer's art.
teaches: The epic stages a marutham refusal of the go-between with the roles turned round, so that the charge of false love the convention lets the wife bring against the man is brought by the man against the courtesan.

note: The fragment takes over Kuruntokai 17's palm-horse, erukku garland, jeering street and heartwood-hard love, and adds baseness, possession and disease.
teaches: The same four acts that the Sangam lover names as love's compulsion, in his own voice, become in a renunciant work the symptoms of a sickness to be avoided: the change of speaker is what changes the verdict.

note: In Akananuru 151 the woman reports the man's reason that the poor cannot support dependents or laugh among kin, and says his heart has set grace aside; verse 44 gives the same reason, feeding kin's hunger, as one no one could fault.
teaches: The argument for leaving to earn wealth is the same in both, but the akam poem lets the one left behind weigh it against grace, while the fragment's voice treats it as needing no answer.

note: Paripadal 12 has Madurai dress, perfume itself and mount she-elephants, horses and chariots in a rush to meet the Vaiyai flood; the Cintamani's city sets out with litters, elephants and carts for its spring water-play by the river.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam river festival's order of dressing, mounting and rushing to the bank, but its festival honours no river or god, and is likened instead to the Jina's assembly, so the old civic rite is re-made as pure pleasure under a renouncer's image.

note: Paripadal 6 sets the river play out as a battle array, with bathers drilling rivalry 'as in war' and carrying syringes (சிவிறியர்); in 966 the bathers spray with syringes (சிவிறி) and the play goes through a campaign's whole course, the enemy's back seen, the offender fined with garlands, tribute taken.
teaches: The Sangam festival's figure of water-play as battle is carried by the epic from the array to the victory and its exactions, and set just before a real terror breaks out (973), so the mock war of desire gives way to a true danger.

note: The Paripadal fragment asks whether Madurai's fame can ever prove false as long as the Vaigai flows; the epic calls the Vaigai the never-failing (பொய்யா) creeper of the clan and has her hide her tears for the wife the city will wrong.
teaches: The Paripadal makes the flowing Vaigai the pledge that Madurai's fame cannot fail; the epic keeps the river unfailing but makes her the first to know that the city's justice will fail, so the pledge passes from the city to the river alone.

note: Paripadal 3 says the god is everything and the essence within everything and calls him one full of maayam (மாயமார் அனையை); the kuravai asks whether the churner of the sea bound by Asodhai's churning rope is maayam, for it bewilders.
teaches: The hymn treats the god's maayam as a doctrine to be stated, his being all things at once, while the herdswomen meet it as an unanswered question in a domestic scene, so the same paradox is shown both as learned theology and as village wonder.

note: Paripadal 5 praises the spear that cut Sur's mango in the sea and split the crane-named mountain and says the velan's praises and veri are neither true nor false; the kuravai names the same crane-mountain killer and calls him foolish if he comes to the velan's rite.
teaches: Both texts hold the god's deeds fixed while keeping the velan's rite at a distance: the hymn suspends judgement on the rite, and the kuravai laughs at it, which shows that doubt about the diviner was compatible with full praise of Murugan.

note: In Paripadal 19 maidens who do not eat the leftover of the god's elephant at Parankunram fail to win husbands; the hill girls pray to Murugan not for marriage in general but that their friend be spared another's match and given her own lover.
teaches: The temple poem treats Murugan as giver of husbands to all maidens who honour him, while the kuravai bends the same belief to the akam crisis of the secret union, asking him to prevent the family's match.

note: Boothappandiyan swears that if he does not see his enemies' backs he may be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that if he does not live with Gunamalai he may be one who turned his weapon on the beaten.
teaches: The vanjinam form stakes one domain against the other in both directions: the king pledges his marriage to secure a victory, and the epic hero pledges his warrior honour to secure a marriage, choosing as penalty an attack on fleeing men, the very thing the king's vow hopes to see.

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, and the speakers neither rejoice that life is sweet nor curse it as bitter; Civakan is freed by a god yet calls the freeing his own former deed and feels neither joy nor grief.
teaches: The pair shows the Sangam sage's 'not from others' being kept even when the rescue plainly does come from another: the epic folds the rescuer into the hero's own deed, the dog he once helped.

note: Purananuru 35 tells the Chola his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects, and warns him the world blames kings when things go wrong; 159 says Saccandan's umbrella already shades the world like a father.
teaches: The Sangam poet gives the umbrella as a duty the king must be urged to keep, the epic as a state already achieved; set together, the epic's praise lacks the warning that the story will soon need.

note: Purananuru 56 equates the Pandya with four gods, one for each of his powers; 160 equates Saccandan with Dharma, Varuna, Death, Vaman and Kama.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam form of measuring a king god by god but shifts it from war powers to grace, giving and beauty, and puts the god of desire in the list, which the story makes the king's flaw.

note: Puram 246's queen rejects the widow's austerities and chooses the pyre; Nandattan names penance and the fire as two equal courses for a widow.
teaches: Where the Sangam queen ranks the fire above the hard widow's life, the Jain epic's speaker leaves the two as alternatives, so the pair shows the choice the queen made was one of two recognised paths.

note: Pisirandhaiyar and many others sit fasting with the Chola; Buddhisenan would follow Civakan in death, but only after vengeance and without knowing he is dead.
teaches: Against the Purananuru's companions who die beside a living king by his own choice, the epic's vow to follow a lord in death rests on an unverified death and a killing first, and the next verse checks it.

note: The Puram queen refuses to be one of the widows who go unanointed, eat cooked leaves and sleep on gravel, and chooses the pyre; Vijayai lives that very widow's life, unanointed, on greens (354), as a Jain ascetic.
teaches: The life the Sangam queen scorns as the wretched alternative to the pyre is the one the Jain epic gives its queen as a penance lived for a son, so the two show the widow's choice valued in opposite ways.

note: Neduncheliyan swears that if he fails to take the kings who scorned him, the poets led by Mangudi Marutan may cease to sing of his land; Civakan swears that if he fails to bring the raiders to bow before the king, his name may not go out in the world of song.
teaches: The epic keeps the Purananuru's vanjinam form, a war vow whose penalty is the loss of poets' praise, but its hero swears it for another man's king and against raiders who prove to be his friends, so the oath of fame becomes a set piece the plot quietly empties.

note: 1919 counts taking the daughters of hill and forest chiefs as the settled custom of kings whose rule stands; Purananuru 336 shows a king hot for a girl whose father will not give her, and the war that waits on it.
teaches: The epic's 'custom' is the king's side of a transaction that the Purananuru shows from the chief's side as a demand refused and a battle coming, so the policy's cost becomes visible.

note: Purananuru 20 says the Chera's guard is not shaken by omen birds coming or going; in the usurper's palace owls cry by day, blood rains and earth and sky shake.
teaches: Read together the two make portents a measure of rule: the praised king's realm is not shaken whatever the birds do, while the usurper's palace is shaken by every sign, though the epic does not itself say his usurpation is the cause.

note: The Purananuru poet asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short of ruin when it saw women made widows beat their breasts and shear their hair; the Cintamani names the widows' lost adornment as what the hero's spear will bring.
teaches: In the Sangam poem the sight of widows is what checks the spear, while in the epic the widows are counted in advance as the spear's work, so the pair shows grief for the enemy's women moving from a limit on war to its foreseen price.

note: In Puram 19 Death itself runs away ashamed from the field where mothers of old houses weep over their sons; in 2233 the Earth goddess, unable to look at the cruelty, veils herself in a red blanket of blood.
teaches: Both poems make a cosmic power recoil from the field, but the Sangam poem turns the recoil into praise of the king's valour, while the epic gives it to the Earth the hero fights to win, so the prize cannot bear the war waged for her.

note: Puram 26 praises a Pandya who cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for the hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in 2235 the slain warriors themselves are the ghoul-woman's feast, their wedding garlands replaced by entrails.
teaches: The Sangam battlefield-feast is the victor's rite and his glory, while the Cintamani tells it from the side of the slain, as bridegrooms whose wedding garlands become entrails.

note: The Pandya Kudumi warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Vipulan will not strike beasts, the wounded, the young or the old.
teaches: Both armies spare the weak, but on different grounds: the Purananuru's warning is the way of right (அறத்துஆறு) protecting those who cannot fight, while the epic grounds each refusal in the striker's own glory, so the same restraint can rest on dharma or on pride.

note: Purananuru 287 says warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the higher world; in 2265 the slain challenger is showered with flowers by celestial women and reaches heaven.
teaches: The Purananuru's reward is promised to one's own unflinching men to steady them; the epic grants it on the field to an enemy killed by the hero's companion, so the heaven of the brave is shown to belong to the fallen of either side.

note: Purananuru 290 tells a king to give toddy to the warrior whose forefathers died for his, because he will shield the king from the spear; the epic's warrior says it is for a day like this that lords keep their men.
teaches: The two show the same exchange of sustenance for service from both ends: the Sangam poet urges the lord to pay in advance, and the epic's warrior, arming, counts himself as that payment falling due.

note: In Purananuru 284 a warrior straightens his twisted sword with an elephant's tusk as lever (மிறையாக ... திருத்தா) and laughs at the fleeing back; Salanidhi straightens his elephant-bent sword in a lever (மிறைக்கொளீஇ திருத்துவான்) and the kings flee.
teaches: The pair shows the epic taking over a Sangam war vignette in its own words, the sword-straightening and the enemy's flight, but turning the Sangam hero's laugh into the foe's fear and making the man a spear-pierced warrior who dies in the next verse.

note: The Purananuru poem says warriors who stand under arrows care nothing for fields because, dying, they wed flawless women in the high world; Ariccandan offers the same heavenly women (கடியரமகளிர்) and adds the poets' praise and the hero-stone.
teaches: The pairing shows the Sangam promise of heavenly brides surviving into the Jain epic as a commander's rallying formula, now stacked with fame and stone into a three-world reward, while the following verse turns its hearers into food for the hero's arrows.

note: Boothappandiyan's vow wishes on himself, if he fails, separation from his wife, a weak sceptre and the loss of friends; Kattiyangaran's vow wishes on himself fear of his wife and the shame of slighting a guest.
teaches: Both are conditional self-curses whose penalties are drawn from household and court rather than the field, so the pair shows the vanjinam form keeping its structure into the epic while the epic gives it to the losing usurper, who dies at once.

note: Kalladanar asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short when he saw the widows of his enemies beating their breasts and cutting their hair; Civakan's anger stops at the usurper's death and he offers the widows a living in the city or gold to leave with.
teaches: Where the Sangam poem praises the conqueror only for holding back his spear at the sight of the widows, the epic makes restraint into provision, the victor feeding or endowing the women his war has widowed.

note: Purananuru 194 sets the dirge drum in one house beside the wedding drum in another and concludes that the maker of the world is unkind; in 2356 one band of women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a sea of joy on the same morning, while the hero washes his face.
teaches: The epic puts the Puram poet's split world of grief and joy inside one palace and makes one man's victory its cause, so what the Sangam poet blames on the world's maker is shown here as the plain consequence of a deed.

note: Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king, so it is the king's duty to know he is its life; 246 puts kings above the gods.
teaches: The Purananuru turns the king's exalted place into a duty laid on the king, while Dharmadattan turns it into a ban laid on the subject who would harm him.

note: Anangamalai pleads that she not be left outside the shade of Civakan's white umbrella, which she calls the shade of dharma; Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects who may come to him for justice.
teaches: The Sangam poem tells a king to keep his umbrella for the sufferer, and the epic shows a sufferer actually using it, which puts the claim to the test of whether a king's sheltering reaches a woman's private petition.

note: 2831 says merit is measured by the gift as iron takes water in proportion to its heating, a gift for the next birth; Purananuru 134 says Ay is no trader who buys virtue with gifts for the next life.
teaches: The verse sets a gift's reward in an exact ledger, and the Sangam poem names that ledger as what its patron does not do.

note: 2907 sets the elephant fed balls of ripe paddy against the elephant that grazes the field and perishes; Purananuru 184 uses the same two elephants for a king who takes his due against one who grabs.
teaches: Both poets reach for the fed and the loose elephant, and the epic puts the old Sangam figure in the mouth of a king handing on power.

note: 2908 says that of rice and water, both life, the king is the world's good life; Purananuru 186 says neither rice nor water is life, the wide world lives by its king.
teaches: The poem makes the king life by denying that rice and water are, while the epic keeps them as lives and adds the king beside them.

note: 2909 compares a king to a driver who must know the ground his chariot runs on; Purananuru 185 compares the realm to a cart that sinks if its driver cannot steer.
teaches: Both set a skilled driver against one who does not know the way, and the epic ties the skill to knowing the land.

note: Puram 62 ends with the gods of the unfading flowers receiving many guests from a field where two kings died; 291 says the dead king became a guest of the gods, adding the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal.
teaches: The Jain epic keeps the Sangam honour of the fallen king as heaven's guest but makes devotion to the Jina part of his passage, so the warrior's heaven is re-founded on religion.

note: Perunkoppendu argues against the elders that the widow's life of plain food and gravel beds is not for her and the pyre is a lotus pool; Saccandan's women make the same choice in a simile and a vow of the other world, without the argument.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam queen's reasoned refusal, the epic's wives choose death as a group and by figure alone, while the one queen who must live, Vijayai, is spared the choice by her unborn son.

note: 3044 has King Senikan call for a feast to the Jina's feet with kings gathered; Purananuru 134 has a patron who does not give to buy merit for the next birth.
teaches: The king's feast here is made an act of worship whose fruit the next lines of the work will tell, and so the poem's patron who gives without bargaining is set against it.

note: Purananuru 359 gives the burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and ghoul-women dancing by pyre lamps that has received even conquerors; 309 has jackals as drums, pyres as lamps, ghosts dancing and owls praising at a prince's birth.
teaches: The same creatures and lights that in the Sangam poem greet the end of kings serve in the epic as the band and lamps of a future king's birth, turning a warning about death into a grim birth-festival.

note: In Purananuru 253 a wife whose husband fell asks how she can go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles; in 351 Vijayai breaks her own bangles in a hermitage among ascetic women.
teaches: The widow's bare hand, which the Sangam wife dreads as a sign shown before her kin, becomes in the Jain epic an act the widow performs herself as part of an ascetic initiation among strangers.

note: Perunkoppendu refuses the widow's life of plain food, gravel bed and no ghee and chooses the pyre; Vijayai refuses the milk offered her and takes up a widow's diet of greens in the forest.
teaches: The diet the Sangam queen calls the lot of wretched widows and rejects for death is accepted by the epic's queen and renamed divinity (வனத்து உறை தெய்வம்), which shows how the Jain frame revalues the widow's abstinence the heroic poem despised.

note: In Purananuru 248 the white water lily that was a girl's garment becomes the alli a widow eats; in 355 the stamens of ripe water lilies and wild rice dry in the hermitage courtyard as Vijayai's food.
teaches: The water lily carries the widow's fall from adornment to bare food in both poems, but in the epic the lily-food sits beside a nursing calf that sends her thoughts to her son, so the widow's diet is joined to a mother's longing the Sangam widow does not have.

note: The Pandya's war proclamation in Puram 9 tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to get clear before battle; Civakan names cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins as those he must protect.
teaches: The same list of the protected is in the Sangam poem those a king spares from his own arrows, and in the epic those a warrior must defend from another's raid, so the duty widens from restraint to rescue.

note: The Purananuru's warrior, with no chariot and no forest fort, watched the enemy's herd go, counted it and turned it with his bow (சிலையின் மாற்றியோனே); Civakan turns the herd by the bow's twang alone (சிலையின் னொலியால் தொறு மீட்டு).
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam feat of turning a herd with the bow but removes even the drawn arrow and gives the deed to a city's darling, so a poor warrior's unsung skill becomes a prince's proof of worth before the town.

note: In the Purananuru poem a king's demand for a girl her father will not give brings war on the town, and the mother who reared her beauty is blamed; here kings rise to seize a bride already won in an open contest.
teaches: The epic removes the father's refusal that drives the Sangam bride-war, since the bride's father set a fair contest and she has chosen, so the suitors' war stands as bare lust and the blame moves from the girl's rearing to the kings and their instigator.

note: Purananuru 369 sings the Chera's battle as a season of tillage, arrows for rain, heads for crop, ghouls threshing; 757 uses the same sowing-and-harvest field, with ghosts fed on flesh and blood, as a warning to rivals before the fight.
teaches: The bard's after-battle praise image, sung to earn a gift, becomes in the epic a combatant's threat spoken before a blow is struck, so the convention moves from rewarding a victory to predicting one.

note: In Purananuru 71 the Pandya swears that if he does not see the backs (புறம்) of the kings who have joined against him, may he be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that unless he sees the kings' backs (புறக்கொடை) and embraces the lady, may his name perish.
teaches: The vow keeps the Sangam form, allied kings and the sight of their backs, but moves the woman from the forfeit to the prize: the Pandya risks his wife, Civakan stakes his name to win a bride.

note: Purananuru 369 sings the battlefield as a harvest where the ghoul-woman holds the corpses and jackals thresh, and the bard asks the king for a gift; in 804 ghouls already fed sing over what was given them.
teaches: The epic hands the bard's role to the ghouls: in the Puram poem the singer asks for a share of the field, while here the scavengers have had their share and their song is thanks, so the field is a patron's gift completed.

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, we neither delight in life nor call it bitter, since life moves by its order like a raft on a river; Kundalakesi 18 says what is due comes, so the wise neither grieve nor exult.
teaches: The Sangam poet draws from the same certainty a rule about others, neither marvelling at the great nor despising the small; the fragment draws only the inner rule, so the pair shows one premise yielding a social ethic in one book and a private discipline in the other.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that food makes the body (உண்டி முதற்றே உணவின் பிண்டம்), so those who bind water to land give body and life, and bids him build tanks; the goddess uses the same phrase, the body is a lump of food, to give Manimekalai a mantra that cuts off her own hunger.
teaches: The same maxim drives two answers to hunger: the Sangam poet makes it a king's duty to feed a people by irrigation, the epic turns it into an ascetic's private release from hunger, the first step before the bowl that will feed others.

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya king that those who give food give life (உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே) and that land waiting on the sky does not serve its ruler, so he must build tanks; Deepathilakai gives the same line (96) after a famine ended only by a god's rain.
teaches: The maxim moves from a king's public works to a renunciant's alms-bowl, and the remedy for a failing sky moves from tanks a ruler digs to a god's gift and a bowl that never empties.

note: Puram 173 praises Pannan's house, where the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) sounds like birds in a fruiting tree, as the home of the doctor of hunger; the epic uses the fruit-tree birds for the crowd at Aputhiran's hall (26 to 27), then tells how the hall's noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவம், 60) fell silent once rain removed hunger.
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise of a patron's noisy kitchen and shows its condition: the sound that proves a giver's fame lasts only as long as others are hungry, so the doctor of hunger is unmade by a world without the disease.

note: In the Purananuru poem the bard hears the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) at Pannan's house and asks where the house of the physician of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்) is; the epic closes with the same noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி, 97) at the public hall, after Kayasandigai has called Manimekalai physician of life (மருத்துவி, 15).
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam scene of the hunger-healer's feast word for word but moves it from a patron's house, reached by a bard's praise, to a public hall with a gate open to all where anyone who will receive is called in.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that those who give food give life and urges him to build tanks; the disguised girl tells the Chola her bowl is life-medicine for embodied beings and asks him to give the prison to the righteous.
teaches: Both poems set a counsellor before a king to teach that feeding is giving life, but the Sangam poet asks for waterworks that bring fame and the other world, while the epic's beggar asks the king to give up a prison, so the duty to feed passes from royal works to a renouncer's bowl the king only endorses.

note: The Purananuru poet names the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort as a deed so great that killing is no longer the living Chola's own fame; Manimekalai's opening makes the hanging-fort Chola the founder of Puhar's festival of Indra.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the epic taking a Sangam war-memory of the Chola line and turning it into a sacred charter, so that a city's yearly rite rests on an ancestor's feat rather than on the reigning king.

note: Both give the rite of laying a king who died of sickness on darbha grass and cutting him with a sword with the words 'go where the warriors go' (செல்வுழிச் செல்க in both); Avvai uses it to praise Athiyaman's battle wounds, Vasanthavai to console and rebuke a queen whose son died in neither war nor old age.
teaches: Held together they show the rite outliving its Sangam use as praise: in the epic it becomes the standard by which a dead prince is found wanting, so that the warrior code is used to stop a mother's grief rather than to honour a king.

note: Puram 189 measures every man's need, king or hunter, by one measure of food and two cloths and concludes that wealth's use is giving; Manimekalai tells the king that dharma for all lives is nothing but food, clothing and shelter.
teaches: The Sangam measure of human need, used to tell a rich man to give, becomes the entire content of a king's dharma toward every life, and the king at once extends it to other kingdoms.

note: Puram 186 says the world lives not by rice or water but by its king, who must know he is its life; the minister tells the king that if he leaves, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone (110 to 111).
teaches: The Sangam duty that a king know himself the world's life becomes, in a Buddhist epic, the argument that holds a king back from renunciation, so the poem's maxim sets a limit even on seeking release.

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan went through the forests to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the stone, the Ganga crossing and the defeat of Kanaka and Vijaya.
teaches: The pair shows the stone-taking already fixed as the defining deed of this Chera in two different kinds of text, and shows the Manimekalai using that known deed only to date and dignify the city where its own Buddhist story continues.
