note: Perunkoppendu tells the elders holding her back that for her, her husband dead, a lotus pond and the pyre's fire are one, and scorns the widow's life of sparse food and bare ground; Madhavi's second kind of pathini enters the blazing fire as into a cool-water pool, and her third wears the body down in vows.
teaches: The queen's single act of defiance, in which the pyre is a cool pond and the austere widowhood she refuses is worse than fire, becomes in the epic a ranked typology of the chaste wife where entering the fire is only the second kind and the vowed austerity she despised is admitted as the third, and all three are then set beneath Kannaki.

note: The Purananuru poem says the world endures because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Sudhamathi calls the Buddha one who lives not for himself but belongs to others (தனக்கு என வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam formula for a class of honourable men who hold the world up and makes it the mark of one being whose living for others is the turning of the dharma wheel, moving the ideal from social honour to religious compassion.

note: The Purananuru poem describes the same burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and dancing demon women, which has taken even conquerors, and urges the patron to give freely and win lasting fame; the goddess draws from it that revelling in wealth instead of desiring dharma is the height of folly.
teaches: The same memento mori leads the puram poet to gift and fame that outlast the body, and the Buddhist epic to dharma, with no word of fame: the cemetery's lesson changes with what each tradition thinks survives.

note: The Purananuru poem says rice and water are not the world's life, the king is, and he must know it; the goddess says the king's swerving kills life through the failing of rain, so the standing of being the beings' life is lost.
teaches: The epic turns the poem's title into a conditional one that a king's own fault cancels, and routes his power over life back through the rain the poem had set below him.

note: Perunkoppendu insists against the elders that her husband's pyre is to her a lotus pool; the sage tells Lakshmi as a plain fact that she will sink into Rahulan's fire, and the epic sends her, through that fire, to a new birth still bound to him.
teaches: The Sangam queen's choice of the pyre is her last word and her karpu's proof, while the Buddhist epic treats the same act as foretold and as no end at all: the bond she dies for carries into the next birth as the attachment that must be undone.

note: Both list Saturn smoking, a comet showing and Venus running south; Kapilar credits the rain that never failed in Pari's land to the king's straight sceptre, while the epic credits the Kaveri's flood to the river.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the same omen formula assigning the land's safety to different powers: to a just king in Purananuru 117, and to the river itself in the epic.

note: Nettimaiyar wishes the Pandya years more than the sands of the Pahruli river of the ancient Pandya; the epic's blessing says the sea took the Pahruli river (பஃறுளி யாற்றுடன்) with the Kumari peak.
teaches: The Sangam poet measures a king's life by a river that still flows, while the epic remembers the same river as drowned and makes its loss the occasion of a northern conquest, so the river turns from a figure of endurance into a figure of loss.

note: Both tie the cattle raid to toddy: in the Purananuru the jar is kept for the raider who will bring a herd; here the toddy seller's refusal sends the hunter out.
teaches: Read together they show toddy as the raid's credit: the poem's kept jar is advance pay, and the epic's refusal is the unpaid debt the seized herd later settles in the seller's yard.

note: The Purananuru raider takes herds yet his own pot shows no curd; the epic names whose yards the seized herds fill.
teaches: The poem's pitied raider who keeps nothing is explained by the epic's list: the herd goes to smith, drummer, bards, augur and toddy seller, so a raid's wealth is a gift economy that leaves the raider poor.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens Cheralathan's sea-raid and felling of the guarded kadambu to Murugan cutting down Sur in the sea; the epic's herdswomen tell the same Chera deed and say he churned the sea, Vishnu's deed.
teaches: Both poets lift the Chera's kadambu raid into a god's sea-deed, but each picks the god of its own setting: the Patitruppattu's war poem chooses Murugan, the herders' kuravai chooses Maal, so the same royal memory is divinised differently by genre.

note: The queen of Bhoothapandiyan refuses the widow's life of alli food and the gravel bed and chooses the pyre; Kannaki asks whether she too must waste away like the widows who keep those observances.
teaches: Both widows refuse the observances of kaimmai, but the Sangam queen turns to the pyre while Kannaki turns to the sun and the king, so the epic moves the wife's refusal of widowhood from death beside the husband to a demand for justice.

note: In Puram 72 the Sangam Pandya Nedunjeliyan of Talaiyalanganam curses himself, should he fail in his vow, to be a king whose people find no cool shade and spread his blame (குடிபழி தூற்றும்); the epic's Madurai spreads the blame of its king (மன்பழி தூற்றுங் குடி) and finds his cool umbrella breeding heat. The two kings share a title, not an identity: the epic's Nedunjeliyan is not the Sangam one.
teaches: The Sangam king's conditional self-curse, a boast of what will never happen, becomes in the epic a description of what has happened to a later Pandya, so the formula of royal disgrace moves from oath to fulfilment.

note: Both show a wife at her husband's wounded chest at the edge of night; the Puram wife reads the omens and dreads the widow's life, while Kannaki asks who will name the deed and blames the king.
teaches: The Sangam lament by the wounded body looks ahead to widowhood, but Kannaki's lament at the same scene turns outward into a charge against the king, so the old mourning form becomes the opening of a plea.

note: Both use the falling star and the broken royal umbrella as signs of a king's death.
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam stock of royal death-omens but moves them into a dream before the death, turning the elegist's after-the-fact proof of grief into a warning that comes too late to be heeded.

note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

note: Both are vanjinam vows in the conditional form 'if I do not, may I', one by a Pandya Nedunjeliyan before battle, one by Kannaki against a Pandya; the epic's king is not shown to be the Talaiyalanganattu victor of the puram poem.
teaches: The puram king stakes his own name as a just king on winning, while Kannaki stakes her name as a pathini on unmaking a king, so the epic turns the royal oath-form against the royal house and makes a widow's virtue the thing pledged.

note: Puram 9's Pandya warns cows, Brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he attacks; Kannaki tells the fire to spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children.
teaches: The protected classes of the just king's war reappear as the limit a wronged woman sets on her own vengeance against a Pandya city, so the code meant to restrain kings now restrains the one punishing a king, and is applied to his own capital.

note: Parasaran hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea (கடற்கடம் பெறிந்த) and carved his bow on the hill; Patitruppattu 11 tells the felling of the guarded kadamba after reaching the sea by Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, whom the Himalaya marks.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam Chera's signature deed as a blessing formula in a brahmin's mouth, and strings it with Mantharam Cheral and the Porunai's Poraiyan, so the separate Cheras of the decades become one praised house.

note: Bhuthapandiyan's queen Perunkoppendu rejects the elders and chooses the pyre after her husband; the Chera queen grants the Pandya queen who died with her king heaven, but chooses Kannaki for worship.
teaches: The Sangam queen's death after her husband is the summit of a wife's virtue in its own poem, while the epic, granting such a death its heavenly reward, ranks above it the wronged wife who survived to accuse a king.

note: The Patitruppattu preface to the fifth decade lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he went for a stone for the goddess Pattini and bathed it in the Ganges; the epic shows him choosing the Himalaya stone over the one from Pothiyil.
teaches: The preface records the stone as one conquest among many, while the epic gives its reason, a king's honour that refuses the near southern stone, so the pairing shows the pathini's cult being written into the Chera king's record of war.

note: Patitruppattu 43 praises Kuttuvan whose army broke kings from the Himalaya to Kumari; Villavan Kothai argues that because of such victories none in the world will resist him.
teaches: The Sangam poem praises conquest as done, while the epic minister uses the same fame as a reason no new conquest is needed, so the reputation of past war is offered as the means of a bloodless one.

note: Villavan Kothai credits Senguttuvan with making the sea-fenced land Tamil (இமிழ்கடல் வேலியைத் தமிழ்நா டாக்கிய); the Patitruppattu preface uses nearly the same phrase of his father Imayavaramban.
teaches: The minister applies to the son the formula the preface gives the father, so the Chera line's fame works as a shared inheritance that the campaign for the stone is said to renew.

note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola who made the Chera of the Himalaya-carved bow fall and withered வாடா வஞ்சி; the epic's king enters வாடா வஞ்சி and the drum boasts of the carved bow.
teaches: The epithets 'unwithering Vanchi' and 'the bow carved on the Himalaya' are the Chera line's own glory in the epic and the measure of a Chola victory in the Sangam poem, so the pairing shows one stock of Chera fame used by both its owners and its enemies.

note: Vellaikkudi Naganar tells the Chola that the world blames kings when rain fails and bids him ignore such talk and guard the ploughmen; Senguttuvan names rain failing and a life wronged as the protector-king's two great fears.
teaches: The Sangam counsellor treats blame for drought as unfair public talk a just king can bear, while the epic king takes the same burden inward as fear and ranks one wronged life above drought, so that kingship itself becomes suffering.

note: Both are royal vows in the conditional form whose penalty is the king's own sceptre turning cruel to his people; the Chera's line almost repeats the Pandya's.
teaches: The Pandya's vow names only his own subjects as the sufferers of a failed king, while the Chera's sets the choice out plainly, a sceptre that makes either foreign kings or his own people tremble, showing that the vow form took the king's power to terrify as fixed and staked the people's peace on a war abroad.

note: Both cook a battlefield meal on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms (முடித்தலை அடுப்பு, தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பு), and both set it beside the king's care for Vedic Brahmins.
teaches: The puram poem makes the battlefield cooking the Pandya's own rite beside his completed Vedic sacrifices, and the epic gives the cooking to demons who call the field an அறக்களம் and then has the king order the fire-keeping Brahmins protected, so the epic keeps the old pairing of war-rite and Vedic rite and adds the name of dharma to the slaughter.

note: The decade's preface says Senguttuvan went for the stone of the goddess pathini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed the stone in the Ganga; the kaathai tells the expedition at length. The epic here does not name the king's parents, so the identity rests on name and deed.
teaches: The preface compresses the campaign to a stone sought, one Aryan lord defeated and a bathing in the Ganga, while the epic gives the war a cause in an insult to Tamil, names two kings Kanakan and Vijayan, and brings the army over the Ganga on allies' boats, so the two show a shared tradition of the pathini's stone told with different enemies and routes.

note: The decade's preface lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he sought the stone of the goddess-pathini (கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள்) and bathed in the Ganga; the epic opens this kaathai with the same phrase and the same river.
teaches: Set beside the preface, the epic's நீர்ப்படை is seen to rest on a Chera tradition that already called the pathini a goddess and joined her stone to the Ganga, and the epic's contribution is the story that makes her one: who she was and why a king would march north for her.

note: The preface says Senguttuvan, son of the Chola Manakkilli, felled Pazhaiyan's neem and made nine heirs of the Chola house fall at the gate; Maadalan praises him for destroying the nine umbrellas that would not bear his cousin Killi's young rule and for felling Pazhaiyan's neem.
teaches: Read together, the preface's nine Chola kin felled at the gate are given a cause in the epic, a war over the succession of a young Chola who was the Chera's cousin through his Chola mother, so the Sangam list of victories becomes a family quarrel among the crowned houses.

note: Both recite the Chola line's ancestors, the king who entered the scale for the dove and the one who destroyed the hanging fort; the puram poem praises a Chola who withered the Chera's unwithering Vanchi, the epic has a Brahmin recite the same lineage in the Chera's own court.
teaches: The praise of the dove-king's line, which in the Sangam poem celebrates a Chola's victory over Vanchi, is spoken in the epic before the king of Vanchi as a pledge that the Chola's sceptre is sound, so the formula once used against the Chera now serves an alliance between cousins.

note: The Chola of the puram poem entered the scale with his own body to save a dove from a hawk; the Chera here gives the Brahmin gold measured against his own weight fifty times over, just after the Brahmin has praised that very dove-king.
teaches: The scale in which a Chola ancestor weighed his flesh against a bird becomes in the Chera's court a scale in which the king's weight is matched in gold for a messenger, so the body-as-measure moves from self-sacrifice to royal gift.

note: The bard of the puram poem hails Athiyaman as the ploughman who yokes white-mouthed donkeys on the bloody fields of captured forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; the Chera's ploughmen sing their king as the donkey-plough ploughman who sowed kavadi on the northern kings' forts.
teaches: The terror title that a Sangam bard gives a patron at his gate is in the epic sung by real ploughmen in their field song, beside their oxen's holiday, so the conqueror's mock ploughing of enemy ground is absorbed into the farming folk's festival of his return.

note: When the Chera Perunjeralathan sits north to die, the ploughmen's cry is forgotten and the village festival forgotten; when Senguttuvan returns, the ploughmen's song and the bathing festival fill the land.
teaches: Holding the two Chera poems together shows the ploughmen's song as the land's own measure of its king, silenced by a king's shameful death and loud at a king's triumph, so the epic's return scene answers the Sangam lament with its exact reverse.

note: Both tell a death by refusing food: the Chera Perunjeralathan, ashamed of a wound in his back, sits facing north with his sword; Kavunthi, after the deaths of her wards, gives up life by the vow of not eating.
teaches: The fasting death that the Sangam poem shows as a warrior king's answer to shame is in the epic taken up by a Jain nun as an answer to failed guardianship, so the same act carries the honour code into the renouncer's vow.

note: Maadalan's list of the king's victories runs close to the wording of the fifth decad's preface on Senguttuvan: சிறுகுரல் நெய்தல் வியலூர், இடும்பின் புறத்து இறுத்து, the nine kings beaten at the gate in standing battle, the sea driven back, the Aryan beaten at the Ganges.
teaches: The preface's bare record of conquests, which names the pathini's stone only as its occasion, becomes in the epic the praise a brahmin recites to cool the king's anger just before telling him that such conquests pass, so the same list serves first as glory and then as the premise of a sermon on impermanence.

note: Among the ancestors Maadalan cites are the king who took a four-Veda man's poem and sent him to the upper world, and (lines 144-146) the one who struck Agappa and bathed in Ayirai and the two seas; the third decad's preface and colophon give Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan these feats and the brahmin poet's reward of heaven through sacrifices.
teaches: The Sangam tradition's sacrifice that sent a brahmin poet to heaven becomes Maadalan's precedent for the sacrifice he urges on the king, yet the same preface says that king went away to the forest, and the epic's counsellor leaves out the renunciation and keeps only the rite.

note: Both tell a king that the rulers before him, many and mighty, are all gone; Puram 363 concludes that he must renounce the whole sea-bounded world before death, Maadalan that he must perform a great sacrifice and rule for aeons.
teaches: The same proof from dead kings yields opposite counsel: the Sangam poet's impermanence ends in giving up the kingdom, the epic's brahmin's in a rite that keeps the king on the throne, so the argument alone does not decide between renunciation and ritual.

note: Puram 264 tells of a hero-stone set up on gravelly ground, crowned with a red flower garland and peacock feathers, with the fallen man's name carved; the epic's kaathai named நடுகல் installs a stone from the Himalaya as a jewelled image with priests and daily rites.
teaches: The epic takes the hero-stone rite, raised by herdsmen for a fallen fighter, and gives it to a woman whose power is chastity, enlarging it with Brahmin sacrifice and a temple, so the old rite of the warrior becomes the founding of a goddess's cult.

note: Puram 9 praises a Pandya who before battle bids cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and the sonless take shelter; the Chola's dictum spares, after battle, men who have made themselves look like non-killers.
teaches: The old dharma of war spares people by what they are, but the epic shows warriors claiming that shelter by what they wear, and a king using the rule not to restrain himself but to belittle another king's captives.

note: The second decade's preface credits Imayavaramban Nedunjeralathan with carving the bow on the Himalaya; the epic's Aryan kings recall the day bow, tiger and fish were all carved there, and say no such kings are left.
teaches: The epic widens one Chera's boast into the shared emblem of the three Tamil crowns and makes the memory a reproach, so the son's campaign is shown as the redeeming of a glory the north said had lapsed.

note: The decade preface on Senguttuvan, son of Nedunjeralathan by the Chola Manakkilli, says in one phrase that he went north wanting a stone for the goddess pathini and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's prose gives the same parentage and campaign, and adds the Aryan kings' taunt and the stone carried on their heads.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Sangam colophon tradition already knew a Chera king's northern stone for a pathini, and the epic turns that bare record into a cause and a ritual: the stone becomes a goddess only after it is won by humbling the kings who mocked Tamil kingship.

note: The Puram poem tells Killivalavan that giving, conquest and justice are not his own fame, since his line already holds the king who entered the scale for the dove and the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort; the ammanai answers its riddle with the Chola who destroyed the hanging forts and names no living Chola.
teaches: Read together, the Puram poet's warning that the ancestors' deeds swallow a living Chola's fame comes true in the epic, where Chola praise sung at the Chera court consists of nothing but those ancestral deeds and the city of Puhar.

note: The Patitruppattu poem names Neduncheralathan as the king who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); the swing song sings the guardian who cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த) and the emblem of the bow, and names no king.
teaches: The pair shows the Patitruppattu's title for one Chera king passing into the epic as an unnamed dynastic refrain, so that in Senguttuvan's court a deed the Sangam decade credits to Neduncheralathan is sung as the house's own.

note: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises Uthiyan Cheralathan as the one who gave the great feast without limit while the Five and the hundred fought until the hundred fell; the swing song gives the feast at the war of the Five and the twice fifty to the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, by house names only, and pairs it with the kadamba deed.
teaches: The Puram poem binds the feast to one named king, while the epic gives it to the Chera house in general and sets it beside another king's deed, so the pair shows a single patron's distinction becoming an heirloom any Chera can be sung by.

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan, seeking a stone for the goddess-pathini, went through the forests, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the last kaathai has the Chera endow the pathini's temple and the freed Aryan kings and Gajabahu of Lanka beg her to come to their lands.
teaches: The Sangam preface records the pathini stone as one deed among a king's conquests; the epic carries the story past the conquest, to the defeated kings themselves asking for the goddess, so the war for the stone becomes the way her worship spreads beyond the Chera land.

note: Purananuru 66 praises Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni but says the defeated king who fasted to death for shame at his back wound is better than he; the epic's Valavan is checked by no rival, only by the Himalaya.
teaches: The Purananuru sets a moral limit on the victor through the vanquished man's honour, while the epic removes every human limit and lets only a mountain halt him, so the later memory of the Chola has lost the Sangam poet's check on royal glory.

note: The Purananuru poem tells Killivalavan that the land of the just sceptre on the Kaveri gets rain when it asks, and that kings are blamed when rains fail; Madhavi's stanza reads the Kaveri's easy flow as proof that the Chola sceptre does not bend.
teaches: The Sangam counsel makes plenty a duty the king must earn and warns he will be blamed for drought, while the epic song takes the river's plenty as already proving his justice, so the pair shows the counsel hardened into a courtly praise that can no longer imagine the failure the older poem warns of.

note: Bhoothapandiyan's queen rebukes the elders who hold her back and chooses the pyre over the widow's austerities, calling fire and a lotus pond one to her; the summary sets the Pandya Nedunjeliyan's queen of flawless chastity lying with him on the throne-couch, her death having come at once at his feet.
teaches: Both remember a Pandya queen who would not outlive her husband, but the Puram queen must argue her way to the pyre against counsel, while the epic's queen dies without fire or argument and the summary counts that death as flawless chastity, so together they show the widow's death moving from a chosen and contested act to a sign of karpu that needs no choosing.

note: The preface to the fifth decad names Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, as the king who went north to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's summary names him by the same epithet (கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி) and the same Ganga, and says nothing of the stone.
teaches: The decad's preface and the epic's summary give the same king the same two marks, the sea driven back and the Ganga reached, but only the Sangam preface keeps the Pattini stone as the purpose of the march, so the epic, which tells the stone's story at length, lets its own summary remember the expedition as the preface's bare royal conquest.

note: Both make the Earth a woman on the battlefield: the Kalavazhi's Earth is wrapped red as in a fine cloth by the king's slaughter, the Cintamani's beats her breast and pines.
teaches: The same personified Earth that the praise-poem dresses in the victor's blood becomes in the epic a mourner, so the pair shows the one figure serving both the glory and the grief of a war.

note: Both set war as a sea with ships: in the epic the two armies meet as two seas with elephants as ships, in the Kalavazhi the blood drags elephants and drums like boats meeting on the sea after the slaughter.
teaches: The epic uses the sea at the moment of the clash, the Kalavazhi uses it for the blood that remains after, so together they show the sea image passing from the armies' living mass to the flood of their dead.

note: The Ainthinai Ezhupathu heroine asks whether the sea, like her, does not sleep because the same shore lord took his fill of it and left; Madhavi's woman tells the neythal that, unlike her, it sleeps free of pain.
teaches: The two neythal women look to the shore for company in sleeplessness and reach opposite answers, one finding in the restless sea a fellow sufferer, the other finding in the closed flower only a sleeper who does not share her pain, so the pair shows the same evening shore read as sympathy and as indifference.

note: The Ainthinai Aimpathu heroine begs the crab not to walk over the tracks of her lover's chariot so she can look at them her fill; Madhavi's woman tells the tide that it has already broken up every trace of that path.
teaches: The Sangam heroine still holds the wheel-track and pleads with a small creature to spare it, while in the song the sea has already wiped it out and she can only ask what to do, so the pair shows the same last trace of the lover first guarded and then lost.

note: The Thinaimalai man says the girl guarding drying fish turns weapon-eyes on him and it is he, not the fish, she guards; the vari says the goddess who afflicts those who see her driving birds from drying fish has taken a woman's form.
teaches: The same fish-guarding girl is a wry reversal of guarding in the akam verse and a goddess in disguise in the epic song, so the pair shows the neithal scene moving from the lover's joke to a performance piece of supernatural praise.

note: Kurinjippattu opens with the friend disclosing to the mother the marriage the girl chose past her father's guard; in 1052 the nurse who sounded Gunamalai tells the mother, who tells the father.
teaches: The epic runs the akam disclosure through the whole household chain and adds the nurse's verdict that the match ripens from past penance, so a convention of love poetry becomes a step in a karmic marriage plot.

note: Maduraikanchi lists a must elephant that kills its goad-men, breaks its post and roams, beside horses drilled in circling courses; 1831 and 1839 give the same post-breaking elephant and the same circling drill.
teaches: The Sangam city poem sets the rampaging elephant and the drilled circles side by side as separate noises of the capital, while the epic joins them as two stages of one hero's mastery, riot turned into drill.

note: The Nedunalvadai's king walks the camp at midnight, a few men with him, looking each wounded man kindly in the face; Civakan tells his uncle to have the wounded tended and lies down to rest with women stroking his feet.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam king who goes out in the cold to see the wounds himself, the epic's victor delegates the duty and sleeps, which shows how far the later court poem has moved the king's care from presence to command.

note: The Mullaippattu's king cannot sleep for thinking of the elephant with its trunk cut, the men who fell and the wounded horses; Civakan sleeps through the noise of wounds, weeping women and drums as if he heard none of it.
teaches: The two kings face the same night after battle with opposite responses, the one kept awake by the wounded and the other asleep amid their cries, so the epic's sleep is a sign of a war ended where the Sangam king's waking is a sign of one still going on.

note: The Sirupanarruppadai paints the kinai bard's hunger in his kitchen, his wife boiling unsalted greens behind a shut door, until a patron's gifts end it; the Cintamani puts the porunar's distress down in half a line, through the carts of paddy and cane.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam bard's want only to cancel it at once, and moves its relief from one named patron's gift to the anonymous traffic of a rich land.

note: The Perumpanarruppadai's girls on sky-touching terraces move like peacocks rejoicing on a great hill's slope; the Cintamani's women on the mansion rows look like peacocks spreading their wings in the mist on a high hill.
teaches: The epic inherits the Sangam figure of terrace women as hill peacocks but makes the hill's mist out of the houses' own perfume smoke, turning a natural setting into manufactured luxury.

note: Both describe the lute part by part with the same names, the bowl (பத்தர், பத்தல்), the pegs (ஆணி), the stem (மருப்பு) and the strings (நரம்பு), and both credit its music with power over the hostile and the wild.
teaches: The Cintamani takes over the Sangam bard's catalogue of the lute but makes it gold, coral and diamond, and makes knowing the instrument's parts and faults the contest itself, so the bard's working tool becomes the test of a prince.

note: Maduraikkanchi 24-42 sets fat-mouthed demon women dancing the tunangai around a battle-sacrifice whose cook serves flesh-rice to the soldiers; in 803 a pregnant ghoul dresses herself in the field's remains while Civakan watches and laughs.
teaches: The Sangam poem makes the ghouls' feast part of a rite the king performs, while the epic removes the rite and keeps the dance as a spectacle for the hero's delight, so the motif survives as ornament of heroism.

note: In the Nedunalvadai the king walks the camp at midnight to look at the sword wounds of the warriors; in the epic the wounded are laid in ghee, have spearheads cut out, and are given purses and ornaments.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows care for the wounded as the king's sleepless looking, and the epic turns that care into a practice of treatment and payment, so the reader sees the duty to the wounded grow from presence into provision.

note: Pattinappalai opens on the Kaveri that does not fail though the white star strays south and the sky withholds rain; the patikam calls the Kaveri the Tamil maiden who does not leave her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens (கோள் நிலை திரிந்து கோடை நீடினும் தான் நிலை திரியா).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise-formula for Puhar's river and turns it into a person, a Chola daughter who bows to the city's goddess and gives the city its second name, so a boast of the land's yield becomes a founding story.

note: Both open on Venus straying south as the sign of drought and say the Kaveri still brings its flood.
teaches: The epic borrows the Pattinappalai's drought omen for the Kaveri on the road out of Puhar, so the couple's departure from the city is set in the same praise that once opened a poem about the city's wealth.

note: The Murukatruppadai hails Murugan among his titles as son of the banyan god, son of the mountain's daughter, and child of Kotravai of victorious war; the vari heaps on Kotravai herself the names of Gauri, Shiva's emblems and the title of Mal's younger kin.
teaches: The Sangam guide poem joins Kotravai to the Saiva household through her son, listing her beside the mountain daughter as Murugan's mother, while the epic's hunters make Kotravai herself absorb Gauri, Shiva's emblems and Vishnu's kinship, so the pair shows the war goddess of the wilds drawn into the great gods' family by two different routes.

note: Maduraikkanchi's dawn in Madurai has the Brahmins chanting the Veda, the elephants fed and the horses in their stalls (பணைநிலைப் புரவி); the epic's travellers hear the same dawn, the Vedic chant and the stalled horses' neighing among it, from outside the walls.
teaches: The epic reuses the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's dawn, phrase for phrase in places, but moves its hearer from the king the idyll counsels on impermanence to the strangers whom the city will destroy, so the idyll's warning that such splendour passes is carried out on the city itself.

note: The Maduraikkanchi's courtesans of Madurai drain the wealth of rich young men and leave them like bees leaving a spent flower; the epic's courtesans of the same city are masters of the two styles of dance and its treatises, paid a fixed fee by rule, before whom kings bow.
teaches: The Sangam poem sees Madurai's courtesans as the drain on the young rich, while the epic sees them as an institution of learned art with a royal tariff, so the pair shows the epic recasting a city's vice as its high culture, the very shift that made Madhavi's art and Kovalan's ruin the same thing.

note: The Maduraikkanchi lists in Madurai's four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவினும்) the shell-cutters, gem-borers, goldsmiths, gold-assayers and cloth-sellers; the epic closes its tour with the gold-assayers, cloth street, grain street and the four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவும்).
teaches: The epic follows the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's trades down to the four streets, but where the Sangam poem lists them as the plenty of a victorious Pandya, the epic shows them through a stranger about to be condemned by one of these trades, so the inherited praise of the city becomes the setting of its fall.

note: In the idyll the old women seek an omen and hear a herd girl tell a distressed tethered calf that its mothers will soon come; in the epic the herd's own signs foretell sorrow and the herdswoman dances so that the cows' and calves' distress may pass.
teaches: Both read a calf's distress among the herds as a sign about an absent man, but the idyll's chance word promises a return and the epic's signs announce a death the herders do not yet know, so the mullai omen-scene is turned from hope to loss.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai places the god at Erakam among Brahmins who chant the six-syllable mantra at the hours; the kuravai names Erakam with Senthil, Sengodu and Venkunru as hills the god never leaves.
teaches: The same shrine is claimed by the guide poem for a Brahmin rite and by the hill women for their kuravai, and their list differs from the six seats, so the roster of Murugan's hills was not yet fixed when the epic was made.

note: The epic's line 21, வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும், is the Pattinappaalai's line 193 on the same city's streets of mingled wealth.
teaches: Pattinappaalai uses the line to close a map of goods arriving from every mountain and sea, while the epic attaches it to a census of Puhar's own craftsmen and traders, so the borrowed praise moves from what flows into the port to who works in it.

note: Pattinappaalai's Thirumavalavan makes the northerners wilt among many regional conquests; the epic's Thirumavalavan marches to the Himalaya and brings back gifts from three named northern kings.
teaches: Read together, the two show a Sangam king's memory being enlarged: one line of the older poem about the north becomes a whole campaign whose trophies are buildings in Puhar, so the epic makes the conquest serve its picture of the city.

note: The Pattinappalai's fishermen count the coloured lights of Puhar's mansions at night; the epic counts the shore's lamps by trade, from perfume-sellers and hawkers to the lighthouse, fishing boats and foreign traders.
teaches: The idyll's lights are a spectacle watched from the boats, while the epic's are a roll of the port's livelihoods, showing how the later poem turns the same harbour of lights into a social survey.

note: The Pattinappalai's speaker, in the poem for Karikal, swears he will not leave his long-haired woman even if given all of Puhar; the epic, invoking Karikal's festival, seats Kovalan beside Madhavi on Puhar's shore, where before evening he will leave her (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The idyll's vow that no city outweighs the beloved is tested on the very shore it praised, and the epic's lover fails it amid Puhar's full splendour.

note: Pattinappaalai says the Kaveri does not fail even when the star goes south and the sky withholds rain; Madhavi's stanza says the Kaveri's unceasing help that sustains life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel.
teaches: The idyll makes the river's reliability its own, a guarantee standing even against a failed sky, while the epic song moves that same unfailing gift under a ruler's grace, so the pair shows the Kaveri's bounty passing from a fact of the land to a token of the king.

note: Both praise the Chola land of Puhar through its water; the Pattinappalai grants that the sky may fail and makes the Kaveri the river that never fails, while the epic's summary sets the divine Kaveri beside a sky that itself never fails (பொய்யா வானம்).
teaches: The Sangam poem rests Puhar's plenty on the river precisely because the sky can fail, and the epic's summary removes that concession, making the sky unfailing too in a line it reuses unchanged for the Pandya land, so the pair shows a Puhar-specific boast about the Kaveri turning into a stock praise that any crowned line receives.

note: Tirumular's Siva-yoga ends in the Lord's abode, given by Nandi; Somaprabha guards his yoga so that his own deeds end, with no god named.
teaches: The two texts use the word yoga for a discipline of release but one gives the release to the Lord's grace and the other to the ascetic's own guarding, so grace and effort part on the same practice.

note: The Tirumanthiram says only the vows kept and the knowledge gained go with the dead; the verse lists what the vow buys after death.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the vow as what travels past death, and the epic adds a ledger of what it buys: Indra's rank, kingship, then the end of deeds.

note: The verse says a vow, worship and gifts conquer the binding deed; the Tirumanthiram says the Lord made the bond that fastens the soul to what went before.
teaches: One text lets the soul loosen its own bond by vow and giving, while the other makes the bond the Lord's work, so the question of who can undo the bond divides them.

note: The brothers destroy both deeds by meditating on the soul, where Tirumular says the worshipped fire burns up deeds.
teaches: The two accounts reach the same freedom from deeds by different agents, the practitioner's own meditation against a fire that burns them, so the dispute is over who does the burning.

note: Austerity and yoga bring the brothers perfection and the rest heaven, as Tirumular says austerity and virtue together are a boat over the sea of deeds.
teaches: The story shows austerity giving two different ends for two sets of people, which the single boat in Tirumular's line does not.

note: This verse praises the lord who burned all old deeds by his own renunciation; Tirumular's sunstone burns the malas only when the Lord's sun appears.
teaches: Jain deliverance burns karma by the liberated one's own effort without a god, while the Saiva text burns it by presence and grace, so the two disagree on whether anything outside the soul does the burning.

note: Tirumanthiram 200 has those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet; the verse has worshippers of a lord who has kept non-killing reach release.
teaches: Both name feet and release for those who keep the vow, but the Saiva verse makes the worshipper the keeper of the vow and the Jain verse makes the lord the keeper.

note: The Jain sage says the son's own austerity will cut his deeds and end birth; Tirumular says austerity and virtue are a boat across the sea of deeds only because the Lord makes them fruitful.
teaches: The same word, tapas, ends karma by the doer's effort in the sage's mouth and by the Lord's grace in Tirumular's, so the release the two promise rests on opposite sources.

note: The prince masters a rutting elephant; Tirumular's body holds five rutting elephants that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The epic's taming is an outward feat of the body, and the Tirumanthiram carries the same image inward to the senses, so the story's word மதம் is read both as rut and as the pride the senses breed.

note: The prince mounts and rides a vicious horse through the streets; Tirumular tells the reader to hold the reins of the running horse firmly.
teaches: The ride of a hero is shown in the epic as skill before a crowd, and in the Tirumanthiram as the discipline of the mind that needs no show, so the two use one image for different ends.

note: Both call the cure of the soul a medicine that leaves it clear: in the Neelakesi the soul takes the three remedies of knowledge, clear faith and conduct; in Tirumular the mind becomes clear when Nandi gives grace, like a madman cured by medicine.
teaches: The shared image of medicine and clarity hides opposed accounts of who heals: for the Jain sermon clarity is one of the remedies the soul swallows itself, for Tirumular it is the effect of the Lord's grace, and on the Jain reading no giver of grace is needed.

note: The Siddhar verse names the Lord as the one who opened his fire-eye and burned Kama; the Neelakesi's hymn says the sage in anger reduced Ananga to white ash.
teaches: A Jain hymn takes the Saiva god's signature deed and gives it to a human ascetic, so the victory over desire that the Saiva texts reserve for the Lord is claimed as something a man achieves by penance.

note: Pattinathar searches hair, skin, blood, bone and worms for the 'I', finds it nowhere, and says that only when the Lord's grace came did he see himself; the Neelakesi praises an ascetic who knows himself other than the body by his own steadfast penance.
teaches: Both hold that the self is not the body, but the Saiva poet reaches that knowledge only by grace while the Jain sage reaches it by enduring, so the shared insight hides a disagreement about how it is won.

note: Tirumanthiram 1616 makes Siva the renouncer who dwells in the burning ground and cuts off the births of those who renounce; Neelakesi 141 praises the ascetic who in the burning ground uprooted all his own karmas.
teaches: The same dwelling place holds two answers to who ends rebirth: in the Saiva verse the god of the burning ground cuts the renouncer's births, in the Jain hymn the renouncer there uproots his karma himself, a disagreement that turns on reading பல்வினையும் பறிப்போய் as his own karma.

note: Both praise the highest being as victor over Death: Siva kicked Death and became king of the south; the Jina passed beyond Death (காலனைக் கடந்தாய்) along with desire, aging and birth.
teaches: The same victory over Death means a deed of force against another being in the Saiva invocation and a leaving-behind of one's own mortal condition in the Jain hymn.

note: Both speak of the two deeds (இருவினை) and their ending: the Jina taught the way they part; Tirumular says that when they balance, grace-power comes as the guru and one's own doing ends.
teaches: On the same pair of deeds the Jain hymn gives the teacher only the role of telling the way, while Tirumular makes the guru a descent of grace that ends the soul's own agency.

note: The Neelakesi praises those who strive (முயல்வார்) with knowledge to wear away their deeds; the Tirumanthiram says deeds end when grace comes as the guru and one's own doing ceases (தன்செயல் அற்றால்).
teaches: Both make knowledge the solvent of deeds, but they disagree on whose act it is: for the Jain land it is the striver's own effort, for Tirumular the end of one's own agency under grace; the tension holds if முயல்வார் is read as self-reliant effort.

note: Neelakesi says we will wear out our own deeds and go; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and ends one's own doing.
teaches: The Jain debater denies that another's compassion can release, and Tirumular makes release depend on a grace that ends one's own agency, so they answer oppositely who removes karma.

note: Neelakesi mocks a teacher who calls release emptiness (சூனியம்); the Idaikkadar Siddhar tells the soul that clinging to what became the void (சூனியமான அத்தை) is beyond compare.
teaches: The void that the Jain debater treats as an absurd account of release is, for a later Siddhar, the goal itself, so the word changes from a target of ridicule to a name of the highest state.

note: 263 mocks the Buddha's void release for giving nothing to hold to; Siddhar 1777 bids the seeker cling close to that which became the void.
teaches: Whether a void can be a goal one holds is exactly where they part: for the Jain debater the void offers no support, for the Siddhar it is the one thing to grasp.

note: Pattinattar counts the begging bowl (இரந்துண்ணும் ஓடு) among the renouncer's wealth without lack; Neelakesi says the bowl is costly, easily lost and useless to one who does penance without fault.
teaches: The begging bowl, emblem of renunciation for the Saiva poet, is for the Jain debater a possession that burdens: whether renunciation keeps even a bowl divides the traditions.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the ochre-wearers with matted hair, water-pots and yoga staffs who leave their wives and beg from house to house; Neelakesi mocks the monk who boils and dyes his cloth as though he had only given up cooking rice.
teaches: Jain and Siddhar both ridicule the ochre-robed renouncer, but for opposite failings: Sivavakkiyar faults him for abandoning home duties, Neelakesi for carrying them on in the monastery.

note: Tirumular keeps the body because without it true knowledge cannot be won; Neelakesi cites as common knowledge that the body lives by food and awareness by the body.
teaches: The same chain, food to body to knowledge, serves opposite ends: Tirumular uses it to justify cultivating the body, while Neelakesi uses it to say the renouncer needs food and nothing more.

note: Neelakesi says deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig; Tirumular says the subtle breath in the soul carries it as wind carries a flower's scent.
teaches: Both answer what carries a soul between bodies with an image of wind, but for the Jain the wind is the deed itself, needing no other mover, while for Tirumular it is the vital breath at the appointed moment, so the same image names karma in one and breath in the other.

note: Neelakesi's fiery body enters another body like a shadow; Tirumular's light born in the womb spreads through the earthly body like a bubble in water, a shadow, and the eight take hold.
teaches: Writers of opposed schools both picture the subtle body that passes into a new one as a shadow, which shows they agreed rebirth needs a subtle carrier and differed only on what it is made of, the Jain fiery and karmic bodies or Tirumular's eight.

note: Both put the renouncer in the burning ground with the same verb: காட்டகத் துறைவான் in the Neelakesi, உறைவது காட்டகம் in the Tirumanthiram.
teaches: The burning ground was the renouncer's accepted dwelling across sects, but for Tirumular its dweller is Siva himself, whom renouncers imitate, while the Jain sage enters it as a stranger in a goddess's shrine whose offerings he will end.

note: Pattinattar lists the five fires, lying in water, plucking hair and going without food and says his devotees reached release without them; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as bringing no gain.
teaches: Buddhist debater and Saiva poet reject the same austerities for opposite reasons: for Mokkalan pain has no power to free, for Pattinattar the god's name frees without it, so a shared rejection hides a disagreement about what does the freeing.

note: Tirumular says that even burning one's bones as firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without melting love; Mokkalan says cutting wounds and leaping from mountains serve no purpose.
teaches: Both reject bodily extremity as the way, but Tirumular keeps it as a measure that love surpasses while Mokkalan declares it simply useless, so the Saiva verse still honours the ascetic's pain where the Buddhist does not.

note: Both give an account of where a child comes from: the Neelakesi's sage assigns the body to the parents' blood and the life to its own former deeds, leaving the deity nothing to give; Tirumular has the Lord sit in the womb and form the embryo, knowing what it will become.
teaches: On the same question, the making of a child, the Jain sage removes every divine agent while Tirumular puts the Lord inside the womb, so karma alone and karma shaped by the Lord are opposed answers, not one view in two idioms.

note: Both list the same abstentions, killing first, then lying and theft; the Siddhar asks the Lord of Chidambaram to grant him a life without them, while the sage tells householders that keeping them wins the world of the gods.
teaches: The same list of abstentions is a gift begged of the Lord in the Siddhar and the householder's own work with a self-acting reward in the Jain sermon, which is the grace-against-effort divide in miniature.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Neelakesi appeals to the Apta's scripture as what leaves nothing unknown, but does so as a move in a debate.
teaches: Both rest final authority on a scripture, but the Saiva verse sets scripture against argument while the Jain debater uses scripture as the ground of argument, so the two disagree about whether debate serves the scripture.

note: Tirumular says the undiscerning take the moon in clouds and in a pot of Ganga water as many, though it is one; Neelakesi asks who ever said the moon differs in each water, to show the Lord's one knowing present to all things.
teaches: Both use one moon in many waters, but the Saiva verse makes the many appearances one reality, while the Jain keeps the many things real and makes only the knowing single.

note: Tirumular says that saying Siva Siva makes evil deeds die and brings the state of Siva (சிவகதி); Neelakesi says that praising the Aptha destroys both kinds of deed and brings the undivided state of Siva (சிவகதி).
teaches: The two verses share the formula of praise, deeds destroyed and சிவகதி, but for Tirumular the word names Siva and only evil deeds must go, while for the Jain hymn it names a godless auspicious state and good deeds must go too.

note: Idaikkadar says a roasted seed will not sprout and those without devotion will not reach the goal; Neelakesi says a burnt seed never sprouts and so the released soul is never born again.
teaches: The same roasted seed is failure for the Siddhar, the soul without devotion that cannot grow toward release, and success for the Jain, the soul whose karma is burnt so it cannot grow into rebirth, so the image's meaning depends on whether sprouting is birth or attainment.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha's reasoning collapses into the void; the Siddhar tells his listener that all arising deeds are seen to be void, appearing without appearing in pure space.
teaches: For the Jain debater reaching the void is a reductio, for the Siddhar it is the seeing that frees; the same word marks defeat in one tradition and insight in the other.

note: 534 mocks the teacher who calls earth, water, fire and city false; Pambatti Siddhar bids the reader be clear that the world is false and dance.
teaches: The Jain realist's retort, that one who calls all things false leaves no ground for his own truth, falls on the Siddhar's world-is-false as much as on the Buddhist's, though the Siddhar makes it a release-giving insight, not a doctrine to defend.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks those who bathe daily crying 'pollution', since the body itself took form from pollution; 561 tells those who hold all things impure to bathe in the gutter, as if that conclusion were absurd.
teaches: The Siddhar draws the very conclusion the Jain debater uses as a reductio: if everything is born of impurity, the ritual bath is pointless, so the same premise ends in mockery of ritual in one text and in mockery of the premise in the other.

note: Tirumular says souls that know what truly is go to grace and release is becoming one with Siva; Neelakesi says understanding the Lord's scripture brings release in due order, with no grace and no union.
teaches: Both put knowledge first, but in the Saiva verse knowledge leads to grace and union with God, while in the Jain verse the Lord gives only the scripture and the soul reaches release by its own understanding.

note: Tirumular tells the devotee to take refuge in the shade of the one God's feet so that the sea of deeds will not reach him; Neelakesi, a Jain convert, prays at the Jina's feet that her old deeds may end.
teaches: A Jain convert and a Saiva poet both bring their deeds to a Lord's feet in prayer, so the difference between Jain release by wearing deeds away and Saiva release by grace is not visible in the act of worship but only in the doctrine behind it.

note: Tirumular says silence of speech alone is mere muteness, true silence being the stilling of mind; Neelakesi says silence of speech proves nothing, since trees and mountains are silent.
teaches: Both deny that outward silence shows attainment, but they move the test in opposite directions: Tirumular inward to a stilled mind, the Jain debater outward to the teaching a knower must give.

note: Tirumular says that as a madman is cleared by medicine, he was made clear when Nandi gave grace; Neelakesi says she, once a demon, was made clear by the dharma a teacher gave her.
teaches: Both use the same image of madness cured, but the cure differs in kind: for the Saiva it is the Lord's grace that stops his doing, for the Jain a teaching she must take in and keep.

note: The Sankhya of 735 counts twenty-five principles that need no maker; Tirumular's Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb for each birth.
teaches: The Saiva verse keeps the Sankhya tally of twenty-five but puts a maker over it, the one element both the Sankhya and its Jain critic do without.

note: Both call birth a sickness with a medicine: the Neelakesi's sage names the medicine as dharma that cuts the diseases of birth; Pattinathar names it as never forgetting the lotus feet of the Lord of the Tillai hall.
teaches: The two traditions agree on the diagnosis and part on the cure: the Jain medicine is a dharma one takes up oneself with no god named, while the Siddhar's medicine is remembrance of the Lord's feet.

note: Neelakesi asks what could bind a soul that is pure and changeless; the Tirumanthiram makes soul and bond both beginningless, so the soul was never first pure and then bound.
teaches: The Jain question to the Sankhya, what first bound a pure soul, is the question the Saiva verse avoids by making bondage as old as the soul, at the price of a soul that was never pure until the Lord draws near.

note: Tirumular says the soul reaches the saving state by seeing through the twenty-five principles, prakriti and maya; 763 says listing the principles can do nothing for a soul that never changes.
teaches: The pair shows what the Saiva use of the twenty-five needs and the Sankhya lacks: a soul that can be bound and freed, so that seeing through the principles is a real change of state.

note: Tirumular makes the five dances the five acts done by grace; the Neelakesi cites the dance and the acts only as the opponent's shield, which 767-775 break.
teaches: The doctrine Tirumular offers as the heart of grace is the very one the Jain debater names in order to refute, and her answer (a god who is all is the author of every harm) is the objection Tirumular's dance never meets.

note: Sivavakkiyar uses the banyan folded in its own seed as the image of Parabrahman grown within a man; Neelakesi mocks the tall palm said to be already in its seed.
teaches: The tree-in-the-seed image that a Siddhar offers as an insight was, for a Jain debater, the weak point of the doctrine that effects pre-exist, so one image carries a mystic's claim and a logician's refutation.

note: In 821 darkness perishes as the disciple understands the three and remembers the Lord's feet; in Tirumanthiram 2293 the malas leave like evening darkness before a flame by grace.
teaches: Both texts end bondage with darkness dispelled, but in the Jain verse the remover is the disciple's own knowledge and remembrance, while the Saiva verse gives the work to grace.

note: Tirumular says there is no dharma that leaves out the Veda, and the wise gave up disputation and recited it to gain release; Neelakesi argues by inference that the Veda is made and, being joined to killing, drives its followers to evil births.
teaches: The two verses disagree both on the Veda and on method: Tirumular sets recitation above argument as the way to release, while Neelakesi makes argument the test that the Veda fails.

note: Pattirakiriyar longs to go about without caste, as the agama of Kapila says; Neelakesi argues that high and low birth is unreal because sight, smell, taste and touch find no difference.
teaches: Both reject caste, but on different grounds: the Siddhar appeals to a scripture, while the Jain debater appeals to perception against scripture, which shows that an anti-caste position need not rest on any text.

note: Tirumular says that when steadfast Brahmins pour the oblation sky, earth, the quarters and their gods flourish; Neelakesi says that rites cannot drive off disease or demons and that gods who delight in killing cannot remove the killer's karma.
teaches: Where the Saiva verse gives the rite power to sustain the world and its gods, the Jain debater denies it any power over karma at all, so the two disagree on whether ritual acts on the moral order.

note: Neelakesi argues that the ascetic's staff and bowl would be wasted unless a soul survives the body; Tirumular says garb put on the body is not for the soul and falls away with the body.
teaches: Both tie ascetic dress to the body-soul question but draw opposite lessons from it: for the Jain debater the gear presupposes a soul, for Tirumular it cannot reach the soul at all, so outward penance is evidence in one text and irrelevance in the other.

note: Neelakesi asks what cause brings the elements together, since they cannot join themselves; Tirumular sets unknowing maya beside the knowing soul and calls the making of elements and senses the fivefold work of grace.
teaches: Both texts deny that unknowing matter assembles itself into a knower, but where the Jain debater leaves the cause in the soul and its deeds, the Saiva verse gives it to grace.

note: The materialist says that when the elements part, all comes to nothing; the Siddhar says he saw the five elements die and fall and the five senses burn and fall.
teaches: The Siddhar describes as his own experience the parting of elements and senses that the materialist says must end awareness, and he remains to report it, which is the case Neelakesi argues for and does not show.

note: Tirumular puts in fire-mouthed hell those who said 'kill, stab'; the Neelakesi puts there those who ate the flesh as well as those who killed.
teaches: A Saiva and a Jain text each carry the guilt of a killing beyond the hand that strikes, one back to the man who ordered it and the other forward to the man who eats, so between them the whole chain around a death is held to account.

note: The Neelakesi's hell has no one to relieve the sufferer (பரிபவரும் இல்லையே); Arunagirinathar asks Murugan to come at speed when Death would drop him into the seven hells, so that his sins go.
teaches: The two answer opposite ways whether anyone can stand between a sinner's deeds and hell: the Jain sermon says no one can, the Murugan song asks that the god do exactly that; the conflict holds if பரிபவர் means one who relieves or rescues.

note: Soolamani 1 praises a god who won the sum of deeds himself and lets those who bow be freed; Tirumanthiram 1649 says by Siva's grace deeds do not cling.
teaches: Release from deeds is credited to a conqueror's own victory in the Jain verse and to the giving of grace in the Saiva one, so the two differ over who removes the deeds.

note: Verse 1024 narrates the youth's heart burning for a woman's body as the natural course of love; Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from such burning.
teaches: What the epic narrates as an unfolding desire, the Siddhar-side verse treats as a trap, so the two disagree about what the heart should do with beauty.

note: Verse 1036 gives a woman setting lamps, incense, flowers and music before the Jina; Tirumanthiram 1005 sets golden lamps and incense in every direction and promises release.
teaches: A Jain maiden's temple rite and a Saiva verse use the same lamp-and-incense offering, though only the Tirumanthiram names its fruit.

note: The astrologer reads a night's dream as true knowledge of what will come; the Siddhar song says all he saw has turned into a dream, like moonlight on a forest.
teaches: One poem trusts a dream to show what is real in the future, and the other uses the dream as the name for the whole of what is seen, so the same word divides prophecy from unreality.

note: Women's perfumes weaken even ascetics here; the Thiruppugazh poet confesses his own ruin from craving women.
teaches: The scenic verse already carries the temptation that the poet of the Thiruppugazh later tells in the first person.

note: 1101 shows the priest's fire fed while the groom's desire is kindled; Siddhar 147 asks when he will kindle the homa fire inside to cross the sea of desire.
teaches: One fire serves desire on one side and ends desire on the other, so the rite is the same fire put to opposite uses.

note: 1113 lets the pair dissolve in a daze of union; Tirumanthiram 1960 teaches union in which the bindu is kept and infatuation dies.
teaches: The epic gives the surrender that Tirumular's discipline of union is set against, and the Saiva verse asks what the daze costs.

note: In 1148 Acuvakandan boasts of turning mountains and rolling the world; Tirumanthiram 1686 lists burning with anger and boasting of greatness among what is not the nature of one near the Lord.
teaches: The Saiva list names as marks of the unripe what the epic's rival king shows as his great-hearted rage.

note: The king is lord of a rutting war elephant and in rage; the Siddhar song kills anger as a mad elephant's rut with the goad of reasoning.
teaches: Anger as a rutting elephant is a royal fact in the epic and a figure in the Siddhar, which shows what the goad of reason would have to stop.

note: The soldiers eager to carry arms and win; the Siddhar says horses, elephants and infantry shine under the parasol and are nothing without the ash.
teaches: The soldiers' pride in their strong shoulders is set beside a verse that says armies are worth nothing without the right mark, so the epic's boasts are weighed against a Siddhar's measure.

note: 1165 makes pride the child of anger's fire; Tirumanthiram 266 says the swollen-headed die without support, fallen into withering anger.
teaches: Pride that grows from anger in the epic is shown by Tirumular to end in a death without any support.

note: Dhumaketu is likened to the Death of the age's end; Tirumular says the Lord's thinkers are beyond Death's messengers.
teaches: The war poem sets Death above all fighters, while Tirumular sets one who thinks of the Lord above Death.

note: 1426 has a king order the destruction of all men; Tirumanthiram 238 says an unlearned king who says 'kill' is worse than Death, since Death spares the good.
teaches: Set side by side, the king who commands total death is judged by a rule the epic's own narrator does not state.

note: 1427 has a spell command Death to finish his work at a king's wish; Tirumanthiram 176 says no one can fight when life leaves and only the thought of the Lord turns Death's messengers.
teaches: The epic's Death takes orders from a spell while the Saiva verse holds Death answerable to the Lord alone, so the two disagree over who commands Death.

note: 1476 asks whether a king who lay on a golden couch with wives rubbing his feet should now lie on an elephant's brow; Siddhar 642 says the throne of pure gold does not go with the body when Yama takes it.
teaches: The epic shows the couch lost by a battle and the Siddhar shows it lost by Yama, so one losing of luxury is told as a war and as the common end.

note: 1517 praises a mountain-lifter whom kings and gods hail; Tirumanthiram 350 tells of a lifter of the great mountain who was crushed by the Lord and then given grace.
teaches: The epic stops at homage to the lifter, while the Saiva verse asks what becomes of that strength before God.

note: 1573 has the jester win debate by beating reciters; Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise gave up disputation and recited the Veda to gain release.
teaches: The jester practises debate for a gift and the verse in the Tirumanthiram says the wise leave debate for recitation, so the farce is set against that view.

note: 1730 gives the dream of a gem as the sign that the child is coming; Tirumanthiram 453 says the Lord, at the moment of the joining, fixes the span and the earthly life of the child.
teaches: The epic reads the conception from omens and the mother's body, while the Tirumanthiram says the life was fixed by the Lord at the joining, so a sign is read against a cause.

note: 1752 likens the returning balls to lovers who will not be held off; Thiruppugazh 586 asks Murugan not to let the poet waste away over women whose palms ache from ball-play.
teaches: One text enjoys ball-play as courtship, and the other treats the same game as the snare from which a devotee asks to be freed.

note: Verse 182 says even calling the Arhat all-knowing does not let one know him; Tirumanthiram 32 says no one knows the lord's nature, and the all-pervading lord is praised only in part.
teaches: Both say naming does not reach the god, but the Jain verse accepts omniscience as a true name while the Saiva verse denies any measure of the lord.

note: 1839 says wealth and heavenly pleasure are the fruit of deeds and bids remembering; Tirumanthiram 267 says joy and sorrow were fixed by earlier acts and that fools who see joy yet do not give know no virtue.
teaches: The poem asks only for remembering the fruit and keeping to the way; the couplet names what that way includes, giving, and what its absence shows.

note: 1850 turns on the body's filth to set aside kingly pride; Thiruppugazh 146 describes the same filth as a house of diseases and asks Murugan for grace.
teaches: The Jain king ends his disgust in a plan to leave and seek sages, while the Thiruppugazh ends the same disgust in a plea for a god's feet.

note: 1862 names the austere sage's feet as the only refuge from Death; Tirumanthiram 2 praises Siva who kicked Death and became king of the south.
teaches: The two refuges differ in kind: a teacher's feet to be reached by one's own austerity, against a god who defeated Death himself.

note: 1906 says no one but the Lord, who harms no life, can be counted as god; Tirumanthiram 1451 says there is one God in all ten directions and bids us take refuge in his feet to dry up the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both hold one God whose feet end the deeds, but they name different ones, and the pair turns on whether the one at whose feet deeds are shed is a Jina who gave up his own, or a God who gives grace.

note: 1920 promises the way of conquering deeds as a thing the sage will teach; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped burns up the many ills of deeds.
teaches: The Jain sage treats conquering deeds as a teaching to be given, while Tirumular treats it as a rite whose fire burns them.

note: 1930 says sufferers entered the pit by their own earlier striving and no one comes when they cry; Tirumanthiram 165 sends those who do not worship Siva to the seventh hell where they cry out.
teaches: The cry in hell is answered by neither text, but the Jain verse locates the cause in deeds and the Saiva verse in worship withheld.

note: 1931 has tormentors tell sufferers to take the fruit of their own deeds; Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind killers and drive them with the very commands they gave.
teaches: Both hells have punishers who echo the victim's own deed, but only the Saiva servants act for Death, while the Soolamani's act for no one.

note: 1932 stages lust's punishment as a forced embrace of fire; Siddhar 450 has the pit of hell say it will eat the lustful and the loins say they will ruin him.
teaches: A Siddhar's warning in the speaker's own body becomes in the epic a scene of wardens and figures, so the same fear is placed inside and outside the sinner.

note: 1939 gives hell as the ripening of the sufferers' own deeds with no one allotting it; Tirumanthiram 2544 says the Lord set hell and heaven for souls by grace.
teaches: The same pain is explained once by deeds ripening and once by a lord's grace, which marks where the Jain and Saiva accounts of hell part.

note: 1951 and the following verses give conduct as the ground of hell; Tirumanthiram 165 puts those who do not worship the Lord's form in the seventh hell.
teaches: The sage's list of sins contains no failure of worship while Tirumular's contains little else, so the two define the sinner differently.

note: 1962 gives the animals' pain at the killers' hands; Siddhar 269 gives the killers' own end, when Death seizes them for the sake of the body's pot.
teaches: The Siddhar says the killer will answer to Death, while the Soolamani implies what answering means: birth as the beast he hunted.

note: 1967 sends the false ascetic to an animal birth; Tirumanthiram 1659 sends those of false austerity to hell and says austerities hold only through true knowledge.
teaches: Jain and Saiva texts agree that false austerity is punished and differ on the place: a beast's birth in the one, hell in the other.

note: 1970 sends those who deny soul and rebirth to the nigoda state; Tirumanthiram 2558 sends those who say there is no higher state to hell.
teaches: Both texts answer denial with a bad end and not with argument, but one end is a lower birth and the other is hell.

note: Soolamani 199 has deeds breed deeds until a refuge is reached; Tirumanthiram 120 has a teacher make the seeds of births like seeds touched by fire, which will not sprout.
teaches: Both see rebirth as a growing seed; the Jain verse tells how the chain runs, the Saiva verse how it is cut at the root by a teacher.

note: 1992 treats giving as graded with a lowest grade; Tirumanthiram 505 says gifts to those without conduct and vows are like milking a barren cow.
teaches: The lowest grade of giving may still be a gift, and the Tirumanthiram says that at some point there is no crop.

note: 1992 grades a gift by the receiver's fault-lessness, the giver and the gift; Tirumanthiram 508 sends giver and receiver to hell if the receiver does not bow in worship of the Lord.
teaches: The two ask what makes a receiver worthy and give different answers, so one cannot tell from either how to judge a fit receiver.

note: Soolamani 200 makes the feet of the beginningless Lord the refuge from great suffering; Tirumanthiram 138 says the holy feet are Sivam, Sivaloka and the path, and a refuge for those clear within.
teaches: Both name the feet a refuge, but the Saiva feet are the goal and the way at once, while the Jain verse sets the refuge apart from the state it leads to, described in 202.

note: 2000 says the gifts of one who knows the true principles lead him among the best gods; Tirumanthiram 1867 says charity to tireless ascetics sinks deep karma and becomes the golden world.
teaches: One text places the fruit of giving in a higher birth, and the other in the removal of karma, which are different ends.

note: 2015 sorts meditation into four kinds by their fruit, two bad and two leading to heaven and release; Tirumanthiram 598 gives three objects of meditation, Shakti, the Supreme and Siva as guru.
teaches: The two works sort meditation differently, by moral fruit in the epic and by the divine object in the Saiva text.

note: 2018 has vision destroy karma's darkness by itself; Tirumanthiram 116 has Nandi remove the malas as fire rises from bamboo, out of grace.
teaches: Release by one's own seeing, without any god, meets release by a lord's grace, and the same fire-and-darkness language serves both.

note: Soolamani 202 describes release as a shining form and limitless, unfailing bliss; Tirumanthiram 136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt returns to water.
teaches: The two release verses differ on whether the freed self keeps its own form and bliss or subsides into another, if the salt image is read as loss of separate being and the Jain 'shining form' as a kept one.

note: 2060 says heaven's wealth ends; Tirumanthiram 184 says time cuts down both the heaven-bound and the deed-bound.
teaches: Both deny that heaven is lasting, but the epic counts the ending in fixed spans of seas and tells of a state beyond, while Tirumular makes time's cutting a general law with no way out in that line.

note: 2065 says the highest gods have no lord over them and none greater; Tirumanthiram 266 says the ripened see the Lord's feet and the resolute rule his heaven.
teaches: The epic's top heaven stands under no ruling god, while Tirumular's heaven is the Lord's own; the conflict depends on reading கோனிலா as 'with no king above' and on taking 'his heaven' as lordship, not only as place.

note: 2072 has the hero reach release by his own vision, knowledge, mastered mind and long meditation; Tirumanthiram 126 has the freed ones climb the thirty-six tattvas as a ladder to release, enter the light of bliss and see Sivam.
teaches: Both texts describe release as a climb by stages, but 2072 ends in a world of release won by the self's own effort while Tirumular's ladder ends in seeing Sivam.

note: 2074 uses three pleasant senses, jewel-light, sandal coolness and flower scent, for the bliss of release, which it calls சிவகதி; Tirumanthiram 325 uses a drink, the nectar of Siva's bliss in samadhi, for the same kind of state.
teaches: Both reach for sensory pictures of a state they say is beyond the senses, but the Jain verse's சிவகதி names a state of release while Tirumular's Siva is the god whose bliss it is.

note: 2086 tells the sons not to trust the goddess and to love the learned, whom she scorns; Tirumanthiram 169 calls bewildering wealth a waning moon and bids the reader seek the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like a rain cloud.
teaches: Both give up trusting wealth but name different things to trust in its place: the Jain king names the learned, Tirumular names a god who is himself wealth.

note: 2088 says the earth has enjoyed countless men and left them, and has not stayed with the next; Siddhar 286 says crowned kings are burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth.
teaches: The two reverse the same image: the king thinks he holds the earth, but 2088 says she leaves him and the Siddhar says he is returned into her.

note: 2099 has the king leave wealth, army and earth to his sons; Tirumanthiram 168 says join the true wealth before the elephants, chariots and wealth pass to others.
teaches: Both tell a king to leave his wealth while he lives, but the epic hands it to sons and takes no god, while Tirumular names the one to join.

note: 2115 has samadhi give the sword that cuts the foe; Tirumanthiram 121 has the Siva-yogi cut bonds and remain with the body as if dead.
teaches: Samadhi is a weapon of conquest in the Jain epic and a quiet stillness in the Tirumanthiram, so the same state is used for opposite pictures.

note: 2117 kills anger and its fellows one after another in a fixed sequence; Siddhar 87 asks when anger, speech and action, the 'I' and the mind will die so that release can be reached.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a battle order for the passions where the Siddhar only longs for them to die all at once.

note: 2125 places the liberated soul in the state called சிவகதி and wins it by its own meditation; Tirumanthiram 6 says apart from the Lord there is no hard penance that can achieve and no way into his city.
teaches: The two texts both speak of an unreturning state but disagree on whether penance alone reaches it or only the Lord opens the way.

note: 2127 has Death and Desire flee the hero who wins by full knowledge; Tirumanthiram 345 tells of burning Death in the fire of yoga at Kadavur.
teaches: Both texts have Death beaten, but one by a man's own knowledge and the other by a god's fire.

note: Tirumanthiram 1006 says that worship brings Indra's wealth, then the siddhis, then release; verse 272 says the world of the gods is reached by the true word and great austerity or by unslackening rule.
teaches: The same prize, Indra's world, is reached by worship in one and by one's own austerity or rule in the other, so the paths differ over whether a god's favour is needed; the conflict holds if Tirumular's worship counts as asking his grace.

note: Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings of the just sceptre and countless great ascetics have fallen; verse 273 says austerity and rule are heavy burdens, harder than lifting a diamond hill.
teaches: The epic stresses how heavy the two burdens are, and Tirumular says that even those who bore both have fallen, so the weight is not the end of the road.

note: Verse 289 names the pleasures of lovers as ripe fruits they taste; Tirumanthiram 201 names a man's wife as the ripe jackfruit he will not eat while he toils for the wild date.
teaches: Both speak of sexual joy as fruit, but the poem lets lovers eat it freely in the grove while the Tirumanthiram asks whose fruit it is, so the image carries opposite moral weights.

note: Tirumanthiram 634 says those who do austerity become lords of Amaravati and live in bliss by the Lord's grace; verse 354 says a king who leaves his rule for austerity becomes lord of the gods, with no god named as the giver.
teaches: The same heavenly kingship is credited to the ascetic's own austerity by the Jain sage and to the Lord's grace by Tirumular, so the two disagree about who gives the reward.

note: Tirumanthiram 258 names austerity and virtue as a boat across the sea of deeds that the Lord makes fruitful; verse 355 says austerity ends all evil and reaches Sivagati, with the god unnamed.
teaches: Both name austerity as what ends deeds, but one adds a god who makes it bear fruit and the other leaves effort alone to do it, so the dispute is over what austerity needs.

note: Verse 395 has the world take refuge in the grace of the first lord who bears the wheel; Tirumanthiram 349 says the bright-flamed First gave the discus to Achyuta.
teaches: Both texts make the wheel the sign of a first lord, but one makes it his own dharma-wheel and the other a gift he hands to a lesser god, so the wheel's source is claimed for two rival firsts.

note: 454 shows the women shaping the face's work with glance and smile; Siddhar 10 prays to forget women who show hand, eyes and face.
