teaches: The siddhar's prayer names the same tools the epic's women use, as the lure to be forgotten, where the epic presents them as skill.

note: Verse 462 has men blame the Creator for making women, whose beauty they take as the cause of desire; Tirumanthiram 204 turns the same beauty into an etti fruit that looks good and poisons, and tells the heart to hold back.
teaches: The men's wonder at the Creator's sin shows desire as a thing done to them, and Tirumular sets it as a choice of the heart, which marks where the epic stops short of the Saiva remedy.

note: Tirumanthiram 244 calls the king's share one sixth of the produce and ties it to keeping dharma without lapse; 54 shows the king taking his sixth only as grace.
teaches: The verse puts the one-sixth rule into practice as restraint on both tax and killing, while the Tirumanthiram makes it a step on the road to release and wealth.

note: Tirumanthiram 1626 says that people who ask for many things get their wealth, but those who do great tapas win the end of birth; verse 547 has Nami ask a god's servant for wealth.
teaches: Nami stands as a case of the first sort, asking for wealth at the feet of a yogi, and the Tirumanthiram supplies a rank by which his wish is lower than release.

note: Tirumanthiram 670 says siddhis come through eightfold yoga and Shakti's grace; verse 548 has Dharanan hand Nami the sky-going lore and a mountain for the asking.
teaches: In the epic, powers are a gift passed through a go-between to a man who asks for wealth, where the Tirumanthiram sets them at the end of discipline and grace.

note: Verse 560 makes kevala the bride whom the renouncer takes and by which he rises above the gods; Tirumanthiram 494 calls those who have left the kevala state the Vijnanars, so the same word marks the state to be left.
teaches: The same word names the goal in one text and the soul's first bound state in the other, so the two cannot be read on the same ladder.

note: Tirumanthiram 140 says the five senses come under one's control of themselves once one has met the Lord; verse 624 says a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer.
teaches: The epic gives self-conquest as a ruler's own work with a public reward; the Saiva stanza makes it follow from meeting the Lord.

note: Tirumanthiram 2030 gives fate's great strength as the sea-girt earth; verse 668 pictures that strength as fate upsetting a city and handing its wealth to others.
teaches: A one-line claim that fate's power is the earth is shown as a scene of one city's wealth passing to another.

note: Siddhar 1790 scolds the stony mind for wanting to rule the whole earth under one umbrella; 69 closes the king's praise on exactly that single umbrella and his pleasure under it.
teaches: The Siddhar treats the one-umbrella rule as a desire to be given up, while the poem treats it as the king's finished wealth, so the same picture means a trap in one and a reward in the other.

note: Tirumanthiram 2026 tells of five lions in a forest whose claws and teeth must be cut before the Lord is reached; verse 723 has a prince seize a lion by the fangs and tear it.
teaches: The same beast is mastered here by force of arm and there by a cutting of the claws, so the lion stands both for an outer foe and for an inner one.

note: Tirumanthiram 724 keeps the body alive because true knowledge needs a living frame; verse 775 holds that a man should give even himself to end the world's pain.
teaches: A Jain epic's praise of the body given away for others and a Saiva text's care for the body to win knowledge set out two uses of the same frame.

note: 79 shows youth as a fire kindled in women; Tirumanthiram 180 has a man recall being sweet as cane juice to women and now bitter as the kanjiram fruit.
teaches: The epic shows only the rising stage of desire's arc, and Tirumular supplies the other end, so together they place the princes' present blaze on a curve that ends in the speaker's bitterness.

note: Verse 927 shows a keeper who knows the elephant's ways re-roping it and handing it to its riders; Tirumanthiram 2023 sets five rutting elephants in the body that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The same craft of the keeper is both a working skill here and the picture of a discipline that fails without a teaching there.

note: Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from smiling women as the etti fruit is poison under a good look; Soolamani 980 shows a man's looks seize a girl's eyes and holds the pull as natural.
teaches: The epic tells love as a force that wins the heart, and Tirumular gives the warning that such pull is the poison.

note: The king mourning a body that was never found is set against the town that wails, buries and forgets in Tirumanthiram 145.
teaches: One poem shows grief for a real death that is quickly ended, the other grief for a false death that the king cannot end, so lament is shown to follow belief and not fact.

note: The jackals and ghouls feeding on the slain in 181 are the carrion eaters the Siddhar names when each claims the body as its own.
teaches: A battle's bodies are the same flesh the Siddhar tells us is only meat for jackals and kites, so the glory of the field is also the end of the body.

note: The verse sheds heavy deeds by right vision; Tirumular burns the many ills of deeds by worship of the fire.
teaches: The deed is shed by sight and understanding in one and burnt away by worship in the other, so the means of release is what they dispute.

note: The Siddhar asks when darkness will leave births as grass, beast and worm; the verse shows one man made a beast.
teaches: The Siddhar names the beast-births without saying why; the verse supplies a cause in a life of drink and lust.

note: Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages; the verse says meditation burns them.
teaches: Both texts burn the deeds with fire, but in one the fire is the Lord's, worshipped, and in the other it is the sage's own meditation, which shows where Jain and Saiva release part ways.

note: The rutting elephant is stilled by the vina's song; Tirumular's five elephants are held by the goad of five letters.
teaches: The same picture of a raging elephant brought to rest differs in who tames it, music held by a captive or a mantra held by the self.

note: The goad in line 4 is the tool of the elephant keeper; Tirumular's goad is the five letters that rein the five elephants.
teaches: The goad that in one poem governs a real elephant becomes the word that governs the senses in the other.

note: Verse 1 says release is taught by leaving cruel deeds behind; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only when the sun-like Lord appears, as the sunstone burns cotton.
teaches: Whether release is something the one freed does by shedding deeds or something the Lord does by his presence is the exact point where the Jain and Saiva ways part.

note: The queen leaves the king for the keeper, as the verse says men leave the ripe jackfruit for the thorny date.
teaches: The poem uses the Tirumanthiram's choice of poor fruit over rich fruit for a woman, and for a far more extreme pair.

note: The Siddhar blames a deceiving demon in woman's form; the king blames desire itself and has just spared the woman.
teaches: The Siddhar locates the theft of understanding in the woman, while the king locates it in desire, and so he can leave her alive.

note: The king's disenchantment with the court and the queen leads him to leave the throne; the Siddhar lists town, kin, women, glory and wealth as things that do not last.
teaches: The Siddhar states what does not last; the king shows the grief and betrayal through which a man comes to accept it.

note: The mother asks a kid for Chandikai; the Tirumanthiram describes Chandika as holding the four directions, without an offering.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram gives Chandika a cosmic form and no offering, while the epic shows how a mother worships her.

note: The townspeople tie sickness to the goddess's anger and ask for worship to prevent it; the Siddhar says the offering of goat and cock at the shrine does not stop the sickness and the family deity is not its cause.
teaches: The two disagree on whether a deity's anger causes disease, so the epic's chain from the goddess's anger to the king's sacrifice rests on a belief the Siddhar rejects.

note: The teller says that understanding that events arise from deeds gives true companions and joy; the Siddhar says the body is the enjoyment of deeds and joins those who think of Siva's feet.
teaches: The epic makes understanding the nature of deeds the first step; the Siddhar names grace at the feet as what takes one beyond them.

note: Tirumular says an unlearned king blind to dharma says 'kill'; the king here, without clarity in dharma, takes the people's advice and goes to the goddess's shrine.
teaches: The epic shows how the unlearned king's killing begins: he is led by piety and the people's fear rather than by anger, so the rule applies to a devout king too.

note: The Jain epic says the fruit of deed cannot be overcome; Tirumular says a teacher's fire makes deed-seeds that do not sprout into births.
teaches: Set together they show the epic's karma as a debt that must be lived through, against the Tirumanthiram's karma that grace can scorch before it grows.

note: The brahmins here claim a fresh-killed buffalo for the rite and eat it as holy; Tirumular names flesh-eaters as vile ones seized by Yama's messengers.
teaches: The two texts judge the same act in opposite voices, one by merit and the other by hell, so the reader sees that the epic leaves the verdict to the story and not to a threat.

note: The Siddhar wishes to see the lives he might kill as his own life; the kid in 197 is, literally, the king's own father.
teaches: The Siddhar's stance of 'thinking of them as my own life' is a wish; the epic gives it a literal case, where the creature eaten is the eater's kin.

note: Tirumular puts the flesh-eaters' pain in hell, after death; the epic spends its verses on the animal's pain first.
teaches: The epic puts the pain first on the animal and sets the eater's suffering later in this same life, where Tirumular's punishment lies only after death.

note: The Siddhar's woman is a pit of sores by nature; here the sores come on one woman as the result of what she did.
teaches: The epic places the body's foulness in a deed and its time, where the Siddhar places it in woman's nature, so the two verses disagree on its cause.

note: Both speak of eight qualities, here a freed soul's own, there the Lord's.
teaches: The Jain verse makes the eight the property of any soul that is freed, and the Saiva verse makes them the Lord's, so the reader sees where the two schools put the one list.

note: The sage makes feeling another's pain as one's own the base of the chief vow; the Siddhar wishes to think of the lives he would kill and eat as his own life.
teaches: The Siddhar offers this as a wish on the way to completing his tapas, while the verse makes it the support without which the vow of not killing cannot stand.

note: The sage says the suffering of births ends only by good dharma; Tirumular names austerity and virtue the boat across the sea of deeds, which the Lord makes fruitful.
teaches: The Jain verse makes dharma sufficient to end the fruit of deeds; Tirumular makes the Lord's act the thing that gives austerity and virtue their effect.

note: The sage says the king's father and mother went into animal births because of their deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to the births he has had as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The Siddhar mourns the animal births without naming a cause; the epic traces the animal birth to a particular killing and makes it the fruit of a deed.

note: The cocks say that the teacher's dharma has freed them from the fever of rebirth; Tirumular's guru makes the deeds into burnt seeds that will not sprout into seven births.
teaches: Both free through a teacher, but in the epic the cocks' own vow and memory do the work while in Tirumular it is the guru's act that burns the seed, and no god is named in the epic's verse.

note: In 270 the fruit follows honour or scorn though the ascetics hold neither favour nor anger; in Tirumanthiram 36 grace comes in the measure of the praise.
teaches: One text lets the result come from the one who honours without any granting, the other makes the Lord answer; the two differ over whether anyone grants the fruit.

note: Tirumanthiram has Yama's messengers seize the flesh-eaters and break them in fire-mouthed hell; here the dwellers of hell burn and split her with no god's order named.
teaches: Both fill hell with fire and breaking, but only the epic leaves the tormentors without a lord, which shows how little each needs a judge.

note: Tirumanthiram has old deeds following the subtle body into a new body; the muni gives the bodies one by one for the king's father, with a vow taken in the cock's body turning the chain upward.
teaches: The epic shows that the following deed can be altered by a vow made in a beast's body, which the Saiva line says nothing of.

note: Tirumanthiram 200 counts killing as a mountain-sized sin that is put away by reaching Siva's feet; verse 321 says the killing's result cannot be undone by anything given, and only the dharma's austerity loosens it.
teaches: The Saiva text frees one from the sin by reaching the Lord, while the Jain verse leaves the deed to be worn away by conduct alone.

note: Tirumanthiram 499 has karma bring the soul to wombs and then knowledge reach Siva; verse 329 says the dharma holds karma off and leads on to release.
teaches: Both give heaven or birth as a stage, but one reaches release through the Lord and the other through the dharma's own power.

note: The brother recalls births among animals driven by old deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The recalled animal births become the very cry of 'enough' that the pair will act on, so the epic gives the Siddhar's wish a remembered cause.

note: The poet says the soul is stainless and other than the body and that its karma is not its own nature; Tirumular says the stains go only when the sun of grace stands over them.
teaches: The epic leaves the stain's end to the soul's own knowledge of itself, while Tirumular needs a light from outside, so the two give opposite sources for the freeing.

note: Bhadragiriyar longs for the day he will stop killing and eating lives and hold them as his own life; in verse 60 the two at the killing ground wish the king to spread mercy to every life.
teaches: The Siddhar states mercy as a vow about his own food and conduct; the epic has it spoken as a blessing by the victims to the one holding the sword.

note: Pattinattar confesses to killing and eating many lives and trusts the Lord to bear the fault; the youth holds that harm to living bodies brings suffering through births.
teaches: Whether the guilt of killing can be borne by another turns on whether a god stands in the account: the verse sets a chain of sin and suffering with no pardoner in it, while the poet's plea counts on one.

note: Verse 70 says hearing the dharma checks karma's influx and sheds it; Tirumanthiram 1527 says grace comes as the guru and, when one's own doing ends through the knowledge it gives, the three impurities end.
teaches: Both make a teacher's word the means of release, but in one the hearer's own checking and shedding does the work, and in the other his own doing must cease and grace does it.

note: Both set grey hair and the loss of women's regard against the pleasure of Kama.
teaches: The Siddhar's youth who spends everything on women ends with a staff in his hand, while Asokan reads his first white hair in time to leave, so the two verses show the same fall averted and unaverted.

note: Both argue that the days before age are few and that austerity should be taken up before it arrives.
teaches: The Saiva verse points to the mountain of great austerity as the use of youth, while Asokan turns to the forest mountain and has no god to appeal to, only the fleeting of youth and kin.

note: The poet says a desiring mind outruns counsel; the verse says even learned men and yogis cannot turn a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The queen's fall is made one case of a general weakness that knowledge and attainment do not guard against.

note: Both epics open by going for refuge to the feet of the tirthankara: the Cintamani's red feet, this poem's feet of Nemi under the pindi.
teaches: Two Jain epics begin with the same act of going to the feet but name different lords, so the invocation is a convention and the chosen tirthankara tells which tradition the poem draws on.

note: Both name the star Arundhati as the measure of a woman's chastity: Mrigalochana is like her, and in the Cintamani a woman is said to put her aside.
teaches: Two Jain epics use the same star as the yardstick of wifely chastity, one saying a queen is equal to it and the other that a woman surpasses it.

note: In both works a former birth's vow explains what happens in this one: a broken vow there, a kept vow here.
teaches: The same cause by a vow of a past birth explains a loss in one work and a gain in the other, so the epics do not tie past deeds to suffering alone.

note: Jayandhara falls in love with a painted woman who is real elsewhere; the Manimekalai prince sees the living girl as a painted image.
teaches: The two works run the same trope in opposite directions, so a reader sees that the poets use the picture to say a desire is shaped by a seen form before the person is known.

note: Both poets defend flaws in speech by an image, the Cintamani's unwashed gem and this poem's lamp with smoke.
teaches: The apology for a flawed poem is a set piece of the Jain epics, but this poem argues from the lamp's worth and the Cintamani from the washing that cures the flaw.

note: Prithidevi fears her senior co-wife will let her fall; the Silappathikaram lists a woman who reared her co-wife's child as her own as a type of pathini.
teaches: The epic sets the co-wife's presumed envy beside the Tamil ideal of the co-wife who cares, so the new queen's fear is read as a convention the other works already know and answer.

note: Kovalan frees a Brahmin from a rogue elephant and tames it, and Naga Kumaran subdues a maddened elephant that has been wrecking the city: the same feat of a hero.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the feat is an act of compassion for one man; in this epic it is a sign of a foretold destiny and a cause of royal suspicion.

note: The prince wins a princess by defeating her at the vina; in the Cintamani the girl goes out to break her opponents with the yaazh.
teaches: Both epics make the vina contest the means by which a king's son wins his bride, so the motif is a standard marriage test rather than one poet's invention.

note: The Vedic logician in the Manimekalai defines perception as fivefold sense knowledge; the Neelakesi's teacher counts as perception also avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala, knowledge without the senses.
teaches: The two epics define the same first means of knowledge incompatibly: for the logician perception ends at the five senses, for the Jain it reaches up to omniscience, which is what lets the Jain claim an all-knowing teacher as a source of valid knowledge.

note: The Manimekalai's Vedic logician lists comparison, scripture, presumption and other means beside perception and inference; the Neelakesi's teacher lists memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture.
teaches: Both lists keep inference and scripture, but the Jain list admits memory and recognition as valid knowledge and leaves out comparison and presumption, so the count of means is itself a point of difference between the schools the epics stage.

note: Manimekalai shows the prince an old woman's body and says flowers, sandal, cloth and jewels hide its flesh; the Neelakesi's sage tells the adorned woman herself that her bath, scents, jewels and garlands only cover filth with skin.
teaches: The Buddhist and Jain epics use one argument with the roles reversed: in the Manimekalai a woman ascetic cures a man's lust, in the Neelakesi a male ascetic rebuffs a woman's, and here the body he unmasks is itself a borrowed disguise.

note: Neelakesi charges that the Buddha does not count enduring austerity a vow; the Kundalakesi fragment calls bodily mortifications, nakedness among them, mere words, and puts tapas in restrained living.
teaches: The Buddhist fragment confirms the position the Jain debater attacks but shows it as a relocation of austerity into conduct, not the plain denial of austerity the charge describes.

note: Kundalakesi's praise of her lord repeats, phrase for phrase, the invocation of the Kundalakesi: great from the first, thinking only good until the end, wanting nothing for himself, toiling for others.
teaches: The Neelakesi argues against the Kundalakesi's actual opening verse, so the surviving fragment is the text under attack and the debate is with a book, not an invented opponent.

note: Both list the five aggregates; the Manimekalai's teacher names feeling நுகர்ச்சி and formation பாவனை, the Neelakesi's Kundalakesi names them உழப்பு and செய்கை.
teaches: The Jain poet reports the aggregates accurately in substance, but naming feeling as pain (உழப்பு) and adding the flame of momentary perishing loads the list toward the points he means to attack.

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation opens 'he stood in greatness from the first' (முன் தான் பெருமைக்கண் நின்றான்); Neelakesi asks what 'first' can mean in a beginningless round of births.
teaches: A word of praise in the Buddhist invocation is read as a doctrinal claim and put to a dilemma, showing how the Jain debater turns devotion into a proposition that can be refuted.

note: The Manimekalai praises the Buddha as one who does not pity his own life and protects others' lives; Neelakesi takes the same countless lives of self-giving as evidence of countless sins.
teaches: The mark by which the Buddhist epic defines its teacher's dharma is exactly what the Jain debater reinterprets as karmic debt, so the two schools disagree over what suffering for others means.

note: A Kundalakesi fragment praises a man who stood unmoved, saying all that had befallen him was the fruit of deeds; Neelakesi cites that same Buddhist tenet to argue the Buddha's sufferings were his own karma.
teaches: A tenet shared by both schools, that suffering ripens from one's own deeds, cuts against the Buddhist claim that the teacher suffered for others.

note: The Buddhist teacher in the Manimekalai accepts only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi says a teacher who knew only through the senses and reasoning lacks subtle knowledge and his word is no scripture.
teaches: The same restriction to perception and inference that the Buddhist offers as rigour is, from the Jain side, the proof that its founder was not omniscient and so cannot ground a scripture.

note: The Manimekalai names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); Neelakesi says three of them are modes of knowing, leaving two.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist's own list, the Jain attack is seen to aim at the split of consciousness from feeling, perception and volition, collapsing the person into a knower and form, which is the Jain soul and matter by another route.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the mind arises like lightning (சித்தம் உற்பவித்தது மின்போல்); Neelakesi asks how, if the mind perishes wholly with what it knew, its perishing could be known.
teaches: The Buddhist offers the lightning-flash mind as a manner of speaking about what has no lasting being, while the Jain treats it as a claim about a knower and asks who is left to witness the flash's end.

note: The Manimekalai says the chain of becoming has no I and no mine, no going and no coming; Neelakesi says whatever carries traces across the moments is a soul, like the thread in a garland.
teaches: The point of disagreement is located exactly: both accept that something continues from moment to moment, and they differ only on whether that continuity needs a thread, a soul, running through it.

note: The Kundalakesi invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good; Neelakesi calls the stories of the Buddha's self-giving the doings of the deluded and possessed.
teaches: The Buddhist poem makes self-giving the very definition of its lord, so the Jain reply that such giving is madness strikes at the ground of the rival's devotion and not at a side issue.

note: Flesh eaten by birds: the Kundalakesi fragment shows vultures and dogs tearing the desired body; Neelakesi 214 says flesh cut off as a gift feeds only crows.
teaches: The same carrion image serves the Buddhist as a reason to stop desiring the body and the Jain as a reason not to throw it away, so contempt for the body and refusal to waste it come from one picture.

note: Aathirai enters the pyre to go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire will not touch her and a voice says he lives; Neelakesi 218 names the wife's death with her husband as the absurd end of praising futile death.
teaches: Neither epic lets a wife's death on the pyre stand as achieved virtue, the Jain by argument and the Buddhist by a fire that refuses her, yet the Manimekalai gives the karmic motive the Neelakesi's reductio leaves out.

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்); Neelakesi 222 mocks the monkey-king's self-offering, which saved no one, as no greatness.
teaches: The dispute is not whether the Buddha gave himself away but whether labour for others counts when, as the Jain argues, it profits no one; the Buddhist praise rests on intention, the Jain rebuttal on result.

note: The Kundalakesi calls covering or stripping the body, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair mere words, and true tapas a subdued life; Neelakesi asks whether the Buddhist rules of eating, shaving and kohl are dharma.
teaches: Both schools use the same test, that outward discipline is not the path, and each turns it on the other: the Buddhist verse includes the Jain's nakedness among empty forms, and the Jain debater counts the Vinaya's grooming among them.

note: The Kundalakesi praises the Buddha as one who kept nothing for himself and toiled only for others; Neelakesi takes the bodhisattva's gift of himself and his wives as proof of a man bound by nothing.
teaches: The same total self-giving is the Buddhist invocation's ground of worship and the Jain debater's first charge, which shows the quarrel was over whether others (a wife) can be given as one's own.

note: Aravana Adigal teaches that seeing that no thing has a self (எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை) is the nature of release; Neelakesi asks how release and relief of pain fit a teaching that there is no soul.
teaches: The Buddhist epic makes no-self the content of release, while the Jain epic treats the same doctrine as making release impossible, since for it someone must be freed; the two verses disagree on whether release needs a subject.

note: 256 parodies 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; the Manimekalai teacher gives suffering as the first truth and clinging as its cause.
teaches: The parody works by dropping the cause: the Buddhist epic ties suffering to clinging and its end to non-clinging, which the Jain song omits so the doctrine sounds like grumbling.

note: The Neelakesi's monk says evil conduct is not evil karma if the mind is pure; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts killing, theft and lust of the body among the ten evil deeds that lead to hell.
teaches: Set beside a Buddhist epic's own list of bodily evil deeds, the monk's mind-only defence shows itself as the Jain poet's construction of Buddhism, not the doctrine a Tamil Buddhist text teaches.

note: Both give the same Jain list, opened with the same epithet (இந்திரர் தொழப்படும் இறைவன் in the Manimekalai, இந்திரர்கள் தொழப்படுவான் here) and framed by the same questions of lord, categories, their workings, bondage and release.
teaches: The Jain categories circulated as a fixed formula that both sects' epics quote; the Buddhist epic lets a Jain recite it and moves on, while the Jain epic puts it in a Buddhist's mouth so that its defence can follow.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says dharma pervades everything and makes things move (பொருள்களை நடத்தும்); Neelakesi calls the reading 'we move by dharma' a quibble and says dharma lets things move as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing.
teaches: A Jain debater rejects as a misreading the very wording a Buddhist epic puts in a Jain's mouth: dharma is a condition of motion, not a mover, a distinction the Buddhist report blurs.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddhist has no space of measureless extent; the Manimekalai's teacher of logic names both 'one who says space is unreal' and 'one who says it is real' as parties to an argument, without taking a side there.
teaches: The Buddhist manual treats the reality of space as a disputed thesis between parties, while the Jain debater fixes the denial on the Buddhist and draws its cost, that the world then has no edge.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says time makes the short occurrence called கணிகம் and the long one of கற்பம்; Neelakesi throws the same two words at the Buddhist who denies time while using them.
teaches: The pair கணிகம் and கற்பம் was the Jain definition of time, so when Neelakesi mocks the Buddhist for speaking of moments she is pointing out that the word for his momentariness belongs to a doctrine of time he rejects.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the first Jina (in Buddhist usage, the Buddha) taught only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise that cures disease.
teaches: The Buddhist rule of two means of knowledge, stated as doctrine in one epic, meets in the other a counter-case from medicine, showing that the dispute over scripture as a means of knowledge was argued in Tamil from practical knowledge, not only from revelation.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) as what is spoken of as a person; Neelakesi names feeling, cognition, perception and action (உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை) and says they belong to one being.
teaches: The Jain debater accepts the Buddhist list of the four mental aggregates term for term and disputes only whether they have one owner, so the quarrel over the self is about ownership of the aggregates, not about what they are.

note: Both give the Jain doctrine that a thing persists in kind while its form arises and perishes: the Manimekalai's Jain with gram cooked into a dish and the sprouting neem, Neelakesi with a gold pot remade as a crown, applied to the soul passing from man to god.
teaches: On arising, persistence and destruction the Buddhist epic's report of the Jains matches a Jain debater's own illustration, so here the polemical account is one the school would accept, and the Neelakesi shows it was aimed at the soul's rebirth.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment says filth pours from every opening of the body, so no fragrance is to be found in it; the Neelakesi says dirt on the ascetic is simply the human body's nature.
teaches: The Buddhist poet's own premise, that the body is filth through and through, is the ground of the Jain reply: if the body is foul by nature, washing it cannot make it clean, and mocking the unwashed ascetic contradicts the Buddhist's teaching on the body.

note: The Manimekalai's drunk pleads with an unwashed Jain ascetic (மண்ணா மேனியன்) that his soul should not suffer in a filthy body; the Neelakesi answers that dirt on the body is nothing to correct, since adornment hinders meditation.
teaches: The unwashed Jain ascetic was a stock target in the Buddhist-Jain quarrel: the Buddhist epic mocks it through a drunkard's pity, and the Jain epic gives the reply, that the filth is the body's own and attending to it is the real distraction.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the faultless forbade liquor and the killing of living beings; Neelakesi argues that those who shun toddy should for the same reason shun flesh.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's own ban joins liquor with killing, not with eating meat, and the Jain debater exploits exactly that gap, asking why the reasoning that forbids toddy stops before flesh.

note: Saathuvan lets the chief stop killing yet still eat beasts that die of old age; Neelakesi holds that flesh is itself a fault and that its renunciation by all would end the killing.
teaches: For the Buddhist story the wrong lies in the killing, so meat from a natural death is allowed, while for the Jain debater eating is wrong in itself because it is what keeps killing going; the two epics draw the line at different acts.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment lists exposure, fire, cold, begging and matted hair as mere words and calls living subdued the true penance; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as profitless.
teaches: The Buddhist dismissal of mortification, stated in the fragment as a positive ideal of restraint, appears in the Jain epic only as a negative charge that it can then answer, so the Neelakesi keeps the attack and drops the Buddhist alternative.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment calls the body a deed-made thing where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live; Neelakesi says the many lives within the bodhisattva's body die when he gives it to the beast.
teaches: The Buddhist verse uses the body's teeming worms to teach disgust for it, while the Jain debater uses the same teeming body to charge the Buddhist hero's gift with mass killing, so one image serves renunciation on one side and non-harm on the other.

note: The Silappathikaram's hunters offer the goddess blood as the price (விலை) of the victory she gives; the Neelakesi's worshippers offer a goat for the child she gave, and the sage denies that she gave anything.
teaches: Both epics show worship to the fierce goddess as an exchange of blood for a boon; the Jain sage attacks the exchange at its first term, the boon, which the hunters' song takes for granted.

note: Mokkalan demands that substance and quality be declared either one or different; the Manimekalai's teacher gives a naya of oneness and a naya of difference as two valid ways of seeing cause and effect.
teaches: Mokkalan's either-or is stricter than the Buddhist doctrine the Manimekalai sets out, which itself allows a thing to be viewed as one with its cause under one naya and as different under another, close to the Jain answer he rejects.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists impermanence, suffering, no-self and impurity as marks to contemplate in order to cut attachment; Neelakesi names the same four as qualities the Buddhists lay on the aggregates.
teaches: The four marks the Buddhist teacher gives as a meditation for release are read by the Jain debater as predicates of a bearer, so the Buddhist list is turned into evidence for the substance-and-quality relation Mokkalan denies.

note: Mokkalan says that to declare a thing inexpressible is self-contradiction; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts keeping silent before an ill-formed question as a proper kind of answer.
teaches: The Buddhist in the Jain epic attacks the Jain mode of the inexpressible with an argument his own school, as the Manimekalai presents it, would have to face, since it too treats not saying as an answer.

note: Both use gram cooked into a mash (கும்மாயம்) as the Jain example of a kind that persists while its form passes; the Manimekalai lets the Jain state it unanswered, the Neelakesi puts it under a Buddhist's attack.
teaches: The same stock example served the two traditions differently: the Buddhist epic records it as the Jain's own illustration and moves on, while the Jain epic has a Buddhist demand to be shown the persisting thing, so the example's weak point is named by the side that wrote it down.

note: The Jain in Manimekalai 27 gives gram cooked into கும்மாயம் as his example of a kind that persists while a form passes; in Neelakesi 390 to 391 the Buddhist attacks that very example and Neelakesi defends it.
teaches: The cooked-gram example is shown to be a fixed Jain teaching case known to both sides, so the Buddhist epic's report of Jain doctrine matches what the Jain epic itself has to defend.

note: Manimekalai's Jain states that every thing takes on origination, persistence and destruction in each instant; Neelakesi 392 has the Buddhist ask what bears those three if they are qualities.
teaches: Manimekalai lets the Jain triad stand unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist's actual objection to it, the missing bearer, and the Jain reply in 393 that quality and bearer are one and different.

note: The Vaisheshika in Manimekalai 27 lists substance and quality as separate categories, substance bearing quality; Neelakesi says the quality is the qualified substance itself and the two are both different and one.
teaches: Against the Vaisheshika separation of substance and quality, the Jain refuses both their separateness and their simple identity, so the two schools disagree on whether a quality can be counted apart from its bearer.

note: Manimekalai's Jain says only that the atom, matter (புற்கலம்), is the outward form of things; Neelakesi 395 to 397 defends how atoms become form against the objection that touching atoms must have parts.
teaches: The bare formula in the Buddhist epic hides a live problem, how indivisible atoms can join, which the Jain epic answers with many atoms sharing one place.

note: Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher gives the hare's horn as the case of what has no arising at all; Neelakesi's Buddhist uses the hare's and donkey's horns to show that some things are non-existent outright.
teaches: The Jain epic's Buddhist argues with the same stock example the Buddhist epic teaches, so here the polemic reproduces Buddhist doctrine fairly before Neelakesi answers it in 405.

note: Manimekalai's teacher lists modes of usage that rest on what is not (இல்லது சார்ந்த வழக்கு), and pairs cognition with the hare's horn; Neelakesi's Buddhist insists that names and cognitions occur for what does not exist.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Buddhist claim in 412 rests on a worked-out doctrine of usage, which is what Neelakesi's reply in 413 must deny by appeal to scripture.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says each thing is both lasting and passing and takes on origination, persistence and destruction in every moment; in 420-421 Mokkalan calls this self-contradiction (milk becomes curd), and Neelakesi answers that change runs only by a thing's own causes.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sets out the Jain both-lasting-and-passing doctrine unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist charge against it and the reply, so together they show the doctrine and where it was attacked.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha himself spoke of six kinds of destinies; in the Manimekalai Aravanar teaches that beings are of six kinds (humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals, ghosts), born by good and bad deeds.
teaches: Neelakesi's retort works because Buddhists did teach six realms on their master's word, as the Buddhist epic confirms, so her appeal to scripture for the place of release matches their own practice.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says release is blocking the way good and bad deeds come in and wearing out past deeds; Neelakesi names that way as yoga activity and uses it to deny that a freed soul could be rebound.
teaches: The inflow that the Buddhist epic's summary only mentions becomes, in the Jain epic, the answer to the charge that a released soul could fall back into bondage.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher describes release as the reverse chain in which birth and all its sorrow cease; Neelakesi says the released soul, like a burnt seed, never sprouts but abides eternally with eight qualities.
teaches: Both epics define release as the end of birth, but the Buddhist account has nothing that remains while the Jain account insists a soul abides, which is exactly what Mokkala's question in 457 asks.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher names the five aggregates simply (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); the Neelakesi's Buddha gives them with numbered subdivisions, three feelings, six consciousnesses and twenty formations.
teaches: The Buddhist epic gives the aggregates as a short list within the four truths; the Jain epic's Buddha gives a scholastic count, so the polemic attacks a more technical Abhidharma than the one the Buddhist epic chose to teach.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives earth as hard, water cool, fire burning and wind moving, borne by eternal atoms; the Neelakesi's Buddha gives the same four marks with functions, borne by octads of momentary form (478, 485).
teaches: Across two polemical epics the marks of the elements are common ground; what the schools dispute is the bearer, eternal unchanging atoms for the Ajivika against momentary eight-fold clusters for the Buddhist.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the collective name (body, water, country) as a Buddhist mode of speech; the Neelakesi's Buddha calls the soul such a name, like 'hand' for five fingers.
teaches: The Jain poet gives his Buddha a doctrine the Buddhist epic itself states, so here the polemic reports Buddhist teaching recognisably before answering it.

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha calls impermanence, suffering, impurity and no-soul his four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and release's cause.
teaches: Holding the two lists together shows the Jain epic replacing the Buddhist's path of cause and cure with four bare marks of things, so that release seems to follow from seeing alone; this depends on reading நான்மை in 493 as the four truths.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says gram keeps its nature when cooked into a dish; the Neelakesi's Jain asks how milk, curd and buttermilk could fill the vessels if nothing lasts.
teaches: Both epics give the Jain the same proof from the kitchen, a substance that persists through its changes; the Buddhist epic reports it unanswered there, and the Jain epic aims it at the Buddha's momentariness.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the joined name as a valid mode of speech: many letters coming together appear as a word; 518 says a momentary mind could never put the letters together.
teaches: The two epics take the same example, a word made of letters, to opposite ends: the Buddhist treats it as a correct conventional name, the Jain as proof that something must last to join the letters.

note: The Manimekalai names the mind's three bad deeds as coveting, anger and wrong view; 529 says pride, deceit and greed are as evil as anger and the Buddhists leave them uncondemned.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's actual list, Neelakesi's charge turns out to be a clash of classifications: she measures a list of ten deeds against the Jain four passions, anger, pride, deceit and greed.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher counts the collective name (the body, water, a country) as a true mode of speech; 533 says naming collections one holds unreal makes every such word a lie.
teaches: The Jain charge of lying presupposes that a name must match one real thing, which is the very premise the Buddhist account of conventional naming in the Manimekalai rejects.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives exactly four bad deeds of speech in a closed list of ten; 535 says there are many more, such as talking alone with a woman.
teaches: Neelakesi quotes the Buddhist list faithfully and attacks its closure, not its content: her additions come from a renouncer's code of conduct, which a list of ten deeds for all people does not try to cover.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists killing, theft and lust as the three evil deeds that arise in the body; 539 takes that very grouping and asks who does them if the mind is not there.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sorts deeds by the door they go out through and counts the mind's three faults separately, so the Jain objection works only by reading a classification of doors as a claim that the body acts without mind.

note: 553 argues that if all is suffering there cannot be four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives four truths in which the fourth is joy, which is release caused by not clinging.
teaches: The reductio holds only against a Buddhism that calls everything suffering without exception; the Buddhist epic's own fourth truth (இன்பம் வீடே) is the exception, which shows the Jain argument aimed at a version the Buddhist teacher would not accept.

note: The Buddha of the Neelakesi offers seed, sprout and branch as a continuity in which release lies; the Manimekalai's teacher uses seed, sprout and stalk as the example of the continuity name, one word for a series.
teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the seed series as a rule of naming, while the Jain epic puts it in the Buddha's mouth as an account of what passes on to release, which is the stronger claim its heroine can then attack.

note: The Buddha here says deed and fruit exist but no doer; Manimekalai 30's teacher says the chain has no maker, no I and no mine, and is itself deed and fruit.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's own teaching, the Jain poem's Buddhist thesis turns out to be stated fairly, so Neelakesi's reply in 575 attacks a view the school holds, not a straw figure.

note: Both heroines of the debate epics take another woman's form: Neelakesi takes a princess's shape to break a sage's vow, Manimekalai took Kayachandigai's shape to teach her former husband birth and death and end his karma.
teaches: The Jain and Buddhist epics use the same device of a borrowed body to opposite ends, one to bind a man in desire and one to free him from it, so the borrowed form itself is neutral and the intent decides.

note: Kundalakesi's invocation praises the lord who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கேயுறு திக்கு ழந்தான்); 587 tells the Buddha that because he laboured for others (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய்), by his own rule that a pain-bringing deed is evil, he must himself suffer those deeds.
teaches: The Jain epic lifts the Buddhist poem's central praise almost word for word and recasts it as a karmic debt, so the same self-giving reads as perfection in one sect and as a self-inflicted evil deed in the other.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the Buddha came down leaving the Tushita world (துடிதலோகம் ஒழியத் தோன்றி); Neelakesi asks how the ascetic who perished could be a god in the Tushita palace at all without a self to carry him.
teaches: The Buddhist epic tells the Tushita descent as sacred history, and the Jain epic takes the same episode as its test case against rebirth without a self.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy as the example of naming by continuity (தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi grants seed-to-flower continuity only because a long branch joins them without a gap.
teaches: The Buddhist example of continuity works only where the stages touch, and Neelakesi uses that condition to deny that it reaches across death to a new body.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher makes release the seeing that the links are sorrow, unstable and without self; the Neelakesi's Jain argues that momentariness would make release the mere perishing of each moment.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist epic's own account, the Jain charge is seen to aim at a version of Buddhism the Buddhist teacher would not own, since there release is an insight gained by those who see impermanence, not the impermanence itself.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says there is no arising for a hare's horn, the mode of denial resting on what is not; Neelakesi says there is no perishing for what does not exist, as there is no size to a crow's tooth.
teaches: Both schools grant the same rule for the non-existent, and the Jain uses it against the Buddhist: if a perished moment is as unreal as a hare's horn, it cannot also be the thing whose perishing gives rise to the next.

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha says the reaper is neither that nor other; the Manimekalai's teacher draws from the nayas a middle that is 'neither that nor what is not that' (அதுவும் அன்று அது அலாததும் அன்று), and that there is no doer apart from the doing.
teaches: The formula the Jain poem gives the Buddha is the one the Buddhist epic itself teaches, so Neelakesi's excluded-middle reply in 645 strikes the school's own middle way, not a caricature.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher calls 'paddy seed gives paddy sprout' the naya of own-nature; Neelakesi uses the same fact, that paddy gives only paddy, to argue that the Buddha's example proves sameness of kind.
teaches: One observation serves the Buddhist as a law of causes without a self and the Jain as proof of a persisting kind, so the two epics agree on the fact and differ on what it shows.

note: In the Manimekalai the Jain's account of things as lasting and passing at once is heard and left among the doctrines Manimekalai sets aside; in the Neelakesi the Buddha himself is made to praise that account.
teaches: Each epic stages the same Jain doctrine before the other side and gives it the opposite fate, so the debate scenes show how each school wanted the meeting to end.

note: Manimekalai asks the Jain for his lord, his categories, their workings, and bondage and release; Neelakesi asks the Ajivika for his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.
teaches: Both epics question rival schools by nearly the same heads, but the Jain examiner puts scripture in place of bondage and release, and her first attack (680) falls on the scripture, so the choice of heads already aims the refutation.

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika spokesman, Puranan, gives as god a knower without limit present everywhere, and five categories, soul and four atoms; Neelakesi's Puranan gives Makkali as god, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories.
teaches: A Buddhist and a Jain polemic agree on the Ajivika spokesman's name and the five categories, which points to the Ajivikas' own teaching, but only the Jain account makes Makkali the god, which sets up its attack on a silent omniscient whose books no one heard.

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another (ஒன்று ஒன்றில் புகுதா); Neelakesi's says they combine and part but one does not enter another.
teaches: Two hostile accounts state the same tenet in nearly the same words, so it is likely the Ajivikas' own, and the Jain debater singles it out for attack (698) where the Buddhist narrator lets it pass.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives water its own coolness and taste and fire its burning; the Neelakesi's gives every sensible quality but sound to earth alone, and Neelakesi argues the other elements would then be imperceptible.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist report, the Jain objection is seen to strike the version of the doctrine that gives the senses' objects to earth alone; the Manimekalai's Ajivika, who gives water a taste, would be harder to hit.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says the atoms never enter one another, yet move, sink and rise; Neelakesi takes the same premises and demands the cause of sinking and rising.
teaches: The two polemics report the same Ajivika premise, atoms that never enter one another and yet sink and rise; the Buddhist leaves it, while the Jain shows it leaves motion without a cause.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before brings what follows; Neelakesi tests this with the infant girl whose womanhood must then already be present.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the claim that a life's course is fixed at conception and walks away from it; the Jain epic answers it with a concrete reductio, the grown woman's features absent from the infant.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are all mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before makes what comes; 707 tests that claim on breasts, teeth, hair and nails that a newborn lacks.
teaches: The Buddhist epic lets the Ajivika's 'all is set at conception' stand and walks away; the Jain epic takes it as a claim about the body and refutes it by the parts that visibly appear later.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika puts all of a life into the moment of conception; 709 shows that this would put a woman's daughter's daughter, and so on, into the first womb.
teaches: Holding the two together shows what the Jain thinks the doctrine costs: if a life is complete at conception, so are all lives to come from it, an infinite nesting the bare report never faces.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another; in 713 the Jain's Ajivika says the same of souls, each with its own length and breadth.
teaches: The rule of non-penetration that the Buddhist account gives for atoms is, in the Jain account, also a rule for souls, and only there does it meet the objection of crowded bodies.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika counts the soul as a category apart from the four atoms, the one that knows; 715 presses an opponent who gives the soul form.
teaches: The Buddhist report keeps the Ajivika soul apart from matter, so the Jain's charge that it has form and can be sliced like a pumpkin is aimed at a version the other report does not give.

note: Both epics give the Ajivika fire rising, water sinking and wind moving; 717 adds that the soul rises with fire, and 718-720 attack the whole scheme.
teaches: Two hostile witnesses agree on the Ajivika theory of natural motions, which makes it likely a real doctrine; the Jain adds the soul to it because a rising soul is what he can refute.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain lists dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, deeds, bondage and release; 729 has the Jain debater close by giving the three-times-three categories.
teaches: A Buddhist's account of Jain doctrine mixes substances with the path, while the Jain epic hands the convert the nine categories as one fixed count, which shows how each side reckoned the Jain list.

note: Both epics give the Sankhya twenty-five, but the Neelakesi counts the unmanifest and the five subtle elements while the Manimekalai counts the five sense objects and thought (சித்தம்) and leaves primal nature outside the list.
teaches: Two rival polemics hand down different lists under the same count of twenty-five, so the Tamil reports of Sankhya were not one fixed table and neither epic's list can stand for the school by itself.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya soul is the knowing awareness, without the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal; the Neelakesi's has the same marks but adds that it does nothing and yet experiences.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain reports agree on the soul's marks, but only the Jain report foregrounds the pair 'does nothing' and 'experiences', which is exactly the pair it then sets against each other in 740-745.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists a thesis that goes against one's own words (சுவசன விருத்தம், 'my mother is barren') among the false theses; 743 says the Sankhya's admission of acting souls destroys his own thesis (மேற்கோள்).
teaches: What the Buddhist manual gives as a textbook fault with a toy example, the Jain debater springs in a live debate, showing how the logicians' catalogue of faults was used as a weapon between schools.

note: The Neelakesi's sage counts four states of birth (நாற்கதி); Aravanar in the Manimekalai counts six kinds of living beings: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts.
teaches: The rival epics disagree even on how many destinies there are, so a reader comparing their karma teaching must first map the Jain four gatis onto the Buddhist six realms.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker counts speech, hands, feet and the two excretory organs among the twenty-five principles; 756 denies these are organs, since they have no object and no knowing.
teaches: Set beside the plain Sankhya list in the Manimekalai, Neelakesi's mockery shows exactly which item of the count she treats as weakest: the organs of action, which fail her test that an organ must know something.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says space gives room to all things; Neelakesi says space is one, formless, non-sentient and extends through world and non-world.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's report of Jain space matches the Jain epic's own voice on its function, while only the Neelakesi adds the non-world beyond the world, the part an outside report left out.

note: The Neelakesi's sage says the hells are seven (ஏழாய்) and spread into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings; the Manimekalai's goddess summons the eight kinds of hell-beings (எண் வகை நரகர்) within the Chakravala.
teaches: The two epics count the hells differently, seven earths stacked below the world against eight kinds of hell-dwellers within one world-system, so hell's shape is itself a point of sectarian difference.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker derives the ear and sound from space (line 214); 760 says sound has form and cannot belong to formless space.
teaches: The derivation the Buddhist epic lets the Sankhya state unanswered is the very step the Jain epic attacks, so the two polemics differ less in what they report of Sankhya than in what they choose to contest.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker lets primal nature unfold and withdraw by itself and names no creator; in the Neelakesi's Sankhya sarukkam the opponent defends a Lord of five acts, with the dance first.
teaches: The two polemical epics give the same school different shapes: the Buddhist account keeps Sankhya godless, while the Jain account hangs a Saiva-style lord on it, so neither can be read alone as what the Tamil Sankhyas held.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker calls the person the one awareness that knows all; Neelakesi takes the seer and enjoyer as the opponent's own words and gives that knowing to every soul.
teaches: Where the Buddhist epic only records the person as one knowing awareness, the Jain epic uses the same attribute to argue that the Sankhya has already granted a knowing soul in every being.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika gives the same six categories (பொருள், குணம், கருமம், சாமானியம், விசேடம், கூட்டம்) and is left unanswered; Neelakesi's opponent gives them in 785 to 788 and she answers them from 791.
teaches: The six-category list was a fixed set piece of Tamil accounts of the schools, and the two epics differ in what they do with it: the Buddhist epic records it and moves on, the Jain epic makes each category a target.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain counts space (ஆகாயம்) as a substance that gives room to all things; in 794 Neelakesi says the Vaisheshika's direction comes down to space.
teaches: Neelakesi's denial of direction is not a denial of space: the Jain list keeps space as a substance, so she can fold direction into it rather than abolish it.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says each thing is both lasting and passing and has arising, staying and perishing (தோற்றமும் நிலையும் கேடும்); 803 names the three as மும்மை.
teaches: A Buddhist epic's report and a Jain epic's own argument agree on the triad as the Jain signature, which shows the Buddhist account of this doctrine is faithful where the Jain uses it.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika makes generality the first common being that lets substance, quality and action work; 813 says the universal is only likeness between things.
teaches: What the Vaisheshika in one epic treats as the ground of all working, the Jain in the other reduces to resemblance, so the dispute is over whether the common is a thing or a relation.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika closes his account with inherence joining quality and bearer, and the Buddhist epic lets it stand unanswered; 815 attacks that very relation with a regress.
teaches: Read together, the two epics show which Vaisheshika category the rival schools found weakest: the Buddhist work records inherence as the school's last word, the Jain work makes it the first thing to fall.

note: In the Manimekalai the Vedic brahmin states that the Veda has no cause, beginning or end, and Manimekalai simply judges that it agrees with no way of truth; here the same thesis is put by Bhutikan as a challenge and answered with five inferences.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the Veda's beginninglessness and dismisses it without argument, while the Jain epic makes it the hinge of a full debate, showing which of the two heterodox poets chose to argue the point.

note: The Valayapathi fragment says not to accept a dharma joined with killing; Neelakesi applies that rule to the Veda, which she says forbids killing and yet permits limitless killing in sacrifice.
teaches: The fragment's maxim gets a named target: the dharma joined with killing is the Vedic sacrifice, and the Neelakesi adds that such a dharma fails even by its own rule against killing.

note: Both epics give the materialist the liquor figure for awareness arising in combined elements; Manimekalai's lets awareness die like a drum's sound, Neelakesi's sends each element back to its kind and counts space among five elements.
teaches: The liquor analogy was the stock materialist argument in both traditions, but only the Jain epic answers it on its own terms (866, 868), while Manimekalai leaves the doctrine and attacks only its theory of knowledge.

note: Manimekalai asks the materialist whether some have not known a former birth, and he waves it off as the delusion of dreams or possession; Neelakesi points instead to the newborn seeking the breast.
teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai, the Jain choice of evidence shows its point: an infant's instinct cannot be dismissed as dream or a god's delusion, the very escape the materialist used against memory of past births.

note: Manimekalai asks whether some have not known a former birth, and the materialist dismisses such knowledge as the delusion of the god-struck or the dreamer; Neelakesi offers the reborn man who leads his kin to the treasure he hid.
teaches: The reborn man's found treasure is a check outside his own mind, so it meets the very objection the materialist raised against Manimekalai's appeal to remembered births.

note: Both epics answer a materialist who accepts only perception: Manimekalai shows him that he knows his own parents only by inference; Neelakesi grants his rule and gives him a perception, the sight of a ghost.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain epic meet the same Lokayata rule in opposite ways: one turns the rule against itself and leaves the materialist answered, the other satisfies the rule and leaves him converted.

note: Both open by praising the Jain god, but the Cintamani defines him by the bliss he reached by himself and his unceasing qualities, while the Soolamani defines him by the sum of deeds he conquered and by the freeing of those who bow.
teaches: One invocation names what the god is, the other what the god did to deeds, so the Jain epics share a god but each praises a different side of him.

note: Kannaki's dream of trouble in Madurai, told to Kovalan before he leaves, and the astrologer's dream of an elephant garlanding the young lord are both dreams that foretell what is to come.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the dream is a warning that cannot turn the course of fate, while here it is a promise that the court at once turns into a plan, so one image serves ruin in one epic and fortune in the other.

note: 1286 taunts a rival with a bride won by another; Cintamani 769 taunts rivals with their wives' sulking looks lost after the battle.
teaches: Both epics make a pre-battle taunt turn on the rival's wife or bride, so the insult reaches his private stake and not his strength.

note: Both Jain epics describe a Vidyadhara city by its splendour, this one as a golden city on the southern ridge, the other as a casket of gems opened.
teaches: Both epics fix the Vidyadhara realm in the reader's mind as a city of gems and gold above the plain, so the genre's convention is clear from the pair.

note: 1470 shows the chief queen failing at her husband's body; Cintamani 293 shows women beating their breasts as the king lies dead.
teaches: In both epics the king's death is felt first by his women, so a fall in battle becomes a household loss and not only a political one.

note: Both make the adulterer embrace a figure of red-hot copper in hell.
teaches: Two Jain epics share the same matched punishment, but only 1932 begins from the secret night-visit and the wardens' mocking words.

note: Both set hell's dogs on the victims; 1933 adds that the wardens raised them in cages and that the victims flee up a tree of thorns.
teaches: The dog and the thorn tree recur as fixed parts of the Jain hell, while 1933 shows the dogs as reared for the work.

note: Both feed flesh-eaters molten metal; the Cintamani calls them to come, 1934 shows them the 'flesh' first.
teaches: The shared molten-metal meal marks flesh-eating as a fixed offence of the Jain hell, with 1934 adding the mocking offer of food.

note: Both give the thirsty a false drink: poison pools here, water that turns to pus in the Cintamani.
teaches: Relief that destroys the sufferer is a standing device of the Jain hell, shown with different liquids in each epic.

note: Both praise the Jain god as light: the Soolamani's light of the world above after splitting the deeds, the Cintamani's holy form that blazes brighter than flame.
teaches: The Soolamani's light is the result of cutting the deeds, while the Cintamani's is a body brighter than flame and marked with signs, so the same image names an act in one and a form in the other.

note: Soolamani 200 recommends refuge in the Lord's feet as the cure for suffering; Civaka Cintamani 380 shows Civakan going to the Wise One as a raft because an old deed drove him.
teaches: The sermon says why to take refuge and the story shows why someone does, adding that the going is itself moved by an old deed.

note: After taking refuge, Manimekalai's teacher begins on the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha; Soolamani 201 gives three things to hold after the refuge in 200: true seeing, knowledge and conduct.
teaches: Both sermons give threes after refuge, but the Buddhist three are what one goes to for refuge and the Jain three are what the follower must hold.

note: 2098 has gods carry the king's crown and cast it into the milk sea; Cintamani 3035 has gods lift the tray with Civakan's hair and let it fall into the milk sea.
teaches: Both Jain epics end a royal career with the same act, gods taking the shed sign of rank to the milk sea, so the image reads as a convention for a king's completed renunciation.

note: 2121 has the sky filled with the gods' regalia, flowers, sandal and powder; Cintamani 3090 has the gods rain flowers, coloured sandal and incense that fill the quarters.
teaches: The same festival of gods is set at the end of the war in the Soolamani and at the teaching in the Cintamani, so it honours victory in one and instruction in the other.

note: 2124 has the liberated one embrace the maiden called முடிவு; Cintamani 3117 has the king embrace the maiden Kevala with unblinking eyes.
teaches: Both Jain epics speak of release as a bride, but the Soolamani's bride is the end of birth and the Cintamani's is knowledge.

note: 2125 has the freed soul swallow the world and non-world together once the coverings are gone; Cintamani 3082 has the hero swallow the three worlds and the world of non-world after the four enemy kings fall.
teaches: The same formula for omniscience appears in both Jain epics, and only the Soolamani names the removal of coverings as its cause.

note: Verse 251 compares a king in love's grip without learned men to a rutting elephant ridden by a fool; Cintamani 9 tells of a king whose dense desire made him refuse counsel and lose to a plot.
teaches: The Cintamani's story gives the cost that the Soolamani's maxim only warns of, a king who would not hear and lost the throne.

note: Verse 254 has the king thank the ministers for his rule; Cintamani 206 has a counsellor press the king to hear counsel he does not want.
teaches: The Soolamani's council shows a king who welcomes counsel, while the Cintamani shows the counsellor who must speak when the king would not listen, so the ideal depends on a willing king.

note: Both poets ask the learned to deal with the flaws of the work, but the Cintamani asks that they wash the flaw out with their wit, while the Soolamani expects the wise to guard the lapses of people like himself.
teaches: One poet asks the reader to correct the flaw and the other to shield it, so the two Jain epics set different tasks for the learned in front of a faulty work.

note: Cintamani verse 44 shows ploughmen and buffalo rushing into the fields; Soolamani verse 31 shows the sugarcane and paddy standing with no one in the field.
teaches: Two Jain epics describing the land differ in whom they let in: the Cintamani fills its fields with the labour that makes the crop, and the Soolamani leaves the crop standing alone.

note: Civaka Cintamani 215 makes a king heedless of a warning because an earlier-formed destiny rose in him; verse 358 has a counsellor name fate as the power over plans and still press counsel.
teaches: One epic makes fate the reason a king ignores counsel and the other makes it the reason counsel must be given with humility, so fate is shown as excusing the king in one and humbling the adviser in the other.

note: Both epics let the washed-off paste and saffron of bathing women thicken a pool, here in the Vidyadhara palace and there in the city's ponds.
teaches: Both Jain epics fix wealth in the cosmetic that the bath washes into the pool, so the image is the genre's mark of luxury.

note: Both place the work before an assembly of the discerning: the Soolamani says the discerning in the king's assembly accepted it, while the Cintamani says it was set out to be told to the assembly of the discerning.
teaches: The Soolamani states the assembly's acceptance as already given, where the Cintamani only offers the story for it, so one poet claims approval and the other asks for it.

note: The Silappathikaram sets Kannaki's wedding under a pearl canopy on diamond pillars; verse 852 hangs gems and pearls on a hall.
teaches: The pair shows the same jewelled hall at two scales: a city wedding and a palace one dressed like the gods' own.

note: Cintamani 1344 has the astrologer fix the day; verse 866 has learned men judge the hour before the girl boards.
teaches: The pair shows the wedding hour as a learned decision in both Jain epics, with the Soolamani making it the king's cue to act.

note: Cintamani 1344 has jewelled women standing guard round the bride before her wedding; verse 868 posts two thousand armed maidens round the princess.
teaches: Both epics guard the bride with women, but this one makes the guard an armed troop of the magic-learned.

note: Both tell of an animal dying while a mantra is spoken to it so that it is reborn a god.
teaches: In the Cintamani the dog must consent and think on the words, while here the elephant is simply spoken to and the change is at once.

note: Vikraman leaves his kingdom to a nephew he has just found, while the Cintamani's Lokamapalan sets his young son on the throne and takes the ascetics' guise.
teaches: Both epics tell of a king handing over rule and turning ascetic, but here the heir is a sister's son and the turn follows childlessness, where the Cintamani's follows the setting up of his own son.

note: Both verses list the tricks of ball play, hiding the ball in a garland and making it dance like a snake.
teaches: Two Jain epics share one catalogue of ball tricks, so the hidden-in-garland and snake-dance play is a conventional set of skills, not either poet's invention.

note: Both show a queen's resentment at a king's divided heart, but Dattai's anger ends in worship and the Pandya queen's sulk ends in the king's blindness.
teaches: The Silappathikaram makes a queen's sulk the opening that lets the goldsmith's lie in, while here the first queen's anger is quickly absorbed; the same domestic feeling has opposite consequences.

note: Both close on a king with tribute-paying kings around him, but Civakan turns away from it in dharma and Udayanan stays in it.
teaches: The same picture of a king whom others serve ends in renunciation in the Cintamani and in enjoyment here, so the minor epic's close is not the great epic's close.

note: In both epics a god gives a hero a spell to call on, and a later need brings him.
teaches: Both Jain epics let a god leave a gift of spells that later serves the hero, so the helping god is a recurring structure of the genre.

note: Sathanikan crowns the heir first and then turns ascetic, in the order the Cintamani's chariot-king lays down: guard the kingdom, give it to a worthy son, and only then renounce.
teaches: The Cintamani states as advice the order that this king follows in the story, and the epic adds that he passes over his two named sons for Udayanan.

note: Both poets ask the learned to take a flawed work for its worth, using a gem as the image.
teaches: A gem image serves the Jain poets as a standing apology, one for flaws washed off and the other for plain wrapping carrying value.

note: Udayanan turns from pleasure after reflecting on past penance; Civakan turns from kingship after hearing the dharma.
teaches: The two epics give a king's renunciation different starting points, one from his own reflection and one from a sermon, and this shows how the Jain epics motivate it.

note: Both name the Charanas as a class of ascetics, one by their powers of flight and one at the mountain where they wash away karma.
teaches: The class appears with its powers in one epic and its purpose, washing karma away, in the other.

note: The Charana appears as a teacher who reads the travellers' minds in the Silappathikaram and as a flier in Udayana.
teaches: One epic shows the Charana's mind-reading and the other his flight, so the powers attributed to him go beyond either.

note: Vasavadatta's dream foretells a taking-away by a man, read by experts as a marriage; Kannaki's dream foretells the carrying off of her husband and a false charge.
teaches: A dream in these epics gives the story's course in advance, but the same image foretells a bridegroom in one poem and a ruin in the other.

note: The Jain five vows and flesh, honey and toddy against the Buddhist ten evil deeds of body, tongue and mind.
teaches: The two lists overlap on killing, theft and lust and differ on the rest, so the reader sees which wrongs the two faiths treat as common ground and which they do not.

note: In both works a king's own greying body is held up as the plain proof that youth does not last.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram a sage says the king need not be told since he sees his grey frame, whereas Asokan draws the conclusion himself and acts on it.

note: The Kural defines தவம் as enduring pain and not harming; 101 gives a king who loses his land and then takes up yoga to end old deeds.
teaches: The verse shows tavam taken up after loss and aimed at ending vinai, which the Kural's definition of endurance and non-harm does not say.

note: Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under the moon-bright umbrella are carried off and spoken of as dead; Jayavarma lays down his kingdom while living.
teaches: A king's leaving rule by his own act, before it is taken from him, is the story's answer to the impermanence the Naladiyar says no king escapes.

note: Kural 3 places the god on a flower and says those who reach his feet live long on the earth; the hymn has the lord seated on a lotus and promises Indra's rank to those who worship his feet.
teaches: Both couplet and hymn set the god on a flower and promise a reward for reaching the feet, but the hymn's reward is rank in heaven while the couplet's is long life on earth.

note: Kural 10 says only those at the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; the hymn says those who bow to the lord on the lion throne become gods and then reach release.
teaches: The hymn makes the crossing of births a graded gain, gods first and release after, where the couplet states it only as a crossing for those who reach the feet.

note: The hero kills Vayuvegan to avenge a father's murder; the couplet makes not killing the whole of virtuous action.
teaches: A Jain-framed epic lets its hero kill a usurper without comment, so the couplet's absolute not-killing meets a case where the story itself counts killing as justice.

note: Vayuvegan kills a king and seizes his land; the hero kills him, as the king's weeding of the cruel in the couplet.
teaches: The couplet puts the punishment of the cruel in a king's hand; here a wandering prince does it, so the story shows the same duty fallen to whoever happens to be there.

note: The hero takes five hundred princesses by the mantra-rite; the couplet praises the man who does not look at another's wife.
teaches: The couplet bars only another's wife, and the poem's heroes win unmarried women, so the epic's polygamy sits outside what the couplet forbids.

note: The couplet calls even the body excess for those who would cut off births; Nagadattan lets go of the body by fasting.
teaches: The couplet calls the body surplus for one bent on ending births, and the story shows that a householder who lets the body go by fasting is rewarded with a god's birth, so the Jain fast does not by itself end births.

note: The quatrain praises those who hold their vows through unbearable trouble; here the trouble of hunger is the vow itself.
teaches: The quatrain sets trouble as the test of a vow, but the fast makes the trouble a part of the vow, so holding firm means keeping a hunger that ends the keeper's life.

note: The couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking; here the death by fast is followed at once by waking as a god.
teaches: The couplet's sleep-and-waking comparison is made literal, and the waking place depends on how the sleeper died.

note: The couplet says to renounce while there is time; the king crowns his son first and then renounces.
teaches: The couplet gives only the timing, and the story adds that a king's renouncing in time includes installing his heir first.

note: A queen leaves her son for the nun's life and is rewarded in heaven, while the couplet asks what a householder gains by going to the outside way.
teaches: The story answers the Kural's question by showing a woman rewarded for leaving, so the couplet's praise of the householder is met by a Jain ideal that holds the opposite.

note: Both make the god the one to whom deeds do not cling; the king praises a lord who himself defeated hard deeds.
teaches: The Kural says worshippers are freed from deeds by praise, while the Jain king hymns a lord who won against deeds by his own conquest, so the same praise stands on different grounds.

note: The king gives up kingship at the height of his state and takes austerity, as the couplet urges renouncing while there is time.
