teaches: The couplet urges haste in the abstract; the king's act shows what haste costs, a throne handed to a son, and what it is paid for.

note: A king on his throne turns from rule at the sight of a vanishing cloud, as the quatrain's best of people see home, youth and wealth fail and renounce.
teaches: The quatrain gives renunciation as a conclusion of reasoning; the story shows the same turn as a sudden sight on a throne after the heir is crowned.

note: The monk conquers both deeds by his own austerity, where the couplet says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The couplet places freedom from both deeds in devotion to a Lord; the story gives the same freedom through a man's own austerity and no god, so the same result has two causes.

note: The closing sermon says nothing helps the soul but virtue and nothing harms it but vice; the couplet says no gain surpasses virtue and no ruin surpasses forgetting it.
teaches: The couplet's ruin is forgetting virtue, while the sermon's is positive vice (maram), so the story hardens the Kural's lapse into a deed that harms the soul.

note: The sermon says to fear a bad rebirth and leave vice; the quatrain gives the bad rebirth as the fruit of wronging others' wives.
teaches: The sermon names fear of an evil birth without a case, and the quatrain supplies one, so the fear gets a concrete deed and fruit.

note: The Kural's எண்குணத்தான் (one of eight qualities) and the verse's இருநான்கு குணமுடைய இறைவன் (the lord with twice four qualities) are the same number.
teaches: The Kural's unlisted eight is matched by a Jain count of eight qualities, so a Jain poet can read the couplet as meaning his own liberated lord.

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; the verse says the lord has ended birth, old age and death.
teaches: The couplet makes ending birth the reward of reaching the feet, and this verse names the three things the lord himself has ended, so the poem tells what is meant by crossing the sea.

note: Both name two kinds of deed; the Kural says they do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise, the verse names the two as what makes becoming, as something the lord taught.
teaches: The Kural states that the two deeds fall away from the devoted, and the Jain verse says it is the lord's own teaching of them that frees.

note: The Naladiyar says the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon bears its spot; the poet asks that one smoky flaw not make the lamp be thrown away.
teaches: The ethics book sets the noble above forgiveness of their stain, while the poet, claiming no such standard, pleads that a stained thing still be kept.

note: The Kural says envy ruins fortune and leads one to a bad place; the verse shows only a new wife's fear of envy and the retreat to the temple.
teaches: The Kural describes envy's results, and the verse shows how its mere expectation sends a wife to the god instead of to the rival.

note: The Kural makes not killing the whole of virtuous action; the verse makes a lord of that vow the one whose worship cuts the evil birth.
teaches: The Kural sets non-killing as the rule, and the verse makes it the lord's own vow, so worship of him is worship of the rule kept to its end.

note: The Kural has the son's merit read back as the father's tapas; the verse has the sage promise a virtuous son when the queen asks for tapas.
teaches: The Kural reads a son as the proof of a parent's penance and the verse reverses it, making the promised son the answer to a request for penance.

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one plans against it; the verse bows to a lord who has conquered fate.
teaches: The Kural makes fate the strongest force and the Jain verse puts one who has beaten it in front of the worshipper, so release means the end of the thing the Kural says cannot be passed.

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother; this verse says deeds already gathered can be shed in a moment.
teaches: The Tamil ethics book makes old deeds unavoidable, while the Jain epic's poet leaves a way to drop them at once, so karma is binding in one book and removable in the other.

note: The sage says austerity will cut away the prince's heated deeds so that he reaches release; the quatrain says austerity drives sin out as a lamp drives darkness, and that evil settles in again when the good deeds that feed it run out.
teaches: The sage's promise of a final release by tapas is answered by a warning that austerity burns sin only while its good is kept up, so the prophecy needs the prince's own lasting effort.

note: The prince is accused through a lie told against him and keeps his bearing; the Naladiyar says the pure of heart are not shaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's flame.
teaches: The Naladiyar's steadiness under slander is shown in the epic as a prince who answers the false charge with a procession and with giving, not with protest.

note: The prince wins at dice from the kings, as the Kural warns that what a gambler wins is like the hook's metal in the fish.
teaches: The Kural treats winning as the lure; the epic gives a winner who is not caught by it because he gives the winnings back, which shows the rule is about the winner's grip on the goods.

note: The king in 78 leaves for forest austerity after crowning his sons, the move Kural 46 asks the householder to question.
teaches: The epic shows leaving for the outside way as a late step after the duty of rule is done, which narrows how far the Kural's rhetorical question reaches.

note: Naladiyar 21 says kings under umbrellas were carried off and called dead; in 78 the king leaves the throne alive and by his own act.
teaches: The same fall of royal pomp appears as chosen renunciation rather than death, showing impermanence can be met before it arrives.

note: Both invocations make knowledge the mark of the god: the Kural's வாலறிவன் (one of pure knowledge), the Neelakesi's எல்லாம் உணர்ந்தான் (one who knows all).
teaches: The Kural's unnamed pure knower is open enough that a Jain poet can fill the same slot with a god defined only by omniscience and freedom from birth, with no creating role.

note: The Kural ranks abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Neelakesi lists the Vedic sacrifice among the deaths that make a beast's birth a suffering.
teaches: The couplet weighs sacrifice and abstention as merits for the actor and leaves the rite standing as a lesser good; the Jain sermon removes it from the scale of merit by counting it as a harm to the slain beast.

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; the Neelakesi names anger, pride, deceit and attachment as the very pains of the unrestrained.
teaches: Both make the passions the root of suffering, but they count them differently: the Kural's three (desire, anger, confusion) against the Jain four (anger, pride, deceit, attachment), so pride and deceit, absent from the couplet, are for the Jain teacher as basic as anger.

note: The Naladiyar's fool hails a pot of filth as a woman because of its skin; the Neelakesi's men perish for a filthy body worm-filled under its cover.
teaches: The quatrain rests its case on disgust alone, while the sermon sets the same disgust beside the evil rebirth and the stained lineage, so the impure body becomes one of three reckonings a restrained man makes rather than the whole argument.

note: The Kural tells the healer to find the disease, its source and the means that subdue it; the Neelakesi sermon classifies suffering as disease in 109-113 and then names its remedy.
teaches: The sermon follows the physician's order the couplet sets down, diagnosis by kinds before the cure, and applies it to the disease of birth, so the Kural's medical rule serves as the shape of a religious argument.

note: The Kural asks what a householder living in dharma gains by taking the outside way; the Neelakesi grades conduct as complete or partial.
teaches: If the partial conduct is the householder's, as Jain usage suggests, the sermon accepts the household as a path of dharma but ranks it below renunciation, which is just the ranking the couplet's question refuses.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, blood, bone and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman; Neelakesi 128 lists the woman's beauties and says lovers, ascetics and jackals each see something else in them.
teaches: The quatrain dissolves the beloved into parts, while the epic keeps the parts whole and moves the difference to the viewer, so the two give two routes to the same detachment: analysis of the object and analysis of the gaze.

note: Both speakers refuse to be swayed by praise of a woman's beauty because they have seen bones in the burning ground: the Naladiyar's speaker has seen the scattered teeth, the Neelakesi's sage lives among the bones.
teaches: The quatrain's resolve rests on having once seen the burning ground; the sage's rests on dwelling there, so the pair shows the same defence held as a memory and as a way of life.

note: Kural 579 calls it the highest disposition to show kindly regard to and bear with even those whose way is to hurt one; the Neelakesi's sage is likened to a mother who in excess of kindly regard (கழிகண்ணோட்டம்) suckles the infant that hurts her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's high virtue an image and a result: the forbearance is maternal, and it converts the one who came to harm, which the couplet's rule does not promise.

note: Kural 314 says the punishment for those who hurt you is to shame them by doing them good; Neelakesi 138 says the sage made her, who came to kill him, bow by his virtues alone.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's punishment by goodness carried through to its end: the would-be killer is not only shamed but turned into a worshipper and, two verses later, an advocate.

note: Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Neelakesi 140 praises the sage who, while rain beat on him and poisonous creatures crawled over him, knew himself to be other than the body.
teaches: The couplet's doubtful question about the soul's lodging becomes in the epic a settled conviction that is practised: knowing the self is other than the body is what lets the ascetic bear the body's torments.

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Neelakesi 147 says souls sunk in the sea of sorrow, born among beasts and in hells, should take refuge in the guileless great one.
teaches: The epic names what the couplet leaves open: the sea is filled with the births of beasts and hells, and the feet are those of the Jina, so a Jain teacher reads the Kural's refuge as his own.

note: Both use the sea of births: the Kural's பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், crossed by reaching the Lord's feet; the Neelakesi's sea of the souls' own evil deeds, crossed on a raft the Jina made.
teaches: The Jain hymn fills in what the couplet leaves open: the sea is made of the swimmer's own deeds, and the Lord's part is to build the raft, not to hold the swimmer.

note: Both say that the two kinds of deed, good and evil, leave the soul: in the Kural, for those who love the Lord's true praise; in the Neelakesi, by the way the Jina taught under the asoka tree.
teaches: Sung in the middle of Neelakesi's own praise, the verse credits release from both deeds to the teaching the Jina gave, not to the praise itself, which the couplet makes sufficient.

note: Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha is that he does not count eating flesh a fault; the couplet argues that flesh is sold only because people eat it.
teaches: The couplet supplies the reason a Jain debater can blame the flesh-eater who kills nothing: the eating is what causes the killing, so silence on eating is silence on killing.

note: The Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by going the outside way; the Neelakesi's ideal land has virtuous householders and also those who leave home's troubles to wear away their deeds.
teaches: The Jain poet answers the couplet's question by naming a gain the household cannot give, the wearing away of deeds already done, while still praising the household's gifts and conduct.

note: Neelakesi quotes the quatrain's first line, 'even if ruined, do not plan the ruin of the worthy', against a teacher who ruined himself for others and taught flesh-eating.
teaches: The quatrain's counsel to forbearance becomes a test of a rival teacher: self-ruin does not excuse doctrine that harms others.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; the Neelakesi praises a land where the four varnas each keep the path given to them.
teaches: A Jain poet could honour the Kural's ethics and still count the hereditary varna order as a land's virtue, so the couplet's levelling of birth was not read by him as rejecting the order, only as asking each to keep its duty.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh can hold compassion; Neelakesi asks the same of a teacher said to be all compassion who eats flesh.
teaches: The couplet's general question becomes a charge against a named teacher's claim to compassion, so the Kural's link between flesh and compassion settles a dispute between schools.

note: Thirikadugam names three seeds of the month's three rains: the priests' virtue, the king's just rule, and the wife who follows her husband; the Neelakesi gives its land three rains a month from its own known goodness.
teaches: The three-rains formula, which Thirikadugam ties to the conduct of priest, king and wife, appears in the epic as a landscape convention that explains away the missing palai tinai, its moral causes left unspoken.

note: Both use the new pot that takes the scent of pathiri flowers: the Naladiyar for the unlearned who gain sense from the learned, the Neelakesi for the Buddhist example of traces that persist after the flower is gone.
teaches: A homely image of borrowed fragrance served Tamil writers for transmission without identity, and the Jain debater shows that the image cuts both ways, since a scent that outlives its flower can be claimed for an enduring soul.

note: The Kural says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Kundalakesi lists the Buddha's literal gifts of eyes, body, wife and child as proof of his compassion.
teaches: The couplet's figure of giving one's bones becomes in the birth-stories a literal record of bodily gifts, and the pairing shows where the figure turns contestable: once it includes wife and child, the Jain opponent can call it madness rather than love.

note: Kural 221 defines giving as giving to those who have nothing; Neelakesi 214 argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot become the receiver's and so fills no lack.
teaches: The Kural fixes a gift's worth by the receiver's want; the debate adds that the gift must also be usable by the receiver, which rules out the heroic gifts of the body.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when one can no longer give; Neelakesi 218 says a death known to achieve nothing is no virtue, and draws the wife on the pyre as the absurd consequence.
teaches: The Kural's rank of giving above life is hyperbole about value; the Jain argument shows where taking it literally leads, and limits the praise of self-loss to a death that does something.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Neelakesi asks whether rules for shaving heads and eating are the path of dharma.
teaches: The couplet's neutral rule that outward marks do not make the renouncer becomes in the epic a weapon against a rival order's rule-book, and the pairing shows the rule cuts against every order with marks, the Jain one included.

note: The Naladiyar says a husband cannot put away even a wife without good qualities; Neelakesi treats the bodhisattva's giving away of his wives as the act of a man no bond restrains.
teaches: Her charge depends on the household norm the quatrain states, that a wife is not the husband's to dispose of, and applies it to judge a renouncer's gift, which the quatrain never contemplates.

note: 255 mocks those who eat a creature's flesh once it has died; Kural 258 says those of faultless sight do not eat flesh that has parted from life.
teaches: The Kural's phrase 'flesh parted from life' already covers the Buddhist allowance for meat from an animal that died, so the Jain jibe can claim the couplet's authority against that defence.

note: Kural 275 says the hidden conduct of those who claim to be free of attachment brings many evils; 258 charges monks who swell attachment while seeming free of it.
teaches: The Kural leaves its 'many evils' unnamed; the Neelakesi names them as a ghost's birth or dark hell, turning a moral warning into a doctrine of rebirth.

note: Kural 256 argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; 260 presses the same point against a Buddhist who says he only eats what another killed.
teaches: The Kural's demand argument is put to work against a named defence, the eater's pure intention, and becomes a claim about karma: the buyer's deed joins the butcher's.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaven head nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 261 says the outward guise is false unless mind and conduct agree.
teaches: Both discount the guise, but for different reasons: the Kural makes conduct the test of renunciation, and the Neelakesi uses that same test against a monk who makes the mind the only test.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one avoids what the world condemns; Mokkalan grants the robe only the small use of making the monk known, and Neelakesi asks what such a sign is for.
teaches: The Kural's dismissal of ascetic marks becomes a live weapon between sects: the Jain debater uses it against the Buddhist robe, while her own tradition's nakedness is a mark of another kind.

note: The Kural says that one who restrains the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs is protected through seven births; Neelakesi says the monk should guard the eyes that stir the mind instead of covering his limbs.
teaches: The tortoise image of drawing in the limbs is exactly what Neelakesi denies is restraint when done with cloth: she moves the Kural's withdrawal from the body to the senses, against the robe.

note: The Kural says outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை) comes by water and inner purity by truth; Neelakesi lists water, betel and the tooth-stick and says that if outer cleaning purified the mind, courtesans would be the purest.
teaches: The couplet's two-part rule is turned into a reductio: Neelakesi supplies the absurd case that proves outer and inner purity are separate, and aims it at monks who tend their robes.

note: Neelakesi says that if only perception and inference counted there could be no medical treatise; the Kural's chapter on medicine states the three humours on the authority of the learned in the books (நூலோர்).
teaches: The Kural's deference to the medical books for the three humours is just the kind of text-borne knowledge the Jain debater cites: neither the patient's sight nor his inference gives it.

note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

note: Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that the sin of killing attaches only where there is intention; the Kural argues that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh for a price.
teaches: The Kural's buyer-and-seller argument is the reply the intention defence needs: the eater need intend no killing for his eating to cause one, so a rule that weighs only intention misses the chain from buyer to slaughter.

note: The objection in Neelakesi 316 is that if pleasure and pain are the fruit of deeds, the pain of penance is too; the Kural defines penance as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life.
teaches: The Kural's definition of தவம் as bearing the pain that comes takes away the force of the objection: if penance is endurance of what arrives, it does not matter that the pain is old karma's fruit.

note: The Naladiyar calls the meat-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Neelakesi places its flesh-eating demon hosts and a goddess's shrine inside a real burning ground.
teaches: The quatrain's metaphor joining flesh-eating and the cremation ground becomes the Neelakesi's literal scene, so the epic's first quarrel over flesh is staged where eating bodies and burning them meet.

note: The Kural asks what other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) can remain for those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; the Neelakesi defends those who teach that at death every tie, even to dharma (அறத்தொடர்ப்பாடு), must go.
teaches: The Kural's list of ties ends at the body, while the Jain teaching carried into the hour of death adds dharma itself to what must be let go, so renunciation's last step is dropping the merit that led there.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can hold to compassion (அருள்); Neelakesi asks a monk who eats flesh so that his body thickens whether he has any compassion (அருள்).
teaches: The couplet's question, put to anyone, becomes in the debate a charge against a school that makes compassion its centre, so its force is to expose a contradiction inside a teaching rather than to state a general rule.

note: The Kural says no one would bring meat to sell if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi tells the monk who calls buying meat fair that by paying the fishermen daily he wants killing always.
teaches: The couplet's market argument is turned on a particular defence, that meat bought or given is clean of killing, and shown to cover the buyer who pays day after day, so steady demand makes him a party to each killing.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi says that if all renounced flesh no one would go near killing, and that the teacher who teaches dharma earns its merit.
teaches: The couplet blames the eating world for the killing; the debate adds that a world's eating follows its teachers, so a teacher who permits flesh carries the demand argument's guilt.

note: Kural 261 makes bearing pain one half of penance; Mokkalan argues that if wasting the body were good, burning or wasting with disease would also be penance.
teaches: The reductio bites only if the couplet's pain is pain one inflicts on oneself; if it is the pain that comes unsought, the Kural and the Buddhist agree, so the pairing shows that the couplet's word உற்ற decides which side it is on.

note: The Kural likens men without kindly regard to trees fixed in the soil; Neelakesi argues that trees feel heat and cold and change as living bodies do.
teaches: Read with the Jain argument, the couplet's tree is not a dead thing but a living being that feels by touch yet has no eye to look with, which makes the comparison exact for a man who has eyes and does not use them kindly.

note: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; Mokkalan and Neelakesi dispute whether a thing can both last and not last.
teaches: The couplet assumes things fall cleanly into the lasting and the passing, and the debate shows that division itself was contested, the Jain holding one thing lasting in substance and passing in its modes.

note: The Kural sets abstaining from one killing above a thousand fire sacrifices; the Neelakesi's sage does not ask the worshippers to drop their vow but to offer a clay goat in its place.
teaches: Between the Kural's flat preference for not killing over ritual and outright refusal of the rite lies a third course the epic shows a teacher using: keep the vow, replace the victim with an image.

note: The Kural ranks not killing first and not lying second; the sage lists killing, lying, theft, going to others' wives and craving for wealth, and promises the world of the gods.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of not killing above not lying is the head of a fixed Jain list of five householder abstentions, which the epic gives whole with a heavenly reward rather than release.

note: Naladiyar 313 describes people who rush to debate on the strength of a word, talk at length and do not know when they are beaten; Neelakesi tells the Buddhist he does not know words and prattles many words like a ghost.
teaches: The Naladiyar's type of the endless talker becomes a charge thrown by one debater at another, which shows the description used as a weapon in debate as well as a moral portrait.

note: The Kural likens the body-life bond to a bird leaving its nest; Neelakesi holds the soul joined with the body it has taken and makes it the one who sees and knows there.
teaches: The Kural's bird stresses how loosely the life sits in the body, while the Jain debater insists the soul fills and works the body as its knower, so the same separability is put to opposite uses.

note: The Kural says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world; in 416-417 both debaters take the giver's reaching heaven as what makes giving worth doing, and Neelakesi calls the identity of giver and god the truth of giving (தானத்தின் உண்மை).
teaches: The Kural's 'even if there were no higher world' is a position neither the Jain nor the Buddhist debater will hold here, since both stake the worth of alms on a rewarded doer.

note: The Kural says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here; Mokkalan asks what makes non-return final, and Neelakesi answers that karma returns only through yoga activity, which the freed soul lacks.
teaches: The Kural names the path of no return without saying what keeps it closed, and the debate supplies a mechanism: return needs the inflow of karma through activity, which release has ended.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the hymn says hunger, disease and enmity perish wherever the Jina goes.
teaches: The three ills the Kural treats as a test of a well-governed land are, in the Jain hymn, ended by the presence of a saint rather than by the king, so the pairing moves the source of a land's welfare from rule to holiness.

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Neelakesi says those who strew flowers and hymn the Aptha lose both kinds of deed and reach the state of Siva.
teaches: The couplet leaves its Lord unnamed and its reward unstated, and the epic fills both, naming the Aptha by the marks just argued for and calling the reward release, which shows how a sect could read the Kural's opening chapter as its own.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh for a price if the world did not kill to eat; 471 makes the market's beasts say the buyers' money sends the netter out to kill them.
teaches: The couplet's demand argument is given a voice and an opponent: in the Buddha's own town the dead animals accuse the buyer, so the rule becomes a charge against a monastic order that buys rather than kills.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; 472 grants the Buddha the greatest self-giving, even of his wife, and still faults him for not forbidding flesh.
teaches: Grace in the Kural is lost by the eater; the Neelakesi adds a teacher's grace lost by silence, so that a life of total giving can still fail the test if it leaves others free to eat flesh.

note: Kural 255 says hell does not open its mouth to release one who eats flesh; 473 says the Buddha, by permitting flesh, will lead himself and his disciples into the burning hell.
teaches: The Kural's hell takes the single eater; the Jain polemic widens it to a teacher and his whole following, so a permission given in doctrine becomes a collective path to hell.

note: Thirikadugam 36 names among the self-deceived the one who eats flesh and claims compassion and the one who says the deed is done without his consent; 474 answers that defence with the middleman who profits from a trade he does not perform.
teaches: The Thirikadugam only lists the excuse 'it was not done with my consent'; the Neelakesi gives the reason it fails, since the eater stands to the killing as a middleman to a sale, profiting from both sides.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 binds the sin of a killing on five: the killer, the one who consented, the one who took the carcass, the cook and the eater; 475 mocks a master who sorts sin so that the killer bears it and the eater does not.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Jain account of shared guilt as a deliberate counter-rule: the Sirupanchamoolam's five sharers are the answer to the very division of guilt the Neelakesi's Buddha is said to make.

note: The Kural says penance can crush one's foes if one so intends; the sage, attacked by Neelakesi, intends instead to make her see her powerlessness and come to the dharma.
teaches: The power the Kural grants penance against enemies is here held back and turned to converting the enemy, which is what the Kural's 'if one so intends' leaves open.

note: The Kural says understanding is seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever nature; Neelakesi says no thing has ever been made clear except through its qualities.
teaches: The Jain makes the couplet's 'whatever its nature' into a method: the true thing is reached through its qualities, not by stripping them away, which is why she can claim the soul is known by knowing and seeing.

note: Kural 35 sets aside envy, craving, anger and harsh words as the four that virtue avoids; 529 names anger, pride, deceit and greed as the faults of the mind.
teaches: Both make anger and greed central, but each completes the list from its own school: the Kural adds envy and a fault of speech, the Jain debater pride and deceit, so the shared pair is common ground and the rest is sectarian.

note: 533 holds that naming a thing one thinks unreal is a lie; Kural 292 holds that even a falsehood stands as truth if it yields faultless good.
teaches: Neelakesi's charge only works on a test of truth by match with things; on the Kural's test by effect, the Buddhist's conventional names, harming no one, would not be lies at all.

note: Kural 91 defines sweet words as moist with love and free of deceit; 536 argues against a rule that gentle speech is good by citing the soft-spoken plotter.
teaches: The Kural's definition already builds in the guard Neelakesi says the Buddhist rule lacks: speech counts as sweet only when it is without deceit, so her gentle conspirator would not qualify under it.

note: Kural 282 says even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; 547 holds that the burglar, the would-be killer and the would-be adulterer carry the karma of their intent even when the act fails.
teaches: Read beside a debate that also condemns the unintended killing, the couplet's thought-crime proves to be only half of the Jain position, which binds karma both to the intent without the deed and to the deed without the intent.

note: The Kural pictures penance as pain burning the ascetic as fire burns gold; Neelakesi fears that the fullness of the sage's penance will burn her.
teaches: The fire of penance faces two ways: inward in the Kural, where it purifies the one who bears it, and outward in the epic, where the assailant feels it as a fire that would consume her.

note: Naladiyar 48 says those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen what the body is; 557 treats 'those who wear garlands and sandal have not found the path' as the absurd outcome of the Buddhist claim that nothing is pure.
teaches: A Jain anthology and a Jain epic part ways on impurity: the Naladiyar finds it in the body and condemns the garland, while the Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist 'nothing at all is pure' because extended to everything it erases the difference between path and no path.

note: The couplet defines a gift by its receiver: what goes to those who have nothing. Neelakesi tests a gift by what is given: persons handed over as alms make their taker a thief.
teaches: A gift can satisfy the couplet's test of the receiver's want and still fail, because the thing given must be the giver's own, which the couplet takes for granted.

note: Both set the ascetic's ஆற்றல் against கூற்றம்: the Kural says those who gain the power of penance can leap even Death; here a demoness likened to Death owns that the fire of the sage's penance would destroy her.
teaches: The couplet's abstract boast that penance outruns death becomes a scene in which Death's likeness itself gives up the fight, and the victory comes without the ascetic acting at all.

note: The Buddha denies any doer behind the deed; the quatrain says an old deed seeks out the very one who did it, as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The quatrain's comfort that a deed finds its own doer depends on there being a doer who lasts, which is exactly what the Buddha's thesis denies, so the proverb takes a side in the Jain-Buddhist debate.

note: The Kural says all pains rest on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்); Neelakesi applies the rule to the Buddha's pain-bearing gifts and says he must himself suffer what they caused.
teaches: Applied without limit, the rule that pain returns to its causer condemns even the giver who bears pain for others, and only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop that.

note: The Kural says to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is show; Neelakesi denies that the mind alone is the deed and argues that action always goes with it and is karma too.
teaches: A mind-first ethic that the Kural states as praise of sincerity becomes, between Buddhist and Jain, a disputed claim about where karma lies, and the Jain side refuses to let the act fall away.

note: The Kural says a fault in the well-born shows like the moon's spot; the Neelakesi says the moon's spot does not stop the world loving it.
teaches: Read together, the moon's spot is both what makes a high fault visible and what proves the loved and high are never spotless, so visibility is not the same as rejection.

note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out the one who did it (தற்செய்த கிழவனை) as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the Buddha in 602 says the doer has perished and the continuum running on from him receives the fruit.
teaches: The quatrain's image needs a doer who is still there to be found, while the Buddha's answer removes him, so the pair shows that the Tamil ethical common sense about karma assumes a lasting self.

note: The Naladiyar's new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers, an image of the unlearned gaining sense from the learned; Neelakesi attacks the same image as the Buddha's proof of a trace that outlives the flower.
teaches: The ethical image of borrowed fragrance only works if the scent has a lasting bearer, the flower-dust in the pot, so the Jain debater's demand to know whose the scent is shows what the Naladiyar's figure quietly assumes about company and influence.

note: The Kural calls the tie of body and life a friendship that ends as a bird leaves its nest; the Neelakesi's sage knows a scripture that cuts the deeds entangled in the soul's oneness with and difference from the body.
teaches: Set beside the Kural, the Jain verse turns the body-soul tie from a bond death simply ends into a knot of deeds that a discipline can cut while one still lives.

note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back to oneself in the afternoon, of themselves; Neelakesi argues that the fruit of deeds falls to the doers themselves (செய்தார்கள் தாம்).
teaches: The couplet's 'to oneself' (தமக்கு) is set within one day of one life, while the debate asks whether the same self is there across births to receive it.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi makes 'the doers themselves reap' the point that silences the Buddha.
teaches: The proverb that a deed finds its doer turns out to presuppose a doer who lasts until the fruit comes, which is exactly what the Buddhist no-self denies and what Neelakesi defends.

note: Kural 356 says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return; Neelakesi says those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release in due order.
teaches: Both make understanding the road to release, but the epic names whose scripture it must be and adds that any being, even a demoness, may walk it, by stages.

note: Kural 4 sets the Lord apart as one without liking or aversion; Puranan argues that a knower who speaks must fall into longing and anger, and Neelakesi denies that speech implies them.
teaches: The Kural defines its Lord by the absence of liking and aversion without asking whether such a Lord can teach; the Ajivika debate shows that the absence was contested, since a rival held that any speaking Lord must have them.

note: The Kural likens the learned who cannot unfold their learning to scentless flowers; Neelakesi ranks a silent omniscient below any man who tells the good he sees.
teaches: The couplet faults those unable to expound, and the verse extends the fault to one who could speak and chooses not to, turning a rule about scholars into a test of a god.

note: Both picture life in a house: the Kural asks whether life, a lodger in the body, has no home of its own; the Neelakesi's sage likens beings across the states of birth to people who live together in one house and do not fear each other.
teaches: The same lodging image serves the Kural to make the soul homeless and the Jain sage to make all souls housemates, so it can teach unrest or fearlessness depending on whether one looks at one body or at all lives.

note: The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which comes first whatever one devises; Neelakesi attacks a fixity that sets in advance what comes, how, how much and when.
teaches: The couplet claims fate outruns human contrivance, but the Jain attack shows that the vulnerable step is the further claim that every particular of an outcome is already fixed, which the couplet does not make.

note: The Naladiyar answers a beautiful woman's appeal by dissecting the body into entrails, blood and bone and asking which part is she; the Neelakesi's sage meets a full display of wiles with one question, what are these to us.
teaches: The Naladiyar's dissection is a method for one still tempted, while the sage needs no method; and since this beauty is a demoness's borrowed shape, the Naladiyar's question of where the woman is in the body has, here, a literal answer: nowhere.

note: Kural 948 tells the physician to find the disease, then its root, then the remedy, and act; 723 says the teachers' instruction does the same for the suffering of many beings.
teaches: The Kural's method of the physician becomes, in a Jain debate, the method of the religious teacher, so that a rival doctrine is treated as a disease to be diagnosed rather than an enemy to be beaten.

note: Kural 358 says understanding is seeing the excellent so that the folly called birth departs; 724 calls birth a disease, names bad deeds eaten as its cause, and makes true understanding the cure.
teaches: Both make birth the evil and understanding the cure, but the Jain verse inserts the deed as the cause between them, so understanding ends birth only by ending the eating of past deeds.

note: Kural 706 has crystal show the colour of what is near it, as the face shows the heart; the Sankhya, in Neelakesi's report, uses crystal beside a coloured thing for a soul that only seems changed.
teaches: The same crystal runs opposite ways: in the Kural its borrowed colour is a true sign of what lies within, in the Sankhya it is a mere appearance over a soul untouched, which is why Neelakesi can call the image an evasion.

note: The Kural's first couplet says the world has the primal Lord as its first; the Neelakesi argues no creator can be first without an endless regress of makers.
teaches: Kural 1 says the Lord is first but never that he made the world, so the Jain regress argument against a creator leaves the couplet standing, which shows why Jain readers could keep it.

note: Kural 5 says both kinds of deed, born of darkness, do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 807 says good and bad deeds and their fruits are qualities of the soul, or birth and release mean nothing.
teaches: Both count good deeds with bad as what binds, but the Jain debater asks what clinging is: a deed can cling or fall away only if it is a quality of the soul, which the couplet takes for granted.

note: Kural 355 calls understanding the seeing of the true thing in a thing whatever its nature; 819 says thing and quality are one from one standpoint and different from another.
teaches: The couplet separates a thing's nature from its truth and asks us to see through to the truth; the Jain standpoint doctrine holds that the separation itself depends on where one looks.

note: The couplet says a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails though the Veda can be relearned; Neelakesi says the Veda itself teaches that birth yields nothing yet fixes the four classes and shuts out the Sudra.
teaches: Both put conduct above birth, but the Kural keeps birth as a rank that conduct can lose, while Neelakesi finds the Veda caught between those two and calls the mixture confusion.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices; Neelakesi says the sacrifice itself is the killing and its heavy deed falls on those who perform it.
teaches: Read beside the Jain charge, the couplet's comparison is seen to be the mild form of an argument the debater presses to the end: the Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention, Neelakesi denies the sacrifice any merit at all.

note: The couplet names tending the ancestors and the gods among the householder's five chief duties; Neelakesi argues that merit done in the name of the eminent dead cannot reach them, or the released would be bound again.
teaches: Set beside the Jain reductio, the Kural's duty to the ancestors is seen to say nothing on whether anything reaches them, which is the question on which the Vedic and Jain views divide.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi says a deed of killing done for the gods ripens in the killer as poison in the one who eats it, whoever it was meant for.
teaches: The quatrain's claim that a deed finds its own doer becomes in the debate a weapon against transferred merit, showing that the proverb rules out offering one's deed to gods or ancestors.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to be will be counted a demon (அலகை); the epic names its materialist Pisasakan, a name that sounds like பிசாசு, and ends the sarukkam by showing him a demon (887-892).
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's label into a plot: the man who denies spirits carries a demon's name and is converted by meeting one, so the Kural's 'demon' becomes both insult and refutation.

note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth are many and should be used for the world beyond; Neelakesi 86 says only the humans of the land of deeds can reach bliss by penance.
teaches: The quatrain treats human birth as one opportunity, while the epic splits humanity by land and says the gain of release belongs only to those born where deeds and penance are possible.

note: The Kural has the five elements laugh inwardly at a deceiver's hidden conduct; Neelakesi argues that no element has theft, lust or generosity as a quality.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's laughing elements must be a figure of moral witness, since the Jain debate shows that moral traits are exactly what the elements cannot bear, and her 'thieving element' mocks any literal reading.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to exist will be set down on earth as a demon; the materialist who denies ghosts is named Pisasikan, the ghost's one, and the demoness claims him as son once he takes the dharma.
teaches: The epic plays the couplet's sentence out and reverses its sting: the denier is indeed reckoned of the demons, but as their adopted kin through dharma rather than as an object of scorn.

note: Kural 255 says hell will not open its mouth to release the flesh-eater; Neelakesi 97 shows the flesh-eater burning inside the fire's mouth, crying out.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell, read beside the epic, becomes a place one is held and burned in, and the epic shows that the Kural's verdict falls on the eater as a sinner in his own right, not only on the killer.

note: Kural 10 has those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Soolamani 1 has those who bowed at the feet lose their deeds, after a god who conquered deeds himself.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry one over births, and the Soolamani names a ground for it: a god who has himself overcome the deeds that bind.

note: Kural 1274 says something lies within the bud of the girl's smile like scent within a bud; in 1004 the friend reads the bride's silent smile and gives it words.
teaches: The couplet's hidden meaning in a smile is shown here as read and spoken for her by a friend, which makes private signal into public courtesy.

note: Kural 685 describes the envoy who speaks briefly, removes what would offend, and brings a smile; in 1011 Madhavasenai carries the bride's greeting to the groom's mother as a go-between.
teaches: The same tact of an envoy is shown in a domestic errand between two households, where the greeting claims kinship before the wedding.

note: Both ask whether a woman is a goddess, a rare bird or a human, but in verse 1017 the question is asked about a painted likeness and answered by reasoning.
teaches: The question that Kural 1081 puts as a lover's reeling is here a calm puzzle about a portrait, so the same three-way wonder can come from sight alone.

note: Kural 1171's woman blames her eyes for showing her the man; verse 1020's youth melts as his eyes take in only a picture.
teaches: Love through the eyes does not need the person present, so the eyes' guilt in the couplet is wider than a meeting.

note: Kural 1224's parted wife meets evening as enemies at a killing ground; verse 1033 gives a lit, scented evening that burns only those who carry desire.
teaches: The epic locates the pain in the viewer's state ('for those who have it'), while the couplet makes evening itself the attacker.

note: Verse 1037 shows lotuses opening in the glow of the feet and worshippers blooming at the Jina's feet; Kural 3 promises long life to those who reach the feet of the one on the flower.
teaches: Both join feet and flowers, but the epic gives the bloom as the worshipper's own joy while the couplet gives a lasting earthly life.

note: Kural 1183 says love has taken the woman's grace and modesty and left sickness and pallor; verse 1045 shows a maiden who tries to hide her sickness and is betrayed by her pallor.
teaches: The epic shows the moment when modesty tries to hold and pallor breaks it, a step the couplet only reports after the fact.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; verse 1049 sets the lovers' union above the state without birth and death.
teaches: The Soolamani friend raises the Kural's comparison from a god's heaven to release itself, the goal her own Jain work teaches.

note: The astrologer sets aside courtesies, waits for the king's sign and speaks; Kural 696 tells a speaker to know the mood, weigh the time and say what is wanted and not disliked.
teaches: The astrologer keeps the Kural's rule of reading the king and timing his speech, but the poet names his aim as showing his learning, a motive the couplet never allows for.

note: The astrologer waits on the king's sign and then speaks to show his learning, with a sight of all three times; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of the stars the most foolish of the foolish, set against the thought of death.
teaches: The story rests its plot on an astrologer who is admitted, heard and believed by the whole court, while the quatrain calls his craft folly, so the two give opposite verdicts on the same trade.

note: Naladiyar 23 says the wedding drums of one hall can be the funeral drums for the bridegroom the same day; verse 1052 reports a drum sounding tomorrow's wedding.
teaches: Read beside the quatrain, the drum of joy carries the warning of the same drum's other use, which the epic's happy scene does not say itself.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that, as darkness rushes in when a lamp's oil runs out, evil takes its stand when good deeds are spent; 1057 sets the passing of good deeds beside the thickening of darkness at night.
teaches: The Naladiyar teaches the lamp-and-darkness figure as a rule; the epic turns it into a description of night, which shows how common the figure was.

note: 1099 has the hill-king give the bride with water before the fire as god; Naladiyar 56 says marriage is called கடி because it binds the husband even to a faulty wife.
teaches: The giving of the bride before the fire is the act that creates the hardship of binding which Naladiyar names, so the rite explains why the husband cannot put her away.

note: Kural 1011 says true shame is shame at wrongdoing and anything else is only the shame of women; 1103 gives the bride's trembling shyness at the first clasp.
teaches: The bride's shyness is the kind the Kural calls a woman's own and not yet the shame of deeds, so the verse shows what the couplet sets aside.

note: Naladiyar 23 sees wedding drums that may be funeral drums by evening; Soolamani 1107 ends the rites with some who leave for the forest and some who go home amazed at the wealth.
teaches: The same festival shows the transience of the day for some and wonder for others, so the Soolamani lets the Naladiyar's lesson be heard only by those who leave.

note: 1111 has the groom's ardour carry her shame off; Kural 1134 has the flood of love carry off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: The same flood that costs the secret lover his standing in the Kural is blessed here, because the epic's shame falls away inside a wedding.

note: 1112 makes two bodies one heart by ripening; Kural 1122 says the bond is as body is to life.
teaches: The epic gives the oneness of lovers a history of slow ripening, while the couplet states only the result as a bond of body and life.

note: 1113 mixes union, delight and sulking in one daze; Kural 1109 lists sulking, making up and union as love's fruits in order.
teaches: The epic blends what the couplet puts in a sequence, so the sulk is a flavour inside union and not a stage before it.

note: 1118 makes the girl both his life and his rare medicine and him her servant; Kural 1102 says she is the cure for the sickness she brings.
teaches: The cure is a bondage in the epic, since the groom who is healed is enslaved by what heals him.

note: 1122 has him gaze unblinking so as not to lose her; Kural 1129 has her not blink lest he be hidden.
teaches: The refusal to blink is common to both lovers, but the epic's reason is that she seems to recede each time he blinks, and the Kural's is that he lives in her eye.

note: 1128 warns the kurava tree not to grow as fragrant as the bride, lest it be plucked; Kural 1111 greets the anicham flower and says the beloved is more delicate.
teaches: Praising a girl by comparing her to a flower carries a threat in the epic, where equalling her gets the flower plucked, and only flattery in the couplet.

note: 1136 shows a minister hiding the lion's death for days; the couplet says the world rests under a king who can bear a bitter word.
teaches: The cost of a king who cannot bear bitter words falls first on his ministers, who delay the news and arrange who tells it.

note: 1139 shows a king's blow breaking a diamond pillar; the couplet says the ruin of one who prizes anger is sure as a hand that strikes the ground.
teaches: The blow succeeds first, so the couplet's ruin is shown as not yet in sight and the story has to come back to it.

note: 1144 shows Arikethu holding back his own view and speaking courtesies at the angry king's feet; the couplet says to stay neither far from nor near a quarrelsome king, as with a fire.
teaches: A courtier's distance from an angry king can be a matter of what he withholds, not where he stands.

note: 1149 has Acuvakandan rage and boast, then say he will gather his people before deciding; the couplet faults a king who does not think with his circle and then lashes out.
teaches: Consulting after the rage has set may offer none of the couplet's protection, because the order of anger and counsel is reversed.

note: In 1153 the kings wonder whether the king rages at Death or at those who rule through the ages; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The courtiers imagine his anger reaching Death himself, the very pride the quatrain says Death gathers in.

note: 1165 calls anger a fire that gives birth to pride and a sword thirsty for blood; Kural 306 calls anger a fire that burns even one's own safe raft of kin.
teaches: The warrior prizes anger as the fuel of his sword, while the Kural counts the same anger as what burns one's own people.

note: 1169 says a lowly jackal rising against lions would only be laughed at; Kural 500 says a jackal can kill an unflinching elephant in mud where its feet sink.
teaches: The speaker assumes the lowly cannot beat the great, while the Kural says the ground can let a jackal beat an elephant.

note: 1173 has the king's anger die at his kin's words; Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like boiled water.
teaches: The king's anger dies at others' words rather than by itself, so the epic shows a cooling the quatrain says only the worthy manage unaided.

note: 1174 has the king thunder that he is faultless and then go to the council hall; Kural 568 says a king who lashes out in anger without thinking with his circle loses fortune.
teaches: The king rages first and consults after, so the epic shows the order that the Kural warns against, though it ends in council.

note: 1175 has the minister Arimanju ask the angry king what he now thinks; Kural 445 says a king must take counsel as the counsellors are his eyes.
teaches: The minister's question is the counsel the Kural asks of a king, asked after the king has already raged.

note: 1179 says a king's justice is to prefer scheming to fighting and see what can be got; Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbent sceptre.
teaches: The counsellor rests victory on scheming and the Kural on the king's justice, so the two name different grounds for winning.

note: The king asks which kind of war to fight; the couplet says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting.
teaches: The Kural states the weighing as a rule; the epic shows a council doing it by splitting war into human, divine and mixed kinds.

note: The king gathers allies after the spy's report; the couplet says a king who does not gather through spies and judge has no victory ready.
teaches: The epic shows a spy's report prompting a council, which is what the couplet calls the ground of victory.

note: Arkakirti's bowstring is named for shame (நாண்) and he prizes the bow above life; the couplet says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic gives the hero's honour a physical thing, the string, that the couplet only states as a rule.

note: Arkakirti's wrath rains arrows and blood; the couplet says to guard against anger, which kills the one who does not.
teaches: A speech that glories in wrath as war's fuel meets a rule that says it destroys its own bearer.

note: The envoys give an ultimatum with no softening; the couplet says an envoy speaks briefly, removes offence and gets the good done.
teaches: The envoys act as the opposite of the couplet's envoy, brief but offering only two harsh options, and it shows the rule's cost.

note: 1210 sends away envoys who brought evil words that burned the ears; Kural 685 says an envoy should remove what would offend.
teaches: The envoys fail the Kural's standard of speech and are still protected, so the immunity of an envoy is shown to stand apart from how well he speaks.

note: 1224 shows enemy kings holding to pride though they know it brings ruin; Kural 969 praises those who give up life when honour is at stake.
teaches: The couplet's honour is tested on the wrong side of a war the poem says is already decided, so pride that kills is shown as heroic and also as futile.

note: The Kural calls an eye that blinks at a flung spear flight; 1247 has whole ranks blind with arrows, puzzled, hiding and falling.
teaches: The Kural counts flinching as flight, but 1247 shows troops struck blind by a dark of arrows, where fear and confusion are not the same.

note: The Kural names the army that does not collapse; 1250 shows drums split, crowns sunk and chariots overturned in a collapsing army.
teaches: A rule that an army must not collapse is tested against the detail of what a collapse looks like in a field.

note: The Kural's warrior laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body; 1255 has a king laugh at his army's rout.
teaches: The laugh of a warrior pulling a spear from his body is a private triumph, while a king's laugh at a lost army is a boast over others' loss.

note: 1256 closes that no one finishes an aim except by hard ripening after kings flee; Kural 473 says many who rose on enthusiasm broke midway.
teaches: The epic offers no cause for the kings' failure, while the couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength.

note: 1279 has warriors who do not fear Death send the fearful away; Kural 765 calls an army one that stands against raging Death.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's test of an army into a selection, since warriors themselves dismiss those who fear.

note: 1280 has victors decline to strike the blinker or shame the fled; Kural 775 calls a blink at a spear flight.
teaches: The epic shows the winners declining to treat a blink as flight, a gentler ending than the couplet's flat verdict.

note: Arisenan names himself and offers the foe the choice to flee; Kural 777 calls the war-anklet an adornment for those who value fame above life.
teaches: The epic shows the cost of the bold stance the couplet praises: the one who proclaims it is among the first to fall in 1294.

note: 1305 sets Kamukan, learned in the arts, with his bow; Naladiyar 386 likens a modest woman's beauty to a sharp sword in a clear-minded hero's hand.
teaches: The epic shows the learned hero whose skill the quatrain only uses as a simile, so a warrior's mind and weapon are tied.

note: The pierced Sarthulakan fights on and kills the thrower, as in the Kural's warrior who sends his spear off and smiles at the one in his own body.
teaches: The poem makes the Kural's warrior who smiles at a spear in his body into a man who turns the wound into a weapon.

note: Dhumaketu's boast of lifting hills and drinking the sea is the kind of word the Naladiyar says the excellent never speak.
teaches: The epic gives the Naladiyar's rule a case in which the boast comes just before a fall.

note: In 1349-1350 the arrow goes through shield and chest and the warrior falls; Kural 774 has a warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: The couplet shows the wound as a thing a brave man shrugs off, and the epic shows the same pierced body falling, so wound-laughter and wound-falling mark two ends of one warrior ideal.

note: 1356 spends the perishing body for fame that stands for ever; Kural 233 holds that nothing in the world stands undying except renown.
teaches: The epic's call to a warrior to give up his body for fame puts into action the couplet's claim, and shows who is asked to pay for it.

note: 1356 asks warriors to stay and die for fame; Kural 780 calls such a death worth asking for if those who sustained one weep for it.
teaches: The couplet makes the dead man's supporters the judge of the death, which the epic speaker, urging flight not to be done, leaves out.

note: 1378 shows an army breaking at the sight of its king's fallen crown; the Kural says an army needs leaders.
teaches: A fallen crown scatters an army that Kural 770 would call leaderless, showing the leader's role as a matter of sight as much as of command.

note: 1380 calls flight from one man loathsome; Kural 775 says even a blink at a hurled spear is flight.
teaches: The two texts set the line of disgrace at different places: the epic at running away, the Kural already at the flinch.

note: 1381 says the mountain Vidyadharas fled from men whom fate has marked; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: The epic gives fate as the one reason a strong flying army can be turned by men with no such powers.

note: 1383 asks whether the flesh body must break for honour's sake; Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic's taunt tests the Kural's rule on men who run, showing it as a shaming speech to the living where the couplet states a private resolve.

note: 1386 has the hero push through slanting spears for honour; Kural 774 has the soldier laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: Both link honour to the warrior's joy in danger, but the epic gives the motive as honour itself and the couplet as the pleasure of the wound.

note: Kural 549 counts guarding the people and removing wrongdoing as the king's work and no fault; verse 140 faults a king on the ground of grace toward the lowest lives, which the Kural's list does not ask of him.
teaches: The epic widens the king's duty to grace toward all lowly lives, where the Kural's duty stops at the people and the removal of wrongdoers, so the two hold different measures of a good ruler.

note: Verse 140 faults a mighty king for want of grace to the lowly; Kural 557 says that a king's lack of tender regard is to his people as lack of rain to the earth.
teaches: The epic names one flaw in a king otherwise perfect, so the Kural's claim that lack of regard undoes all else is tested against a ruler praised for everything else.

note: 1420 shows an army scattering before a mountain-lifter; Kural 765 sets the standard of an army that stands together even when Death comes at it.
teaches: The scene gives the Kural's test a failure that the couplet only describes as a standard, and shows the Kural's army needs a leader to hold.

note: 1425 has a king's grief and anger lead him to loose a spell that destroys the world; Kural 305 says anger kills the one who does not guard against it.
teaches: The epic shows anger as a power that reaches the world and not only the angry man, which limits the couplet's 'yourself'.

note: 1437 compares the bow's arrival to a friend won in a former life; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother.
teaches: The simile gives the old deed a good side: what returns can be a helper in need, not only a penalty.

note: 1448 sets brave speech among one's own against facing the foe; Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one has said is hard.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's remark a speaker and a test: the hilltop boaster must now act, which the next verses show.

note: 1449 shows anger rising at insult and arrows poured out; Kural 305 says to guard against anger or it kills the one who has it.
teaches: The arrows are beaten away in 1450, so the epic shows the Kural's warning working out in the battle rather than as a rule.

note: 1463 says a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender; Kural 319 says hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself.
teaches: The couplet makes the return a rule of time, while the epic makes it happen through the victim's own hand turning the weapon back, so the return has an agent.

note: 1464 shows a king who rode elephants under the umbrella brought low; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants fall when their deeds turn against them.
teaches: The quatrain gives the cause as the king's own deeds and the verse gives the scene, so the pair joins the rule to a particular fall.

note: 1465 says that the man who came yesterday under the umbrella is felled today; Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today.
teaches: The verse gives a king's fall as the proof of the couplet and adds that the end comes by his own weapon, so impermanence is shown with a cause the couplet leaves out.

note: 1467 lists strength, wealth and beauty that do not last; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd gathering and breaking up at a dance hall.
teaches: The verse names what is lost, the couplet gives the image of its loss, and together they show loss as an ending without warning.

note: 1471 shows wives falling and beating their faces at a husband's death; Naladiyar 25 shows kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground.
teaches: Both pass from mourners' grief to what it shows about life, but the epic keeps the grief in the scene and the quatrain turns it into a reason to give up household life.

note: 1482 has the women's tears put out the victor's wrath like water on fire; Kural 555 says the tears of the afflicted wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: Tears are a force against a king in both, but the epic turns them to a mercy that ends the fire while the Kural makes them a loss that grows.

note: 1483 lays a king on a bed of silk and gives him to the fire; Naladiyar 21 says kings under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The fire takes the proud king as the quatrain says it takes all, and the honour of his funeral does not alter that.

note: 1485 shows the queens barring desire with the fence of chastity and the lock on the senses; Kural 57 calls a woman's own restraint the best guard.
teaches: The epic's widows guard themselves by their own restraint, which is the kind the Kural prefers to confinement.

note: 1493 has the father say he reached fatherhood through penance; Kural 70 says the son's help to the father is the question of what penance he did.
teaches: The father in the epic asks the question the couplet puts in others' mouths, so the son's worth is credited back to the father's penance.

note: 1499 crowns the hero because the discus won the war; Kural 546 says victory comes from the sceptre that does not bend, not from the spear.
teaches: The epic gives the title to the winner of the weapon, which the Kural would call a lesser ground than justice.

note: 1508 counts a discus-lord's wealth in jewels, treasures, lands, cities and gatherings of kings; Kural 381 counts a king's parts as army, people, resources, ministers, allies and fort.
teaches: The epic's list is of things owned and has no ministers or fort, while the couplet's list names the organs a state cannot do without.

note: 1510 has the hero without swelling pride at the moment feats are listed; Kural 979 calls greatness the absence of pride.
teaches: The epic shows modesty arising from counting those who came before, a source the couplet does not name.

note: 1523 shows the pearl parasol bringing joy to the people and the sea-ringed world; Kural 389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The epic's parasol is the sign of conquest, while the couplet makes shelter depend on a king's patience with harsh speech.

note: 1552 gives the prince's elation at fortune with no hint of its cause; Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time comes and leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: The Naladiyar supplies a karmic account the epic withholds in these verses: his elation is for a fortune whose source and end are deeds, though the verse says no such thing.

note: 1553 shows great treasure arriving and the king drowning in it; Kural 332 compares wealth's coming to a crowd gathering and its going to the crowd's scattering.
teaches: Read together, the epic shows only the gathering of the crowd, and the couplet supplies the scattering that the festival hides.

note: 1556 shows the king settled under the moon-white umbrella; Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode under umbrellas have fallen when their deeds turned.
teaches: The poem sets Tivittan at the top of his glory, and the quatrain supplies the warning that such a place is held by deeds and can be lost.

note: 1559 shows a king with the homage of three realms taking pleasure like Kama; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The poem offers pleasure at its largest scale, and the quatrain asks whether one who has all of it is looking at its pain.

note: 1571 has the king test a gift-seeker by Vedic learning; Kural 134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda but loses his birth if conduct fails.
teaches: The king's test is of learning, and the couplet's is of conduct, so the jester's comic case falls under both and passes neither.

note: 1597 has the jester fear a spirit that is not there; Kural 428 says the knowing fear what should be feared while the fool does not fear it.
teaches: The couplet names the fool who feels no fear where it is due, and the scene shows the other fault, a fear aimed at something unreal.

note: 1600 has the jester shown his own acts in his shadow, which does what he does; Kural 208 compares the ruin that follows evil deeds to a shadow that stays at the foot.
teaches: The shadow that is a comic false spirit here is the same thing the Kural uses as a sign that a person's deeds follow them, so the pairing shows the image in two uses.

note: 1608 has the queen burn with anger at the king's praise of a stranger's footprint; Kural 1313 has a woman angry at a wreath she says was worn for another woman.
teaches: The epic gives the wife a real occasion where the couplet's wife sulks on a pretext, and shows the husband pleading as the couplet's man does.

note: Verse 161 likens the wealth of the worthless to kongu trees that bloom without scent; Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unwanted to a poison tree fruiting in the town.
teaches: Both name a tree whose outer splendour fails its purpose, one for giving no scent and one for giving poison, so wealth without worth is shown useless in one case and harmful in the other.

note: 1611 has the queen turn to leave and the king bow with his crown at her feet; Kural 1302 says sulking is like salt in right measure and a little more ruins it.
teaches: The king's bow comes before the sulk can become too much, so the scene shows the couplet's measure kept.

note: 1614 has the queen, once the king has bowed, smile and turn her anger into a game on the jester; Naladiyar 384 praises the wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly.
teaches: The queen relents by moving her anger on to the jester in garlands, which the quatrain's wife does not do.

note: 1616 has the king end the quarrel by embrace and plea; Kural 1304 says that not reconciling those who sulk is like cutting a withered creeper at its root.
teaches: The king's embrace shows what the couplet's warning needs: the sulk is healed by the one who gave cause, and the quarrel comes to an end in a wedding scene.

note: 1628 calls the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet to all; Kural 63 says people call children their wealth because their wealth comes through their own deeds.
teaches: The poem's child is a tree that has no deeds, so its sweetness comes wholly from rearing, which tests whether the couplet's reason is the only one.

note: 1632 builds the women's beauty out of gold, leaves and sprouts to delight the king's eyes; Naladiyar 46 asks which part of the fresh-garlanded woman is she, among entrails, fat, blood and bone.
teaches: The poem makes the body a thing of ornament and the quatrain takes it apart into its parts, so the two disagree on whether the adorned body is a person to be praised.

note: 1637 has the women paint the king and themselves sulking at him; Kural 1329 has the man wish the woman would go on sulking so that he may go on pleading.
teaches: The women fix the sulk in paint, where no pleading can follow, so the picture keeps the lovers' quarrel without its making-up.

note: 1642 has the women say a garland bent their slender waists; Kural 1115 has the man say a woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems has a waist too weak for good drums to sound.
teaches: What the couplet gives as a lover's praise of a woman's delicacy the poem gives to the women as their own complaint, so the delicacy becomes something they offer to be noticed.

note: Naladiyar 160 says the base follow the rich as their one hope; verse 166 says people leave the rich once their sweetness turns.
teaches: Naladiyar shows the crowd that clings to wealth and the cuckoo shows it is not loyal, since it goes the moment the taste turns.

note: 1663 names the rutting elephant with a spread face-cloth; Kural 1087 likens the cloth on a woman's breast to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes.
teaches: The same elephant's face-cloth marks erotic danger in a couplet and is used as a stage prop to scare women into a man's arms in the epic.

note: 1666 ends by saying the king did a great penance that gives him whatever he wishes; Kural 265 gives wish-fulfilment as the reason penance is practised.
teaches: The wish that penance buys here is a prank to win an embrace, which tests whether the Kural's reason for tapas needs any worthy wish.

note: 1697 has the envoy take the letter, wait for the king's order and then bow and speak; Kural 687 says the best envoy knows the protocol, the moment and the place.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy in the sequence of bows, seating, gifts and leave to speak that the couplet names but does not show.

note: 1706 shows pleasure on the bed as the cause of the longed-for son, while Naladiyar 54 says the wise see pleasure's pain and keep away from household life.
teaches: The poem lets the pleasure that Naladiyar condemns bear fruit in an auspicious child, so the householder's pleasure is not shown as barren.

note: 1713 lets the drums sound for the birth, and Naladiyar 23 says drums that sound for a wedding can sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The rejoicing of the birth is set beside the quatrain's warning that the same drum serves joy and death, so the festival is read against impermanence.

note: 1720 has brahmins, kings and elders praise those who bore the child, and Kural 70 says a son's worth lies in making others ask what penance his father did.
teaches: The epic voices the praise at the newborn stage, before any deed, while the couplet says the praise belongs to the father only after the son has proved himself.

note: 1738 has the child grow in the guard of women who tend him; Naladiyar 20 says Death takes even the newborn while the mother wails.
teaches: The poem's guarded growth is the thing the quatrain says cannot be guaranteed, so the child's safety is read against death's stealth.

note: 1743 calls the teachers 'rich in unfailing learning' (பொய்யாக் கல்விச் செல்வர்); Kural 400 says learning is the one wealth that does not perish.
teaches: The epic uses the language of wealth for learning, which Kural 400 claims for it alone, but gives it to men who serve a king whose other wealth is shown at length.

note: 1743 has Tivittan give his five-year-old son to teachers 'rich in unfailing learning'; Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to put him first in the assembly.
teaches: The Kural names the goal of a father's care, the seat in the assembly; the epic shows the first step toward it, early schooling in the hands of learned men.

note: 1745 has the father sink in a sea of joy at the naming and the gathering of kin; Kural 69 says a mother is gladder to hear her son called worthy than at his birth.
teaches: The epic's joy comes at the naming and the kin's praise, while the Kural puts the greater joy later, in the son's worth, so the verse's delight is the first joy, not the last.

note: Verse 175 draws spring shoots as copies of the women's hands and waists; Naladiyar 48 tells those who praise sandal and garland without knowing the body to look at vultures tearing the carcass.
teaches: A court poet delights in the body's beauty while a moral quatrain holds the same body as carrion, so the same poem tradition holds two views of the body.

note: 1763 beats a drum to announce a wedding; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded for a wedding may sound the same day as funeral drums.
teaches: The same drum that proclaims joy is, for the Naladiyar, the sign of how quickly joy passes into death.

note: 1764's herald prays for the king's life, virtue and cool rain and harvest; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather where the ruler wields his sceptre justly.
teaches: The herald's prayer asks for the rain and crops that the Kural says come as a fruit of just rule, so the blessing doubles as a claim on the king.

note: 1766 has the drum summon the world's kings to a marriage open to all; Naladiyar 86 praises a wife married with drums beaten for many to know.
teaches: A marriage announced to all is a mark of honour in the Naladiyar, and the swayamvara pushes the same openness to where the bride is chosen before the world.

note: 1783 has conches and a great drum sound the hour of the kings' entry; Naladiyar 23 says the drums of a wedding hall can be the funeral drums of that very day.
teaches: The same drums that open a wedding hold the thought that joy and loss come under one roof.

note: 1790 has kings of five great lines wait with elephants and hosts for the choosing; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The kings' show of force at the choosing is the same show that the quatrain says does not save a king.

note: 1792 has young women's eyes fall on a handsome prince; Naladiyar 102 says beauty, youth, wealth and awe do not last.
teaches: The pull of the prince's looks is shown at full strength by the very verse that the quatrain would call short-lived.

note: 1797 sets her procession to the sounds of praise and music from all quarters; Naladiyar 23 shows wedding drums in a hall turning to funeral drums for the groom.
teaches: The poem fills the bridal march with music and hope, and the quatrain says the same drums can announce the end of the groom.

note: 1798 shows kings' desire swelling as she enters; Naladiyar 17 tells the man not to desire a spear-eyed girl, who will stoop on a staff.
teaches: The poem lets the reader see her with the kings' eyes, and the quatrain supplies what those eyes will not see.

note: Verse 180 says the shrine and its god end births; Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
