teaches: The epic locates the ending of births in the shrine and its god, where the Kural puts it in the devotee's reaching.

note: Verse 181 praises him who conquered the harsh dust of karma; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The epic names the conqueror of karma whose praise the Kural says keeps deed from clinging, so it names the one the couplet leaves as 'the Lord'.

note: 1810 praises a king for the line that bred him; Naladiyar 195 says a lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort, not by name.
teaches: The herald's whole mode of praise is descent, and the quatrain offers another test for the same kings, what each has done.

note: 1815 says women who reached this king's chest had done austerity; Naladiyar 31 says present comfort comes from earlier austerity and is lost without more.
teaches: The herald's line puts a marriage on the same ledger of past austerity that the quatrain keeps, and the quatrain adds that it runs out.

note: 1824 says the herald's showing was needless because her lot of enjoyment had already ripened; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which reaches first even when one tries another way.
teaches: A choice that looks free and quick is shown to have been set before the guide's words, which a bare general rule about fate does not show.

note: 1827 has kings with every means to win her calm themselves because deeds ripen as they will; Kural 377 says even those who have gathered millions enjoy only what the apportioner has apportioned.
teaches: Fate's apportioning is shown over a bride and not over wealth, among men whose rank and army were equal, so the rule is tested where effort was all in place.

note: 1827 shows kings who lose the bride calming themselves by seeing the loss as karma; Naladiyar 33 contrasts the fool who sighs hotly at the fruit of deeds with the wise who call it old desert.
teaches: The same step from sighing to calm is shown as a group's act on a public loss, where the quatrain gives only the principle.

note: 1843 reads the kingship and the bowing kings as the gift of the good-deed deity; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants under umbrellas fall when deeds turn.
teaches: Read together, the umbrellas that 1843 credits to past merit are the same ones Naladiyar says a turn of deeds can remove.

note: 1847 concludes that nothing is better than austerity; Kural 46 asks what is gained by going the outside way if household life is lived in virtue.
teaches: The pair turns on whether household virtue is enough: the king answers from the certainty of death, the couplet from the sufficiency of aram.

note: 1849 shows the adorned body undone by one small prick; Naladiyar 41 says a bit of skin torn off needs a stick to drive away crows.
teaches: Both break the body's finery with a trivial injury, but the epic does it for a king examining his own display, the quatrain to answer a lover's praise.

note: 1850 has crows and kites guarded off with a hand stick; Naladiyar 41 has the stick that drives the crows from the torn body.
teaches: The same stick appears for two different speakers, a king guarding himself and a poet mocking the lover, which shows how fixed the picture was.

note: 1856 tests whether any statecraft can escape Death; Naladiyar 6 says none here has leapt clear and bids the wealthy give.
teaches: The king tries the four expedients the quatrain never names, and by their failure the quatrain's rule is shown by a ruler's own attempt.

note: 1859 shortens the term to a blink before Death; Kural 334 calls the day a blade that saws the life.
teaches: The epic shortens the quantity: the couplet measures life as days, the verse measures it by the blink the minister names.

note: 1866 makes the Lord the foe of deluding deeds and rewards the festival's onlooker with the world of merit; Kural 5 says both kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The epic ends in merit's world, a reward the couplet's two-fold deeds would also refuse to cling to, so the pair shows two ways of reading what freedom from deeds amounts to.

note: 1869's people hear the drum as the sign of a long life and a blessing; Naladiyar 23's wedding drums turn to funeral drums the same day.
teaches: The same drum is a promise of long life in the epic's crowd and a warning of death in the quatrain, and the pair shows how a listener's state decides what it announces.

note: Verse 187 hails the god as walking above the lotus, as Kural 3 speaks of the one who walked upon the flower.
teaches: The same lotus-walker of the opening couplet appears here as an epic's praised Arhat, so the image carries a Jain form where the Kural leaves the Lord unnamed.

note: 1870 piles up festoons, banners, drums and conches that drown the sea; Kural 34 calls virtue the mind's spotlessness and the rest a noise (ஆகுலம்).
teaches: The epic lingers on the din of worship while the couplet measures a rite by the mind within, so the pair asks whether the festival is aram or only clamour.

note: Verse 188 says the god takes no joy in praise yet is loved; Kural 4 says the god without liking or aversion frees those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's rule of the one without liking into a devotional posture: love offered without any hope of being pleased.

note: 1880 sets the king under his umbrella with fly-whisks at the head of his army; Naladiyar 3 says those who rode in such state fall when deeds turn.
teaches: The quatrain's fall of the umbrella-borne is forced by deeds, while the epic king's glittering display is the height from which he will walk away by choice.

note: 1902 has the crowned king bow until the gem-crown touches the earth; Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-quality one is a useless organ.
teaches: The couplet's useless head becomes the crowned one of a king who sets power on the ground, which shows what the bow costs a ruler.

note: 1904 says the Lord cut off the dark garlands of fierce deeds; Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The Lord is shown in 1904 as the one who has already done what the couplet promises his devotees, so the cause of their freedom is his own freeing.

note: 1906 says there is no other god to count, and the Lord is easy for those who worship his feet; Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without a peer can remove the mind's anxiety.
teaches: The hymn names its peerless one by what he does to living things, while the couplet leaves the feet unnamed and so open to any tradition.

note: 1921 turns the soul like a cart wheel through four states; Naladiyar 2 turns wealth like a cart wheel, never level with anyone.
teaches: The same cart wheel is used for what turns beneath a person in Naladiyar and for the person who is turned in the Soolamani.

note: 1931 has the sufferers receive the fruit of former deeds; Naladiyar 33 says the fool sighs hotly when the fruit arrives, and the wise who treat it as old debt pass beyond confusion.
teaches: 1931 shows the fruit received with no way to reinterpret it, which is the state Naladiyar 33 says the wise avoid.

note: 1935 carves and feeds back to meat-eaters their own limbs; Kural 255 ties eating flesh to hell.
teaches: The Kural's single claim about meat and hell becomes a punishment that mirrors the meal, limb for limb.

note: 1937 tears out the tongue of those who slander their betters; Kural 183 says death is better than living by backbiting and falsehood.
teaches: The couplet's preference for dying over slander assumes death ends the matter; the epic says it does not and takes the tongue after death.

note: 1951 names those who leave their wives for others' as falling into deep sorrow; Naladiyar 84 lists disgrace, a cut leg and long suffering in hell for the adulterer.
teaches: Naladiyar counts the worldly penalties before hell; the epic puts only hell and gives the torment in detail.

note: 1953 puts those who hoard without householder's dharma and die hard-fisted in hell; Naladiyar 273 says the hoarder is laughed at by his own wealth.
teaches: The miser is mocked in life by the wealth he stored and punished after death for it, two sanctions for one fault.

note: 1965 lists animals killed as offerings to deities among their torments; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing one creature and eating.
teaches: The Kural ranks abstention above sacrifice, and the Soolamani shows from the victim's side what the offering costs.

note: 1967 says that those who take austerity and then practise deceit are born as beasts; Kural 274 pictures the false ascetic as a hunter hidden in a bush, snaring birds.
teaches: In the Kural the hypocrite hunts the innocent, and the Soolamani turns him into the hunted: the same fault, paid back in the animal's birth.

note: 1975 says that a people is human only in the bare fact of birth and otherwise animal for want of shame and conduct; Kural 1071 says the base look just like human beings.
teaches: The Kural tests humanness by conduct in each person, while the Soolamani ties the same test to a whole island people's birth.

note: Kural 351 says the joyless birth comes from a confusion that takes the unreal for real; Soolamani 198 says deeds grow from a seed of lacking true knowledge and ripen into pain through a chain of births.
teaches: The sage supplies a growth path (seed, deeds, ripening, rebirth) for the couplet's bare claim, while the couplet says what kind of knowledge fails.

note: Kural 361 names craving as the seed that produces unceasing birth; the Soolamani's sage names lacking true knowledge as the seed of the deeds that bind.
teaches: Two Tamil teachers name different seeds of rebirth, so the root of bondage is a question of doctrine and is not common ground.

note: 1985 says only those who hold firmly to good karma come to the human body, out of eighty-four lakh births; Naladiyar 34 says to take the great fruit of the rare body.
teaches: The epic gives the count and cause of the rare body that the quatrain only calls rare, so the urgency has a reason.

note: 1987 draws childhood, youth and old age as a wilderness ending in another state; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come.
teaches: The epic shows what lies past old age, another birth, and so the quatrain's renunciation at the start is not a mere fear of aging.

note: 1988 pictures pleasure as honey tasted by a man hanging above a pit with an elephant and a snake; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in any pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The parable explains why fools do not renounce: the honey is real, and the danger is out of sight while one tastes it.

note: 1997 promises the giver of food a later kingship; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic's giving is promised its fruit, and the Kural says it is worth doing without one, so the reward is a bonus to a duty and not its ground.

note: 2002 offers the vow of not killing to kings as one that leaves no conquest out of reach; Kural 325 ranks not-killing highest among those who renounced.
teaches: The epic recasts non-killing as a king's way to win, where the couplet ranks it only among renouncers.

note: 2009 defines compassion as melting for another's life and counts a moist heart where rescue fails; Kural 315 calls understanding useless without guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The pairing shows compassion as both the test of understanding and a state that stays even when help fails.

note: Kural 355 says knowledge is seeing the real in whatever thing; Soolamani 201 sets discerning true things as the first of three, followed by knowledge and conduct kept to the text.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seeing the start of a sequence that does not end until conduct is kept, not the whole of release.

note: 2010 asks equal calm toward abuse, praise and neglect; Kural 151 asks the bearing of scorn only.
teaches: Level calm includes praise, so the couplet's forbearance covers only half of what the sage asks of the clear-minded.

note: 2014 makes hearing the meaning of the texts a lamp that clears delusion; Kural 423 makes wisdom seeing the true thing in whatever is heard.
teaches: The sage trusts the text as source, where the couplet makes the hearer's seeing the test of any source.

note: 2017 says those with the lamp of vision reach heaven or the bliss without return even without vows; Kural 356 says those who learn and see the true thing reach the path of no return.
teaches: The epic loosens the couplet's chain, holding that sight alone, even without vows, opens heaven or release.

note: 2018 has the lamp of vision end the darkness of deeds; Naladiyar 51 has the lamp of austerity end sin as darkness dies, and darkness return when the oil runs out.
teaches: The lamp's light is credited to vision in the epic and to austerity in the quatrain, with only the quatrain saying the light can fail.

note: 2024 ranks beings best, middle and lowest by the fruit of earlier good deeds; Kural 37 points to the bearer and the rider of a palanquin as the visible proof of virtue's fruit.
teaches: Rank that Kural 37 reads from one palanquin is stretched in 2024 into a ladder of births, so one visible difference becomes a whole order of worlds.

note: Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight darkness leaves and joy arises; Soolamani 203 has the light of knowledge from the sage's words split the darkness of evil deeds in the whole assembly.
teaches: The two verses use darkness and light, but the epic has the light come to a crowd from a teacher's words, while the couplet leaves it to one's own clear sight.

note: 2031 has the youth's lotus-like eyes and the girl's blue-lily eyes meet and press; Kural 1082 has the girl's answering look strike like an army.
teaches: The same meeting of eyes is a fated, gentle union in the enjoyment land but a conquest in the Kural's world of passion.

note: 2033 gives the pair unbroken pleasure for their whole span; Naladiyar 16 says the joy of youth is fleeting like the lamb eating the garland before the slaughter.
teaches: The epic can promise pleasure that lasts a full span only by moving it out of this world, which is exactly what the Naladiyar's warning denies is possible here.

note: 2034 says the painless pleasure is the fruit of what was given to austere kings; Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who have let go.
teaches: A householder's gift to renouncers, a duty in the Kural, is shown in the epic as the cause of a later birth in a land of ease.

note: 2051 itemises the gods' mansions, couches and cars as the whole of heaven; Kural 50 says the one who lives life as it ought to be lived will be counted among the gods.
teaches: What the couplet offers as the reward of right householding is shown by the epic as a list of comforts and then, in 2060, as a reward that has an end.

note: 2052 lists the gods' play, Indra's company and jewelled terraces as heaven's whole stock; Naladiyar 137 asks whether heaven's city is sweeter than the gathering of learned men.
teaches: Naladiyar weighs heaven against the company of the learned and finds it no sweeter; the epic describes the gods' pleasures as only entertainment and ranks them below the teaching of 2067.

note: 2060 says heaven's pleasure comes by austerity yet ends, and that something is higher; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'.
teaches: The couplet's 'higher than the gods' is given a reason in the epic: the gods' world has a measured end, so only what lies above it can be a goal.

note: 2070 traces how birth turns to desire and hatred toward sense objects, heaps up deeds and brings the same nature back after death; Kural 349 says that the very moment attachment ends, births are cut.
teaches: The couplet's moment of cutting is shown in 2070 to be the point where the chain from senses to desire to deed to return is broken.

note: 2079 has the king's own ministers urge him to give up the crown for the austerity that ends the disease of birth; Naladiyar 53 says the best people, seeing that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last, renounce them without delay.
teaches: Naladiyar 53 describes a person giving up a house and wealth, but 2079 shows the same renunciation asked of a king, where the crown and a kingdom's charge must be laid down.

note: 2082 makes wealth a woman who leaves the men she has joined and always wants someone new; Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like the crowd breaking up.
teaches: The couplet's crowd goes without any reason in itself; in 2082 the going has a will, the goddess who tires of her man and wants another.

note: 2083 compares the departing goddess of wealth to courtesans who leave the penniless; Naladiyar 371 says harlots' friendship ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends when the oil is gone.
teaches: The epic turns the Naladiyar's warning about courtesans into a figure for wealth itself, so a man is asked to see in his fortune the same cold arithmetic.

note: 2093 has the king say his own days are few and he has resolved today; Kural 342 says renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural's urgency to renounce in time becomes, in the epic, a king's own reckoning of his remaining days against those of his people.

note: 2096 has the ministers put down the heavy burden they bore through the disease of birth; Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The burden of the body in the epic is lifted by a king's grace, whereas the couplet lays it on the renouncer's own will.

note: 2099 has a king give army and earth to his sons and put off his crown by choice; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas have been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same fall of a king from rank that Naladiyar reads as death's work is here done by the king's own hand while alive.

note: 2101 shows the princes wailing as the crown falls from the lord; Kural 347 says griefs hold those who hold attachment.
teaches: The princes' grief shows the couplet's point from the other side: the renouncer is free while those who still cling to him suffer.

note: 2109 posts five great captains of the vow-army against incoming karma; Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all desire let go.
teaches: The epic's five are vows that hold karma back, not the five senses of the couplet, so the same number is taken from two different disciplines.

note: 2111 shuts the five sense-gates of a fortress and posts guards; Naladiyar 59 names the five gates (body, mouth, eyes, nose, ears) and promises release to one who can guard and steer the craving that comes through them.
teaches: Guarding the senses is shown as one wall among several defences and not a lone act, so restraint looks like the start of a campaign and not its end.

note: 2113 has the lord ride the elephant of knowledge with a diamond goad that is awareness; Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness.
teaches: The same goad turns from a means of guarding the senses to a means of driving the army that kills the karmic enemy.

note: 2124 throws away the sword of meditation once the karmic kings are dead; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, so as to let clinging go.
teaches: A useful hold, whether the sword or the clinging to the unclinging one, is to be dropped at the end of its work.

note: 2129 has Tirumal lift a straight sceptre with the gods guarding him; Kural 547 says the king guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter.
teaches: The guard of a king comes in the epic from the gods and in the couplet from his own justice, so the pairing asks what really protects a ruler.

note: Kural 3 gives the Lord as the one who walked on the flower, at whose feet one arrives; Soolamani 214 gives the girl's hymn to the primal Lord who gave the scripture, who stood on the flower, at whose holy feet she bows.
teaches: The hymn uses a flower-footed epithet close to the couplet's and gives it to the Jain Lord with titles that name him, which the couplet does not.

note: Naladiyar 274 uses a daughter of the house, enjoyed by a stranger, as a figure for wealth that others will use; verse 228 calls a girl the jewel beyond all earthly and heavenly jewels.
teaches: The Naladiyar's picture treats a daughter's going to another house as a thing to be expected, while the epic makes her the treasure whose giving is a king's weightiest care.

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors a ruler's eyes; verse 234 pictures a king opening like a lotus by the sun only through the learned who consider.
teaches: The epic gives a picture of how counsel acts, a bloom that opens only at the sun's touch, where the Kural gives a rule that counsel should be taken.

note: Kural 445 tells a ruler to take counsel from ministers as his eyes; verse 237 says that kings' lives and even Indra's lordship do not flower without counsel.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's rule from a ruler's prudence to a claim about all rule and even the gods' rule.

note: Verse 242 has the king say he can grasp subtle things only through the learned treatises; Kural 637 says that even one who knows the method must act by knowing how the world goes.
teaches: The council's first claim makes the treatise the king's only guide, where the couplet warns that a treatise's method must still be tested against the world, so the two disagree on where good judgment is found.

note: Verse 243 says the learned keep blame and fierce deeds from a king whose sceptre is unbent; Kural 547 says justice guards the king if he does not falter in it.
teaches: The epic names who keeps a king from faltering, the learned counsellors, where the couplet names only the law that guards him if he does not.

note: Verse 244 makes the ministers the king's mind, eye, living, strength and sceptre; Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes and says he must take them after testing them.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's single image of eyes to the king's whole body of rule, while the couplet adds a duty of choosing that the epic leaves unsaid.

note: Verse 247 makes a king one who acts calmly on what the learned choose and tell him; Kural 638 says the man at the king's side must tell him what is good even if the king knows nothing and spoils wise counsel.
teaches: The epic sets the king's duty to act on counsel beside the minister's duty to give it, where the couplet shows only the minister's duty when the king will not hear.

note: Verse 248 says counsel, not strength of arm, is the quality of a king; Kural 546 says it is not the spear but the unbent sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: Each puts a different power above the weapon, counsel in the epic and justice in the couplet, so the pair shows that the Tamil tradition names more than one winner of a war.

note: Verse 249 says even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of counsellors; Kural 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts fate and effort together in the council hall and finds that deliberation is where fate takes shape, while the couplet says effort can turn fate back.

note: Verse 249 says what comes like fate takes shape in the counsellors' deliberation; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The epic lets fate arrive through chosen acts of counsel, while the quatrain says the old deed finds its doer whatever he does, so the two differ on how far deliberation shapes what comes.

note: Verse 252 says failed counsel turns on the king like an angry snake whose charmer's art has failed; Kural 448 says a king with none to rebuke him perishes even without a foe.
teaches: The epic shows a king with counsellors destroyed by counsel gone wrong, where the couplet shows a king destroyed by having no counsellor who dares to rebuke him.

note: Verse 262 says lords who bear the lowly's lapses, like sandal under the rutting elephant, are bowed to by the earth; Naladiyar 66 says the well-born bear the base's stone-like words and let them pass, held back by their lineage.
teaches: The epic names the reward of forbearance in the king's public standing, where the quatrain names its reason in birth.

note: Kural 559 says that when a ruler bends justice the sky bends the rain; verse 263 says that a cruel king is to the world as a sea-scorching sun is to its creatures.
teaches: The Kural names rain as the lost gift, but the epic names the people's suffering as the creatures' in a burning sea, so the ruler's fault is one of heat, not drought.

note: Kural 389 puts the world under the parasol of a king who can bear bitter words; verse 264 says that a parasol grown hot scorches the cool ponds and groves under it.
teaches: The Kural gives the cool shade as a gift of the king's patience, and the epic gives the reverse: when the king is hot the shade itself scorches.

note: Kural 544 says the world holds to the feet of the great king who embraces his people; verse 266 says no one has anything better than the shade of such a king's feet.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's embrace of his people the condition of the world's clinging to his feet, and the epic gives the reason: they cling because men are wounding one another.

note: Kural 388 calls the king who protects with justice the இறை of his people; verse 267 calls him god-like because he orders a man's lot in both worlds.
teaches: The epic gives a reason for the Kural's word இறை as god: his rule reaches the next world's lot as well as this one's, which the couplet leaves untouched.

note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters, learning, are the eyes of living beings; verse 268 names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun.
teaches: The Kural calls learning the only eye of life, and the epic puts learning beside the king and the sun, so what learning sees is made one of three lights the world needs.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; verse 274 says a deed done in a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real.
teaches: The epic uses karma's sureness as the model for counsel, so a plan's result is as certain as a deed's fruit, a use of karma that the quatrain does not make.

note: Naladiyar 137 doubts that the city of those in the wide heaven is sweeter than learned men gathering and laughing together; verse 279 praises a heaven-like realm that only the meritorious can enter.
teaches: The quatrain tests the heaven the epic praises against the pleasure of a company of the learned, and the epic's heaven is praised for its senses while the quatrain finds its sweetness no better than conversation.

note: Naladiyar 14 says a once-desired woman, bent and shaking on a staff, torments men who still desire her; verse 286 describes lovers whose desire sprouts without end in a heaven-like city.
teaches: The epic's desire without end belongs to a realm without death (278), so the quatrain's old age has no place there, which shows that the quatrain's argument depends on this world.

note: Kural 731 names unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people as the marks of a land; verse 29 gives only the yield, in stored grain that does not shrink as it is eaten.
teaches: Read against the Kural's three-part definition, the epic's country is first described by what it yields, and the people and the rich come only later, so the poet is building the land from its harvest outward.

note: The minister lists Asvagriva's army, its order and the food supply among the reasons none equals him; Kural 381 counts army, people, resources, ministers, friends and fort as a king's six limbs.
teaches: The minister's praise follows the Kural's list for army and food but adds the discus, the lineage and learning, so the poet counts as kingly worth what the Kural's checklist leaves out.

note: The minister's praise rests on law-treatise, omen-books and learning; Kural 636 says that natural wit joined to treatises cannot be matched by any scheme.
teaches: The poem's model minister is made by treatises alone, where the couplet gives native wit the first place, so the court poet and the Kural weigh a counsellor differently.

note: The Vidyadhara kings pay tribute and send word out of fear of Asvagriva's anger; Kural 680 says those of small domains, afraid, bow to the great and take what is offered.
teaches: The kings' tribute is the couplet's counsel carried out, but the minister then asks for the girl to be given, which shows how bowing to a great king can end in a marriage and not only in a payment.

note: Bhavachutan says that he saw a fault and will speak though the other has praised; Kural 638 says the one at the king's side must speak what is good even if the king is ignorant.
teaches: The couplet binds a minister to speak against a king's folly, and the scene shows the harder case where he speaks against a fellow minister's persuasive counsel.

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes, to be taken after counsel; verse 330 asks that the worthy suitor be examined and then Pavachchuthan's word settles it.
teaches: The epic shows counsel working as the Kural wants, by examining before choosing, but one man's word still carries the room.

note: Kural 504 says to examine qualities and faults and take what predominates; the roll of princes names only qualities, and verse 334 ends on a danger.
teaches: The council's list of suitors names only merits and the last verse adds a warning, which shows the Kural's rule to weigh faults was missing from the roll.

note: Kural 1228 has the herdsman's flute as a weapon that kills the lonely woman at evening; verse 34 has the herdsmen's konrai flute so sweet that the asunam beast sleeps.
teaches: The same herdsman's flute soothes the beast and wounds the parted woman, so its effect lies in the listener's state and not in the music, a point neither verse shows alone.

note: Naladiyar 11 says that the wise renounce in childhood because they know grey hair will come; verse 351 shows a youth who turns from music, dance and heaven-like pleasure while still young.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason for early renunciation and the epic gives a young man living it, so the reader sees how the reason looks as a character.

note: Naladiyar 27 praises the firm who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end their wandering; verse 356 says the body's nature of leaving, with austerity and knowledge, brings the mind to the divine seat.
teaches: The quatrain stops at the resolve born of seeing the body pass, and the epic names where that resolve is said to lead.

note: Kural 380 says that nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one devises another way; verse 358 says that when they plan, fate gives the result and a strong plan may end otherwise, and Sumantiri still goes on to counsel.
teaches: The couplet gives fate as a rule; the minister uses it as a caution that does not stop deliberation, so the rule is shown as bounding counsel and not replacing it.

note: The counsellors tell the king to go in at once and not let counsel drag; Kural 638 says a minister must tell even a king who has ruined wise counsel what is good for him.
teaches: Here the counsellors' advice is a plain urging of haste that the king accepts, so the Kural's hard case of an unheeding king meets its easy one.

note: The verse thickens a pool with the washed paste and saffron of women's bodies; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is.
teaches: The epic's picture of the bath as pure delight is set against a Jain verse on the same bodies as flesh for vultures.

note: The time-keepers tell the king the hours that have passed; Kural 482 says acting in season is the rope that binds fortune.
teaches: The epic shows the machinery of a court that keeps its king aware of the hour, which is what the couplet's rule needs before it can be followed.

note: The king ends the day in song and pleasure; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The chapter shows a whole day of enjoyment with no word of its pain, so the quatrain's test of pleasure is left unanswered by the story here.

note: The attendants read the king's sign and withdraw unasked; Kural 701 praises one who reads what is meant before it is said.
teaches: The reading of a sign here serves privacy and not counsel, so the Kural's praise of sign-readers is shown at work in a small court habit.

note: Verse 385 names the first lord as the light who bore the wheel of dharma (அறக்கதிர் ஆழி); Kural 8 calls the god அறவாழி அந்தணன், where ஆழி can be taken as sea or as wheel.
teaches: A Jain epic uses the words aram and aazhi for a god where the Kural's phrase leaves open sea or wheel, so the same wording is read two ways across the corpus.

note: Verse 396 gives the lord who has no taste of the senses the work of opening doors that end hunger; Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger behind that of those who remove it.
teaches: The epic's lord is at once the senses' renouncer and the hunger-remover, so he fills both places the couplet sets in rank order.

note: Verse 418 gives the saying that the childless are like trees and the queen's joy at a daughter; Kural 61 holds children valuable only when they come to know what should be known.
teaches: The Kural makes the worth of a child depend on understanding, where the epic king's praise rests only on having a child at all and on her marriage prospect.

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi as envoy because he is learned and can put kin and affairs into words; Kural 686 names learning, fearlessness and sense of the time as the envoy's marks.
teaches: The ministers' test for an envoy stops at learning and speech, where the Kural adds fearlessness before hostile eyes and a sense of the moment, so the gaps show what the court has not yet asked of Marusi.

note: 450 sets the women's eyes above the deer's; Kural 1085 finds the deer, the eye and Death all in one look.
teaches: The epic uses the same deer-and-eye comparison as the couplet but lets the deer lose, where the couplet lets the look hold the deer's frightened shyness as one of its three natures.

note: 453 calls the women's sword-like eyes the mark of every killing art of love; Kural 1083 learns what Death is from a woman's large war-making eyes.
teaches: Both name the glance as a killer, but the couplet is one man's astonished cry and the epic makes it a settled doctrine of the women's whole equipment.

note: 453 hails the women's eyes as the killing sign of love; Naladiyar 44 refuses the sword-and-lily praise and sees only a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The two cannot both stand: one accepts the eye as a weapon, the other denies the image on the ground that the eye is only flesh, and which holds depends on whether the speaker is praising or renouncing.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe; verse 458 says the women's long dark eyes are skilled at killing.
teaches: The eye as Death is a shared trope of the lover's tradition, which the epic makes the plea of many men at once.

note: Verse 458 has men grant that the women's long dark eyes kill and bow to them; Naladiyar 44 refuses to call eyes spears or carp, since he has seen the eye is a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Soolamani gives the lover's image of the lethal eye a scene of surrender, and the Naladiyar answers with a renunciant who would not give way, so a reader sees the image only works on one who agrees to be struck.

note: Verse 463 puts a fire of desire within the women that sends up lines like smoke; Naladiyar 89 says desire burns the mind itself and is more to be feared than arrow, fire or sun.
teaches: The epic shows the fire of desire as marks on the body, and the Naladiyar says what the fire burns, the mind, so each supplies what the other lacks.

note: Kural 84 says a glad face towards good guests draws the goddess of wealth; verse 471 shows the host women doing every service to the guest for the Vidyadhara.
teaches: The Kural's rule is given a court in which welcome is a trained skill and not a feeling, and the Kural shows what the women's service is for.

note: Naladiyar 17 warns against the woman's spear-like eyes, since she too will age and lean on a staff; at 486 the blue-eyed women pour out their hearts to the princes.
teaches: The epic shows love's pull in full while the quatrain names its price, so the two together show what a reader is warned off and why.

note: Kural 1183 says the lover has taken a woman's modesty and given her sickness and pallor; at 487 many women grow pale and sigh for men who have only passed by.
teaches: The Kural's single lover is replaced by two princes and a crowd, so pallor from love is shown as a common mark of beauty's reach as well as a private ache.

note: Naladiyar 221 says the faults of those taken as good are kept within, as rice has its husk; Soolamani 5 asks that the poet's fault count for nothing before the good.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule keeping faults hidden between friends becomes a poet's plea that readers apply it to his own work, which turns a rule of friendship into a rule of reading.

note: Kural 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows the protocol, weighs the moment and place, and speaks after thought; at 500 Maruci opens with a bow and a courtesy that honours the princes before any message.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy meeting the Kural's test of protocol, and shows that what he first says is praise and not the matter of his errand.

note: Naladiyar 115 says the words of the poor glance off while the rich are heard; Marusi says that anyone who speaks wanting something is slighted, even when he speaks for the stronger lord.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds the cause of being ignored in the speaker's poverty, while Marusi finds it in the act of asking, so a rich lord's messenger can be slighted too.

note: Verse 52 gives Payapati a gentle face for those who come near; Kural 386 says a king easy to see and gentle in speech is praised above others.
teaches: The epic's king is gentle only to those who draw near and hot to foes, so the Kural's single ideal is shown split in two by the king's own enemies.

note: Naladiyar 27 sets the body as a bubble in pelting rain; 520 calls the human body a frothy hollow. The first uses it to urge ending the cycle of births, the second to bar men from a Vidyadhara's wealth.
teaches: One image of the body as foam serves a teacher of release and an envoy's claim of rank, so the image shows weakness only and takes its direction from who uses it.

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak briefly, to leave out what offends and to say it so that it wins a smile; Marusi's words in 518 to 523 offend the king and end by calling men of the earth unable to know what is fitting.
teaches: A couplet of what an envoy should do is seen broken in a scene where the envoy's anger grows from the court's silence rather than from ill will.

note: Kural 377 says that even those who amass millions enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned; verse 527 has the king say that only former deeds strive and later effort does not win what is not due.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's unnamed apportioner a face, the person's own earlier deeds, and uses it to settle who may marry whom, where the couplet only consoles about wealth.

note: Verse 528 reads the Vidyadharas' high wealth as the fruit of earlier austerity; Naladiyar 265 reads the wealth of the unjust as the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The same rule that makes the Vidyadhara's wealth a sign of past austerity makes a rich man's wealth no sign of present merit, so the epic's reasoning holds only for those of known past.

note: Naladiyar 72 says to bear in silence the unfit words of those who are not one's equals; verse 529 has Marusi ashamed because the king bore his unfit words.
teaches: The quatrain shows forbearance as the superior's duty, and the epic shows what it does to the one borne with: shame and a calmed anger rather than a grudge.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from work; verse 531 says Vidyadharas are men, distinguished only by their lore.
teaches: The couplet is turned from a general saying into the reason a marriage across a supposed divide may go ahead.

note: Kural 133 says that conduct is nobility of birth; verse 535 has the first lord make the five royal lineages and teach each its conduct and occupation.
teaches: In the epic, lineage is a thing made, with conduct as one of its parts, so the couplet's identity of conduct and birth is the made thing's own mark.

note: Kural 550 allows a king to put the cruel to death as weeding the crop; 54 has this king subdue even opponents by bowing them, and not slay in anger.
teaches: The couplet's weeding is the harsher rule, and the verse shows a king who treats killing as what grace avoids, so the two differ on whether death is part of a king's work.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering; verse 541 sings of the Lord as one who put away every desire and yet gives his servants unfailing bliss.
teaches: The hymn lets the desireless Lord be a giver, which the couplet avoids by saying only that no suffering reaches those at his feet.

note: Verse 549 judges the match fit because both houses have high lineage and wealth; Naladiyar 195 says high and low caste are only words and that austerity, learning and effort, not famous wealth, make a lineage.
teaches: The two disagree about what equality of houses rests on: the epic points to descent and riches, the quatrain to conduct and learning, and the clash holds only if lineage in 549 means inherited standing.

note: Verse 268 says all living beings worship the one who has gained his own self; verse 556 has kings bow at the feet of a man who left a throne and let creepers climb him.
teaches: The beings who worship the self-conquered man in the story are kings and serpents together, as the couplet does not say.

note: Kural 388 gives the title of lord to the king who guards by justice; verse 561 claims the title by a line of kings who never drew reproach.
teaches: A clan's boast of blamelessness is a debt to be repaid in each reign, which the couplet makes clear and the priest's speech blurs.

note: Verse 561 presents the king's greatness as coming from a high clan; Naladiyar 195 says good and bad caste are words and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage, which holds if 'clan' is taken to mean birth alone.
teaches: The priest's boast of birth is checked by the poem's own ancestor, who gained his rank by renouncing, which is the test the Naladiyar sets.

note: Kural 681 names birth in an honourable family among the first qualities of an envoy; verse 564 comes after the two clan recitals and praises the envoy's knowledge of clans and customs.
teaches: Family is not a bare boast but a thing the host tests by having the envoy recite and understand it.

note: Kural 685 asks the envoy to speak in brief, remove offence and gain the good; verse 566 has the king bid the envoy show faultless virtues in sifted words.
teaches: The host asks for the craft the couplet describes and does not simply receive it, so the envoy's skill is put on trial at the host's court.

note: The king reads the outcome of the errand from the envoy's face before he speaks, as Kural 706 says the face shows what the heart holds strongest.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet from a feeling to a piece of news, so a returning envoy's face can carry the result of a mission before his words do.

note: Kural 447 prizes counsellors who rebuke the ruler; 58 shows a court where no one proposes anything except at the king's hint.
teaches: The couplet praises the courtier who dares to rebuke, and the verse depicts a court where none speak unless prompted, which shows what the king gives up by having no one to correct him.

note: Marusi adds, beyond his message, his own eye-witness judgement that no other king he has seen equals the host; Kural 688 asks of an envoy purity, support, resolve and truthfulness in delivering the message.
teaches: The envoy's truthfulness here covers a judgement of the other king that the message does not carry, which is more than the couplet's duty of faithful relay.

note: Marusi calls the king hard for kings to reach yet easy for his own servants; Kural 386 praises a king who is easy to see.
teaches: The epic limits the couplet's easy access: it is a favour kept for a king's own men and withheld from rival kings.

note: Marusi's pairs, fire in command and cool in giving, name two of the four things Kural 390 calls the light of kings: giving and a straight sceptre.
teaches: The envoy's pairs put two marks of the Kural's ideal king into the temperature of one man, so command and giving are shown as tempers, not as separate duties.

note: Marusi says the world would not be without the king's gentle grace; Kural 544 says the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people with the sceptre.
teaches: The envoy states the Kural's idea of the world's dependence on the king's grace as a bare condition for existence, and in the mouth of a rival's envoy.

note: Marusi describes those under the king's umbrella as learned men bound by love who give their lives; Kural 389 says the world dwells under the umbrella of the king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella's shelter is filled by learned retainers who die for the king, and the couplet shows what keeps them there: a king who can bear their bitter words.

note: Kural 542 has the people looking to the sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 598 runs it the other way, with the king glad or hurt as the world is.
teaches: The pair shows rule as a two-way dependence, where the couplet states only the people's need of the king.

note: Kural 549 says guarding and caring for the people is the king's work and no stain; verse 599 shows that work as sleeplessness.
teaches: What the Kural calls work, the verse shows as a worry that costs a king his sleep.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed finds its doer like a calf its mother; verse 604 says merit joined this pair.
teaches: The Naladiyar's law of the old deed is shown working for good here, where its examples elsewhere fall on the wicked.

note: Kural 920 puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of the man Fortune has left; verse 615 makes desire itself the liquor.
teaches: The verse folds two of the Kural's three vices into one, so the women's eyes are the cup.

note: Kural 539 bids one swollen with joy think of those ruined by negligence; verse 619 shows Acuvakanthan so swollen.
teaches: The couplet's advice is the thing Acuvakanthan does not heed, so the story reads as its example.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure though suffering mounts, and the higher look to the pain in it; 619 shows a king past all noticing.
teaches: A verse of ethics gets a king's case, where the cost is a realm and not one man's comfort.

note: Kural 389 says the world rests under the umbrella of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear; verse 620 names a king by the opposite temper, striking in anger and unable to bear a word against him.
teaches: The couplet's virtue is given its negative portrait in a ruler whose pride goes with his intolerance.

note: Kural 617 says the goddess of misfortune lives in sloth and the lotus goddess in the labour of the unslothful; in verse 621 the goddess of fortune takes offence and looks for another place, because the king has not come to her.
teaches: In the Kural fortune leaves a man for sloth; here she leaves a king for his pleasure, so the fault is attention given elsewhere.

note: Kural 385 names a king as one able to create, gather, guard and apportion wealth; verse 626 gives the same four acts and says it is the learned man who becomes the protector of others.
teaches: The couplet's four tasks are tied to learning, so the verse makes the king's wealth-work depend on what he has studied.

note: Kural 431 says the wealth of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality; verse 627 makes arrogance a frost that destroys the lotus of wealth.
teaches: The couplet says what spoils the dignity of wealth; the verse shows how, with arrogance falling on wealth like frost on a lotus.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants at the head of armies fall and change when their deeds turn against them; verse 635 has a king boasting that mere men cannot shake him.
teaches: A king's claim of strength is read as the very certainty that, in the Naladiyar, precedes the fall of such rulers.

note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the king's eyes and he should take counsel; verse 641 has the king, who has already said he will fight regardless, tell his ministers to counsel.
teaches: The couplet's rule is shown with its limit, as counsel asked after the king has made up his mind.

note: Kural 674 says what is left over of a deed or a feud scorches like a fire's remnant; verse 643 draws the same fire but warns of a foe still small.
teaches: The epic's counsellors aim the couplet's fire at an enemy not yet seen to strike, which turns a rule about unfinished business into a case for striking first.

note: Kural 879 tells the king to cut a thorn tree young lest the hand that cuts it be hurt; verse 644 adds a nail for the sprout and that axe and hatchet fail once it has grown.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's thorn tree an argument for haste, though Arimanju's reply in 646 to 648 shows the story doubts that the tree is a thorn at all.

note: Kural 871 says no one should want enmity even in jest; verse 647 says that making foes of the harmless and trusting the ill-hearted both burn later.
teaches: Arimanju's caution answers the counsellors' haste with the Kural's own rule against courting enmity, so the epic stages two readings of Kural 879 and 871 as rival counsel.

note: Kural 756 counts what falls to the king, customs and what he takes from crushed foes as his wealth; verse 665 lists treasure and royal marks demanded of a king who has not been crushed.
teaches: The epic shows the third kind of the couplet's royal wealth being claimed before any war, by an overlord's letter and not by victory.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than fate, and that it arrives first even when one devises another course; verse 668 has the king put fate's power to use as the ground of giving way.
teaches: The couplet's law of fate is turned by the king into a reason to submit, which the hero rejects in the same chapter.

note: Kural 902 says shame follows the man whose desire for his woman makes him careless of other things; 67 has two wives bind a king so that he lets the work of ruling go.
teaches: The couplet speaks for any man and the verse shows the cost to a king, whose neglected work is the world's guarding, so the stakes are larger than shame.

note: Kural 680 says those with a small domain, afraid of unrest within, bow to the great and take what they are offered; verse 670 has the king bowing on the strength of earlier kings who pleased their overlord.
teaches: The king's submission follows the couplet's prudence step by step, so the prince's later refusal is a refusal of that prudence and not of mere cowardice.

note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool grieves when the fruit of past deeds comes, while the wise take it as an old desert crossed; verse 670 accepts the fruit of deeds without grief and answers by paying.
teaches: The same calm acceptance of deeds' fruit that the quatrain offers as freedom is here the mood in which a king submits.

note: Kural 894 says a weak man who harms the strong beckons Death with his hand; verse 686 makes the demander, who counts himself strong, the fool who beckons.
teaches: Strength is not settled by who sends the demand, and the couplet's rule can be turned against the one who thinks himself the strong party.

note: Naladiyar 3 says that kings who rode under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 69 shows a king at the height of his umbrella-wealth, with no word of what deeds will bring.
teaches: The quatrain says the umbrella's glory lasts only while deeds hold it up, and the verse stops at the glory without the fall, so the reader supplies the warning from the quatrain.

note: Kural 636 says no over-subtle scheme stands before keen native wit joined with learning; verse 695 rests the scheme on the target's lacking the sense to tell good from bad.
teaches: A scheme's success is shown to depend on how the target is judged, which the couplet alone does not say.

note: The verse praises the land by festival and wealth only; Kural 738 lists freedom from disease, protection and yield as a land's ornaments.
teaches: The epic shows a land's greatness by its splendour alone, so the reader sees what the Kural's list adds that this praise leaves out.

note: Kural 698 warns against belittling a ruler as young; in 703 Acuvakanthan waves off the prince as a child and the story then lets the prince take up his challenge.
teaches: The verse shows the belittling the couplet warns against and what it provokes, a prince who vows rather than withdraws.

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak so as to bring a smile and remove what would offend; here the envoys carry the king's taunt whole, because the minister of 700 wants the youth angered.
teaches: The envoys' offence is the lord's chosen means, a purpose the rule for envoys does not allow for.

note: Kural 471 says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting; in 708 and 709 the prince sends away his elephants, chariots and men and goes with no allies.
teaches: The prince's vow sets aside the allies' strength that the couplet counts, leaving the outcome to his own strength.

note: Kural 382 names fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive as a king's nature; in 719 the prince taunts a lion in its own cave.
teaches: The couplet's first quality is shown here as a deed done before a foe with no help, so fearlessness is seen at its cost.

note: Naladiyar 198 holds up the lion's strength as the measure of a man who would die poor rather than shame himself; in 724 the lion is the foe whose strength the gods marvel to see overcome.
teaches: The lion is first the model of honour and then the thing a stronger man destroys, so strength is not a single measure.

note: Kural 774 has the warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his body; in 726 the victor of a harder fight shows neither joy nor wonder.
teaches: The Kural's soldier takes pleasure in the fight and the epic's prince does not, so the same bravery is shown with two moods.

note: At the princes' birth the clinging moisture of evil deeds is said to dry up for many; Kural 5 says deeds of darkness do not cling to those who delight in the Lord's praise.
teaches: The Kural lifts the hold of deeds through the devotee's own praise, but the epic lifts it for many through the birth of a great being, so each work places the loosening of karma somewhere different.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's killing of the cruel to pulling weeds from young corn; verse 772 praises a prince's killing of a beast that preyed on the herds, as a gift of safe sleep to the world.
teaches: The epic carries the weeding rule from criminals to a beast, and gives the reason in the world's sleep, though a Jain poet still has to justify a killing.

note: Kural 388 makes the ruler who does justice and protects an இறை for the people; verse 773 sets the king's sons under the same duty and says it outweighs their own lives.
teaches: The duty to protect reaches the king's sons and is stated as a willingness to lose their lives, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one to take the great fruit of a rare body while it lasts; verse 774 says the body yields no fruit if it cannot help the afflicted.
teaches: The body's fruit is named as aid to others in trouble, where the quatrain leaves what the fruit is to the word virtue.

note: Kural 235 speaks of a death that is really existence, a growth through ruin; verse 776 says the flesh body goes while the form of fame stands.
teaches: The verse supplies the two-body picture that explains the couplet's death that is existence, as the fame body that survives.

note: Kural 1067 begs the beggars not to beg of those who conceal; verse 784 likens a deer's thirst to a high-born man who begged from a low man's eyes and earned blame.
teaches: The verse makes the cost of begging of the wrong person a stain on rank, where the couplet gives only a warning.

note: Kural 742 counts a shady forest as one of a fort's four parts; verse 785 shows who holds the forest, men who live by violence and serve the king.
teaches: A forest that guards the realm is held by violent servants, a cost the couplet's list of fort parts does not show.

note: 80 likens the women's sidelong glances to Kaman's arrows; Naladiyar 17 warns against desiring a woman of spear-like eyes, for she too will lean on a staff.
teaches: The epic shows the glance as a weapon at the moment of its force, and Naladiyar names the later fall of the same weapon, so the pair sets the glance's power against its short life.

note: Kural 65 says touching one's children is joy to the body; the king here holds both sons in both arms as soon as he sees them.
teaches: The king's embrace shows a father's bodily joy in his sons coming before any royal question.

note: Kural 550 likens the king's removal of the cruel to weeding a crop; 824 gives a lion ruining the king's forest, removed by his sons.
teaches: A king's clearing of harm to his land can be done by a beast-slaying prince, which widens the weeding image beyond wrongdoers.

note: Kural 65 also names the joy of hearing children's words; in 825 the king revives when his son tells him he went along.
teaches: The king's lifting at his son's words gives the couplet's pleasure of the ear a sudden effect on life itself.

note: Kural 676 says to act only after weighing the finish, the hindrance and the yield; verse 829 has the king consult his kin and then press on with the wedding.
teaches: A king's deliberation can be a formality over a choice already made by the deed of the suitor.

note: Kural 381 counts an army first among a king's six limbs, while verse 838 raises the host as a marriage escort, in the likeness of a sea swallowing the world.
teaches: The pair shows an army used for display and escort, a use the couplet's list of royal strengths does not name.

note: Kural 57 holds that guarding women by confinement is no use and their own steadfastness is the best guard; verse 861 sets armed women round the princess.
teaches: The pair shows the guard of arms as outward show beside the inward guard the couplet values.

note: Kural 761 calls a complete army the chief of a king's wealth; verse 874 shows the host as a spreading display round a bridal vimana.
teaches: The pair shows that the host here is wealth on show, not strength at work as the couplet rates it.

note: Kural 381 counts the army among the six limbs of a king; verse 898 shows an army encamped with allied kings rimming the forest around the royal banner.
teaches: The camp shows the army as a ring of allies as well as a limb, which the couplet's list of six does not show.

note: The soldiers hold that only bound fate may take a life; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: A warrior class that claims only fate may kill makes its own arms the servants of fate, which the couplet's praise of fate's strength never says.

note: The prince stocks the city's feast for guests as each desires; Kural 81 says a household exists to tend guests.
teaches: The wedding feast is a state's display and a political courtesy, which shows a limit of the couplet's household hospitality that needs no such display.

note: Verse 934 shows the king's white umbrella raised in the ride that cools the world; Kural 389 says the world lives under the umbrella of a king who can bear bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella cools only for a king who has the character the Kural names, which the display of the ride cannot show.

note: Verse 934 shows a king riding an elephant under a high umbrella; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under umbrellas like the moon over a hill have been carried off.
teaches: The same pomp that the Soolamani shows as the king's splendour is the thing the Naladiyar sets against death, so the display is also a reminder of its end.

note: Verse 936 gives the roar of pipes, drums and horns at the wedding ride; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sound for a wedding may sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The wedding's noise is the same instrument as the funeral's, so the Naladiyar turns the verse's joy into a warning without changing the sounds.

note: Verse 941 shows women along the route losing their composure at the sight of the young men; Kural 1254 says the restraint she boasted of passes beyond concealment into the open.
teaches: The public street is the occasion where the Kural's private breaking of restraint becomes visible to all.

note: Verse 944 gives the host's standing by its look: elephants like hills, banners like streams, warriors like tigers; Kural 768 says an army without striking power still gains standing from its martial bearing.
teaches: A host at a wedding is shown by its bearing alone, which is the standing the Kural says an army can have even before it fights.

note: Kural 680 has a small ruler bow to the great out of fear; verse 960 has the princes fold hands before the king at a meeting arranged for a wedding.
teaches: The bow of a wedding visit is shown as courtesy between equals, where the couplet sees bowing as a way of buying safety.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing him; verse 963 has the host drink in the guest's beauty and seat him on his own elephant.
teaches: The welcome here is warmer than a kept face, since the host shares his own mount, a test the couplet does not set.

note: Kural 1251 has the axe of desire break the door of restraint bolted with shame; Soolamani 981 has restraint vanish because desire runs straight on, and puts it in the poet's voice about the girl.
teaches: The Kural gives restraint a lock that desire can break, while the Jain epic says the restraint was not broken but given to the one she loves.

note: Kural 1094 has the man see that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he does not she smiles; in 982 the lad looks boldly while her modesty holds her back and she melts.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's inference from the lowered eye, and the epic shows the same shyness from within, as a pull she cannot hide.

note: Naladiyar 47 has the fool call a body of nine seeping openings 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' because skin dazzles his eyes; Soolamani 987 has Prajapati marvel that the Maker gathered all beauty into one girl.
teaches: The same dazzled look at a woman is a fool's error in the Naladiyar and a bride's honour in the epic, so the epic's praise stands on a view of the body the Jain text refuses.

note: Kural 1125 has the man say he would recall her only if he forgot, but he does not know how to forget; 990 has the girl say that if she tried to forget, fate itself would drive her back to remember.
teaches: Both deny forgetting, but the Soolamani lays the compulsion on fate, which the Kural leaves to the lover's nature.

note: Kural 1102 says the cure for a disease is usually other than its cause but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; Soolamani 991 says love's sickness has no cure and that looking coolly at loved ones only doubles the wound.
teaches: The Kural finds the remedy in union with the beloved, and the epic denies any remedy before the union.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists beauty among the things that fail to last, which the best renounce; 999 praises the bride's beauty as so bright she cannot be looked at, and says nothing of its end.
teaches: The poet gives full praise to beauty that his school's moral verse calls perishable, so the reader sees the praise and the warning side by side without either answering the other.

note: The poet bows to a named tirthankara; the couplet praises the feet of one free of liking and aversion without naming him.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a name and a seat under the pindi tree to the one the Kural leaves unnamed, so the same freedom from liking and aversion can be read as a particular lord.

note: Yugi's deceit is for keeping a sworn vow; the couplet says wealth gained by deceit does not hold.
teaches: Deceit that serves a promise and not wealth is not judged by the couplet, which shows how far its warning reaches.

note: Udayanan stands under a rain of arrows and answers with his bow; the couplet gives the bull elephant under a sheaf of arrows.
teaches: The couplet's elephant only stands firm; Udayanan stands firm and also shoots back, so endurance in the story includes acting.

note: Verse 123 calls the lady's breast a raft in the sea of desire; Naladiyar 17 warns that the same woman will one day walk bent on a staff.
teaches: The epic's rapture and the quatrain's warning use the same woman and cannot both be the last word on her.

note: Kural 539 bids a man remember the ruined when swollen with joy; the king of verse 124 forgets even his own ruin.
teaches: The couplet's remedy needs a remembering mind, and the poem shows the king in whom nothing remains to be reminded.

note: Kural 638 makes it the minister's duty to tell a king what is good for him; Yugi, given a king who will not hear, chooses a trick.
teaches: The couplet assumes the king can be told, while the poem shows a minister who judges telling useless and acts in secret.

note: Kural 901 says desire for a wife costs a man what action needs; Yugi concludes the same of the king's union, and cures it by a stratagem, not by the king's restraint.
teaches: The couplet speaks to the man who must resist his own desire, while the epic gives the cure to a minister who engineers an absence.

note: The ministers' counsel to a grieving king meets Kural 638 on a minister's duty to speak to a king who will not listen.
teaches: The Kural rule covers a king who destroys good counsel, but the epic shows a king who accepts counsel and is still deceived because the advisers' facts are false.

note: Disguised ministers sell jewels in an enemy camp, as the Kural describes a spy who takes an unsuspected form.
teaches: The epic's spies are the king and his own minister, and gems are the means, which the Kural's spy has no word for.

note: The spies' report in 169 is confirmed in 170 by a second voice, the minister's.
teaches: The king rejoices only once a second voice agrees, which suggests the second confirmation is a habit of a court and not only a rule.

note: The ministers, army and friend the king adds to the dowry in 176 are the same things the Kural counts among a state's six parts.
teaches: A king who has lost a state can rebuild its parts by marriage, which the Kural's list of parts does not say.

note: After the victory by arms, the king in 185 tends the wounded and rewards them, which is the work of a ruler's rule and not of the spear.
teaches: The epic shows victory first by the sword and then by care, so the Kural's claim is borne out only in the part after the battle.

note: The king ends his queen's sulk by praise and an embrace, which is what the couplet urges for a sulker.
teaches: The couplet says not to leave the sulker unembraced, while the scene adds that he first praises her beauty and wins her mind.

note: Quarrel (201-202), making up (203) and union (204) run in the order the couplet gives.
teaches: The couplet lists the three as a gain of love, and the run of verses shows them as one evening in a king's house.

note: Udayanan divides towns among those who served him; the couplet names apportioning as one of a king's tasks.
teaches: The poem shows apportioning as reward to friends who risked themselves for the king, which the couplet names without saying to whom the share goes.

note: Vikraman's grief at having no child (verse 21) meets the Kural's praise of children who know what should be known, and the epic gives him a sister's son in place of his own.
teaches: The epic shows that the heir the Kural praises can come by a sister's son, not only by birth, and that the want of a child can lead to renunciation.

note: The letter softens the wrong of the seizure with words of pardon; the couplet asks the envoy to remove what offends.
teaches: A letter that must confess a seizure can keep to the couplet's rule of avoiding offence only by naming the fault and asking for pardon in the same breath.

note: Pradyotan pleads the tie of uncle and nephew; the couplet tells a man not to presume on kin degree with a king.
teaches: Here the stronger party pleads kinship and not the lesser, which shows the couplet's warning running the other way once the king has wronged his kinsman.

note: The king says that without such counsellors there is no kingship; the couplet makes counsellors the king's eyes.
teaches: The couplet asks the king to choose counsellors after counsel, but the verse shows a king recognising the worth of a minister who had worked against him.

note: Vikraman gives up his kingdom and goes to the forest, as the quatrain's best of men renounce home and wealth on seeing they do not last.
teaches: The epic shows a king doing what the quatrain says, with the order of arranging his heir first and then leaving, which the quatrain does not mention.

note: The Kural's wife calls her husband a philanderer because all women feast on him with their eyes; Dattai's anger at his second marriage is the same grievance.
teaches: The epic shows what the Kural's grievance leads to when the husband is a king who really does take another wife, so the complaint is tested rather than only voiced.

note: The Kural's friend clears distress at once; the god's help waits to be called.
teaches: The god's reproach shows a friend's help can be bound by the call, which limits the Kural's picture of friendship that acts in the moment of trouble.

note: The Kural's bewildered first sight is here mutual and immediate.
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's bewilderment through to union within a single verse, with no doubt, no gossip and no delay, so the bewilderment is a path to union and not a state of suffering.

note: The captor confines her and then tries to break her steadfastness; the Kural says only her own firmness guards a woman.
teaches: Here the confinement works as the couplet says it must: the captor holds her body, yet only her silence and thought of her husband stand in the way, so the guard is inside her.

note: Desire breaks through the restraint of the one who was to be the tempter.
teaches: Vegavati was sent as the instrument of a plan, and she meets desire the Kural says does not stop to ask whether one is firm in restraint, which makes the plan itself the thing that fails.

note: Sathanikan gives up the throne while living, where the quatrain says kings under the umbrella on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The epic's king keeps his rank by choosing to leave it before death, which the quatrain does not allow for.

note: At the height of empire and eight thousand queens, the Naladiyar says kings on elephants under umbrellas are carried off like all others; the next kandam is a renunciation.
teaches: The peak of enjoyment is set right before the work's renunciation kandam, so the Naladiyar's warning is the story's own turning point.

note: The epic makes merit's fruit a throne and pleasure in this life, where the couplet calls virtue the companion that stays when you die.
teaches: Merit gathered earlier is repaid here as sovereignty, so the couplet's 'companion' is shown paying out in the same life it began.

note: The king's vow follows earlier merit, as the couplet says austerity comes only to those who already have it.
teaches: The couplet's circular rule is shown working in a life, with the vow following earlier merit.

note: A king of full worldly success leaves pleasure behind, which tests the couplet's question about going outside.
teaches: The couplet asks what is gained by leaving the household that keeps virtue, and the story answers with a king who leaves out of disgust at its pleasures, not out of failure.

note: The couplet makes austerity and giving depend on the sky's rain; here the ascetics themselves send the rain.
teaches: The dependence of austerity on rain in the couplet is reversed in the unit, where the austere supply the rain.

note: The quatrain praises those who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end wandering; the unit shows a sermon only heard.
teaches: Hearing a sermon on suffering is not yet the resolve the quatrain praises, so the unit stops short of its conclusion.

note: Both give hell as the fruit of the deed; the verse adds animal rebirth to it.
teaches: The epic widens the couplet's hell into an order of fruits that includes animal birth, which the couplet does not name.

note: The verse promises release for gifts to ascetics; the couplet says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: The verse pays giving in release, while the couplet holds that giving is good without any reward, so the two differ on why one gives.

note: Both warn that women and liquor ruin a man; the verse follows the ruin past this life.
teaches: The couplet counts the loss in fortune; the story counts the loss in the next birth, so the harm reaches beyond this life.

note: Naladiyar tells the listener to do what good he can at once, because Death comes; the king acts at once on the news of the elephant.
teaches: Naladiyar's warning comes with no figure to act on it; the king gives up a throne, a wife-court and his lands within a verse of the warning, so the rule is shown at its full price.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside if the household is led in virtue; the king takes his queens and ministers with him.
teaches: The Kural weighs the household against leaving it, while the king's whole household leaves together, which tests whether renunciation is abandoning dependants.

note: The Kural makes it the duty of a minister at the king's side to tell him what is good for him; in 36 the ministers tell Pradyota of Udayana's merits.
teaches: The ministers do speak, as the Kural asks, but to a king in anger the truth ends in a plot, so the duty to speak does not guarantee it is heard.

note: Kural 126 praises drawing in the five senses like a tortoise; the verse lists holding the five senses as one item of a numbered discipline.
teaches: The couplet states restraint as a single act with a reward over seven births, and the verse sets it as one part of a long catalogue, so restraint becomes one limb of a trained life.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; the verse says they are burned in meditation.
teaches: The couplet makes freedom from the two deeds a gift of praise, and the verse makes it the fruit of effort, so the cause of release differs while the word for the two deeds is shared.

note: The Kural says a king who does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger sees his fortune shrink; in 37 Pradyota rages after the ministers have spoken.
teaches: The king here has taken counsel and yet his anger still rules the outcome, so the Kural's warning is about whether counsel is heard, not just whether it is asked.

note: The verse allows deeds to be shed in order, where the couplet says fate gets there first whatever one devises.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves room for undoing deeds that the Kural's fate overrides, though the dispute is over what one can do to a deed.

note: The Kural's picture is of binding a rutting elephant by means of an elephant; verse 40 builds an elephant of wood and hide, filled with ninety-six men, to take a king.
teaches: The ministers use the Kural's own method in a worse form, a false elephant with men inside and a king as the catch.

note: The Kural ranks the slackness of great joy below anger as a cause of ruin; in 47 the king goes on though omens and Vayantakan warn him.
teaches: The Kural's slackness is not ignorance: Udayana is told and warned, and in the verse it is his gladness at sight of the elephant that wins.

note: Veeranathan's rain of virtue in verse 5 is set beside the Kural's rain that comes where the king rules justly.
teaches: The epic gives the rain to the tirthankara's teaching, where the Kural makes it the reward of the ruler's sceptre.

note: The Naladiyar gives it as a rule that kings who rode in state are carried off and spoken of as dead; here a king's sword snaps and he is seized, but he is afterwards to be rescued.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule of the ruined proud king is true of the captive here, but the epic makes the ruin a seizure to be undone by a minister, not a final end.

note: Yugi falls as if speared (65) and then rises and sets his plan; the couplet's strong in mind who do not give way where things fall apart.
teaches: The couplet's firm elephant is a person who stays upright; Yugi shows the other half, a man who is struck down and then gets up to act.

note: Yugi removes the king's kin to safety, appoints rulers and plans to answer force with guile, which are three of the minister's skills in the couplet: dividing, holding his own side close, bringing back those who left.
teaches: Kural 633 lists a minister's skills as bare terms; this verse shows one minister doing them in order at a moment of loss.

note: The couplet wants a spy in a guise that raises no suspicion; Yugi's mad guise draws every eye but carries speech meant for one hearer, the king.
teaches: A disguise can be conspicuous to everyone and still be a secret to all but one, which the couplet's rule of unsuspected appearance does not allow.

note: Yugi and Vayanthakan wait for the right hour and rope, as the couplet says nothing is hard for one who knows time and means.
teaches: The rescue is built on the couplet's rule, but at the cost of others, which the couplet does not weigh.

note: Yugi uses the king's own rutting elephant to break the king's hold, as the couplet binds a rutting elephant with another.
teaches: The Kural's image of one task serving another is shown as a plan that also costs lives.

note: The freed elephant kills the keepers who try to enclose it, as the quatrain says an elephant may kill even its keeper.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's keeper-killer elephant as a weapon someone else has deliberately loosed.

note: The king fears the blame of sending a captive before an elephant but admits the capture was by a lie.
teaches: The king dreads the stain of one act and ignores the one before it, which the couplet's test of fame would catch.

note: Udayanan, a captive, rides in triumph on the elephant; the quatrain says kings who rode elephants fall when their deeds turn.
teaches: The story reverses the quatrain's fall, showing a captive king raised through skill and not through deeds, which limits how far the quatrain's warning is the whole account.
