note: The friend asks the queen to confine her restraint; the couplet says desire breaks that bolted door.
teaches: The couplet's door of restraint is shown here as one a friend urges the queen to keep shut and which the queen has already broken.

note: The friend answers desire by loathing the body's foulness, as the quatrain does with every body.
teaches: The remedy of disgust works in the quatrain as meditation and fails in the story, where one repellent body cannot cool a mind already taken.

note: The quatrain weighs great fear against small pleasure and counsels against another's wife; the keeper, who has just said the king will kill him, then calls the queen's love his best reward.
teaches: The quatrain's reckoning of fear against pleasure is tested on a man who does the sum and then goes ahead.

note: The king has the power to strike and the cause, and holds his anger.
teaches: The couplet separates guarding anger where it can take effect from guarding it where it cannot; the king's stand is the first kind, with a sword drawn.

note: The king spares the woman and the man, but for reasons of sex and rank, not because life is dear.
teaches: The couplet bars killing even to save one's own life without exception; the king's reasons here are narrower, and only at 139 does he come to the couplet's rule.

note: The king lists what desire destroys; the couplet says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion lose even their names.
teaches: The couplet states the cure; the king's list shows what it costs when desire is not removed, and he begins the cure by leaving the court.

note: The king takes the nature of women as a reason to leave; the quatrain says no guard will keep them from fault.
teaches: The quatrain says guards cannot hold women's conduct; the king's answer is not a stronger guard but his own departure.

note: A mother asks for one killing as an offering to a goddess; the couplet says not killing beats a thousand offerings.
teaches: The couplet compares not killing with great offerings, while the story puts the offering on a mother's lips as a cure for her son's fear.

note: The king refuses to kill even to save his own life, and gives the cost in the next world and the shortness of this one.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule alone; the king adds the reason that makes it bear on a man whose own life is threatened.

note: The king asks who can turn aside the ripening of deeds.
teaches: The couplet says fate outruns any other device; the king acts that out, trying the mother's device and finding the fruit still comes.

note: Hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself, as the king's offering returns on him through the poison.
teaches: The couplet says the hurt returns of itself; 153 shows it returning through a third person's crime, so the doer suffers without being punished by the doer's own victim.

note: A deed that seeks out the one who did it, like a calf finding its mother in a herd.
teaches: The quatrain's image says deeds find their doer; 153 shows how: they come in at the hour of the poison and ripen into animal births.

note: The quatrain says kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn; the epic shows the fall as the same soul living on as a timid bird in his son's house.
teaches: The couplet's fall of kings is made concrete: the king does not end, he is reborn lower, and at his own son's door.

note: A calf finds its mother among many cows as an old deed finds its doer; here the mother, now a dog, finds the son in a bird's body and kills him.
teaches: The quatrain's mother-finding image is turned over: the deed that finds the doer wears the face of a mother meeting her child.

note: The kural's evil that follows the doer like a shadow that never leaves is shown in the snake who becomes a crocodile and follows the fish into the river.
teaches: The pursuit shows that the shadow of deed can pass through the animal births, which the couplet's one life does not show.

note: The couplet says pains rest on those who caused pains; here the crocodile's pain comes but at the hands of men who themselves do harm.
teaches: The epic shows deed's return working through the very cruelty of new doers, so the rule is true but puts another debt on those who carry it out.

note: The couplet ranks not killing and eating above a thousand sacrifices; the epic's rite of the dead is a sacrifice whose flesh is the dead man.
teaches: The couplet states the rule; the epic's story shows its cost to the rite's own beneficiaries, so that the rule is tested by a case where the dead eat the dead.

note: The lamb in the slaughter ground nibbles the garland unaware; the kid in 197 knows its fate and its son.
teaches: The Naladiyar's lamb stands for the heedless; the epic sets beside it a lamb that knows, so the reader sees what the heedless have lost.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf seeks its mother; the kid in 199 is a king found by his own deeds.
teaches: The quatrain gives the mechanism and the epic gives the case: the doer is found even across births and in a lower body, and still hears the deed named as its own.

note: The Naladiyar's lamb nibbles the garland in the slaughter ground; here pairs of animals are brought together at the shrine as victims.
teaches: The quatrain uses the victim's unawareness as an image for the thoughtless, and the epic shows the gathered victims themselves, so the image can be read back onto the sacrifice.

note: The couplet calls a king who torments his people crueller than a killer; here the king seizes merchants' goods over a horse.
teaches: The epic's king acts from a sudden anger, not from habit, so it shows how the couplet's cruelty can come from one incident and an unexamined report.

note: The king holds that worship of the goddess is rightly done by killing, beginning with humans; the Kural says refraining from killing and eating one creature is better than a thousand sacrifices.
teaches: The two rank sacrifice and non-killing in opposite orders, and if the Kural is read as applying to blood offering as well as to oblations, the king's rite is the very thing the couplet ranks lowest.

note: The couplet asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can hold to compassion; here the flesh is possibly her victim's.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's general 'another creature' into a creature that may be her own victim's next body, which sharpens its question.

note: The couplet says sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; here a wife crosses, and the fruit falls on her.
teaches: The couplet is spoken to a man; the epic carries the same four ills onto a wife and adds the one the couplet lacks, the disease of her own body.

note: The onlookers name the fruit of a woman's cruelty as leprosy, coming to her body; the couplet says only that harm returns of itself.
teaches: The epic shows the return of harm as a long delay in which the doer is first shown eating and then rotting, which the couplet's afternoon-for-forenoon image cannot show.

note: Both say a deed finds its doer; the epic adds that it outlasts her death.
teaches: Putting 217 beside the calf-and-mother image shows that the Jain epic makes the deed's claim reach past the doer's body, a step the quatrain does not take.

note: The king orders a pair of human children brought for sacrifice to avert the goddess's anger; the Kural says not to do a deed that takes another's life even if one's own life be lost.
teaches: The king takes lives to avert harm to his city, whereas the Kural allows no exception even for the life of the one who decides, so the scene tests the rule against the case of a ruler who thinks he acts for his people.

note: The couplet pictures the life as a lodger in the body; the verse argues it by the conch's sound.
teaches: The couplet takes the soul's separateness for granted and the verse offers a reason for it, so the reader sees what the couplet's picture assumed.

note: Verse 243 puts truth after not killing and gives each its fruit, as the couplet puts not lying second to not killing.
teaches: The couplet only names the order of the two virtues, and the verse adds what each is said to yield.

note: The couplet says a life lives on not eating flesh and keeps hell closed; the verse adds worldly beauty, victory and birth.
teaches: The couplet gives the reason for not eating flesh as fear of hell, and the verse gives a gain in this life, so the reader sees two arguments for one abstention.

note: The sage says kings who kill to keep the body last only a few days and then sink in rebirth; the couplet forbids taking a life even to save one's own.
teaches: The couplet gives a bare ban; the sage supplies the reason that the life one kills to save is brief and the killing makes the next birth worse.

note: Naladiyar says even kings who rode elephants under the white umbrella have been carried off and no one is left over; the verse says kings who kill to last also die and then sink in rebirth.
teaches: The quatrain ends at death; the verse adds that for a king who killed to last, the end is only a sinking into more births.

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the sage says the pain of killing returns to the killers birth after birth.
teaches: The couplet states the return of pain as a rule; the verse shows it falling across births on two named kin who thought their killing was only a rite.

note: Kural 28 says the greatness of those whose word is full shows in their hidden words; 269 says what such ascetics will comes about, even the cloud, and puts this under fate.
teaches: The epic places the ascetic's power in his will and under fate, where the couplet puts it in the word.

note: 271 says the ascetic thinks of pain inflicted as his own deed; Naladiyar 58 says the worthy grieve for those who scorn them, fearing the hell that will follow.
teaches: Together they show that holding hurt as one's own deed does not leave the ascetic cold: Naladiyar adds the pity for the offender that 271 omits.

note: 272 grounds 'all lives are like my own' in an ascetic's grace and a result beyond karma; Kural 315 tests understanding by guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The epic puts the rule into a speech to a hunting king, so that guarding other lives has a named cost to him: his hounds and spear.

note: Naladiyar 53 has the best renounce home, youth and wealth at once to save themselves; 275 renounces for the pleasure-rich heaven.
teaches: The epic shows that the same reflection on impermanence may end in heaven rather than in release.

note: 278 has the ascetic hold neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit; Kural 346 says cutting off 'I' and 'mine' reaches a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic adds a third term, benefit, to the Kural's pair, so letting go includes even what one might claim as one's own good.

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; 281 forbids the king to take his own life even to atone.
teaches: The couplet's rule against killing is shown to cover the doer's own life, which the couplet does not say.

note: The Kural says that for the flesh-eater hell does not open its mouth; here the flesh-eater is told 'you ate' and hot copper is forced into her mouth.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell becomes a scene in which hell feeds the eater, and the penalty is shown to match the eating.

note: In both, the flesh the eater took from another is answered in the eater's own body: the crab-eater's fingers rot, the queen's limbs are cut off for her to eat.
teaches: Together they show the deed answering in kind, once in a diseased human body and once in a hell where the body will not die.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; here the old deed 'stands and burns' the queen in hell.
teaches: The calf's search takes the deed to its doer, and the epic shows what the deed then does once it has arrived.

note: The quatrain has mother seeking mother through the world; here father, mother, son and daughter change places among themselves across births.
teaches: One shows kin passing the world on, the other shows kin turning into each other, so grief for kin has no fixed object.

note: The Kural says all pain falls on those who caused pain; the king reads his own life as a ripening of the pain he gave his father and mother in their births.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes a confession in which the doer sees the pain return across several births.

note: The Kural names not killing as the chief virtue; the king names the lack of mercy joined to seeking wealth and pleasure as his fault.
teaches: The king adds the motive of wealth and pleasure to the couplet's plain count of killing, so greed becomes part of the fault.

note: Naladiyar 4 tells the hearer to do good at once because Death comes in anger; verse 317 grades austerity to each one's strength.
teaches: Urgency in the quatrain is made practicable by the epic's graded vows, which say how those not yet able to renounce fully are to begin.

note: Kural 321 calls not killing the first of dharma and says killing brings every other kind of deed; verse 321 shows one killing without a real life still following across births.
teaches: The couplet's rule is tested at its smallest case, the effigy, which shows how far the epic extends the rule beyond the couplet.

note: The epic says fear can neither stop the coming harm nor do anything but add pain and fresh deeds; the quatrain says the fool sighs when the fruit arrives while the wise take it as old desert.
teaches: Fear is shown as a new cause of karma before the fruit comes, which extends the quatrain's advice on taking fruit that has arrived.

note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; verse 330 names dharma, giving up anger, knowledge and the vow as what to do.
teaches: The couplet names what must perish and the epic's last verse names the practices that make it perish.

note: The epic says deeds whirl the soul like a wheel through the four states; the couplet names craving as the seed of unceasing birth.
teaches: The epic gives the wheel's driver as deeds and the Kural gives craving, so the two books hold different roots of the same round of birth.

note: The Kural says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord's true fame; verse 4 promises a poem that shows the fruit of deeds, good and bad, as they actually ripen.
teaches: A story shows karma bearing fruit in merit and fear, which limits the couplet's picture of deeds that simply do not cling to the devout.

note: The epic says even Indra-like lords of the gods lost their forms; the quatrain says kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left over.
teaches: The quatrain's visible proof that kings die is stretched by the epic to the gods, so no rank in any world offers refuge from loss.

note: The epic likens death and birth to putting off a cloth and leaving a house for another; the couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking.
teaches: The epic's cloth and house are things a person does and leaves, while the Kural's sleep is something that happens to one, so the two images differ on whether the change is in the soul's hands.

note: The brother's thought is that women's minds lack firmness; the Kural names firmness, called karpu, as the greatest thing in a woman.
teaches: Both books turn on a woman's firmness, but the epic locates it in renunciation and the Kural in chastity, so firmness is not the same virtue in the two.

note: The brother bids his sister think of the soul as other than the body and leave it in the victors' refuge; the couplet likens the tie of body and life to a bird flying off from its nest.
teaches: The couplet calls the tie light and the epic makes it a choice to be carried out, so the same lightness is turned into an act of leaving.

note: Kural 259 ranks refusing to take and eat one creature's life above a thousand oblations; verse 58 shows the rite at its far end, a man led to the goddess's place with the king's sword drawn.
teaches: The couplet weighs a ritual's merit against one life in general; the epic puts the weighing at the altar, where the offering is a man and the weigher is the king holding the sword.

note: Naladiyar 16 sets a kid nibbling the leaf garland before it in the fierce ritual ground; verse 59 sets two youths at the place of killing, smiling.
teaches: The kid is glad because it does not know where it stands, while the youths' smile at the same kind of place rests on knowing, so the doomed creature's calm turns from ignorance to composure.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; the youth traces the pair's sufferings over many births to harm done to living bodies.
teaches: The quatrain gives the deed's aim but not its kind; the epic names the kind, injury to living beings, and spreads its return over many births.

note: Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone to cure desire; verse 71 calls the body a hut of filth and the dharma what ends desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing.
teaches: The quatrain cures desire by looking at the parts; the epic ties the same look to a dharma that also ends killing, so the contemplation of foulness shares a root with the mercy that stays the king's sword.

note: Naladiyar praises those who renounce in childhood for foreseeing grey hair; Asokan renounces only after he sees it.
teaches: The king meets the Naladiyar's test late but still before the staff, so renunciation after the first white hair counts as wise, not foolish.

note: Kural 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue; verse 86 says the cause: pride of wealth turns the prince to forget it.
teaches: The Kural names forgetting as the worst loss but not its cause, and the epic gives it as the pride of wealth.

note: The turtle in the heated pot plays on unaware of its end, as the king and city sit in wealth without seeing release.
teaches: Both place the danger in comfort that blinds, but the Naladiyar names death as the one waiting, while the epic leaves the danger as the loss of the road to release.

note: The king's plunge into a sea of pleasure is set beside the quatrain's lamb eating the garland before its slaying.
teaches: The epic scene only lists pleasure's delights and the quatrain adds the shadow of the slaughter ground over them.

note: Amritamati in a guarded palace chamber is moved by a song from the stable: the confinement fails and her own steadfastness is the real guard.
teaches: The Kural says that only a woman's own steadfastness guards her, and the epic shows the guard fails through the ear, not the door, so steadfastness is a matter of the mind.

note: Both verses show evening birds going to their nests and young while one who is away or lovesick suffers.
teaches: Pairing the two shows that the happy birds are used as the measure of the lover's loneliness in both, only here the sufferer is a youth and there it is a wife.

note: Verse 1029 compares closing lotuses to chaste women whose beloved has left; Akananuru 71 compares bees leaving pool flowers for branch flowers to graceless men.
teaches: The same evening scene casts the flower as a faithful wife and the bee as a leaving man, so each poet gives the figure a different party to blame.

note: Both set the cowherds' flute in the evening pastures: a sign of plenty here, a torment to the waiting wife there.
teaches: The same flute is joy in the public landscape and pain in a private heart, so the reader sees how the sound takes its meaning from who hears it.

note: 1680 has the king and his wives clinging to a float in the pond; Akananuru 266 has the husband bathing with young women on a float, whose gossip the wife throws back at him.
teaches: The same float-play is a king's marital pleasure in the epic and a husband's scandal in the akam poem, so what makes it fair or shameful is who the partners are.

note: 1759 has the father hold his sweat-brow daughter after ball-play; Akananuru 17 recalls a girl too tired for a ball game who lay in her mother's arms.
teaches: The tired child resting in a parent's arms is the last scene before she leaves for a husband, by public choice in the epic and by flight in the akam poem.

note: 1816 places a king at Urandai among swans, drums and banners; Akananuru 385 uses Uranthai as the standard of a house rich in festival.
teaches: Urandai is the name of wealth in both books, so the herald's list of its splendours carries a meaning already known from the Sangam poem.

note: Peacocks dance to the clouds' roar here, and in Akananuru 82 the hill is a stage where the peacock is the dancer.
teaches: Both make the hill a stage on which weather and creatures perform together, but the Akananuru names the full orchestra while the epic gives only clouds and peacocks.

note: Akananuru 84 sets a rainbow on the mountain under rain clouds as the season of return; verse 754 uses Indra's broken bow among dark clouds only as a likeness for blossom.
teaches: The same bow-on-the-hill image works as a season marker in the Sangam poem and as a bare comparison here.

note: Akananuru 38 has the ashoka as the lovers' old swing-tree now empty; verse 757 has the ashoka in red pollen and humming bees, likened to adorned youths.
teaches: The ashoka stands for young lovers in both, one time in their absence and one time as their likeness.

note: Akananuru 45 has the lover cross a summer forest with rattling dry pods and a tiger on the waterless track; verse 781 shows the same dry forest, with trees keening like a mourning house.
teaches: The same summer forest is a woman's dread in the Sangam poem and a mourning house in the epic.

note: Purananuru 34 cites dharma as granting expiation (கழுவாய்) for killing cows, destroying unborn children and wronging elders, but none for ingratitude; in Neelakesi 148 the demoness asks expiation for her sins and is told to teach the Jina's path.
teaches: Both assume that grave wrongs admit expiation, but the Sangam maxim treats it as a provision of dharma with exceptions while the Jain sage turns it into a lifelong mission of persuasion.

note: Purananuru 43 praises a Chola as descendant of the king of limitless giving who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk; Neelakesi says no living person asks for another's flesh, eyes or head.
teaches: The gift of one's own flesh to a creature in distress, a dynastic boast in Sangam praise and a credential of compassion for the Buddhist, is denied any worth by the Jain debater's test of need, so Tamil tradition did not hold it as a settled virtue.

note: Perunkoppendu argues for her place on her husband's pyre against the elders who hold her back; Neelakesi 218 cites the wife who burns with her guardian husband as the futile death no one should call virtue.
teaches: The Sangam queen gives the pyre a reason, escape from the widow's diet and gravel bed, that the Jain reductio ignores when it calls such death one that achieves nothing; the two disagree on what the wife's death is for.

note: Given audience by the Chera, Nariveruuthalaiyar asks for nothing and tells him to guard the realm with grace and love; offered jewels, land and treasure, Neelakesi refuses them and tells the king to keep to the path of dharma.
teaches: The visitor who turns a king's favour into counsel persists from bardic to religious poetry, but the counsel shifts from ruling with grace to following a doctrine, and the refusal of gifts becomes a renouncer's mark.

note: A war of men without trickery is proposed; the Pandya Kudumi proclaims dharma to the weak before battle.
teaches: Both limit war, one by limiting means, the other by sparing those who cannot fight.

note: 1207 shows the hero's anger at petty words in his body; Purananuru 72 turns Neduncheliyan's rage at kings who mocked him as young into a vow with named forfeits.
teaches: The Sangam king binds himself in public speech to avenge a taunt, while the epic hero is let burn first and be confirmed by gods afterwards, so anger at a taunt is lawful in both but sanctioned differently.

note: 1233 sets cloud against cloud and sea against sea as two hosts meet; Purananuru 17 sees the Chera king's host as an army like the sea.
teaches: The sea-army that praise sets at rest as a king's glory here meets another sea, and the figure turns from praise into clash.

note: 1355 warns that fleeing warriors will be shunned by women; Purananuru 278 shows a mother who swears to cut off the breast that fed a son she thinks has fled.
teaches: The shame of flight is placed in the women's mouths in both, but the epic's speaker uses it to threaten, while the Sangam mother tests the rumour before she acts.

note: 1380 condemns a fleeing swordsman; Purananuru 278 gives a mother's vow to cut her breast when told her son fled.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows what the epic's taunt costs the one who runs: the family's shame, not only his own.

note: 1395 shows the flood of blood and broken tusks as a spectacle; Purananuru 62 asks what victory there can be when both armies have died.
teaches: Set side by side, the epic dwells on the field's carnage without cost where the Sangam poem measures it by the widows and the empty claim to victory.

note: 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy; Purananuru 227 calls Death a fool that cooked and ate its own seed by taking Valavan.
teaches: The epic shows the king as the agent of his death while the Sangam poet blames Death as an outside foe, so the two poems disagree on who ends a king.

note: 1814 puts a moon-line king under a tall umbrella with cloud-like elephants; Purananuru 3 puts the Pandya under a white umbrella like the full moon.
teaches: The poem makes the moon-line king's umbrella the sign of his kind, as the Sangam poem does for the Pandya, so the herald's king reads as the Pandya of that tradition.

note: Purananuru 73 has the fool who ignored a king's strength as a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; verse 686 has the demander as a fool reaching for the jewel in a cobra's hood.
teaches: Both pictures make provoking the strong a blind mistake, and the epic moves the blame from stumbling to coveting.

note: Both set the regions of the Tamil land together in one country: the four regions mingled here, the tunes and creatures of each region exchanged there.
teaches: Both poems prove a country's wholeness by letting the four regions share each other's things, but the epic only lists them while the Pattupattu ties the mingling to the king's just rule.

note: The Pattupattu's mullai is wild woodland of avarai and kaanthal on a hunters' road ending in a meal of roast game; verse 30 gives the mullai as cropland of sesame, avarai and tuvarai pods.
teaches: The same named tract is a place of hunters' hospitality in the older poem and a place of pod crops in the epic, so the epic poet has turned the mullai from forest road to farmland.

note: In the Pattupattu the fishers sing the kurinji tune, the hill people wear neythal chaplets and the tracts are said to gather under one umbrella; in verse 33 each kind of woman wears the flowers of her own tract.
teaches: Both poems sort a land by its peoples and flowers, but the Sangam poem mixes the tracts to show one king's rule, while the epic keeps each tract's women with her own flower and ends in a catalogue.

note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.

note: Acharakkovai 31 forbids passing between brahmins (பார்ப்பார்) as between gods; Tirumanthiram 231 denies the name of brahmin to those who lack truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion.
teaches: The Acharakkovai's deference attaches to the birth-name with no condition, while the Tirumanthiram makes the name itself depend on inner qualities, so the second would void the rule's deference for a brahmin who lacks them.

note: Acharakkovai 42 treats the menstrual days as days of no touch and sets the twelve days after the bath apart for the wife; Sivavakkiyar 134 says the monthly pollution is what grows into the body once the months stop, so no birth is free of it.
teaches: The ritual rule and the Siddhar's attack both join menstruation to conception, but one draws a line of pollution across the cycle while the other uses the same cycle to deny that any body stands outside pollution.

note: Acharakkovai 5 bars one in எச்சில் from touching brahmins and other sacred things; Sivavakkiyar asks why water in the mouth is called எச்சில் while the Veda churned in the same mouth is not.
teaches: The Siddhar turns the category the Acharakkovai uses to protect the brahmin against the brahmin's own recitation, showing that the purity rule depends on exempting the sacred mouth from it.

note: Acharakkovai 7 classes sexual union and eating as kinds of எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the pure body itself came from எச்சில், and honey and milk are எச்சில் too.
teaches: The Siddhar takes the Acharakkovai's own classing of union as எச்சில் to its end: if union pollutes, every body and every food is born of pollution and the category cannot separate clean from unclean.

note: Acharakkovai 8 bars recitation while in எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the mantra one recites is itself the mouth's எச்சில்.
teaches: One text guards recitation from impurity and the other calls recitation impure in itself, so the rule that protects the mantra is the Siddhar's evidence that purity of the mouth is a fiction.

note: Acharakkovai 90 sets rules toward the பார்ப்பார், from whose hand a cow is not taken, and the புலை, to whom leavings are not held out; Sivavakkiyar asks what a Paraiyar woman and a Brahmin woman are, since no mark on flesh, skin or bone divides them.
teaches: Read against each other, the rule that ranks two birth-groups by what may pass between their hands meets a denial that the body carries any rank, so the purity rule is shown to depend on a mark the Siddhar says is not there.

note: Pattinathar says not to talk of எச்சில் and of fit and unfit, since people do not know where the impurity lies; Innaa 2 counts animals entering a brahmin's house as a pain, on the reading that the pain is ritual defilement.
teaches: The Innaa locates defilement in what crosses a brahmin's threshold, while Pattinathar denies that impurity sits in outward things at all, so the pair shows the purity code and its later Siddha rejection.

note: Nanmanikkadigai ranks the brahmin's birth above all others; the Siddhar verse asks whether a number is marked on flesh or bone to tell a Paraiyar woman from a Brahmin woman.
teaches: Set together, a birth-rank stated as plain fact meets a later denial that birth leaves any mark on the body, showing the claim the ethics work takes for granted being contested.

note: The Siddhar song says forest, rags and begging bowl gain nothing without inner love; Pazhamozhi 339 says the sect's mark is not penance without an even mind.
teaches: Both deny that garb makes the ascetic, but they put different things in its place, love for the Lord in the Siddhar and Jain-style equanimity in Pazhamozhi.

note: The Siddhar verse asks what use ash and bathing are without learning to be born otherwise; the verse ranks worship on the Ganga's bank lowest, below restraint.
teaches: The Siddhar dismisses ritual bathing outright, while the ethics verse keeps Ganga worship as a merit but ranks it beneath restraint of presence and speech.

note: Kannaki cites the Chola who crushed his own son under the chariot for a cow's grief; Pazhamozhi 242 tells the same episode and adds that the worthy had hidden the deed.
teaches: Kannaki uses the episode to shame a king who killed without inquiry; Pazhamozhi makes it a rule about age, so one exemplum serves both as indictment and as maxim.

note: In Akananuru 146 the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for the husband who goes to the courtesans' street; Pazhamozhi 333 sets the same refusal of the bard in four lines and closes it with the proverb that a feigned sleeper cannot be woken.
teaches: The ethics work takes the akam wife's refusal of the bard and turns it into a general judgement, that a husband who strays knowingly is beyond persuasion, where the Sangam poem left the charge in images and pity.

note: Acharakkovai 16 makes the teacher one of five elders to be worshipped as gods; Purananuru 183 says learning is worth serving and paying the teacher, and that learning outweighs both seniority and the order of birth.
teaches: Puram 183 gives the reason for the teacher's place and also cuts against the list: the elder brother the Acharakkovai reveres yields to the wiser younger, and a learned man of the lowest order draws the highest to him.

note: Acharakkovai 83 says those who would live long do not tell the size of the king's army; in Patitruppattu 77 the poet, asked by travellers how large Poraiyan's army is, says he could not count it and describes its elephants.
teaches: Read together, the courtier's rule of silence and the bard's praise give the same answer to the same question: no figure is told, and the bard turns the forbidden number into the uncountable.

note: Purananuru 43 recalls the Chola ancestor who entered the scales for a dove; Elathi 20 praises one who delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb.
teaches: Read with Puram 43, Elathi's simile carries the memory of the king who gave his own flesh: the heroic deed of an ancestor becomes the measure of ordinary giving for anyone.

note: Purananuru 330 praises one man who, sword raised, stopped a king's army from passing him as the shore stops the sea; Iniyavai calls checking the army of great kings in the crowded battle sweet.
teaches: The Purananuru makes the stand one hero's glory, and the counted verse files it with civic zeal and tireless effort, showing heroic memory folded into a general ethic of exertion.

note: In Purananuru 101 Avvai tells her heart that whether Athiyaman's gift is delayed or not it is sure, since he greets her on the hundredth visit as on the first; the Innaa line counts a poet held back by the giver as painful.
teaches: The poem shows the pain the Innaa line names and how it is borne: a patron's constant welcome makes the delay of the poet's send-off endurable.

note: Innaa 9 counts the absence of patrons as the foremost pain of gift-seekers; in Puram 375 a drummer finds no patron but Ay and wishes that, with Ay gone, there be no patrons at all, lest bards praise kings of worthless wealth.
teaches: The bard in the Puram poem prefers the very lack the Innaa ranks first among his pains to service under the ungenerous, which the Innaa counts as a separate pain in its third item.

note: Purananuru 195 tells grey-haired elders in useless age that Death will bind them and urges them at least to refrain from harm; saying 50 says age without knowledge of the next birth is not old age.
teaches: The puram poet shames old men by the coming of Death, while the saying denies them the name of age unless they know what follows death, so the heroic warning about the end becomes a doctrine of rebirth.

note: Purananuru 204 says giving at 'take' is high and refusing a gift is higher still (கொள்ளேன் என்றல் அதனினும் உயர்ந்தன்று); the line says no distinction exceeds giving to those who ask. The tension holds on the plain reading of the line's 'nothing greater'.
teaches: The bard's poem ranks the proud refusal of a gift above the gift, where the ethics line puts the giver at the summit, showing the puram ethic of honour placing the poet's self-respect above the patron's generosity.

note: Purananuru 27 reports as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்) that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives; the line states flatly that heaven is easy for those who desire fame.
teaches: The heroic poem hedges its heaven as something heard and grants it to the man others praise, while the maxim drops the hedge and grants it to the man who wants fame, so the pair shows a court belief hardening into a saying and its condition moving from the poet's praise to the seeker's own desire.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels Killivalavan that in a land of just rule, where the humble can reach the king when they seek முறை, rain comes when sought, and that if he protects his people the unsubmitting will bow; 99 states the bare rule that security needs just order.
teaches: The poem shows to a named Chola what just rule looks like and what it brings, the king reached by the humble and the enemy bowing, and the line reduces the same counsel to a maxim any ruler can carry.

note: Purananuru 192 opens with every town as ours and everyone our kin, as the stance of one who sees through the wise; Nanmanikkadigai says every town belongs to those with something in hand.
teaches: The heroic poem makes belonging everywhere a philosophical stance; the ethics verse observes that wealth secures the same welcome, which sets the ideal against how towns in fact receive people.

note: Purananuru 187 says a land is good only where its men are good; Nanmanikkadigai says kings gain glory by the land they rule.
teaches: The pair runs the credit in opposite directions: the Purananuru makes the land's worth depend on its people, the ethics verse makes the king's glory depend on the land, so his glory rests on men he does not make good himself.

note: Purananuru 39 tells a Chola that, with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his own fame; Pazhamozhi 155 recalls the same Chola feat of the fort in the sky.
teaches: The puram poem treats the hanging fort as inherited glory a descendant cannot claim, while the ethics verse turns it into a lesson anyone can use: the fort fell to force applied by the right means.

note: Purananuru 196, a bard to the Pandya Nanmaran, says that saying yes to what one can and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, while false promises and false refusals wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame.
teaches: The bard's complaint to a king and the ethics verse state the same rule about refusal, which shows the norm of the honest 'no' is older than the ethics works and was first argued from a suppliant's side.

note: Pisirandhaiyar tells the Pandya to take his due like an elephant fed paddy in balls, not one loosed in the field; Pazhamozhi 244 gives the same rule of revenue through the bee that takes and leaves.
teaches: The Sangam poem warns one king of the ruin a greedy collection brings on him and his land; the ethics verse lifts the warning into a general rule of royal taking that should leave no mark at all.

note: Purananuru 290 has a warrior's king give him toddy before drinking himself, and the warrior will take the spear meant for the king; Pazhamozhi 266 turns the toddy already drunk into the reason a king's man cannot shrink from his task.
teaches: Held together they show the heroic custom of the king's toddy hardening into a courtier's proverb of obligation: what the war poem offers as honour freely returned, the ethics verse states as a debt that forbids hesitation.

note: Purananuru 73 has Nalankilli say the fool who scorned him will hardly escape, like a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; Pazhamozhi 281 tells the king's wronged servant not to wake the sleeping tiger by acting on his grievance.
teaches: The pairing shows the same sleeping tiger from both sides: the Chola king boasts of being the tiger that the careless rouse to their death, and the ethics verse teaches the king's own servant to treat that tiger as a standing danger to be left asleep.

note: Purananuru 341 tells of a father who will not give his young daughter even when the king pleads and takes up arms with his tiger-like kin, torn between her wedding tomorrow and death; Pazhamozhi 326 says even the girl's brothers will refuse the king and the only outcome is battle.
teaches: The Sangam poem holds the refusal as a tragic choice and grieves for the town's beauty; the ethics verse keeps the heroic memory but removes the dilemma, so the refusal becomes a fixed rule of a proud house and war the only remedy, said with a kitchen proverb.

note: Purananuru 116 shows Pari's daughters after his fall, in a thorn-fenced hut counting salt carts; Pazhamozhi 381 shows Pari's daughter giving a bard gold in a drought.
teaches: The Purananuru remembers the daughters as the dispossessed; Pazhamozhi keeps one of them as a giver who feeds a bard even when rain fails, so the ethics work turns the elegy of Pari's house into proof that his giving outlived his fortune.

note: Purananuru 142 says Pekan is foolish (மடம்) only in giving, like rain on salt land, never foolish in battle; Pazhamozhi 74 says knowing foolishness (அறிமடம்) is an ornament to the worthy, citing the mantle given to a peacock.
teaches: The puram poem already calls Pekan's giving மடம் and limits it to the gift; the ethics verse adds அறி, knowing, and so makes the patron's folly a chosen virtue rather than a lapse.

note: Purananuru 200 presents Pari's daughters as the children of the man who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper that never sang for him; Pazhamozhi 74 cites the same gift as hearsay of old givers.
teaches: The heroic poem uses the chariot to the creeper to claim a husband for the daughters, while the ethics verse turns the same act into a maxim that knowing folly adorns the worthy, so the patron's deed becomes a proof text.

note: Purananuru 203 tells a king that refusing a returning suppliant with 'you took before' is cruel and that protecting suppliants is his duty; Pazhamozhi 84 says those who took in seekers do not cast them off as worthless.
teaches: The puram poem closes the excuse of past giving and the ethics verse closes the excuse of the seeker's unworthiness, so together they show the protector's duty answering two different pretexts for withdrawal.

note: Purananuru 195 tells aged worthies that the axe-bearing one will bind them, so if they cannot do good they should at least avoid harm; Sirupanchamoolam 25 sets four commands under the certainty of Death's coming.
teaches: Both rest counsel on the certainty of death, but the Sangam poem bargains down to a minimum (at least do no harm) while the ethics verse turns the same ground into four positive and negative rules and adds a reckoning after death.

note: Purananuru 183 says learning is good even at the cost of serving the teacher, giving him wealth and accepting the lower place; Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the true teacher seeks no gain and the fit pupil serves with love.
teaches: The Sangam king accepts payment and service as the price of learning; the Jain verse keeps the pupil's loving service but denies the teacher any gain, and adds that learning without casting off the three faults is a sickness.

note: Purananuru 9 praises a Pandya who warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five who give up in battle and must not be approached.
teaches: The Sangam king protects those who never fight by warning them before battle; the verse protects those who stop fighting during it, so together they give both ends of the period's code of sparing in war.

note: Purananuru 18 urges the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan to build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water win wealth hereafter, sole rule and fame; the verse makes tank-digging one of five works that take any doer to heaven.
teaches: The duty the Sangam poet urged on one king becomes in the ethics work a merit open to any man of means, and the promised reward narrows from rule and fame to heaven.

note: Purananuru 219 addresses a warrior wasting his body as he sits to die, with many sitting with him; the verse counts those who sit facing north among the needy to be fed.
teaches: The act the Puram honours as heroic resolve the Jain ethics verse counts as a state of need beside age and disease, so the dying hero becomes a receiver of care.

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya that those who join water to land give bodies and life; Thirikadugam says one who digs a drinking well without stint gains an undying body.
teaches: The puram poem credits the builder of water works with the lives of his people; the ethics verse credits the well-digger with his own undying body, so the same act of providing water is rewarded outward in one and inward in the other.

note: Porunaratruppadai says Karikalan received his inheritance while still in the womb; Pazhamozhi 239 tells of a Chola's son who survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled justly, a prince tradition identifies as Karikalan.
teaches: If the traditional identification holds, the same accession is told once as a birthright fixed before birth and once as a survival against fire, and the pair shows the ethics work turning a praised royal memory into proof that a living man can still come to anything.

note: Ainkurunuru 44 says the tortoise's young grow by looking at the mother's face; Siddhar 176 says the sea tortoise's eggs take form as the mother thinks of them, and asks when the poet will so reach God.
teaches: The same belief, that the tortoise nurtures without touch, serves the Sangam friend to argue that a wife needs only her husband's presence and the later siddhar to describe grace given by attention alone, so a piece of animal lore carried a model of care at a distance from household love into devotion.

note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.

note: Kuruntokai 0 knows Murugan by his lotus-red feet, the spear that split the mountain and the cock banner, and says his guarding keeps the world safe; Thiruppugazh 323 names the same spear that pierced Krauncha, the cock banner and the golden anklet feet, and asks for release from desire.
teaches: The same three marks of Murugan pass from a guarantee of the whole world's safety in the oldest invocation to one devotee's plea for rescue from his own lust, so the iconography stayed fixed while the god's protection moved from the world to the self.

note: Natrinai 0 builds the discus-bearer's body from the cosmos: earth his feet, sea his garment, sky his body, the quarters his hands, moon and sun his eyes; Tirumanthiram 2774 gives Shiva the same map, space his body, the eight directions his hands, the three lights his three eyes, as he dances.
teaches: The body made of sky, quarters and heavenly lights is a frame older than either sect: the Sangam invocation fills it for the discus-bearer as a fact the Veda reports, and Tirumular fills it for Shiva and sets it dancing with a third eye of fire, so the image passed between gods while its parts stayed fixed.

note: The eloping man in Natrinai 362 vows that if a fight comes he will not fear and will drive it off, but if her kin come he will hide (நுமர் வரின் மறைகுவென்); Pattinathar's antadhi verse 922 gives the hero the same two conditions, hill men he will make food for kites, but if they are her kin he will hide (உமராயின் மறைகுவனே).
teaches: Pattinathar kept not only the eloping lover's boast but its exact limit, courage against strangers and concealment before her family, which shows the devotional kovai inherited the Sangam udanpokku speech as a fixed thurai with its own logic, since striking her kin would undo the marriage the flight is meant to make.

note: Both make the cause of love-sickness its cure; in Kural 1102 the man says the girl is the medicine for the sickness she gives, in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother the lord's chariot is the medicine for the sickness the girl's eyes caught.
teaches: Valluvar states the paradox as the lover's private wonder, while the Sangam friend uses the same paradox as evidence before the mother, so the idea that only the beloved can cure love began as an argument for marriage before it was a maxim of delight.

note: In Kural 1209 the woman's life fails as she dwells on the lack of grace of one who said they were not apart; in Ainkurunuru 109 the friend asks what the many days of his grace were worth now that he has left.
teaches: Valluvar turns the memory of past grace into a slow inward death, while the Sangam friend turns it into a reproach spoken to the mother, so the same memory serves as private lament in the couplet and as public evidence in the decade.

note: In both the wife's shoulders waste and she will not call him cruel; in Ainkurunuru 11 she says he is good while her own shoulders say he is not, in Kural 1236 she is pained that others call him cruel because her shoulders and bangles slacken.
teaches: The Sangam poem sets the accusation inside her own body, against her own words, while Valluvar moves it to other people reading her body, so the couplet's defence of him against outsiders presupposes the older poem's private split between what she says and what her shoulders show.

note: In Kural 1130 the woman says he lives in her heart while this town (இவ் வூர்) says he is loveless and far; in Ainkurunuru 110 the friend says we call him ours while this town (இவ்வூர்) says otherwise, and asks fate to make it so.
teaches: Both set the lovers' word against the town's, but Valluvar's woman rests in her inner certainty while the Sangam friend turns to fate to make the bond public, so the couplet's private comfort appears in the older poem as a demand for marriage.

note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Ainkurunuru 111's woman says she is no performer of hard penance and so could not live apart from him.
teaches: The heroine's disclaimer assumes exactly the Kural's definition of penance as the bearing of suffering, so the pair shows that the endurance of separation was already counted as an ascetic feat, and that the lover's refusal of it is a refusal of tapas.

note: Both are the woman's own words: Kural 1257 says she knows nothing called modesty when the beloved does what love wants; Ainkurunuru 112 tells her modest heart they have forgotten, as they wait to see him come.
teaches: The Kural's general claim that shame vanishes before love is shown in the poem as a single moment, the heroine speaking to the heart that owns modesty just as she gives it up to watch him arrive.

note: Both pair the town's gossip with the mother's word: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and mother's words water to this sickness; in Ainkurunuru 113 the town names her the lord's woman, mother calls her, and she says it is only a fever (வெம்மை).
teaches: The Kural calls the love a sickness that gossip and the mother feed, and the poem shows the girl turning that very likeness into her alibi, naming the fever and hiding its cause, so the couplet's metaphor began as the lover's cover story.

note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.

note: Kural 1235 has the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel man (கொடியார் கொடுமை); in Ainkurunuru 117 the woman says it is cruel (கொடிதே) that beauty comes to this in those who do not forget him.
teaches: The friend in the Kural lays the cruelty on the man, while the heroine in the poem lays it on the condition of loving him, so the same lost beauty is a charge against him from outside and a lament without an accused from within.

note: Kural 1284: she went to sulk, but her heart forgot it and went to unite; Ainkurunuru 118: she went meaning to rage at the unjust man and hold him back, but thought again, relented and came away.
teaches: Both women set out angry and lose the anger on the way, but the Kural's anger turns into union while the Sangam heroine's turns into retreat, so a failed quarrel need not end in an embrace: it can end in pity and silence.

note: Kural 1265 wishes to see the கொண்கன் with full eyes so that the pallor of her soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) may leave; Ainkurunuru 120 reports that her soft shoulders (மெல் தோளே) have become beautiful because the lord has come.
teaches: The Kural states as a hope that the sight of the shore lord will cure the shoulders, and the Ainkurunuru records the cure as done, so the couplet's optative has an older poem in which the wish was already fulfilled.

note: In Ainkurunuru 131 the woman says the lord's friendship is good only while no gossip rises in the town; in Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is the manure on which her love-sickness grows.
teaches: Valluvar's woman turns the gossip into nourishment for her love, while the Sangam woman, speaking to the man's bard, treats the same gossip as the limit the bond cannot outlive, so the couplet's paradox rewrites a fear the older poem left plain.

note: Both have the woman's bangled shoulders lose their beauty when her partner leaves (Kural: துணைநீங்கித் தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்; Ainkurunuru: பிரிந்தெனப் புல்லென்றன என் புரிவளைத் தோளே).
teaches: The couplet describes the wasted shoulders as a fact, while the poem puts them as a helpless question to the absent man's own bard, so the same bodily sign becomes in the older poem a complaint lodged with his side of the household.

note: In Kural 1265 the woman wishes to see her husband (கொண்கனை) and says the pallor of her shoulders will then leave; in Ainkurunuru 134 she tells the bard her dark-gold beauty has come back with the chariot of the shore lord (கொண்க).
teaches: Valluvar states as a wish that only the sight of the husband will cure the pallor; the Sangam poem shows the cure already happened, the beauty arriving in his chariot, so the couplet's claim that news is not enough rests on the older scene of the bodily return.

note: Ainkurunuru 14 praises the chest of the ford-town lord for its softness that gives cool sleep; Naladiyar 389's wife of the field-town lord looks at the same chest smeared with sandal by other women's breasts.
teaches: The marutham husband's chest is the wife's place of rest in the Sangam poem and the evidence of his other women in the Naladiyar, so the later moralist turns the older image of comfort into the record of its betrayal.

note: In Kural 1157 the woman says her slipping bangles spread the news that the shore lord (துறைவன்) has left her; in Ainkurunuru 140 she asks the bard to tell the lord of the ford (துறைகெழு கொண்கன்) the state of her bangles since he left.
teaches: Valluvar makes the bangles themselves the gossips who publish his departure, while the Sangam woman needs the bard to carry that sign to the man, so the couplet's bangles that speak for themselves compress a scene in which the body's testimony still had to be delivered.

note: Ainkurunuru 142's heroine resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep; in Kural 1207 the woman says she does not know how to forget and asks what would become of her if she did.
teaches: The Sangam heroine treats not-thinking as a cure she can choose for her sleeplessness, while Valluvar's woman declares forgetting impossible and fatal, so the couplet denies exactly the resolve the older poem lets her voice.

note: In Kural 1188 people say only that she has grown pale and never that he has left; in Ainkurunuru 145 the friend says the shore lord has now taken her pallor away.
teaches: The friend names the man as the one who can remove the pallor, which makes him its cause, so the Sangam poem supplies the very attribution that the couplet's woman complains no one makes.

note: Both are spoken to the man about to leave, by the friend on one reading of the Kural: Ainkurunuru 149 asks him not to become able to go after causing her affliction, Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return only to those who will survive it.
teaches: The Sangam friend still appeals to the man's character, asking him not to be the kind who can leave, whereas the couplet has given up persuasion and answers his promise with the threat of her death.

note: Ainkurunuru 150's heroine calls the shore lord bitter in union (புணர்வின் இன்னான்) and hard to unite with; in Kural 1152 the woman says union now holds pain for fear of parting.
teaches: Valluvar gives the reason the Sangam poem leaves implicit, that union turns bitter because parting is foreseen, while the poem's pun of the ever-embracing wave (புணரி) shows what that bitterness is measured against.

note: Both are the woman speaking of her heart against the man in oodal: the couplet says the heart's anger is false because it yields at the sight of him; Ainkurunuru 151 grants that the heart has already melted and refuses all the same.
teaches: The couplet treats a heart that yields as proof the quarrel was never real, while the poem keeps the refusal standing after the heart has gone over, so the Sangam woman's oodal is a decision of will against her own feeling rather than a mood that the man's presence dissolves.

note: Same situation and speaker: the woman of the shore says the lord of the ford (துறைவன்) has left her and her bangles slip from her forearm; the Kural keeps the Ainkurunuru's words துறைவன், துற, முன்கை, இறை and வளை.
teaches: The couplet lifts a neythal formula whole, but gives the bangles a new office: in the Ainkurunuru they imitate his desertion, in the Kural they broadcast it like gossip, so the later poet turned the body from mirror of the man into witness to the town.

note: The Kural tells friends to read a painful act of an old friend as folly or deep intimacy; the heroine of 167 calls the man who promised grace and gave none an old companion, தொல் கேள்.
teaches: The heroine applies the ethics book's rule of old friendship inside love, and the poem shows its cost: the same rule that keeps a long bond alive lets a broken promise go unanswered, so the wronged side carries the whole duty of forbearance.

note: In both the woman has accepted the man's part with her mind, in Kural 1181 by consenting to his absence, in 169 by knowing the truth of his heart, and still the pallor spreads on her.
teaches: The couplet makes her consent the reason she cannot complain of her pallor, and the Ainkurunuru adds that even trust in his heart does not stop it, so pallor in this tradition is a bodily fact beyond the will rather than a charge against the man.

note: On the plain reading the claims are incompatible: in 170 the woman holds up her pallid eyes as evidence against the friend's word that he is good, while in Kural 1190 she would rather be called pallid than have the friend blame his unkindness.
teaches: Read together, the two show the heroine taking the side opposite to whoever speaks to her, so her pallor is not a fixed verdict on the man but an argument she turns against his praise or for his defence as the friend's stance requires.

note: Both have the man in secret love say the girl keeps his eyes from sleep at night: Ainkurunuru 172 likens his wakefulness to the never-resting waves of Thondi; Kural 1136 has him, sleepless at midnight, think of riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 172 stops at the sleepless night and gives it the image of the restless sea, while the Kural shows where that night leads, to the threat of the madal, so the pair marks sleeplessness as the stage of love just before shame is given up.

note: Both have the man name the girl's power with the word அணங்கு: in Kural 1081 he cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Ainkurunuru 173 her fragrant hair is the அணங்கு and those it seizes lose their sleep.
teaches: The Kural leaves the smitten man's question open, and the Sangam poem answers it not by settling what she is but by the symptom, sleepless nights and a cutting pain, so that in the tradition the afflicting goddess is known by what she does to the one who sees her.

note: In both the wife recalls that he promised not to leave (பிரியலென், அஞ்சல்) and then left; Ainkurunuru 18 ends on her weeping eyes and the question, Kural 1154 asks whether those who believed his assuring words are at fault.
teaches: The Sangam wife quotes his broken promise as an accusation, while Valluvar's wife turns it into a question of blame for having believed, so the couplet adds to the older scene a moral reckoning about trust that the poem leaves unasked.

note: Kural 1150 says the town raises the very talk we want and the lover will grant (நல்குவர்) if he wishes; Ainkurunuru 181 says if the shore lord grants (நல்கின்), this clamouring town will be sweet to live in.
teaches: The Kural names the town's clamour as a lever that can push the lover to grant marriage, and the Ainkurunuru poem shows the far side of that lever: once he grants, the same noise becomes the festive kuravai of a town she can live in happily, so gossip and celebration are one sound judged before and after his word.

note: Kural 1225's woman asks what good she has done the morning and what wrong the evening, so morning is the friendly hour; Ainkurunuru 183 ends that even if morning comes there is no one to clear her pain.
teaches: The Kural's separated woman still has a kind hour in the morning, while the Ainkurunuru heroine denies even that, so the pair shows two degrees of the same grief: one that rises and falls with the day, and one that the day's turn no longer touches.

note: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and blooms at evening; in Ainkurunuru 183 evening arrives early in the harsh day while the neythal of the backwater closes.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for evening pain gains a real flower in the Sangam poem, and the two move in opposite directions: as the shore's neythal closes at evening, the sickness opens, so the landscape's hour of rest is the lover's hour of full bloom of pain.

note: Kural 1171's woman asks why her eyes weep when it was they who showed him to her; Ainkurunuru 190's woman says the lord of the shore surely is the one who made her eyes weep.
teaches: For the same tears the Kural's woman blames her own eyes for having looked, while the Ainkurunuru woman blames the man with an emphatic மன்ற, so the pair shows the two directions in which the abandoned lover can turn the fault, inward on her own seeing or outward on him.

note: The Kural man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Ainkurunuru man knows she is a shore girl and says she is harder to win than the mountain nymphs (வரையர மகளிரின் அரியள்).
teaches: The likeness to a goddess can carry two different fears: in the couplet it is bewilderment at what she is, in the shore poem it is despair of reaching her, so the divine comparison in akam measures distance as often as beauty.

note: Both have the woman of the shore say her bangles registered the lord's leaving (தணந்தமை ... உணர்ந்த வளை; பிரிந்தென நெகிழ்ந்தன); Ainkurunuru 192 adds that they have grown tight again (வீங்கின).
teaches: The Kural treats the bangle only as an early witness of separation, while the Ainkurunuru poem shows it registering his return as well, so the convention is a two-way gauge of the man's presence and not merely a sign of wasting.

note: Both men say the bangled girl has given them suffering, with the verb of a gift (துயரம் நல்கி; தந்தாள் ... துயர்); in the Kural the gift is the palmyra horse and the evening's pain, in Ainkurunuru 195 a grief that will not pass and lost sleep.
teaches: Read together they show the stages of the same plea to the friend: the Ainkurunuru man stops at sleeplessness, and the couplet shows where his complaint goes next if no one answers it, to the threat of riding the palmyra horse.

note: In the Kural the slipping bangles spread the news (தூற்றா) that the lord of the shore has left; in Ainkurunuru 199 the woman names him by the bangles he loosened and asks to climb the high dune to gaze at his land.
teaches: The couplet's woman fears her bangles will publish the loss to the town, while the Ainkurunuru woman makes the loss her name for him and climbs where all can see her looking, so the same token can be suffered as exposure or claimed in the open.

note: In both the wife's bangles slip from her wrist because of the man; in Ainkurunuru 20 they loosen as she thinks of him, in Kural 1157 they broadcast that he has left.
teaches: The Sangam poem treats the slipping bangle as the private effect of memory, while Valluvar makes the same bangle a gossip that announces his desertion to everyone, so the couplet turns an inner sign into public scandal.

note: Both turn on assurance (தெளிப்பவும், தெளித்தசொல்): in Ainkurunuru 21 the friend sets the man's assurances against the girl's paling eyes; in Kural 1154 the woman asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The Kural asks who bears the blame once a trusted promise fails, while the Ainkurunuru shows the body already failing while the promise is still being spoken, so the couplet's moral question comes after a doubt that the older poem places in the girl's eyes before any leaving.

note: Ainkurunuru 212: the girl asks why they should be parted from a man of virtue (அறவன்). Kural 1154: the woman asks whether those who trusted the assurances of the one who said 'do not fear' are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The girl rests her whole security on the man's being virtuous, while the Kural imagines that very assurer leaving and moves the blame onto him, so the pair shows that in secret love the only guarantee was his character and the Kural tests it to the point of failure.

note: Ainkurunuru 213: the girl says she can live only if he comes. Kural 1263: the wife says she still lives on the longing for her husband's return from war.
teaches: For the wife the longing for return is already enough to keep her alive, while the unmarried girl says life itself waits on his coming, so the pair grades the same dependence: hope sustains in marriage, only presence sustains in secret love.

note: Ainkurunuru 215: at evening the bee hums sweeter than the musicians' flute, and those who leave then will do worse. Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon.
teaches: The Kural makes the evening flute itself the weapon, while the Ainkurunuru keeps the music sweet and turns its sweetness into the measure of the leaver's cruelty, so together they show evening music wounding the parted woman not by harshness but by sweetness heard alone.

note: Ainkurunuru 217: the friend asks why the girl pales even though the man keeps coming. Kural 1187: the woman says pallor came on her thickly the moment she turned a little in his embrace.
teaches: The friend's puzzle, pallor despite his visits, finds its answer in the Kural's hyperbole that the least gap in union breeds pallor, so the pair shows that secret visits, each ending in parting, feed the pallor rather than cure it.

note: Ainkurunuru 218: throbbing eyes and tightening bangles promise his coming. Kural 1203: a sneeze that starts and dies away makes the woman fear he began to think of her and stopped.
teaches: Both women read the absent man in involuntary signs of their own bodies, but the girl's signs come to completion and promise him while the Kural's sneeze aborts and suggests his forgetting, so the pair shows the same bodily sign-language turned to hope or doubt.

note: Ainkurunuru 219: the friend asks why the girl's forehead pales since the hill man went away. Kural 1188: the woman complains that people say she has grown pale, and no one says that he left her.
teaches: The friend's question names the man's leaving together with the pallor, which is exactly the acknowledgement the Kural's woman says the world withholds, so the pair shows the friend as the one voice that ties the girl's pallor to the man who caused it.

note: Kural 1156 says that a man who can speak of leaving leaves no hope; Ainkurunuru 221 shows the heroine's beauty fading at the quoted word செல்வல், before any journey begins.
teaches: The couplet judges the announcement as a moral sign of hardness, while the poem shows it working on the body at once, so together they make the spoken intention, not the absence, the first wound of parting in Tamil love poetry.

note: Kural 1188 says people call her pale but no one says he left her; Ainkurunuru 225 asks whether the lover himself does not perceive the paling of her brow.
teaches: Held together they show the pallor seen by the whole town yet unread by the one man it concerns, so the symptom that exposes her to gossip fails at the only task she wants of it, reaching him.

note: Kural 1155 asks the friend to prevent the departure of the man fit for her, since union is hard once he goes; Ainkurunuru 228 asks what becomes of their life if he leaves without having pleaded for favour.
teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: in secret love the man's suit must pass through the friend, so the heroine's plea that the friend stop his leaving is a plea that she accept his pleading.

note: Kural 1265 says the pallor of her shoulders will leave once she has seen her husband her eyes' fill; in Ainkurunuru 229 the friend sees the brow's golden beauty returned and asks whether he came in the night.
teaches: The couplet makes the lover's presence the cure for pallor, and the poem turns that rule into a means of detection, so the cure that the heroine longs for is also what betrays her secret meeting to the friend.

note: Kural 1213's woman says she lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; in Ainkurunuru 234 the friend tells the lover that the girl sees his chest in dreams and not awake, and that is why she pales.
teaches: The same split between dream and waking presence is the woman's own comfort in the Kural and the friend's evidence of harm in the Sangam poem, so the couplet's consolation is shown to be what an onlooker reads as wasting, and the dream becomes a lever for marriage rather than a way to live.

note: Ainkurunuru 24 says he takes the beauty (நலங்கொண்டு) of the women he embraced and abandons them; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns the friend's accusation of plain taking into an exchange in which pallor is the payment, so the same loss that the Sangam friend calls the act of a kin-destroying creature becomes, in the couplet, the woman's own bitter bookkeeping.

note: Both use the belief that the crab is killed by its own young: Ainkurunuru 24 names the crab born at its mother's death (தாய்சாப் பிறக்கும்), Sirupanchamoolam 10 lists its own brood as death to the crab (ஞெண்டிற்குத் தன்பார்ப்பு).
teaches: The pairing shows a piece of field lore surviving from the akam landscape into the didactic list: the Sangam friend uses it to charge a man with destroying his own, while the later moralist uses it to say a thing's own offspring or speech is its death, so the same belief turned from accusation of another into warning to oneself.

note: Both say the man's chest belongs to many women: Ainkurunuru 25's friend says the ooran's chest (மார்புபலர்க்கு) brings grief to many; Kural 1311's wife refuses his chest (மார்பு) because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The friend counts the cost to the many women his chest has harmed, while the Kural wife refuses that chest because it is shared even by looks, so held together they show the same charge of a common chest used first as report to the mother and then as the wife's own ground for refusal.

note: Both have the man, on seeing the girl, take her for an அணங்கு (Kural: அணங்குகொல்; Ainkurunuru: ஆர் அணங்கினளே).
teaches: Valluvar's man hesitates between goddess, peahen and woman, while the Sangam man has settled the question and pins it on her youth (இளையள் ஆயினும்), so the couplet's doubt is a refinement of an older certainty that a hill girl can be a striking power.

note: In both the friend (on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural) speaks to the man who is about to leave, to hold him back.
teaches: The couplet holds the man back with a threat that she will not live, while the Sangam friend holds him back with the girl's worth, a daughter begged from the god, so the pair shows two arguments for the same refusal: her death against her value.

note: Both are spoken by the woman about the pallor that the man's presence will remove: Kural 1265 wishes to see him and says the pallor will then leave; Ainkurunuru 263 says he has come and her beauty has come back.
teaches: The Sangam poem gives as an accomplished fact, in two verbs set side by side, what the couplet can only promise, showing the restored beauty as the very event of his arrival rather than its later result.

note: Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; Ainkurunuru 278 says the lord gave a sickness never forgotten and took the beauty onlookers never tired of.
teaches: Valluvar keeps only the exchange as the woman's own complaint, while the Sangam poem sets it in an image of a bamboo springing back like a rod that has landed a fish, which shows the taking and the man's unharmed recoil that the couplet's bare bargain leaves out.

note: Both mark the loss in the shoulders and the slipping bangle: Ainkurunuru 28 has the bright bangle loosening as the soft shoulders pale (ஒண்டொடி நெகிழ, மென் தோள் பசப்பது); Kural 1234 has the bangle slipping from shoulders that have lost their old beauty.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru friend uses the paled shoulders to tell the mother that a man, not the ford goddess, is the cause, while the Kural keeps only the signs, so the couplet's portrait of wasting shoulders was in the older poem a piece of evidence in a disclosure.

note: Both have the friend (for Parimelazhagar in the Kural) speak to the man about to part: Kural 1151 refuses his promise of a quick return, saying tell it to those who will be alive; Ainkurunuru 285 asks how he can part and leave her here with her bangles slipping.
teaches: The Kural states the friend's refusal as a bare threat to the girl's life, while the Sangam poem sets the same refusal in the girl's daily field life and names the visible sign, the slipping bangle, so the Kural's abstract 'those who will be alive' is shown as wasting already begun.

note: Both have the girl hold to the man's goodness while her pallor spreads: in Kural 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits yet pallor comes; in Ainkurunuru 286 she says he seems to have loved her without blemish yet takes her beauty.
teaches: In both the girl refuses to blame the man and lays the loss elsewhere, on the pallor as a cheat in the Kural and on his love itself in the Sangam poem, so the pair shows a fixed rule of her speech: the waste of her beauty is never his fault in her own mouth.

note: Kural 101 says that help given unasked cannot be repaid by earth and heaven together; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man, knowing the good of the parrots' help, asks his heart what he can do in return.
teaches: The Kural's unrepayable help is a deliberate kindness, while the parrots helped without knowing or meaning it, so the lover's echo of the gratitude maxim stretches it to an unintended benefit and makes the debt even less payable, since the helpers cannot know they are owed.

note: Both have the man in love rank a small favour of the beloved above the highest good: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep in her soft arms; Ainkurunuru 290 says parrots merely looked at and shooed by the hill girl are more fortunate than a just king.
teaches: The Kural sets union against heaven, while the Sangam poem sets far less, a glance and a shooing given to birds, against a righteous kingdom, so the pair shows the measure working at both ends: even the least share of her notice outweighs the highest worldly good.

note: Both have the woman speak of her heart that has gone after the man: in Ainkurunuru 295 she wonders whether the heart that went with the hill man will come back or settle there; in Kural 1248 she calls her heart foolish for following the one who left, pining that he will not show grace.
teaches: The Kural judges the following heart a fool because the man has gone and withholds his grace, while the Ainkurunuru girl, with no doubt of him, only wonders whether her heart will return, so the pair shows that the same act of the heart going after the man is not folly in itself and is judged by how the man answers it.

note: Both give the man the same words for constancy: Kural 1125 உள்ளுவன் ... மறப்பறியேன், answering the friend who asks whether he remembers; Ainkurunuru 298 உள்ளுபு மறந்தறியேமே, said of a girl who shows him no grace.
teaches: The Kural's joke that he cannot remember what he never forgets answers a doubt about absence, while the Ainkurunuru sets the same claim against her coldness, so together they show the man's never-forgetting was the stock answer to both doubts the friend tests him with: will he stay away, and will he give up if she is unkind.

note: Both have the man say the blue water-lily (குவளை) cannot match the girl's eyes: Ainkurunuru 299 says the lily of her own hill spring can hardly open as her eyes do, and Kural 1114 that the lily, if it could see, would bow its head ashamed.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru states the defeat of the lily as a plain fact of the girl's own hill, and the Kural gives the lily sight and a modest bowed head, so the pair shows the Kural's conceit growing out of the akam habit of measuring the hill girl against her land's flowers, with the lily now made to act out her own modesty.

note: Kural 1151 refuses any promise of quick return and asks only whether he is leaving; Ainkurunuru 302 grants that his work for wealth has its own right and argues only that the woman has an equal one.
teaches: Read together they show the friend's dissuasion in two registers, the couplet's flat ultimatum of death and the poem's balanced concession of rights, so the Kural's line is an extreme the Sangam friend reaches only after first admitting the claim of wealth.

note: Kural 64 makes the gruel stirred by children's small hands sweeter than amrita; Ainkurunuru 309 asks whether wealth gained across the waste is sweeter than an unborn son's smile.
teaches: The couplet's household ranking of children above every delicacy becomes, in the friend's mouth, a direct argument against the wealth journey, showing that the Kural's measure of sweetness was already a tool for weighing a husband's absence against his family.

note: Both blessings are said by the woman to a thing of nature that governs her sight of the man who has left: the Kural blesses the moon on condition that it not set (படாஅதி வாழி மதி); Ainkurunuru 312 blesses the hill that has already hidden him (மறைத்த குன்றே).
