teaches: The Kural's blessing is a bargain for sight, while the Sangam woman blesses the hill after it has hidden him, so her wish can only be for what the hill will do to him on the way, which shows the blessing turning from her own need to his safety.

note: In both the woman's heart has followed the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்; இறந்தோர் தேஎத்துச் சென்ற நெஞ்சம்); the Kural calls it a fool, Ainkurunuru 317 asks the friend why it is so slow to come back.
teaches: The Kural judges the heart's going as folly, but the Ainkurunuru woman takes the going for granted and worries about the heart's delay, so the same flight of the heart becomes, in the older poem, a second absence that mirrors the man's.

note: Both state the same sign of separation on the same body part: the broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்; பணைநீங்கி) waste and the bangles slip once the partner is gone.
teaches: The Kural gives the slipping bangle as a plain effect of the partner's absence, while the Ainkurunuru woman names the departed men as those who killed her longing, so the poem shows the bodily sign being used as an accusation, which the couplet's general statement leaves out.

note: Both turn on the woman's own inability to forget (மறப்பறியேன்; மறவா நம்மே); the Kural asks what would become of her if she forgot, Ainkurunuru 319 asks whether he has forgotten her.
teaches: The Kural keeps the question inside her (remembering burns, forgetting would kill), while the Sangam poem turns the same constancy outward into a charge against him, so read together they show the two directions the claim 'I do not forget' could be pointed.

note: The Kural's man says the fire she gives burns when he moves away from her (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம்); Ainkurunuru 322's man, far from her on the summer road, says the thought of her makes the burning path cool (தண்ணிய).
teaches: Held together they give opposite laws for distance: in the couplet absence from her is the source of heat, while in the desert poem absence is already given and her remembered presence is the only coolness, so whether she burns or cools depends on whether the man is measuring his desire or the land.

note: The Kural's man says love is sweeter than toddy because merely thinking of it brings unfailing joy; in Ainkurunuru 325 the man says the scorching waste does not harm him because he has her nature as companion.
teaches: The couplet states that remembered love never fails to give joy, and the Ainkurunuru puts that claim to a hard test, the peopleless summer waste, where the memory works as a travelling companion (துணை), so the maxim gains a situation in which its truth is a matter of survival.

note: Both have the woman's foolish heart following the man who has left (Ainkurunuru: பேதை நெஞ்சம் பின்செல; Kural: பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு).
teaches: With the same words the couplet blames her own heart for going after an unkind man, while the Sangam wife lets the heart go and blames the man as harder than stone, so the following heart was an image that could lay the fault on either lover.

note: In both the wife, parted from her man, speaks of the evening: the Kural asks the evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru 339 asks whether evening exists in the land he went to.
teaches: The couplet gives evening a hard partner of its own, and the Sangam wife supposes his land has no evening at all, so the pair shows the same assumption from two sides: evening is the hour that should force lovers together, and only an absent or hard-hearted partner escapes it.

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven for those who pine with their eyes on the day of return (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு); Ainkurunuru 350 is spoken on that day, the time he named, and he has not come.
teaches: The couplet measures the waiting before the fixed day as the long part, while the poem shows the fixed day arriving empty, so the Kural's pain has a limit that the Ainkurunuru woman has already passed, when waiting no longer has a date to count toward.

note: In Kural 1170 the woman says her eyes would not swim in a flood of tears if they could go to him as her heart does; in Ainkurunuru 358 the eyes, which have become a flood however often they are wiped, will not let him stay away long.
teaches: The couplet makes the flood of tears a sign of the eyes' helplessness, bound to the house while the heart travels, whereas the Sangam poem turns that same flood into a power that pulls him back, so the tears are complaint in one and pledge of return in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 36 says that if he forgets them, they too could forget and be content, were it not that her eyes go pale; Kural 1207 has the woman say she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
teaches: The Sangam speaker claims forgetting is in her power and lays the failure on her paling eyes, while the Kural woman denies she can forget at all, so the older poem places love's hold in the body against the will and the couplet moves it into the mind itself.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, the eye and the doe all in the young woman's look; Ainkurunuru 361 grants the eyes are fierce, then ranks her breasts fiercer and her shoulders fiercer still.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the first sight puts all the deadliness in the look, and the Ainkurunuru poet answers that the eyes are only the first and mildest weapon, which shows the old akam poets could treat the same stricken lover as half joking where the couplet keeps him grave.

note: Kural 1081: on first sight the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels; Ainkurunuru 363: the man tells the hunters' sister that what she calls freckles (சுணங்கு) his stricken heart calls a goddess (அணங்கு).
teaches: Where the couplet leaves the goddess as one of three guesses about the whole woman, 363 pins the striking power on one small mark she herself thinks a blemish, so the pair shows the anangu is not in her but in the gap between how she sees herself and how he is struck.

note: In Kural 1151 the friend tells the departing man to promise a quick return only to those who will still be alive; in Ainkurunuru 368 the friend invites him to stay and enjoy the cool summer with them if the girl is not to be ruined.
teaches: Both hold the girl's life against the journey, but the couplet does it by refusing his comfort and 368 by tempting him with the season's pleasure, so together they show the two strategies of the friend who would stop a departure, the bitter and the sweet, around the same threat.

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says she saw him on one day only and the gossip has spread like the snake seizing the moon; in Ainkurunuru 369 the friend tells the man that his tryst of yesterday (நெருநல்) is already louder in the town's mouth than the seasonal koel.
teaches: Both measure a single meeting against a public noise, the eclipse in the couplet and the koel's cry in 369, and holding them together shows the alar topic's fixed shape: the smaller and more recent the secret, the larger the natural event the gossip is said to outdo.

note: Ainkurunuru 37 has நயந்தோர் உண்கண் பசந்துபனி மல்க, the eyes of those who loved him pale and brimming; Kural 1232 has நயந்தவர் ... பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண், pale eyes streaming that seem to tell of the beloved's unkindness.
teaches: Valluvar keeps the Ainkurunuru's very words for the pale, wet eyes but changes their office: in the Sangam poem they are evidence the wronged woman cites against his lying oath, in the couplet they become speakers that publish his unkindness to others, so the image moves from accusation to involuntary gossip.

note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common pond (பழனம்). Kural 1311: the wife refuses her husband's chest because all women feast on it in common with their eyes.
teaches: The fear the Ainkurunuru girls voice before marriage, that his chest may become common property, is the very charge the Kural's wife brings in a sulk after it, so the two show the marutham husband's straying anticipated as a danger and then turned into a reason to refuse him.

note: Both say the lute is outdone by one's child: Kural 66 that only those who have not heard their children's prattle call the lute sweet; Ainkurunuru 410 that the bard's lute did not match the hour when the son rode on his father's chest.
teaches: The Kural's maxim has a scene behind it in which the lute is actually playing in the courtyard while the child plays, so the comparison was first a judgment between two pleasures heard together, and the child's worth lay in the whole family hour, not in speech alone.

note: The Naladiyar says the passing joy of youth is not found among the wise; the Ainkurunuru hero says youth spent together is sweet and the union is sweet now.
teaches: Both accept that youth passes, but the Naladiyar draws from that fact a duty to withhold delight, while the Sangam hero draws from it a reason to spend youth in shared pleasure, so the same premise yields opposite counsel in the old love poetry and the later ascetic quatrains.

note: The Kural's man says an embrace no breeze can part is sweet to two who love; the Ainkurunuru hero asks if his wife, who held him close against her breasts (மாண்முலை அடைய முயங்கியோயே), is a woman of the sky.
teaches: The Kural names the close embrace as a pleasure common to all lovers, but the Ainkurunuru hero, after absence, finds the same embrace so beyond the human that he takes his own wife for a celestial, so the general sweetness is shown as wonder when it is regained.

note: The Kural's man says the bond between him and the girl is like that of body and life; the Ainkurunuru hero speaks of their faultless bond as lives mingled into one (உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய).
teaches: The Kural states the life-bond as a lover's private claim, while the Ainkurunuru hero, past a parting, finds it acted out by the scrub's mating beasts and makes the couple the measure of them, so the general likeness gains a witness in the season of return.

note: In both the wife refuses the straying husband's chest: in Ainkurunuru 42 the friend reports it to him as if it were joy-drunk folly; in Kural 1311 the wife herself refuses it because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The refusal of the chest was a recognised act of the sulking wife before Valluvar; the Sangam friend presents it with mock surprise to shame the man, while the Kural gives the wife her own reason, so the couplet supplies the motive that the older poem leaves to irony.

note: Both dissuade the man from leaving, in the friend's voice on Parimelazhagar's reading of the couplet: the Kural argues from her survival, 423 from the rain already falling and her filled eyes.
teaches: The two show that the dissuasion of a departure had two set arguments, the season and her life, and the Kural keeps only the harsher second, while the Ainkurunuru friend leans on the order of the seasons that a man who leaves in the rains breaks.

note: Both set the home feast against the king's war: the couplet says let the king fight and win and let us feast at evening; 442 says if the king's war subsides she will receive guests in plenty.
teaches: The poem names whose feast the couplet's விருந்து is, the wife as hostess of guests and mother of a son, so the couplet's private wish is shown to be the restoration of a whole household that the king's war holds in suspense.

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty (தொல்கவின்) and the bangles slip; Ainkurunuru 455: the shoulders, their bangles loosened, have lost their old beauty (தொன்னலம்) just as the rains begin that stop the kings' war.
teaches: The couplet states the wasting of the shoulders as the general mark of separation; the Ainkurunuru poem times it to the rains that end the campaign, so the slipping bangle becomes evidence that he is overdue, not only that he is away.

note: Kural 1231: thinking of him who went far, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers; Ainkurunuru 458: the rain-beaten kondrai flowers have come to resemble her eyes, which lost their beauty when he left.
teaches: The couplet's eyes lose a contest with flowers they once outshone; the Ainkurunuru poem reverses the direction, bringing the flowers down to the state of the eyes, so the wasted eyes become the measure the season is read by.

note: Kural 1265: once she has seen her husband to her eyes' fill the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave; Ainkurunuru 459: she asks whether she can embrace his chest so the pallor of her shoulders goes, while he is away with the king.
teaches: Both name the husband's presence as the cure for pallor, but the couplet makes the cure sight while the Ainkurunuru wife makes it embrace and doubts it is possible at all, because the king's war, not the man, decides when he comes.

note: Both have the waiting woman put a question to or about evening: the Kural asks evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru asks whether his land has this loveless evening at all.
teaches: The Kural explains the man's calm by a hard heart that evening shares, the Ainkurunuru by a land the evening may not reach, so the two give the waiting woman two answers to why he does not suffer the hour she suffers.

note: Both set the king's war against the home feast in the man's mouth: the Kural lets the king win and the man feast at evening with his wife; Ainkurunuru says one more day with the victorious king would be an age.
teaches: The Kural states the two duties as a calm pair of wishes, while the Sangam poem shows the strain inside that balance, since the king's victory is honoured in a line and then a single day of further service is weighed as an aeon.

note: The Kural's woman says he went away with his resolve as companion (உள்ளம் துணையாக) and she lives only by longing for his return; 496's friend says he has come back to be the companion of her shoulders (தோள் துணையாக).
teaches: The word துணை marks the turn of the plot: the reproach that he chose his resolve as companion over her is answered on his return, when the companionship is given back to her as embrace, so the Kural's complaint is a stage the akam story expects to close.

note: The Kural's woman says the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only once she has seen him to her eyes' fill; 498 says her shoulders have regained their beauty because he came.
teaches: The Kural states as the woman's own condition that only his presence cures the pallor, and 498 shows that condition met and observed from outside, item by item on her body, so the couplet's claim is confirmed as the accepted course of the return.

note: Kural 1303 says that not embracing the one who sulks is like adding pain to those already in distress; Ainkurunuru 50 tells the husband who gives no refuge that the household and they suffer, and his wife weeps too.
teaches: The Kural states the cost of withheld grace for one sulking woman, while the Ainkurunuru friend counts it across the whole household, its wealth and its people, so the older poem makes the husband's refusal a failure of the house and not only of love.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Ainkurunuru 55 the friend tells the man that because he desired her beauty and left her, her brow has paled for many to see.
teaches: The Kural keeps the exchange of beauty for pallor as the woman's private complaint, while the Ainkurunuru friend turns the same exchange into public evidence held up to the man, so the pallor that is a lament in the couplet becomes an accusation in the town.

note: Kural 1102 says the woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes the man; in Ainkurunuru 59 the friend says she was once the cure for his love-sick heart but can be no cure for the girl now.
teaches: The couplet makes the beloved the only remedy for the man's love-sickness, but the Sangam friend shows a third person who served as that remedy by bringing them together, and who has none for the woman once he strays, so the cure flows only toward the man.

note: Both are the wife in oodal refusing the husband's chest; Ainkurunuru 63 because other women have lain on it, Kural 1311 because all women consume him with their eyes.
teaches: The couplet raises the bar of the older refusal: where the Sangam wife needs the touch of other women to refuse him, Valluvar's wife refuses for their looks alone, so the Kural turns a grievance about deeds into a jealousy of glances.

note: Ainkurunuru 8: the mother wishes that the king rule justly and there be no theft (and in poem 10, that the rains come). Kural 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The mother's prayers for just rule and for timely rain stand as separate wishes in the decade, while the Kural makes the second follow from the first, so a household's prayer list shows the belief that the Kural later states as a law of kingship.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife, saying she is not sulking, reads his reddened eyes after the flood-bath as a sign of the women he bathed with. Kural 1313: the husband says that even if he wears a wreath of branch flowers, she grows angry, saying he wore it to show another woman.
teaches: Both turn the husband's body into evidence in a love-quarrel, but the Kural's husband protests that the sign is innocent and the suspicion hers, while the Ainkurunuru sign comes from a bath with women he did take, so together they show that the oodal's reading of marks on the man can be either jealous fancy or plain proof, and the couplet's comedy depends on the scene being the first.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are so red after he bathed in the first-rain flood as the shoulder-companion of fine women. Naladiyar 387: the wife complains that the man who embraced other women comes to embrace her too without bathing.
teaches: In the Naladiyar the husband's fault is that he comes to his wife unwashed from other women, while in the Ainkurunuru the bath itself is the scene of his straying and its red eyes the evidence, so the pair shows bathing in the field country as both the cleansing a wife expects after his absence and the occasion of the absence.

note: Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman calls his chest a Thai bathing pond that many plunge into. Kural 1311: the wife refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The Kural wife's complaint that his chest is common property is made, in the Ainkurunuru, by one of the women who share it, who boasts of it rather than complains, so the same image of the common chest serves as reproach from the house and as triumph from outside it.

note: Ainkurunuru 89: the other woman tells the bard the wife is greatly graced, only because she wants the name of wife. Naladiyar 390: the wife tells the bard not to lie that he will be kind; she is the dry end of the cane and the others its sweet middle. On a plain reading each woman says the other has his favour.
teaches: Each woman tells the same messenger that the other is the favoured one, so the bard meets the identical complaint at both doors and the triangle has no one who admits to being loved; the Naladiyar files that voice under the chaste wife, the Ainkurunuru gives it to the rival.

note: Ainkurunuru 9: the girls wish that their bond with the lover not become town gossip (அம்பல்). Kural 1143: the man welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, since it feels like having her already.
teaches: The same talk of the town that the women pray to escape is a pleasure the man savours, so read together the two show that in secret love gossip threatened the woman's standing while it flattered the man's hopes.

note: Ainkurunuru 98 has the friend tell the lover that the girl's parents guard her more strictly than she guards herself; Kural 57 asks what use guarding a woman by confinement is, since the guard of her own steadfastness is the best.
teaches: The Kural's rule ranks a woman's own guard above confinement, but the Sangam friend relies on the confinement exactly because in courtship the girl's own guard has already given way, so the household's watch the couplet finds useless is what turns a lover into a husband.

note: Both say the woman is the cure of the love sickness: Kural 1102 says every other illness has a different cure but hers is cured by herself; Ainkurunuru 99 says the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for his sickness.
teaches: The couplet's paradox that the cause is the cure is put by the Sangam poem as something that has already happened (ஆகிய), placing the claim after the first meeting, which is where the Kural sets it too, under the joy of union.

note: Both speak in the woman's voice after a promise not to part is broken by his leaving: the Kural asks if the believer is at fault; Akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ).
teaches: The Kural turns the broken promise into a question of blame, while the Sangam heroine keeps it a question of memory; the poem shows a woman who will not yet say he broke his word, which the couplet's moral question has already assumed.

note: Kural 210 says that ruin is rare for one who does not stray into evil; the heroine of 101 quotes the same rule as an old proverb (நன்றுசெய் மருங்கில் தீதுஇல்) and asks whether it has turned false, since she did nothing hateful and is still left. On her reading the rule has failed.
teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's assurance was already an old proverb in the Sangam age, and that akam poetry was where it was tested: a blameless woman's abandonment is the counter-case the maxim does not answer.

note: Kural 551 judges the king who harasses his people and does wrong to be crueller than murderers; Akananuru 109 sets the murderers' road, with cairns over men shot though they carried nothing, in hills ruled by a king without aram (அறன்இல் வேந்தன்).
teaches: The Kural ranks the bad king against killers in the abstract, while the akam poet already draws the lawless realm and the murderous road as one landscape, so a lover's journey becomes the evidence of what a king without aram costs those who travel his land.

note: Kural 657 says the worthy prefer utter poverty to wealth gained under blame; the friend in Akananuru 112 says the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்), and so the hero should marry.
teaches: The same rule of the worthy, refusing any gain that brings blame, governs wealth in the Kural and love in the Akananuru, and the friend turns it from a counsel of going without into an argument for marriage, which removes the blame without removing the pleasure.

note: Same situation: a man held by the king's war who longs to be home at evening. Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and we will hold the evening feast with the household; in Akananuru 114 the war is done and the hero urges his charioteer to reach his wife before the evening's grief.
teaches: The couplet's two clauses, victory and then the evening at home, become in the poem a race against dusk, and the poem adds what the couplet leaves out: evening is the hour when the waiting wife suffers most, so his haste is to end her sorrow as much as to begin his feast.

note: Both are the man's words after first seeing the girl, about her eyes: the Kural says her look eats the life of those who see it; the Akananuru man tells the friends who rebuke him that they would not rebuke him if they had seen her look.
teaches: The Kural states the power of the look as a general truth, while the Akananuru puts it into a defence before the man's companions, showing that the couplet's claim first served as the hero's answer to rebuke (கழற்றெதிர்மறை).

note: Both answer the man's announced departure: in Kural 1151 the reply (the friend's or the woman's) is a sharp refusal, tell your quick return to those who will survive; in Akananuru 143 the friend only reports the woman's tears at his 'small word', and the colophon says he stayed.
teaches: The same thurai had two answers, the Kural's barbed argument and the Sangam friend's report of tears, and the poem shows the second one succeeding, which the couplet's general statement cannot show.

note: The man's maxim quoted in 151 is that the poor cannot support their dependants or laugh among their kin; Kural 1047 says poverty makes a man a stranger even to the mother who bore him.
teaches: The Kural states as a rule the claim the akam hero uses to justify leaving, and the poem shows what the rule costs when it is acted on: the wife says it leaves no room for grace.

note: Kural 760 says that for those who make bright wealth the other two (virtue and pleasure) come easily together; in Akananuru 155 the man says two things come from wealth, a life free of wrong and a wealth that never begs, and leaves.
teaches: The hero's version of the Kural's claim drops pleasure from the pair, and the poem makes that omission visible: the household pleasure is exactly what his errand for wealth suspends.

note: Kural 1157 has the woman say her slipping bangles already announce that the lord of the shore has left; in Akananuru 161 the friend tells the man the girl's tears show she has already understood his plan to go.
teaches: The poem turns the couplet's body-as-herald into an argument: the friend uses the tears that announce his going as the reason he should not go, so the sign the Kural records becomes a plea.

note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; in Akananuru 173 the man says that dharma and helping kin in ruin are not for those who sit at ease, and leaves to earn.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's premise about wealth working inside a marriage: it becomes the husband's reason for leaving and the friend's ground for comfort, and it shows the cost the maxim omits.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault when the one who said 'do not fear' leaves; in Akananuru 175 the woman recalls his vows, the hand on her wrist and the promised season, which has now come.
teaches: The poem supplies the concrete pledge the couplet only names (a vow, a grasped wrist, a named season) and fixes the moment of testing at the arrival of the promised rains.

note: Kural 1151, which Parimelazhagar gives to the friend, refuses to hear of a quick return; in Akananuru 179 the friend asks the departing man whether he can bear to live away while she is left alone.
teaches: The couplet compresses the friend's dissuasion into a threat of death, and the poem shows the fuller form of the same speech, arguing from the dangers of the road and the woman's beauty.

note: Kural 1081 is the man's first sight: goddess, peahen or woman, his heart reels; in 198 he has already held her and still decides she is not a woman but the dread maiden of a mountain spring, having likened her coming to a peahen in cloud.
teaches: The couplet places the doubt at first sight and the commentators settle it in favour of a woman, but the poem keeps the same three terms after the union and settles them the other way, so the awe of the anangu was not only a first impression.

note: Both join the town's gossip (கவ்வை, கௌவை) and the mother's response: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and the mother's words water to the woman's sickness; in Akananuru 20 the mother acts on the gossip and puts the girl under guard.
teaches: The Kural reads gossip and the mother as feeding love from within, while the Sangam poem shows their outward effect, confinement, and uses it to press the hidden lover to marry, so the couplet's paradox has a practical role in the akam plot.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the man who said 'fear not' are at fault if he leaves; in 205 the woman names his oath 'we will not part' a lie and yet wishes his journey success.
teaches: The couplet treats the broken promise as a question of blame, while the poem shows the same woman blaming and blessing him at once, so the trust the Kural judges was not withdrawn when it was betrayed.

note: Both answer a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell your quick return to those who will be alive then; 215 says wishing you a safe journey is for those who can bear to stay.
teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's refusal works in practice: the friend withholds the ritual farewell and fills the road with killers and vultures, so the threat of death the Kural only implies is made visible.

note: Both measure gossip against a public spectacle: the Kural against the serpent swallowing the moon, the Akananuru against the shout at Katti's flight.
teaches: The Kural keeps the old akam habit of sizing a private scandal by a famous public event, but trades the historical rout for a cosmic eclipse, losing the political sting while keeping the scale.

note: Both set the absent man's wellbeing above the woman's pallor: the friend's blessing நோய்இலராக, the Kural's 'let my body pale, if he is well'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into the woman's own mouth a blessing that the Akananuru gives to the friend, showing how the anthology's go-between voice was absorbed into the single speaker of the later couplets.

note: Both refuse the promise of a quick return: the girl quotes his 'we will come right away' against the spring, the Kural says tell your quick return to those who will be alive.
teaches: Read together they show the same refusal of comfort in two registers, the Kural as a sharp retort before parting and the Akananuru as proof gathered afterwards from the season's signs.

note: In both the girl looks and bows her head; the Kural takes it as water poured into the bond, while here the bowed head with checked tears leaves the hero in pain.
teaches: The Kural fixes the bowed head as a sign of consent, but the Akananuru shows the same gesture as unreadable to the man at the moment it happens, so the maxim is a reading made after the fact.

note: Both give the man's reason for parting as the pursuit of glory or strength (நல்லிசை, உரன்), which takes his resolve as companion instead of her.
teaches: The friend's argument that glory is not for those who stay home is the very reason the Kural's woman lives on in longing, so the same heroic value comforts in one poem and wounds in the other.

note: Both have the returning man wish to finish the work and reach home for the evening; the Kural's evening feast at home is the poem's dusk arrival when the wife loosens her braid.
teaches: The Kural states as a wish what the mullai poem stages as a drive at dusk, showing that the evening return was the fixed goal of the man's speech in both traditions.

note: In both the evening comes with cold and brings the woman's sorrow to its height.
teaches: The Kural names the evening's chill and the swelling grief in two lines, while the Akananuru supplies the season's things, the north wind, the rain and the flowers, that make the evening cold, so the couplet presupposes the landscape.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: Kural 1268 has a man serving in the king's war wish the king victory so that he may feast at home with his wife by evening; Akananuru 24 is such a man in the king's camp at the end of the rains, measuring the camp's sleepless night against his wife's lonely one.
teaches: The couplet states the soldier-husband's wish as a sentence; the poem gives the night that produces it, the blunted tusks, the drums and the cold rain, so the Kural's two clauses read as the end of a long vigil.

note: Both name former deeds as the cause of suffering: the woman's தொல்வினைப் பயன், the Naladiyar's fixed mark that cannot shrink or grow.
teaches: The Naladiyar draws from fixed former deeds the lesson that grief is useless, but the Akananuru woman names the same cause through streaming eyes and says she cannot bear it, so the explanation was available to akam speakers long before it was offered as a cure.

note: Kural 1323 asks whether any heaven equals sulking with one joined to you as water to earth; in Akananuru 26 the wife cannot sulk because her husband melted like ploughed red earth taking the rain.
teaches: The couplet makes the earth-and-water bond the reason sulking is sweet, while the poem uses the same image to end the sulk, which shows the likeness can either sustain lovers' quarrel or dissolve it, depending on who is melting.

note: In Kural 1236 the woman tells her friend that with bangles and shoulders slackening what hurts is hearing him called cruel; in Akananuru 267, when the friend says the oath-breaker has changed, the wife replies that he is not at fault and her shoulders, which let the bangles slip, are.
teaches: Same speaker, addressee and occasion: the Kural states the defence of the absent man as a feeling, and the poem shows its rhetorical move, turning the blame on her own body, so the couplet's restraint is seen as an argument with the friend.

note: Kural 1151 (the friend's words for Parimelazhagar) tells the departing man to promise his quick return to those who will still be alive; in Akananuru 271, the friend tells the departing man to prosper, but asks whether there is any medicine for the girl in the land where he will stay.
teaches: Both turn the farewell into a threat of her death, but the poem argues it through the road, whose nelli fruit revives dying travellers, so the couplet's bare warning is given a reason: the waste has remedies for strangers and none for her.

note: Kural 1147 has the woman say her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water; in Akananuru 273 she says the sickness sprouted between her breasts, grew a trunk, spread branches of gossip and budded with scandal into a tree shading the world.
teaches: The Kural's two-line plant metaphor, gossip feeding the disease, is the seed of Avvaiyar's full tree, which adds the stages of growth and makes the scandal not only food for the love but its flowering.

note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of a man who gives nothing to the needy to a beautiful woman growing old alone; the courtesan in Akananuru 276 likens her own beauty, if she fails to win the man, to the wealth of one who hoarded and never gave to those who asked.
teaches: The two verses run the same comparison in opposite directions, beauty as vehicle for hoarded wealth in the Kural and hoarded wealth as vehicle for beauty in the poem, which shows the pairing was a shared idea in which each term could explain the other.

note: Both use the beaten drum (அறைபறை) for love exposed to the town while the man is away; in the Kural it is her own eyes, in 281 it is the gossip he left behind.
teaches: The Kural takes the stock drum of gossip and turns it on the woman's own eyes, so the pairing shows the couplet moving the blame for exposure from the town, as the Sangam poem has it, to her own body.

note: Kural 467 says to deliberate and then resolve, never resolve and then deliberate; the friend in 286 says the great weigh virtue, wealth and their own worth before carrying out what they intend.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule of deliberate action used as a lever in courtship: if the great think before they promise, a lover who swore cannot later plead haste, so the maxim becomes a way to bind a promise.

note: Both are the friend telling the wife not to prolong her sulking: Kural 1302 says sulking is salt and too much spoils it; Akananuru 316 shows women who sulked too long left alone, poor and nursing hungry sons.
teaches: What the Kural calls spoiling by too much salt the Sangam friend spells out as the loss of fortune and household, so the couplet's measured image stands for a social and economic ruin, not only a lost pleasure.

note: Both are spoken to a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell me if you are not going, and keep your promise of a quick return for those who will still be alive; Akananuru 319's friend says go and get your wealth, since the girl cannot even say she will stay behind.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows why the friend speaks in this situation at all: the girl is too young and loving to answer him herself, which supports reading the couplet's 'tell me' as the friend speaking for her.

note: Kural 81: all of keeping house is for receiving guests; in Akananuru 324 the attendants announce the husband's return by saying his wife will now have guests to feed too.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule from the inside of an absence: hospitality belonged to the couple, so a wife alone could not host, and the husband's return is announced as the return of guests.

note: Kural 629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain; Akananuru 327 tells the heart that joy and grief come by turns like day and night, so it need not go seeking hardship for wealth.
teaches: The same doctrine of joy and grief in turn, which the Kural uses to teach calm under misfortune, becomes in the lover's mouth an argument for staying home rather than chasing gain.

note: Kural 467 says to think before resolving and calls rethinking after resolve a lapse; in Akananuru 33 the man tells his heart it did not think then, and that to halt the work now would make him a thing others laugh at.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule against second thoughts applied by a lover to his own heart, and adds what the maxim omits: the resolved deed costs a wife left behind, and the man accepts that cost rather than the shame of turning back.

note: Kural 247 grants that this world is not for those without wealth; Akananuru 335 opens by conceding that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, then gives up the journey for wealth anyway.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's premise about wealth in so many words yet refuses its practical pull, showing that the premise alone did not settle whether a husband should leave home to earn.

note: Kural 1122 calls the bond with the girl that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை ... நட்பு); 339 has the same word and image, friendship like life joined to the body (யாக்கைக்கு உயிர்இயைந் தன்ன நட்பின்).
teaches: The shared image and even the shared word நட்பு show the Kural's couplet as a distilled form of an akam figure that the poem still spends a scene of departure to earn.

note: Kural 1124: she is living to my life when with me and dying when she leaves; Akananuru 339 ends with love like the life's living and parting like dying, spoken by a husband as he sets out.
teaches: The Kural says it in courtship as praise; the poem puts the same claim in the mouth of a man choosing to leave, so the saying becomes the cost he knowingly pays, burning at both ends of the firebrand.

note: The Kural's woman has worn her fingers marking the days since he left; 351 names the marks drawn on the wall that she counts each day.
teaches: The couplet speaks only from the woman's side, while 351 puts the same tally marks in the returning man's mind, so the counting of days on the wall was a known practice that both partners could picture, not a private secret of the one who waits.

note: Both start from the coming of age: the Naladiyar's wise renounce early because grey hair will come; 353's hero refuses to leave his wife because the days pass like a dream and age is coming.
teaches: The same premise, that youth is short, yields opposite counsels, renunciation in the Naladiyar and staying in married love in 353, so impermanence was a shared starting point that the akam poets turned toward the household and the didactic poets away from it.

note: Both are the man at the king's war: the couplet wishes the king victory so that he may join his wife for the evening feast; in 354 the king has won and raised his flag, and the attendants urge the hero home before her pallor deepens.
teaches: The couplet's wish has two conditions, the king's victory and the evening at home, and 354 shows them met in order (the flag raised, the herds coming in at dusk), so the Kural's line compresses a whole mullai homecoming whose hinge is that the hero's private return waits on the public war.

note: Both make the man say that the sweetest thing is an embrace that lets nothing come between: in the Kural not even a breeze, in the poem not even a thread, at which she sulks.
teaches: The couplet states the delight as settled, while the poem quotes it as the argument the man lost to his heart's desire for wealth, so the Kural's claim is shown being tested and overruled inside the paalai situation.

note: The Kural says to give and live with renown (இசைபட) as the only gain; the poem names those who give with renown (இசைபடப் பெய்தல்) as the men who must sleep in ruined halls on the road to wealth.
teaches: The poem shows what the Kural's rule costs a married man: renown from giving needs wealth, and wealth needs the wasteland and separation, so the maxim's single profit is bought with the akam hero's loneliness.

note: Both say great wealth does not last: the Kural likens its coming and going to a crowd at a dance hall, the poem likens its passing to a night's dream.
teaches: The poem turns the Kural's general warning about wealth into a reason for a husband to stay home, using impermanence not to urge giving but to set the wife's embrace above a second journey for gain.

note: Both are the plea of the one left behind against a departure: the couplet says tell your quick return to those still alive; 387 asks him to say he will return, and then shows a road where great men turn back at a lizard's cry.
teaches: The couplet only doubts the traveller's promise; the poem shows why it is empty, since on that road a return depends on omens and beasts, not on the man's word.

note: Both are the man's account of a first sight, and both set a simple girl (பேதை) against eyes that make war (அமர்த்தன / அமர்த்தனள்).
teaches: The couplet's paradox of war-making eyes in an artless girl gets a cause in the poem: she glares because a stranger blocks her road and jokes about her body, so the 'deadly' look is her self-possession, and it ends in a smile.

note: Both speak of a lover who took a woman's beauty in exchange: the couplet's woman says he took grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor; the courtesan of 396 demands her beauty back before he goes.
teaches: Read together they show the claim that a lover owes back the beauty he took was not the wife's alone: the courtesan states it as a debt to be repaid, which the couplet's wife can only lament.

note: Both liken the beloved's coming to rain on those who live by it: the Kural states it as a rule of lovers' grace, Akananuru 42 makes it a drought broken at dawn over a whole countryside.
teaches: The Kural's two-line rain simile is the compressed form of a scene the Sangam poet builds at length, so the couplet's image carries the whole drought-and-tank picture behind it.

note: Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and let us feast at home in the evening; Akananuru 44 opens with the king's work done and the tribute paid, and bids the chariot race home to sleep on her breast.
teaches: The Kural's couplet is the akam homecoming formula of the returning warrior reduced to its two clauses, the king's victory first and the household's evening second.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Both answer a man's announced departure for wealth: in Kural 1151 she says 'if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive'; in Akananuru 5 she says nothing, and he gives up the journey.
teaches: The Kural gives the refusal its sharpest words, and the Sangam poem shows the same refusal working without any: from the man's side, it is the unspoken sign and the withering garland on the child that stop him.

note: Kural 1155 says if he leaves, union becomes hard (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு); in 51 the man tells his heart that wealth is joined only by parting, and chooses to stay.
teaches: The same word புணர்வு carries both sides of one exchange: the Kural's woman counts what parting costs union, and the Sangam man counts what union costs wealth.

note: Kural 1138 says love breaks through secrecy into the public square whatever the lover's restraint; in 52 the heroine, her pallor already visible, still forbids her friend to name it even at the cost of her life.
teaches: The Kural's rule that love cannot be hidden is qualified by the Sangam heroine's will: the body discloses it, but the naming is still hers to refuse.

note: Kural 223 counts not saying 'I have nothing' and giving as the mark of the well-born; in 53 that very inability to refuse the needy is what drives the man away from the heroine.
teaches: The Kural's praise of giving has a cost the Kural does not count: in akam the generous man's virtue is the cause of the woman's abandonment.

note: Kural 62 says evil will not touch for seven births those who have children free of blame; Akananuru 66 quotes a saying of the same kind (blameless sons bring fame here and a stainless next world) and finds it true when a toddler stops his father from marrying another wife.
teaches: The pair shows a maxim about a child's merit protecting the parent being tested in a household quarrel, where its proof is not the next world but a husband held at home, which shifts the rule from the father's destiny to the mother's marriage.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Akananuru 69 says the man left for wealth wanting exactly that joy (ஈதல் இன்பம் வெஃகி), and the friend draws from it that he will not delay.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's joy of giving as the stated motive of the akam journey for wealth, so the separation the paalai poems lament is grounded in a virtue, and the friend can use that virtue as a promise of his return.

note: Kural 247 sets wealth and grace side by side as what this world and the next require; the man in Akananuru 75 quotes the saying that effort for wealth, not grace, is a man's task and refuses it, since nothing in this world can give back what parting wastes.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's balance of wealth and grace becomes a choice in a marriage, and the akam man qualifies the Kural's grant of this world to wealth by naming one thing in this world that wealth cannot restore.

note: Both speak in the voice of the man returning from work to an evening at home: Kural 1268 wishes the king's war won so that he may feast with his wife at evening; Akananuru 9's work is done and his heart has gone ahead to her at the evening when calves come home.
teaches: The Kural names the evening the man looks forward to, and the Sangam poem fills it from the woman's side, her prayer at the lizard's chirp and the game of covered eyes, with his heart arriving before his chariot.

note: Kural 524 says the fruit of gaining wealth is to be surrounded by kin; the man in 93 gives exactly this reason (ending the kin's ruin, feeding relatives, making strangers kin) for the journey that took him from his wife.
teaches: The Kural's purpose for wealth is the very reason the paalai hero gives for leaving, so the akam poem shows what the maxim costs in separation, and puts the return to the wife, not the kin, at the end.

note: In Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip manures her love-sickness and her mother's words water it; in Akananuru 95 the mother answers the gossiping women in her daughter's defence, and that trust is what the girl cannot face.
teaches: The Kural's couplet assumes a scolding mother whose words feed the love; the Sangam scene shows the harder case, where the mother's kindness against the town's gossip is what leaves the girl helpless, so the same two pressures can work through trust as well as blame.

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: Kural 1150: the friend says the town raises the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant marriage if asked; Kalittokai 104: the friend tells the girl that her kin have gladly agreed to give her to the herder who leapt on the black bull, trampling on the heads of the town that raised the gossip (அலர் எடுத்த ஊராரை உச்சி மிதித்து).
teaches: The couplet hopes that the town's talk will move the lover to marry; the herders' poem shows a second way gossip ends, through the kin's public consent once the bull is taken, so in the mullai village it is the girl's family the gossip moves, and the wedding then silences the town.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness of love grows long with the town's gossip for manure and the mother's words for water; Kalittokai 105: the girl asks what joy equals this, that her mother beat her with a stick and the town made gossip linking her to the herder (யாய் என்னைக் கண் உடைக் கோலள் அலைத்ததற்கு... அலர் செய்துவிட்டது இவ் ஊர்).
teaches: The same two forces, the town's talk and the mother's harshness, feed a growing pain in the couplet but are welcomed as joy by the herd girl, because once the bond is public her marriage follows from the bull-catch; whether exposure hurts depends on whether an open road to marriage lies ahead.

note: Kural 1083: the man says he now knows Death, which has a woman's grace and big eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு); Kalittokai 108: the man calls the girl the warrior who took up arms against his life, and mocks her trust in her mullai-bud teeth and battle eyes (பேர் அமர் உண் கண்ணும்), while she answers back and at last sets the tryst.
teaches: The couplet's lone confession of being slain by her eyes appears in the herders' poem as a line of banter that the girl hears, throws back and answers with a meeting place, which shows the conceit of the killing eye at work as courtship speech addressed to the woman, not only as the man's inner wonder.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Kalittokai 109: the man watching the buttermilk girl reports that the town's wives, judging her fit to be an anangu to everyone (யார்க்கும் அணங்கு ஆதல் சான்றாள்), keep their husbands in and shut their doors when she comes.
teaches: Beside the couplet, the herders' poem shows that the word அணங்கு named a real danger, a beauty that strikes whoever sees it: what is one man's private bewilderment in the Kural becomes in Kalittokai a judgment the whole town shares and acts on by guarding its men.

note: Kural 1229 says that when evening spreads the whole town is bewildered and suffers; Kalittokai 118's refrain says evening torments those parted but cannot dim (கடிகல்லாய்) the beauty, sweet speech and smile of lovers who are together.
teaches: Read beside the poem, the couplet's 'the whole town suffers' shows itself as the lonely woman's projection, since the kali poem insists evening harms only the parted, so the grief belongs to separation and not to the hour.

note: Kural 1221 tells the hour it is not evening but the time that eats the lives of the wedded; Kalittokai 119, after a long catalogue of dusk, says those who call it evening are deluded, not knowing it is the hour that unwraps women's lives.
teaches: The couplet compresses into one address the argument the kali poem builds through fifteen lines of homing birds, closing flowers and lit fires, so the Kural's 'not evening but a killing hour' is a summary of an established neythal rebuttal rather than a fresh conceit.

note: Both say death comes unseen and no one knows the last day; the Naladiyar concludes that one must lay up provisions of virtue in time, Kalittokai 12 that one must not let the days of embrace pass for wealth.
teaches: The same reminder of death is used to opposite ends: the Jain moralist spends the uncertain time on merit, the love poet on love, so the memento mori did not belong to renunciation alone.

note: Kural 1224: in the lover's absence evening comes like enemies to a killing field; Kalittokai 120 makes evening a hunter aiming at a deer, a mocker of the beaten, a man pushing a spear into a burn, and Death grinning with the crescent as its tooth.
teaches: The poem unfolds the couplet's single image of evening as executioner into a series of cruelties each aimed at someone already wounded, which shows that the Kural's 'like enemies' means an attack on the defenceless, not just a hostile arrival.

note: Kural 1246 tells the heart its anger is false, since it cannot stay angry on seeing the man who ends quarrels by union; Kalittokai 122 has the woman, chided for sulking, say she knows he keeps other women, yet when he tends her a little her shameless heart melts and is calmed.
teaches: The kali poem supplies the setting the couplet leaves out, a friend mocking her sulks as causeless, so the Kural's confession that the heart's anger is false turns out to answer that reproach: she knows his fault fully, and her heart still gives way.

note: Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for following the man who left while lamenting his lack of grace; Kalittokai 123 asks the simple heart (மட நெஞ்சே) that went to him at night whether it saw, embraced or knew him, and pities it for tossing like the backwater tide.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's 'you go after him' looks like as an event, the heart's nightly journey met by three questions it cannot answer, so the Kural's rebuke of the foolish heart is the end of a scene in which the heart keeps coming back empty.

note: Kural 1235: the friend says the shoulders, bangles gone and old beauty faded, declare the cruel man's cruelty; Kalittokai 124: the friend tells the man the woman hid her pain even from her, but her pale forehead, wasted shoulders and streaming eyes could not hide it.
teaches: Together they show the body as a witness that overrides the woman's own silence: the poem adds that she tried to keep the pain even from her closest friend, so what the couplet calls the shoulders 'declaring' is a betrayal of her will to conceal, which the friend then turns against the man.

note: Kural 293: do not lie about what your own heart knows, for after the lie your heart burns you; Kalittokai 125 opens with the maxim that those who think no one saw may hide what their heart knows, but no witness is closer than the heart, and then charges the lover.
teaches: The akam friend turns the ethical maxim into a weapon of courtship: the Kural's inner witness, a general law of truthfulness, becomes the ground on which she charges a lover with knowing his own neglect, so the doctrine of conscience was already available to love poetry as rhetoric.

note: Kural 1218: when I sleep he is on my shoulder, when I wake he runs into my heart; Kalittokai 126: the friend says the woman, thinking of him, believes him on her shoulder (தோள் மேலாய்), embraces him as if awake, finds nothing and knows it was a dream.
teaches: The poem tells the couplet's moment from outside and counts its cost: what the Kural's woman offers as a defence of her lover (he never leaves me) the friend reports as the last of three daily delusions ending in grief, so the shoulder-dream is comfort in the first person and harm in the third.

note: Kural 1157: the bangles slipping past her wrist announce that the lord of the shore has left; Kalittokai 127: the friend tells the lord of the shore that her bangles slip (இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த) and asks him to give grace as the wave shelters the adumbu creeper.
teaches: The couplet has the bangles accuse the man to the woman herself; the poem has the friend carry the same evidence to the man's face and pair it with a remedy, so the slipping bangle moves from private proof of desertion to an argument for his return.

note: Kural 1213: my life lasts because I see in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Kalittokai 128: the woman tells of a dream in which she quarrelled with the man and he bowed at her feet, and says her life held at the brink hoping he would come awake too.
teaches: The poem shows the mechanism the couplet only asserts: the dream keeps her alive by letting her act out the quarrel and his submission and by feeding the hope of a real coming, so the Kural's 'my life lasts' rests on both satisfaction and expectation.

note: Kural 1222 asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Kalittokai 129 asks the sea, the anril on the palmyra and the little flute in turn whether, like her, they have someone who loved and left them.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's question as one move in a round of addresses to sea, bird and music, so the Kural's single address to evening reads as a compressed survival of a sung form in which each sound of nightfall is asked whether it too was abandoned.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds at morning and blooms at evening; Kalittokai 130: as the great backwater flowers close at evening, her heart closes in ruin (அழிவொடு கூம்பும்).
teaches: The two invert one flower image: the couplet makes the evening sickness bloom, the poem makes the heart shut with the evening flowers, so love's pain at dusk could be figured as opening or as closing, and the Kural's paradox depends on reversing the shore's ordinary evening closure.

note: Kural 1154: if the man who said 'do not fear' leaves, is the fault in those who trusted his word; Kalittokai 132: the friend asks the man whether the woman's pallor and lost beauty are not the fruit of his 'do not fear' (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு) and 'trust me' (தெளி) at their secret meetings.
teaches: The couplet's question of who bears the fault is answered in the poem by the friend, who reads each reassurance as the direct cause of a named loss, so the Kural's moral question has a speech situation behind it in which the promise is handed back to the man as a debt.

note: Kalittokai 133 defines அறிவு as bearing the words of fools (பேதையார் சொல் நோன்றல்) and பொறை as bearing with those who do not cherish you; Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths.
teaches: The same act is filed under different virtues: the kali friend calls forbearance toward fools wisdom and keeps patience for those who neglect you, while the Kural calls it strength, so this forbearance had no fixed place yet in the lists of virtues, standing under wisdom in one and strength in the other.

note: Kalittokai 133: justice (முறை) is taking life without favour (கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்); Kural 541: justice is to examine, show favour to no one (கண்ணோடாது) and act after weighing.
teaches: Both define justice with the same word கண்ணோடாது, but the love poem gives its harshest form, taking life, in a list meant to shame a lover, so the definition of முறை as unbending punishment was common coin a friend could quote, and the Kural's procedural version tempers a stock definition centred on the death sentence.

note: Kural 1164: the sea of love is there but there is no raft of safety to cross it; Kalittokai 134: her grief ends as a man whose ship broke in a shoreless sea is saved by a raft the waves bring, the lovers hastening home. One says no raft exists, the other that the sea itself brings one.
teaches: The two use the same sea and raft with opposite outcomes, which shows that in love the raft is not something the sufferer can find for herself: the couplet's woman has none, and in the poem it arrives only with the beloved's return.

note: Kalittokai 135's friend tells the shore lord that abandoning the girl would lie as a great fault on his lineage (குடிமைக் கண் பெரியது ஓர் குற்றம்); Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out high like the spot on the moon.
teaches: The couplet's rule that high birth makes a fault more visible is what gives the friend's threat its force: she aims at his lineage rather than his love because a lord's desertion, unlike a commoner's, would be seen by all, so the maxim is already a working argument in akam persuasion.

note: Kalittokai 136 likens the girl's joy at each meeting to a gambler's winning throw and her grief at his leaving to the loss of a stake; Kural 932 says the gambler gains one and loses a hundred.
teaches: Read with the couplet's arithmetic of the dice, the friend's simile becomes a warning: a secret love that runs on wins and losses must end in ruin on balance, which is why she ends by telling him to take the girl in marriage and stop the game.

note: Kalittokai 137 says his gentleness burns her worse than fire (தீயினும் கடிது); Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, while love's sickness burns when the lover is away.
teaches: The couplet states as a single paradox what the kali poem reaches through three graded steps (word above bow, kindness above enmity, gentleness above fire), so the Kural's compressed contrast between fire and love was the end point of an argued rhetoric the longer form still displays.

note: Kalittokai 138's madal rider sings that grief and the palmyra horse are what she gave (படரும் பனை ஈன்ற மாவும் நல்கியவை); in Kural 1135 the man says the girl gave him the madal and evening's anguish.
teaches: Both men list the madal among the woman's gifts, so the convention made the beloved the author of the lover's public shame; the kali poem adds the outcome the couplet leaves open, her coming in grace, which shows the gift was meant to be returned.

note: Kalittokai 139 calls the horse she gave a shelter (ஏமம்) against the army of love; Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard (ஏமம்) and no strength but the madal.
teaches: Both use the same word ஏமம் for an act of humiliation, and the kali poem shows how the safeguard works: it is spoken to the worthies whose duty is to treat another's pain as their own, so the madal protects by putting the assembly under obligation.

note: Kalittokai 139's rider swims the sea of love with the madal as his raft (மடல் புணையா நீந்துவேன்); Kural 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: Where the couplet's flood sweeps away the raft of shame, the kali lover takes the shameful act itself as his raft, so the two together show the madal as what is left when shame has failed: a raft made of the loss of one.

note: Kural 113 says to give up at once gain made by leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Kalittokai 14 says wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next.
teaches: The Kural allows that unfair gain may bring good and asks for sacrifice anyway, while the love poem denies it brings good in either world, so the woman's argument is stronger than the ethics book's rule.

note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; Kalittokai 14 puts the like saying (காதலார் எவன் செய்ப பொருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு) in the mouths of strangers and rejects it.
teaches: A maxim the Kural states as fact is quoted in the love poem as hostile outsiders' talk, so the wealth maxim was public wisdom that akam speakers could set against love and refuse.

note: Kalittokai 140's rider complains that the town sees his sickness and does not soften (கண்டும் கண்ணோடாது இவ் ஊர்); Kural 576 says those who have eyes and do not turn them kindly are like trees fixed in the soil.
teaches: The madal rider appeals to the civic virtue the Kural names கண்ணோட்டம், so the madal is shown to work through the town's duty of kindly regard, and the town that will not soften is, by the Kural's measure, as insensible as a tree.

note: Kalittokai 141's rider says she made him, who rides the war horse in battle, ride the madal to the common; in Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The couplet's before-and-after inventory is spelled out in the kali poem as three lost ranks (warrior, protector, orator), which shows that the manliness the Kural says is lost is a public standing, not only a private virtue.

note: Kalittokai 142's girl, once laughing with hidden teeth, now laughs aloud and weeps so all hear and sings her love to the worthies; Kural 1138 says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks secrecy and comes into the open.
teaches: The couplet states as a law what the kali poem stages as a scene with an audience and a song, and shows the price: once love breaks into the open, the woman faces two pains, love and gossip (காமமும் கௌவையும்), where the couplet names only the first.

note: Kalittokai 144's girl says that when she opens her eyes to seize him he runs and hides in her heart; Kural 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
teaches: The same fancy of the lover fleeing into the heart on waking appears in both, but the kali poem frames it as a madwoman's complaint to the sea, so what the couplet offers as consolation (he never leaves her) is also a sign of her derangement.

note: Kalittokai 145's woman begs the sun not to set and speaks of bearing evening's enmity (மாலைப் பகை); Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what enmity (பகை) to evening.
teaches: The couplet's riddle about why evening is hostile is answered in the kali poem by an action: she asks the sun to stay and hopes the man will come at dawn over the sea, so the hours are enemies or friends according to when the parted can expect his return.

note: Kalittokai 146's woman says that if she told her pain to the night that puts many to sleep (பலர்த் துயிற்றும் யாமம்), it would not sleep; Kural 1168 says the night that puts all beings to sleep has no companion but her.
teaches: Both make the night, the one who puts all to sleep, the only wakeful companion of the deserted woman; the kali poem goes further and threatens to keep the night itself awake with her song, turning the couplet's pity for the night into her power over it.

note: Kural 1137 says nothing is worthier than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the madal; Kalittokai 147's woman, maddened in the street, begs Kama's arrows so that the man will come riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: The kali woman keeps the rule the couplet praises, she does not mount the madal, but she gets around it by wishing the madal on him, so the restriction on women survives even in the most extreme akam scene and shapes the form her desire takes.

note: Kalittokai 148 calls evening a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; in Kural 1226 the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband was still with her.
teaches: The couplet records the discovery and the kali poem the double nature behind it: the same hour is a raft and a suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for lovers together and a sickness for the parted, which is why she learned its cruelty only after he left.

note: Kalittokai 149's friend warns that failing those who helped in want will strike the doer even in his descendants; Kural 110 says one who kills a good done to him has no escape.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's gravest moral rule to a lover's delay, so the woman who gave herself in secret is counted as a benefactor, and his failure to marry her becomes ingratitude, the one wrong with no escape.

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband commands rain; Kalittokai 16 calls the woman the chaste one who gives rain to the world in drought and says virtue will not let her pale.
teaches: The power the Kural states as a marvel works in the love poem as an argument: a woman who can bring rain cannot be left to waste, so the belief served to bind husbands as well as to praise wives.

note: In both the friend (for one Kural commentator) tells the man who announces his going that the woman will not survive him: 'tell your quick return to those who will be alive' and 'she will not live a blink without you'.
teaches: The couplet's bare refusal of comfort becomes in the kali an argued case: the friend first sets his two promises against each other and shows that wealth cannot be earned, and only then says the girl will not live, so the Kural's line reads as the last move of a dispute the long poem spells out.

note: The friend argues that wealth moves from one to another by former deeds (பழ வினை), so leaving to earn it is pointless; Kural 619 holds that even when fate denies, effort pays the wage of the body's labour.
teaches: The friend uses the doctrine of former deeds to keep the man home, while the Kural grants that doctrine only to deny that it excuses idleness, so the same belief about fate served the akam poets as an argument against striving and the moralist as one to be overruled.

note: Naladiyar 45 scorns men who praise teeth as jasmine buds, having seen fallen teeth in the burning ground; in Kalittokai 22 the woman asks the man who praised her teeth like jasmine buds whether he praised them falling out.
teaches: Both deflate the same compliment with the same decay, but to opposite ends: the ascetic uses the fallen teeth to free a man from desire, the wife uses them to bind him to her for life, so the image of the body's ruin cut both for and against staying with a woman.

note: In both the woman tells her friend, before the man leaves, that she cannot survive his going: Kural 1155 asks her to stop it since union will be impossible once he goes, and Kalittokai 24 says her life has already gone with him.
teaches: The kali adds how she knows and why she yields: she learned of the journey from his sleep-talk and gives up her life to save his name from blame, so the couplet's plea to prevent the departure is shown coming from a woman who has already lost the chance to plead.

note: Kural 557: as the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of grace (அளி) is to those who live; Kalittokai 25: as is this world when the sky withholds rain, so is her beauty when his grace (அளி) is withdrawn.
teaches: The kali poet takes the moralist's image of rain and royal grace and applies it to a husband, so the man stands to his wife as a king to his realm and his leaving becomes a failure of rule, not only of love.

note: Kural 820 warns against the bond of those who are friendly at home and slander in the assembly; Kalittokai 25 compares her eyes, which shine while he is near and weep when he goes, to the bond of mean men who praise to the face and slander behind.
teaches: The friend turns the moralist's type of false friend into a figure for the woman's own body, whose eyes, bangles and brow publish her state once he leaves, so the danger the Kural sees in other people becomes, in love, the betrayal of the self by its own signs.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the generous man to a fruit tree ripening in the town; Kalittokai 27 likens the riverbank trees flourishing in spring to the wealth of a man who gives without stint and lives by virtue.
teaches: The comparison runs one way in the Kural (wealth like a tree) and the other in the kali (trees like wealth), showing that the moral image had become common enough for a love poet to turn it round and use the giver's wealth to describe the season.

note: Kural 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm; Kalittokai 27 has spring encamp like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister let it in.
teaches: The Kural states the danger of a bad counsellor as a maxim, while the kali shows its outcome, the enemy camped inside the land, and uses that sight for spring's assault on a lonely woman, which shows the statecraft maxim already worked as a picture poets could borrow.

note: Kural 555: the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction wear away the wealth of the king who causes it; Kalittokai 34: her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed.
teaches: Read with the Kural, the woman's tears carry the threat the moralist gives to the subjects' tears, that they wear down the ruler who causes them, so her weeping is an accusation against the absent husband as well as a sign of grief.

note: Kural 788: friendship clears distress at once, as the hand of a man whose garment slips; Kalittokai 34: the lover has come on the promised day as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
teaches: Both use the hand that moves to the body without thought as the figure of help that needs no asking; the Kural gives it to friendship, the kali to a husband returning on the counted day, so the reflex image measures the ideal of timely help in both public and private bonds.

note: Kural 1257: the woman says she knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she longs for. Kalittokai 37: the girl says that, since he could not speak and she might not, she resolved (துணிதந்து) to do one shameless deed (நாண் இன்மை செய்தேன்), staging a fall into his arms.
teaches: The Kural makes the loss of shame something that happens to a woman when the lover acts, while Kapilar's girl chooses the shameless act herself because the man will not, and then praises him for the restraint that sends her home; held together they show that akam allows the heroine to set aside naanam as a tactic when the rules of speech leave both lovers mute.

note: Kural 55: the wife who rises worshipping her husband, not a god, commands rain. Kalittokai 39: the girl, embraced by the man who saved her from the flood, could bring rain at need (line 6), and because hill women rise worshipping their husbands (கேள்வர்த் தொழுது எழலால்) the hunters' arrows do not miss.
teaches: The Kural's claim appears in the friend's disclosure as a belief the hill folk already hold, extended from rain to the whole hill economy and staked on a single premarital embrace, so the maxim on the wife's power was a shared folk conviction that the friend could use to argue the girl was already a faithful wife.

note: Kural 1152 says that union, which once gave delight even at a glance, now carries the pain of fearing separation; Kalittokai 4 shows the woman reading his coming departure in caresses that exceed the usual.
teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: the fear spoils union because his tenderness itself has become the sign of leaving, so the more he gives the surer she is he will go.

note: Kural 957: a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon. Kalittokai 41: if a falsehood appeared in the hill lord's truth it would be like fire appearing in the moon (திங்களுள் தீத் தோன்றியற்று).
teaches: The Kural uses the moon to say a noble man's fault cannot be hidden; the girls use it to say such a fault is impossible, so the same figure that warns the great serves in akam as a pledge of trust sung for the lover to overhear, binding him to live up to it.

note: Kural 428: not to fear what should be feared is folly, and to fear it is the work of the wise. Kalittokai 42 line 26: the friend checks her own reproach, saying he is not a lawless man who fears nothing that should be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சா அறன் இலி அல்லன்).
teaches: The Kural's prudence about danger is turned by the friend into a moral standard for a lover, where what should be feared is breaking a girl's heart, and failing it makes a man அறன் இலி; the pair shows the maxim already working as a test of character in love, not only in counsel.

note: Kural 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach. Kalittokai 43 lines 26-27: the lover is praised as one who, if he could not fill the want of one who told him of poverty, would give up his body (தன் மெய் துறப்பான்).
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is sung by the girls as a fact about one man to cure a girl's wasting, so the ethical maxim served in akam as the highest praise a lover could receive, and the praise itself works the cure before he comes.

note: Kural 980: greatness hides another's weakness, smallness tells only faults. Kalittokai 44: the girl hid the man's ungraciousness from her friend, the street and her companions, ashamed that others would blame him, and the friend calls this a nature rare even in a mother.
teaches: The Kural's mark of greatness is shown in the one wronged, a girl hiding her lover's fault, and the friend's report of it becomes a reproach, since the man learns that the greater one in the affair is she; the pair shows the maxim working as leverage in a love quarrel.

note: Kural 1112: the man scolds his heart for reeling at flowers, thinking her eyes resemble what many can see. Kalittokai 45: the friend asks whether he ruined the girl's eyes because they resembled the flowers of his hill's springs (மலர் ஏய்க்கும்). On one reading the claims are incompatible: the Kural's lover refuses the likeness as beneath her, Kalittokai's friend holds him to it as the motive of harm.
teaches: The flower comparison that the Kural's lover rejects to honour the girl is used by the friend against the man as an accusation, so the same convention of beauty can be denied as praise or pressed as a charge, depending on whether the lover or the friend wields it.

note: Kural 1192: the grace a lover shows the one who loves is like rain to those who live by it. Kalittokai 46: the girl longed for his grace like the bird that sings up to the sky for raindrops (துளி நசை ... அளி நசை), yet it was a stormy midnight (கனை பெயல் நடுநாள்) that kept him from the tryst.
teaches: The Kural's image of grace as rain is set in Kalittokai against real rain, which is what stopped the meeting, so the girl craves one rain while the other keeps it from her; the pairing shows the kali poet testing a stock equivalence against the weather of the kurinji night.

note: Kural 1133: the man says he once had shame and sound manliness and now has the palmyra horse. Kalittokai 47: the girl says a man of great strength and restraint has put off his manliness (தன் ஆண்தகை விட்டு) to tell her he cannot live without her.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's own account of losing his manliness, the threat behind the madal, while Kalittokai gives the girl's hearing of it, weighing whether to believe it and what consenting would cost her name, so the pair shows both sides of the same pressure in secret love.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
