teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

note: Kural 1095: the man says she does not look at him directly but smiles with one eye narrowed. Kalittokai 51: the girl says the young man looked at her from the corner of his eye as if to kill and smiled (கடைக் கண்ணால் ... நகை கூட்டம் செய்தான்).
teaches: The Kural reads the sidelong smile as the girl's sign of consent, seen by the man; Kalittokai gives the same sign to the man, seen by the girl after she has lied for him, so the gesture of kurippu is not tied to one sex and seals a secret both have now chosen.

note: Kural 1117 asks whether a woman's face has spots as the moon does; Kalittokai 55 has the man make the same correction six times over (not the moon, for it has no stain; not the crescent, for it does not wane), reported by the girl.
teaches: The Kural's single corrected simile is shown in the Kalittokai as a wooing technique that the girl sees through, so the man's praise-by-correction is not only admiration but a calculated approach she names as such.

note: In Kural 1081 the man, first seeing her, cannot tell if she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Kalittokai 56 he asks if she is a craftsman's doll, a woman assembled from all women's best parts, or Death in a form it chose.
teaches: Both stage the first sight as a failure to classify the woman, but the Kalittokai adds Death and a girl too young to know her effect, so the Kural's bewilderment turns into a complaint that her beauty is a public danger no one has announced.

note: Kural 1102 says the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Kalittokai 60 the man tells the friend his only medicine is to see the girl's face, and there is no other.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as the man's private discovery after union; in the Kalittokai it is relayed by the friend as a plea before union, so the same conceit serves as an argument that obliges the girl to grant the cure.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palm-stem horse; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the tusker-like warrior who threatens the mocked madal is truly without shame (நாண் இலன்).
teaches: The Kural gives the man's own confession that madal means the loss of shame and manliness; the Kalittokai gives the woman's side seeing that loss, and shows it is what persuades her that he will not stop.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

note: Kural 316 says one must not do to another what one knows to be painful; in Kalittokai 62 the girl states that rule and the man answers that sweetness lies in the one who needs, and that seizing moon-faced women is virtue.
teaches: The Kalittokai lets the lover contest the Kural's rule with an argument from pleasure rather than ignore it, showing that the love poets knew the non-harm maxim and staged its failure under desire.

note: Kalittokai 67's three refrains say 'I would say I will sulk' (புலப்பேன் யான் என்பேன்மன்) and the heart says it will join him; Kural 1284 has the woman go to sulk and her heart go to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது).
teaches: The Kural's couplet is one turn of a song the Kalittokai performs three times with three different marks on the man's body, and the Kalittokai names the heart's act outright as treason (அறைபோகு), showing that the couplet's quiet split between woman and heart was heard as betrayal from within.

note: Kural 1215 says what was seen awake was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet while it is seen; Kalittokai 68 says the husband's embrace is like wealth won in a dream, different on waking.
teaches: The Kural's lover levels waking and dream, both sweet while they last, but the Kalittokai wife uses the dream to name a possession that vanishes, so the dream simile can console a parted lover or indict an unfaithful husband depending on whether the absence is chosen.

note: Kural 1192 likens a lover's grace to the rain that sustains those who live by it; Kalittokai 71 likens the husband's once-a-year visit to a drizzle that cannot satisfy paddy withering for want of rain.
teaches: The Kural's rain stands for grace given in its season, and the Kalittokai shows the same image under neglect: a token visit is not rain but drizzle, so the wife measures grace by its sufficiency, a test the Kural's simile assumes but does not state.

note: Kural 580 praises those who, wanting a refinement worth loving, see poison poured and drink it; Kalittokai 74 calls the women who trust the husband's words though they see his graceless ways deluded, like those who eat poison knowing it kills.
teaches: Knowingly swallowing poison is a mark of courtesy in the Kural and a mark of delusion in the Kalittokai, so the same act is judged by whom it is done for: forbearance toward a friend is refinement, forbearance toward a faithless lover is folly.

note: Kural 1143 welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, because it gives as if already got what is not yet got; Kalittokai 76 ends that if the town has done what their kin would do at the wedding, nothing is left to do.
teaches: Both turn alar from shame into a kind of marriage, and together they show the two uses of the same claim: the Kural lover savours the gossip as a foretaste, while the Kalittokai friend uses it as an argument that the wedding is already public and must now follow.

note: Kural 1254 says she used to call herself restrained (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்) but desire breaks out in public; Kalittokai 77 asks whether restraint (நிறை) is easy for one who lives with an enemy, her own heart.
teaches: The Kural blames desire in general for breaking restraint, while the Kalittokai wife places the failure in a precise moment, the sight of the unfaithful husband at her door, so the same loss of நிறை turns from a lover's confession into a wronged wife's helplessness against her own grievance.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so do at once what does; Kalittokai 8 says wealth is less stable than a lute, Fortune or a cruel king, so do not go after it.
teaches: From the same premise the two draw different conclusions: the Kural says to spend unstable wealth on lasting good, the love poem says not to leave love to seek it, so impermanence argued for staying home as well as for giving.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

note: Kural 70 says a son repays his father by making people ask what penance the father did; Kalittokai 86 has the mother wish the son to resemble the father in valour, justice and giving but not in leaving women.
teaches: The Kural assumes the father is the standard the son's goodness reflects back on, while the akam mother makes the son's goodness a correction of the father, so the same likeness that honours a father in the Kural reproaches him in the Kalittokai.

note: In Kural 1259 the woman went to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him; in Kalittokai 87 the wife tells her heart that sulking at a shameless man is pointless and gives up her complaint.
teaches: Both wives abandon the sulk through the heart, but for opposite reasons: in the Kural the heart's desire overrides her, in the Kalittokai the heart concludes that a man without shame cannot be moved by sulking, so ending an oodal can be resignation as well as longing.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that even if he wears a garland she accuses him of wearing it for another woman; in Kalittokai 88 the wife points to his faded garland, the pollen of other women's hair and the nail marks on him.
teaches: The Kural presents the wife's suspicion of a garland as groundless jealousy from the man's side, while the Kalittokai wife reads the same evidence correctly, so the couplet's comic complaint rests on an akam scene in which the garland really was a sign.

note: Kural 1325 has a faultless man delight in being kept from his beloved's arms; in Kalittokai 89 the husband says he has done no wrong (தீதோ இலேன்) and the wife calls the claim deceit and expects him to fall at her feet confessing.
teaches: The Kural builds the pleasure of oodal on the man's real innocence, while the Kalittokai shows the same plea of innocence as the stock defence of a straying husband, so the couplet's playful exclusion presupposes a faultlessness that akam wives treat as the thing in dispute.

note: Kural 1260 asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in fire can say 'we will join and then sulk'; Kalittokai 90 ends with the wife asking whether women whose hearts cannot hold restraint (நிறை ஆற்றா நெஞ்சு) can say they will not bear his wrongs.
teaches: The Kalittokai gives the couplet's rhetorical question a full case: a detailed charge of a night visit, his dream defence and his plea, so that the wife's collapse comes after she has proved him guilty, showing that the melting heart of the Kural overrides evidence and not only pride.

note: In Kural 1288 the woman says his chest is to her as liquor is to drinkers, though it does shameful harm; Kalittokai 91 ends with the wife saying her heart melts when she sees him whatever wrong he does, so he need not try to please her.
teaches: The Kural states the compulsion as the woman's confession, while the Kalittokai draws its consequence for the man: because she always yields, he has no motive to behave, so the wife's helplessness becomes part of the reason the straying continues.

note: Kural 559 says that if the ruler bends justice the sky withholds rain; Kalittokai 99 praises the king for rains that come by his rightness and then asks whether his wife alone lies outside that rightness.
teaches: The Kural ties rain to the king's public justice only, while the Kalittokai grants the rain and still finds injustice at home, so the friend shows that the doctrine's measure of a ruler can be met in full while a wife is wronged.

note: Both have the man set the gods' world against lying in the beloved's arms: the Kural asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter, Kuruntokai 101 puts earth and heaven together on one pan of a balance against a single day of embrace.
teaches: The Kural's open question about heaven has an older Sangam answer: the poet had already weighed both worlds together against one day and found them light, so the couplet's question reads as an allusion to that verdict rather than a doubt.

note: Both put the woman in the same bind, nearly in the same words (உள்ளின் உள்ளம் வேமே; உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்): remembering burns her and not remembering is impossible.
teaches: The Kural keeps Avvaiyar's bind and drops her last line, the charge that the man is not noble, so set side by side they show the couplet turning a complaint against him into a pure description of her state.

note: Both make the woman's pain open with the evening: the Kural's sickness buds at dawn and blooms at evening, and in Kuruntokai 108 the jasmine opens red in the sunset as the cows go home and she says she will not survive.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for the sickness rests on a real mullai sight that Kuruntokai 108 shows, the jasmine opening at red dusk as the herds return, so the couplet's conceit is that scene folded into the body of the woman who watches it.

note: Kural 1248 has the woman call her heart a fool for running after the man who left; in Kuruntokai 11 the woman herself bids her heart rise and follow him even past the land of the Vadugar, since staying here cannot be survived.
teaches: The heart that the Kural woman scolds for following is the one the Sangam woman sends out on purpose, so the same impulse is folly in the Kural's chapter and the only means of survival in Maamulanar's poem.

note: Both hang the woman between love and shame: the Kural has the two hung from a carrying pole that is her life, Kuruntokai 112 names the town's talk as the fear and pictures her as a branch an elephant has snapped that still hangs by its fibre.
teaches: Kuruntokai 112 gives the Kural's evenly balanced pole a cause and a breaking point: the weight on shame's side is the town's gossip, and the balance is already a break held only by a strand, which the couplet's still image does not show.

note: Both tie the slipping bangles to the absence of the lord of the shore (துறைவன்): in the Kural they announce his leaving to the town; in Kuruntokai 117 the friend says let him stay away, smaller bangles can be bought from the sellers.
teaches: The same sign of wasting is grief in the woman's mouth and a weapon in the friend's: Kuruntokai 117 shows the slipping bangle could be turned into mockery meant to shame the man, which the Kural's lament never does.

note: In the Kural the woman pities the evening as a fellow sufferer and asks if its mate is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 118 the evening is loveless (நாரில்) and the birds and beasts that settle in loneliness are company she gets no comfort from.
teaches: Read together they show two answers to the same hour: the Kural's woman finds a companion in the grieving evening, while the Sangam woman finds the whole world, beasts and gatekeepers included, going home around her, so the evening isolates rather than consoles.

note: Both have the man say that his strength has been broken by a young girl: the Kural by her bright forehead alone, though foes in battle feared him; Kuruntokai 119 by the likeness of a hatchling snake felling a wild elephant.
teaches: Kuruntokai 119 supplies the image behind the Kural's paradox of the mighty man undone by a forehead: the elephant brought down by a hatchling snake, a picture of poison not strength, which explains why the couplet's warrior has no defence.

note: In both the woman says her lover gave her sickness and pallor: Kuruntokai 13 says plainly he gave the sickness and pallor fills her eyes; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns Kapilar's single complaint of a gift into an exchange with two sides, naming what was taken (சாயல், நாண்) as well as what was given, so the pair show the 'he gave me pallor' formula growing into an account of loss.

note: Kural 1151 (the friend or the woman to the man): if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the woman he himself said men are women's life, so he will hold back.
teaches: The couplet states as a threat what the Kuruntokai friend leaves the man to infer from his own words: if men are the women's life, then his going kills her and any promise of a quick return is addressed to the dead, which is why the friend can be sure he will stay.

note: Kural 1227 (the woman) calls love a sickness that buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 136 (the man) says love is neither a spirit nor a disease and does not swell and subside, but has its season like an elephant's musth when it finds one to look on.
teaches: The two agree that love keeps time but disagree on what kind of thing it is: the Kural's woman makes it a disease with a daily clock inside her, the Kuruntokai's man denies it is a sickness at all and makes it a latent season set off from outside by sight, so whether love is illness depends on whether one is waiting or seeing.

note: Kuruntokai 140: the woman asks how the gossiping town came to know the grief she bore in silence; Kural 1180: the woman says it is not hard for the town to learn the secret of those whose eyes beat it out like a drum.
teaches: The Kural answers the Kuruntokai woman's question: she kept silent, but her eyes told the town, so the gossip she resents is her own grief made public by her body, not betrayal by anyone else.

note: Kural 331 calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for lasting. Kuruntokai 143's friend says impermanence alone is permanent, and draws hope from it.
teaches: The Kural uses impermanence to rebuke attachment, but the friend of the love poem applies the same truth to grief, showing that the doctrine was a two-edged tool: what cannot last includes the pallor of longing, so it consoles as readily as it warns.

note: Naladiyar 2: wealth stays level with no one but turns like a cart wheel, so share it the day it comes. Kuruntokai 143 uses the wealth that does not stay with a generous man as the image of pallor that will pass.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues from wealth's instability to giving, and the love poem had already fused the two into one image, the giver whose wealth leaves him, and turned that ethical commonplace into a promise that sorrow too is the kind of thing that leaves.

note: Kural 1168: the night that puts all living things to sleep is pitiable, having no companion but her. Kuruntokai 145: the long night here has only sleepers who will not talk with the sleepless.
teaches: Both women stay awake while everyone sleeps, but the Kural turns her loneliness into a mock pity for the night, while the Kuruntokai blames the sleeping village; together they show that the wakeful heroine's complaint can fall on the night or on the people, and that the couplet's wit grows from the poem's social grievance.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover met in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 147: the hero says the dream, as if it had brought her, rouses him from sweet sleep.
teaches: The Kural's woman blames waking and spares the dream; the Kuruntokai's man blames the dream itself for ending his sleep, so set together they show that the dream meeting was felt as both gift and cheat, and that the blame shifts with which side of it the lover dwells on.

note: Kural 1134: the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (the man speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty is a small sand dam that holds as long as it can and gives way when the sweet flood presses (the woman speaks).
teaches: Both picture desire as a flood against shame, but for the man shame is a raft that is swept away with him on it, and for the woman it is a dam that holds the water back, so the shared image is divided by gender: his shame rides the flood, hers resists it.

note: Kural 1251: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame (the woman speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty struggled long, held as long as it could and now gives way.
teaches: The Kural states the collapse of restraint as a single blow of an axe, while the Kuruntokai gives it duration and fellowship, a modesty that 'suffered with us' long before giving way, which shows the couplet compressing a process the older poem tells as a struggle.

note: Kural 1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near. Kuruntokai 150: the woman says the pain swells when she thinks of his chest and vanishes when she embraces it.
teaches: The Kural's man finds the paradoxical fire in the woman, but the Kuruntokai heroine finds the same sickness in herself and sets it off by memory, not distance, so the pair shows that the burning-and-cooling belongs to both lovers and that thinking of the absent one is itself the burning.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart where it goes seeking, since the lover lives within it. Kuruntokai 153: her heart, once timid, now goes along the night slope to him without tiring.
teaches: The Kural mocks the heart's going out as needless because he is already within, while the Kuruntokai heroine marvels at the same going as courage, so the pairing shows the couplet's wit resting on an older picture of the heart as a traveller on the lover's road.

note: Kuruntokai 156: the lovesick hero asks the Brahmin whether his unwritten learning holds a medicine to unite the parted. Kural 1102: the man says other illnesses have other cures, but this woman is herself the cure for her sickness.
teaches: The couplet reads as the answer to the Kuruntokai hero's question: no learned remedy exists, because only the woman herself cures the sickness she causes, so the pair turns the hero's doubt of the Brahmin's lore into the Kural's general rule of love's medicine.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 163 she asks the sea who has hurt it, since she hears it crying at midnight.
teaches: Both women treat a natural thing as a fellow sufferer, but the poem shows how the projection is built: she knows the sea grieves because she herself is awake to hear it, so the sympathy is evidence of her sleeplessness rather than a fancy.

note: Kural 1090 says liquor delights only one who drinks it while love delights at a look; in Kuruntokai 165 the man, having only seen her hair and grace, says the sight came on his desire like toddy on top of joy.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's claim that love works by sight alone but denies the contrast with liquor: for the man who has looked, seeing acts exactly like a second drink, so the couplet's rule holds while its comparison is turned around.

note: Naladiyar 363 calls a wife who does not enter the kitchen at dawn a disease and one who does not serve what she cooked a demon; Kuruntokai 167 shows a young wife, smoke in her kohl eyes, cooking and serving with delight at her husband's praise. On the Naladiyar's reading the act is a duty enforced by threat; on the poem's it is the wife's own joy.
teaches: The same kitchen duty that the ethics book defines by the horror of its failure is shown in the Sangam poem as freely chosen pleasure, so the pair shows the domestic norm seen from the husband's fear and from the wife's satisfaction.

note: Both are the man speaking of the madal: Kuruntokai 17 lists as a general rule what men do when love hardens (ride the palm horse, wear erukku, become a street spectacle); Kural 1133 says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The Kuruntokai poem supplies the public ritual (the erukku garland, the mocking street) that the Kural compresses into a single inventory of loss, and the Kural adds what the older poem leaves unstated: that taking up the madal costs a man his shame and manliness.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse; in Kuruntokai 173 he mounts it with shame killed (நாணட்டு) and says the town will name her fault.
teaches: The Kural counts only what the madal costs the rider, his shame; the poem names what it is for, turning his public shame into her blame on the town's tongue, which is the pressure that makes the threat work on her kin.

note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth and the other world not for those without grace; Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves for wealth, in this world wealth alone is wealth and grace has no one.
teaches: The heroine grants the Kural's premise about this world in its own words (இவ்வுலகத்து) and drops its consolation: with no other world in view, the couplet's balance of wealth and grace collapses into a world where grace has no owner.

note: In Kural 1148 the woman says hoping to quench love with gossip is like quenching fire with ghee; in Kuruntokai 175 she refuses to tell everyone she is not grieving and asks what the gossip matters.
teaches: The Kural's woman answers the town with an argument that talk only feeds love, while the poem's woman refuses the remedy the friend proposes, public denial, so the pair separates two defences against gossip: rebutting its power and declining to perform the concealment that would silence it.

note: Kuruntokai 18 says her love hangs on her small life like a great jackfruit on a small stalk; Kural 1163 says love and shame hang from the two ends of a carrying pole that is her life.
teaches: Both picture love as a weight hanging from life, but the Kural adds shame as a counterweight, so the Sangam image of a stalk about to snap under one load becomes in the couplet a pole balanced between two loads that will snap either way.

note: Kuruntokai 182: the lover asks whether throwing off his great shame (பெருநாண் நீக்கி) and riding the palm horse through the street will win her after the messenger failed; Kural 1132: body and life will mount the palm horse once shame is put aside (நாணினை நீக்கி).
teaches: The Kural states the madal threat as a general law of the unbearable, while the Kuruntokai shows its occasion (a failed go-between) and counts its price in other men's mockery, so the Kural's 'putting shame aside' is a public cost the hero weighs, not a private loss.

note: Kuruntokai 184: the hero tells his companions his heart is caught in the net of the fisher girl's eyes; Kural 1084: the man says the artless girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them.
teaches: Both men describe a first sight as the girl's eyes acting on them, but the Kuruntokai draws the weapon from her own people's trade (the fishermen's fine net), showing that the Kural's abstract killing gaze was, in the older poetry, given a landscape and a craft.

note: Kuruntokai 185: the girl asks what use it is to tell him she has wasted because of him; Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts her is hearing him called cruel.
teaches: Both heroines decline to blame the man for their wasting body, but for opposite reasons: the Kural's woman defends him, the Kuruntokai's expects no answer from a man as unmoved as the rock under the beaten kaanthal, so the same refusal can be loyalty or despair.

note: Kuruntokai 187: he is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts; Kural 1291: she asks her heart why it is not hers when his heart stays with him.
teaches: Kapilar gives the image and the Kural the argument of one complaint: the man's heart keeps to itself like stone while hers goes over to him, and together they show the heroine's quarrel is with her own heart's softness more than with his hardness.

note: Kuruntokai 188: evening has come, aiming at her beauty, when the mullai has budded and he has not come; Kural 1221: she tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the lives of wives.
teaches: The Kuruntokai shows why the evening attacks: it arrives with the season he promised to return by, so its hostility is the broken promise made visible, which the Kural's address to the evening leaves unstated.

note: Kuruntokai 190: at midnight in the storm she hears the cattle stall's one bell ring with every step of the bull; Kural 1168: the night that puts all beings to sleep has her alone for company.
teaches: The Kural's claim that she alone keeps the night company is proved in the Kuruntokai by what she hears: only a wakeful listener counts the bull's every step by its bell, so the single sound measures the sleepless solitude the couplet asserts.

note: Kuruntokai 199: the lover tells his heart his love-sickness will last on into the other world; Kural 1315: he told her they would not part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
teaches: The Kural's joke works only because Paranar's belief was the convention: love was expected to outlast this birth, so a lover who promised only 'this birth' had set a limit the older poem's lover would not accept.

note: In both the man praises the woman he has just joined by addressing a creature of the flowers: Kuruntokai 2 asks the bee whether any flower is more fragrant than her hair; Kural 1111 tells the anicham it is soft but she is softer.
teaches: Valluvar keeps the Sangam device of praise through an apostrophe to nature but changes the sense judged, from smell to touch, and drops the witness: the Kuruntokai man asks the bee for evidence, the Kural man simply declares the verdict.

note: Kuruntokai 200: surely he has forgotten, but we do not forget; Kural 1207: what would become of her if she forgot, when she knows no forgetting and remembering burns.
teaches: The Kural keeps forgetting inside the woman, as a danger she cannot afford, while Avvaiyar turns it outward as a charge against the man, proven by the rains that came on time, so the same refusal to forget can be self-torment or an accusation.

note: Kuruntokai 202 sets the nerunji's flower, sweet to the eye, before its thorn as the lover's kindness before his cruelty; Kural 1120 uses only the nerunji fruit, the thorn, to say how soft things feel to her feet.
teaches: Both poets know the nerunji as a plant that pleases first and pricks after; the couplet takes only the prick to praise a woman's delicacy, while the Sangam poem uses the order of flower and thorn to tell the history of a love, so the same plant can measure a body or a story.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover is going; look here, the pallor is spreading on my body. Kuruntokai 205 asks how the pallor on her forehead knew so soon, when the shore lord has only now driven away.
teaches: The couplet's two pointing words make his going and her paling one instant; the Kuruntokai poem has the same instant but turns it into a question to the pallor itself, and supplies the scene the couplet leaves out, the white chariot rising like swans and the sea spray on its wheels.

note: Kuruntokai 206 tells the wise to keep from love because the woman is too sweet, her words like ambrosia; Naladiyar 41 tells men to turn from desire because the admired body is a frail bag the crows would tear.
teaches: The same counsel, keep away from love, rests on opposite judgments of the beloved: the Sangam lover flees because she is ambrosia and the pain is love's own, the Jain moralist because she is carrion under skin, so the later ethic keeps the advice and reverses its reason.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 207: he left without telling her, thinking that if he spoke, going would become hard, and she heard of it from others.
teaches: The couplet's demand to be told assumes the parting is spoken; the Kuruntokai man knows the power of that speech so well that he avoids it, so the heroine is denied even the chance to answer him that the Kural's speaker uses.

note: Kural 1209: her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of one who said they were not separate. Kuruntokai 218: he, like life to her life, who could not bear a parting even a blink long, can now forget her and stay away, and she will still think of him.
teaches: The couplet names the wound as the broken claim of oneness; the Kuruntokai poem gives the claim its measure, not a blink apart, and adds what the woman does with the wound, vows, omens and thought, so the poem shows the couplet's dying as a life kept busy with ritual.

note: Kural 1255: the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to those sick with love. Kuruntokai 219: her restraint has gone far and her mind urges her to go to him, but she holds back for fear he will ask 'who are you?'
teaches: The couplet says the lovesick cannot know the pride of not following; the Kuruntokai heroine, lovesick, still stays, held back not by pride but by fear of being met as a stranger, so the poem shows a restraint that survives the loss of honour and the couplet's claim is too absolute.

note: Kural 1227: this sickness buds in the morning, swells through the day and blossoms in the evening. Kuruntokai 220: in the evening the jasmine opens its small buds like a wild cat smiling, and the man who left for wealth has not come.
teaches: The couplet makes a flower's day the shape of love-sickness; the Kuruntokai poem shows the real flower, the mullai opening its buds at dusk in the season he named, at the moment her grief opens, so the metaphor rests on the evening flowering of the jasmine land.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life; in Kuruntokai 222 the man says she takes the head of the raft when he does, the tail when he does, and would follow him into the current.
teaches: The couplet names the inseparability as a metaphor, and the poem shows how a lover knows it: she mirrors his every movement in play and would follow him into danger, so the body-and-life bond is proved by action before it is stated.

note: Kural 110: there is escape for every other killing of good, none for one who kills a benefit; in Kuruntokai 225 the friend promises the girl's hair to the man only if he does not forget kindness as an enthroned king does.
teaches: The Kural's absolute rule becomes a condition of marriage in the poem: the friend uses ingratitude, the one unpardonable fault, to define in advance what deserting the girl would be.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes to seek when the lover is inside it; Kuruntokai 228: though he left for a far country, he is near to her heart.
teaches: The same indwelling is used two ways: the couplet makes it a reason to scold the restless heart, while the poem makes it a consolation that cancels the distance, so the lover in the heart can either rebuke longing or quiet it.

note: Kural 1247: the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; Kuruntokai 231: neglected by the man in her own town, she says her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like a loosed arrow.
teaches: The couplet presents a choice still open between desire and shame, while the poem shows it already made and past recall, desire having killed shame on its own, so the Kural's dilemma is the moment before the poem's confession.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftover (மிச்சில்) needs sowing at all; Kuruntokai 233 praises her father's town where the leftover (மிச்சில்) of rice poured out for the great is shared with all without limit.
teaches: The love poet measures a bride's family by the very household ethic the Kural states, even with its word for the leftover, so the hospitality rule was already a mark of a good marriage before it was a maxim about prosperity.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 234: for those without a partner the dawn and the day are evening too.
teaches: The couplet keeps evening as the climax of a daily growth, while the poem refuses any such gradation and makes every hour evening, so on one reading the parted woman has no easier morning at all, which the Kural's flower image allows.

note: Kural 1183: the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange; Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the man that if he means to leave he must first give back the beauty he has consumed.
teaches: The couplet records the exchange as done, and the poem turns the same commercial idea into a demand for repayment that cannot be met, which makes it an argument that he must stay.

note: Kural 1108: an embrace so close not even the wind can part it is sweet to two who desire each other; Kuruntokai 237: the man far away says he cannot count what now stands between their embrace, groves where tigers roar.
teaches: Read together, the measure of separation is the same embrace the couplet praises: where once not even a breeze passed between them, now forests and tigers do, so the poem's distance is felt as a gap inside the embrace.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders lose their old beauty and her bangles slip; Kuruntokai 239: her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there shame left to give up?
teaches: The couplet lists the slipping bangles as a sign of grief, while the poem draws from the same sign a conclusion: since the body has already told, modesty has nothing left to hide, so the wasting licenses the woman to speak out.

note: Kural 1171: the woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her and brought on the sickness; Kuruntokai 241: she bears her desire, while her eyes, which saw the hill man, weep out of their own intimacy.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes as the cause that now complains, while the poem excuses them as loyal intimates of the man, so the same weeping eyes can be charged as culprits or honoured as the part of her that keeps faith with what it saw.

note: Kural 1207: she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns; Kuruntokai 243: she resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep.
teaches: The poem tries the remedy the couplet says is impossible, a vow not to remember, and the very need to vow it confirms the couplet: remembering keeps her awake and forgetting cannot be chosen, only resolved.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has grown pale, and no one says he left her; Kuruntokai 245: worse than her lost beauty would be his unkindness becoming known to many.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women want opposite things from the town: the couplet's woman resents that the blame falls on her body and not on him, the poem's woman dreads exactly that blame reaching him, so the lover can either demand that the fault be named or shield it at her own cost.

note: Kural 791: nothing is as ruinous as befriending without inquiry, for once formed a friendship cannot be left; Kuruntokai 247: the friend says she knew then that the man's friendship is flawless, fruitful, righteous and a raft for kin.
teaches: The Kural's test of friendship is meant to come before the bond, but in secret love the bond comes first, so the friend's knowing it to be flawless arrives after the fact and has to argue, in the Kural's own terms of fruit and kin, that the inquiry would have passed.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 250: the man tells his charioteer to drive the swift horses before evening comes, for her distress.
teaches: The couplet names evening as the feast the returning man looks to; the poem shows why it is a deadline as well as a reward: evening is the hour the stag is with its mate and the hour she suffers most alone, so he must beat it.

note: Kural 1286: when she sees him she sees no fault, when she does not see him she sees only faults; Kuruntokai 252: urged by her friend to reproach him, she says the worthy cannot speak blame to a face.
teaches: The couplet presents her silence before him as a blindness of love; the poem's woman sees the fault plainly and calls him crooked, yet keeps silent by a rule of the noble, so the same silence can be read as love's blindness or as chosen restraint.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Kuruntokai 256: before he could say he would return when the work was done, her weeping eyes blocked his chariot.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's spoken refusal of the promise of a quick return; the poem shows that refusal made without words, before the promise is spoken, and records that it worked: the chariot stopped.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders have lost their fullness and the bangles slip; Kuruntokai 260: the bangled shoulders are filling out again, read with heron and bush as a sign he will return.
teaches: The couplet makes the shoulders a record of his absence; the poem reads them forward as an omen of his return, so the body that registers separation is also consulted to foretell its end.

note: Kural 804: the wise welcome the unasked acts of old friends; Kuruntokai 265 likens the kaanthal bud opening to the bee to duty-knowing men opening to the worthy they have long known, then shows the man ashamed and ready to act once told.
teaches: The Kural's ethic of intimacy is used in the poem as a simile for nature and then as a forecast of the lover's conduct, so the old-friendship rule becomes the friend's evidence that he will marry without being pressed.

note: Kural 335 says that, because death stops the tongue unannounced, good deeds must be rushed to; the man of Kuruntokai 267 argues from Death's crooked, daily taking that those who know it do not leave their women to go after work and wealth.
teaches: The same awareness of death leads to opposite conduct: the Kural spends the short life on merit done in haste, the lover on staying with her and refusing the journey, so impermanence by itself does not decide between duty and love.

note: Kural 1189: the woman says let her body turn pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is well. Kuruntokai 27: her beauty, of use neither to her nor to him, is left for pallor to eat, like milk spilt on the ground.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman accept pallor as a price paid for his welfare, while the Kuruntokai poet counts it pure waste, a yield that reaches no one, so the same pallor in absence is read as sacrifice in one and as loss with no gain in the other.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my wife and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 270: his work done, the man lies on her hair and bids the rain pour.
teaches: The couplet's wish is the poem's fulfilled state: the evening feast he pictured while the king's work held him is given its weather and its pillow, and the rain he dreaded on campaign becomes a blessing once he is home.

note: Kural 1269: for those who wait for the day of return, one day passes like seven; Kuruntokai 271: one day of union has turned into very many days of sickness.
teaches: The couplet stretches the waiting days, the poem multiplies the one day of joy into a long illness, so the woman's suffering is measured not only by slow time but by a debt that a single meeting keeps collecting.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Kuruntokai 272 likens her eyes to the bloody arrow her brothers drew from a stag near a doe parted from its herd.
teaches: The poem stages the couplet's three-way question as one hunt: doe, killing shaft and eye stand together, and because the shaft belongs to her brothers, the deadliness of her look is also the threat of her kin to the suitor.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating without favour and acting after judgement toward everyone; in Kuruntokai 276 the lover thinks of taking his case to the just king's court and at once asks what would become of her.
teaches: The lover's question shows where the Kural's impartial justice stops: a harm done without intent by an innocent girl is real but cannot be judged, so the just court is imagined only to be abandoned.

note: Kural 1168: the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, for it has no companion but her. Kuruntokai 28: she wants to strike, butt or cry out at the town that sleeps unaware of her pain.
teaches: Both set one sleepless woman against a sleeping world, but the Kural turns the loneliness into pity for the night, while the Sangam poem turns it into rage at the town, which shows that the same isolation could be voiced as tender complaint or as a wish to wake everyone.

note: Kural 1229: when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and suffers (on the reading that the town shares her pain). Kuruntokai 28: the town sleeps, not knowing her grief.
teaches: On that reading the Kural imagines the town grieving with the lovesick woman, while Kuruntokai 28 has the town sleep through her grief, so whether the community shares a private sorrow is answered both ways in the love poetry.

note: Kural 1124: she is to him as life when present and as death when she goes; Kuruntokai 280: for one day's union he would not want half a day of life after.
teaches: The couplet equates her presence with life, the poem goes further and trades the rest of life for one day of her, so the man's praise of love moves from equation to sacrifice.

note: Kuruntokai 283 reports the man's maxim that the life of those who have nothing is more shameful even than begging, and he leaves for wealth; Kural 1064 says the worth that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for the world to hold. On the reading that 283 ranks poverty below begging, the two rank the same states in opposite order.
teaches: The Kural makes the destitute man who refuses to beg the height of dignity, while the akam hero's maxim makes destitution itself the deepest shame, so the poems show that the urge to go for wealth rested on a ranking of poverty and begging the Kural explicitly reverses.

note: Kural 1103: the man asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; Kuruntokai 288: the woman asks whether the world of the gods is sweeter even than the hurt that comes from kin because of her lover.
teaches: The couplet weighs heaven against the joy of love, the poem weighs it against love's pain, so the woman's claim is the stronger: not only the embrace but even the suffering it brings outweighs the gods' world.

note: Kural 1130: he lives joyfully in her heart, while the town says he is unloving and lives apart; Kuruntokai 289: she grieves for him out in the rain, and the clamouring town grieves for her more.
teaches: In both the woman's thought goes out to the absent man while the town's goes to her plight, but the town's verdict differs, blame in the Kural and pity in the poem, so the town's talk in akam is not fixed as hostile gossip and can be her chorus.

note: Kural 660: making wealth by deceit and feeling safe is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. Kuruntokai 29: the heart, passing over good counsel, is like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain, plunged into a flood it cannot hold.
teaches: In both the unfired pot is ruined by what it is made to hold, so the image locates the fault in the vessel rather than the water: wealth got by fraud undoes its keeper as desire taken in against counsel undoes the heart.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now seem to announce the parting; Kuruntokai 299: the woman's shoulders gain beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves, after the tryst on the shore.
teaches: The couplet gives the swelling and the wasting as public evidence that others read, while the poem gives them as the woman's own bewildered discovery, tied to the day her eyes saw him and her ears heard him, so the same bodily sign is both the town's proof and her private record.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 30: a lying dream of his embrace deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed, alone.
teaches: The Kural blames waking in the abstract, while the Kuruntokai poem shows the very moment, the hand on the empty bed, so the couplet's complaint gains a scene and the scene gains a name for its cause.

note: Kural 1218: in sleep he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart. Kuruntokai 30: on waking from the dream she finds only the empty bed and calls herself alone and pitiable.
teaches: The Kural consoles the dreamer that waking only moves the lover inward, while the Kuruntokai woman finds no such refuge and is left alone, so the two disagree on whether the waking after a love dream is a loss or a passage into the heart.

note: Kural 1179 says her eyes do not sleep when he fails to come nor when he comes; in Kuruntokai 301 he does not come, and the bell of a chariot that is not there rings in her ear at midnight while her eyes give up sleep.
teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's 'when he does not come' still keeps the eyes open: the ear makes his chariot out of the night, so absence is lived as an arrival that never quite happens.

note: Kural 1150 says the town is raising the very gossip they want, since it will bring the lover round; in Kuruntokai 302 the gossip that calls the pair inseparable is what she fears has kept him away. On this reading the same talk helps in one and harms in the other.
teaches: The pair shows alar cutting both ways in secret love: the talk the Kural's speaker welcomes as a lever toward marriage can, as the poem fears, frighten a lover into staying away altogether.

note: Kural 1205 rebukes the man for barring her from his heart while he keeps coming into hers; in Kuruntokai 302 the man likewise comes only into her heart at midnight, and she asks whether fear of gossip keeps him away.
teaches: Together they give two verdicts on the same phantom visit: the couplet calls it shameless trespass, the poem excuses it as fear of the town, so whether his absence is a fault depends on the reason the heroine allows him.

note: Kural 1171 says the eyes showed him and so she came to see an unending sickness; Kuruntokai 305 opens with the bright fire of love that the eyes brought and follows it to a sickness no one can stop.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes and stops at 'unending'; the poem carries the same sickness to its end in the dunghill cocks' fight that only death stops, so 'unending' is shown to mean ending only in death.

note: Kural 1288 tells the thief that his chest is to her as toddy is to drinkers, though it does them shameful harm; Kuruntokai 309 says the women are like the neythal that blooms again in the field it was weeded from, though he does them many unkind things.
teaches: Both say she cannot leave him though he harms her, but the Kural calls the bond an addiction while the poem calls it rootedness in his own field, so the pair shows the same dependence judged as weakness and as loyalty.

note: Kural 1222 asks the dim evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 310 sees the sky dazed like herself at day's end and then says she may yet live if someone will carry word to him.
teaches: The couplet stops at fellow-feeling with the evening; the poem turns that fellow-feeling into a need for a messenger, so the evening lament is shown as the point where the heroine starts to seek a go-between.

note: Kural 1271 has the man tell the girl that though she hides it, her eyes go beyond her control and speak; in Kuruntokai 312 the man marvels that by dawn she is wholly one of her kin again, face unmoved. On the poem's reading her concealment holds.
teaches: The pair sets two views of the girl's secret side by side: the Kural's man reads it in her eyes, Kapilar's man admires a disguise he cannot see through, so concealment in kalavu is both a failure and an art.

note: Kural 791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since for the faithful there is no leaving once the friendship is made; Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the shore lord is tied and settled, hard to untie.
teaches: The heroine states as her settled joy the very fact the Kural gives as the reason for caution, so the pair shows that love's bond is the friendship the ethics book warns about, entered without the inquiry it prescribes.

note: Kural 1288 addresses the lover as thief whose chest is like toddy that harms; Kuruntokai 318 calls the man thief too, but also the one bound by his oath and the raft who must carry her across.
teaches: The Kural's 'thief' names only the sweet harm, while the poem turns the same title into a claim: whoever stole is bound to restore, so the word becomes the ground of her demand for marriage.

note: Kural 1221 says the hour is not evening but a spear that eats the life of the wedded; in Kuruntokai 319 the rain-evening comes as the stag and the elephant take shelter with their mates, and she asks what will become of her life if he does not come.
teaches: The poem shows why the evening kills: it is the hour when every creature goes to its mate, so the Kural's bare claim that evening eats life gets its cause in the paired beasts the heroine watches.

note: Kural 1131: for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse. Kuruntokai 32: to ride the madal in the street is shame, and to live apart is shame too.
teaches: The same lover's threat is a safeguard in the Kural and a disgrace in the Kuruntokai, which only weighs it as the lesser of two shames, so the madal was argued both as the lover's last strength and as an equal dishonour to living on without her.

note: Kural 1227: love-sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening. Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is a lie.
teaches: The Kural gives love a daily clock with evening as its worst hour, while the Kuruntokai lover says true love cannot tell the hours apart, so the two set the convention of the evening's pain against the claim that real longing knows no time.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on one day only, yet the talk has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; Kuruntokai 320 says they have not even the blame of laughing together one day, yet the town spreads gossip.
teaches: The Kural concedes one meeting behind the talk while the poem denies even that, so the pair shows the gossip of kalavu needing ever less fact, until in 320 it rests on nothing but the town's cruelty.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether heaven is sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; in Kuruntokai 323 the man calls every other day chaff and counts as lived only the days spent sleeping on her shoulders.
teaches: The couplet ranks the embrace above heaven's pleasure; the poem turns the same ranking on time itself, so the pair shows the claim growing from a comparison of joys into a measure of which days of a life count as lived.

note: Kural 1192 says a lover's grace to those who love is like rain to those who live by it; Kuruntokai 327's man has learned to withhold grace from those who live only if he is gracious (நல்கின் வாழும்), and water reaches her as a flood from his hill.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's rain of grace is shown in reverse: the one who lives by it is denied it, and the water that does come down from the lover's hill is muddy and destroys, so dependence on grace is seen from the side of its failure.

note: In Kural 1167 the woman swims love's flood without seeing a shore and at midnight is the only one awake; in Kuruntokai 329 she cannot sleep in midnight's thick dark, thinking of the man on the desert road.
teaches: The couplet gives the midnight wakefulness as a bare state; the poem gives it a content, the road he took buried under fallen iluppai flowers, so the pair shows the sleepless mind of separation travelling the absent man's road.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 330 she asks whether the sorrowful evening (புன்கண் மாலை) and its loneliness exist at all in the land he went to.
teaches: Both make the evening testify against the absent man, but in opposite ways: the couplet makes it a fellow sufferer, the poem imagines a land without it, which would explain why he stays away, so the pair shows the evening serving as companion and as accusation.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman tells her friend to prevent the departure of the one fit for her, since once he goes union is hard; in Kuruntokai 334 she tells her friend that if he leaves, what they lose is only their one life.
teaches: Both speak to the friend before a parting, but the couplet asks for help to stop it while the poem asks for none and names the price, her life, so the pair shows the same plea in two moods, one still bargaining and one already resigned.

note: In Kural 1081 the man cannot tell whether she is an anangu, a peahen or a woman; in Kuruntokai 337 he is sure she is an anangu (அணங்கென) and adds that she herself does not know it.
teaches: The couplet's bewilderment is about what she is; the poem moves it to the gap between her power and her ignorance of it, the one-sided love of kaikkilai, so the pair shows the anangu figure turning from a lover's confusion into an observation about a girl not yet aware of herself.

note: In Kural 1249 the woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking, since the lover is within it; in Kuruntokai 340 her heart, where he dwells, can settle on neither side and sways like a kandal with ebb and tide.
teaches: The couplet treats the heart's going out to him as an absurdity to point out; the poem's rooted kandal, bent out by the ebb and back by the flood, makes the same divided heart a rhythm she cannot stop, so the paradox becomes a condition rather than an error.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should at once do what lasts; in Kuruntokai 350 the friend calls the wealth for which the man left நிலையாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, and regrets they did not stop him.
teaches: The ethicist's premise that wealth does not stay becomes in akam an argument against the journey itself: the Kural spends unstable wealth on lasting good, while the friend counts the lasting thing given up as the woman's company, so the same premise judges the pursuit of wealth from the household's side.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the woman the town raises the very gossip they want, since the lover will grant marriage when asked; in Kuruntokai 351 the friend tells the girl to rejoice because their kin have declared the marriage, and asks whether the gossiping town is still the same.
teaches: The couplet hopes the town's gossip will force the marriage, and the poem shows the end of that hope: once the kin declare the marriage, the talk that pressed for it has nothing left to say, so the gossip served its purpose and the friend can mock it.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not left; Kuruntokai 352: the woman says she knew the reality of the small dull evening only when she could not see him.
teaches: The couplet states the late discovery of evening's pain as a bare fact, and the poem gives the sign through which she learned it, the creature that leaves its day-tree lonely at dusk, so the knowledge the Kural reports is shown arising from a scene in which the hour itself repeats the parting.

note: Kural 1261: the woman's fingers are worn from marking the days since he left; Kuruntokai 358: the friend speaks to the woman who scores lines and clings to the wall, and points to the mullai buds as the season he promised.
teaches: The couplet gives the counting of days only as the woman's wasting, while the poem lets the friend answer it with a sign outside the wall, the season's buds, so the count the Kural leaves open is closed by the promised season and becomes ground for comfort.

note: Kural 1151's friend refuses comfort with an ultimatum about who will still be alive when he returns; Kuruntokai 363's friend asks whether crossing the waste is sweet when even the bull there stays by its doe.
teaches: The same dissuasion of a man about to leave is made by threat in the couplet and by the example of the road's own creatures in the poem, so the pair shows the friend has two arguments, death of the one left and the shame of being less faithful than a beast.

note: Kural 1104's man asks where she found a fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near; Kuruntokai 376's man says she is cool in summer and warm in the cold season.
teaches: Both men praise her as a reversal of temperature, but the couplet makes it depend on his distance and the poem on the season, so together they show the convention of the beloved as a climate of her own, which the Kural turns inward into the lover's desire.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not yet left; in 386 the woman knew evening only as the festival hour of jewelled women and did not know its sorrow wide as the earth.
teaches: The poem fills in what the couplet's woman did know of evening before: the public festival hour of the women's gathering, so the Kural's 'I did not know' is the reversal of a known, shared evening into a private sorrow.

note: Kural 1167: the woman swims the fierce flood of desire and sees no shore, and at midnight only she is awake; in 387 she swims across the evening to reach the night as its bank, and finds the night's flood larger than the sea.
teaches: The couplet's shoreless flood gets its hours in the poem: the evening is the first water and the night a second, larger one, so the shore the Kural's woman cannot see is the bank of evening that only opens onto the night.

note: Kural 1146: gossip about one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; in 395 the woman says no one frees her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, nor even tells her not to fear.
teaches: The eclipse served both as a spectacle everyone sees and as a rite in which everyone rushes to help: the Kural takes the first sense for gossip, the poem the second for rescue, and the woman's complaint is that her eclipse draws the town's eyes but none of its help.

note: Kural 1187: she lay in his embrace and turned aside, and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up; in 399 pallor is moss on the village well that parts where he touches and spreads where he lets go.
teaches: The couplet's instant hyperbole is given a mechanism by the poem: pallor is a surface like well-moss that closes the moment the hand lifts, so the Kural's 'at that very moment' is not exaggeration but what anyone at a village well has seen.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life. Kuruntokai 40: the man says their mothers, fathers and they themselves were strangers, yet their loving hearts have mingled like rain in red earth.
teaches: Both men declare an inseparable bond, but the Kuruntokai first denies any tie of kin, so the union it praises is made between strangers and inseparable only after mingling, which the Kural's body-and-life image, a pair joined from birth, does not show.

note: Naladiyar 125 says the bond (தொடர்பு) with small men wanes (தேயுமே) of itself like the moon while friendship with the great grows; Kuruntokai 42 asks the hill lord whether our bond (எம் தொடர்பும்) will wane (தேயுமோ) even if desire ends.
teaches: The same two words, bond and waning, show the friend putting the lover to the Naladiyar's test of character: a bond that wanes once its first cause, desire, is spent marks the small man, so her question demands that he prove himself one of the great.

note: Kural 1151 has the woman (or her friend) speak at once: if you are not leaving, tell me; your quick return, tell those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 43 says neither spoke: she thought he would not go, he thought she would not bear it.
teaches: The couplet is the sentence whose absence Avvaiyar's poem mourns: set beside it, the poem shows a parting that happened because pride on both sides kept that sentence unsaid, so the Kural's bluntness reads as the cure for the silence that undid the Kuruntokai pair.

note: Kural 1222: the woman tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed as hers. Kuruntokai 46 asks whether the sad evening (புன்கண் மாலை) is absent in the land where he has gone.
teaches: Both women make the evening's sorrow a test of the absent man: the couplet asks whether the evening's partner is as hard as hers, the poem asks whether he has any evening at all, and its sparrows settling with their young supply what the couplet leaves out, that evening is when every creature with a home returns to it.

note: Kural 1119: the man tells the moon that if it would resemble her face it must not appear for many to see. Kuruntokai 47: the friend tells the long white moon it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
teaches: Both speakers wish the moon would not shine for others, for opposite reasons: the Kural's lover wants her face kept to himself, the Kuruntokai friend wants the meeting kept from watchers, so the moon's openness, which the couplet turns into a compliment, is in the older poem the danger that ends secret love.

note: Kural 1315: the man says they will not part in this birth, and her eyes fill with tears. Kuruntokai 49: the woman asks that even when this life turns into the next he be her husband.
teaches: The couplet's joke rests on a wish it never states, that the bond reach past this birth; Kuruntokai 49 is that wish in the woman's own mouth, so the pair shows why 'in this birth' wounds her: she had asked for the next one too.

note: Both have the woman in separation with eyes that cannot sleep; Kuruntokai 5 uses the sleeplessness to ask whether this is love-sickness, Kural 1179 says the eyes do not sleep when he is away nor when he comes.
teaches: The Sangam woman learns from sleepless eyes that she is in love, while the Kural woman, past that discovery, finds the sleeplessness survives even his return, so the couplet assumes and goes beyond the moment the older poem records.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness and her bright bangles slip. Kuruntokai 50: the shoulders he embraced have wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, adorned with loneliness.
teaches: The couplet names the wasted shoulder and slipping bangle as the sign of separation; the poem shows what the sign was used to say, setting it against his town's ford adorned with flowers, so the body's loss becomes an accusation of a place that still flourishes.

note: Kural 1143: the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not welcome, since it is like having what he has not yet obtained. Kuruntokai 51: the friend says the gossiping town too speaks of the girl with him, and her mother and father favour him.
teaches: The couplet values gossip as a foretaste of a union not yet had; the poem shows the next step, when talk that pairs the lovers joins the parents' consent, so the gossip the Kural's lover enjoys in fancy becomes one of the voices that brings the marriage about.

note: Kural 447: who can ruin those who keep companions that rebuke them? Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking companions (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்) that it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread past bearing.
teaches: The Kural makes the rebuking companion a ruler's best protection; the lover grants the rebuke its good intent and shows where it stops, since love has spread like butter on hot rock before any word could check it, so the ethic of correction meets its limit at kaamam.

note: Both set the sleeping world against the one woman awake in separation; Kuruntokai 6 leaves her alone awake under the dead night, Kural 1168 makes the night itself her companion, pitied for having no one else.
teaches: The Kural turns the bare Sangam contrast of a sleeping world and one waking woman into a conceit in which the night shares her vigil, so the couplet adds a companion, even a mocked one, to a solitude the older poem leaves complete.

note: Kural 1199: though the one she longs for gives no grace (நல்கார்), even word of him is sweet to her ears. Kuruntokai 60: even if her lover does not grace her (நல்கார்) or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
teaches: Both women claim sweetness from a lover who gives none, with the same verb; Paranar's simile of the cripple licking his empty palm beneath the honeycomb shows what the couplet's maxim hides, that this sweetness is tasted only in imagination, a pleasure that is also the measure of what is withheld.

note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; the heart in Kuruntokai 63 states that premise, and the man answers it only by asking whether she can come along.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the poem shows the Kural's blunt premise as a voice inside a lover's head that he can neither refute nor obey, so the maxim's truth is granted and its price is made visible in the separation.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but this woman is the cure of the sickness she gives; Kuruntokai 71: if medicine, she is medicine; if treasure, she is treasure.
teaches: The man's claim that she is his medicine is the same in both, but the poem adds treasure (வைப்பு), so under its paalai colophon the cure-paradox of the couplet becomes an argument against leaving to seek wealth.

note: Kural 1084: the eyes of this artless girl devour the life of those who see them; Kuruntokai 72: the eyes of the girl scaring sparrows from the millet have, like arrows, made him sick for all to see.
teaches: The poem places the couplet's paradox, the simple girl with killing eyes, in her actual work of chasing small birds off the hill millet, and adds what the couplet lacks: the wound is public, known to everyone.

note: Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts the woman is hearing him called cruel; Kuruntokai 77: there is no fault in him, or if any, it is that her soft shoulders proved easy to leave.
teaches: Both women defend the absent man with their wasted shoulders as the evidence, but the poem goes further than the couplet by moving the blame onto those shoulders, while its desert of dead travellers' cairns lets the reproach stand unspoken.

note: Kural 906 says men who fear their wife's shoulders are worthless even if they live like gods; in Kuruntokai 8 the other woman mocks the man for doing his son's mother's bidding like a mirror image, and on the akam reading this obedience is the household holding him, which the poem does not condemn.
teaches: Read together they show that the conduct the Kural brands as a man's vice appears in akam only as the other woman's spiteful jibe, so the ethical charge of wife-obedience and the love poem's victory of the wife are the same act seen from opposite sides.

note: Both use the saying 'eating one's own in one's own house': Kural 1107 for the joy of the beloved's embrace, Kuruntokai 83 for jackfruit hanging sweet on the lover's own hill as the mother announces he will come.
teaches: The pair shows the phrase was a common measure of untroubled, owned pleasure; the Kural applies it to union itself, while the Kuruntokai friend lays it on the lover's land at the moment marriage is promised, so the image belongs to the settled household rather than to secret love.

note: In Kural 1168 the woman says the night that lulls every creature to sleep has only her for company; in Kuruntokai 86 she asks at midnight whether anyone else hears the cow's bell.
teaches: The Kural asserts that she alone is awake; the Kuruntokai poem tests the claim with a question and finds one other wakeful thing, a lonely cow whose bell rings with her, so the solitude the Kural states is shown as a search for a companion.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has paled, no one says he left her. Kuruntokai 87: the god destroys the false, my lover is not false, yet my brow has paled.
teaches: Read together they show why the blame lands on her body: in the Kuruntokai the woman herself clears him before the avenging god, so the only visible sign of the wrong is her pallor, which is exactly the one-sided verdict the Kural's woman complains of.

note: Kural 1222 asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 92 at sunset watches birds hurry home with food for their young.
teaches: The Kural guesses that the evening suffers from a cruel partner like hers; the Kuruntokai's dusk answers that every creature in it is hurrying home to its own, so the hard-heartedness is her man's alone and not the hour's.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering where there is no lover who knows you suffer; Kuruntokai 93: what is sulking worth when love is gone; do not speak against him, he is mother and father to us.
teaches: The Kural gives the reasoning that sulking needs a lover who will notice; the Kuruntokai wife draws the conclusion in her own case and adds the reason she cannot quarrel, her total dependence on him, so the maxim is shown ending in silence rather than in oodal.

note: Kural 1088: my might, feared in battle, broke before her bright brow; Kuruntokai 95: her grace like water quenched my strength like fire.
teaches: The Kural reports the man's defeat as a wonder of scale, so great a strength and so small a brow; the Kuruntokai explains it by kind, water putting out fire, so his strength was not outmatched but met by its natural undoing.

note: On the Kural reading where gossip feeds love and keeps it from drooping, Kuruntokai 97 disagrees: the secret turned to talk in the square is one of four things scattered apart, with her beauty lost and the man in his own town.
teaches: The man in the Kural can welcome gossip as fuel for love, while the woman in the Kuruntokai counts it among her losses, so the pair shows that rumour's value in the akam world depends on which lover bears it.

note: Both use the formula of the world that cannot do without water (நீர் இன்று அமையா உலகம், நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு): Kural 20 as the first step of an argument that all conduct depends on rain, Natrinai 1 as the measure of how she cannot live without him.
teaches: The same clause is a step in Valluvar's proof about rain and a simile of a woman's dependence in Kapilar, which shows it was a common saying both drew on, apt to the akam poet for a lover's need as it was to the moralist for the world's.

note: Natrinai 1's heroine calls her man sweeter the longer one knows him (நீடுதோறு இனியர்) and the bond of the noble lofty; Kural 783 says the companionship of people of character delights the more it is practised, as a book does the more it is studied.
teaches: The heroine uses the Kural's rule about friendship with the noble as the premise of a love argument, reasoning from his character that he cannot leave her, so a maxim about good company served in akam as evidence against a report of parting.

note: Both are the man struck by the girl's look and both find a doe in it: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Natrinai 101 says the shore hamlet was sweet to live in before he saw her deer-like look.
teaches: The couplet says what the look contains, the doe beside Death; the Natrinai man shows what Death in it did, measuring the wound as the loss of his home's sweetness from the day he saw her.

note: Both have the woman's heart following the man who has left; Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for going after him, Natrinai 107 says the heart that went has the good share and she who stayed has the pain.
teaches: The same split between a heart that follows and a self left behind is judged in opposite ways: Valluvar's woman despises the following heart, the Natrinai woman envies it, because she is the one left to bear the town's gossip.

note: Both are the separated woman at evening in a pastoral scene: in Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; in Natrinai 109 she stands alone like a cow tied by the head in a dripping shed.
teaches: The pastoral evening gives the Kural woman a sound that attacks her and the Natrinai woman a posture she shares, so the mullai hour wounds in one from outside and in the other makes her one of its own tethered creatures.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife as one who lives within the means of the man who took her; Natrinai 110 shows a spoilt girl who once refused honeyed milk now eating only at alternate meals in her husband's poor house, refusing her rich father's food.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's rule costs and how strange it looks to her own family, who ask where she learned it, so living within his means appears as a change of person rather than a skill.

note: Both are the deserted woman facing the town's gossip: in Kural 1149 she asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her; in Natrinai 116 the bond has burst like a fallen jackfruit yet the women still keep up their talk of her.
teaches: In the Kural his leaving cancels the shame of the gossip, while in Natrinai the gossip outlives the bond it was about, so the pair shows two answers to the same abandonment: indifference to talk or bearing talk about a love that is already gone.

note: Both are the woman's love-sickness at evening in separation: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds at morning, grows through the day and blooms at evening; Natrinai 117 sets her evening on the shore, where the neythal closes and birds go home together while he does not think of her.
teaches: Set beside the shore's evening, where the neythal shuts, the couplet's sickness that blooms at evening reads as the one flower that opens when the others close, and the poem supplies the scene the couplet compresses into a single growth.

note: Kural 90 says a guest withers when the host's face changes; in Natrinai 120 the man brings a guest into the house because his sulking wife will not show an angry face to a guest and he will see her smile.
teaches: The rule of the welcoming face that the Kural lays on the host becomes, in the poem, the husband's lever against the wife's sulk, so the guest is both the object of hospitality and the akam go-between (வாயில்) that ends an oodal.

note: Kural 1268 has the man wish that the king fight and win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer reports that the king has let them go and drives him home to the wife preparing the evening feast for guests.
teaches: The couplet is a wish spoken while the war still holds him, the Natrinai poem the same wish granted and on the road, so together they show the full arc of the mullai return, and that the king's release and the evening guest-feast were the fixed terms of it.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman asks her friend, if she would guard her, to stop the man's departure; in Natrinai 124 the friend does exactly that, telling the man not to go and pointing to the season.
teaches: The Kural gives only the request, while the Natrinai shows the friend carrying it out, adding the rainy-season argument and the anril image, so the couplet's appeal is revealed as the opening move of a known scene in which the friend speaks for the woman to the man.

note: Naladiyar 16 says the fleeting pleasures of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling its garland, are not found among the wise; Natrinai 126 says no wealth surpasses youth and that love must be taken in youth because wealth cannot buy it later.
teaches: Both start from the shortness of youth and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar to refuse youth's pleasure, the Natrinai hero to refuse wealth for its sake, so the same premise of impermanence served the akam poets as an argument for love and the didactic poets as one against it.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 129 mocks as a great joke the man who says he will go and that we will live on at home until he returns.
teaches: Both turn the man's promise of return into a question of whether she will survive to see it, but the Natrinai supplies what the couplet leaves out, the midnight thunder she must hear alone, so the Kural's bitter one-liner has behind it a scene in which the waiting itself is the threat.
