note: Kural 1168 has the sleepless woman say the night, which puts all creatures to sleep, has only her for company; Natrinai 132 begins with the great town asleep but fills the house with the cold wind, a trembling dog, guards by the bed and watchmen ringing the bell.
teaches: The couplet's solitude of the one waker is qualified by a poem in which others do wake, but only to keep her in, so the sleepless night of the guarded girl is not loneliness but confinement.

note: In Kural 1236 the woman, bangles slipping, is hurt when her friend calls the man cruel; in Natrinai 133, with the same slipping bangles, the friend says he will not cause them suffering, and the word gives the woman a little relief.
teaches: Held together they show the friend's two possible speeches and the woman's response to each, blame wounds her and defence of him comforts her, yet the Natrinai measures that comfort as a smith's sprinkle on a furnace, small and passing.

note: Kural 1157 says the bangles slipping past the wrist spread the news that the lord of the shore has left; in Natrinai 136 the father fits the girl with golden bangles that cannot slip, which hide the blame of her shoulders.
teaches: If, as the Kural says, slipping bangles are the body's gossip, the Natrinai shows that gossip could be silenced by a tight bangle, so the sign of separation was something a household could conceal, though only the lover could cure what it signified.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on only one day yet the gossip spread like the eclipse; Natrinai 138 says that their meeting at the ford was once known only to their eyes and asks whether the whole festive town does not know it today.
teaches: The Kural compresses into an eclipse the leap from one private sight to public talk that the Natrinai spreads over a remembered garland and a dancing town, and the Natrinai's overhearing hero shows the complaint was spoken to push him toward marriage.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world can give back to the rain, whose obligation seeks no return; in Natrinai 139 the hero blesses the rain cloud as his helper for the night rain that fell while he lay with his wife.
teaches: The Kural's rain serves the world and gets nothing back, while the Natrinai hero answers its private help with a blessing, so the poem shows the one return a person could make to the rain and turns the rain's public good into a favour done to two people.

note: In Kural 1102 the man says every disease has a cure other than itself, but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Natrinai 140 the refused man tells his heart there is no other medicine for the sickness he has.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox from the side of a man already united with her, the Natrinai from the side of a man refused, so the same claim that she alone is the cure is a joke in fulfilment and a sentence of endless pursuit in refusal.

note: Kural 84: the goddess of fortune dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face. Natrinai 142 sets the wife who rejoices at a guest even at night in a woodland of unfailing plenty (பொய்யா யாணர்).
teaches: The poem gives the couplet's householder a face and a hour: the glad host is the waiting wife, her welcome extends even to guests who arrive after dark, and the plenty the Kural promises is already the landscape the returning husband drives through.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 148 ends, after the man has gone for his work, with 'I will not grieve, friend; may his journey prosper'.
teaches: On the same departure for work the two voices take incompatible stands, the couplet refusing all comfort as if the going were a death, the poem blessing the journey; the iraicchi of the tiger hunting for its mate shows how the friend's comfort turns the one stance into the other.

note: Kural 1147: the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness. In Natrinai 149 the street women spread the gossip, the mother beats the girl with a cane, and she resolves to leave with the shore lord.
teaches: The couplet says that gossip and the mother's scolding feed the love they mean to kill; the poem shows what that fed love finally does, turning the same two pressures, the street's finger at the nose and the mother's cane, into the reason for elopement.

note: Both are about restraint that can no longer keep love hidden: Kural 1254's woman says she used to think herself restrained but her love now breaks out in public; Natrinai 15's friend tells the man they have let go even their long modesty and the town may gossip.
teaches: The Kural records the loss of restraint as an inner confession, while Natrinai 15 makes the same loss a threat spoken to the man, likened to a mother forced to give her child to a demon, so the collapse of naanam also served as a lever to force marriage.

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the palmyra horse that lovers ride. Natrinai 152: love gave him the madal, the erukku gave him gossip, the sun gave loneliness, night gave helplessness.
teaches: The couplet records one exchange, virtues lost for a madal; the poem turns it into a chain of gifts in which each thing hands on the next harm, so the madal is not the end of the loss but the first link of a day-long sequence.

note: Kural 338: the bond of body and life is like a bird that flies off leaving its nest alone. Natrinai 153: her heart has gone after him and her body, left behind, lives on by eating, like the lone man guarding a ruined town.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's departure without the death: the heart flies off as the life does in the Kural, yet the body stays, sustained only to keep watch over its own emptiness, so separation in love is a death the body is made to outlive.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman. Natrinai 155: at their second meeting he asks her aloud whether she is the goddess of the sea or of the backwater, and she answers with a smile and tears.
teaches: The couplet leaves the man's doubt as a question in his head; the poem puts the same question to the girl and lets her answer it, since a smile and tears are a woman's reply, not a goddess's, so the doubt is settled by her response.

note: Both hold that wealth does not stay: Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance and goes as it disperses; Natrinai 16 says wealth vanishes like the trail of a fish in a pond.
teaches: The Kural uses wealth's impermanence to counsel detachment, while the Natrinai man uses it to choose his wife's gaze over a journey, so the same doctrine served an argument for staying at home in love as well as one for letting go.

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the madal. Natrinai 160: shame, decency and good conduct he knew better than his friend, before he saw her.
teaches: The couplet says the virtues were possessed and are now gone; the poem says they are still known, better than the rebuker knows them, and simply no longer govern him, so love takes away their rule, not the knowledge of them.

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; in Natrinai 166 a husband says that seeing his wife he is like those settled in virtue, and gives that and his son's first play as reasons he will not leave.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's claim used as an argument against the paalai journey: a husband offers the household's settled virtue as his answer to the pull of wealth abroad, which makes the maxim a reason to stay.

note: Both rank modesty above life: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for it but never shame for life; Natrinai 17's girl says she almost forgot the modesty dearer than life when her mother spoke softly.
teaches: The Kural states the ranking as a firm rule, and the Natrinai girl who holds it nearly breaks it not under threat but under a mother's tenderness, so the poem shows the rule's weak point to be a kindness the maxim does not foresee.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her man's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 174 the wife, told she should be well now that he is back and never leaves her side, says he gave his chest to another woman and an embrace is worth nothing without love.
teaches: The Kural grounds the refusal in shared possession; the poem grounds it in absent love even when he is wholly present, so the pair separates two grievances the oodal chapters run together: that he is shared, and that he is there without love.

note: Kural 1147 says love's sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Natrinai 175 shows a mother who has never met the man, believing the hamlet women's petty talk, glaring at the girl's pale body at midnight.
teaches: The poem supplies the order the couplet only implies: the gossip reaches the mother first and her watch follows from it, so she acts on hearsay about a man she does not know, which is why her words feed the sickness instead of curing it.

note: Kural 1276: the woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking hold the hardship to come and the thought of his lack of love; in Natrinai 177 the girl tells her friend she reads his going in his being more tender than before, along with his spear wiped and his shield decked.
teaches: The couplet names one sign, excess tenderness; the poem shows it read together with the readied weapons, so the Kural's inference is the abstract of a scene in which caress and war gear together give the man away.

note: Kural 212 says wealth earned by effort exists to do good to the worthy; in Natrinai 186 the wife says her husband crossed the waste for wealth with a heart that strives for others.
teaches: The wife in the poem defends a painful separation with the Kural's ethic of earning in order to give, so the household rule appears here as the reason that made the paalai journey honourable in her eyes.

note: Both answer a lover's departure by saying she will not live until he returns: Kural 1151 says to tell his quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 19's friend says go, knowing well she will not live the few days till you come.
teaches: The couplet's bitter refusal of comfort appears in Natrinai 19 inside a friend's demand for marriage in the secret stage, so the claim that she will die before he returns worked in kalavu as pressure to marry and not only as grief.

note: Kural 211: duty seeks no return, and the world makes none to the rain. Natrinai 194: the friend asks what return (கைம்மாறு) they can make to the elephant and the parrot.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's word for repayment to beasts who helped without meaning to, the parrot that raided the millet and so kept the girls in the field, so her mock gratitude turns the rule of unrepayable benefit into a teasing way of announcing that the meetings are over.

note: In both the separated woman speaks to the moon about the man who is gone: the Kural asks it not to set so she may see him; Natrinai 196 asks it to show where he hides.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one blessing and plea a scene the Natrinai poem argues at length: the moon sees all worlds, so its silence is a witness's lie and its waning the punishment, which shows how much reasoning lies behind the Kural's single request.

note: Both are a wife's sulk at the husband's straying, fixed on his chest: Kural 1311 refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes; Natrinai 20 describes the girl who slept on the lord's chest and walked off at dawn with crushed earring and withered garland.
teaches: The Kural states the wife's charge in general terms, and Natrinai 20 shows the single scene behind such a charge, the rival's disordered body read as proof and blessed in irony, so the couplet's reproach rests on a convention of reading the other woman's appearance as evidence.

note: Natrinai 210 says grand speech and harsh riding are not wealth, only the fruit of deeds, and the wealth of the worthy is a gentle-eyed nature; Kural 241 says the wealth of grace is the wealth of wealths, since the base also hold goods.
teaches: The friend aims the Kural's general ranking of wealths at a particular rich husband who has hurt his wife, and narrows grace to fear of the dependant's distress, so the maxim is shown at work as a rebuke inside a marriage.

note: Kural 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute and lute sweet; in Natrinai 212 the bards tune their strings on the road while at home the child's sweet voice asking to be held made the mother anxious each time.
teaches: The child's voice that the Kural ranks above music becomes, while the father is away, a reminder of his absence, so the couplet's household joy assumes the father is present to hear it.

note: Kural 613 says the pride of generosity rests on effort; the man of Natrinai 214 leaves saying fame, pleasure and giving do not come to those who sit idle.
teaches: The akam poem shows the Kural's rule as a departing husband's stock reason, quoted by the wife he leaves and then mocked by the thunder, so the maxim that giving needs effort was already common speech, and the poem counts what it costs the one left behind.

note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress at once, like the hand of one whose garment slips; the other woman of Natrinai 216 says her lovers do not help her sorrow as the hand helps a hurt eye, yet the town they live in is still sweet.
teaches: The parathai admits her lovers fail the Kural's test of friendship, the hand's unthinking help, and still finds their mere presence in town enough, so the pair shows love surviving a failure that by the Kural's measure would end a friendship.

note: In Kural 1260 the woman says those whose hearts melt like fat in fire cannot say they will join and then hold out in a sulk; in Natrinai 217 the wife says that though the man is very sweet she will brood and sulk, since making him feel it drives off her loneliness.
teaches: The Kural woman doubts that a loving heart can keep a sulk, while the Natrinai wife resolves to keep one precisely because she loves him and wants the long loneliness to end, so the two disagree on whether the sulk is weakness overcome or a strategy of love.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; in Natrinai 218 the girl, past the promised season, lists the evening's creatures, the bats going home, the cock calling his mate, the owl, and asks if she must hear the andril alone.
teaches: The Kural woman makes evening a fellow sufferer, while the Natrinai girl finds every creature of the evening paired or going home, so the same projection onto nightfall can give companionship or prove isolation, and the unmarried girl gets only the second.

note: In Kural 1188 the woman says people speak of her pallor but none says he left her; in Natrinai 219 the girl says she will not blame him though pallor spreads and she dies, since he and she joined of their own accord.
teaches: The Kural woman complains that blame falls on her skin and not on him, while the Natrinai girl takes the pallor as her own because the union was her own choice, so the pair shows how a self-chosen secret union changes who can be blamed for the suffering.

note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting (ஒப்புரவு) lives and others are counted among the dead; in Natrinai 220 the lover says the townspeople, if they knew ஒப்புரவு, would side with him and tell him not to be a stranger to the girl.
teaches: The lover appeals to the Kural's civic duty of fellow-feeling to claim the town's support for a love match it is condemning, so the pair shows ஒப்புரவு invoked against the town's own idea of propriety.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and keep the evening feast. Natrinai 221: the work done, the man bids the charioteer hurry to the wife who loves to host guests and the son who now calls him.
teaches: The Kural states the soldier's wish to trade the king's war for the evening feast at home in two lines; the Natrinai scene fills that home with a hospitable wife and a child just learning to walk and call him father, so the 'feast' of the couplet is shown to be a whole household's welcome, not only the wife's.

note: Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word? Natrinai 224: what can I say now to those who assured me 'we will not part' and set off for the waste?
teaches: The Kural poses as a moral question who is at fault when an assurance is broken; the Natrinai woman, using the same verb of assuring (தெளித்த), cannot even ask it aloud and lets the budding kuravu and the koel's 'stay joined' do the accusing, so the broken word is judged by the season instead of by her.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 229: so go, finish the work, but do not linger, for the north wind has come.
teaches: Faced with the same announcement of departure, the Kural's speaker refuses any promise of a quick return as useless to the dying, while the Natrinai friend bargains for exactly that promise and binds it to a season already arrived, so two stances to a leaving husband stand side by side: refusal by death, and consent with a deadline.

note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.

note: Kural 1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that not even a breeze can part. Natrinai 240: even the closest embrace is such that sleep comes between, yet the forest road stands like a mountain.
teaches: The Kural makes the gapless embrace the ideal of union; the Natrinai lover admits that even such an embrace is parted by sleep, and that admission is what lets his heart argue for leaving, so the ideal of perfect closeness becomes, in the man's mouth, a reason that union is already imperfect.

note: Kural 754 says wealth rightly gained yields virtue and pleasure, placing wealth below and in service of aram; Natrinai 243's woman says that if parting for wealth in such a season is men's nature, wealth must be dearer than aram itself. On the plain reading men's conduct, as she sees it, contradicts the Kural's ordering.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's ordering of virtue over wealth being turned into an accusation from inside the household: the woman accepts the scale but finds that men's going inverts it, so the ethical rule became a weapon in the akam speaker's mouth.

note: Kural 1102 has the man say that this jewelled girl is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes; Natrinai 247's friend tells the man that for the girl's pallor there is no medicine other than him.
teaches: Read together, the cure that is also the cause belongs to both lovers, and the Natrinai shows the claim used as pressure: what the man says of her in delight, the friend turns back on him as an argument that only marriage can treat the girl's sickness.

note: Kural 616 says effort brings prosperity and its absence brings want; Natrinai 252 states the same as the man's resolve (no rare wealth for those who stay) and then shows the planned work blocked by the woman's beauty.
teaches: The pair shows the maxim of effort accepted in full by the lover and yet not acted on, so the Natrinai marks the limit of the Kural's rule: it decides nothing while something dearer than prosperity stands in the way.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 256 is the man telling his grieving wife that he has given up going, through the burnt forest and even through the cool forest of the rains.
teaches: Read together, the Natrinai supplies the one answer the Kural's speaker would accept, a plain 'I am not going', and shows that to be believed it had to renounce the pleasant season as well as the harsh one, since a man who stays only while the road is burnt will go when it rains.

note: Kural 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words; Natrinai 262's man, seeing his wife already wasting, ends on 'hard indeed is the shame of having nothing' (இன்மையது இளிவே).
teaches: The Natrinai shows what Valluvar's shame of poverty weighs against in a man's life: it is the one argument strong enough to set beside a wife's midnight suffering, so the couplet's social fear turns out to be the engine of the paalai parting.

note: Both are, on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural, the friend trying to stop the man's departure: Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 269 sets before him his son climbing down his chest and his wife's eyes on his face.
teaches: The pair shows two opposite tactics for one thurai, the Kural's friend making the woman's death the stake and the Natrinai's friend making the man's own pleasures at home the stake, so the couplet's threat is one option among the friend's arguments, not the only one.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a house is for tending guests; in Natrinai 280 the wife, urged not to sulk at her philandering husband, says she cannot even sulk because her house, like the Velir's Kunrur, is never free of feasting guests.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the Kural's household duty turned into a weapon in love: hospitality is a reason no one can fault, so the wife uses it to refuse both the sulk and the husband, and the virtue becomes the frame of her pride.

note: Natrinai 284 has the man's body as an old rope pulled at both ends by two tuskers, heart against reason; Kural 1163 has the woman's life as a carrying pole with love and shame hung at its two ends, in a body that cannot bear them.
teaches: Set side by side, the two show one figure, a load-bearing cord or pole strained between two claims, serving both the man's conflict of love against duty and the woman's of love against shame, so the tradition pictured a lover's divided mind as a physical strain whatever the second claim was.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die half done; in Natrinai 284 the man's own reason says the same, that leaving work unfinished brings ignorance and disgrace, while his heart urges him home.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's maxim on unfinished work already living inside an akam man as the voice of his reason, and the Natrinai adds what the maxim leaves out: obeying it costs a body torn like a rope between two tuskers.

note: Natrinai 289's woman says her lover would not shift from his word even if the earth shifted, though the promised rains have come without him; Kural 1154's woman asks whether any fault lies with those who believed the assuring words of one who then left.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women answer the same broken promise in incompatible ways, one keeping her faith in his word intact and blaming only her unpitied state, the other turning the promise into a charge against him, which marks out the range a waiting woman's speech could take.

note: Kural 1102: the jewelled woman is herself the cure of the sickness she causes; Natrinai 294: at the wedding, the friend says the man's chest has become both the sickness and the joy, as the sky bore both fire and wind.
teaches: The couplet states the paradox as the lover's private discovery in secret union, while Natrinai 294 has the friend confirm it at the wedding, so the pair shows the same claim moving from a lover's wonder to a public fact once marriage makes the cause of the sickness its lawful cure.

note: Kural 1156: if he is hard enough to speak of leaving, the hope of his grace is vain; Natrinai 296: told he will go, the woman asks what will become of her, since he leaves with a heart set on work even in the season when the kondrai blooms and the parted grieve.
teaches: Kural 1156 finds the man's hardness in the announcement itself, and Natrinai 296 adds a second measure the couplet does not give, the timing: to leave in the very season made for grieving apart shows a heart given wholly to work.

note: Both set a sleepless woman against a night in which everyone else sleeps: Kural 1168 says the night that lulls all creatures has only her for company; in Natrinai 303 the hamlet has fallen silent and only the paired anril cries.
teaches: The couplet's lonely vigil turns out, in the Natrinai scene, to have one other waker, a bird that has its mate, so her sleeplessness is measured against a pairing she lacks, and her question is whether he lies awake too.

note: Both make pallor the immediate price of the lover's absence: Kural 1187 says it came the moment she turned in his embrace; Natrinai 304 says beauty joins her when he joins and pallor wrecks it when he parts.
teaches: The couplet records the speed of the pallor; the Natrinai woman draws the moral that the same chest is joy and harm at once, like the hand that plays to the asunam and then kills it.

note: Both are the moment the man announces departure: in Kural 1151 she answers with a sharp demand, tell me if you are not going; in Natrinai 308 she can neither ask nor stop him and only presses against his chest.
teaches: The Kural gives the woman a defiant sentence to stop the journey, while Natrinai shows wordless grief doing what the sentence could not, since it is her silence that melts his resolve.

note: Both start from the same premise, that youth passes and does not return; Naladiyar 11 concludes that the wise renounce desire from childhood; Natrinai 314 uses it to condemn the man who left an embrace for wealth.
teaches: The same commonplace of fleeting youth served opposite ends: for the akam woman it is a reason to spend youth in love now, for the didactic poet a reason to give love up, so the ascetic use of the maxim takes over an argument love poetry had already made.

note: Both argue from an unknown lifespan against putting something off: Naladiyar 19 says do not defer good deeds because the wind may drop the unripe fruit; Natrinai 314 says no one knows the measure of a life, yet he left her for later gain.
teaches: The pairing shows that 'do not defer, life is short' was a shared argument whose object changed with the genre, virtue in the Naladiyar and love in the Natrinai, where wealth-seeking is the deferral blamed.

note: Natrinai 32's friend ends with the saying that the great take a friend after inquiry and do not inquire after befriending, and that once accepted it is hard to undo; Kural 791 says nothing brings ruin like befriending without inquiry, since there is no leaving once the bond is formed.
teaches: The Kural's rule and its reason, inquire first because a formed bond cannot be left, already serve in the Natrinai as a proverb a friend applies to a girl choosing a lover, so the ethics of friendship framed the irrevocability of a love match before Valluvar set them apart in his book on polity.

note: Natrinai 327's girl stakes her life on the belief that the noble do not fail in what they owe; Kural 990 says that if the worthy declined in worth the earth could not bear its load.
teaches: The Kural makes the failure of the worthy a cosmic impossibility, while the Natrinai girl turns the same belief into a private wager on one man, so the pair shows what the maxim costs when a single life rests on someone being counted among the worthy.

note: Both have a woman awake at midnight with a love too great to get past: the Kural's flood with no shore and only herself awake, Natrinai 335's great love with no one to clear it while moon, surf, wind, anril and lute keep the night going.
teaches: The couplet's 'only I am here at midnight' is filled in by the older poem with a crowd of sounds and scents that will not stop, showing that the woman's solitude is not silence but a shore night that keeps working on her.

note: Kural 1222's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Natrinai 343's woman asks whether there is no such evening in the land where her lover went.
teaches: Both turn the woman's grief into a question about where evening reaches, but the Natrinai grounds it in a village dusk of cows, offerings and a crow going home to its kin, so the couplet's bare question gains the scene that makes the absent man's freedom from evening seem unnatural.

note: Kural 1168's woman says the night that puts every creature to sleep has only her as companion; Natrinai 348's woman lies sleepless while moon, festival town and paired bees all rejoice, and asks whether the world fights her or she the world.
teaches: The couplet makes the sleepless woman the night's one companion in a sleeping world, while the Natrinai wakes the whole world in celebration around her, so the same sleeplessness becomes either a bond with the dark or a quarrel with everything else.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the girl, the man overhearing, that the town is raising the very gossip they want; in Natrinai 354 the friend tells the man to his face that his friendship has become gossip as loud as the salt traders' din.
teaches: The pair shows the friend aiming the same town gossip toward marriage from two sides: told to the girl in his hearing it is the talk they hoped for, told to the man directly it is a public noise that shames his friendship.

note: Kural 580 says that those who want a refinement worth loving will drink poison they see poured; Natrinai 355's friend says the very refined (நனி நாகரிகர்) drink even poison if old friends give it, and asks the man to be kind to the girl by கண் ஓடி.
teaches: Valluvar files the poison saying under கண்ணோட்டம; the Natrinai quotes it and then asks for exactly that kindly regard, so the pairing shows the courtesy ideal of the chapter on statecraft working in love poetry as the friend's lever to bind a man to a girl who has no one else.

note: Kural 1207's woman says she does not know forgetting and that even remembering burns; Natrinai 357's woman says the remembered day of play with the man has scarred her heart and will not fade, and on that she says she can bear the delay.
teaches: In both, memory cannot be shed, but the couplet makes it a burn and a danger, while the Natrinai makes one remembered day the scar on which the woman rests her claim to endure, so the same unfading memory is wound in one and support in the other.

note: Kural 1311's woman refuses the philanderer's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 360 the friend, or on the colophon's second reading the wife in oodal, refuses him at the door and pictures yesterday's women left like a doll after the festival.
teaches: Both refuse the straying husband, but the couplet objects that he is shared, while the Natrinai shows how he uses and discards each courtesan, so the wife's scorn reaches past her own wrong to the rivals he abandons.

note: Kural 1228 has the waiting woman say the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Natrinai 364's heroine says the herdsmen's kondrai flutes and the cattle bells at evening will take her life if they come with the rain after the named season has passed.
teaches: The couplet's flute that kills is given its setting by the Natrinai poem, cows driven home, bells that never knew thunder and the season he named already gone, which shows why a sweet pastoral sound became deadly: it marks the homecoming hour, and the season promise turns it into proof that he has not come.

note: Kural 1137 holds that nothing is nobler than a woman who suffers a sea of desire yet does not ride the madal, that is, does not make her love public; in Natrinai 365 the friend proposes that they slip the mother's watch, go to the common in daylight before everyone and ask the way to his town to rebuke him.
teaches: The couplet makes the woman's silence a virtue, but the Natrinai friend uses the threat of breaking it, a daylight public walk being the woman's form of the madal, as a lever on the overhearing hero, so the restraint the Kural praises was also a weapon that worked only while it might be dropped.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say love's axe breaks the door of restraint (நிறை) barred with shame; Natrinai 369's heroine, left unmarried while he seeks wealth, says she cannot swim across a love that breaks her restraint (நிறை அடு காமம்) like the Ganga in flood breaking dams.
teaches: Both name the same loss, restraint broken by love, but the Kural's image is a single blow to a closed door while the Natrinai's is a flood from the Himalaya that keeps coming each evening, so the poem adds what the couplet lacks: that the breaking recurs at a fixed hour and the woman's question is endurance, how to swim, not resistance.

note: Kural 1268 has the man, held by the king's war, wish that the king win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast for guests; Natrinai 374's man, returning from his work, asks travellers about the wife who longs to feast guests yet weeps.
teaches: The couplet gives the feast for guests as the man's own goal after duty, while the Natrinai poem puts the same wish in the wife and shows it unfulfilled in her tears, so the household's guest-feast was the shared picture of reunion that each partner ascribed to the other.

note: In Kural 1133 the turned-away man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal that lovers ride; in Natrinai 377 the turned-away man, speaking for the friend to hear, asks whether riding the madal and praising the girl through lands and towns will not kill him like a disease.
teaches: The Kural states what the madal costs the man, his shame, while the Natrinai shows what it would do, carry her beauty's praise through every town, so the threat works on the friend because his loss of shame would become the girl's public exposure.

note: Kural 791 says nothing is as ruinous as making a friend without inquiry, since the devoted cannot leave once the bond is made; Natrinai 378 ends with the friend (or the heroine) calling her sleepless nights and the neighbours' gossip the measure of the bond made without inquiry (நாடாது இயைந்த நண்பு) with the lord of the shore.
teaches: The akam poem applies the ethics book's rule for choosing friends to a love made at a girl's sand-house, and its suffering shows the second half of the couplet at work, that she cannot leave the bond once made, so the maxim on friendship was available as a verdict on unwise love.

note: Kural 1161: she would hide this pain, but it wells up like spring water when drawn. Natrinai 382: at evening she must hide her grief even if her life goes.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's wish to hide her pain without a reason and says it fails; the Natrinai woman supplies the reason, that the slander of his enemies would shame him, so concealment in separation is shown to be a duty to his name and not only her modesty.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but the sickness this jewelled woman causes she alone cures. Natrinai 384: eloping, the man calls her the one who was the medicine when he suffered after casting off shame.
teaches: The Kural's paradox that the woman is the cure for the sickness she causes becomes in Natrinai 384 the eloping man's reason for taking her across the waste: he now carries his medicine with him, so the couplet's moment of union is extended into the whole journey of udanpokku.

note: Both concern the town's gossip about a secret love: Kural 1143's man asks whether gossip the whole town knows is not good for him, since it is like having what he has not yet got; Natrinai 4's friend fears that gossip reaching the mother will end the meetings and asks whether the man will take them to his own town.
teaches: The gossip that the Kural's man welcomes as a foretaste of union is, for the women of Natrinai 4, the danger that ends their meetings, which they can only turn into pressure to marry, so the worth of alar in the secret stage depends on who bears its cost.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a household is for caring for guests; Natrinai 41's friend says men suffer far off in the waste because they want the household where the wife cooks for a night guest.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes, in the friend's mouth, a reason for the separation itself: if the house exists for the guest, then the husband's absence earning for it is the rule at work, so the Kural's praise of hospitality is shown to carry the cost the wife bears in paalai.

note: Kural 1151, in Parimelazhagar's reading the friend's words: if you are not leaving tell me, your quick return tell those who will be alive. Natrinai 43: the friend tells the departing man his going is joy to him and ruin to her.
teaches: Both friends answer an announced departure by saying she will not survive it, but the poem adds the grounds the couplet leaves out: the man once said 'fear not', so his leaving is a broken pledge of protection, which explains why the couplet treats talk of a quick return as worthless.

note: Kural 1094: when I look she looks down, when I do not she looks and softly smiles. Natrinai 44: after bathing she gave him an unaimed look and a smile and went home, and now, confined, he asks his heart whether she knows.
teaches: The couplet treats the averted look and smile as a sign the man can read with confidence; the poem shows the same sign after the girl has been shut in, when there is no second meeting to confirm it, and the reading collapses into doubt, so the Kural's reading of hints depends on continued access to her.

note: Kural 333: wealth does not stay, so when you get it do at once what stays. Natrinai 46 calls the wealth the man leaves for மன்னாப் பொருள், wealth that does not last.
teaches: Both call wealth impermanent, but the Kural still tells a man to get it and convert it into lasting good, while the friend uses its impermanence to argue against going after it at all, which shows the couplet's maxim leaving room for the very journey the akam poem condemns.

note: Naladiyar 16: the fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the garland leaves at the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise. Natrinai 46: pleasure and youth pass like an arrow's shadow, so the man should not leave her for wealth.
teaches: The two start from the same premise, the speed with which youth passes, and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar says renounce its pleasure, the Sangam friend says spend it in love and despise wealth instead, which shows that impermanence was an argument both renouncers and lovers used, and settles nothing by itself.

note: Kural 508: one who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble without end. Natrinai 50: the friend failed to guard the girl because she trusted the man without seeing, taking his smallness for greatness.
teaches: The couplet is a rule for a king choosing men; the friend applies the same failure to herself in the household and names its cause, a public reputation (even his enemies admire him) taken in place of examination, so the pair shows the akam go-between bound by the same duty of testing the Kural lays on the king.

note: Kural 616: effort produces prosperity and its lack ushers in poverty. Natrinai 52: the heart set on ஆள்வினை is loveless, and wealth made by toil is a slight thing.
teaches: The Kural makes effort the source of fortune and the duty of a man; the husband of Natrinai 52 calls the heart that obeys that duty loveless and declares its fruit slight, so read together they show that the ethics of ஆள்வினை and the akam of the home make incompatible claims on the same man.

note: Kural 1102: medicine for a disease is something other than it, but for the sickness this woman gives, she herself is the cure. Natrinai 53: the mother prescribes the stream water from the lover's hill as medicine for the girl's shivering.
teaches: The couplet states as a paradox that the cause of love-sickness is its only cure; the poem shows the mother unknowingly obeying it, sending the girl to water that comes from the lover's own hill, and the friend reports it so that the man listening learns he is the medicine and must come to marry.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know evening brings sickness while he who wed her had not left. Natrinai 54: the small dull evening is deeply lonely, she tells a heron going home to its kin, and begs it to carry her plight to him.
teaches: The couplet says evening hurts only when he is gone; the poem shows why, through the heron that at evening flies home to its flock, so the hour that sends every creature to its kin is the hour that marks her lack, and her plea that the bird delay its homing for her is the couplet's sickness acted out.

note: Kural 1293: heart, do you follow him as you please because the ruined have no friends? Natrinai 56: has my heart stayed with him to return together, or has it seen my lost beauty and left me as a stranger?
teaches: The couplet gives only the bitter answer, that the heart deserts her as fair-weather friends desert the ruined; the poem holds that answer beside a kinder one, that the heart is loyally waiting with him, so the Kural's accusation is shown to be one horn of a doubt the woman cannot settle.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is, since their own steadfastness is the best guard; in Natrinai 68 the friend says shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for the household.
teaches: Both reject confinement, but the Kural does so for the wife because her virtue makes it needless, while the Natrinai girls reject it for the unmarried daughter because it blocks a love headed for marriage, so the same verdict rests on opposite views of what the woman's will is for.

note: Both have the wife alone at evening hearing the cowherds' flutes; Kural 1228 calls the flute the messenger of evening and a killing weapon, Natrinai 69 sets the flutes and cow bells among the evening's signs and says that if such an evening came where he is, he could not stay at his work.
teaches: The couplet makes the evening's music a weapon only against her, while the Natrinai wife imagines it falling on him too and so excuses his absence by supposing his land has no such evenings, turning the same lament into a defence of his love.

note: Both are the friend's speech to a man about to leave: Kural 1151 says tell me only if you are not going, and tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 71 grants the woman may let him go and asks whether he can stroke her eyes and leave.
teaches: The couplet argues from the woman's death, the Natrinai friend from the man's own tenderness at the moment of leave-taking, so the two show the dissuasion speech had two separate levers, her survival and his ability to bear the parting.

note: Natrinai 71 opens by calling wealth impermanent (மன்னாப் பொருள்) to keep the man at home; Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should do at once what lasts.
teaches: The same premise, that wealth does not last, yields opposite advice: the Kural tells a man to seek and spend it on what endures, the friend uses it to argue he should not seek it at all, which shows nilaiyaamai served the akam poets as a rhetorical weapon before it was a doctrine.

note: Both are the friend speaking to the woman while the man overhears, about the town's gossip; in Kural 1150 the gossip is welcome because it will push him to marry, in Natrinai 72 his anxiety about gossip is read as a sign his love is drying up.
teaches: In the same speech situation the friend can treat gossip as an ally or as a threat depending on how the man reacts to it, so the pair shows that alar works on the lover's resolve, not on the woman's name.

note: Both concern the woman's indifferent glance in early love: Kural 1099 says looking at each other like strangers is found only in lovers; in Natrinai 75 the rejected man says her glance that does not look has wounded him like a hunter's arrow.
teaches: The look the Kural's observer reads as proof of love is, to the man who receives it, a fatal wound, so the pair shows the same sign read from outside as a disguise and from inside as a refusal.

note: In both the woman tells her friend that the man's departure must be stopped because union after he goes will be hard; Natrinai 79 rehearses the words she might say and asks by what means to stop him.
teaches: The Kural gives the friend a reason to act, while the Natrinai woman supplies the argument she would use, that rejoining after parting makes another parting harder, and then doubts any words will work; the poem shows the couplet's advice as a thing she has already tried in her head.

note: Both are the man at first sight of the girl: Kural 1081 asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, his heart reeling; Natrinai 8 asks whose daughter she is, blesses her father and wishes on her mother the fortune of Thondi.
teaches: Valluvar's man asks what she is and the Natrinai man whose she is, his first words going to her parents, so the Sangam poem shows the couplet's stunned wonder already turning toward the kin and the marriage that will need them.

note: Both have the man say that the woman herself is the only cure for the sickness she causes; the Kural states it as a paradox of medicine, Natrinai 80 says it to his own heart so that the friend who keeps him off will hear.
teaches: The couplet's general paradox becomes in the older poem a lever in a negotiation: by declaring the girl his only medicine where her guardian can overhear, the rejected man turns a private conceit into a claim on the friend's pity.

note: Kural 1268 wishes the king victory so that the man may join his wife and keep an evening feast for guests; Natrinai 81 is that moment reached: the king has quelled the enemy and the man hurries home to a wife whose grief was her longing to host guests.
teaches: Held together they show that the soldier's picture of home was a feast for guests, voiced as a wish before victory in the Kural and as a race home after it in the Natrinai, which adds that the wife's sorrow was her inability to host alone, so hospitality is a couple's act that war suspends.

note: In Kural 1082 the man is struck by her answering look as by a goddess with an army; in Natrinai 82 the man says he cannot bear to look at her form, which strikes his eyes like Valli joined with Murugan.
teaches: The Kural puts the wound in her returned glance, the Natrinai in his own looking at her beauty, and only the Natrinai can name the goddess as the hill's own Valli, so the divine attack of the Kural's abstract couplet is, in the older poem, a local deity of the land where the love happens.

note: Kural 81 says that all of keeping a home and guarding its goods is for caring for guests and doing good; Natrinai 84 says the man leaves his wife for the waste because he cannot live a home life that fails to relieve those who come begging.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the cost of the Kural's rule: if a household exists to give, a household without wealth fails its purpose, so the very ideal that defines home life is what sends the husband away from home and leaves the wife to grieve.

note: Kural 620 says those who toil on without flagging see fate's back; in Natrinai 88 the friend tells the girl not to be stricken as though by their own old deeds but to rise, go and speak to the man.
teaches: The Kural states for the man of affairs that effort overturns fate, and the Natrinai shows the same refusal of fate in a girl's friend inside a secret love, where the effort is speech to the man, so the rule had a domestic use, and the friend's action is an answer to the household's fatalism.

note: Kural 1222 pities the sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) evening and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed (வன்கண்ணது) as hers; Natrinai 89 calls the evening sad (புன்கண் மாலை) but makes it the ally of the hard-hearted (வன்கணாளர்) who do not come. On this reading the evening is a fellow victim in one and an accomplice in the other.
teaches: The same two words, புன்கண் and வன்கண், are distributed differently: the Kural gives the evening its own hard partner and so makes it a sister in grief, while the Natrinai joins the evening to her own hard man, so the woman's view of the hour turns on whether she sees it as abandoned or as sent.

note: Kural 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse; in Natrinai 94 the woman herself says that speaking out desire suits a man while womanhood makes her hold it in, and asks what kind of man he is not to know.
teaches: The Kural's praise of the woman's silence becomes in the Natrinai a grievance spoken by the woman under that rule, aimed at the man who is free to speak and does not, so the restraint the couplet admires is shown from inside as a constraint she resents.

note: Kural 1185 is built on the pointing words உவக்காண், இவக்காண்: look there, he goes; look here, the pallor spreads. Natrinai 96 points with இதுவே, உதுவே, அதுவே to the places where she met him, and ends on the pallor.
teaches: Both make pallor out of pointing, but the Kural points across the distance of a departure seen as it happens, while the Natrinai friend walks back through the places of meeting before an overhearing man, so pallor comes in one from the sight of leaving and in the other from memory of place, used to press for marriage.

note: Paripadal 5 opens by hailing the spear that cut down Sur; in Kalittokai 93 one of the husband's 'goddesses' sang of the red-speared slayer of Sur with him on the hill through the rains.
teaches: The pair shows the Murugan hymn in two settings: in the Paripadal it is temple praise, while the Kalittokai places the same theme in a lovers' pastime on the hill in the rainy season, so devotional song at Murugan's hill was also an occasion for courtship that the wife can use as evidence.

note: Purananuru 243's old man remembers garlanding a doll of packed sand and leaping into deep water as the untaught youth he has lost; Ainkurunuru 124 shows a girl with a sand doll punishing the sea that took it.
teaches: The same shore games of sand dolls and leaps into water are, in the puram elegy, the innocence age mourns, and in the akam barb, the proof that a man has taken up with a child, so the scene of youth carries nostalgia or contempt according to who recalls it and for what end.

note: Purananuru 168 praises Kotran's hill, where hill people sow millet unploughed in the earth a boar has turned and feast on the first new grain; in Ainkurunuru 270 the hunters reap the first crop from the boar-ploughed slope and leave the hill bare.
teaches: The same unploughed tillage and first harvest is plenty and hospitality in the praise of a patron but, for lovers who met at the millet watch, the end of their season and a bare hill, so akam reads the hill's farming calendar as a calendar of meeting.

note: Purananuru 188 says a rich man's days are fruitless without toddling children (குறுகுறு நடந்து); Ainkurunuru 403 shows a toddler (தளர்நடை) pulling a toy chariot and named after his grandfather.
teaches: Purananuru gives as general counsel that toddling children are what make a life worth having, and Ainkurunuru adds, through the grandfather's name the boy bears, that the toddler is valued also as the next link of a famous line.

note: In Purananuru 144 bards see a woman weeping over Pekan's neglect and rebuke him; in 475 the heroine says the bard wept over her wasting more than his master.
teaches: Puram shows the bard's pity for the neglected woman turned into a public rebuke of his patron, and akam shows the woman herself noticing that pity and setting it against her lord's coldness, so the bard's tears were a recognised charge against the man in both genres.

note: In Purananuru 145 Paranar asks as his only gift that Pekan ride to the grieving woman tonight; in 480 the bard, unheard, declares that he is no longer the man's bard.
teaches: Puram's bard spends his claim on the patron to win the woman's cause, while the Ainkurunuru bard, his plea having failed, gives up the claim itself, so the pair shows the patron bond as the bard's leverage and its renunciation as his last resort.

note: Both have winged termites pouring from a red anthill (Purananuru: செம்புற்று ஈயல்; Ainkurunuru: நெடுஞ்செம் புற்றம் ஈயல்); Purananuru makes them the one-day life of kings who defied Vazhuthi.
teaches: The swarm of the first rains meant short-lived ruin in a war poem and food that ends the beasts' hunger in a love poem, and 497's war-loving lord stands between the two, come home from the kind of war in which other men were the termites.

note: Ainkurunuru 74: a young woman climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water, her hair spreading like a descending peacock. Purananuru 243: an old man recalls how in youth he climbed the low marutham branch at the ford and leapt into the deep pool to the wonder of those on the bank.
teaches: The leap from the riverside marutham was a common game of youth in the field towns, and the two books use it oppositely: the akam poet freezes it as the height of a woman's beauty seen by a lover, while the puram poet, leaning on his staff, makes the same leap the measure of what age has taken.

note: Both invocations, ascribed to Perundevanar, list Shiva by the same marks: the konrai garland and chaplet, the bull, the dark throat, the crescent, the matted hair. Akananuru 0 says Umai is joined to him (சேர்ந்தோள் உமையே); Purananuru 1 says the woman's form is one part of him that he can hide within himself.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two openings show each anthology choosing the god's form that suits its matter: the love anthology gives him a consort beside him, the outer anthology a body that holds the woman within it and shelters all lives.

note: Both make the Chera port Thondi famous for its shore and its fragrance: Purananuru 48's bard calls it his own town, smelling of neythal, to direct another bard to its king; Akananuru 10's friend likens the girl's beauty to rich Thondi.
teaches: The friend values a girl in the terms a bard used for a king's town, so a woman's worth in akam could be stated in the public currency of puram praise, as a reason for open marriage rather than secret meeting.

note: Purananuru 158 names Ezhini among the seven dead givers, with his horse and sharp spear; Akananuru 105 names Ezhini of many spears with his horse, whose bowmen drive off cattle on the daughter's road. That both mean the same chief is likely but not certain.
teaches: The chief keeps the same epithets of horse and spear in both books, but the bard remembers him as a lost giver while the mother sees only his raiders on her daughter's road, so a patron's fame looked different from the path his men made dangerous.

note: Purananuru 233 is a bard's cry at the dawn news of Evvi's wounds, wishing it false; Akananuru 115 recalls the battle where Evvi fell and, on our reading, the bards breaking off and laying down the curved necks of their harps in worship.
teaches: The puram poem gives the bards' words at Evvi's fall and the akam poem their gesture, so together they show that his death was mourned with a known bardic rite that a love poet could cite as an image for seed pods on a road.

note: Purananuru 76 praises Chezhiyan, who alone defeated the seven who joined against him; Akananuru 116 recalls Chezhiyan at Koodal routing two great kings who rose together. The battles may not be the same.
teaches: Both poets make the Pandya's fame the defeat of an alliance, seven kings in the puram praise and two great kings in Paranar's simile, so one king against a coalition was the shape his fame took, whichever battle is meant.

note: Both turn on Karikalan's victories: Purananuru 66 praises the king but sets above him the defeated king at Venni who, ashamed of a wound in the back, starved himself to death; Akananuru 125 likens the fleeing north wind to the nine kings who abandoned their umbrellas on the Vaakai field.
teaches: Read together they show the warrior code from both sides: the loser who dies of shame earns more praise than the victor, while the losers who run are proverbial for disgrace, so an akam poet could call a wind cowardly by naming Karikalan's battle.

note: Both praise the lord of Kodai (கோடைப் பொருநன் / கோடைப் பொருந) for giving elephants: Purananuru 205 says the bard's troupe never leaves him without elephants and chariots; Akananuru 13 says he gives to suppliants without limit, pausing only to tame a pit-caught elephant.
teaches: The friend in Akananuru 13 takes the very generosity that Purananuru 205 praises and makes it a ceiling: even wealth that large is not worth a winter apart, so puram praise becomes an akam argument against seeking wealth.

note: Both describe the hero-stone of a man killed recovering cattle, crowned with peacock feather and inscribed with his name (பீலி சூட்டி, பெயர் பொறித்து); 264 mourns the dead man, 131 lines the road with such stones.
teaches: Purananuru 264 shows one stone as a single loss to the bards who depended on the man, and Akananuru 131 shows rows of them as the reason a lover will not travel, so the same memorial carried grief in puram and deterrence in akam.

note: Purananuru 170 praises Pittan as soft to those who come in hope (நசைவர்க்கு மென்மை) and iron to enemies; Akananuru 143 calls him the giver of fine vessels to those who live by hope (நசையின் வாழ்நர்க்கு) and sets the woman's tears in a pool on his hill.
teaches: The akam poet takes from Pittan's fame the same formula of giving to the hopeful that the praise poem uses, which shows a patron's epithet passing whole between the two kinds of poetry.

note: In Purananuru 343 a father refuses suitors even if they bow and offer wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) like Muziri's, where ships bring gold for pepper; in Akananuru 149 the man refuses precious wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) even if easily won, beside Muziri where Yavana ships bring gold and take pepper.
teaches: Muziri's sea trade was the stock measure of the wealth a woman outweighs, used by the war poem for a father keeping his daughter and by the love poem for a husband keeping his wife.

note: Akananuru 152 names Aay as the one who gives to all who come, whether able or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்); Purananuru 134 says Aay is no trader in virtue who gives in this life for a return in the next.
teaches: Together they make Aay's giving unconditional on both sides, asking nothing of the receiver's skill and nothing of the next world, which neither poem says alone.

note: Akananuru 168 compares the roar of the waterfalls to the kitchen of Udhiyan, bound to the duty of giving; Purananuru 2 praises the Chera king who gave great food without limit to the armies of the war.
teaches: The akam poet can borrow the noise of Udhiyan's kitchen as a simile because his feeding was proverbial in puram praise, so a king's fame for food had become a stock measure of uproar.

note: Akananuru 173 places the man's road on the gold-bearing slopes of Nannan of the swift chariot; Purananuru 151 names a patron as kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, whose hill was shut against poets.
teaches: Both books know Nannan by his chariot and his hill, but the puram poem remembers his line for a door shut against singers while the akam poem uses his range only for its gold and its danger, so the same name carries blame in one genre and mere geography in the other.

note: Akananuru 175 compares the lightning to the spear Chezhiyan raised after he won the battle at Alangaanam (ஆலங் கானத்து அமர்கடந்து); Purananuru 23 praises Nedunchezhiyan with the same phrase.
teaches: The identical phrase shows the victory at Alangaanam was already a formula, so an akam poet could use a celebrated battle to light up a love poem's rain clouds.

note: Akananuru 177 places a fertile mango grove on the Kaveri's north bank in the land of Pannan of the warrior anklets; Purananuru 173 praises Pannan of Sirukudi as the healer of hunger whose house rings with feeding.
teaches: If this is the same Pannan, akam uses the puram patron's land as a byword for fertile beauty, so a patron's renown for feeding becomes a measure of a woman's beauty.

note: Akananuru 179 line 1 and Purananuru 151 line 2 are the same line (விண்தோய் சிமைய விறல்வரைக் கவாஅன்); in puram it is the slope of a patron's hill, in akam the slope of the dangerous waste.
teaches: The repeated line shows the poets shared formulas across akam and puram, and that the setting decides whether the same sky-touching slope means a patron's wealth or a lover's danger.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori who ruled Kolli and Malaiyan who rode the horse Kaari side by side among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kaari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
teaches: The bards' roll of the seven great givers sets a killer and his victim together as equals in generosity, and only the akam simile keeps the memory that one of them ended the other.

note: Purananuru 396 praises Ezhini Aathan of Vaattaaru as strength to the weak and kin to the kinless, in a land where the Kosar drink toddy; Akananuru 216 recalls the spear of the lord of Chelli, a Kosar town, pressed into Aathan Ezhini's chest.
teaches: If the two name the same chief, the patron the bard praised as a protector was remembered in akam only for his death wound, which a courtesan uses as a measure of how much she can hurt her rivals.

note: Thazhumban's Unur stands as the measure of wealth in both, here as the region beyond which the lover's noisy departure is likened to Marungur's market, there as the town a girl's beauty is compared to.
teaches: A chieftain's town famous in puram praise was reused by akam poets as a ready scale of plenty, so a patron's fame circulated as a stock of comparison across the two kinds of poem.

note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.

note: Karikal's victory at Venni: Purananuru 66 praises the defeated king who starved himself facing north in shame at his back wound; 246 measures gossip against the victory shout at Azhundur.
teaches: The puram poet honours the loser of Venni above the victor while the akam poet borrows only the victor's roar, which shows how differently one battle served praise of honour and a scale for noise.

note: Both name the rock-cut road the Moriyar's chariot wheels made: in the Purananuru the sun's disc standing over that pass is the image of the patron's daily charity; here the pass is the far road the lover crossed.
teaches: A northern dynasty's road through the southern hills was common knowledge to both kinds of poem, so the same landmark could stand for a patron's open-handedness and for the distance that keeps a lover away.

note: Purananuru 142 (Paranar) praises Pekan as giving like rain that falls everywhere without choosing; Akananuru 262 (Paranar) gives Pekan's hill as கொண்டல் மாமலை, the rain-cloud hill whose drizzle wets the bushes, and lends its scent to the girl's voice.
teaches: The same poet's figure for Pekan's indiscriminate giving, rain, is carried into akam as the smell of his rain-soaked hill, showing a patron's praise-image reused as a lover's sensory measure.

note: Purananuru 233 is a lament that wishes false the dawn report of Evvi's many wounds; Akananuru 266 measures the gossip about the husband by the roar of the feast at Uraththur after Evvi's victory.
teaches: Evvi's name travels with loud public report in both books, a victory feast in akam and a death rumour in puram, so the akam poet uses his fame precisely as a gauge of how far news spreads.

note: Purananuru 264 sets up a stone for a man who recovered cattle, crowned with red flowers tied with marral fibre and peacock feather and inscribed with his name; Akananuru 269 shows such stones on the road, names inscribed, washed, smeared with turmeric and crowned with red karanthai for men who held off the Mazhavar to recover cattle.
teaches: The puram poem gives the stone on the day of grief, when the bards still come not knowing; the akam poem shows the same rite kept up later on a travelled road, so together they show the hero-stone moving from mourning to a standing roadside cult.

note: Purananuru 343, a maganmaruttal poem, has the father refuse his daughter even if suitors bow and give நலஞ்சால் விழுப்பொருள்; Akananuru 280 has the lover say she cannot be had even for நலம்சால் விழுப்பொருள் given by the shipload, and resolve to serve her fisherman father instead.
teaches: The near-identical phrase shows the akam suitor speaking inside the puram convention of the father who refuses wealth, and gives the convention's other side: where puram suitors bring siege, the akam lover answers the refusal with servitude.

note: Purananuru 175 likens a patron's lasting charity to the rock-cut pass of the Moriyar's chariot wheels, a public way open to all; Akananuru 281 sends the lover over that same pass.
teaches: In praise poetry the Moriyar's cut road stands for something permanent and shared, while the akam poet uses it as the point past which a man is lost to one woman, so one piece of remembered history carried opposite values in the two kinds of poetry.

note: Purananuru 48 says Thondi smells of the neythal flowers blooming in its great backwater; Akananuru 290 says the woman's eyes were once like the great cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour.
teaches: Thondi's neythal was the town's own emblem in praise of its king, so when the akam poet says her eyes have lost that likeness he is measuring her pallor against a flower the audience knew as Thondi's pride.

note: Purananuru 264 tells of a hero-stone newly set up with his name engraved and crowned with a peacock feather; Akananuru 297 shows such a stone grown old, its inscribed name passed unread by weary travellers.
teaches: The puram poem records the moment a name is carved to outlast death, and the akam poem shows the same kind of stone generations on with no one reading it, so the pair qualifies the promise of the engraved name.

note: Akananuru 303 calls Paari the giver of hill-like elephants to any suppliant and makes his Parambu the place sparrows always return to at evening; Purananuru 108 says Paari never answers a suppliant with 'I will not come'.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the certainty of Paari's giving, famous from the puram poems, to make the sparrows' return seem certain, so that the heroine's disappointment is measured against a patron who never failed anyone.

note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

note: The same poet, Maruthan Ilanagan, praises Vazhuthi's war in Purananuru 52 and in Akananuru 312 likens lightning to the spear Vazhuthi raises against fleeing enemies.
teaches: One poet's war praise for a Pandya becomes, in his love poem, the measure of a storm's power, showing puram fame travelling into akam as a simile that its first hearers would recognise.

note: Both describe the waterless road where bowmen shoot travellers and birds feed on the dead; in Purananuru 3 suppliants brave it for the Pandya's gifts, in Akananuru 313 the husband crosses it for wealth.
teaches: The same death road is crossed for the same motive, gain, by the suppliant and by the husband; puram counts the crossing as praise of the patron, akam as the measure of what the wife fears.

note: Purananuru 158 names Kolli as the hill Ori ruled, among seven givers now dead; Akananuru 338 calls Kolli the Porai's and makes it the measure of a love that must not perish.
teaches: The puram poem remembers Kolli by a dead patron and the akam poem by its new Chera master, so the hill a lover swears by already carries the record of a fallen lord.

note: Purananuru 126 praises Malaiyaman Kari as lord of the Pennai country and giver to bards; Akananuru 35 likens a daughter's hair to the fine sand-ripples of the Pennai at Kari's ford.
teaches: A patron's river, praised in puram for the gifts it brings bards, became in akam a stock likeness of a girl's beauty, so a chief's fame lent its landscape to love poetry.

note: Both show hero-stones by a stony cairn (பதுக்கை) crowned with peacock feathers (பீலி சூட்டி) for men who died over cattle; Purananuru 264 is the lament for one such fallen man, Akananuru 35 sees such stones only as worship on the road a runaway daughter took.
teaches: The puram poem tells who lies under the stone and who will miss him; the akam poem shows how the same stones looked to a mother who saw only their danger, so a hero's memorial became a mark of the perils of the wild road.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Both tell Nedunchezhiyan's one-man victory over seven kings at Alankanam in the same phrase, எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க; Purananuru 76 praises it as unheard of, Akananuru 36 uses its victory shout to measure the noise of gossip about a husband's new wife.
teaches: The identical phrase in a praise poem and in a wife's complaint shows the battle had a fixed formula that akam poets lifted whole, so a private quarrel could borrow the loudest public event the audience knew.

note: Evvi is the unsparing giver (ஓம்பா ஈகை மாவேள் எவ்வி) in the Purananuru poem and the lord who gives toddy to the fishermen to end a brawl in 366.
teaches: The Purananuru names Evvi's giving as a title, while the akam simile shows it as a scene of keeping peace between farmers and salt-makers and makes his shade a measure of a woman's comfort, so a patron's fame for protection became an akam image of shelter.

note: Both use the figure of the ஓர்எயில் மன்னன, the chieftain of a single fort set against crowned kings: in 338 he will not give his daughter to them, in 373 he lies sleepless under their siege.
teaches: The kaanchi poem on a daughter refused to kings shows where the akam poet's image came from: the lone fort's siege was a known situation of puram, and the akam poet borrowed only its sleepless watch to picture the wife.

note: Karikal is the victor of Venni in the Purananuru poem and the onlooker at Atthi's flood-dance at Kazhar in 376.
teaches: The conqueror praised in puram appears in akam only as a royal spectator who dates and places a love legend, so akam poets used a war king's fame as a frame for a story of loss rather than of victory.

note: Puram 2 praises the Chera as வான வரம்பன், whose realm runs from the sea of sunrise to the sea of sunset; in 389 the husband goes beyond Vaana varamban's good land into tiger country.
teaches: The title that in puram means a king bounded only by the sky becomes in akam the edge of the safe world: the lover's journey is measured as going past a realm that claims to have no beyond.

note: Both place a spot by the formula 'east of Uranthai' (உறந்தைக் குணாது): in Akananuru 4 the tall hill whose kanthal she smells of, in Purananuru 395 Pidavur, the patron Sathan's town.
teaches: The same coordinates serve a patron's address and a woman's fragrance, which shows that akam's landscape was drawn on the real map of Chola country that puram poets used for their patrons.

note: Pannan of Sirukudi is praised in Purananuru 173 as the healer of hunger whose house feeds crowds; in Akananuru 54 his village's gooseberry gives the simile and he is called one who lives not for himself but for others.
teaches: An akam poet could fold a puram patron's reputation into one epithet inside a love poem, which shows how well-known Pannan's generosity was.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Akananuru 54 calls Pannan தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்.
teaches: The kaanchi poem's general ideal and the akam poem's praise of one patron use the same contrast of self and others, so the maxim was already a phrase of praise for real patrons.

note: Both tell of Cheralathan, ashamed of his back wound from the fight with Karikalan, sitting facing north to die; Purananuru 65 laments the king, Akananuru 55 turns to the noble men who died with him.
teaches: The akam poem keeps a detail the puram lament leaves out, the companions who followed the king into death, and uses it to measure a mother's wish that her life would follow her daughter.

note: Both use the formula of Thithan the great giver (மாவண் தித்தன்) and his paddy-rich Uranthai: Purananuru 352 likens the fine gifts offered for a girl, and refused, to Uranthai; Akananuru 6 sets the husband's riverside affair at Uranthai.
teaches: A single praise formula for a Chola chief served the puram poet as the measure of a refused bride-price and the akam poet as the stage of a husband's betrayal, which shows how much shared fame the two kinds of poem drew on.

note: Purananuru 93 describes the rite of cutting with a sword the body of a king who died of sickness, so that he goes where battle-slain warriors go; Akananuru 61 opens with the saying behind that rite (blessed are those who die at others' hands, not seized by Death) as the reason a man leaves home.
teaches: Together they show the warrior's creed about a good death working at two scales: as a royal funeral rite in puram, and in akam as a proverb that sends an ordinary man away from his wife to strive.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for giving the great feast without limit; Akananuru 65 likens the girls' joy at eloping to that of the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral.
teaches: The king's puram fame as a feeder of bards had become a proverbial measure of gladness, so an akam friend could express release from a watchful mother by the bards' delight at his court.

note: Both use nearly the same words for the Moriyar, whose chariots under sky-touching umbrellas cut a path through the rock with their wheels: in 69 that rock marks how far the man has gone, in Purananuru 175 the cutting's circle is a likeness for a patron's constancy.
teaches: The northern invaders' cut through the hills was a shared memory that akam used as a mark of distance and puram as an image of something fixed and open to all, showing one historical feature serving both kinds of poem.

note: Akananuru 70 likens the town's silence after the wedding to the banyan Rama hushed at Kodi for his secret counsel; Purananuru 378 likens a bard's kin, putting on jewels the wrong way, to the monkeys who found Sita's jewels on the ground.
teaches: These are two early Tamil uses of the Rama story, both of minor episodes and both as similes, one akam and one puram, which shows the story was familiar enough to be drawn on for a passing likeness rather than told.

note: Purananuru 172 praises Pittan, lord of the hard country, for his spear that wins hard battles and his great giving; Akananuru 77 names Pittan, Chera's warrior with unending toddy, and likens the woman's tearful eyes to the spear he raised against hostile kings.
teaches: The pair shows a chief's puram praise (his spear and his gifts) reused in akam, where his famous spear becomes the measure of the pain her eyes will cause, so the poet trusts listeners to know the patron's weapon.

note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

note: Kuttuvan's land is the measure of wealth in both: in Purananuru 343 a father refuses wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri as bride-price; in Akananuru 91 the man would not stay for Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, forgetting his wife.
teaches: Kuttuvan's riches stood in both books as the outer limit of wealth, and both poems use it to say a woman outweighs it: in puram the father refuses it for his daughter, in akam the husband refuses it for his wife.

note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola assembly at Uraiyur where justice stands unfailing; Akananuru 93 compares the man's hard-won treasure to the virtue-filled assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur.
teaches: The justice of Uraiyur's assembly, a praise theme in puram, was famous enough to serve an akam poet as a simile for something precious, so the court's moral fame had become a byword for worth itself.

note: Purananuru 55 wishes the Pandya the heat of the sun, the coolness of the moon and the giving of the rain; Kalittokai 100 praises the husband, as king, with the sun's harshness to foes, the moon's coolness to those under his parasol and the rain's giving, then says each praise is ruined by his wife's tears, bangles and pallor.
teaches: The akam friend takes the stock triad of royal praise found in the Purananuru and makes each term hostage to a woman's body, showing that the same encomium could be turned into a reproach by asking whether its subject meets it at home.

note: Kalittokai 101 says the herd girl's shoulders go to the one who seizes a bull that does not fear even a rutting tusker (கடாஅக் களிற்றினும் கண்ணஞ்சா ஏற்றை); Purananuru 342 says the chieftain's daughter's beauty is for fighters alone (பொருநர்க்கு அல்லது பிறர்க்கு ஆகாதே), her brothers threshing the battlefield with elephants for oxen.
teaches: Both give the girl only to proven courage, but the chieftain's family proves it in a war that uses elephants as threshing oxen, while the herders stage the proof on their own working animal inside a fenced pen, so the mullai contest is the puram bride-test turned from a siege that ruins the town into a bounded festival.

note: Purananuru 343: the father refuses even wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri humbly offered, and suitors' armies crowd the town; Kalittokai 103: the herd girls say they want no price (விலை வேண்டார்), only a man who will fall between the killer bull's horns as between their breasts.
