teaches: Read together they show who sets the bride's terms: in the puram town the father refuses wealth and the girl becomes the cause of a war, while in the herders' song the girls voice the refusal themselves and name the one price they accept, so the mullai poem gives the woman the choice the puram poem leaves to her father and the kings.

note: Kalittokai 104 likens the pen strewn with gored men to the field where the five archers killed the hundred (நூற்றுவர் மடங்க... ஐவர் அட்ட பொரு களம்); Purananuru 2 praises the Chera who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five and fell on the field.
teaches: The Bharata war that Purananuru 2 treats as a dated occasion for one king's generosity is already, in Kalittokai, a stock picture of any heap of the fallen, used even for a village bull-catch, so the epic had passed from a remembered event into the common image store of the poets.

note: Purananuru 278: the old mother, told her son fled, searches the field and rejoices more than at his birth to find him cut to pieces; Kalittokai 106: the herd girls sing that they will bind the bull-gored wounds against their breasts and that the tamer's blood on their curd-spotted shoulders is an ornament.
teaches: Akam takes over the puram pride in wounds taken facing the foe and moves it from the mother to the beloved: the wound that proves in Purananuru 278 that a son died well proves in Kalittokai 106 that a man is fit to be embraced, so the herd girls' desire is built on the warrior ethic.

note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.

note: Purananuru 34 quotes dharma that there is expiation for many crimes but none for those who kill a benefit; Kalittokai 149's friend says ingratitude to helpers will not spare a man, however good his sword.
teaches: The rule the puram poet uses to praise a king's gifts to bards is turned in the akam poem against a lover, which shows the ethic of gratitude ran across both halves of Sangam poetry and could bind a man's private love as tightly as a patron's duty.

note: Kalittokai 2 calls the wife's chastity bright as the northern star (வடமீன் போல்) and sets her shoulders above wealth for suppliants; Purananuru 122 says Kari gives his land to brahmins and his tribute to bards and keeps as his own only the shoulders of his wife chaste as the northern star (வடமீன் புரையுங் கற்பின்).
teaches: The puram poem shows the patron's answer to the dilemma the akam friend poses: a giver can give everything away and still keep the wife's shoulders as his only possession, so generosity and staying home need not be traded off as the man in Kalittokai 2 supposes.

note: Purananuru 22 praises the Chera on campaign abroad, under whose white umbrella's shade the unarmed sleep safe while he does not sleep; Kalittokai 26 has the woman say her man guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade, praised by the world, while he lives in a stranger's land.
teaches: The akam woman quotes the very virtue the puram poet praises, shelter given abroad to all who seek it, and asks why it does not reach her, so the pairing shows the cost of the heroic ideal falling on the household the hero leaves.

note: Purananuru 165 opens with those who wished to last in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து மன்னுதல் குறித்தோர்) and set up their fame; Kalittokai 54 ends with the girl wanting it said she acted from love, which in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து) is what lasts.
teaches: The akam heroine takes over the puram formula for lasting fame and applies it to a woman's choice of lover, so the Sangam ideal of a name that outlives one could be earned by love as well as by giving.

note: Purananuru 12 asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma to take others' land so that it is painful to them (இன்னா ஆகப் பிறர் மண் கொண்டு) and do sweet things for his admirers; in Kalittokai 62 the girl asks whether forcing on others what pains them because it is sweet to oneself (தமக்கு இனிது என்று, வலிதின் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்வது) is good.
teaches: The same sweet-for-oneself, painful-for-others test is put to a conquering king and to a forceful lover, and in both the one questioned claims it as virtue (அறன்), so the Sangam poets judged seizure in war and in love by one moral rule.

note: Purananuru 92 says a son's prattle keeps no tune and makes no sense, yet moves fathers to grace; in Kalittokai 80 the mother hears the son's sweet 'attatta' but the father is away with other women.
teaches: The puram poet's comparison assumes a father present to be moved by the prattle, and the Kalittokai shows the house where he is not, so the grace the prattle should draw from the father falls to the mother and is mixed with pain.

note: Purananuru 312 assigns bearing the son to the mother and making him worthy (சான்றோன் ஆக்குதல்) to the father; in Kalittokai 86 the mother herself teaches the son which of his father's qualities to copy and which to refuse.
teaches: Read together, they show the puram division of duties failing inside the house: when the father is the bad example, the mother takes over his task of forming the son, sorting his public virtues from his private fault, which the puram poem's neat allocation never anticipates.

note: Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade from the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, and that rain comes in the land of the just sceptre; Kalittokai 99 asks the husband, addressed as king, whether his wife fell outside the shade of the parasol he calls virtue's shade and the working of his sceptre.
teaches: The friend in the Kalittokai uses the same counsel a puram poet gave a king, that the parasol exists to shade those who suffer, and turns it on the household, showing that the akam poets could hold a husband to the standard of kingship and find him failing his nearest subject.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Kuruntokai 129 he tells his comrade, 'friend of poets', that a girl's brow has bound him like a new-caught elephant; in Purananuru 216, fasting to death, he tells doubters his poet-friend, whom he has never seen, will surely come.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices turn on the same bond of male friendship: in the love poem the comrade is the one he confides his captivity to, in the death poem the friend's coming is the proof of his worth, so the paangan of akam convention is, for this poet, a role he filled with a real friendship of poets.

note: Purananuru 233 refuses to believe the dawn news that Evvi, leader of the bards' families, lies with spear wounds in his chest; Kuruntokai 19 compares the man's grieving heart to the flowerless heads of the bards impoverished by Evvi's loss.
teaches: The puram lament gives the moment of the news, and Paranar's simile gives its aftermath, bards going bare-headed without flowers, so the pair show a patron's death becoming a recognised mourning custom that akam could borrow to measure a lover's estrangement.

note: Kuruntokai 196: the husband who once called neem sweet now calls the cool spring water of Pari's Parambu hot and brackish; Purananuru 176: the poet regrets the days lost like people who scorned the clear spring of Parambu because it was in their own town.
teaches: Read with the Purananuru, the friend's choice of Parambu's water carries its proverbial lesson: the sweetest thing is scorned when it is near, so she diagnoses the husband's turning as contempt bred by having the wife at home.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Purananuru 216 he says his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar calls himself 'the foolish Chola's'; in Kuruntokai 20 his heroine says let the leavers be wise and let us be fools.
teaches: The same king, in puram and in akam, gives the name of folly to loyalty that prudence would abandon, his friend's in the one and the waiting woman's in the other, so the akam poem's irony has a model in the king's own creed of friendship.

note: Purananuru 150: Nalli, unnamed, roasts fat in his forest for a starving poet and gives him his own chain. Kuruntokai 210: the friend prices the meal owed to the crow that called a guest in the ghee of the herds of Nalli's forest.
teaches: Holding the two together shows why Nalli's forest is the measure in the love poem: he was remembered as the host who fed a stranger in the woods unasked, so the friend, repaying a bird for bringing a guest, reaches for the most famous hospitality she knows and still calls it too little.

note: Purananuru 34 states that there is no expiation for killing a benefit and binds the poet to praise the king who fed the bards; Kuruntokai 225 makes a king who forgets, once enthroned, the help he had in ruin the type of ingratitude the lover must not imitate.
teaches: The puram poem casts the king as the benefactor to whom gratitude is owed, while the akam friend can cite the king who forgets his helpers as a familiar figure, so the same norm of gratitude was also turned against kings, and borrowed to bind a lover to marriage.

note: Purananuru 233 names Akuthai as the strong one whose elephants never ran short for those who came for gifts; Kuruntokai 298 recalls the young she-elephants Akuthai's father gave to singing women and likens the lover's long waiting to that gift.
teaches: The puram lament knows the house of Akuthai only as givers of elephants, and the akam friend turns that known generosity into a figure for a lover's patience, so a patron's fame for gifts served akam as a ready image of an act that waits on a return.

note: Kapilar praises Malaiyan in Purananuru 123 as giving more chariots than the raindrops on the heights of Mullur; in Kuruntokai 312, also Kapilar's, the girl comes at midnight filling Malaiyan's Mullur forest with her fragrance.
teaches: The same poet uses his patron's hill both as the measure of a king's countless gifts and as the secret ground of a tryst, which shows a court poet setting his love scenes inside the land he praised in puram.

note: Purananuru 151 refuses the young Vicchi lord the poet's embrace because of a door shut against singers; Kuruntokai 328 measures gossip by the uproar of Kurumbur when bards saw the Vicchiyar chief stand like a tiger against the kings.
teaches: The Vicchi house is remembered by singers in two ways at once, its war-cry loud enough to be an akam poet's yardstick for noise and its door shut against bards in puram, so the pair shows that a chief's fame for valour could circulate apart from, and despite, his name for giving.

note: Purananuru 71: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not rout the allied kings he may be parted from his wide-eyed wife. Kuruntokai 36: the lover swore a vanjinam that he would not leave her.
teaches: Separation from the beloved is the penalty the king stakes on his battle vow and the very thing the lover's vow forswears, so the akam vow borrows the puram form and the friend's trust in it rests on the warrior's honour that a vanjinam is never broken.

note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya that even if the earth shifts his word must not; Kuruntokai 373's friend says that even if the earth shifts and fire and water change places, the lovers' bond suffers no harm from gossip.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram formula for a king's unbreakable word and gives it to a secret love, so the pair shows that the lovers' bond was claimed in the language of royal oath, and that a pledge, not a feeling, is what kalavu asks to be trusted.

note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

note: Purananuru 189 concludes that the use of wealth is giving, since king and hunter alike eat one measure; Kuruntokai 63's heart argues the same, that there is no giving and enjoying for the penniless, to drive the man to work.
teaches: The puram maxim that wealth exists to be given becomes, in the akam poem, the very reason a man leaves his wife, so the pair shows the giver's ethic carrying a private cost the praise poem never counts.

note: Perunkoppendu in Purananuru 246 refuses a widow's life and chooses the pyre; the female monkey in Kuruntokai 69, unable to bear widowhood (கைம்மை உய்யா), leaves her young with kin and leaps to her death.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram queen's refusal of widowhood and gives it to a creature of the hill, making the girl's not outliving her lover a law of nature for the night-visitor to weigh, not a royal vow.

note: Purananuru 230: while Ezhini lived, the herds rested in the forest unguarded and safe; Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan tells the wife to guard her husband like the great herds at Ezhini's war front.
teaches: The courtesan's taunt rests on Ezhini's puram fame as the protector of herds, so she casts herself as the cattle-raider and the husband as plunder that only a war-chief's watch could keep, using the heroic guard to mock a household one.

note: Avvaiyar's Purananuru 97 warns Anji's enemies that his worn swords, spears and elephants prove resistance is hopeless; her Kuruntokai 91 makes the night terror of a frontier town fearing Anji the measure of a wife's sleepless marriage.
teaches: The same poet supplies both sides of Anji's war: the puram poem speaks for the conqueror's threat, the akam poem borrows the sleeplessness of the threatened town, showing that the fear puram praise produces was available to akam as an image of domestic misery.

note: Purananuru 123 makes chariot-giving Malaiyan's mark, chariots given sober outnumbering the raindrops on Mullur; Natrinai 100 names him only as தேர் வண் மலையன் and borrows his musicians' drum to measure a frightened husband's trembling.
teaches: The akam poet can name Malaiyan by the epithet the puram poems established and rely on his fame being known, and turns it to mockery: the drum of a great giver's festivals throbs for a man afraid of his wife, so puram glory serves akam as a scale for comic smallness.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for the great food he gave at the war of the hundred and the five; Natrinai 113 likens the heroine's sob to the ambal pipe the musicians blow on the hushed field after Udhiyan's loud battle.
teaches: Where the praise poem remembers Udhiyan's war for its feeding of the armies, the love poet remembers its aftermath, the silent field and the mourning pipe, so akam took from the same king's fame the grief that puram praise leaves out.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are men who would give their lives for fame; Natrinai 115 says the absent lover, of great love, would not stay away even for endless fame.
teaches: On one defensible reading the two rank the same goods in opposite order, puram putting fame above life and akam putting love above fame, so the friend's comfort works only by overturning the heroic scale the puram poem praises.

note: Purananuru 127 praises Aay, whose bards led away his elephants and whose palace stood bare from giving; Natrinai 167 makes the rattle of the chariots bards won at Aay's feast the sound of a heron's cry on the shore of the man whose bard the friend turns away.
teaches: The pairing shows an akam friend borrowing Aay's puram fame as the measure of a generous patron, so the bard who in puram goes home rich is in akam the go-between sent home empty: one profession seen from the giver's hall and from the wronged wife's door.

note: Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan for chariots given more freely than the raindrops on the peak of Mullur; Natrinai 170 recalls Malaiyan's single spear routing the many Aryans at Mullur, as the image of wives helpless before one rival.
teaches: Held together they show a chieftain's fame had two faces, giving and lone valour, and the akam poet chose the war face because the household's problem was one woman beating many: akam borrowed from puram exactly the facet its situation needed.

note: Both poems call on the potter of the town: Purananuru 228 to make the burial urn for a dead Chola king; Natrinai 200 as the crier who proclaims festivals, asked to proclaim the bard a liar.
teaches: Taken together, the potter appears as the town's public servant for both its funerals and its festivals, and the friend's commission parodies the solemn address to him by making the crier's voice carry a domestic quarrel.

note: Purananuru 184: a king who takes his due like an elephant fed balls of paddy keeps the land rich, but one who grabs is like an elephant loosed in the field. Natrinai 226: kings do not take gold that ruins the land's wealth, yet her lover does not know the measure of the wealth he seeks.
teaches: The counsel that a king must take tribute without ruining its source had become a proverb a wife could quote, and Natrinai 226 turns it on the household: a husband who leaves to make wealth regardless of her life is the elephant loose in the field.

note: Purananuru 133: go and see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain. Natrinai 237: the rain clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered for suppliants.
teaches: The puram poet likens Ay's giving to rain, and the akam poet turns it round and likens the rain clouds to Ay's gift elephants, so the patron's bounty and the monsoon were interchangeable images and the friend can offer the season as a promise as sure as a great giver's word.

note: Both are by Kapilar: in Purananuru 109 the kings besieging Paari's Parambu, with its jackfruit and its springs, cannot take it by force, but bards who come singing will be given it; in Natrinai 253 the girl, grown beautiful and hard to reach, is like Paari's jackfruit hill closed in by rain.
teaches: Read with the puram poem, the akam simile carries its argument: Parambu yields not to siege but to those who come asking, so the friend's comparison tells the man that the girl will not be had by stealth but only by asking for her in marriage.

note: In Purananuru 337 a girl courted by kings is hard to see, like the cold spring of Paari's Parambu, shut in the house while her brothers fight the suitors; in Natrinai 253 the girl, guarded like Paari's hill, is hard to reach for her secret lover.
teaches: The pair shows Parambu as the standard image of the guarded marriageable girl in both akam and puram, and sets two kinds of suitor against the same closed house: kings who would take her by war and a lover who must now stop coming by night.

note: Kapilar in Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan of Mullur for chariots given while sober, more than the raindrops on Mullur's heights; Kapilar in Natrinai 291 measures a girl's ruined beauty by the herd-owners whose cattle the king of Mullur drove off at nightfall on his horse.
teaches: Read together, the same poet's two Mullur poems show the giving king's other face: the wealth praised in puram as countless gifts came partly from night raids on herds, and akam borrows the raid from the side of those who lost everything.

note: The bereaved mother in Natrinai 293 wishes that the young man's mother may suffer great anguish like hers (எம்போல் பெரு விதுப்புறுகமாதோ); the mourner of Purananuru 291 wishes the same on the king (என்போற் பெருவிதுப்பு உறுக) whose garland sent the man to his death.
teaches: The shared curse formula shows that akam treated a daughter's elopement as a bereavement in the full puram sense: the mother speaks in the words a mourner uses over a warrior's body, aimed at the one who caused the loss.

note: Paranar in Purananuru 348 compares a girl to rich Unur of truthful Thazhumban and pictures suitors' chariots in every shade and elephants tied at every place for her; Paranar in Natrinai 300, with strangers' marriage offers in the colophon, has a chariot set at the gate as her bride-price and likens the lover to Unur's begging elephant at the kitchen.
teaches: Holding the two Paranar poems together shows him using Thazhumban's Unur for the same occasion, a girl besieged by suitors with chariots and elephants: in puram the siege threatens the town, in akam the friend turns it into a goad to make the hidden lover ask for her before others do.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori of Kolli and Malaiyan who rode Kaari side by side among the seven great givers; Natrinai 320 remembers the street where Ori was killed and Kaari entered as a byword for a stricken town.
teaches: The bards' canon of seven generous patrons hides that two of them were enemies, one killing the other, and the love poem shows that killing had become a proverb for a town in panic.

note: Purananuru 158 names Ori as the one who ruled Kolli (கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரியும்) among the seven givers now dead; Natrinai 346 measures the wife's fragrant hair by the kulavi of the great cool Kolli of Porayan.
teaches: Set beside the elegy that names Ori as Kolli's dead lord, the love poem's passing epithet shows the hill in the Chera Porayan's hands, so the pair records that Kolli changed masters after Ori, which neither poem states.

note: Purananuru 281 has women guard a wounded warrior from ghouls with neem, music, mustard seed and incense; Natrinai 349's man likens himself, ever behind the fisher girl, to the ghoul that hovers by men gravely wounded on the battlefield.
teaches: Read with the warding rite, the lover's simile casts him as the very presence a household drives from its wounded with neem and smoke, so his self-portrait as tireless follower carries his knowledge that he is the unwanted one at her door.

note: Purananuru 67 asks the swan, flying from the ford of Kumari to the northern mountain, to stop at the Chola king's palace with the poet's name; Natrinai 356 likens the man's toiling heart to the swan that grazes the southern sea and carries food to its chicks on the Himalaya.
teaches: Both send the swan between the southern sea and the northern mountain, but puram makes it a messenger to a king while akam makes its tireless feeding flight the lover's own heart, so the long-flight swan served as a go-between in one genre and as the self in the other.

note: Purananuru 101: Avvai tells her heart that Athiyaman's gift, late or soon, is as sure as the food an elephant holds between its tusks. Natrinai 381 (also Avvaiyar): the rain has settled in like Neduman Anji's seat from which he keeps giving chariots.
teaches: The same poet who in puram counts on Anji's giving as something that never fails makes that unfailing giving the image of a rain a waiting woman cannot bear, so the patron's plenty is a blessing to the bard and a torment to the lover depending on who receives it.

note: Purananuru 72 has Neduncheliyan vow to rout the kings who mocked him and seize them together with their drums (முரசமொடு); Natrinai 39 names Cheliyan as the one who took the drums and crossed the foes' guarded walls (முரசு கொண்டு ஓம்பு அரண் கடந்த) and likens the girl's shoulders to his Koodal. The Natrinai does not say which Cheliyan; the drum-taking matches.
teaches: The pair shows a king's battle vow hardened into a stock epithet inside a love simile and turned on the lover: the city of the king who took walled forts becomes the measure of shoulders that overpower the man, so puram conquest lends akam its language of love's assault.

note: Purananuru 39: because justice stands firm and unfailing in the Chola court at Uranthai, justice is not this king's own fame. Natrinai 400: like justice that never fails in the Uranthai court of the warlike Cholas, he knows no failing in her heart.
teaches: The puram poet says Uranthai's justice is too settled to count as any one king's merit, and the courtesan borrows exactly that settledness for her lover's place in her heart, so an inherited institution, not a person's virtue, was the akam poet's measure of a love that cannot change.

note: Purananuru 152: Ori, met as a hunter in the wilds, gives a strange troupe meat, toddy, gold and gems unasked. Natrinai 52: even wealth equal to the giving of Ori, lord of the Mazhavar, would be slight against his wife's embrace.
teaches: The puram poem shows Ori's giving as so lavish it reached strangers in the wilderness, and the akam poem takes exactly that giving as the upper limit of what a man could hope to gain and still sets it below love, so the pair shows a patron's fame serving akam poets as a fixed measure of wealth.

note: Purananuru 108: in Pari's Parambu the firebrand a hill woman lights is sandalwood, its smoke reaching the vengai. Natrinai 55: the friend explains the bees on the girl by pointing to a burning sandalwood firebrand.
teaches: The puram poem records that hill households burned sandal as ordinary firewood, which is what makes the friend's lie in Natrinai 55 credible to the mother: the girl could smell of sandal from the hearth, so the trick depends on a fact of hill life the puram poet praises as the land's wealth.

note: Both name வல்வில் ஓரி: Purananuru 152 shows the hunter whose single arrow kills an elephant, a tiger, a stag, a boar and an iguana, and who feeds the bard venison; in Natrinai 6 the girl's hair smells of Ori's forest, where the ripe fruit of the kumizh falls as food for young deer.
teaches: The love poet takes from the hunter-patron's fame only his forest's scent and plenty, a place where the very deer his bow kills feed unharmed, so akam borrowed a puram name for the bounty of a land and left its violence behind.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Malaiyan who rode Kaari and won great battles among the seven givers; in Natrinai 77 Kapilar likens the relief the girl's look once gave the lover to Malaiyan riding his horse into enemy land, breaking forts and breathing out his weariness.
teaches: The puram poem keeps Malaiyan as a rider and giver in a public roll, while the akam poem takes the same rider at the private moment after the raid, his sigh of relief, so akam used the king's fame for the feeling of a finished deed rather than for the deed.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend calls the season of humming bees and a forest in bloom the medicine for the heroine's pallor (பசலை மருந்து); in Ainkurunuru 342 the bees revel on the flowering nunavam and he has not come.
teaches: The friend can call the flowering season a cure only because it guarantees his return; Ainkurunuru 342 shows the same flowering turning into the sickness once the season arrives without him, so the convention's comfort is only as good as the man's timekeeping.

note: Both set peacocks in their finery and the konrai-lovely forest of the rains before a waiting woman; Kar Narpathu's friend names the season the cure (மருந்து) for her pallor.
teaches: Kar Narpathu spells out that the season's beauty is a promise of return and so a cure, while Ainkurunuru only calls his road good for having it, so the decade's bare praise of the road is the same reassurance left unspoken.

note: 449 has the chariot and horses ready on condition the king finishes his work (வேந்துவினை முடினே); Kar Narpathu 20 reports the king's work done (வேந்தன் வினையு முடிந்தன) and the road grown pleasant.
teaches: The pair gives the two moments of the mullai return, the chariot readied in the camp while the king's work hangs, and the fulfilment when the work is done and the rain-cloud itself seems an army going home.

note: Both say the rain-season flowers have opened like eyes (கண்ணெனக் கருவிளை மலர; கண்மலர்போற் பூத்தன) as the friend's season sign.
teaches: In Kar Narpathu the eye-like flowers speak and announce the man's return, in Ainkurunuru they only mark a season he cannot forget, so the same flower simile let the friend present the hedge either as a messenger or as a calendar.

note: Kar Narpathu 20's hero says the king's work is finished and the roads are pleasant; Ainkurunuru 466's friend says the king has released him after the great work and she is sure of his coming.
teaches: The hero announces the release as a fact on the road, while the friend can only infer it at home and stake her certainty on it, so the release from the king's work was the one event both ends of the mullai separation waited on.

note: Kar Narpathu 12's friend takes the dark clouds rising on the right (ஏரும் வலம்) every day as a sign beyond doubt of his coming; Ainkurunuru 469's cloud rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு) to bring him.
teaches: Kar Narpathu treats the rightward rising cloud as evidence to be read, Ainkurunuru as an escort that brings the man and an occasion to go out and watch, so the omen of the right side could serve the friend both as proof and as a reason to act.

note: Kar Narpathu's friend sees flowers bloom like the woman's eyes and hears them announce his return; in 492 the man sees peacock, mullai and deer as likenesses of her and comes home.
teaches: The same likening of the season's things to the woman works from both ends of the separation: for her the flowers that resemble her eyes are messengers of his return, while for him the creatures that resemble her are what sent him home, so the comparison is the bond that carries the promise across.

note: Both say the fragrant cool rain-season laughs with mullai buds for bright teeth (முல்லை ... இலங்கெயிறு ... நறுந்தண் கார் ... நகும்); in Kar Narpathu 14 the friend reads the laugh as proof he will come quickly, in Kuruntokai 126 the woman hears it mocking her: where are they?
teaches: The later poet took the older line almost word for word and reversed what it means: the same laughing season is a sign of his return to the friend who comforts and a jeer at the deserted woman, which shows that the image itself carries no fixed mood and the speaker's place in the situation decides it.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend shows the bloomed konrai and the dancing peacocks and calls the season medicine for the pallor. Kuruntokai 148: the friend denies that the konrai and kurundham mean the rains, and the heroine asks if she is dreaming.
teaches: The friend's proof from the season only works before the season is spent; once the konrai has bloomed and he has not come, the same flower proves his breach, so the comforter must deny the season and the heroine turns the argument against her.

note: Kar Narpathu 10: as thunder roars and the bull bellows back, the swift chariot comes with the sound of a forest stream. Kuruntokai 155: the evening of the season has come, but not the word that his chariot with its ringing bells is on its way.
teaches: The venba lets the sound of the chariot arrive with the season, but the Kuruntokai keeps season and chariot apart and has the heroine wait first for the report of it, which shows the chariot-sound of mullai as a promise the older poem could leave unkept.

note: Kar Narpathu 17: on the high rock-ledged hill the thunder crushes snakes and the sky, thick with dark, shows the season; the friend reads it as his return. Kuruntokai 158: the heroine asks the cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes dead on the tall slope, whether it has no pity on lone women.
teaches: The same storm with its snake-killing thunder is a sign of comfort when the friend reads it as the promised season and a terror when the lone heroine faces it at night, so the image carries whatever the speaker's situation gives it rather than a fixed meaning.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend points to the bloomed konrai that has made the forest lovely as proof that the season of his return has come. Kuruntokai 21: the woman says that even if the konrai forest declares the rains, she will not believe it, since he does not lie.
teaches: The same konrai sign is proof of his return in the friend's mouth and a sign the woman refuses in her own, so the season argument of the mullai poems could be turned around: faith in his word can deny the season rather than read it.

note: Kar Narpathu 1: the friend says the man who promised to come when the rain hung low can hardly fail to come now that the clouds roar and pour. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the great cloud pours, thunders and flashes with no pity, aimed at her life.
teaches: The rain of the promised season is the same sign in both, but the friend reads it as his oath falling due and the heroine as the deadline passing on her; set side by side, the poems show the rainy season carries both senses at once, and the speaker decides which is heard.

note: Kar Narpathu 3: the friend, showing her own distress, says the wind, hail and thundering sky act as if all aimed at one lone woman. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the thundering cloud flashes with her life as its aim.
teaches: The complaint that the storm is aimed at her is the heroine's own in the older poem, and in the later venba the friend speaks it for her about 'one woman', so the charge against the rain had become a formula that could be handed from the sufferer to her companion.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend says they are sure he will come quickly, since the rain cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its bright teeth. Kuruntokai 220: the jasmine buds open like a wild cat smiling, the evening is here, and he has not come.
teaches: Both poems read the opening jasmine as a smile with teeth, but in the friend's venba it is the season laughing in welcome and in the heroine's Kuruntokai poem it is a wild cat's grin, so the one image turns from promise to mockery once the day of return has passed.

note: Kar Narpathu 12 has the friend say that his coming is certain, shown beyond doubt by the dark clouds that rise every day; in Kuruntokai 314 the full rain cloud flashes lightning at evening and the heroine says he still does not come. On this reading the sign the friend calls certain has failed.
teaches: Set beside the Kar Narpathu's confident friend, the poem shows the other side of the season-sign: the cloud that is offered as proof of return becomes, when he does not come, the measure of his broken word.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend points to the bloomed konrai as the season and the cure of pallor; Kuruntokai 66's friend calls the bloomed konrai foolish, fooled by stray rain, and denies that the season has come.
teaches: The friend's comfort can use the konrai either way, as proof the promised season is here or as a false sign to be dismissed, which shows that the consolation lies in the friend's argument and not in the flower itself.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: his coming is certain; every day the dark clouds, like elephants anointed with oil, rise on the right. Natrinai 237: look, the clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered.
teaches: Both friends point a pining woman to clouds that rise like elephants as proof of the season's return, but Kar Narpathu's anointed elephants and the rising on the right make the cloud an omen, while Natrinai's patron's elephants make it a gift laid up for those who wait, so the same image could reassure by augury or by the ethic of giving.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend reassures the woman with a lizard chirping on the lucky side, a koel on the house's nochchi and the season's flowers; in Kar Narpathu 12 she calls his coming certain because the dark clouds rise every day on the right.
teaches: The pair shows that the friend's reassurance in the rains rested on reading omens, the right side being lucky in both, and that the rainy season itself was read as one more omen of return, which is why Natrinai 246 can end its certainty as a question.

note: In Kar Narpathu 1 the friend says that with the sky roaring and pouring, the man who said 'we will come' can hardly fail to come now; in Natrinai 248 the friend says the same roar is false thunder and not the promised season. On the plain reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what the rain shows.
teaches: Set side by side, the same evidence serves the friend either way: when the season must mean his return she affirms it, and when his absence would make him a liar she denies it, so the season's sign was something the friend argued about rather than read off.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's frenzy-ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among Murugan's abodes, with red millet and blood scattered and the god called down (முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த), where seekers gain what they ask; Akananuru 22 describes the same rite and the heroine laughs that it was wasted on a stranger priest, since her lover was the cure.
teaches: The devotional idyll and the love poem share the rite's very words, but the akam poem limits its power: the god may come, yet the velan's diagnosis of a girl's sickness is wrong, so the rite's authority stops where secret love begins.

note: Both describe the king's war camp at midnight with the long-tongued bright bell (நெடுநா ஒண்மணி) and the roaring drum; Mullaippattu's king lies awake thinking of the enemy while his queen waits, and Akananuru 24's soldier speaks of his wife alone at home.
teaches: The shared bell formula shows the midnight camp was a stock scene, and the two poems use it from different ranks: the idyll gives it to the king, the short poem to a man in his army whose wife waits like the idyll's queen.

note: Both show a lighthouse lamp on a tall tower that calls ships to the shore at night: the idyll as a sight of the port on the guide's road, the poem as the pilot's sign of landfall.
teaches: The idyll records the harbour light as a fact of the port; the akam poet turns the same light into the sure sign of a voyage's end and sets it against the woman's lack of any messenger, so a civic fixture became an emblem of return.

note: Both list the signs of dusk, with the anril calling or settling in the palmyra's inner frond (பெண்ணை அகமடல்) among them.
teaches: Kapilar's idyll uses the dusk catalogue as the moment the man promises marriage, while 260 uses the same signs to open a night of dread, so the formula of nightfall was shared and its turn at the end set its meaning.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veriyattu ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among the true places where Murugan comes to those who seek him; in Akananuru 98 the same rite, with kadambu, palm leaf and the god's great name praised, is a misreading of love-sickness by deluded women.
teaches: The same veriyattu rite is a real dwelling of the god in the devotional idyll and a comic error in the love poem, so the Sangam akam convention could treat Murugan's possession as a cover story without denying the god, who here might even cure her.

note: Paripadal 13 orders the elements sky, wind, fire, water by how many of the five each is known through; Tirumanthiram 385 tells the same chain as emergence, space, air, then a doubtful கான், water, the five together.
teaches: Because the Paripadal's count puts fire between wind and water, it supports reading the Tirumanthiram's obscure கான் as fire, and shows the creation chain the later Saiva text tells already present in an early Tamil hymn as a theory of how each element is known.

note: Paripadal 1.32-33 says Thirumal's coming is hard to know even for sages free of confusion; Tirumanthiram 13 puts Vishnu who measured the earth among the gods who, measuring by thought, still cannot conceive the Lord. On the plain reading the two give the unknowable highest place to different gods, and one puts the other's god among the baffled seekers.
teaches: The same argument from unknowability served two rival theologies, and the Saiva poet reuses it by moving Thirumal from the place of the unknown into the place of the seeker, so ineffability became a way to rank gods.

note: Paripadal 2.5-12 tells the ages of the world in the order sky (as sound), wind, fire, water, earth; Thiruppugazh 21 names Mayon as the one who became sky, wind, fire, water and earth in the same order, and the seven worlds, yet touches none of them.
teaches: The five-element order credited to Thirumal survives a thousand years into Arunagirinathar, but what the Sangam singer told as successive ages of the world's making the later poet states as the god's present pervasion of all things.

note: Tirumanthiram 7 declares the Lord elder to the three (மூவர்க்கும் மூத்தவன்) and father to the one who calls him father; Paripadal 2.20-23 makes Thirumal younger to those who call him younger than the conch-white brother and elder to those who call him elder.
teaches: Both poets let the god become the kin-name the worshipper uses, but only the Paripadal applies the rule to seniority itself, so where Tirumular fixes his Lord as eldest the earlier hymn shows rank among gods as a matter of the believer's tradition.

note: Paripadal 3.63 says 'you are the fragrance in the flower' (பூவினுள் நாற்றம் நீ) in a run of identities; Tirumanthiram 2639 says the Lord is like the fragrance in the flower, the ghee in milk and the juice in fruit (பூவினுள் நாற்றமும் போலுளன்), mingled everywhere.
teaches: The same image of fragrance in the flower is an identity in the Sangam hymn, where the god is the essence of each thing, and a simile in Tirumular, where the Lord is like that essence and stands mingled in things, so the pair shows the later Saiva poet keeping the image while holding the god at one remove from the world he pervades.

note: Paripadal 4.11-21 tells of பிருங்கலாதன் tormented by his father, the god embracing the son and tearing the father's chest with his claws from the broken pillar (ஒடி தூண்); Thiruppugazh 870 tells of a child chanting நம நாராயணாய, the father asking where his god is, and the lion bursting from the pillar to tear Hiranya's chest.
teaches: In the Sangam hymn the story turns on the god's two acts on two chests, the embrace and the tearing, while Arunagirinathar's version turns on the child's recitation of the name and the father's challenge, so the pair shows the Prahlada story shifting its centre from the god's protecting hand to the power of the uttered name.

note: Tirumanthiram 10 says he himself is the earth, the sky, the fire, the sun, the moon, the rain and the sea (தானே opening each line); Paripadal 4.25-34 says only that two of the god's qualities are in each of the sun, moon, rain, earth, flower, water, sky and wind, and that these came about by parting from him (நிற் பிரிந்து).
teaches: The two lists cover nearly the same things, but the Sangam hymn keeps the god outside them, each element holding a pair of his qualities as a share that left him, while Tirumular erases the gap and makes him the things themselves, so the pair shows identity with the elements was a later and stronger claim than participation.

note: Tirumanthiram 3021 asks where he is and answers that the Lord stands everywhere like rain; Paripadal 4.65-70 names the banyan, the kadamba, the river islet and the trackless hill, where he dwells under a different name in each, and concludes எவ் வயினோயும் நீயே, you are the one in every place.
teaches: Tirumular reaches omnipresence through the image of rain falling on all places alike, while the Sangam poet reaches it by gathering particular shrines with their own local names, so the pair shows the claim 'he is everywhere' first serving to unite many local cults under one god before it became a claim about space.

note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

note: Paripadal 5 has six of the seven sages' wives bear him; Thiruppugazh 372 names him the six-faced one who drank at the breasts of the six (அறுவர் முலையுணு).
teaches: In the Paripadal the six are mothers by conception through the fire, while in the Thiruppugazh they have become nurses he drank from, so the pair shows the six mothers' role shifting from bearing to nursing as the Krittika story settled.

note: Paripadal 5 asks Murugan for love (அன்பும்) instead of wealth; Thiruppugazh 986 asks for love growing ever greater, with tears, melting and faltering speech, and only then for the stainless meaning.
teaches: The Sangam prayer names love as one of three ethical gifts, while the Thiruppugazh makes love itself the whole request and describes its bodily signs, so the pair traces anbu changing from a virtue asked for into the felt experience of bhakti.

note: Paripadal 8.96-108 shows the crowd at Parankundram carrying flowers, incense and lamps and asking for children, wealth and victory; Thiruppugazh 8, sung at Parangiri, confesses that the poet never worshipped with flowers or walked round the hill and asks only that Murugan come at the hour of death.
teaches: The rites the Sangam festival performs as means to this-world ends become, at the same hill a thousand years later, the list of duties the devotee confesses he failed, and the request moves from children and wealth to rescue at death.

note: Thiruppugazh 12, a Parankunram song, has Indra's daughter and the hunter girl both embrace Murugan's twelve shoulders; Paripadal 9 sets the same two wives at the same hill in a quarrel with blows of garlands.
teaches: The later hymn keeps the two consorts side by side in a single embrace, while the Sangam song lets them fight over him at the same shrine, which shows the co-wives' rivalry was once part of the hill's sacred lore and was smoothed away as the pair became fixed icons of devotion.

note: Thiruppugazh 18 names Murugan of south Parankunram as the one who took the girl the hill people gave (குன்றவர்கள் தந்தபெண்); Paripadal 9.67-69 has Valli's kin, the kurinji hill-men (குறிஞ்சிக் குன்றவர் ... வள்ளி தமர்), turn the wives' quarrel into a thumbai battle on that hill.
teaches: In the hymn the hill people appear only as givers of the bride, while in the Paripadal they stay her partisans after the marriage and fight for her against the sky-born wife, so the pair shows Valli's marriage remembered as an alliance with her kin that carried on into the god's household.

note: Thiruppugazh 11 names Murugan's uncle as the one who sleeps on the serpent and who churned the sea of old (பனகம் துயில்கின்ற ... கடல் முன்பு கடைந்த); Paripadal Thirattu 1.68-75 gives the churning to the serpent, who lifted the mountain and was the rope while the discus-bearer (ஆழியான்) only pulled.
teaches: By Arunagirinathar's time the churning is simply Mal's act and the serpent his bed, while the Sangam hymn praises the rope for not breaking, so the pair shows the serpent losing its share of the myth as it became the god's couch.

note: Kural 211 measures giving without return by the rain, to which the world gives nothing back; Paripadal 10.125-127 measures the Vaigai's flood over the fields by the Vazhuthi who pours gold into poets' hands.
teaches: The Kural makes nature the model for the giver, while the Paripadal makes the king the model for nature, so the pair shows the comparison between rain and royal giving could run in both directions, with the Pandya's gift treated as the surer standard.

note: Kural 1145 says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is craved each time one is drunk; Paripadal 10.63-68 likens lovers who hide their love from gossip to drinkers who hide their drunkenness.
teaches: Both join love and toddy, but the Kural's lover welcomes exposure while the Paripadal's festival lovers hide from it, so the same comparison serves to praise and to fear gossip, and the couplet's bravado reads as one stance among those the poets knew.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even water for a cow; Paripadal 10.87-88 has bathers who, seeing what they lack, do good works in hope before they speak the shame of asking (இளிவரவு கூறாமுன்).
teaches: The festival bathers apply the Kural's horror of asking even to what they want from the river, choosing an offering over a spoken request, so the ethic against begging shaped how people framed a petition in worship.

note: Paripadal 11.122-123 has onlookers call a girl a striking goddess (தாக்கு அணங்கு) whose eyes are Kaaman's army (காமன் படை); Kural 1082 has the man say that her returning his look is a striking goddess come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்ன).
teaches: The rare compound and the army come together in both, so the Kural's lover is speaking a festival idiom: what the Paripadal's crowd shouts as a warning to all who see the girl, the Kural turns into one man's private experience of a single returned glance.

note: Paripadal 11.37-38 asks who notices the days run down (நாள் குறைபடுதல் காணுநர் யாரே) as the flood wanes like the moon; Kural 334 says the day is a saw cutting life, for those who can perceive it (உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்).
teaches: Both turn on the same observation, that daily loss goes unseen, but the Paripadal draws from it a request to the river to slow down and keep its plenty, while the Kural draws a warning to the perceptive; the image of unnoticed waning could serve plenty as well as renunciation.

note: In Paripadal 11.80 unmarried girls bathe under the brahmins' fire rite praying 'may the wide land not be scorched'; Kural 55 says it rains at the word of the wife who does not worship a god but worships her husband. On the plain reading these name incompatible sources of the rain women can bring: public worship by maidens, or a wife's devotion that sets worship of a god aside.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows two rival accounts of women's power over the rain, the festival rite of the unmarried at the river and the wife's domestic devotion, and the Kural's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் reads as a choice of the second over the first.

note: Kural 1321 has the woman say that though he has no fault, his grace has the power to bring on a sulk; in Paripadal 12.55-60 the man has eyed another woman's breasts, and when beaten he 'sees no fault' (பிழை ஒன்றும் காணான்) and bows asking to be told it, and the onlookers call him the pure one (தூயவனைக் காண்மின்).
teaches: The couplet takes the faultless lover of the oodal at the woman's word, while the hymn shows a crowd that has watched him look and mocks his innocence as he begs to hear his fault, so together they show that the faultless husband of the sulk was a convention its audience knew to be a pose, and that the Kural's version is the inside view of a scene the festival saw from outside.

note: Kural 1064 says the dignity that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for all the world to hold (இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளா); Paripadal 12.101 ends by telling the Vaiyai that this flower-topped world cannot hold its fame (நின் புகழ் கொள்ளாது, இம் மலர் தலை உலகே).
teaches: The same measure, a greatness the world is too small to hold, is given by the hymn to a river's yearly plenty and by the Kural to a destitute man's refusal to ask, so the pair shows the ethical book taking the praise formula of abundance and fixing it on the one thing that has no abundance at all.

note: Both name the same five, taste, light or sight, touch, sound and smell; the Kural, in its chapter on renunciants, puts the world in the grasp of the one who discerns them, while Paripadal 13 says the five and the faculties that take them are the god.
teaches: The Kural's five, which the renunciant must master, are in the Paripadal the god himself, so the same old list of five could ground either a discipline of withdrawal from the senses or a worship through them.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Paripadal 13 line 47 says the two deeds are absent where his feet are praised, and gives the god a heart set on a single deed.
teaches: The Paripadal sets the Kural's claim inside a theology: the praisers are free of both deeds because the god himself is beyond the three times and holds to one deed, so the Kural's freedom from karma through praise is grounded in what the praised one is.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere at any time; Paripadal 15.49-53 says the god appears in whatever world and removes suffering when people are troubled, and sends worshippers with their families to his hill.
teaches: The Kural puts the movement on the devotee who reaches the feet, while the hymn puts it on a god who comes into each world and on the pilgrim's journey to one hill, so release from suffering is framed as both an inward arrival and a visit.

note: Kural 215 likens the wealth of a wise man who helps the world to the village tank filled with water; Paripadal 16.1-4 likens the banks, worn away as the flood carries off pepper, sandal and curd foam, to the giving of a generous lord.
teaches: The Kural uses full water as the image of a giver's wealth, and the Paripadal uses a giver as the image of water taking from its banks, so the pair shows the river-and-giving figure running both ways, with the Paripadal stressing that giving is a wearing away.

note: Kural 18 warns that if the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods; Paripadal 16.48-55 prays that the sky never refuse, so that the sandal, garlands, smoke and offerings of the river festival never dry and the Vaigai never runs dry.
teaches: The Kural states the dependence of worship on rain as a general warning, and the hymn turns the same dependence into a prayer said at the festival it describes, so the couplet's rule is shown at work in the Vaigai rites.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty of the householder the care of ancestors, gods, guests, kin and self; Paripadal 17.42-46 says the god's festival and the fine feasting of guests pass in turn between the hill, the Vaiyai and Koodal, and the song closes with a prayer made with kin (யாமும் எம் சுற்றமும்).
teaches: The Kural lays the duties to god, guest and kin on one household, while the hymn shows the same duties carried by a whole region in turn, hill, river and city, so the pair shows the couplet's private order also lived as the civic round of Madurai's festivals.

note: Kural 1320 has the man say that even when he looks at her thinking, she flares up: whom were you thinking of as you looked? In Paripadal 18.8-14 the woman sees him gaze at a peacock and think, says she knows his thought and demands it, and he answers that he was thinking how the peacock had stolen her bearing.
teaches: The couplet ends on the woman's suspicion with no reply, while the hymn supplies the reply that disarms it, that the thought was of her through the bird that took her grace, so the pair shows the silent gaze as a fixed cause of sulking and the lover's answer as part of the same convention.

note: Kural 37 tells us to see the way of aram in the difference between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it; Paripadal 19.10-13 likens the festival riders on horses and in chariots, in fine ornament and cloth, to those who have done much aram and set out for the world of the excellent to take its fruit.
teaches: Both picture the fruit of aram as riding in finery, but the Paripadal puts that ride in the passage to the next world and uses it only as a simile for festival-goers, while the Kural reads it in this world's ranks, so the pair shows the Kural's hard claim taking a shared image of heavenly reward and pressing it into a judgement on living people.

note: Kural 25 names Indra, lord of the wide heaven, as witness enough to the strength of one who has quenched the five senses; Paripadal 19.50-52 records visitors at the Parankunram painted hall explaining a picture: Indra as the cat, Ahalya, Gautama who had gone out, and her form turned to stone in his anger.
teaches: On the reading that Indra is witness through his own fall, the Kural's single name assumes a story that the Paripadal shows painted on a Madurai temple wall and told aloud to anyone who asked, so the couplet's allusion was not learned lore but a tale ordinary pilgrims were taught from pictures.

note: Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without comparison (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்) are freed from the mind's care; Paripadal 1.53-68 finds no likeness for the god (நின்னோர் அனையை) and ends with hearts made secure (ஏமுறு நெஞ்சத்தேம்) worshipping the shade of his feet.
teaches: The couplet's two terms, the incomparable one and refuge at his feet, appear in the hymn as a sequence: the singer first tries and fails to find a simile, and only then turns to the feet, so the Kural's maxim reads as the summary of a hymn's movement.

note: Naladiyar 385 has the wife wonder how women who embrace many chests for gain can do so daily; Paripadal 20.48-51 has the wife's companion call the courtesan a bought woman whose womanhood is common to all (பெண்மைப் பொதுமைப் பிணையிலி).
teaches: The Naladiyar's contrast of chaste wife and common woman is a private wondering, while in the Paripadal the same contrast becomes public abuse at the river, worked out as a farmer's claim on a straying ox, which shows the wife's chastity defended as a household's ownership of the husband and not only as her own shame.

note: Kural 913 makes the embrace of women who love for wealth a falsehood, like holding a stranger's corpse in the dark; in Paripadal 20.79-82 the paid woman herself argues that the payment was fair (விலை தந்தான்) and that the falsehood is the man's.
teaches: The Kural judges the bought embrace from the client's side, so the deceit is hers; the Paripadal lets the woman answer from inside the bargain, and on that reading the two cannot both stand, since one places the lie in her love and the other in his gift of what was not his to give.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say desire's axe breaks the door of restraint; Paripadal 20.91-94 has the onlookers say no one can bar men's chests from women and ask whether love stays within its bounds (கட வரை நிற்குமோ காமம்?).
teaches: In the Kural the claim that desire breaks every bound is a woman's confession about her own longing, while in the Paripadal the same claim is turned into an excuse for the husband's straying and urged on the wife, which shows how one maxim about love's force served opposite ends depending on whose desire it named.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; Paripadal 20.88-89 has onlookers tell a wronged wife that worthy women praise and bow to their husbands even when the husbands slight them (கேள்வரை ஏத்தி இறைஞ்சுவார்).
teaches: The Kural offers the wife's worship of her husband as a source of power over nature, but the Paripadal shows the same ideal used in a quarrel to silence a wife whose husband has given her bangle away, so the couplet's praise of devotion could serve in practice as counsel to put up with a man's straying.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 20.109-112 says it is the Vaiyai's nature to join lovers so that quarrel, friendship, parting, love and toddy are praised together.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the sulk sweetens union is a statement about two lovers, and the Paripadal extends it to a whole town's festival, closing a poem whose centre was a bitter public quarrel by counting that quarrel among the river's pleasures, so the couplet's private economy of oodal is shown working at civic scale.

note: Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet (இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்) cross the sea of births; Paripadal 21.16 asks only that dwelling at the foot of the god's hill (குன்றத்து அடி உறை) be granted, and line 68 repeats it as dwelling at the god's feet (நின் அடி உறை).
teaches: The Kural's feet are a way out of rebirth, while the Paripadal makes the same feet a place on the ground, the foot of one hill where worshippers ask to go on living, so the pair shows the god's feet as a refuge of release in the ethical book and as a home on earth in the older festival hymn.

note: Kural 1090 says brewed toddy (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights those who see it; Paripadal 21.20 has a dancer held by the joy of brewed toddy (அடு நறா மகிழ்) sulking at her husband, and the poet says such scenes, when recalled, are a painting's beauty.
teaches: The Kural separates the drinker's private pleasure from the beholder's pleasure in love, while the Paripadal mixes them in one woman, drunk and sulking at her husband, and makes her a picture for onlookers on the hill, so held together they show that at the shrine festival even the drinker's mood became something seen and enjoyed by others.

note: Kural 1 takes the letter அ, first of all letters, as the figure of the First Lord who is first of the world; Paripadal 2.58-59 uses the pointing letters அ, உ and எ (அவ்வும், உவ்வும், எவ்வயினோயும்) to say the god is that, this and whatever place.
teaches: Two early poets built theology from the Tamil alphabet in different ways: the Kural uses the order of the letters to make God the origin, while the hymn uses the pointing letters to make God every possible referent, origin set beside pervasion.

note: Paripadal 2.62-65 counts the seizing of the goat in the sacrifice and the fire oblation as the god's own food; Kural 259 says not to take one creature's life and eat it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices. On the plain reading the hymn honours the animal sacrifice that the couplet ranks below abstention.
teaches: The hymn's aside that others will not accept the brahmins' rite (பிறர் உடம்படுவாரா) and the Kural's ranking of not killing over sacrifice show the same quarrel from both sides, so the dispute over animal sacrifice was live within the Tamil tradition itself.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 3.53-58 makes Maal first of the immortals and first also of the asuras who fled from him into the sea, and asks whether there is any 'these are enemies, these friends' for those who know his nature.
teaches: The Kural states the god's freedom from liking and aversion as a bare attribute, while the hymn tests it against the war of gods and demons, where the god plainly took a side, and saves it by making him lord of both, so the pair shows the attribute had to be defended against a mythology of partisan war.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 4.49-55 says the god has harm and grace, cruelty and rightness wherever these are found and none where they are not, and treats the lives of those who praise him and those who do not without exchange, having neither foes nor kin.
teaches: The Kural defines the god by what he lacks, while the hymn shows what that lack allows: he can hold cruelty and grace alike because they answer what is in things rather than his own preference, so freedom from liking and aversion is seen to include, not exclude, the god's harshness.

note: Kural 241 ranks the wealth of அருள் above the wealth of goods, which even the base possess; Paripadal 5.80-81 refuses பொருளும் பொன்னும் and asks அருளும் அன்பும் அறனும்.
teaches: The Kural makes the ranking a general maxim about kinds of wealth, and the Paripadal turns that same ranking into the content of a prayer, showing the ethical scale used as the measure of what to ask a god for.

note: Kural 18 says that if the sky dries, festival and worship cease even for the gods; Paripadal 6.1-13 shows the rain that has come ending in incense, flowers, oblation and fire (புகை, பூ, அவி ஆராதனை, அழல்) at the river's arrival.
teaches: The Kural argues from absence that worship hangs on rain, and the Paripadal shows the positive side as one continuous scene from sea to cloud to river to offering, adding what the couplet leaves out: the same flood that feeds the rite also brings lovers together, so festival here means love as much as worship.

note: Kural 1251 has desire's axe break the door of restraint (நிறை); Paripadal 6.22-23 has the flood break its dam as lovers of one desire break the restraint that fills the heart (உளம் நிறை உடைத்தென).
teaches: The Kural's woman speaks of restraint broken as her private defeat, while the Paripadal makes the same breaking of நிறை the measure of a flood the whole town celebrates with drums, so the pair shows the Kural's image of a lost guard was also, in the festival, a public and welcome release.

note: Naladiyar 370 says fresh floodwater and a courtesan's friendship are alike, both ending when their source ends; Paripadal 6.72-75 has the wife say love's shrinking and swelling is the Vaiyai's flood.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the flood's ebb to condemn bought love and spare the household, but the Paripadal puts the same flood image in the wife's mouth against her own husband, so the didactic contrast of faithful wife and fickle courtesan breaks down once the river festival shows the husband's love rising and falling like the stream.

note: Kural 1134 says love's fierce flood carries off the raft (புணை) of shame and manliness; Paripadal 6.80-81 says the husband's chest, like a log in the river, became a raft (புணை) for women skilled at seizing.
teaches: In the Kural the raft is the lover's own virtue swept away by his desire, in the Paripadal the man himself is the raft that others ride, so the same river figure moves from an inner confession to a wife's accusation, and the festival's real floats show where the Kural's metaphor came from.

note: Naladiyar 222 says those who live by water do not rage when the flood breaks the dam but dam it again, as one bears a valued friend's repeated wrongs; Paripadal 6.83-87 says that even when the breached sluice is closed the spray still wells, as her burning goes on after he returns.
teaches: The two poems use the same breached dam for opposite claims: the Naladiyar makes re-damming the picture of calm forbearance that works, while the Paripadal wife says closing the breach does not stop the leak, so the pair shows that the moralist's patience is exactly what the wronged wife declares impossible.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that whatever garland he wears she says he wore it for another woman; in Paripadal 6.91-92 the wife asks who pressed into his garland and what touched it, and he blames the river.
teaches: The Kural states the suspicious garland as a pure case of love's jealousy, with no cause given, while the Paripadal gives the garland a real crushing and a real crowd in the water, so the pair shows the couplet's general complaint distilled from a festival in which the evidence truly could point either way.

note: Kural 1302, spoken by the friend, says sulking is like salt and a little too much spoils it; Paripadal 6.98-99 has those around the wife say that if the sulk festers much love is spoiled (துனி நனி கன்றிடின் காமம் கெடூஉம்).
teaches: The same counsel to a sulking wife appears in both, but the Paripadal shows it said aloud at the festival and then acted on by skilled pleaders until the sulk is understood, so the Kural's measure of salt turns out to belong to a social practice of reconciliation, not only to one friend's private advice.

note: Kural 17 says even the wide sea would lose its nature if the cloud that drew from it gave nothing back; Paripadal 7.1-10 begins with clouds that have drawn the dark sea fully (பௌவம் செவ்விதா அற முகந்து) and ends the sentence with the land's good and beauty swelling as the Vaiyai comes.
teaches: The couplet states the exchange between sea and cloud as a warning about withholding, while the song follows the same water through rain, falls and river into the Pandya fields, so together they show that the Kural's abstract cycle was the felt shape of the flood festival, praised in the hymn as the return the couplet only demands.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her lover's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Paripadal 7.69-75 the woman's fury falls on her lover because he looked at the ornaments of the bathing women (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட).
teaches: The couplet makes the man's being looked at enough for oodal, the hymn makes his looking the offence, and the song's crowded bathing shows why both could be true at once: in the festival everyone sees and is seen, so the sulk needs no act of straying, only the eyes.

note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

note: Kural 17 says even the great sea loses its nature if the cloud withholds rain; Paripadal 8.128-130 prays that the hill's streaming falls and springs last even when the sky dries and the earth cracks (மண் பரிய வானம் வறப்பினும், மன்னுகமா).
teaches: The Kural makes every water, the sea included, depend on rain, and the Paripadal asks that the god's waterfall be exempt from that law, which is what marks the shrine's water as sacred rather than natural.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 9.12-22 ranks love, equal union and karpu, and places the courtesan, the reproach and the சுணங்கறை inside karpu, with their fruit in the sulk (ஊடல்).
teaches: The Kural gives the sulk's worth as a man's two-line saying, while the Paripadal builds it into a ranked theory addressed to Vedic scholars and then uses it to excuse a god's wives, so the pair shows oodal already held as doctrine of Tamil porul, citable to outsiders and to the gods.

note: In both a wife refuses the husband who has been with other women: Kural 1311 says 'I will not come near your chest, philanderer' (நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு); in Paripadal 9.30-40 the wife blesses him ironically and cries 'don't come near' (குறுகல்), while the rival gives him her chest (மார்பு அளிப்பாளை).
teaches: The Kural's refusal is private and the rival only imagined, while the Paripadal stages the same refusal with the rival present and offering the very chest the wife denies, so the pair shows the one gesture of refusing the chest working as a quarrel between two women, not only between wife and husband.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called the good path to heaven, and giving good even if there were no higher world; thirattu 12 praises a city that rejoices to see receivers (ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்) and ranks its life above heaven. On the reading that ஏற்பார் are those who take gifts, the fragment honours the very taking the Kural calls bad.
teaches: Both cut the value of giving loose from heaven, but the Kural does it by condemning the receiver while the Paripadal makes the receiver's presence a joy of the city, so the two hold opposite views of whether asking belongs to the good life.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the one you love; Paripadal Thirattu 1.33-46 lists the shrine crowd as matched men and women and says the god's town is like the heaven where ripened deeds are enjoyed.
teaches: The couplet sets lovers' joy against Mal's heaven as rivals, but the hymn builds its likeness of heaven out of the paired lovers in the god's own crowd, so the opposition the Kural plays on was not one the temple festival felt.

note: Kural 1014 asks whether shame (நாணுடைமை) is not an ornament of the worthy; thirattu 6 calls modesty the girl's ancient ornament (நாண் எனும் தொல்லை அணி) at her first union.
teaches: The same figure of shame as an ornament serves the Kural for the moral restraint of the worthy and the Paripadal for a bride's reserve at first union, which shows that naanam named both and that the poets ranked the bride's reserve above her jewels as the Kural ranks restraint above pride.

note: Kural 118 likens the worthy man's impartiality to a balance that levels itself before it weighs; thirattu 7 has poets weigh the world against Koodal with the balance of their learning (புலக் கோலால் தூக்க).
teaches: Read beside the Kural's just balance, the fragment's praise borrows the authority of an impartial weighing, so the poets present their verdict on Koodal as fairness, the ornament of the worthy, rather than as a court singer's flattery.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; thirattu 9 says Madurai's fame will stand and blossom as long as the king's hill exists (குன்றம் உண்டாகும் அளவு).
teaches: The Kural makes fame the one thing that does not perish, while the Paripadal blessing gives even the city's fame a term measured by a hill, so the poets' praise of undying renown was bounded by the oldest lasting things of the land.

note: Akananuru 296's friend turns the hero away because he bathed in the great Vaigai with the dark girl (பெருநீர் வையை அவளொடு ஆடி) and the talk is like Koodal's clamour; Paripadal 10.19-23 lists chaste wives and courtesans (பதிவத மாதர், பரத்தையர்) going together to the Vaigai at Koodal.
teaches: Since the festival put wives and courtesans in the same flood openly, the friend's charge in Akananuru 296 cannot be the bathing itself, a licensed public pleasure, but the companion he chose, so the akam poem turns a shared civic rite into private evidence.

note: Kuruntokai 37's tusker strips yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger, left for the heroine to read as the hero's love; Paripadal 10.42-52 has a tusker turn back to embrace his terrified mate and says outright சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்.
teaches: The Paripadal poet spells out in one line the sense that Kuruntokai 37 leaves implied, which shows that the caring elephant pair was read by the poets themselves as an image of the lover who removes the beloved's distress.

note: Akananuru 266's wife says her husband played in the evening flood with young women and lost his shame (நாண்இழந்து), and the talk is loud as a feast; Paripadal 10.63-68 shows lovers in the flood hiding their joy for fear of gossip (அலர் அஞ்சி).
teaches: The Paripadal shows that the flood-play crowd expected lovers to hide, so the wife's charge that he 'lost his shame' accuses him of breaking a restraint the festival itself kept, not of joining the play.

note: Paripadal 11.120-121 has the bathing women ask that for seven births, without growing old, their rich kin last and bear children; in Kuruntokai 49 a wife asks her husband that even when this birth gives way to the next he be her husband and she the one close to his heart.
teaches: What the Kuruntokai wife says privately to one man, the Paripadal's women ask together of the river at a public festival, so the wish to keep the same spouse beyond this birth was a recognised petition of the Thai rite, not only one woman's vow of love.

note: Paripadal 11.62-71 praises the Vaigai water-sport of men with gold-garlanded women as an open custom (கரவா வழக்கிற்று); in Akananuru 296 the friend refuses a husband who bathed in the great Vaigai with another woman and says it is already common talk.
teaches: The same Madurai river festival that the devotional song celebrates as a public glory with nothing hidden is, seen from the wife's door, the proof and occasion of a husband's straying, so the openness the Paripadal praises is exactly what feeds the alar of the marutham quarrel.

note: Natrinai 80 names in one line a girl who bathes in the cold pond of the month of Thai with her jewelled companions (தைஇத் திங்கள் தண் கயம் படியும்); Paripadal 11.74-92 sets out the rite itself: Aathirai, the brahmins, the elder women of the ford, the dawn bath and the fire.
teaches: The akam poem's passing mention of a Thai bath points to a guarded public rite with priests, elder women and mothers, so the girl a lover sees there is seen at a sanctioned gathering of maidens, which is why such a meeting could happen and why shyness must restrain her.

note: Paripadal 11.106-110 tells literally of a youth whom the Vaigai's current carries off while a girl takes his heart (கடும் புனல் கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க); in Kalittokai 98 a husband swears he was delayed bathing in the Vaigai's new flood, and his wife answers that people saw the new flood drag him off, a flood that was a woman.
teaches: The wife's figure of the woman as a flood that carried him off is the Paripadal's festival event turned into an accusation, so the river festival was both the occasion of a man being swept away by a look and the stock excuse for it, and the Kalittokai's irony depends on the audience knowing the Paripadal scene.

note: In Kalittokai 67.6-9 the wife says she will sulk when her husband comes showing the wounds and scars (புண், வடு) that other women's garlands (கோதையால் அலைத்த) left on him, and her heart gives way when she sees him; in Paripadal 12.57-73 the wife herself beats her husband with her garland (கமழ் கோதை கோலாப் புடைத்து), then fears a scar on his chest (வடு அஞ்சி) and her quarrel passes.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the garland-wound is evidence against the husband, written on him by rival women, while in the hymn the wife wields the garland herself and her fear of the scar is what ends her sulk, so the pair shows the garland-blow as a festival game of the Vaiyai town whose meaning, accusation or claim, depends on whose hand struck it.

note: Kalittokai 67.3-5 says the Vaiyai beating against the wall (மதில் பொரூஉம்) is the only enemy the walled town has known; Paripadal 12.9 has the town hear that the Vaiyai has come beating against Madurai's wall (மதுரை மதில் பொரூஉம்) and rush out in finery to meet it.
teaches: The akam poem turns the river's assault on the wall into a boast that no army ever reached Madurai, and the hymn shows what that only siege was like inside the walls, a summons that sends the whole town to dress and ride out, so together they show the flood as the city's one welcomed attack, the festival standing where war stands for other towns.

note: In Akananuru 194 the heroine hears the peacock cry in the very rains her lover named for his return and he has not come; in Paripadal 14 the peacock's cry on the god's rainy hill is like the words calling the departed lover 'do not delay, come'.
teaches: The Paripadal's simile only works for a hearer who knows the mullai convention the Akananuru poem dramatises, the rains as the deadline of return, so the devotional poet borrows the heroine's grief as an ornament of the god's hill and makes the peacock say the summons she can only feel.

note: Ainkurunuru 47 has the woman tell the man that her companions know he tells many lies, just like his bard; Paripadal 18.16-22 shows her making the bard see the nail marks, the embrace and the ornaments on the man and calling his song a bloom of lies (பொய் வளம் பூத்தன).
