teaches: The Ainkurunuru gives the charge that the bard lies as his master does, and the hymn gives the proof shown to the bard's face, the marks the hill's women left, so together they show the god's festival hill as one of the places where marutham's straying was caught, with the bard's song refuted by the body.

note: Kuruntokai 1 says the hill of the Red One, who killed the demons till the field ran red, is thick with kanthal clusters the colour of blood (குருதிப் பூவின் குலைக்காந் தட்டே); Paripadal 18.35-36 says the close-packed kanthal of the god's hill are like the hands of men defeated in war and bound.
teaches: Both poets make the kanthal of Murugan's hill a sign of his war, but the Kuruntokai reads it by colour, the blood of the slain, and the Paripadal by shape, the clasped hands of the captured, so the pair shows the flower fixed as the god's war emblem while each poet chose a different basis for it.

note: Kalittokai 95 has the husband say he only watched a quail fight (குறும்பூழ் போர்), and the wife turns each kind of quail fight into a figure for his affairs; in Paripadal 18.12-14 the man says he looked at the peacock and at a quail dazed with revelry, and the woman looked at him as a stranger.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the man's watching of birds is an alibi that the wife exposes, while in the Paripadal his gaze at birds is a lover's thought of her that he can explain away, so the pair shows the same excuse of bird-watching used once for a lie caught and once for a sulk mended on the god's hill.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that if Murugan, the tall Vel smelling of veri, should actually relieve her at the mother's rite, her lover will hear that her pain was something else; Paripadal 19.89-94 says maidens will not reach young men's arms, nor wives their husbands' grace, unless they eat the leftover of the god's elephant at his hill.
teaches: The akam girl's dread makes sense only if Murugan really does rule a girl's union, and the Paripadal states that power openly as a festival rite that maidens and wives perform, so together they show that the akam irony about the veri rite rests on a public belief in the god as the giver of husbands, not on disbelief in him.

note: Akananuru 186 has the courtesan say, for the wife's women to overhear, that the wife's real enemy is the husband who leaves women pale and lives in her own house; Paripadal 20.79-82 has the courtesan tell the wife to her face that he is the thief and she is not (அவன் கள்வன்; கள்வி நான் அல்லேன்).
teaches: Together the two show that shifting the blame onto the husband was the courtesan's settled defence in marutham, and that what the Akananuru gives as an overheard boast the festival poem stages as a face-to-face exchange, with the husband's gift on her body as the evidence and a crowd to hear both sides.

note: Akananuru 82.1-10 makes the hill country a stage: wind in bamboo the flute, the waterfall the drum, bees the lute, monkeys the audience and the peacock a dancer; Paripadal 21.30-38 has the peacock dance, the thumbi as flute, bees as lute and the waterfall as drum on the god's hill.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hill's orchestra is a love poem's setting, praising the hill man's country and ending in the woman's lonely night, while the Paripadal keeps the same instruments, drops the monkey audience and the lovers, and gives the scene to the god with the drum, so the pair shows a figure from akam landscape reused as worship of the hill's own god.

note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

note: Akananuru 296 makes the husband's bathing in the great Vaigai with a dark girl the gossip of Koodal; Paripadal 6.26-43 shows the whole town, young and old, rich and strong, going down to play in the same river.
teaches: Read against the Paripadal's crowd at the fords, the Akananuru friend's charge cannot be that he bathed in the Vaigai, since everyone did; the scandal lies in whom he bathed with, so the akam reproach depends on a public festival that the akam poem itself never describes.

note: In Akananuru 266 the wife says the husband's water-play with young women in the evening flood is gossip but that what hurts is his oath by Murugan of Alaivay; in Paripadal 6.88-96 the husband, accused after the water-play, swears by cool Parankunram.
teaches: Both husbands answer a water-play charge with an oath to a Murugan shrine, but the Akananuru wife treats the oath as the worse betrayal while the Paripadal lets the oath pass into a reconciliation brokered by others, so the pair shows the festival hymn softening into play what the akam anthology records as a wound.

note: Ainkurunuru 69 has the wife say she has seen the husband's woman crying, eyes reddened, when the cool flood with its flowers swept her sand-play away at the crowded ford; Paripadal 7.25-26 lists among the town's cries the young women weeping that the flood broke the dolls they drew in the sand.
teaches: In the hymn the weeping over sand dolls is one anonymous cry among many on flood day, while the akam wife picks out one such girl to mock as her husband's new woman, so the pair shows the akam poet taking a stock festival scene and turning it into a mark of the rival's childishness.

note: Akananuru 266 has the wife tell her husband that his bathing yesterday in the new flood with young women, gazing again and again at one woman's rain-cool eyes, is now loud gossip; Paripadal 7.65-76 shows the scene itself: a bard praises a bather's eyes, the lover who looked at the bathers is pulled into the mud and his head trodden on by the woman in her sulk.
teaches: The Akananuru gives only the aftermath, the wife's reproach once talk has spread, whereas the Paripadal shows the gazing at the eyes and the quarrel breaking out at once in the river, so together they show the river bathing as the very occasion of the marutham sulk, with its offence and its punishment both public.

note: In Akananuru 166 the husband soothes his wife by calling on the Velur god to afflict him if he went to the other woman, and the other woman exposes the lie; in Paripadal 8.65-66 the wife forbids such an oath by Murugan, since the god's true spear would eat him.
teaches: The Akananuru shows the god-oath used lightly as a husband's comfort, the Paripadal shows a wife who takes the same self-curse seriously enough to block it, so together they reveal that the oath was believed to bind the swearer bodily and that a knowing wife could protect a lying husband from it.

note: Kuruntokai 53 says the oath the man swore at the sandy ford with the hill goddesses as witness is what afflicts us, the women (எம்மணங் கினவே); Paripadal 8.66 says the god's spear will devour the man himself if he swears falsely.
teaches: On the plain reading of each, the two poems disagree on whom a broken god-witnessed oath strikes, the deceived women in the Kuruntokai and the perjurer in the Paripadal, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to where the god's punishment falls.

note: In Natrinai 386 the girl refuses the hero's offer of a dread oath by the god (அணங்குடை அருஞ் சூள்) because men of his kin do not need it, and he comes with marriage; in Paripadal 8.65-71 the wife refuses her husband's oath by Murugan because the god's spear would devour a false swearer.
teaches: Both women stop a man from swearing by the god, but for opposite reasons, trust in his kin in the courtship poem and certainty of his guilt in the marriage quarrel, which shows that refusing the god-oath was a recognised move whose meaning depended on the stage of love.

note: Kalittokai 35 counts Koodal's seasonal pleasures (bees on the Vaigai's sandbank, the festival, the townsmen savouring poets' new words) as the times the absent man promised to return; thirattu 13 lists the Vaigai flood, the god's hill and spear-eyed women as pleasures among which Koodal's people lose their way daily.
teaches: The same catalogue of Koodal's pleasures marks the hour of a promised return in the Kalittokai and causes daily indecision in the Paripadal, so the city's festive plenty was a stock that akam used to sharpen absence and city praise used to show abundance.

note: Kalittokai 98 has the husband excuse his absence by the Vaiyai's new flood (வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்); Paripadal thirattu 2.36-39 has the rival excuse the lover's garland in her hair by the same flood (தானே புறன் தந்து வேய்தந்தது ... அறிந்து புனல் புணர்த்தது).
teaches: Held together, the two show that the festival flood was the stock excuse of the whole triangle: the man pleads it to his wife, and the other woman pleads it to the wife too, so the wife's scorn in the Kalittokai answers an alibi that every party in the Vaiyai festival could use.

note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

note: Kalittokai 35 line 2 likens humming bees in the boughs to the enjoyment of those who live on a diligent man's wealth; thirattu 8 likens those who live on gifts (பரிசில் வாழ்நர்) to bees eating pollen.
teaches: The bee and the dependent were interchangeable figures that ran in both directions, a season described through patronage in Kalittokai and a society through a flower in the Paripadal, and only the Paripadal says whom the dependents feed on: the households, not the palace.

note: Purananuru 3 counsels the Pandya Vazhuthi that suppliants have crossed deadly roads and his strength is to read their need and end their poverty; Paripadal 10.125-126 names the Vazhuthi who pours gold into the hands of poets in want (இலம்படு புலவர்).
teaches: What the puram poet urges on a Vazhuthi as a duty to be kept, the devotional poet takes as so settled a fact of the Pandya house that it can serve as the vehicle for praising the river itself.

note: Purananuru 56.3-6 sets out the conch-white plough-bearer with the palmyra banner and the gem-dark one with the bird banner as two of four separate gods; Paripadal 1.3-11 gives the same emblems (வால் வளை மேனி, நாஞ்சில், சேவல் அம் கொடி) to one god addressed in the singular.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows that the emblem sets of Balarama and Thirumal were fixed common iconography, but that the Paripadal's Vaishnava singer had already fused the two brothers into one object of worship that the puram poet still counted as two gods.

note: Purananuru 59 tells the Pandya he is like the sun to his foes and like the moon to us (ஞாயிறு அனையை ... திங்கள் அனையை); Paripadal 1.41-45 tells the god he is grace to those who love him and terror to foes, the moon and the burning sun, with no marker of likeness.
teaches: The devotional poet took the king-praise formula of grace to friends and fire to foes and dropped its marker of comparison, so what the court poet offers as a simile becomes in the hymn a statement of identity.

note: Purananuru 56 makes the Pandya equal (ஒத்தீயே) to each of four gods in one quality; Paripadal 1.53-57 says no one can be found of whom to say the god is like them, so he is like only himself (நின்னோர் அனையை); both describe the bird-bannered god's body with the same formula, மண்ணுறு மணி (Pura 56.5, Pari 1.62).
teaches: The pairing shows a limit to the பூவைநிலை way of praising a king by the gods: the likeness runs one way only, since a king can be measured by a god but the hymn finds nothing by which to measure the god.

note: Purananuru 107 answers the poets who praise Pari alone: there is also the rain (மாரியும் உண்டு) that sustains the world; Paripadal 22.8 says the sky poured water like the king's bounty (அவன் வண்மைபோல் வானம் பொழிந்த நீர்), after likening clouds, thunder, drops and lightning to his elephants, drum, arrows and spear.
teaches: Kapilar measures the patron against the rain and lets the rain win, while the Paripadal measures the rain against the king and makes the whole storm a copy of his war and gifts, so held together they show the rain-and-giving comparison run in both directions, with the river hymn making the king the original and nature the likeness.

note: Purananuru 35.14-21 tells Killivalavan that his sky-touching umbrella is not to keep off the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, under a sceptre like aram itself; Paripadal 3.74-76 says the god, with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, made the twenty-one worlds a single shade with no second shade.
teaches: The puram poet has to argue the king into reading his umbrella as protection, a meaning the king may fail, whereas the hymn makes protection the umbrella's very substance in the god and takes over the royal boast of one shade with no rival, so the pair shows divine kingship and the counsel to kings using one ideal to measure each other.

note: Purananuru 56.1-8 gives four gods four banners: the bull, the palm (பனைக்கொடி) of the conch-white one with the plough, the bird of the sapphire-dark one, the peacock; Paripadal 4.37-41 gives the dark god the bird, the palm, the plough and the elephant, and says there is no banner that is not his. On the plain reading the palm banner belongs to a different god in one poem and to Mal in the other.
teaches: The puram poet needs four separate gods so that the king can match each in one excellence, while the devotional poet folds the elder brother's palm and plough into Mal's own emblems, so the pair shows how a hymn's claim of sole lordship rearranged the very iconography the court poets used as a fixed set.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Purananuru 38 says bards think of Killivalavan's land even in the gods' golden grove, because there no one with means gives and no one in want asks (உடையோர் ஈதலும் இல்லோர் இரத்தலும்); thirattu 12 says Koodal honours givers and rejoices at receivers, so who would go to the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு)?
teaches: Purananuru 38 supplies the reason the fragment leaves unsaid, that heaven is poorer for lacking the exchange of giving and asking, so the Paripadal's preference for Koodal over heaven rests on an older argument first made for a king's land and here transferred to a city and its god's hill.

note: Patitruppattu 31.1-10 shows crowds from the four quarters who go unfed (உண்ணாப் பைஞ்ஞிலம்), bathe at the cold ghat and praise the red feet of the tulasi-garlanded lord before going home glad; Paripadal Thirattu 1.43-46 shows the crowd at the god's town bearing food offerings, umbrellas, incense and flowers, in a town like a heaven of enjoyment.
teaches: Read together the two give two modes of early Mal worship, a fasting and bathing crowd in the Chera poem and a feasting, paired and pleasure-seeking crowd in the Koodal hymn, so devotion to the same god was already practised as abstinence in one place and as festival in another.

note: Purananuru 55.1-4 gives the mountain bow strung with a snake (பாம்புஞாண்) and the three forts burned with one arrow as the blue-throated god's feat, an emblem to measure the Pandya by; Paripadal Thirattu 1.80-82 says the serpent became the string of the Himalaya bow when the bull-rider destroyed the three cities and that it was they who gave him that ancient fame.
teaches: The same snake-strung bow is Shiva's glory in a court poem and the serpent's own merit in a shrine hymn, so the pair shows that a fixed myth could be re-credited to whichever power a cult served, the bowstring becoming the hero once it had a temple.

note: Kalavazhi Narpathu 30 likens the pooled blood of the battlefield, dragging killed elephants, to a flood that rolls boulders down the hill (மலையுருட்டு நீர்போல்); Paripadal 12.84-85 sees the Vaiyai in the morning of the rains red with turbid blood (கலிழ் செங் குருதித்தே) and names it the river of the king whose army kills in war.
teaches: The war poem uses the hill torrent as the image for battle blood and the hymn uses battle blood as the image for the monsoon torrent, so held together they show the comparison running both ways for Tamil poets: the king's killing is a flood and his river's flood is his killing, the river's redness counting as his fame.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai describes the twice-born at Eragam in full, never failing in the six duties, keeping the three fires and chanting at the proper hour; Paripadal 14 compresses them to a riddle of counts, இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ஒரு பெயர், and says the god delights in their aram.
teaches: The idyll's full portrait supplies what the Paripadal's terse count assumes, so its இரு பிறப்பு is the same இருபிறப்பாளர் the idyll names, and the brahmins' ritual life is shown to be, for both poems, one of the things Murugan is praised for enjoying.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 67-77 marks the god's dwelling on the hill west of Koodal by the bees that sleep in the lotus and hum round the pool flowers opening like eyes; Paripadal 17.37-38 says that when the swingers leap together on festival day the bees that suck the pool flowers' pollen cannot reach them.
teaches: The guide poem gives the hill west of Koodal at rest, its pool bees the sign of the god's ordinary dwelling, and the hymn uses the same pool bees to measure the festival, when the crowd drives them off, so the pair shows the same place on its common day and on its feast day.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the god's hill west of Koodal of crowded mansion streets, among wide muddy fields of lotus and bees; Paripadal 19.8-18 fills the whole stretch between the hill and Koodal (குன்றொடு கூடல் இடையெல்லாம்) with a pre-dawn procession of riders, chariots and garlanded heads.
teaches: The guide poem gives the pilgrim the hill's place relative to the city and its quiet fields, and the hymn shows the same stretch on festival day as one continuous human garland, so together they show Parankunram as Madurai's own shrine, whose road from the city was itself part of the festival.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 206-217 describes the god as red, in red clothing (செய்யன் சிவந்த ஆடையன்), dancing on every hill with the women's soft shoulders in his arms; Paripadal 19.97-100 tells him his dress and cloak are red, his weapon coral-coloured, his form like fire and his face like the young sun.
teaches: The guide poem's red god is roaming from hill to hill in the kurinji dance, while the hymn addresses the same red figure as the image standing by the kadambu at one shrine, praised by a gathered company, so the pair shows one colour iconography carried from the wandering god of the hill people to the fixed god of a temple.

note: Paripadal 5.1-4 (பனிக் கடல் ... புக்கு ... சூர் மா முதல் தடிந்து) and Thirumurugatruppadai 45-46 and 60 (பனிக்கடல் கலங்கவுள் புக்குச் சூர்முதல் தடிந்த ... மாமுதல் தடிந்த) tell the Sur deed in nearly the same words.
teaches: The near-identical phrasing in two different collections shows the Sur killing already had a fixed verbal formula, a shared stock of Murugan praise that both poets drew on rather than one poem borrowing a picture from the other.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 151-154 shows Siva only as one of three lords who come to see Murugan, with Uma, three unwinking eyes and the three forts destroyed; Paripadal 5.22-47 tells how that same god's union with Uma led to Murugan's birth.
teaches: The guide poem gives the kinship only as epithets (son of the god of the banyan, line 256) and shows Siva as a visiting lord, while the Paripadal narrates the birth in full, so the pair shows the story was known to both but told only where a poem chose to narrate rather than to direct a pilgrim.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 253-255 (நெடும்பெருஞ் சிமையத்து நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை ... அறுவர் பயந்த) and Paripadal 5.48-49 (இமயத்து நீலப் பைஞ் சுனைப் பயந்தோர்) set the birth in the same blue pool and give him six mothers.
teaches: Both poems use நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை and the six who bore him, but only the Paripadal says who the six were and why their chastity stayed whole, so the guide poem's single epithet is seen to presuppose a full birth story its hearers already knew.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai ends with the god giving the suppliant a rare gift (பெறலரும் பரிசில்) that makes him stand alone in the world; Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram.
teaches: The guide poem frames devotion in the bard's economy of gifts, while the Paripadal explicitly refuses material gifts, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to what one should ask of Murugan, the patron's reward and the ethical state.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 167 gives the attending gods as a sum (நால்வேறு இயற்கைப் பதினொரு மூவரொடு); Paripadal 8.4-7 names the same thirty-three group by group: twelve, two who speak of medicine, eight, and eleven from the lord of Aathirai.
teaches: The guide poem's 'eleven times three of four kinds' is spelled out in the Paripadal as four counted groups, showing that the Vedic thirty-three were known in Tamil by their divisions and that both poets made Murugan the one they attend.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the hill west of Koodal, with bees humming over pool flowers that open like eyes; Paripadal 8.17-28 makes the same bees, pools and flowers the god's procession, the coming from your hill to Koodal (குன்றத்தான் கூடல் வரவு).
teaches: The guide poem fixes Parankundram by its position beside the city, while the Paripadal turns the road between them into a seasonal procession of sound and bloom, so together they show the shrine defined by its tie to Madurai rather than as a lone mountain retreat.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 6 names the god only as husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity (மறுவில் கற்பின் வாணுதற் கணவன்); Paripadal 9.8-11 names her as the daughter of the thousand-eyed one and sets the wedding at Parankunram, marked by rain in summer.
teaches: Held together, the guide poem's opening epithet turns out to rest on a wedding story that the Paripadal ties to one hill, which explains why Parankunram, the hill of that marriage, is the first abode the guide poem then visits.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 101-102 gives one of the six faces to smiling with Valli, the hill-dwellers' daughter, after its opening epithet for the chaste wife; Paripadal 9.81 names the god as lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu (கற்பு இணை நெறியூடு அற்பு இணைக் கிழமை).
teaches: The guide poem lists the two marriages separately, one as an epithet and one as a face's work, while the Paripadal joins them in one phrase after teaching the order of love, so the pair shows the two consorts being read as the two branches of akam, karpu and the love of free choice, united in one god.

note: Both name the god by his marks, the konrai, the matted hair and the woman who is part of him; Purananuru 1 lists them without a name, Tirumanthiram 16 calls him the one whose part is the bright-browed woman.
teaches: Set beside Tirumular, the anthology's invocation shows that konrai, matted hair and the woman-part were already a fixed set of marks that identified the god without his name, and it adds what Tirumular's verse lacks: the god may also hide that female form within himself.

note: Tirumanthiram 157 calls the mourners who burn the body and bathe unjust for returning to life; 245 is a mourner who burned his wife and is appalled that he still lives.
teaches: The king's poem complicates the Tirumanthiram's charge: survival after the pyre is shown not as forgetting but as grief's own failure to kill, which the survivor feels as shame.

note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

note: Kural 211 makes the rain the model of giving that seeks no return; Patitruppattu 18 says that even if the rain-cloud fails for many years, Cheralathan will not fail the bards' hope.
teaches: The Kural treats rain as the standard for duty-bound giving, but the Chera poem ranks the king above that standard because rain can fail, so the bards' praise claims for a patron a reliability the ethics book grants only to nature.

note: Kural 86 says the one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Patitruppattu 21 calls the king's kitchen-fat an ஆவுதி (oblation) beside the sacrificial one and says the two smells together please the gods who abide in the sky.
teaches: The Chera poem shows the mechanism the Kural only asserts: feeding guests reaches the gods because the kitchen smoke is itself counted as an oblation, so hospitality was understood as a second sacrifice rather than merely compared to one.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's power; Patitruppattu 22 puts தெறல் கடுமை, severity of punishment, in one list with too much kindness and too much love as obstacles to dharma's wheel.
teaches: Read together, the Kural treats harshness on its own while the Chera poem sets it beside its opposite excesses, so the older list frames royal justice as a mean between cruelty and indulgence rather than as the avoidance of cruelty alone.

note: Kural 578 gives the world to those able to show kannottam without spoiling the task; Patitruppattu 22 lists கழிகண்ணோட்டம், excessive kindly regard, among the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, beside anger and harsh punishment.
teaches: The Chera list names as a fault exactly the excess the Kural's condition guards against, which shows that the Kural's praise of kannottam was already bounded in older court ethics where too much mercy blocked a king's justice.

note: Kural 559 says if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain; Patitruppattu 24 ends that even if the rain-cloud forgets its season the king's wealth will keep its yield.
teaches: The Kural binds the land's rain to the king's justice, but the praise poem claims the just king's plenty survives even a failed monsoon, so court praise pushed royal power past the cosmic dependence the ethical maxim keeps.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; Patitruppattu 24 names the six duties (ஓதல் வேட்டல் அவைபிறர்ச் செய்தல் ஈதல் ஏற்றல்) and says the king walks by the word of those who keep them, so that the world walks by his.
teaches: The Kural makes the Brahmins' learning depend on the king's protection, while the Chera poem makes the king's conduct depend on the Brahmins' word, so the pair shows the relation running both ways: guarded by the king, they in turn guide him.

note: Kural 301 says anger is truly restrained only where it could take effect; Patitruppattu 32 marvels that the king, having broken the enemy and taken their land, is not angry even in the country of those who reviled him.
teaches: The Kural's rule names the only test of restraint that counts, and the Chera poem shows a king passing it at the one moment conquest gives his anger full power, which is why the poet calls it a wonder rather than a duty.

note: Kural 750 says that whatever excellences a fort has, it is nothing without men excellent in action; Patitruppattu 33 makes the marching army itself a fortress, swords for wall, spears for hedge and arrows for moat.
teaches: The Kural makes the defenders the real worth of a fort, and the Chera poet takes that to its end by removing the walls altogether, so that the fort exists wherever the army camps.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Patitruppattu 37 lists the king's victory (வலம்படு வென்றியும்) and his unbending principle (கோடாக் கொள்கையும்) as two separate things he has.
teaches: The Kural makes straight rule the cause of victory, while the Chera poet sets the two side by side as distinct possessions, so the praise poem lacks the causal claim the maxim adds and shows the two were first counted as separate royal goods.

note: Kural 322 ranks sharing food (பகுத்துண்டு) first among all that the authors gathered (தொகுத்தவற்றுள்); Patitruppattu 38 praises the king for the manliness that gathered the sharing of food (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை) and for living for others.
teaches: The same pair of words, sharing and gathering, ranks a virtue in the Kural's list of teachings and names a king's acquired valour in the Chera poem, so a virtue the Kural places among the vows against killing appears here as a warrior's manhood.

note: Kural 776 says the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound; Patitruppattu 42 says the king's men wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies already hold arrows and whose chests show the surgeon's needle-scars.
teaches: The Kural keeps the ledger of wounds inside one man's private reckoning, while the Chera poem turns it into a rule of the company, so that scars decide who may stand in the thumbai line and the wound becomes a public credential rather than a personal measure.

note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; Patitruppattu 43 likens the king's giving to rain that breaks a drought and floods the river banks.
teaches: Both take rain as the model of giving, but the Kural uses it to show giving without return, while the Chera poet uses drought-breaking rain to show giving measured by need and graded by receiver, so the same image yields a rule of disinterest in one and a rule of fit in the other.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called a good path, and giving good even without a higher world; Patitruppattu 52 says the king's hand bends down to give to suppliants and does not know how to open upward to take (இரப்போர்க்குக் கவிதல் அல்லதை இரைஇய மலர்பு அறியா).
teaches: The poem turns the couplet's two verbs into two postures of one hand, palm down to give and palm up to receive, so the rule against taking becomes a bodily habit the king cannot break.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Patitruppattu 54 wishes that the giving king not go to the high world (உயர்நிலை உலகத்துச் செல்லாது) but stay long on the earth.
teaches: The couplet sets heaven aside as irrelevant to the worth of giving, while the bard treats the giver's heaven as a loss to those who live on his gifts and wishes it postponed, so the same detachment of giving from heaven appears once as an ethic and once as the suppliants' self-interest.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world gives back to the rain, to show that obligation seeks no return; Patitruppattu 55 wishes the giving king's days to pass like white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and go up to rest on the hill.
teaches: Both use the rain cloud for the giver, but the Kural stops at the absence of return, while the Chera poem imagines what the cloud has after giving, rest on the hill, and makes that the blessing on the king's lifespan.

note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Patitruppattu 57 says the king fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of the women of his house (ஒண்நுதல் மகளிர் துனித்த கண்ணினும் இரவலர் புன்கண் அஞ்சும்).
teaches: The couplet names the giver's discomfort in general, and the poem measures it against the strongest private disturbance of akam, a wife's sulk, so the giver's pain is ranked above domestic love.

note: Kural 120 says true trade for merchants is caring for others' goods as their own; Patitruppattu 59 tells the king that protecting the land, where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads stay unblocked in the way of dharma, is his duty.
teaches: The Kural places fair trade in the merchant's conscience, while the Chera poem names the condition it assumes, open roads that the king must keep, so the trader's ethic depends on a ruler's duty the couplet does not mention.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty the care of five: ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself; Patitruppattu 70 says the king, with his kin around him, fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, put elders before his sons, and so paid the ancient debts (தொல்கடன்).
teaches: Read together, they show two accounts of what a man owes: the Kural spreads the duty over five equal claims including guests and himself, while the Chera poem counts it as an inherited debt to gods, sages and elders paid off by sacrifice and learning, so the king's virtue is framed as settlement rather than care.

note: Kural 467 says to think and then resolve, and that to think after resolving is a lapse; Patitruppattu 72 says the king's foes, from the greatness of their enmity and their folly, resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்), unlike the wise who know his nature, and meet him as the doom-fire.
teaches: The Kural gives the rule as prudence in any task, while the Chera poem applies it to war and shows its breach as ruin, setting the wise counsellors who know the king against the foes who resolve unthinking, so deliberation becomes the line between the king's servants and his victims.

note: Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the one who has no comparison; Patitruppattu 73 calls the Chera one to whom others are no comparison (நினக்குப் பிறர்உவமம் ஆகா) and ends with the poet grieving (வருந்துவல் யானே) that people will not believe his praise.
teaches: The Kural makes the incomparable one the end of anxiety for those who come to him, but the Chera poet shows the same attribute, given to a king, bringing anxiety to the one who praises, since what has no comparison cannot be made credible to hearers.

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because whatever is wanted is gained as it is wanted; Patitruppattu 74 says the king told his grey-haired elder that generosity, dignity, wealth, offspring, the divine and everything belong to those who have tapas (தவம்உடை யோர்க்கென), and let him go to the wide forest.
teaches: The Kural states the promise of tapas as a reason to strive, while the Chera poem shows a king applying it to another, releasing his aged counsellor from court to the forest, so tapas appears as the last stage of a life of royal service and its grant as a king's virtue.

note: Kural 443 says that to cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of rare things; Patitruppattu 79 says the king honours the great and cherishes the small (பெரியோர்ப் பேணிச் சிறியோரை அளித்தி), between lines on not sparing his life in war and sparing nothing in giving.
teaches: The Kural singles out honouring the great as a ruler's hardest gain, while the Chera poem pairs it with care for the small and sets both beside courage and giving, so the maxim appears as one term of a balanced royal portrait rather than a rarity standing alone.

note: Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others; Patitruppattu 86 tells how the report of the king's killing in war made the poet fear him, until he found him the patron of singers who ends the misery of the poor and is gentle as cool river water.
teaches: The couplet treats being easy to approach as a plain royal virtue, while the poem shows what it has to overcome: a king's fame for killing keeps suppliants away, so his accessibility has to be proved against his own reputation.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by the right way; Patitruppattu 89 lists the rain in its season, the paired deer, the humming boughs, unfailing fruit and tubers, grazing herds and endless grain, then gives the cause: because your sceptre is straight (நின்கோல் செம்மையின்).
teaches: The couplet states the link between a just sceptre and rain as a rule, while the poem spreads its consequences over a whole countryside of herds, forest creatures and grain, which shows how wide a land's well-being the belief was taken to cover.

note: Kural 744 says a fort is that which destroys the besieging enemy's spirit (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்); Fragment 2 lists a fort with tall wall, battlements, guard forest and deep moat and says that it is the defending kings who lose heart (நெஞ்சுபுகல் அழிந்து) at the Chera march.
teaches: On the plain reading the two make opposite claims about the same contest of nerve: the Kural gives the fort the power to break the attacker's spirit, while the praise poem says a perfect fort could not keep its own kings' spirit from breaking, so the war of morale the Kural assigns to walls the poet assigns to the king's army.

note: Kural 610 says a king without sloth (மடியிலா மன்னவன்) gains the whole earth; Fragment 4 praises a king who does not stop for the rains nor slacken for the cold (பனிஎன மடியாய்) and keeps his army in foreign land.
teaches: The Kural states freedom from sloth as a ruler's general virtue, while the fragment shows what it meant in war: refusing the seasonal halt of the rains and the cold that normally ended a campaign, so the king's tirelessness was measured against the calendar of war.

note: Kural 541 makes justice an inquiry without favour to anyone (கண்ணோடாது); 10 praises a king who lessens the penalty when the offender submits.
teaches: Read together they show that the old ideal allowed mercy after the verdict but not favour within it: the Kural bars kindly regard in the inquiry, while the Purananuru king reduces the sentence for submission, not for kinship or closeness.

note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

note: 100 ends with the eyes that glared at foes staying red even when he looks at his small son; Kural 775 calls it defeat if the glaring eye blinks when a spear is thrown.
teaches: The Kural asks the warrior's glare not to waver before a spear, and Avvai shows it cannot waver even before his own child, so together the fixed red eye is both the warrior's ideal and a cost the poem lets the reader feel.

note: Kural 495 says the crocodile wins in deep water and is killed by anything once out of it; 104 makes the young king a crocodile that kills an elephant in a foot-deep children's pool.
teaches: The Kural uses the crocodile to teach that strength belongs to the ground, while Avvai uses it to claim a strength that needs almost no ground, so a court poet's praise could deny the very limit the ethics book counsels kings to respect.

note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to slight him as young (இளையர்); 104 warns the enemy's warriors not to slight Avvai's lord as young (இளையன்).
teaches: The warning against scorning a young king is a rule of court conduct in the Kural and a battlefield threat in Avvai, which shows the same caution was voiced to subjects as duty and to enemies as danger.

note: Kural 221 calls giving only what goes to those who have nothing, all else being a measured exchange; 106 says Pari holds himself bound to give even to the foolish and the weak, as the gods accept even the erukkam flower.
teaches: The Kural defines true giving by the asker having nothing to return, and Kapilar supplies the image for it, the god who accepts a worthless flower, so the giver's duty is modelled on a god's acceptance rather than on a bargain.

note: Kural 211 says obligation seeks no return, for the world gives nothing back to the rain; 107 says Pari is not the only one, for the rain too sustains the world.
teaches: Kapilar's mock rebuke works only because the comparison of the giver with the rain was already accepted, as the Kural makes it a principle, so the joke assumes the doctrine and the doctrine has here a named man as its model.

note: Naladiyar 97 sets the rain and the world's doing what it should side by side as the two things the world survives by; 107 sets Pari and the rain side by side as sustainers of the world.
teaches: The Naladiyar's pairing of rain with human giving is the background against which 107's line reads as praise, and 107 shows that pairing applied to one patron centuries before it was stated as a general rule.

note: Kural 223 praises giving without uttering the misery of 'I have nothing'; 108 says Pari would not say 'I will not come' even if suppliants asked for him.
teaches: The Kural forbids the giver one refusal, the plea of having nothing; 108 imagines the case past it, where nothing is left and the giver offers himself, so the poem tests the maxim at its limit.

note: Naladiyar 3 says even kings who led armies under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and their enemies take their wives; 112 has a giver's daughters say the kings took their hill and they have no father.
teaches: The Naladiyar explains a ruler's fall by his own spent deeds, but 112 gives no cause and its subject is a famous giver, so the lament qualifies the moral account: here loss falls on the blameless and the poem does not explain it.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a ruler who wields the sceptre rightly; 117 says Pari's land never lacked rain, even under the omens of drought, because of the straightness of his sceptre.
teaches: The Kural's rule is given to crowned kings, and 117 grants it to a hill chief and sets it above the stars' omens, so the poem shows the doctrine of the just sceptre extended to any lord who rules well.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of a kindly man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 119 likens Pari to a lone tree on a long road without shade.
teaches: The Kural puts its tree where everyone can reach it, while 119 puts it where nothing else gives shelter, so the poem adds that a giver's worth is measured by how few others give.

note: 12 asks whether gifts made from others' land, taken so that it pains them, are dharma; Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears.
teaches: Nettimaiyar leaves his question to the king, and the Kural answers it with a law of return, which shows that the poet's courteous irony carries a real moral charge against the plunder that pays for the bards' gifts.

note: 121 tells Kari to give up the common gaze (பொது நோக்கு) and know each bard's rank (வரிசை); Kural 528 says a king who looks by rank (வரிசையா) rather than in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) draws many to live around him.
teaches: The Kural's two technical words for graded favour already stand in Kapilar's advice to a patron, so the Kural's rule for a king's kin was first argued by poets about how gifts should be ranked among themselves.

note: 127 sets Ay's emptied palace against the cities of drum-owning kings who eat alone, give nothing and lose their fame; Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, though they hold crores.
teaches: The Kural's paradox that unshared wealth is poverty is shown in 127 from the other side, a bare palace that is rich in fame, so the pair gives both halves of one reckoning: the miser's full store is empty and the giver's empty hall is full.

note: 134 says Ay does not give as a trade for the next world but because it is the path of the worthy; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: Both refuse to found giving on reward hereafter, but they put different things in its place: the Kural a bare judgment that giving is good, the Purananuru the example of the worthy, so the same denial could rest either on principle or on custom.

note: 134 rejects as a merchant of virtue anyone who gives because what is done in this life serves the next; Naladiyar 95 tells the giver to give with an eye to the next world and this one (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் நோக்கி).
teaches: The Naladiyar's advice is the very motive the Sangam poet holds up for scorn, which shows that giving for the next birth was a live doctrine both poets knew, and that the older praise poetry judged it a lesser reason than custom and honour.

note: 136 argues that those who give to the bard give to others and those who give to others give to themselves; Kural 221 says only giving to the destitute is giving and all else is a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை).
teaches: The starving bard is exactly the Kural's destitute recipient, yet he argues that such giving does come back to the giver, so the Kural's line between true gift and loan was drawn against an older view in which even giving to the poor was defended by its return.

note: 139 urges the lord of Nanjil to give now, since he does not fear death for his king and a battle may come any day; Naladiyar 5 says not to hold back a gift thinking it can be given later, since Death drags all away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's general reason for giving now, the certainty of death, appears in 139 as a bard's practical argument tied to the warrior patron's own courage, which shows how the moralist's maxim was already a working plea in the bard's trade.

note: 14 praises the king's hands, hardened by goad, bowstring and giving, against the soft hands of his poets, which do nothing but eat; Kural 1035 honours those who eat from their own hands' work, who do not beg and who give to those who ask.
teaches: In the Kural the hand that works for its food is the hand that gives; Kapilar reverses the order and makes the poets' soft, idle hands the proof of the patron's care, so the court valued being fed as a sign of the giver's greatness where the Kural values self-support.

note: 141 says Pekan's giving does not look to the next world (மறுமை நோக்கின்றோ அன்றே) but to others' want; Kural 222 says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Kural's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, is already the bards' test of a true patron, and 141 adds the positive motive the couplet leaves unstated: the giver looks at the receiver's want, as the useless gift to the peacock proves.

note: Both liken giving to rain; Kural 211 makes the rain a duty that asks no return, while 142 notes that rain also wastes itself on salt land and calls Pekan's giving கொடைமடம், folly.
teaches: The Kural keeps only the dutiful side of the rain image, but the Purananuru poet saw its waste as well, so the rain figure for generosity carried an admitted cost of indiscrimination that the maxim leaves out.

note: 154 makes asking for a little water from someone known the natural image for seeking out the generous; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the greatest degradation of the tongue. On the plain reading the same act is natural in one and shameful in the other.
teaches: The bard and the moralist used the same smallest request in opposite ways: for the poet it shows that seeking the generous is as natural as thirst, for the Kural it shows that no request is small enough to be clean, though 154 itself concedes that asking is hard (இரத்தலோ அரிதே).

note: 157 counts among Erai's virtues being ashamed at others' destitution (பிறர் கையறவு தான் நாணுதல்); Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace as for their own the dwelling of shame.
teaches: The Kural's widened shame, felt for what others suffer, appears first as a chief's virtue praised by a woman poet of his hill, where its object is concretely other people's want rather than their disgrace in general.

note: 159 will refuse an elephant given grudgingly and take a kunri seed given gladly; Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural names the asker's joy at a gift without contempt; 159 turns it into a rule of conduct for the asker, who must refuse a grudging gift even while his family starves, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard could accept at all.

note: Kural 1061 says not asking even from those who give gladly is worth ten million times more; 159 treats asking a glad giver as honourable and refuses only the grudging gift.
teaches: The bard's code and the Kural's draw the line of dignity in different places: for the bard the giver's gladness makes asking clean, for the Kural even the gladdest giver does not, so the Kural's chapter on the dread of asking rejects the very compromise the parisil poems lived by.

note: 160 asks to be sent off quickly (வல்லே விடுதல் வேண்டுவல்); Naladiyar 111 says keeping a seeker waiting till hope dies is worse than ingratitude.
teaches: The Naladiyar faults delay as the giver's breach of truth; 160 shows what the delay costs at the other end, a mother distracting a hungry child at home, which is why the bard asks for speed before size.

note: 162 says to Ilaveliman: see that askers exist and that givers exist; Kural 1055 says askers stand before others because there are people in the world who do not withhold.
teaches: The Kural explains asking by the existence of givers in general; 162 uses that same general truth as a weapon against one particular chief, so the principle that kept the asker's dignity also let him walk away from a mean patron.

note: Kural 230 says death is the bitterest thing, yet sweet when one cannot give; in 165 the giver says a bard going away disappointed is worse than losing his country and gives his head.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is a figure of speech in a couplet; 165 gives it a narrative in which a dispossessed chief literally prefers death to failing a bard, so the maxim had a heroic story behind it.

note: 165 opens: those who wished to last in an unlasting world set up their fame and died; Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame.
teaches: The Kural states the rule abstractly; 165 places it as the premise of a gift poem and adds its converse, that the ungiving rich are forgotten, so fame here is something the bard both records and withholds.

note: Kural 776 makes the day without a noble wound a wasted day; 167 grants the king's scars are sweet to hear of but says they are harsh to see, and the enemies' whole skins sweet to see.
teaches: Where the Kural counts the wound only as the warrior's own ledger of worth, 167 adds the onlooker's split response, so the wound's value lies in report and fame, not in how it looks.

note: Naladiyar 100 says the word 'they gave' is heard through the three worlds, further than drum or thunder; 168 says bards praise Kotran across the Tamil land every day, shaming kings who do not give.
teaches: 168 shows the mechanism the Naladiyar leaves out: the fame of giving travels because the bards who received the gifts carry it, and it is aimed at the kings who did not give.

note: Naladiyar 159 says the excellent honour a frequent visitor each time they see him; 171 says Kotran gives whether we come today, later or every day, never saying he gave before.
teaches: The Naladiyar states as a mark of character what 171 records of one chief's practice with bards, so the later maxim about the frequent visitor had its model in the patron who gave daily without reproach.

note: Kural 227 calls hunger a fierce disease (பசியென்னும் தீப்பிணி) that will not touch one who shares food; 173 calls Pannan the physician of the disease of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்).
teaches: Both books treat hunger as a disease, but the Kural says sharing protects the sharer while 173 makes the giver the healer of other people's hunger, so the image moves from the giver's safety to the hungry crowd's cure.

note: Kural 107 says one remembers the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow for seven births; 175 says the poet will forget Athanungan only when he forgets himself, when life leaves the body.
teaches: The Kural stretches gratitude across seven births, while the Purananuru poet bounds it by this one life and locates it in his body, which shows the older poem's gratitude making no claim on rebirth.

note: 18 opens its argument with bodies that cannot exist without water (நீர்இன்று அமையா யாக்கை); Kural 20 says the world cannot go on without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு).
teaches: The two share the phrase but draw different conclusions from it: the Kural derives the world's dependence on the sky, the Purananuru the king's duty to store water, so one premise supported both a praise of rain and a policy against relying on it.

note: Kural 542 says the whole world lives looking to the sky and the people to the ruler's sceptre; 18 says land that sows and looks to the sky (வித்திவான் நோக்கும் புன்புலம்) does not help its ruler however wide, and tells him to build tanks.
teaches: Where the Kural sets rain and the sceptre side by side as the two things people depend on, Kudapulaviyanar makes the ruler answerable for freeing the land from the sky, turning dependence on rain into a duty of public works.

note: 182 opens its catalogue with not eating alone even the nectar of the gods; Kural 322 makes sharing one's food the chief of all virtues.
teaches: Sharing food heads the list in both books, which shows that in early Tamil ethics the shared meal, not an inner disposition, was the first test of a good person.

note: Both say the world stands because of a certain kind of person: 182 names those who strive for others, Kural 996 those of courtesy (பண்புடையார்), without whom it would sink into the earth.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a two-line rule what the Pandya prince builds as a list of concrete refusals, so the reader of the Kural can see which deeds (not eating alone, dying for honour, refusing blame-tainted gain) its abstract பண்பு was taken to mean.

note: Both rank learning above birth: in 183 a man of the highest order defers to a learned man of the lowest, and Kural 409 says the unlearned high-born lack the worth of the learned low-born.
teaches: The Kural's maxim was already a king's teaching in the Purananuru, where Nedunchezhiyan keeps the four orders by name and lets learning reverse them, so neither text abolishes birth rank: both use it as the measure that learning overturns.

note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

note: Kural 552 calls the sceptre-holder's demand a robber's demand at spear-point; 184 likens the greedy king to an elephant loose in a field.
teaches: The Kural condemns excess levy from the subject's side as robbery, while Pisirandhaiyar argues from the king's side that grabbing wastes more than it yields and leaves the king himself unfed, so the same rule is given both a moral and a prudential ground.

note: Kural 542 sets the world's dependence on the sky beside the people's dependence on the sceptre; 186 denies rice and water the name of life and gives it to the king alone.
teaches: The Kural keeps rain and rule as parallel supports, but Mosikeeranar ranks the king above food and water and then turns the claim into the king's own duty to know it, so the pair shows the same dependence read once as praise and once as a burden laid on the ruler.

note: Kural 737 defines a country by its limbs: waters, a well-placed hill, the water from it and a strong fort. 187 says no kind of ground, plain, forest, low or high, makes a land good, only the goodness of its men. On the reading that both answer what makes a land good, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the land lists natural and built assets, while Avvaiyar dismisses terrain altogether, so a reader sees two answers to one question, resources or people, and that the Purananuru gave the moral answer before the treatise gave the material one.

note: Both turn on a small child's hand in the food: Kural 64 says gruel stirred by children's small hands is sweeter than nectar; 188 lists the child's touching, biting, stirring and scattering of ghee rice.
teaches: The Kural makes the image a measure of sweetness, while the Pandya king makes its absence a verdict that a rich man's feasting life is profitless, so one scene serves as delight in one book and as the test of a wasted life in the other.

note: 189 says the use of wealth is giving and whoever means to enjoy it alone loses much; Naladiyar 9 says the man who neither eats, gives nor relieves his kin but guards his wealth is counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Both declare kept wealth already lost, but for different reasons: Nakkeerar from the fixed measure one body can eat and wear, the Naladiyar from the miser's failure in every use, so the pair gives the conclusion one ground in the body and one in duty.

note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who accept good when it comes grieve when it does not; 192 neither rejoices that life is sweet nor calls it bitter, because a life follows its order.
teaches: Both ground equanimity on an order the person does not control, but the Kural names it ஊழ் and argues, while Kaniyan gives the picture of a raft carried on a flood, so the abstract fate of the Kural is given an image of how it works.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why anyone stays unlearned; 192 says every town is ours and everyone our kin, with no condition of learning.
teaches: The Kural makes belonging everywhere a reward of learning, while Kaniyan makes it a consequence of seeing that good and ill are not given by others, so the pair shows the same cosmopolitan claim earned once by study and once by insight.

note: Both set a wedding drum against a funeral drum. Naladiyar 23 draws the lesson that the worthy hold to the way of escape; 194 tells those who know the world's nature to look for what is sweet (இனிய காண்க). On the reading that இனிய means good deeds in this life, the two conclusions diverge.
teaches: The same sight of joy and mourning side by side leads the Naladiyar to renunciation and the Purananuru poet to seeking good within the world, which shows the later didactic book reusing a Sangam image for a different, ascetic conclusion.

note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the death rattle stops the tongue; 195, facing old men who have done no good, asks at least that they refrain from harm.
teaches: The Kural's urgency assumes one can still act well, while the Purananuru poet sets a floor for those who will not, so the pair shows that early Tamil counsel allowed abstaining from harm to count as a road to the good when doing good had failed.

note: Kural 1051 says if those worth asking withhold, the blame is theirs; 196 says a false promise or a false refusal lessens the giver's fame.
teaches: The Kural states as a rule that withholding shames the giver, not the asker, and Avur Moolankizhar applies it to a named king's delay, so the rule had been used as a poet's weapon before it became a maxim.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: Kural 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than the poverty of the good; 197 says the poet thinks nothing of the riches of the unfeeling and thinks of the poverty of the wise with joy.
teaches: The Kural's comparison is spoken by a poet to a Chola king's face in the Purananuru, which shows that the maxim's ranking of the wise poor over the ignorant rich was first a bard's claim on his own dignity before a patron.

note: Naladiyar 206 says saltless millet gruel among one's own is sweeter than milk rice from strangers' hands; 197 prizes the small chief's greens and varagu rice given with regard over kings' wealth.
teaches: Both value a poor meal for the regard it is given with, but the Naladiyar finds that regard among kin while the Purananuru finds it in a patron who knows a poet's worth, so the pair shows the bard's patron standing where the family stands in the later book.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

note: 20 ends: all living beings fear (அஞ்சும்) you; Kural 563 says a ruler who acts so as to cause dread perishes quickly. On the reading that the beings fear the king, 20 praises what the Kural condemns; on the reading that they fear for him, the two agree.
teaches: The ambiguity of 20's last line matters because the Kural's chapter against causing dread makes a feared king a doomed king, so Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar's praise only holds if the people's fear is anxiety for their ruler and not dread of him.

note: 203 calls it cruel (இன்னாது) for a patron to refuse a returning bard with 'you took before'; Kural 224 says being asked is itself painful (இன்னாது) to the giver until he sees the asker's glad face.
teaches: The same word marks the pain of the asking moment from opposite sides, the giver's in the Kural and the refused bard's in 203, so the couplet's candour about the giver's discomfort is answered by a poet who names what that discomfort costs the asker.

note: 204 says those who come in hope blame the omens and the hour, never the patron; Kural 1051 says that when the worthy withhold, the blame is theirs and not the asker's. On the plain reading the two place the blame for a refused request in incompatible places.
teaches: The bard's courtesy in 204 is a deliberate refusal to lay the blame that the Kural says belongs to the withholder, so the poem shows the decorum that kept a disappointed poet in a patron's favour against the moral rule.

note: 204 ranks four acts: asking low, refusing lower, giving high, refusing a gift higher; Kural 222 ranks two: taking is bad even on a good path, giving good even without heaven.
teaches: The Sangam poet's ladder adds a rung the Kural lacks, the refusal of what is offered, which shows that the Kural's verdict against taking had a heroic form in which the proud receiver outranks the giver.

note: 205 says the bard does not want even the three kings' gifts if given without regard (பெட்பின்றி); Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural states the receiver's joy at a gift given without contempt; 205 turns it into a condition of acceptance, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard would take the gift at all, not only how he felt about it.

note: 206 shows the bard leaving in pride when kept waiting at the gate; Kural 1060 says the asker should not be angry when refused, since his own want shows wealth is hard to come by.
teaches: Avvai is not refused a gift but denied recognition at the gate, so the pair separates two cases the Kural's counsel of patience joins: want may excuse a refusal, but the bards held that a slight to their rank was not to be borne.

note: 207 rejects a gift that does not make the heart glad and leaves the face fallen (அகம்நக வாரா முகன்அழி); Kural 786 says friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship, only that which makes the heart smile.
teaches: The Kural's pair of face and heart (முகநக, அகநக) already stands in a bard's test of a gift, so the measure the Kural applies to friendship was first a poet's measure of patronage.

note: Kural 743 defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; 21 describes Kanapper with a moat beyond depth, a sky-high wall and a sunless guard forest, and praises the king who took it.
teaches: The puram poet uses the full list of what makes a fort good only to measure the man who took it, so the Kural's criteria guarantee nothing to the defender: in the praise poem a perfect fort is the conqueror's ornament.

note: 211 tells of a patron who showed the gift as if in hand and then stood by a lie; Kural 1067 begs all who beg not to ask of those who conceal.
teaches: The Kural's advice not to beg from concealers is given from outside; 211 shows from inside what the bard does when the advice comes too late, shaming by praise (நாணக் கூறி) as his only remedy.

note: 213 counsels the king that a war with those who rose against him (traditionally his sons) is lost whichever side wins; Kural 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed, holds ruin.
teaches: The Kural asserts that enmity within brings ruin; 213 gives the reason in a single case, since in a war inside the house the king loses his heirs if he wins and his honour if he loses.

note: 214 reasons that even if there is no joy beyond, good deeds may end rebirth or leave fame; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: Both test good conduct on the supposition that there is no heaven, but the Kural rests there while the king reaches for a further reward, release or fame, so the pair shows two ways of answering doubt about the next world.

note: 215 says Pisiron may stay away in prosperity but will not stay away in trouble; Naladiyar 238 is an oath to rush to a friend in distress and put one's life in his hands.
teaches: The Naladiyar's oath is a figure of speech, but in the tradition this chapter records the friend did come to share the king's death, so the puram poems supply a case in which the oath was taken literally.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: 218 says the worthy join the worthy as gems from distant places meet in one jewel; Naladiyar 236 says the water-lily and the kuvalai grow in one pool, yet the small do not equal the great.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows that nearness does not make likeness and the Sangam poem that distance does not prevent it, so together they make nature, not place, the ground of fellowship.

note: Kural 771 boasts that many who stood against the speaker's lord now stand as stones (கல்நின் றவர்); 221 ends with the generous patron himself become a hero-stone (நடுகல் ஆயினன் புரவலன்), mourned by poets.
teaches: In the Kural the hero-stone is the fate a warrior threatens on his enemies, while in 221 it is the end of the patron the poets loved, so the same stone that marks a foe's defeat also marks the giver's fame, and the boast of 771 is one side of a monument that kaiyarunilai shows from the other.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as a bond that never curtails the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை); 223 says the king, even as a hero-stone, gives room to friends of old intimacy (கிழமைத் தொன்னட் புடையார்) who come to him.
teaches: The Kural's definition is carried past death in 223: the claim of intimacy that a friend may exercise unasked includes the right to follow the king into death, and the stone honours it by making room, so pazhaimai is tested at its extreme.

note: Naladiyar 20 pictures merciless Death roaming for its victims and seizing even the unborn while the mother wails; 226 says Death could not have taken Valavan by rage or force and must have begged him like a bard.
teaches: On the Naladiyar's account no one escapes a Death that takes by force, while 226 claims that this king was beyond Death's force and fell only to his own generosity, so the bardic lament denies the very powerlessness before Death that the moralist uses to urge virtue.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except unmatched renown; 231 says Anji's fame will not perish whether his pyre shrinks or rises to the sky.
teaches: Avvai's poem gives the Kural's general claim its occasion: fame is undying precisely at the pyre, where everything else of the man is being burned, so the maxim's 'nothing else stands' is shown in the act of the body's ending.

note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; 234 grieves that Evvi, who always ate with many at a gate open to the world, is now fed alone a small rice ball on grass by his wife.
teaches: The Kural condemns solitary eating as the miser's choice, and 234 shows death forcing that very condition on the most open-handed host, so the bitterness the Kural assigns to the hoarder becomes, in the lament, the injury done to the giver by his funeral rite.

note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of one who gives nothing to a beautiful woman growing old alone; 235 ends by likening the many lives that die without giving to pakanrai flowers that wither unworn.
teaches: Both books picture what is not given as beauty that no one enjoys, but Avvai moves the image from the miser's wealth to the miser's life and sets it against a giver who has just died, so the waste is measured by the loss of one who did give.

note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; 237 says a tiger that misses the elephant it stalked will not stalk a rat, and the poet resolves to seek great gifts.
teaches: The Kural's warrior maxim about aiming high is used in 237 by a bard to turn from mourning to his next patron, so the ethic of the great target governed the bard's choice of patron as well as the soldier's choice of foe.

note: Kural 922 says not to drink toddy, and that only those who do not care to be counted by the worthy should; 239 lists draining jars of sweet toddy among the deeds of a man who 'did all that should be done' and so earned fame.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree about whether drinking belongs to a praiseworthy life: the Kural excludes the drinker from the esteem of the worthy, while the Purananuru lament counts the toddy jar beside justice and giving in a life complete enough to make the manner of burial indifferent.

note: 24 ends: those who knew say the ones who truly lived are those who did not go as the many go but stood and died with lasting fame; Kural 240 says those who live without renown do not live.
teaches: The Kural's flat verdict appears in 24 as a saying the poet attributes to the wise and sets after a blessing of royal pleasure, so the maxim was already proverbial and served to bend a feast poem toward the thought of death.

note: 241 presents Andiran's giving of chariots as what announces him in heaven; the Kural says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Kural's hypothetical answers a real habit of praise: poets like this one tied giving to a welcome in the sky, and the couplet deliberately cuts that tie so that giving no longer needs the reward.

note: Both picture old age on a staff, but the Naladiyar calls youth faulty and the wise renounce it in infancy, while 243 calls its untaught youth precious and grieves for it.
teaches: The same image of the old man on a staff serves the Jain moralist as a warning against enjoying youth and the Sangam poet as proof that youth was the best of life, so the later book is arguing against a value the older poetry held.

note: The Kural likens the false ascetic to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 252 says this ascetic really was a hunter, snaring women with words, before he became one.
teaches: Both use the hunter and the snared bird for the ascetic, but in opposite order: for the Kural the hunter hides inside the ascetic, for the Sangam poet the ascetic has replaced the hunter, so the same image can accuse or praise a renunciant.

note: The Kural's mother rejoices more at hearing her son called worthy than at his birth; 254's mother praises her son daily, and the speaker dreads her hearing of his death.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows the other side of the Kural's maxim: the mother whose joy rests on hearing her son praised is the one whom the word of his death will strike hardest.

note: The Kural says shame turns her back on drinkers; in 258 the toddy jar is reserved for the raider as an honour before his deed.
teaches: The pairing shows that drinking was an honour of the warrior's rite (உண்டாட்டு) in the older poetry, so the Kural's chapter against liquor is rejecting a heroic custom, not only a private vice.

note: The Kural says a death that is really existence is hard to achieve save for the skilled; 260 shows the hero's body left shaking with arrows while his name passes onto the stone.
teaches: 260 gives the Kural's abstract paradox a concrete form: the 'death that lives' was a practice with a body left on the bank, a stone set in a narrow path, and a name crowned with peacock feathers.

note: Kural 771 threatens enemies that many who stood before the lord now stand as stones; in 265 the stone is the hero's own, and the poet grieves that patronage and victory went with him.
teaches: The Kural's boast treats the hero-stone as the enemy's fate and a mark of the lord's might, while 265 shows the same stone from the side of those left behind, so the pair shows that the honour Valluvar's warrior wields as a threat was, for the bards, a loss of livelihood.

note: Naladiyar 286 says the man who cannot give to those who come hungry had better leave his village; 266 asks the king to end such poverty quickly, as a plea in the assembly is answered.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the poor host's shame his own to solve by leaving, while the Purananuru poet places the remedy on the king as a matter of justice, so the pair shows two answers to the same shame: private withdrawal and a public claim on the ruler.

note: Naladiyar 287 says want takes away good nature and sharpness of mind; 266 names its poverty as அறிவுகெட நின்ற, which has ruined his understanding, and as making him hide from guests.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim that poverty destroys the mind is given here as a poet's own testimony with a concrete symptom, hiding from the guest one longed for, which shows that the loss of hospitality was felt as the loss of reason itself.

note: 27 reports the saying that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car that no charioteer drives; Kural 234 says that if one wins long fame on earth, the gods' world does not honour the புலவர்.
teaches: The belief that poets' praise carries a man to heaven, which 27 gives as current hearsay, is the background the elliptical couplet assumes when it ties earthly fame to the gods' world, so the Purananuru supplies the premise the Kural leaves out.

note: 27 line 6 மரைஇலை போல மாய்ந்திசினோர் பலரே (many died like the lotus leaf); Naladiyar 359 ends மரையிலையின் மாய்ந்தார் பலர் (many perished like the lotus leaf).
teaches: The Naladiyar repeats the Purananuru's half-line almost word for word but moves it from nobly born kings who died without a poet's praise to people whose expectations came to nothing, and the earlier poem shows what the lotus-leaf death meant: dying without a name, beside the flower that is remembered.

note: Kural 774's hero sends his spear away with an elephant and laughs as he pulls one from his own body; 274's warrior hurls his spear at the oncoming elephant and, weaponless, takes the enemy's attack upon his body.
teaches: The Kural's couplet compresses a set scene that the Purananuru gives at length with dress and enemy horse, which shows that Valluvar's chapter on martial pride was built on stock battle episodes the audience already knew from heroic song.

note: Kural 69: the mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him (ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும்); 277: the old mother's joy at hearing her son died killing an elephant is greater than on the day she bore him (ஈன்ற ஞான்றினும் பெரிதே).
teaches: The Kural keeps the heroic measure of a mother's joy but moves its object from a son's death in battle to his being called worthy, so the pair shows Valluvar civilising a formula of the battlefield into one of learning and character.

note: Kural 69's mother rejoices on hearing her son praised; 278's mother hears a report of his flight, refuses it, searches the field, and rejoices more than at his birth only on seeing his body.
teaches: Where the Kural makes a mother's greatest joy depend on what she hears said of her son, 278 makes hearsay the thing to be refuted by sight of the wounds, which shows that the heroic mother trusted only the body's evidence of honour.

note: 28 tells the king his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failure would be his own neglect; Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means without wrong yields virtue and pleasure.
teaches: The Kural makes the yield of virtue and pleasure depend on how wealth was gained, while the court poet makes it depend on whether the king takes care to use it, so the two books place the moral test of wealth at opposite ends, getting and spending.
