note: 282: the hero's body is gone and only his split shield remains, but he is in the mouths of poets; Kural 235: a death that is really existence comes only to the skilled.
teaches: The Kural's paradox of a death that is life gets in 282 its working mechanism: the poets' tongues are where the vanished hero now exists, so the Kural's 'skilled' death depended on someone to sing it.

note: 284: the warrior who killed an elephant laughs at the back of the man who fled; Kural 774: having sent his spear off with an elephant, he laughs as he pulls one from his own body.
teaches: Both place a warrior's laugh just after an elephant kill, but 284 turns it on the coward and the Kural turns it on the hero's own wound, which shows the Kural moving the scorn of fear from the enemy to the self.

note: 287 says the warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the high world; Kural 777 names only world-circling fame as what those who do not want life seek.
teaches: The Kural names fame alone and its commentator adds heaven; 287 already makes heaven the reward and dismisses land, so the commentator's addition had a Sangam warrant that the Kural itself left out.

note: 289: like a ploughman choosing the best bull, the king picks the man among the old fighting houses and gives him his own gold bowl; Kural 517: having reasoned that this man will do this by this means, leave it to him.
teaches: The Kural's choice of the right man for a task appears in 289 as a public honour, the king's own bowl handed over before battle, so the selection the Kural treats as reasoning was also a gift that bound the chosen man to go first.

note: 29 sets its blessing in a world where people pass in turn like players at a festival; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd that gathers at a dance hall and disperses.
teaches: Both books reach for the festival stage to show transience, but the Purananuru applies it to the players, the people themselves, and draws the counsel to turn stored wealth into fame, while the Kural applies it to the audience, wealth itself, so the same image grounds two different lessons about what passes.

note: 290: this man's grandfather died beside the king's grandfather, and he too will take the spears meant for the king; Kural 764: an army is one with courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்).
teaches: The Kural's 'courage that has come down' is, in Avvaiyar, a three-generation bond between one fighting family and one royal family, so inherited courage meant inherited loyalty to a particular house.

note: 294: no one approaches the warrior standing alone, as no one approaches the gem the serpent spits (அரவுஉமிழ் மணியின் குறுகார்); Kural 763: a host of rats roaring like the sea perish when the cobra breathes.
teaches: The Kural's cobra verse never mentions an army and its commentator reads it as one hero against a crowd; 294 uses the serpent exactly so, for a lone fighter in a confused battle whom the crowd will not approach, so the allegorical reading follows an image of the war poems.

note: 295: seeing her son broken in the battle press, his mother's dry breasts flow; Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him.
teaches: The Kural's mother hears praise and her joy exceeds the birth; Avvaiyar's mother sees the body and her breasts give milk as at the birth, so the Kural's comparison with childbirth has a harsher Sangam form in which the worth was proved by dying.

note: 299: the poor chief's gram-fed horse cleaves the front while the rich kings' ghee-fed horses hang back; Kural 769: an army wins if it is free of shrinking, lasting grievance and poverty (வறுமை).
teaches: The Kural counts poverty among the things that lose a war, while 299 makes the poor chief the winner and the rich the ones who shrink, so the Kural's rule is about an army's supply and the poem's point is that wealth does not supply courage.

note: 3 ends by calling the ending of suppliants' poverty the king's true strength (வன்மை); Kural 225 ranks the strength of removing others' hunger above the strength of enduring one's own.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of strengths is abstract, and the Pandya counsel turns it into a test of practice: the giver must read the need from the face before it is spoken, and the deadly road the suppliants crossed measures what that strength owes them.

note: 301's hero will lift his spear only against the king's mounted elephant (வேந்தூர் யானைக்கு அல்லது); Kural 772 prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare.
teaches: The Kural states the warrior's preference for a worthy target as a maxim of honour, and 301 shows the same preference working as a tactic, since the enemy camp is warned that a man who ignores lesser blows is saving himself for their king.

note: 303's speaker killed an elephant yesterday and now waits for a young rider's spear in his chest; Kural 774's warrior sends his spear off with an elephant and laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: Both pair the elephant killed with the spear received, so the couplet's laughing warrior is the same type as 303's boaster, and the poem supplies the couplet's missing sequence: the elephant was yesterday, the wound is today's test.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one said is hard; in 304 the king's camp trembles because the hero's word is never two (இரண்டா காது அவன் கூறியது).
teaches: The Kural treats word and deed as a gap to be closed by effort, but 304 shows a man whose record has closed it so firmly that his spoken vow alone frightens an army, so keeping one's word becomes a weapon and not only a virtue.

note: Kural 685 says the envoy speaks briefly and brings good; 305's brahmin says only a few words (சொல்லிய சொல்லோ சிலவே) and the siege ladders and elephants' bells are put away.
teaches: The couplet's rule for the envoy, brevity that achieves its end, has a historical scene behind it in which the good brought was a war called off, and the poem credits that to the words' fewness rather than to the speaker's power.

note: Kural 81 says all household life is for receiving guests; 306's woman prays at the hero-stone first that she may have guests (விருந்து எதிர் பெறுகதில்) and then for her husband's war.
teaches: The Kural's claim that household life exists for guests was a prayer before it was a maxim: in 306 a warrior's wife asks the hero-stone for guests before she asks for her husband's victory, so hospitality ranked first even in a house that lived by war.

note: Kural 780 says a death that fills the patron's eyes with tears is worth begging for; in 307 the enemy king himself, seeing the fallen hero, says nothing is finer than to stay on this field.
teaches: The Kural measures a good death by the tears of one's own lord, while 307 goes further and makes the enemy king the witness who envies the death, so the honour of a field death did not depend on whose side mourned it.

note: Both are spoken by a follower of 'my lord' (என்னை): 309 says enemies fear at the report that he is in the camp, Kural 771 warns enemies not to stand before him, since many who did now stand as stones.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on martial pride keeps the Purananuru's speaking voice, the retainer boasting of என்னை, and 309 shows what the couplet compresses: the lord's power is the fear his name spreads before any blow, which is why the stones of 771 are the result rather than the boast.

note: 31 opens: as wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, so the two other kings' umbrellas follow behind Nalankilli's; Kural 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy.
teaches: The ordering the Kural states as an ethical rule is used by the court poet as a ready image to rank three crowned kings, which shows the precedence of virtue over wealth and pleasure was a commonplace secure enough to carry a political claim.

note: Kural 67 says the father's duty is to make his son first in the assembly; 312 says the father's duty is to make him a worthy man (சான்றோன்) but the son's own duty is to kill elephants and return.
teaches: Both assign the father the son's standing among men, but 312 places that standing inside a chain of duties ending in war, so the 'worthy man' of a warrior house was finished by the battlefield, not by the assembly the Kural has in mind.

note: Kural 69 says the mother rejoices more to hear her son called சான்றோன் than at his birth; 312's mother says bearing him is her duty and making him சான்றோன் is the father's.
teaches: The same word marks the same two stages, birth and being called worthy, and 312 shows why the Kural's mother only hears of it: in this division of duties the worthiness is made by others, so her joy is at a work she began but did not finish.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not fail in obligation even when without means; 313's hero has nothing in hand yet is bound (கடவ) to give elephants and chariots to suppliants.
teaches: The couplet's abstract duty, giving even without means, is shown in 313 with its practical answer: a warrior without wealth gives what he will win, so the obligation was made possible by the economy of plunder the Kural does not mention.

note: Kural 1027 likens the one who carries the family's burden to the stout-hearted in battle; 314 shows one man as lamp of his house and dam of the routed army.
teaches: The Kural uses the battle hero as a simile for the family's mainstay, while 314 shows that in the warrior village they were literally the same man, so the couplet's comparison grew from a social fact that it turned into a figure.

note: Kural 490 says to fold up like the heron when it is time and strike like its beak when the moment comes; 315 says Anji can stay unseen like the fire-drill in the eaves and blaze like its fire when he appears.
teaches: Both reduce right timing to one object with two states, but Avvai's image puts the force inside the waiting thing (the fire is already in the stick), which adds to the couplet that restraint is stored strength rather than mere patience.

note: Kural 926 says sleepers are like the dead and toddy-drinkers eat poison; 316 praises as 'our lord' a man asleep in a drunken drowse who pawns his sword for guests.
teaches: On the plain reading the two judge the same figure oppositely, since the drunken sleeper whom the Kural calls as good as dead is in 316 the generous lord of the bards, which shows that the Kural's ban on drink rejects a heroic ideal the Sangam village celebrated.

note: Kural 89 calls neglect of guests poverty in the midst of wealth; in 319 the wife, with an empty jar and only roasted hare, takes in the bard and promises a golden lotus on her husband's return.
teaches: The couplet defines the failure, poverty inside wealth, and 319 shows its converse, generosity inside poverty, where what is lacking is paid on credit against the husband's next war, so hospitality was measured by readiness to give, not by stores.

note: Kural 780 calls a death that makes one's patron weep worth begging for; 324 praises a companion who will die when his king dies.
teaches: The Kural places the good death before the lord's, earning his tears, while the poem binds the companion's death to follow the king's, so together they show two orders of loyalty in Tamil war ethics: dying for the lord and dying with him.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; 327 praises a chief who begs millet face to face from small farmers to feed bards and his kin.
teaches: The Kural's limit case (begging even for a good cause is degrading) is exactly what the Purananuru holds up as heroic, so the pair shows that the shame of asking was a later ethical rule, while the older warrior ethic counted begging for others as part of generosity.

note: Kural 219 defines the generous man's poverty as being unable to do what he should; 331 says its chief, though very poor, can make what is not there and still give.
teaches: Valluvar treats poverty as the one thing that disables the generous man, while the Purananuru poet shows a poor chief whose skill in contriving, rationing and scattering defeats that disablement, so the pair shows generosity measured in the Kural by means and in the poem by craft.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of a man who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; in 333 the wife has fed guests until she must pound the seed millet itself.
teaches: The Kural's rhetorical promise that the hospitable house needs no seed is played out literally in the poem, where hospitality has eaten the seed, so the pair shows the real cost that the maxim's confidence passes over.

note: 34 quotes dharma: there is expiation for killing cows' udders, destroying unborn children or wronging elders, but none for killing a benefit; Kural 110 says those who killed any good may escape, but not one who killed a good done to him.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a rule what the Purananuru presents as a known saying with its list of lesser crimes, and the poet turns it on himself, so the maxim was already used to bind a bard to praise his patron: gratitude here is the poet's own obligation, not only the patron's claim.

note: 35 says the king's umbrella is for sheltering his people and his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; Kural 1034 says those with the shade of grain-ears see many kings' umbrellas under their own king's umbrella.
teaches: Both texts set the royal umbrella against the farmer and make conquest depend on the plough, but 35 says it to the king as counsel while the Kural says it of the farmer as praise, so the same economic claim is spoken from both ends of the realm.

note: 35 says rain comes when sought in the land of the just sceptre, but also that the world blames kings for failed rains and harvests; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules rightly.
teaches: The Kural states the link between just rule and rain as a fact, while the court poet adds that people will blame the king for drought whatever its cause, so in the Purananuru the doctrine is also a political danger the king must manage.

note: The Kural calls it the world's 'greatness' that one here yesterday is gone today; 356 gives that greatness a place, the burning ground that has seen everyone's back.
teaches: The Kural's bitter abstraction becomes a physical place in the Purananuru, and the ground that outlives all men is the 'greatness' the couplet names without showing.

note: Both use crossing water as the image of what one needs at death; the Kural's swimmer needs the Lord's feet, 357's needs a raft that wealth is not.
teaches: The crossing image the Kural gives a god already stood in the Purananuru without one, carried by what a man keeps in place of wealth, so the Kural's theology was laid on an older ethical figure.

note: Both turn on one verb of holding or leaving repeated across the lines; the Kural says griefs cling to clingers, 358 that Fortune leaves those who cling and stays with those who let go.
teaches: Read together they give both halves of one argument the Kural states only negatively: holding brings grief, and letting go is what keeps Fortune, so renunciation is offered even to kings as a gain.

note: The Kural says nothing but renown stands undying; 359 says blame stands too.
teaches: Adding that blame lasts as well turns the Kural's consolation into a warning, so giving is urged not to earn a name but to escape the other lasting name.

note: Both say give now because death is certain; the Naladiyar warns that wealth is useless after the funeral drum, 359 promises a fame that outshines the burning ground.
teaches: The same deathbed counsel serves two motives: the Naladiyar argues from the uselessness of hoarded wealth, the Purananuru from the name left behind, so the later book drops the reward the earlier one offered.

note: 36 tells the besieging king that to have fought a rival who sits at ease behind his walls is a matter of shame; Naladiyar 241 says the worthy, seeing their enemies humbled, feel shame and do not advance.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim about shame before a humbled foe is in 36 an actual plea to stop a siege, which shows the poets used this sense of honour to bring wars to an end, and that the shame was felt to fall on the victor.

note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; 360 says even great rulers' wealth does not stay, so fill the hands of gift-seekers.
teaches: The Kural leaves 'what stays' unnamed, and the Purananuru names it as filling the hands of those who seek gifts, which shows the bard's claim behind the maxim.

note: Naladiyar 5 says those who gave first escape the waste land through which Death drags its captives; 361 tells Death to its face that a king who has given to brahmins, bards and suppliants does not fear its coming.
teaches: The Naladiyar's promise that givers escape Death is a future reward, while the Purananuru poet shows the same claim as a present state, a king already fearless, so the Jain maxim restates as doctrine what the court poets had staged as a king's achieved confidence.

note: Naladiyar 21: even umbrella-kings on elephants were carried off and none is left; 363: kings who ruled the whole earth alone are more than the sand and went to the burning ground, so act now and renounce.
teaches: The Naladiyar's general observation about dead kings appears in the Purananuru as an argument put to one living king, with the outcaste's saltless rice as its sting, which shows the impermanence of kings was a counsel form before it became a moral commonplace.

note: 364 answers the nearness of the burning ground with feasting: roast ram, toddy, gifts, joy now. Naladiyar 16 says joy that does not last, like the lamb nibbling its garland at the place of slaughter, is not found among the wise. On the plain reading, the feast 364 urges is exactly the lamb's pleasure the Naladiyar condemns.
teaches: Both poems draw their conclusion from the same nearness of death, so the disagreement shows that impermanence by itself did not settle how to live: the Sangam kaanchi poet drew enjoyment and giving from it, the Jain poet withdrawal.

note: In 365 the Earth, personified as a woman, weeps at being claimed by king after king like a bought woman; in Kural 1040 the good woman called Land laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty.
teaches: The personified Earth judges men in both, but the Purananuru's Earth grieves at being owned by a succession of kings while the Kural's mocks those who do not work her, so the same figure speaks for the land against its rulers in one and against its idle tenants in the other.

note: Naladiyar 120: nothing goes with a person but the deeds they did; 367: the lands do not go with their owners, only the good done in living is a raft when one sinks, so give to brahmins and suppliants and drink the toddy women bring.
teaches: Avvaiyar and the Naladiyar hold the same doctrine that only deeds accompany a person, but Avvaiyar counts the court's feasting alongside giving as the way to use the allotted days, so the doctrine did not by itself require the ascetic conclusion the Jain anthology draws.

note: 371 recalls the king's fame as 'ploughing with the bow' (வில்லேர் உழவின்) and sings his battle as threshing; Kural 872 says one may take on the enmity of bow-ploughmen (வில்லேர் உழவர்) but not of word-ploughmen.
teaches: The Kural's bow-ploughman is a set epithet from the களவழி poems, where the battle is literally worked through as tillage and threshing, so the couplet takes the bards' highest praise of a warrior king and ranks it below the work of words.

note: Kural 1061: not begging, even from those who give gladly without hiding, is worth ten million times more; 376: after one night's gift the drummer has not thought of begging since, and his drum has not sounded at other givers' gates.
teaches: The Kural reaches not-begging by self-respect, while the Purananuru bard reaches it because one patron gave so fully that no further asking was needed, so the poem shows the ideal attained from the giver's side rather than the asker's.

note: 38 says heaven lacks giving and asking, so gift-seekers prefer the king's land; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: Both books cut the worth of giving loose from heaven, but from opposite sides: the Kural says giving is good even without a heaven to reward it, and the Purananuru says heaven is poorer than earth because no one gives there, so giving becomes what makes this world worth more than the next.

note: 386 praises the king because his bards knew only the sweat of eating hot food and never the sweat of work; Kural 1065 says nothing is sweeter than even thin gruel earned by one's own effort.
teaches: On the plain reading the two rank the same pair in opposite order: the bard's highest praise is to be spared labour by a giver, while the Kural makes self-earned food the sweetest, so the Kural's ethic of not asking is written against the very economy of patronage the Purananuru celebrates.

note: 387: the king did not look at the bard's smallness but gave by the measure of his own greatness; Kural 87: the fruit of hospitality has no set measure, being as great as the guest's worth.
teaches: The Kural measures hospitality by the guest's worth, while the poem praises a king precisely for ignoring the guest's low worth and measuring by his own, so royal giving runs on a scale opposite to the household's.

note: 389: as he gives, Athanungan asks the bard whether he will remember him in the drought; Kural 1059: what renown would givers have without people who ask?
teaches: The Kural states abstractly that the giver's fame needs the asker; the poem shows a giver who knows it, asking to be remembered as he gives, so the bard's memory is the very return the giver seeks.

note: 393: the bard's family sings lineages by inherited order (குடிமுறை பாடி) and asks the king for food and cloth; Kural 1062 curses the maker of the world if anyone must live by begging.
teaches: What the Kural treats as an outrage against the world's order, a life that depends on asking, the bard presents as a hereditary office with its own proper order of song, so the two disagree on whether living by the gift is a shame or a calling.

note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

note: 395: the chief shows his wife to the bard and tells her to care for him as for himself; Kural 81: the whole of keeping house and guarding goods is for tending guests.
teaches: The couplet says the household exists for the guest; the poem shows the moment that claim is enacted, when the master hands the guest over to the mistress of the house, so the guest is taken into the household rather than merely fed by it.

note: 397: under the king's protection the bard will fear nothing even if the sea ends or the sun rises in the south; Naladiyar 1: those who once ate six-flavoured food may go begging for gruel, so wealth cannot be counted as lasting.
teaches: The bard claims a security from his patron that survives cosmic upheaval, while the Naladiyar denies that any wealth or provision lasts, so the two make incompatible claims about whether a gift can make a life safe.

note: 399: the bard lived on bitter-gourd gruel his wife cooked with fish he caught himself and called it ruin (அழிவுகொண்டு) until the chief's gift came; Kural 1065: thin gruel from one's own effort is the sweetest food.
teaches: The poem gives the exact case the Kural imagines, gruel from one's own catch, and judges it the opposite way, as ruin to be ended by a patron, so the couplet is seen to argue against the bard's way of life and not merely in the abstract.

note: 40 asks the conqueror to be sweet of speech and easy of access (இன்சொல் எண்பதத்தை); Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others.
teaches: The Kural's two marks of a praised king are in 40 exactly the two requests a poet puts to a victorious king, so the couplet's criteria were the counsel bards gave in person, and the poem ties them to the king's fame among his poets.

note: 400: besides driving off his own enemies, the king can drive off the hunger-enemy of those who come to him; Kural 225: the strength to bear hunger ranks behind the strength to remove others' hunger.
teaches: The Kural ranks hunger-removal above ascetic endurance as a kind of strength; the poem makes it a second warfare of the king, so the couplet's ranking appears to draw on a heroic vocabulary in which feeding was counted as victory.

note: 41 opens 'காலனும் காலம் பார்க்கும்' (even Death watches for its time) to say the king does not wait; Naladiyar 36 tells the reader not to ask whether Death comes today or another day, for it stands right behind.
teaches: Both treat Death as an agent that chooses its hour, but the Purananuru makes that patience the measure a king exceeds, while the Naladiyar makes the unknown hour the reason for doing good now, so one belief about death supports a war boast in one book and a moral urgency in the other.

note: Kural 544: the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people and rules by the sceptre; 42: under his unbending sceptre the land knows no war cry, and all poets turn to him as rivers run to the sea.
teaches: The Kural states the reciprocity abstractly, while 42 shows what the embrace consists of (fields that feed guests, no raid-cry heard) and what the turning to the king looks like (poets flowing in like rivers), so the couplet's 'world at his feet' can be read as a picture of a watered, hospitable country.

note: Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for another's fault as for their own the dwelling place of shame; in 43 the prince, wronged by the poet's words, is ashamed 'as if you had erred' (நீபிழைத் தாய்போல் நனிநா ணினையே).
teaches: The Kural's definition of the finest shame is acted out in 43 by a prince who blushes for the man who insulted him, and the poem adds the consequence the couplet omits: that shame shown this way disarms the offender, who then takes the fault on himself.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: 5 tells the king not to side with those who cast off grace (அருள்) and love and take a hell that never leaves; Kural 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the dark, painful world.
teaches: The Kural makes grace a person's safeguard against hell; the Chera counsel turns the same link into a rule of government, where grace is shown by guarding the realm as one rears a child and hell is the lot of rulers who drop it.

note: 50 says the king spared and fanned the poet as if he had heard that the higher world has a dwelling only for those with fame here; Kural 234 says that if one wins wide fame on earth the world of the gods does not honour the learned (or the gods) instead.
teaches: Both tie fame on earth to standing in the world beyond, and 50 shows the belief at work in a single act of royal mercy, while the Kural states it as a rule whose terms are disputed; the poem suggests that for a Sangam king fame was a practical reason for forbearance.

note: Kural 1055: askers can stand before people because there are those on earth who do not hide what they have; 54: suppliants walk into the king's court 'as if they owned it' (உடையோர் போல), because he gives without stint.
teaches: The Kural explains why asking is possible at all, and 54 shows the confidence such a giver creates, a beggar entering a court with raised head; the poem also adds the other face the Kural omits, the same king's land as a tiger's ground to his rivals.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting after inquiry without favour to anyone; 55 asks the king not to bend the rod because a man is 'ours' and not to destroy merit because he is 'others'.
teaches: The Kural forbids favour in one direction only, while 55 names both failures, favouring one's own and injuring outsiders, so the poem shows that impartiality was understood as a double duty, protecting strangers' merit as well as resisting kin.

note: 55: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors are excellent, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; Kural 546: it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: The Purananuru poet already ranks the four-limbed army below righteous rule before the Kural's couplet does, and he spells out the straight sceptre as impartiality toward one's own and others, so the Kural's maxim had a court-counsel form addressed to a named Pandya.

note: 58 warns two allied kings against outsiders who come between them 'seeming good, seeming kind, seeming to follow the old ways'; Kural 826 says the words of the unreconciled, though they speak good things like friends, are soon seen through.
teaches: The Kural's general warning about feigned friendship is applied in 58 to an alliance of kings, where the danger is not the enemy's attack but his pleasant counsel, so the pair shows the couplet's subject was already a matter of statecraft.

note: Both use the weighing balance for leaning to no side: 6 wishes the king may not hold to one side, like the beam of a balance (தெரிகோல் ஞமன்ன் போல); Kural 118 makes not leaning, like a levelled scale, the ornament of the worthy.
teaches: The same balance serves as a king's blessing in the Purananuru and as a general virtue in the Kural, which shows that impartiality was pictured as a public act of weighing done by whoever judges, before it was a disposition of the private person.

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows; 6 asks the king's umbrella and head to bow before the god's shrine and the sages, his garland to wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands, and his anger to yield before his women's sulking.
teaches: Where the Kural makes humility a constant trait of the great, the Purananuru poet gives it addresses: the king bows to god, sages and wives and to no one on the field, so royal humility was a question of before whom, not of always.

note: Kural 970 says the world praises the radiance of those who will not live when disgrace comes; 66 says the king who sat north ashamed of his wound reached the world of great fame (மிகப் புகழ் உலகம்).
teaches: 66 shows what the Kural's general praise of honour could mean in practice: a dishonour as small as a wound's place on the body, a death chosen for it, and a poet ranking the dead man above the living victor in public.

note: 68 promises the bard a lord who will give so much that he forgets other men's doors (பிறன்கடை மறப்ப); Kural 1053 says even asking has a grace when one stands before those who hide nothing and know their duty.
teaches: The Kural allows asking only before the right giver, and the guide poem is the bard's practical answer: it tells him which door to stand at so that he need never stand at another, which shows ஆற்றுப்படை solving the Kural's problem of asking.

note: 70 says the king's giving is no windfall like woodcutters finding gold; Kural 216 likens the wealth of the good-hearted man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: 70 makes explicit what the Kural's tree in the town only implies: the value of a generous man's wealth to those who ask is that it can be counted on, unlike a lucky find, so reliability is part of what giving means.

note: Among the curses 71 accepts is to put an incapable man in office in his assembly out of fondness (அன்பின் அவையத்துத் திறன்இல் ஒருவனை நாட்டி); Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every kind of folly.
teaches: The Kural names fondness as the cause of a bad appointment; 71 shows how grave such an appointment was held to be, since a king lists it among the curses on himself beside losing his wife, his friends and his birthright.

note: In 72 the king accepts, if he breaks his vow, that his people will find no shade under his rule and will weep and blame him as cruel; Kural 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering are what wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: The Kural names the people's tears as a force that destroys a king's wealth; 72 shows a king himself choosing those tears as the worst penalty he could stake, so the Kural's warning was already a ruler's own measure of failure.

note: 73 says the fool who ignored the strength of the strong (ஆற்றல் உடையோர் ஆற்றல் போற்றாது) will hardly escape alive; Kural 891 says not slighting the strength of those able to act (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை) is the chief of all safeguards.
teaches: The near-identical wording shows the Kural turning a king's threat into a general safeguard: what 73 says from the side of the strong man about to strike, the Kural says to everyone who might provoke him.

note: 74 asks whether a warrior line would bear a son who begs a little drink to quench his hunger; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow degrades the tongue more than anything.
teaches: The Kural makes asking shameful even for the worthiest cause; 74 roots the same horror in a warrior code that will not let even a stillborn child go unmarked by the sword, so the shame of begging is shown as a matter of lineage as well as of general ethics.

note: 75's petty heir begs dues from his people (குடிபுரவு இரக்கும்); Kural 552 says the asking (இரவு) of a king with his sceptre is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over'.
teaches: Both books call a king's demand on his people begging, and 75 adds the cause the Kural leaves out: the petty heir values the throne as wealth to take from, where the worthy one counts the same fortune as light as a dry stick.

note: 84 says her lord has great shoulders though he eats புற்கை (coarse gruel); Kural 1065 says that even gruel thin as water (அடுபுற்கை) is sweetest when one's own effort earned it.
teaches: The Kural's gruel of the self-reliant poor already stood in the older poem for a strong man's austere fare, cited by a woman as proof of his strength, so the couplet's dignity of plain food draws on a heroic image, not only on poverty.

note: Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him; in 86 a mother likens her womb to a tiger's empty den and says her son will be found on the battlefield.
teaches: The Kural's mother waits to hear others praise her son, while the Purananuru mother does not know where he is and stakes her pride on her womb and the battlefield, which shows that the worth a mother hoped for could be a warrior's death as readily as a good name.

note: 87 opens களம்புகல் ஓம்புமின், தெவ்விர் (enemies, beware of entering the field); Kural 771 opens என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் (enemies, do not stand before my lord).
teaches: The Kural's chapter on an army's pride keeps a whole Sangam speech-type, the warning to foes addressed as தெவ்விர் with a prohibitive verb, and swaps Avvai's craftsman's image of strength for the hero-stones of the slain, so the couplet is the genre cut down to its threat.

note: 9 praises the Pandya who, before battle, tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter; Kural 773 calls generous help to the foe in misfortune the cutting edge of valour.
teaches: The Kural puts mercy at the end of valour, once the foe has fallen; the Purananuru shows a king putting it before the first arrow by warning those who cannot fight, so the restraint of the brave had a set procedure as well as a maxim.

note: 90 asks whether deer herds can stand where a fierce tiger rages; Kural 599 says even a huge, sharp-tusked elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
teaches: In both the tiger is the spirit that neither numbers nor size can resist, but Avvai sets it on a herd to praise a king while the Kural sets it on an elephant to teach ookkam, so one image served both royal praise and a general maxim on energy.

note: Kural 82: even if it were the medicine of deathlessness, eating it alone while the guest waits outside is not to be wished; in 91 Anji gives Avvai the nelli fruit that keeps death away instead of eating it.
teaches: The Kural's extreme case, the food of immortality not eaten alone, has a remembered instance in a chieftain who gave a poet the fruit of long life, so the maxim's hyperbole was also a story the tradition told of a real giver.

note: 92: a child's prattle does not keep to the lute and makes no sense, yet moves fathers; Kural 66: those who call the flute and lute sweet have not heard their children's prattle.
teaches: The Kural leaves unsaid that prattle fails every test of music, and Avvai says it outright and builds on it, so read together the father's delight is shown to be grace rather than taste, which is what lets her use it for a patron's love of an imperfect poem.

note: Kural 776: the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound (விழுப்புண்); 93 tells how a king who died of sickness was cut with a sword on darbha grass so as to go where the battle-slain go, and ends on Anji's விழுப்புண்.
teaches: The poem shows why a day without a wound could be counted lost: a death without one had to be given a wound by rite before the dead could reach the heroes' world, so the Kural's ledger rests on a belief about where the dead go.

note: Kural 227: the disease called hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; 95 praises a lord who shares when he has and goes without together with his dependants when he has not.
teaches: The Kural promises the habitual sharer freedom from hunger, while Avvai's lord shares and still has empty days, so the poem shows the virtue the Kural rewards at work in a world where sharing did not prevent want but made it common to all.

note: Patitruppattu 17 says the king's great victory drum was made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய வலம்படு வியன்பணை); in Akananuru 347 the heroine compares the street's gossip to the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadamba (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய பண்ணமை முரசின்).
teaches: The near-identical wording shows an akam poet borrowing the Chera's victory drum, a puram fact, to measure how loud gossip is, so the king's war trophy had become familiar enough to serve as a household simile for noise.

note: Akananuru 199 measures the wealth a man refuses to leave his wife for by the land Narmudi Cheral regained when Nannan fell in the battle at the great ford of the vakai; Patitruppattu 40 praises the same Narmudi Cheral for cutting down Nannan's vakai at the root.
teaches: The love poem adds that the country won from Nannan was one the Chera had lost before (இழந்த நாடு), which the praise poem does not say, and it shows the king's greatest gain already serving akam poets as the very largest wealth a lover could turn down.

note: Akananuru 347 measures the town's gossip by the drum of Cheralathan made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea; Patitruppattu 44 shows the making of such a drum from the Mohur neem.
teaches: The puram decade shows how a Chera trophy drum was made from a felled guardian tree, and the akam poem shows that drum so well known that a heroine can use its roar to measure the gossip about her, so a war trophy had passed into the household's common speech.

note: Akananuru 214 has a soldier in the rain-soaked camp where the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, asking how his wife bears the evenings alone; Patitruppattu 50 asks how the sleepless king himself passes the camp days away from women's embrace.
teaches: The akam poem treats the king's sleeplessness as the cause of the soldier's separation, while the puram poet lends the king the soldier's own longing to praise his endurance, so the same camp night is a lover's grief in one book and a king's virtue in the other.

note: Akananuru 61 tells the heroine not to suffer looking at the tall wall where the days are marked (நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்), and pictures Pulli's men trading white elephant tusks for toddy; Patitruppattu 68 has the king's warriors hoping to trade white tusks (வெண்கோடு) for toddy while women at home draw the days on the painted wall.
teaches: The tusk bartered for toddy and the days scored on a wall were a stock pair of the far campaign and the waiting house: the akam poet splits them between the land the hero crosses and the heroine's room, while Kapilar keeps both inside one king's war, so the cost of conquest is counted at home.

note: Akananuru 135 likens the heroine's shaken heart to Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir attacked it together; Patitruppattu 71 has Kazhuvul, chief of those who live by cattle, bow his head (கழுவுள் தலைமடங்க) when the Chera's archers drove off the herds.
teaches: Kazhuvul is besieged by a coalition of Velir in one poem and humbled by the Chera in the other, which shows his herders' stronghold as a repeated prey of greater powers and explains why an akam poet could use it as a byword for a heart under assault.

note: Akananuru 44 has a man bid his charioteer hurry home to his wife because the king's war is finished and the foes have paid tribute; Patitruppattu 81 has the poet ask the king himself, in the rainy season with the siege still on, to yoke his chariot for one day to see his wife, so that the sleepless besieged kings may sleep too (துஞ்சா வேந்தரும் துஞ்சுக).
teaches: In the akam poem the homecoming waits until the war is over, but the court poet asks the king to go home in the middle of the war and gives the besieged enemy's rest as a reason, so the mullai motif of the rainy-season return becomes, in praise poetry, a way of asking for a pause in the fighting.

note: Fragment 1 says enemies cannot escape except by heaping rare jewels with elephants and speaking submissively (யானையொ(டு) அரும்கலம் ... பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல்); Akananuru 124 opens with the same formula (நன்கலம் களிற்றொடு ... வணங்கினர், வழிமொழிந்து) as the condition on which a soldier waiting in camp may go home to his wife.
teaches: The submission the praise poet demands as the enemy's only course is, in the akam poem, the event a homesick soldier waits for, so the formula of tribute served both genres and the end of the king's war was imagined from the camp as the start of a lover's return.

note: Fragment 3 has a woman say that another, for all her excellence, is not her equal and knows who her equals are (என்னொடு புரையுநள் அல்லள்); Ainkurunuru 67, a wife's speech in marutham, says the hero's new woman, foolish, sets herself against the wife who is no match for her (தன்னொடு நிகரா என்னொடு நிகரி).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 67 supplies the frame the three-line fragment lacks: claims of who is whose equal are the weapon of the marutham quarrel between wife and new woman, which makes it likely the fragment is such a speech and that its point is standing in the household rather than beauty.

note: The preface says the king carved his bow on the Himalaya and brought costly vessels with diamonds (அருவிலை நன்கலம் வயிரமொடு கொண்டு) to his old city and gave to others; Akananuru 127 recalls Cheralathan who drove off the sea, cut the kadamba, carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped the foes' tribute of fine vessels with diamonds (நன்கலம் ... வயிரமொடு) at Maanthai, leaving it for the earth to eat.
teaches: The two record the same hoard with the same jewel list but different fates, given away in the preface and left buried in the akam poem, so an akam poet could cite a puram event precisely while turning its moral from royal giving to abandoned wealth, the wealth the lover will not linger for.

note: Kuruntokai 73 says the Kosar killed Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land; the preface of the fourth ten says Narmudi Cheral beheaded Nannan of Peruvaayil and felled his gold-bearing vakai.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on which tree was Nannan's guardian and who destroyed him, so either the name Nannan covers more than one chief or felling his guarded tree was a victory several conquerors claimed, and neither poem alone shows that the deed was told of more than one enemy.

note: 101 argues at length that Athiyaman's gift never fails however long it is delayed; the akam poem 162 calls Athikan, of the same house, one who never let a suppliant's hope fail (நசைபிழைப்பு அறியா).
teaches: What 101 has to argue as a bard's private reassurance had become, in an akam poet's line, a fixed epithet of the Athiyaman house, so the praise poem shows the experience behind the epithet.

note: 103 is Avvai's guide poem sending a viraliyar to Anji; Akananuru 352 cites a bard's song that set down Anji's good fame (அஞ்சி நல்லிசை நிறுத்த) as a model of fine craft.
teaches: Read together they show the life of a praise song: Avvai directs performers to Anji, and a later akam poet can take a bard's song of Anji's fame as the standard of a well-made song, so the guide poems made the fame the akam poets borrowed.

note: 109 says Parambu needs no ploughing because its hill yields four foods by itself; Akananuru 303 describes flocks of sparrows of Pari's Parambu flying out at dawn to bring back red paddy and returning at evening.
teaches: Both describe food coming into Parambu without its people farming, which suggests the self-feeding hill was a known part of Pari's legend that an akam poet could use as a ready simile for something sure to return.

note: 110 tells the three kings that Parambu is hard to take though they join forces; Akananuru 78 recalls Pari, with Kapilar beside him, driving off the tusked kings after years of fighting.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled history what 110 states as a boast during the siege, so the pair shows the defence of Parambu passing from Kapilar's own war-speech into the shared stock of akam similes.

note: 121 asks the patron to stop treating all poets alike; Akananuru 152 praises Ay for giving freely to those who come whether skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும் சென்றோர்க்கு). On the plain reading the two ideals of giving are incompatible.
teaches: The akam poet borrows as an ornament exactly the indiscriminate giving that Kapilar argues against, so the ideal of the patron who gives to all was common fame, and 121 is a poet's dissent from it, not the standard view.

note: 123 praises Malayan of unfading fame (தொலையா நல்லிசை) at Mullur; Akananuru 209 names the Mullur king Kari whose fame does not pass (செல்லா நல்லிசை), who killed Ori and gave the Kolli hills to the Cheras.
teaches: The akam friend uses Kari's lasting fame as a fixed point to measure the heroine's beauty, which shows that the bards' praise of Kari had become a shared reference that akam poets could cite to measure something else entirely.

note: 126 calls Malaiyaman Kari lord of a land of palmyra groves (பெண்ணையம் படப்பை நாடு); Akananuru 35 names Kari of the long chariot, lord of Kovalur, and the great river Pennai (பெண்ணையம் பேரியாறு) at his ford.
teaches: The mother's lament in Akananuru 35 places her daughter's flight on the river of Kari's land, so a puram patron's territory supplies the akam poem's geography, and the shared பெண்ணையம் suggests that 126's phrase may name the river land rather than palms alone.

note: 128 says Ay's Pothiyil may be approached only by a dancing woman, while proud kings can hardly come near; Akananuru 322 compares the beloved, hard to win, to Pothiyil, hard to enter (புகலரும் பொதியில் போல).
teaches: The akam lover's simile takes its force from the puram boast: Pothiyil's inaccessibility was a known fact of Ay's power, and the akam poet turned a chief's closed hill into a measure of a woman's reserve.

note: Paranar rebukes Pekan in 144 for leaving his wife for another woman; Paranar in Akananuru 262 has a lover compare his beloved's fragrance to Pekan's rain-cloud hill (வண்மகிழ்ப் பேகன் கொண்டல் மாமலை).
teaches: The same poet uses Pekan's hill as a sweet image of union in akam while rebuking Pekan's own broken marriage in puram, so the patron's name entered akam similes as pure fame, cleansed of the scandal the puram poems record.

note: Akananuru 238 names Nalli for rain-like giving of chariots and elephants to suppliants (மழைசுரந் தன்ன ஈகை) as a simile's backdrop; 150 tells one of his gifts in full, a chain from his chest given to a ragged poet in the forest.
teaches: The akam epithet compresses into a formula of chariots and elephants a fame that the puram poem shows was made of personal, unannounced gifts, so the akam poet's shorthand assumes hearers who knew stories like 150.

note: 151 explains a snub: the poets shunned the hill of Nannan's kin because of a door shut against singers; Akananuru 152 praises Nannan for famous giving, flinging elephants (இசைநல் ஈகைக் களிறுவீசு). On the reading that the same line of Nannan is meant, the two reputations are incompatible.
teaches: Whether one Nannan or two, the name carried opposite reputations for giving in the two anthologies, which shows that a patron's fame among bards was contested and could be undone by one shut door.

note: 158 lists Malaiyan (who rode Kari) and Ori among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras (ஓரிக் கொன்று சேரலர்க்கு ஈத்த).
teaches: The canon of the seven givers sets side by side two men one of whom killed the other, so the list honours giving alone and is silent about the wars among the givers, which the akam poet remembers in a simile.

note: Both name the Kosar of many spears: in Akananuru 113 as loyal guards whose rich land stands for the heroine's lover, in 169 as young men practising spear throws at a murukku post, the simile for Pittan's strength.
teaches: The Kosar were a byword for spear-skill and fidelity known to both genres: the akam poet borrows their loyalty to measure a lover's land, the puram poet their training post to measure a chief, so their fame served as a ready image in both kinds of poem.

note: 17 praises the Irumporai as lord of cool Thondi, with screwpine, wide fields, sandy groves and backwaters; Akananuru 60 compares a fisherman's guarded daughter's beauty to Thondi of the Porayan of the strong chariots.
teaches: The Poraiyan port that the praise poet counts among the king's possessions became, in akam, the standard for a girl's well-guarded beauty, which shows love poets taking their measure of value from the Chera wealth that puram poets praised.

note: Both use the formula of the Moriyar with sky-touching umbrellas whose chariot wheels cut a pass through rock (Akananuru 69 lines 10 to 12; 175 lines 6 to 8).
teaches: The same Mauryan landmark serves akam as the far, dangerous road the hero crosses for wealth and puram as a figure for the fixed, unfailing care of a patron, so the formula's sense came from the poem it was set in, not from the place.

note: Both name Nedunchezhiyan's victory over the seven at Alankanam (ஆலங் கானத்து; எழுவர் நல்வலம்): 19 shows the field where mothers wept and Death fled ashamed, Akananuru 36 makes the victors' shout there the measure of how loud the gossip about the hero is.
teaches: The akam poet borrowed only the victors' roar from Alankanam to measure a scandal, while the puram poem on the same battle keeps the weeping of the old houses' women, so one battle served love poetry as a byword for noise and praise poetry as a field of grief.

note: 201 is spoken after Pari's fall, with his daughters taken to another chief; Akananuru 78 measures the heroine's brow by the flowers of the pool of Pari, the giver who drove off kings (வேந்தர்ஓட்டிய).
teaches: The akam poet keeps Pari as the victor whose hill still blooms, while Kapilar's poem records the aftermath in which his daughters need a protector, so akam fixes a hero at his height that puram follows past his death.

note: 202 closes by wishing Irungovel's spear victory; Akananuru 36 lists Irungo Venman among the seven defeated in one day by Chezhiyan at Alankanam.
teaches: If the two name the same house, the akam friend's list of fallen kings shows the defeat that Kapilar's parting blessing does not foresee, and shows akam poets drawing on puram battle-lists as common knowledge to scale a quarrel.

note: 204 praises Ori as a giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit; Akananuru 209 names Kari of Mullur, who killed Ori of the strong bow and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
teaches: The puram poem preserves Ori as a living patron while the akam friend cites his killing as a famous deed of another chief, so one man's fame survives in the anthologies as both a patron's praise and a rival's trophy.

note: 205, by Perunthalai Sathanar, praises the hunter lord of Kodai whose bards never leave without chariots and elephants; Akananuru 13, by the same poet, names the Kodai lord who gives to suppliants without limit (வரைநிலை இன்றி) except the captured elephant.
teaches: The same poet turns his patron's giving into an akam measure of what the hero would forgo by leaving, and his akam line keeps a detail the puram poem omits, that one gift, the captured elephant, was only promised by word.

note: Akananuru 55 recalls Cheralathan sitting facing north (வான்வடக் கிருந்தென) after his wound at Venni and the worthies who went with him to the other world; in 222 the poet reproaches his king for telling him to come only after his son was born.
teaches: The akam simile shows that companions dying with a king who sat facing north was a known and honoured act, which explains why being told to wait for a son's birth is felt in 222 as a lack of love: the friend was barred from an honour the custom gave him.

note: 224 mourns the king of the colophon, Karikalan, listing his battles, feeding of bards and sacrifice; Akananuru 55 recalls Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni, after which the defeated Cheral sat facing north and worthies died with him.
teaches: Karikalan is remembered in the akam simile through the mourning his victory caused in the defeated court, and in 224 through his own women's stripped ornaments, so the same king stands in the corpus at both ends of the grief that war produces.

note: 23 praises the victor of Alankanam; Akananuru 175 compares the lightning of the returning rains to the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alankanam.
teaches: The heroine's speech in an akam poem borrows the Pandya's Alankanam victory, which 23 celebrates as fact, to measure the flashing of the rains that mark her lover's promised return, so a war became a stock image of brilliance within the poets' own generation.

note: 233 refuses the dawn report of spear wounds on the chest of Evvi, leader of the bards' families; Akananuru 115 uses the bards who, in the battle where Evvi fell (எவ்வி வீழ்ந்த செருவில் பாணர்), broke off the curved necks of their lutes, as a simile for konrai pods on a desert path.
teaches: The akam poet assumes his hearers know that bards mourned Evvi by breaking their lutes, so the death the puram poet cannot bring himself to believe became, in the akam tradition, a fixed public memory usable as a passing image of curved pods.

note: 24 names the Mizhalai of Evvi, the generous Vel, among the lands Chezhiyan holds; Akananuru 266 names Evvi of Needur, true of sword, and the uproar after his men's victory.
teaches: One chief is remembered in the Purananuru for open-handed giving and for lands that passed to the Pandya, and in the Akananuru as a byword for the din of his war victory, so the akam poets kept a lesser king's martial name alive as a measure of loud gossip.

note: 240 calls Aay Andiran never stinting singers of horses, elephants and chariots; Akananuru 152 names 'Aay's forest' after the Aay who gives elephants to all who come, skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Aay's open-handedness to name a place, while the puram poem records what followed his death, his poets scattering to other lands, so the patron's giving outlived him as a landmark in love poetry even as the household it fed dissolved.

note: 246's speaker is the queen of Bhoothapandiyan; the colophon of Akananuru 25 names Bhoothapandiyan as its poet, whose hero vows 'let my life suffer' at parting.
teaches: Through the colophons, the akam poet who wrote a lover's promise not to stay away is also the husband whose wife refused to outlive him, so the anthologies let a convention of inseparable lovers stand beside one recorded marriage.

note: 26 calls Chezhiyan அடுகளம் வேட்ட, the one who sacrificed the killing field; Akananuru 36 measures the town's gossip by the roar when Chezhiyan at Alankanam களம்வேட்ட, after killing seven kings in one day.
teaches: The same phrase for the battlefield sacrifice appears in a praise poem and in a heroine's quarrel with her husband, which shows the Pandya's war rite was famous enough as a phrase to serve an akam speaker as the loudest noise she could name.

note: Both describe the making of a hero-stone: 264's name carved, red flower garland bound with maral fibre and peacock feather; Akananuru 269's names washed, turmeric, and a karanthai garland tied with fibre on the stone by the road.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the puram rite almost item by item to fill the heroine's fear of the road, which shows that the hero-stone was a fixed, widely known ritual whose details an akam audience would recognise as danger without being told.

note: 283 line 6 names the assembly hall of the Kosar (கோசர் அவைக்களத்தானும்); Akananuru 262 names the town-elder Kosar (ஊர்முது கோசர்) who blinded Anni Mignili's father.
teaches: Both poets know the Kosar as a body that sits in judgment, an institution in the puram fragment and the source of a borrowed story in the akam poem, so the Kosar's council was famous enough for an akam speaker to cite it as a known wrong.

note: 283 names the Azhumbil man who will not submit (அழும்பிலன் அடங்கான்); Akananuru 44 uses Azhumbil (அழும்பில் அன்ன அறாஅ யாணர்) as the measure of unfailing plenty, in a Chola king's praise.
teaches: The akam poet uses Azhumbil only as a by-word for wealth, while the puram fragment remembers it as the seat of a man who resisted, so the same place carried prosperity in love poetry and defiance in war poetry.

note: Akananuru 60 calls the mother who will guard the girl அறன்இல் யாய்; 336 calls the mother who reared the girl's beauty அறன்இலன் and பண்புஇல் தாய்.
teaches: Both poems blame the mother with the same word, but the akam friend blames her for guarding the girl too closely and the puram poet for rearing a beauty that draws war, which shows that the girl's beauty, a private matter in akam, becomes a public danger in the kaanchi poems.

note: Akananuru 60's friend says the mother will keep the girl under closer guard than the Chola treasure and asks the hero not to crush her bangled girl; 337 says the girl is confined to the house (மனைச்செறிந் தனளே) and asks who will crush (ஞெமுக்குவோரே) her young breasts.
teaches: The same confinement of the maturing girl and the same verb for the lover's embrace appear in both, but in akam the guard is a mother keeping off one lover while in puram it is brothers with bloody spears keeping off kings, which shows the puram poet enlarging an akam household scene into war.

note: Akananuru 90's friend says that even the Kosars' town would not be accepted as the price of the girl; 338 says the father will not give his daughter even if the three crowned kings bring gifts, unless they bow.
teaches: The akam friend's boast that no price is enough for the girl is the same claim the puram father makes against kings, so the pair shows a shared convention of the priceless daughter that in akam keeps a lover waiting and in puram starts a war.

note: Both describe Musiri's trade: gold arriving by ship and pepper going out.
teaches: The same port appears from both sides of the genre line, and in both the speaker refuses Musiri-scale wealth for a woman: the father will not sell her, the hero will not leave her for it.

note: Both name Thazhumban and his town Unur.
teaches: The puram poem praises Thazhumban for truthful speech and the akam poem for never turning comers away, so his fame reached akam poets as that of a host and landmark, and both use his rich Unur as a byword for plenty.

note: Both name Eyinan; 351 likens the girl's beauty to his vaakai, while Akananuru 208 recalls his death at Paazhi. Uncertain: வாகை may be a victory or a place.
teaches: The puram poet uses Eyinan's vaakai as a measure of beauty while the akam poet uses his fall in battle as a measure of shame avenged, so one chieftain's name served both as a token of victory and of a hero's death.

note: 378 likens the bard's kin decked in misplaced jewels to the monkeys who wore the jewels Sita dropped when Ravana took her; Akananuru 70 likens the hushed town to the banyan at Kodi that Rama silenced for his secret counsel.
teaches: The two Sangam allusions to the Rama story both use a marginal episode, dropped jewels and a silenced tree, as a simile for a crowd, so the story was known in enough detail that poets could cite its by-ways without telling it.

note: 385 blesses Aruvanthai with years more than the raindrops on புல்லிய வேங்கட; Akananuru 61 names Pulli, the chief of the cattle raiders, as lord of the festive Venkatam where toddy is bartered for paddy.
teaches: If புல்லிய in 385 names Pulli, a bard of the south uses another chief's hill as the measure of his own patron's blessing, and akam remembers the same hill as a frontier reward the hero would not stay for, so Venkatam served both genres as the edge of the known Tamil world.

note: Akananuru 54 calls Pannan of Sirukudi one who does not live for himself but belongs to others, and sets the hero's homecoming by the gooseberries of his garden; 388 tells how Pannan fed a drummer in famine.
teaches: The akam poet can use Pannan's name as a byword for living for others without explaining it, which shows that the puram reputation 388 records was common knowledge by the time an akam homecoming could borrow it as a landmark.

note: 389 describes Venkatam where a captured elephant calf is tied in the common while its mother grieves; Akananuru 83 shows Pulli's young men separating a calf from its wailing mother and tying it at the toddy houses of the Venkatam town.
teaches: The calf-taking scene was a fixed picture of Venkatam shared by both genres, and the pairing shows the akam hero's heart racing past a scene that the puram poet offers as plain proof of the lord's wealth, the same image put to opposite uses of distance and of plenty.

note: 395 places Pidavur east of Uranthai of Tittan of the small-eyed elephants; Akananuru 122 compares the many obstacles to secret love to the guarded walls of Tittan's Uranthai.
teaches: Tittan's Uranthai is a fixed point on both maps: puram uses it to locate a small chief's village and akam uses its fortifications as a measure of how hard a meeting is, so a king's fame became the grid by which smaller places and private feelings were placed.

note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

note: 45 warns two Cholas that their quarrel will give deep delight to other kings; Akananuru 346 closes on a Chola, Killi Valavan, worsted at Koodal and 'Kothai Marban's joy was great'.
teaches: An akam poet's closing allusion records exactly the outcome Kovur Kizhar predicted in puram, a rival Chera rejoicing at a Chola defeat, which shows that akam poets drew on the same remembered politics of the three crowns (whether this Killi Valavan is 45's Chola is not certain).

note: 48 praises Thondi of the seaside grove, the Chera's town, as fragrant with the king's garland and the neytal of its backwater; Akananuru 60 likens the heroine's bright bangles to Thondi of Poraiyan of the strong chariot.
teaches: The same Chera port that a puram poet offers as his home and his king's glory becomes in an akam poem a measure of a girl's beauty, which shows that akam poets used a king's famous town as a byword for desirable wealth.

note: 49 asks how to name Kothai of the raised sword; Akananuru 346 ends on Kothai Marban rejoicing when a Chola was worsted at Koodal.
teaches: The Chera whom a puram poet praises as lord of three landscapes appears in akam as a rival who delights in a Chola defeat, which shows akam poets citing a living king's partisanship, not only his wealth, and lets the reader see the three-crown politics behind the praise (whether both name the same Kothai is not certain).

note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

note: Akananuru 55's mother, sleepless after her daughter's elopement, compares her lot to the noble men who, hearing Cheralathan's bitter words when he sat north after Venni, went with him to the other world; 65 laments the same king's sitting north (வடக்கு இருந்தனன்) out of shame at a back wound.
teaches: The akam poet can use the king's death as a simile for a mother's loss only because puram poems such as 65 had made it known, and the akam poem adds what 65 does not say: that men of his court followed him into death, so the two together give the event and its aftermath.

note: Akananuru 246's friend says the gossip about the hero was louder than the uproar at Venni when Karikal broke the strength of kings and eleven Velir and their drums were left on the field.
teaches: The akam poet remembers Venni for the noise of Karikal's victory over many kings, while 66 remembers it for the defeated king's honourable death, so one battle served akam as a measure of loudness and puram as a lesson in honour.

note: The half-line எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க (the strength of the seven brought down) stands in 76 line 12 and in Akananuru 36 line 20, both of Cheliyan's victory at Alankanam; Akananuru 36 names the seven kings.
teaches: The identical half-line shows that the Alankanam victory had a fixed formula that passed from praise poetry into akam, where the war-cry of that day becomes the measure of how loud the town's gossip is about the hero's new bride.

note: Akananuru 6 calls Tittan of Uranthai the great giver who brings the wealth of rain (மாவண் தித்தன்); 80 asks Tittan to witness the hero's victory 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Tittan's fame as a giver as a byword, while 80 makes his grace toward one man uncertain, so the same chief appears as a public giver and as a withholding judge whose favour must be won.

note: 91 calls Anji lord of the Athiyar with கழல்தொடி தடக்கை; Akananuru 162 names a கழல்தொடி அதிகன் who never fails the hope of suppliants and owns a hill of jackfruit and vengai (probably the same Athiyar house, though the akam poem does not say which chief).
teaches: An akam poet uses the same epithet and the same fame for never failing those who ask, which 91 shows in one deed, to set the hill where a lover recalls a hard-won meeting, so the Athiyar chief's giving was a byword love poets could lean on.

note: 99 says Anji is beyond ordinary singers and that Paranar sang his victory at Kovalur; in Akananuru 352 the heroine calls her friend's news sweeter than a bard's famous song that set Anji's renown.
teaches: The akam heroine's comparison assumes that songs fixing Anji's fame were well known and loved, which 99 confirms by naming a poet who sang it, so a puram repertoire stands behind the love poem's simile.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

note: Kural 785: shared feeling alone, without meeting or acquaintance, gives the claim of friendship. Ainthinai Aimpathu 23: the bond of those who know needs no bard to plead for the man's grace.
teaches: The wife turns the Kural's rule about friendship into an argument against intercession in marriage: if feeling alone makes the bond, then the presence of a go-between is itself proof that the feeling is gone.

note: Kural 66: only those who have not heard their children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல்) call the flute and lute sweet. Ainthinai Aimpathu 25: the son's மழலைவாய் talk eases the pain of longing for the husband.
teaches: The Kural ranks prattle above music as a pleasure; the venba gives it a harder task, standing in for an absent husband's embrace, so the general praise of children is tested in the one place it might fail.

note: Kural 1309: sulking, like water in the shade, is sweet only with those who love. Ainthinai Aimpathu 27: the faded wife asks whether she is still one the man would sulk at.
teaches: The Kural's rule that a quarrel belongs inside love lets the wife read the man's absence of pulavi as the absence of love, so the venba shows the rule used as evidence by someone on the losing side.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering when there is no lover who knows we suffer? Ainthinai Aimpathu 29: she would refuse his embrace, but he has no thought of her refusal, so she will serve him.
teaches: Both say a protest needs a lover who registers it, and the venba draws the practical end the couplet stops short of: with no such lover, the wife abandons oodal and goes back to service.

note: Kural 1330: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to embrace after it. Ainthinai Aimpathu 30: even while sulking, union with the man's fragrant body is sweet, like the south wind in the cold season.
teaches: The Kural places the embrace after the sulk, while the wife finds it sweet during the sulk itself, so the venba collapses the Kural's sequence and shows desire overriding the quarrel instead of crowning it.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; if you mean to come back soon, tell it to those who will still be alive. Aimpathu 34: the friend asks the man whether he will cross many wastes of killing robbers, leaving the woman of sword-bright eyes.
teaches: Both are said to the man at the point of departure to stop him, but the Kural argues from the woman's death and the Aimpathu from the man's own danger among robbers, so the pair shows the two levers the dissuading speaker can pull against the journey, her life and his.

note: Naladiyar 398: the girl answers the friend who asks whether she can walk tomorrow behind her man through the hard forest: one who gets a great horse learns to ride it at once. Aimpathu 37: the mother asks whether the girl who faltered at play can keep pace behind her lover on the stony path. The mother doubts the feet that the girl says love will make able.
teaches: The same question, can her feet go with him, gets opposite answers: the mother measures the girl by her weakness at childhood play, the girl by the man she has gained, so across the two books the pair stages the quarrel of the elopement between the generation that remembers and the one that goes.

note: Naladiyar 203: the great never say they will not support those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந் தவரை), as a branch bears its own fruit. Ainthinai Aimpathu 48: can those who do not hold to the distress of those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந்தார்) carry great renown?
teaches: The shared word தற்சேர்ந்தார் shows the friend borrowing the maxim of supporting one's dependents and turning it on the lover: the girl in secret love is made a dependent with a kinsman's claim, and his renown is staked on marrying her.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ainthinai Aimpathu 6: evening, sweet with the bee at the jasmine for those who have company, comes and saws those who have no one.
teaches: Both women make evening a killer, but the venba adds that the same hour is sweet to the companioned, so it locates the couplet's hostility in the absence and not in evening itself, which the couplet's 'when the lover is absent' only implies.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, envoy of the burning evening, is a weapon that kills. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7: at red evening the herdsman's fine little flute, played in joy once the cattle have fed, is to her like a spear thrown.
teaches: The couplet states that the flute is a deadly weapon, and the venba supplies the scene that explains it: the herdsman plays for joy at his own day's return, so the weapon is someone else's homecoming.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now announce loudly that he has gone. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 14: because he is said to be good, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he leaves.
teaches: On a plain reading the two make incompatible claims about the same sign: the Kural takes wasting shoulders as the body's certain witness to separation, while the venba says trust in the man's goodness can stop the body from giving that witness at all.

note: Kural 1224: with the lover absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ezhupathu 17: as kodal buds and thunder greet the rains, the little evening comes like killers so that those with no one to embrace them tremble.
teaches: The Kural's image of evening as executioner, spoken by one woman of one absent man, appears in the Ezhupathu tied to the rainy season and widened to a class (those with no one to hold them), which shows the image was a mullai convention of the promised-return season before or beside its use as a private complaint.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know, while her husband had not yet gone, that evening brings sickness. Ezhupathu 21: before he returns, the evening comes with the rains to torment her, and no one lives in such folly as she.
teaches: The Kural names the woman's ignorance at the time of parting as the cause of her suffering, while the Ezhupathu's மடம் is a folly she still lives in now, knowing the evening, so the pairing separates ignorance that excuses from folly that the speaker mocks in herself.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is an envoy of the burning evening and a weapon that kills. Ezhupathu 22: herdsmen blow konrai flutes, the herd goes in, evening comes as she watches, and the sky thunders and draws its bow.
teaches: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute the evening's envoy and weapon, and Ezhupathu 22, which names no pain at all, gives the same evening a second weapon, the rainbow drawn as a bow, so the reader of the Kural sees that the evening's arming was a scene the venba poets could show without comment.

note: In Kural 1247 the woman in separation tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 34 she foresees her heart throwing off shame and going with her life after him.
teaches: The couplet poses the choice between desire and shame as a demand on the heart, and the venba shows the heart's answer and its cost, since choosing desire there means the life leaving the body with it.

note: Kural 782: the friendship (கேண்மை) of the wise waxes like the crescent moon, that of fools wanes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 4: the friendship of the worthy (சான்றவர் கேண்மை) stands firm and grows into strength, so the mountain lord's will too.
teaches: The venba lifts the Kural's maxim about friendship with the worthy into a girl's mouth as her proof that her lover will not fail, which shows the ethics books' rule of friendship being used, within the akam frame, to judge a lover's character before marriage.

note: Kural 1203: a sneeze that seems to come and then dies away makes her think he seems about to think of her and does not. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 41: sneezes come one after another, so he is thinking of her. On the plain reading the same sign gives opposite verdicts.
teaches: Both women read the sneeze by the same folk belief, but the Kural uses its failure for a wry doubt while the venba piles it up as proof, which shows the belief was firm enough to support either despair or hope depending on what the body did.

note: Kural 1102: the man says the jewelled woman (அணியிழை) is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 5: the friend tells the man there is no medicine but him for the bright-jewelled girl (வயங்கிழை).
teaches: The same paradox of the lover as the only cure runs in both directions, the woman for the man in the Kural, the man for the woman here, and the change of speaker turns the Kural's private wonder into the friend's demand that he give the cure.

note: Kural 773 calls generous help to a fallen foe (ஊராண்மை) the cutting edge of valour. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 52: the friend mocks the husband for treating his going to the other street as ஊராண்மை, manliness before the town.
