teaches: The Kural makes ஊராண்மை a virtue of restraint toward the weak, while the friend uses the same word for the husband's public swagger in neglecting his wife, so on a plain reading the two give the word opposite contents, and the venba's sarcasm depends on the higher sense the Kural fixes.

note: Kural 572: the world's ways rest on கண்ணோட்டம், and those without it are a burden on the earth. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 54: the husband who resolves to withhold கண்ணோட்டம் while taking the wife's devoted service is told the blame falls on him.
teaches: The Kural states kindly regard as a duty of public life; the venba brings it inside the marriage and makes its withdrawal a husband's blame, which shows the ethical term was already at work in the language of domestic quarrel.

note: Kural 1157: do not the bangles slipping from my wrist spread the news that the shore lord has left me? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 66: will the thief-hearted shore lord walk off by another path while her good bangles slip?
teaches: The couplet makes the slipping bangle a herald announcing his departure, while the venba places it at the moment of his going and calls his heart a thief's, so the pair qualifies the Kural's sign: the bangle that tells the town of his leaving also convicts him of planned deceit.

note: Kural 1182 has pallor ride the woman's body proud that 'he gave it'; Kainnilai 1 has her body waste pale as if saying 'the forest lord joined with her'.
teaches: Set in the guarded millet field of the secret love, the Kural's private conceit of pallor naming its giver becomes a public danger, since a body that names the lover undoes the secrecy that kalavu depends on.

note: Kural 1151: the friend (or the woman) tells the man that his promise of a quick return should be told to those still alive then. Kainnilai 13: told of his going by the long wasteland, her eyes went soft with tears.
teaches: Both answer the man's announcement of departure, but the Kural puts the threat to her life into argued words while the Kainnilai lets the friend report only the eyes giving way on hearing, so the pair shows the same reply could be made as a sharp argument or as a bare bodily fact laid before him.

note: Kural 1265: the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with her eyes. Kainnilai 19: the friend says the brightness returning to her forehead shows he is coming, before he has come.
teaches: On the Kural's reading the body recovers only from the sight of him and news cannot cure it, while the Kainnilai friend reads a recovery already begun as a sign of his return, so the two disagree on whether the body answers his presence or foreknows it.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes out looking for, since the beloved is already within it. Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart has gone after the man, swimming the long way through the scorched forest.
teaches: Both women speak of a heart that leaves to follow the man, but the Kural calls that going needless because he lives inside her, while the Kainnilai takes the heart's long swim as real, so the pair sets an inward answer to absence against the older picture of the heart travelling the road.

note: Kural 1182: the woman says pallor rides over her body (மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு), claiming it is his gift. Kainnilai 27: at the rainy evening, thinking of his coming, pallor spreads over her body (ஊர்தரு மேனி பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet says only that pallor rides her body by his right; the Kainnilai fragment gives it an hour and a cause, the rain-season evening and the thought of his coming, so expectation, not only absence, is what sets the pallor moving.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Kainnilai 35: the herders, heedless, blow the sweet pipe at that hour.
teaches: The couplet makes the flute a weapon; the Kainnilai adds that those who wield it do not know they are wounding anyone, so the evening's weapon kills without a killer who intends it.

note: Kural 1311: the woman refuses the chest of the man she calls a philanderer, because all women feed on him with their eyes. Kainnilai 38: the wife bars him from her house from today because he lives desiring young women's shoulders.
teaches: The couplet's refusal rests on a witty pretext, that other women merely look at him, while the venba's rests on his actual desire for other women, so the pair shows the Kural turning a real grievance of the marutham poems into the fine point of a lovers' quarrel.

note: Kural 1157: do the bangles slipping from her wrist not already proclaim that the shore lord has left? Kainnilai 55: if the shore lord leaves without embracing her, the bangles will not stay on either hand.
teaches: The venba states as a condition what the couplet packs into a past tense, so it supports reading the Kural's 'has left' as anticipatory: the bangles slip at the mere prospect of the shore lord going.

note: Kural 1262: if she forgets him today her beauty will leave and her bangles slip. Kainnilai 58: if she sits thinking of him, her bangles will not hold. On a plain reading forgetting ruins her in one and remembering in the other.
teaches: The couplet makes memory the thing that keeps her body whole and the venba makes memory the thing that wastes it, so together they show the bangle as a sign the two traditions could hang on either side of remembering the absent man.

note: Kural 1249's woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking when he is within it; Kainnilai 6's girl lets her heart go unspoken to his jewelled chest.
teaches: The heart's going out to the lover is chided as foolish in the Kural's separation chapter but is a silent secret gift in Kainnilai's secret stage, so the same movement of the heart is judged by whether he is still near.

note: In Kural 1157 the slipping bangles proclaim that the lord of the shore has left; in Kainnilai 7 they slip at the mere telling of the hill lord's friendship.
teaches: The Kural gives the bangles as a sign without a scene, and Kainnilai supplies the scene that explains them: a monkey that snatches the fruit and bolts, so the bangles fall because the 'friendship' was a theft and the leaving was already in it.

note: Kural 597 holds up the elephant that plants its feet under a sheaf of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு) as the model of a mind that does not give way; Kalavazhi Narpathu 10 shows elephants pierced everywhere by arrows that cannot move and sink wearily where they stand (செல்கலா தொல்கி யுயங்கும்).
teaches: Seen from the battlefield, the Kural's emblem of steadfastness is ambiguous: the same arrow-struck elephant that stands its ground is, for the victor's poet, a beast too spent to move, so the maxim's courage depends on reading stillness as resolve rather than as defeat.

note: Kural 599, in the chapter on energy (ஊக்கமுடைமை), says the elephant, for all its bulk and sharp tusks, fears a tiger's attack; Kalavazhi Narpathu 16 shows horses, urged on (ஊக்கி) by picked warriors, leaping onto the elephants' brows like tigers springing up a hill.
teaches: The battle verse turns the Kural's animal fable into tactics: the tiger's assault on the elephant is what cavalry does to war elephants, so the couplet's claim that drive overcomes size had a familiar picture on the field, and Poigaiyar's simile names the driving force with the Kural's own word.

note: Kural 774 praises the warrior who sends his spear off in an elephant and laughs as he plucks another from his own body; in Kalavazhi 23 the strong men (வயவர்) hurl and split the elephants' foreheads, and the field is Chempiyan's.
teaches: The Kural keeps the spear-thrower's own pride and wound in view, while the battle-song shows the same feat only through the speared elephants and credits it to the king, so the pair shows the warrior's deed moving from his ethic into his lord's fame.

note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great manhood, but help given when misfortune befalls the foe is its cutting edge; Kalavazhi 35 ends with the enemy king falling with his royal elephant, struck like a lion on a thunder-struck mountain, and goes no further.
teaches: The Kural locates the height of valour in the moment after the foe falls, and the kalavazhi, built to stop at the field of killing, has no place for that moment, so the couplet names exactly what the battle-song leaves out.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

note: Kural 1187: she turned aside a little from his embrace and the pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. Kar Narpathu 27: if we sulk that he left without a thought for us, pallor spreads over her in bed (பள்ளியுட் பாயும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole, that the least turning away from him in bed brings pallor, becomes in the friend's mouth a practical warning against sulking at an absent man, so the venba shows the Kural's figure used as an argument for bearing up.

note: Kural 231: to give and live so that renown arises; there is no other gain for a life. Kar Narpathu 32: bees glad as the hearts of wealthy men who crave undying fame (கெடாஅப் புகழ்வேட்கைச் செல்வர் மனம்போற்).
teaches: The couplet states the craving for renown through giving as the one gain of life, and the venba treats that craving as so familiar that a returning lover can measure a bee's gladness by it, which shows the puram ideal already turned into common stock for akam imagery.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover goes; look here, the pallor spreads on my body. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear, the lover's chariot does not, the pallor appears.
teaches: The couplet times the pallor to his leaving and the venba times it to his failure to return, so the two together show pallor at both ends of the absence, first as its shadow and then as its proof.

note: Kural 1269: for those who long for the day of the far one's return, one day passes like seven. Thinaimalai 101: since the man of the decorated chariot went, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
teaches: The couplet stretches each day of waiting while the venba empties the calendar of the one day she waits for, so together they show waiting as both a lengthening of days and an endless supply of the wrong ones.

note: In Kural 1222 the parted woman pities the dim evening as a sufferer like herself; in 110 the hills weep in pity for her while the wild jasmine laughs.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman lend her grief to one hour of the day, while the quatrain divides the whole landscape into those who mock her and those who mourn with her, so the pathetic projection becomes a judgment on which things are great.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, herald of the burning evening, kills like a weapon; 112: at sunset the sweet flute turns hot, and the friend answers that he will not fail and they must stand ready to receive him.
teaches: The Kural stops at the killing flute, while the quatrain gives the friend's reply to that very hour, turning the evening's heat into the household's readiness for a guest, so the flute is shown to be a test of trust as well as a pain.

note: Kural 1225: the parted woman asks what enmity she did to evening; 121: she says not one foe but many, the anril, the evening, the rain, the flute, the sea and the dark cloud, have made her their living.
teaches: The Kural names evening as the single enemy of the parted woman, and the quatrain multiplies the enemies across landscapes, showing that the evening of the Kural was the type of a whole hostile world of sights and sounds, each taking its share of her.

note: Kural 319: harm done to others in the forenoon returns of itself in the afternoon; 123: what is done in this life bears fruit in this life, as the women who tormented us have now been burned.
teaches: The Kural's impersonal rule that harm returns soon is here voiced by an injured wife about her rivals, showing how the ethical maxim of quick retribution was taken into akam as a scorned woman's satisfaction rather than a warning to oneself.

note: Naladiyar 85 says men who forced themselves on other men's wives in a former birth are born eunuchs in this one; 123 says those who think deeds bear fruit in the next birth do not understand, since the fruit comes here.
teaches: The Naladiyar defers the reckoning to a later birth while the quatrain insists on this one, so the pair shows a live disagreement in the didactic age about where retribution is seen, with the love poet choosing the visible, present punishment.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that does not cut down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை). Thinaimalai 134 uses both words (கிழமை, பழமை) as two alternative reasons why she, the humble one, received the man's grace when the many women he took did not.
teaches: The Kural states as a definition that old intimacy survives the liberties a friend takes, while the wife applies the same two terms to a husband who has taken many women and cannot decide whether his return came from enduring character or from reckoning the use of old ties, so the pair shows the friendship ethic carried into marriage and the doubt it leaves when the one taking liberties is the stronger party.

note: Kural 1311: all women feast on you in common with their eyes, philanderer; I will not come near your chest. Thinaimalai 152: the wife refuses her husband's marked chest under cover of the son's drool and her milk.
teaches: The Kural's wife refuses the chest openly and for the least offence, being looked at; the Thinaimalai's wife has proof printed on the chest and still refuses only by indirection, so the couplet's open charge and the quatrain's domestic pretext mark two registers of one refusal, the second keeping the house's peace while making the charge.

note: Kural 1285: as the eye does not see the brush that lines it, I do not see his fault when I see him. Thinaimalai 153: my eyes never see the lord, in sulk, in union, or when he leaves in anger.
teaches: The Kural finds one moment when the eye cannot see, nearness blinding it to his fault; the Thinaimalai extends that blindness to every phase of the marutham quarrel and to the man himself, so the couplet's single paradox becomes a whole cycle in which closeness and distance alike keep him out of view.

note: Kural 1306: without துனி and புலவி, love is like over-ripe and unripe fruit. Thinaimalai 153: in துனி, புலவி and ஊடல், and in the கனி union after, her eyes never see the lord.
teaches: The Kural justifies the graded quarrel as what keeps love ripe, while the Thinaimalai uses the same three words from inside the cycle and finds that none of its stages, quarrel or ripe union, lets her look at him, so the pair sets the doctrine of the quarrel as seasoning against its cost to the one who lives it.

note: Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and strength but the palmyra horse; in Thinaimalai 16 the man stands on the madal in the street and will not leave until she grants him her breast.
teaches: The couplet names the madal as the lover's only strength in general terms, and the quatrain shows what that strength is in use: a public siege in the street with a single stated condition and no second way, so the 'safeguard' is pressure on her household, not comfort for him.

note: Both men fear the girl's waist will break: the Kural through the flowers' stems, Thinaimalai 17 if she walks even a little.
teaches: The Kural keeps the snapping waist a joke of praise, a mock funeral drum, while Thinaimalai 17 lets the same fear spill into the man's own body, whose heart sways wherever she sways, so the conceit of her fragility becomes a measure of his surrender.

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death; the man of Thinaimalai 22 says her two eyes shot him as her brothers shoot beasts.
teaches: The Kural names the killing look in the abstract, and Thinaimalai 22 grounds it in her people's trade, measuring her two eyes against her brothers' single killing arrow, so the deadly glance of the couplet turns out to be a hunter's weapon of the hills.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, an eye and a doe in the young woman's look; Thinaimalai 32 calls the fish-guard's long eyes a weapon (படைநெடுங்கண்) whose guarding falls on the man.
teaches: The couplet lists in the abstract what a first look can be, and the poem supplies the scene that makes 'death' concrete: a girl posted to guard the drying fish whose watch is turned on the man who looks, so the Kural's killing glance is a guard's weapon.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Thinaimalai 41: the heart melts day after day while the talk swells, like a storm cloud pouring.
teaches: The Kural makes the gossip the food of the love-sickness, and Thinaimalai 41 makes the two one weather, the swelling talk and the melting heart pouring together like a cloud, which shows the girl suffering the growth the couplet describes as a cause.

note: Kural 1081: the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Thinaimalai 47: she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess (ஏரணங்கு) those who look without thinking.
teaches: The Kural's man hesitates over what she is, while the Thinaimalai speaker has settled it and turns to blame, saying her kin have let such a danger loose unguarded, so the pair shows the first-sight wonder of the couplet hardening into a lover's complaint.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும்). Thinaimalai 60: the hero names the long-eyed girl plucking neythal as the fisherman's daughter who has made him mad (மையல்).
teaches: The couplet's lover reels because he cannot tell what she is, while the venba's lover knows exactly who she is, a fisherman's daughter at the shore, and is mad all the same, so the scene shows the bewilderment surviving the answer to the Kural's question.

note: Kural 101: for help given unasked, earth and heaven together are hardly a return. Thinaimalai 62: no one on this sea-girt earth matches the shore lord who once helped in the salt land; seek his equal in heaven.
teaches: The venba takes the Kural's measure of unrequited help, earth and heaven, and applies it to the helper himself: the lover's one service makes him without equal in either world, so the ethical rule of gratitude becomes the friend's argument for the man.

note: Kural 1085 has the man at first sight find in her look Death, an eye and a doe; Thinaimalai 8 has the man at the fields find Kaman's arrows, five twice over, in the girl's two eyes.
teaches: Both men read a killing power in the first look, but the Kural names it Death while the field poem gives it to the love god and counts the arrows, which shows the same wound drawn once as mortal danger and once as a wound meant to be healed in union.

note: Naladiyar 11: knowing grey hair will come, the wise renounce in childhood, while those who delight in fleeting youth rise later on a staff. Thinaimalai 85: because youth cannot be brought back, the man should stay with his wife rather than chase wealth. On a plain reading the same fact counsels withdrawal in one and staying for love in the other.
teaches: From the one premise that youth does not return, the Naladiyar argues for leaving pleasure early and the paalai friend for keeping it while it lasts, so the impermanence of youth was an argument that served the householder's love as readily as the renouncer's flight.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Thinaimalai 86: told that he will surely go, the heroine says to name anyone who could bear it.
teaches: Both meet the news of his going by sending the message elsewhere, to whoever can survive it, and the venba supplies the starving elephant's waste that the couplet leaves out, so the Kural's bare retort is shown to be the stock reply of the paalai heroine to the announcement of departure.

note: Kural 1230: thinking of the man whose nature is wealth, in this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) my life that would not die is dying. Thinaimalai 94: in the bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை), when the moon pours a false day, my life does not stay within but rides away.
teaches: The venba takes the couplet's own phrase for the hour and adds the cause the couplet leaves out, a moon that fakes daylight, so the bewilderment of the evening becomes a trick of the sky rather than only a state of her mind.

note: Kural 1221: you are not evening but வேலை, the time that eats the life of the once-wed. Thinaimalai 96: the dark like Maayon's colour and the milk-white moonlight are like a spear (வேல்) to those without a partner.
teaches: The Kural's pun on வேலை (hour, and the sense that kills) is made literal in the venba as a spear, and it moves from the evening to the moonlit night, showing a later poet turning the couplet's wordplay into a simile.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is away, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground. Thinaimalai 97: the sun sets like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and she cannot bear the evening.
teaches: Both make evening a killing, but the couplet gives the killers no face while the venba names them through the land's own god, so the waiting woman of the mullai sees her evening through the war myth of the god of her own landscape.

note: Kural 1261: my eyes have lost their lustre (வாளற்று) and my fingers are worn from counting the days since he left. Thinaimalai 99: like my lustre, my eyes have lost their light (வாள் இழந்த), my shoulders their beauty, my soft fingers worn with counting the days.
teaches: The venba keeps the couplet's two proofs of waiting, dim eyes and worn fingers, but sets them as a retort to a friend who called the grief idle (வாளா), so the Kural's private lament is turned into evidence in an argument.

note: Kural 1151, the friend (for Parimelazhagar) to the departing man: tell me if you are not going; tell your quick return to those still alive then. Thinaimozhi 12, the friend to the man leaving for wealth: who can know her helplessness better than you?
teaches: Holding them together shows two moves in the friend's attempt to stop the journey: the couplet threatens with the woman's death, while the venba appeals to the man's own knowledge of her, making him the witness who cannot claim ignorance.

note: Kural 1264: thinking of the return of the man who left the love they shared, her heart climbs up as on branches. Thinaimozhi 14: though he left for wealth even after seeing the koel's season, her heart watches for his coming.
teaches: The couplet's heart rising in hope of his return gains in the venba a bitter premise, that he chose to leave in the very season of love, so the longing is shown to persist against her knowledge of his choice, not out of ignorance of it.

note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 19: the woman, picturing him halting in the stony waste where the doe cries with the stag, says her shoulders slip with her bangles.
teaches: The couplet gives the wasting shoulders as the plain sign of absence, and the venba supplies what she is thinking of while they waste: his fear on the road and the paired deer that keep together, so the symptom is tied to an imagined scene rather than to absence alone.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 22: the friend asks what will become of the pallor now that the rain says he will come. Kural 1265: the woman says the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading they disagree on whether news of his return can touch the pallor.
teaches: The friend treats the pallor as already beaten by the season's promise, while the couplet's woman refuses any cure short of seeing him, so the couplet sounds like the heroine's unspoken reply to the friend's teasing question.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 24: the friend rests her comfort on the man who swore an oath (வஞ்சினம்) and held to it, with the rain as his token. Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word?
teaches: The friend builds her comfort on his oath, while the couplet asks who is to blame if such an oath fails, so together they show that the whole mullai argument of waiting rests on trusting a man's word, and the Kural names the risk the friend leaves unsaid.

note: Both name the bewildering evening (மருண்மாலை, மருள்மாலை). Kural 1222: the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 27: the friend calls the darkening rainy evening the sign the man set for his return.
teaches: The same evening the Kural's woman mourns as a fellow sufferer abandoned like herself is presented by the friend as the very token of his return, which shows that the evening's meaning in love poetry depends on who is speaking and whether she still trusts him.

note: Kural 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses the friendship of those who are friends while there is profit and leave when there is none; Thinaimozhi 33 calls the husband's conduct exactly such a friendship.
teaches: The Kural can shrug at the self-serving friend because a friend can be dropped, but the wife cannot treat a husband with that indifference, since what he consumed was her youth, so the akam poem shows where the maxim's calm stops working.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Thinaimozhi 36 the friend tells the man that he both gave the beauty and took it back.
teaches: The Kural's exchange is a loss suffered in separation, but the friend makes the same giving and taking an argument against the husband: since he alone gave and took, there is no one else to blame and nothing anyone can do to him, which turns the woman's lament into an accusation.

note: In Naladiyar 390 the wife tells the bard not to lie that the man will be kind, since to him she is the tip of the sugarcane, and to tell it to those who are its middle joints; in Thinaimozhi 37 she tells the bard not to keep pressing, since she never had the gracious regard 'our younger sisters' have.
teaches: The same refusal of the bard, by the same speaker, is filed by the Naladiyar under the chaste wife, so the didactic book reads her sharp tongue to the go-between as a mark of karpu, while the akam venba keeps it as wounded pride with the ironic family word for the rivals.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base, like sugarcane, only when crushed; Thinaimozhi 39 has the wife say she has become the crushed cane's refuse.
teaches: The Kural looks at crushed cane from the side of the one who extracts the juice, as a way to get use from the mean, while the akam poem speaks from the cane's side, so the same image shows that what is crushed for its sweetness is left as waste.

note: Naladiyar 390 has the wife call herself the tasteless tip of the sugarcane to the lord of the town; Thinaimozhi 39 has her say she has become the chewed pith of the cane after he ate her beauty.
teaches: The marutham wife reaches for sugarcane in both books, but the Naladiyar places her at the less sweet end of a cane still whole, a matter of rank among his women, while the Thinaimozhi has the cane already chewed and spat out, so the same image measures either neglect or use and discard.

note: Kural 782: the friendship of the worthy grows like the waxing moon. Thinaimozhi 41: the worthy man's bond has waned since the day she saw him, and his trysts proved false; on a plain reading the heroine's case contradicts the maxim.
teaches: The heroine's question ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு tests the Kural's rule against one man and finds it failing, so the akam poem uses the ethical maxim as a weapon: either the rule is wrong or he was never one of the worthy.

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bright bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 47: the heroine asks her friend whether he has abandoned her, as pallor spreads and the bangles of her soft shoulders slip.
teaches: The couplet states the sign as a fact of separation, while the venba makes the heroine read it as a question, has he left me?, so the slipping bangle becomes the evidence by which she learns his desertion rather than its mere effect.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels. Thinaimozhi 49: the man asks whether she was a peacock, a young woman or a goddess of the sea waves, and his heart aches from her eyes.
teaches: The same three-way doubt in both shows the first-sight ஐயம் was a fixed form of kalavu, and the venba adds what the couplet leaves open: a place for the seeing, the njazhal grove, and a goddess native to that place, the one who lives in the waves.

note: Thinaimozhi 7 uses ஊரறி கௌவை, gossip the town knows, as the harm that a night visit will bring; Kural 1143 has the man welcome the ஊரறிந்த கெளவை as a foretaste of having her. On a plain reading the town's gossip is a threat in one and a gain in the other.
teaches: The same phrase is a warning in the friend's mouth and a prize in the lover's, so the Kural's couplet reads as his reply to exactly the argument the friend uses to keep him away.

note: Both are the woman saying that his coming will take the pallor from her shoulders: Kural 1265, after she has seen her husband with full eyes; Thinaimozhi 9, if the hill lord comes in this vengai evening.
teaches: The Kural states the cure as a rule in the wife's mouth, while the earlier stage in Thinaimozhi ties it to the flowering vengai, the season sign of weddings, so the coming that cures the pallor is, before marriage, the wedding itself.

note: Natrinai 142: returning, the man tells his charioteer of the young woman of mullai-fitting chastity who rejoices when a guest comes even at night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 10: returning, he tells the charioteer to hurry to see her who stands with the bolt of her chastity drawn shut, hand to cheek.
teaches: The same speaker on the same road imagines the wife's chastity as an open door to guests in one poem and as a shut bolt in the other, so the pair shows karpu as both the household's hospitality and its closing against the world while the husband is away.

note: Natrinai 259: the friendship made with the hill lord in the millet field, chasing parrots and bathing in the falls by the vengai slope, now looks hard to keep because the millet heads have ripened dry. Ainthinai Aimpathu 11: the few days in the vengai grove of the millet field have gone, sweet because no one gave orders.
teaches: Natrinai gives the crop's ripening as the reason the meetings end and Ainthinai names what made them possible, the absence of anyone to command the girls, so together they show the secret love as lent by the harvest calendar and taken back by it.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man finding the swing, the pool and the reaped field empty, and regrets that she forgot to tell him 'the high hill crowned with that white waterfall is our village'. Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 is that telling: the guarding is over, and this village by the clean waterfall is our place.
teaches: The longer poem shows the cost of not telling him where the house is when the field closes, and the quatrain makes the telling itself, so the pair shows pointing out the village by its waterfall as the friend's expected move at harvest, the step that turns field meetings toward the house.

note: In Natrinai 213 the man asks the girls which is the small rock-fenced village near the roaring falls, and whether the guarding of the millet is theirs too. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 the friend says their guarding of the millet is over and this village by the waterfall is their place.
teaches: The man's question and the friend's answer use the same two markers, the waterfall village and the guarding of the millet, which shows the exchange as a set dialogue of kurinji courtship in which the friend's answer comes only when the guarding has ended.

note: Akananuru 388: a young hunter with a hound comes to the millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker has passed through their field. Ainthinai Aimpathu 14: he came like those who ask after a beast, but there is something else he means to ask.
teaches: Akananuru stages the hunter's question in full while Ainthinai compresses it into a simile, 'like those who ask after a beast', which shows that the asking-after-game approach was a recognised pretext the girls themselves could name and see through.

note: Natrinai 44: the man remembers the girl after she bathed in the falls with her companions, her large eyes reddened by the beating water. Ainthinai Aimpathu 15: the friend says the girl's red-lined eyes reddened because they bathed in the leaping falls after plucking vengai.
teaches: The eyes reddened by the waterfall are a cherished sight for the lover in Natrinai and an explanation offered to others in Ainthinai, so the same bath serves both the love and its concealment, which is why it is safe for the friend to name.

note: Akananuru 308: a tusker worn from fighting a tiger, its long wound unwashed, marks the hill of a man who comes by night; the friend asks him to come by day. Ainthinai Aimpathu 16: an elephant that escaped the tiger shrinks at every footfall on the path, and the girl cannot sleep remembering that path.
teaches: In Akananuru the tiger-wounded elephant only marks the hill while the friend argues for day visits, whereas Ainthinai carries the beast's after-fear onto the path itself and into the girl's sleepless eyes, showing how the same hill emblem can move from scenery to the measure of a lover's dread.

note: Natrinai 151: even if the girl's forehead pales and her shoulders grow thin, may the hill lord not come by night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 17: because he comes without fail, the girl, afraid for him, loses her bloom and wastes away.
teaches: Natrinai offers her wasting as the lesser harm to be borne so that he stays away at night, but Ainthinai shows the night visits themselves causing the wasting through fear, so neither his coming nor his staying away spares her and only marriage can.

note: Natrinai 306: the millet is being reaped and the hill girl sent home; how will he come now to see her? Ainthinai Aimpathu 18: not even the parrots come to the millet field now; do not forget your bond with her.
teaches: Natrinai states the practical loss at harvest, no place left to meet, and Ainthinai names the risk behind it, that like the parrots he may stop coming once the field is empty, so the pair shows the end of the guarding feared as a test of his memory as well as of access.

note: In Natrinai 104 the girl asks whether anyone but her thinks of the narrow midnight path he takes while thunder strikes and floods block the way. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 19 the friend, picturing him swimming the falls at midnight, says her heart asks what will become of the girl.
teaches: The girl fears the night path for the man, and the friend fears it for the girl who would not survive his harm, so the pair shows the danger of the night meeting passing through two hearts, with the friend's fear one step removed and therefore usable as an argument for marriage.

note: In Akananuru 388 the old velan says 'my lord's seizure brought this sickness; I know the cure', and the girl mocks him. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 20 the velan, not knowing that the hill man took her nature, says a spirit has seized her and sheds the kid's blood.
teaches: Akananuru lets the velan claim knowledge of the cure and Ainthinai calls him plainly the one who does not know, so together they show the veri rite built around the diviner's ignorance, with the girl's secret as the one thing his craft cannot read.

note: Both wives turn away the bard over the husband's வாய்மொழி: Akananuru 146 pities the woman who will trust that deceiver's word as she once did; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 says the bard who asks her to trust it is hawking needles in the smiths' street.
teaches: Akananuru 146 shows the wife as a past victim of the man's word, and 21 shows why that history makes the bard's pleading absurd: she is the one market where his word cannot be sold.

note: Natrinai 200 has the friend warn the town's women against the bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 treats his pleading not as dangerous but as pointless.
teaches: The two refusals name two faults in the go-between, falsehood that endangers others and futility before the wife who already knows, so the refusal of the bard had both a public and a private argument.

note: In Akananuru 56 the wife tells the bard who blundered into her house 'இம்மனை அன்று; அஃது உம்மனை'; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 22 she tells him 'நெறிஅதுகாண் எங்கையர் இற்கு'.
teaches: The same retort appears as a told comic incident in Akananuru and as a direct taunt in the four-line venba, which shows that pointing the bard to the other house was a fixed refusal move the later poet could use bare, without the story.

note: In Kuruntokai 376 the man says his beloved is cool like Pothiyil sandal in summer and warm like a lotus heart in the cold; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 24 the wife says her shoulders were once sandal paste to him and are now hotter than caustic.
teaches: The lover's praise of a body that tempers every season is answered by the wife's claim that the same body's heat follows his conduct, not the weather, so the courtship image is shown to depend on fidelity.

note: In Kalittokai 81 the son's prattle is praised as 'நோய் நாம் தணிக்கும் மருந்து', the medicine that eases our illness; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 25 the pain of longing for the man's chest is met by the son's மழலைவாய் கட்டுரை.
teaches: Both make the child's prattle the cure for the wife's love-sickness in a marutham quarrel, and Kalittokai's longer scene shows what the venba compresses: the boy repeats words learned in the street, so his chatter can carry the father back into the house.

note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, dressed for a new wedding, stops his chariot when his son runs to him and gives the wedding up; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 26, as the drums of his new wedding sound, the little one who goes after his chariot comes to grief. On the reading of இவன் as the son, the appeal that succeeds in one fails in the other.
teaches: Akananuru 66 presents the son as the force that turns a husband back from another marriage, and 26 shows the same scene with the opposite outcome, so the son's claim emerges as a hope the wives hold rather than a rule the poems guarantee.

note: Akananuru 66: seeing the son run to him, the man cries 'நெடுந்தேர் தாங்குமதி, வலவ!' and climbs down. Ainthinai Aimpathu 28: the son stands yearning, the man sees him and drives the chariot on without a look.
teaches: Set side by side the two chariots mark the test of a straying husband as whether he stops for his child, and 28 makes the wife's hardening a verdict on his failing that test rather than on his other women.

note: Natrinai 69: if the evening came like this in the land where he went for work, he could not hold to his resolve. Ainthinai Aimpathu 3: is there not this rain in the land where our man went?
teaches: The pair shows a single argument of the waiting wife, that the season must reach him too and would bring him home, carried from evening in the long poem to the rain in the venba, where its failure becomes the sharper doubt whether the rain is in his land at all.

note: Akananuru 99: the man leading the eloping girl bids her admire a forest strewn with murukku buds like the gripping claws of the striped tiger (கோள்உகிர் அன்ன). Aimpathu 31 uses the same simile, murukku buds like a tiger's blood-dyed claws, for the spring that breaks the waiting woman's heart.
teaches: Aimpathu 31 says outright that this season gives joy only to those who are together (எதிருநர்க்கு இன்பம்), and Akananuru 99 is that joy spoken by a man walking beside his girl, so the pair shows one flowering read as delight or as wound according to whether the lovers are together.

note: Kuruntokai 37: the friend tells the heroine that the road he took is a loving one, where the tusker strips the yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger. Aimpathu 32: on his road the tusker pours the little water of a rock pool over his heat-worn mate's head.
teaches: Kuruntokai 37 states the friend's conclusion itself, that the road is loving (அன்பின), while the Aimpathu gives only the tusker's act and leaves the inference to the heroine, so the pair shows the same comfort working first as a stated argument and then as an image she must read.

note: Akananuru 369: after the daughter's elopement her parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and her doll gets no offering. Aimpathu 33: the girl herself has stopped thinking of doll, ball, parrot and playmates.
teaches: Aimpathu 33 says the girl has forgotten her toys and companions, and Akananuru 369 says those toys and companions still mourn her, so together they show the mother's grief as a forgetting that runs one way: the house keeps faith with a child who has already left it in mind.

note: Akananuru 49: the foster mother remembers seeing that the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds (கிளியும், பந்தும், கழங்கும்) was not as before, without guessing why. Aimpathu 33: the girl no longer thinks of doll, ball, parrot and playmates, and the mother asks whether she will go after her lover.
teaches: In both the neglected playthings are the sign that the girl has passed out of childhood into love, but Akananuru 49 reads the sign too late and dwells on the mother's missed chance, while the venba reads it and turns at once to the burning road, so the pair shows the same evidence serving regret or foreboding.

note: Akananuru 53: the woman says the man who loves wealth more than her crossed a waste where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the sweet shade of a lettered hero-stone (எழுத்துடை நடுகல் இன்நிழல்). Aimpathu 35: on the road of the man bent on wealth a ghoul gorged on the fat of the slain sleeps in a hero-stone's wide shade.
teaches: In both the hero-stone's shade is the only rest on the wealth-seeker's road, but Akananuru shelters a hungry pair there and the Aimpathu a sated ghoul alone, so the pair shows the stone's shade turned from a picture of shared hardship into one of the road's appetite for men, which is the woman's fear.

note: Akananuru 395: the woman says the man crossed a forest where a fork-horned stag, chasing the mirage, strays off the path and calls for its grazing doe in a failing voice. Aimpathu 36: an elephant pair takes the white mirage for water, runs to it together and falls with tangled legs.
teaches: The two poems take the same chase after a mirage to opposite ends: in Akananuru it parts the stag from its mate and gives the abandoned woman her own cry, in the Aimpathu the pair are fooled and fall together, so the image can either mirror her loneliness or shame the man who leaves when even deceived beasts do not part.

note: Akananuru 153: the foster mother says the girl who grew hot and tired even running after a ball with her friends has gone into the burning summer forest, and asks whether her tender feet can manage it (வல்லுநள் கொல்லோ). Aimpathu 37 asks the same with the same verb (வல்லவோ), recalling her faltering at play by the ford.
teaches: The verb வல் and the evidence from play recur in both, which shows the mother's doubt as a set argument of the form: she judges the girl's strength for the road only by her weakness at games, a measure that the girl's going has already overturned.

note: Akananuru 371: a twist-horned stag whose mate was shot will not drink the little water of the pool (சில்நீர் உண்ணாது) and lies stricken; the man crossing alone sees it and thinks of his love's eyes. Aimpathu 38: the stag feigns drinking the pool's little water so the doe may drink.
teaches: Held together, the two stags at a pool of scant water show the paalai poets making the stag's not drinking the sign of love both while the mate lives and after she dies, and Akananuru 371 bears out the friend's hope in 38, since there the traveller does see such a stag and his thoughts turn home.

note: Kalittokai 11: the woman recalls that the man, calling the forest cruel, told her the tusker there lets his mate drink the little muddy water first and the stag gives its own shade to the doe. Aimpathu 38: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant, feigns drinking so the doe drinks.
teaches: Kalittokai puts the beasts' care in the man's own report, so the woman reasons that one who saw and told it will not let her wither; Aimpathu 38 adds the stag's pretence, a deceit in the service of love, and sets it on the road his heart has already taken, so the same proof is offered from the friend's side and made finer.

note: Akananuru 5: the man tells his heart he gave up the journey when his wife, without a word, showed her grief in her face and her sigh over their son. Aimpathu 39: the man calls his heart foolish, for when they stir to leave for wealth she sobs and sighs; how will she bear it once they are gone?
teaches: Akananuru 5 shows the journey given up on the sight of her mute grief, and Aimpathu 39 shows the man reasoning from her sobs at the setting out to the harder grief to come, so the pair gives the decision against wealth both as what he saw and as what he foresees.

note: Akananuru 167: the man asks his heart whether, after tonight with his wife in the tall mansion, they will lie tomorrow sleepless in the ruined hall of a deserted village. Aimpathu 40: after tonight on the shoulders of her of the cool garland, where will they lie tomorrow, alone beyond the hill paths?
teaches: Akananuru 167 answers its own question with a ruined lodging described in full, while Aimpathu 40 leaves the place unnamed (என்கொலே சேக்கும் இடம்), so the pair shows the same tonight-and-tomorrow argument against the journey working either by the horror of a described shelter or by the bare want of any.

note: Akananuru 50: the hidden-tearful girl says the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted even once from its mate. Ainthinai Aimpathu 41: the anril cries though its mate has come and rests beside it.
teaches: The anril's wakefulness is a fixed proof of sleepless separation, and the venba reverses its case: the long poem argues from a parted bird by likeness, the four-line poem from a joined bird by greater reason, so the same bird can carry both the analogy and the a fortiori.

note: In Akananuru 170 the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 42 she begs the crab not to trample his chariot's tracks.
teaches: Taken together they show why the crab is the neythal heroine's confidant: it alone moves where the lover moved, so she can ask it either to carry her word to him or to spare the one trace of him she still has.

note: Natrinai 378: the bond began when the shore lord came and broke up their little striped sand-house and spoke soft words. Ainthinai Aimpathu 44: the weeping girl tells her mother that the sea came and wrecked her sand-house.
teaches: Natrinai 378 shows that the wrecked sand-house is the very scene where the secret love began, which turns the girl's excuse in Ainthinai Aimpathu 44 into a coded confession: the 'sea' that broke her play is the man of the sea.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the thief was there, and only a heron watching for aaral fish, so if he lies she has no recourse. Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go? On a plain reading one heron is no witness and the other herons are.
teaches: The same bird stands at the secret oath in both, but Kuruntokai's heron, intent on its fish, proves that a kalavu vow has no witness, while the venba's herons are made guarantors, so the pair shows the heroine's two answers to the oathless union: despair, or a trust that invents its witnesses.

note: Natrinai 283 and Ainthinai Aimpathu 46 both have the friend ask the shore lord, beside girls decking their sand-houses (with neythal flowers, with pearls), whether it is fitting (தகுமோ, தகுவதோ) that the girl's beauty should waste.
teaches: The friend's reproach has a fixed form, the girls' sand-house play set against the heroine's wasting beauty with the question 'is it fitting?', and Natrinai adds the ground the venba leaves implicit: his word was held truer than the sun, so the wasting is a breach of his truth.

note: In Akananuru 80 the friend tells the shore lord that they spend the day scaring birds from the fish their father brought, and bids him come by day; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 47 the hero sees the girl scaring birds from the fish her brothers brought and finds her a tormenting goddess.
teaches: Guarding the drying catch is the neythal girl's appointed work and so the one place she is seen by day: the friend can offer it as a meeting place, while the hero's first sight of her there already places her among the kinsmen whose catch she guards, which is why the sight brings fear.

note: In Akananuru 4 the returning man has tied his chariot's bell-tongues so as not to startle the paired birds sleeping in the flowering boughs; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 50 the waiting girl takes the noise of birds for his horses' bells.
teaches: Held together, the two poems make the chariot bell the sound by which each lover's attention is measured: the man who has come home to his wife silences it out of care for mated birds, while the girl still in secret love hears it in every bird.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine could hold firm on her friend's comfort if the hard-mouthed small flute (வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) of the unlettered herdsmen did not torment her in the evening. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7 calls the same small flute fine (சீர்சால் சிறுகுழல்) and its player glad, yet it strikes her like a spear.
teaches: One heroine blames the flute's harsh mouth and the other concedes its sweetness, so together they show the evening flute's pain moving from the instrument to the hearer, which is why the venba needs the simile of the spear.

note: Akananuru 318: the friend tells the man who comes alone at night by a path made fearful by elephants, snakes and tigers not to come from today, and to blow his horn on reaching home so they know he is safe. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 10: the girl asks her friend to tell the lord of the snake-haunted groves not to come by night, to keep a life safe.
teaches: The long poem spells out what the four lines only hint, that refusing the night meeting is an act of care for the man's life on a dangerous path, and the venba moves the plea into the girl's own wish (குறையொன்று உடையேன்), showing the same refusal felt from inside.

note: Akananuru 242: the mother, not knowing of the man who chased parrots from the millet with them, calls the ignorant velan, and before the kid's life is given he should come and embrace the girl. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 12: parrots raid the millet, the girl has embraced him fully, and the velan has resolved to cut the kid.
teaches: Both set the embrace against the kid's sacrifice, but the older poem makes the embrace the remedy that must come before the rite, while the venba gives both as done, which leaves the velan preparing a useless sacrifice for a cure already taken.

note: Natrinai 57: while the herd of wild cows sleeps with their calves, a female monkey creeps up, squeezes the swollen udder and wrings the milk into her young one's hands. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 3: the monkey strokes the udder and the wild cow, glad as with her calf, lets the milk flow.
teaches: Held together they show one scene turned from theft to gift: the older poem's monkey steals while the cows sleep, fitting a friend who warns of the girl's ruin, while the later venba makes the cow consent, fitting a girl who says she cannot part, so the speaker's case decides whether the milk is stolen or given.

note: Both mothers lament a daughter gone with a man through the bowmen's wasteland; Akananuru 35 prays to the god that the stranger may adorn her and lull her on his chest, while Ainthinai Ezhupathu 30 can only wonder whether the girl pines or walks on behind him with reddened feet.
teaches: Together they give the mother's lament two stages, first not knowing whether the girl regrets her going and then accepting it and praying for the man's care, so the venba catches the moment the Akananuru poem has already passed.

note: In Akananuru 91 the elephant that shrinks with its hungry mate in drought lets the friend reassure the heroine after the man has gone; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 31 the elephant sleeping with its mate in the burning forest comes when the man only speaks of going, and her tears answer it.
teaches: The same iraicchi of the elephant pair keeping together in the heat serves to comfort after the parting and to dissuade before it, which shows the image carries the lovers' bond itself and the speaker turns it to whatever the moment needs.

note: Akananuru 53: past the lettered hero-stone of men felled by the archers' fine arrows, the heroine says his love is for wealth more than for her (பொருளே காதலர் காதல்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 32 keeps the lettered stones, the archers' fine arrows and the claim that his love's longing has become hard-won wealth.
teaches: The venba compresses Akananuru 53's scene and accusation into four lines but drops the friend's defence that he goes from a giving heart, putting his 'fitting labour' in its place, so the later poem shows which part of the older argument had become formula and which part it chose to change.

note: Akananuru 35's road is held by bowmen of வில் ஏர் வாழ்க்கை, 'the life whose plough is the bow', and their cairns; Ainthinai Ezhupathu 33's road by வில்லுழுது உண்பார், 'those who eat by ploughing with the bow', among the cairns.
teaches: Held together they show the bow-as-plough figure for the wasteland robbers passing intact from the Sangam anthology into the later venba, while its use shifts from a mother's fear for a daughter on the road to a wife's reproach that the man can see the road's dangers but not her.

note: In Akananuru 297 the man on his way for wealth sees a wildcat's fluffy kitten following its mother like stars round the moon; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 40 the heroine hears that on his road the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
teaches: Each lover sees the wildcat with its young on the wealth road from his or her own side, the man as the household he leaves behind and the woman as the provision he goes to win, so the creature gathers both halves of the paalai argument about leaving for wealth.

note: In Akananuru 289 the man on his journey imagines her praying 'speak good' each time the lizard chirps; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 42 the lizard chirps at the favourable side, together with a throbbing eye and good dreams.
teaches: The man's imagined picture of her waiting on the lizard and her own report that the lizard has spoken well are the two ends of one practice, which shows that the omen was a shared language the separated lovers each expected the other to be reading.

note: In Kalittokai 85 the mother shares out her milk in mockery to the 'other mothers' who wept after trusting the father's deceiving oath (மாயச் சூள்); in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 44 a woman says she believed his words long ago, not knowing them for a false oath (பொய்ச்சூள்).
teaches: Read together, the false oath is the wound the wife shares with her rivals: Kalittokai's mother pities the other women it deceived, and the venba's speaker finds herself among them, so the oath binds all the man's women in one injury.

note: Kalittokai 79: the wife tells the husband not to take up their son, whose hands will pull the pearl chain and garland by which the other women marked him (அணி சிதைப்பான்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 45: he comes with the son on his chest, the boy's pearl ornaments crushing his frontlet (பட்டஞ் சிதைப்ப).
teaches: Kalittokai spells out what the four-line poem only shows: the son's hands spoiling the father's finery are spoiling the other women's tokens, so the venba's ironic 'he is resourceful' means the child he brings as a shield is also the one who exposes him.

note: Natrinai 380: refusing the bard, the friend says they smell of ghee, smoke and new birth, holding the son with milk at the breast, and are no match for the man of the bright-jewelled women's street. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife says the son is suckled and she is old, and sends the bard to the street of the budding-breasted women.
teaches: The pair shows that the nursing mother's body is a set argument in refusing the go-between: the friend in Natrinai offers it as humble unfitness, the wife in the venba turns it into scorn by sending the bard to dance for his food, so the same motherhood can be pleaded as modesty or thrown as contempt.

note: Akananuru 46: the friend refusing the husband entry describes his town's red-eyed buffalo breaking its tether in the night, scattering fish and grazing the lotus. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its wooden clog, eats the field crop and rests in the shade, and the bard is told to carry this to the flower-like women.
teaches: The same hidden comparison is aimed at different hearers: in Akananuru 46 it shames the husband at the door, in the venba it is sent through the bard to the other women as a warning, which shows the buffalo ullurai was a portable accusation that could be addressed to either party of the triangle.

note: Natrinai 330: the male buffalo plunges into the pond and rests from the day's labour in the sweet shade of the marutham (இன் நிழல் வதியும்), and the friend blames the courtesans' mean hearts. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the buffalo breaks its clog, eats the crop and then rests in the shade (நிழல்வதியும்).
teaches: The resting buffalo is innocent after labour in Natrinai and guilty after plunder in the venba, and the blame follows suit, falling on the courtesans in one and on the husband in the other, so what the beast did before the shade decides whom the poem accuses.

note: Kalittokai 85 says the father uses the lying bard as a fishhook to bind the hearts of the women he wants. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 tells the bard to go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women.
teaches: Kalittokai names the bard as the husband's lure for other women, which explains the venba's order to keep going to that street: the wife is sending the go-between back to his real work, so refusing the bard and accusing him are one act.

note: Akananuru 66: the husband, dressed to wed another, is drawn home by the little son who runs to his chariot, and the wife says the old saying about sons has proved true. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: the wife sends the bard away, saying her little son with gold bangles is her companion.
teaches: The son works on both sides of the marutham quarrel: in Akananuru 66 he pulls the straying father back into the house, in the venba the wife holds him up as companion enough to refuse the father's go-between, so the child is at once the husband's way in and the wife's reason to keep him out.

note: Akananuru 146: refusing the bard, the wife asks who the woman will be who now trusts the deceiving philanderer and will weep and pale as she did. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 55: the wife tells the other women directly not to embrace him to love's end or pine for him, but to give up their longing.
teaches: Akananuru 146 only pities the next woman from a distance, while the venba turns to the rivals and counsels them, so together they show the wife's grievance passing into a warning to the women who will suffer as she did.

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the husband not to embrace her body that bore their son, since it would spoil his chest. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 56: with the son trampling him, he praises her slackened breast, though he presses the budding breasts of a girl elsewhere.
teaches: In both the body that bore the son is the ground of the wife's sulking: in Ainkurunuru she withholds it as unfit for his groomed chest, in the venba she sees his praise of it as a cover for his taste for younger bodies, so the mother's body is what she bars him from and what he flatters to come back.

note: Natrinai 335: the sea's sound never stops and the tide comes and goes, and with the anril and the lute the night cannot be survived. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 60: the sea, like her, does not sleep as the tide shifts, because the shore lord took her beauty and left.
teaches: In the Natrinai the restless sea is one of the things that keep the heroine awake, while the venba makes the same tide sleepless for her own reason, so the pair shows the neythal sea turning from a cause of sleeplessness into a fellow sufferer.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief, only a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him go and turn graceless?
teaches: Kuruntokai's heron proves that the secret union had no witness worth the name, and the venba goes one step on, upbraiding that same silent witness for not knowing what it saw, so the heron of kalavu moves from absent proof to complicit bystander.

note: Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the shore lord to go if he must, but first give back the beauty he consumed (நீ உண்டவென் னலனே). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 63: the heroine would accost him herself and say 'give back the colour' (வண்ணந்தா).
teaches: The demand to give back consumed beauty belongs to the friend in Kuruntokai, but the venba puts it in the heroine's own mouth and doubts that only looking at him would suffice, so the pair shows the reproach moving from the go-between to the injured woman herself.

note: Akananuru 170: since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak, the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, at midnight when the sea-crow dreams beside its mate. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 65: she bids the anril, joined with its mate, to tell him 'give back the colour'.
teaches: The long poem shows why a creature is her messenger, since the land itself is mute, while the venba chooses a messenger whose own paired life is the reproach, so together they show the creature-messenger used first for its reach and then for its example.

note: Akananuru 380: the shore lord, wooing, showed the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate in its burrow and said 'this is a fine way'. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 68: the friend tells the shore lord of the crab with its mate on the dune, and that her friend has paled.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hero himself offers the crab that cares for its mate as a sign of how he will behave, and in the venba the friend returns the same crab to him as a reproach while the girl pales, so the pair shows a courting pledge turned into the evidence against the man who gave it.

note: Both have the hill lord of the vengai coming at midnight with spear in hand; Kainnilai 10 is the girl's eager forecast, Akananuru 298 her words when he has come, sweet yet unable to speak her love for fear of the mother.
teaches: Read together the two give the before and after of the night tryst: the quatrain's sleepless certainty that he will come turns, once he is there, into fear of the household and a plea for marriage, so the midnight visit is never the end the girl longs for.

note: Akananuru 351: the returning man imagines the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him sounding at her ear as medicine for her aching shoulders. Kainnilai 18: the friend tells her the truthful lizard has chirped, seeing the traveller come.
teaches: The man in the Akananuru counts on the lizard to announce him and the friend in the Kainnilai reports that it has, so the pair gives both halves of one belief, that the traveller's approach reaches home through the lizard before he does.

note: Akananuru 387: on the road, a lizard's small click by the hero-stones makes even lords with elephants halt and turn back. Kainnilai 18: at home, the truthful lizard chirps as if it has seen the traveller's return.
teaches: Held together they show that the lizard's voice was trusted at both ends of the journey with opposite force, as a warning that turns travellers back on the road and as a promise of return to those at home, so the omen's sense depended on which way the hearer faced.

note: Akananuru 29: the returned man tells his wife that only his body stayed in the burning waste for the work, while his foolish heart was with her. Kainnilai 22: the friend asks whether she thinks the heart of the man who crossed the robber forest has parted from her.
teaches: The friend's question in the Kainnilai presumes exactly what the man asserts on his return in the Akananuru, that the body went and the heart stayed, so the pair shows the body-heart split was a shared assurance used by the comforter before and by the man after the journey.

note: Natrinai 84: the woman reports that he will go (they say) by the hard waste where the mirage lures the deer, and excuses him as one who cannot live a home life unable to relieve beggars. Kainnilai 24: the woman reports that the hard waste where the deer runs after the mirage is, they say, the road of the loveless one.
teaches: The same reported road with the same mirage-chasing deer ends in opposite verdicts on the man, a duty that excuses him in the Natrinai and a want of love that condemns him in the Kainnilai, so the landscape fixed the scene while the poet chose the moral.

note: Akananuru 23: in the rains the stag embraces his doe (பிணை ... தழீஇ), and the woman asks if this is the time her man meant. Kainnilai 29: kurunthu blooms, the stag embraces his doe and the rain-cloud thunders; the rest is lost.
teaches: The Akananuru poem shows the stag's embrace being weighed as the promised season's clock, which tells a reader of the broken Kainnilai verse what such an embrace was there to measure, even though its own ending is gone.

note: Both set a hill creature that has handled ripe fruit against snares; in Kuruntokai the hunter sets nets on every tree after the fruit is already touched, in Kainnilai the monkey tastes the fruit and is caught.
teaches: The same fruit-and-snare economy of the hill serves two speakers opposite ways: the friend uses the late snares to tell the man the girl is now guarded too late, while the girl uses the caught monkey to say she herself is the one bound by the sweetness she tasted.

note: Akananuru 14: the wife asks what will become of them by morning if he does not remember even in the evening when the cattle crowd into the common (மன்றுநிறை புகுதரும் மாலையும்). Kainnilai 30: the hour when the cowherds with konrai pipes enter the common (மன்றம் புகுதரும் போழ்து).
teaches: The Akananuru wife names the homecoming to the common as the hour by which a man who remembers would be back, which explains why the Kainnilai poet could mark the waiting by that hour alone: the village's return is the measure of his not returning.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could bear the friend's comfort but for the harsh small pipe the unlettered cowherds blow (கல்லாக் கோவலர் ஊதும் வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) at evening. Kainnilai 35: the herders who do not know (தெரிவிலர்) blow the sweet pipe (தீங்குழல்).
teaches: Both poets excuse the herders by their ignorance, but one calls the pipe harsh and the other sweet, which shows that the cruelty is not in the sound itself but in the hour and the ear that hears it.

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man his bard is a bigger liar than he is and swears many oaths. Kainnilai 37: the wife tells the bard to stop pouring out lies before her.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's, and Kainnilai 37 lets her silence the bard directly while the man is only named, so together they show the wife's anger moving onto the go-between as the safer target.

note: Natrinai 250: the man tells the bard how, coming near to hug his toddling son, his wife took it otherwise and shied away. Kainnilai 39: the wife says he comes bringing the garlanded son, pointing to him, to torment her. On the man's telling the son is a real tenderness she misreads; on hers it is a tactic.
teaches: Read together the two poems give both sides of the same approach through the child, the husband insisting his affection was misjudged and the wife calling it harassment, so neither poem's account can be taken as the plain fact of the scene.

note: Kuruntokai 42's friend asks the hero whether their bond will wane even if desire ends; Kainnilai 4's friend asks the girl whether he is one to join and then forget.
teaches: The one doubt about the man's constancy is put by the friend as a challenge to him in Kuruntokai and as a comfort to the girl in Kainnilai, so the pair shows the friend's double office of pressing the hero and calming the heroine with the same question.

note: Kalittokai 81: the wife asks the toddling son to repeat the words the 'mothers' of the big street taught him, and the husband blames the bard. Kainnilai 41: she knows his doings, having the sweet babbling son as her own.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 shows a son's prattle betraying where his father has taken him, which supports reading Kainnilai 41's 'we know' as knowledge gained from the boy's babble rather than only as a mother's comfort.

note: Kuruntokai 127: because the man's one bard proved a liar, every bard looks like a thief to the women he left. Kainnilai 47: the wife calls the bard a liar (பொய்ப் பாண) and bars him from her house.
teaches: Kuruntokai 127 states the general effect of one lying go-between and Kainnilai 47 shows its consequence in a single house, the door shut to the bard himself, so the pair shows distrust of the messenger hardening into exclusion.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying our breasts ooze milk, we smell of new birth and are no match for the man of the jewelled women's street. Kainnilai 48: the man does not embrace the sandal-cool breasts; we have grown old with sagging breasts; come for no answer.
teaches: Natrinai 380 makes motherhood the wife's disqualification and Kainnilai 48 makes age, so the pair shows the wife's body at two stages of marriage offered in the same mocking way as the reason the man has gone elsewhere.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief and a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her, so what can she do if he lies. Kainnilai 50: she will tell neither him nor the anril, only the stork of the grove that saw his hard oath.
teaches: The heron that in Kuruntokai only proves how alone the heroine was becomes, in the venba, the one hearer she trusts with the broken oath, so the bird witness of kalavu moves from a sign of her helplessness to the only court left to her.

note: Natrinai 167: the friend refuses the bard who came with the shore lord's message (துறைவன் தூதொடும் வந்த ... பணி மொழி). Kainnilai 51 uses the same words for a bird (தூதொடு வந்த பணிமொழிப் புள்ளே) and tells it to fly off.
teaches: The formula that names the bard refused at the door is given in the venba to a bird, showing the short form compressing the social scene of வாயில் மறுத்தல் into a creature of the shore while keeping the old wording.

note: Akananuru 20: the friend, with the man listening unseen, says that on the town women's talk of a chariot on the dunes the mother has forbidden their shore play (அன்னை கடிகொண்டனளே). Kainnilai 52: the mother has kept the girl in (அன்னையும் இல்கடிந்தாள்), and the speaker asks whether to tell the man of the blame.
teaches: The long poem lets the man overhear the mother's ban, while the venba weighs telling him outright, so the pair shows the ban as the friend's lever for marriage, worked by indirection in one and nearly by open message in the other.

note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

note: Akananuru 20: the friend recalls chasing birds from her father's drying fish (எந்தை தந்த கொழுமீன் உணங்கல் படுபுள் ஓப்பி) among the shore pastimes now forbidden. Kainnilai 56: while driving the birds from the fish her kin brought (எமர் தந்த ... வன்மீன் கவரும்புள் ஓப்பின்), the shore lord took her beauty.
teaches: The same chore, keeping birds off the family's catch, is innocent play in the Akananuru list and the very hour of the theft in the venba, which explains why the mother's ban in the long poem falls on just those shore tasks.

note: Akananuru 315: the mother who saw the girl grow and suspected, yet did not shut her in (செறியேன்), mourns her elopement. Kainnilai 59: the mother, seeing the young man come through the gap, at once blocks it and shuts the door.
teaches: The confinement one mother blames herself for omitting is done at first sight by the other, and the friend reports it as the pressure that forces marriage, so the pair shows the mother's guard as the hinge between the two endings of kalavu, marriage and flight.

note: Natrinai 138: the lord of the cool ford where the white heron lays its eggs (வெண் குருகு ஈனும் தண்ணம் துறைவன்) is now known to the old town. Kainnilai 59: the lord of the cool ford where the heron lays its eggs in the thaazhai (குருகுஈனும் தண்ணந் துறைவனை) is now known to the mother, who shuts the door.
teaches: The epithet of the nesting heron frames in both poems the moment the secret becomes known, to the town in one and the mother in the other, which supports reading the breeding heron as a call for the man to set up house now that kalavu is over.

note: Ainkurunuru 200: the lord of the golden chariot has come, her bangles fit again and they can laugh at the pallor. Kainnilai 60: her golden pallor is gone, for here is the chariot of the man who saw the backs of fleeing kings, nearing Koodal.
teaches: Both mark the end of pallor by the chariot's arrival, but the venba arms the returning lover with a victor's epithet and the Pandya's Korkai and Koodal, showing a late akam poem borrowing puram glory to make homecoming a triumph.

note: Kalavazhi 36 sings the day the Kaveri lord took Kalumalam (கழுமலங் கொண்டநாள்), the enemy umbrellas overturned like mushrooms; Akananuru 44, a hero hurrying home after his king's war, names the Chola Senni who took Kalumalam and captured Kanaiyan (கணையன் அகப்படக் கழுமலம் தந்த) and likens the heroine to that king's rich town Kudavayil.
teaches: Kalavazhi leaves the loser at Kalumalam unnamed and shows only the carnage, while the akam poet names the captive Kanaiyan and spends the victory as a mark of the Chola's prosperity, so together they show one battle remembered both as a field of dead and as a byword for a well-kept land.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend tells the heroine not to weep, since the rain now spreading is the season he named when he assured them 'வருதும் யாம்'. Kar Narpathu 1 quotes the same promise, வருதும், and asks 'will he not come?'
teaches: The promise is the same word in both, which shows the friend's argument as a fixed form, quote his 'we shall come' and point to the rain, with the older poem supplying the peacock calling its mate as the proof the four-line verse leaves out.

note: Akananuru 134: the returning hero tells the charioteer that if she hears the sound of the swift-horsed chariot (கடுமான் தேர்ஒலி) there may be union at midnight. Kar Narpathu 10: the friend hears the swift-horsed chariot coming like a forest stream and says the heroine will bloom.
teaches: The chariot's sound is the hinge of the reunion from both sides: the hero hopes she will hear it and the friend reports that it is heard and what it does to the heroine's body, in the same phrase கடுமான் தேர்.

note: Both liken the opening kodal cluster to a snake's raised hood in the rain-fed woodland; in Akananuru 154 the returning man sees it from the chariot, in Kar Narpathu 11 the friend points to it as the sign of his quick return.
teaches: The same flower-image is seen by the man on the road home and offered by the friend at home as a promise, so the shared stock of mullai images lets the two halves of a separation read the same sign in the same season.

note: Akananuru 9 ends with the returning man asking whether his heart, which went ahead longing for her soft shoulders, has reached her; Kar Narpathu 19 has the man say his heart has gone the long road wanting her as companion.
teaches: Both returning heroes speak of a heart that outruns the chariot, so the figure belongs to the set speech of return; the long poem follows the heart into the house and to her touch, while the venba stops at its setting out.

note: Akananuru 44: the king has finished his work, the enemy has paid tribute, and the man bids the charioteer drive ahead to sleep on his wife's breast. Kar Narpathu 20: the glorious king's work is done, the roads are pleasant, and the rain moves like an army.
teaches: Both make the king's finished war the condition of the husband's return, and the pair shows the venba compressing the long poem's catalogue of kings and battles into one simile in which the rain-cloud marches like the armies he leaves.
