note: Kuruntokai 240: the waiting woman sees mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth (வெருக்குப்பல் லுருவின் முல்லை) crowding the bush as the north wind comes and his hill sinks at evening. Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the mullai buds pointed like the teeth of his girl.
teaches: The same bud-and-teeth simile becomes a predator's teeth for the waiting woman and the beloved's teeth for the returning man, so the mullai bud's meaning in these poems is set by which side of the separation is looking, not by the flower.

note: Akananuru 47: if we have finished the work here, rise quickly, heart (வினைஇவண் முடித்தனம் ஆயின்). Kar Narpathu 24: rise, heart, leaving all the work lying (எல்லா வினையுங் கிடப்ப). On a plain reading they disagree on whether the task must be done before he turns home.
teaches: The older poem holds the man's return behind the finishing of his task, while the venba's man drops the task once the rain and the memory of her hair reach him, so the same address to the heart sets duty and love in two different orders.

note: Both see the thonri open like a lamp in the rains: in Akananuru 235 (சுடர்கொள் அகலின்) the heroine asks whether he has forgotten them; in Kar Narpathu 26 (கார்த்திகை ... விளக்கிற்) the friend says the rain has come with his message.
teaches: The lamp-like thonri is evidence that he has forgotten for the heroine and evidence that he has sent word for the friend, so the one sign of the promised season can be read against him or for him depending on who speaks.

note: Ainkurunuru 447: may the king's work be released, and then we shall see her bright brow, when the bee opens the red thalavu bud shaped like a kingfisher's beak (சிரல்வாய்ச் செம்முகை). Kar Narpathu 36: the man returning from the work sees the thalavam buds, lovely as kingfishers' beaks (சிரல்வாய் வனப்பின), opened in rows.
teaches: The same thalavu bud is the hour hoped for in the man's prayer while the king's work holds him and the sight on the road once he is released, so read together the bud marks the two ends of a single wait.

note: Kar Narpathu 37: will our man, who took up the king's hard work, not come even in the season of great rains? Akananuru 304: in the king's war camp as the first rains fall, the man fears she will think him unkind, not knowing his pain.
teaches: The friend's confidence rests on the season alone, and the Akananuru shows that season from inside the king's camp, where the man is still held and can only dread her reproach, so the king's work she counts to his credit is the very thing keeping him away.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend says the cool rains, when the elephant feeds his young mate and calf with bamboo shoots, are the season he promised, so do not weep. Kar Narpathu 38: the bull elephant plays with his mate in the cool season, yet he has not come, and the colophon says the friend tells her he lied.
teaches: The elephant pair in the rains is the friend's proof of his promise in one poem and her proof of his breach in the other, so the creatures' act carries the same sense in both while the verdict on the man turns on whether he has come.

note: Natrinai 267: crabs of the sand dune with eyes like the nochchi's dark buds (நொச்சி மா அரும்பு அன்ன கண்ண). Kar Narpathu 39: nochchi buds opened like crabs' eyes (அலவன்க ணேய்ப்ப).
teaches: The simile runs in opposite directions: the neythal poem makes its shore crab the subject and borrows the nochchi as image, while the mullai venba makes its nochchi the subject and borrows the crab, so each poet takes the tenor from the poem's own land.

note: Both carry the same thurai, the friend showing the season to reassure the heroine, with the konrai in bloom; Akananuru 4 ends with his chariot in sight, Kar Narpathu 4 with the season as medicine for her pallor.
teaches: Set together they give two endings to one speech: the long poem can produce the man himself on the horizon, while the four-line venba has to stop at the season and so makes the season itself the cure.

note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

note: Kuruntokai 148: if you say this is not the rainy season (காரன்று என்றி), is this a dream? Thinaimalai 103: you say the season has not come (பருவந்தான் பட்டின்றே என்றி); with tears I have cooked my life for it.
teaches: Both women quote the friend's denial of the season with the same என்றி, but the Kuruntokai woman answers with the evidence of the flowers and the Thinaimalai woman with the cost to her life, so the reply moves from disputing the fact to declaring the dispute too late.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain is unseasonable (வம்பு); if this were the true season, would he not come? Thinaimalai 103: to the friend who says the rain is unripe and the season not yet come, the woman says she has already wasted her life in tears.
teaches: Kuruntokai gives the friend's consolation in full and lets it stand, and the Thinaimalai venba shows it being received and failing, so the pair shows the stock argument of the false season from both the side that offers it and the side it does not reach.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend says the konrai are foolish (மடவ) to take the stray rain for the season and bloom. Thinaimalai 104: the woman says the konrai, blooming at the cloud's word, has killed her (கொன்றாய்).
teaches: On the friend's reading the konrai's early flowering is a harmless mistake that proves nothing, and on the woman's it is a killing, so the same tree judged foolish in the consolation is judged guilty by the one it was meant to console.

note: Kuruntokai 290: do those who tell me to bear my love not know what it is, or are they so strong? Thinaimalai 106: who are they who tell the parted to bear it? They are so only for themselves, for the bees already sing in the mullai.
teaches: Kuruntokai answers the counsel to endure by doubting the counsellors' knowledge, while the venba adds the season's evidence against it, the bees already singing in joy, so the refusal to bear up gains in the later poem a reason drawn from the landscape.

note: Kuruntokai 183: the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck in the poor forest. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal fears the budding kaayaa as a flock of peacocks.
teaches: The kaayaa-peacock likeness that Kuruntokai offers as the poet's own comparison is in Thinaimalai mistaken by a flower in the scene, so the later poet makes a stock simile into an error committed inside the landscape.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend sees the golden konrai and the rumbling sky and says this is the season he named, so he will come; in 109 the heroine sees the same konrai under the sea-fed clouds and says he will not appear.
teaches: The same golden konrai is read as proof of return by the friend and as proof of desertion by the heroine, which shows that the flower settles nothing by itself: it only fixes the day by which his failure becomes certain.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage with bamboo flute, waterfall drum, bee lute and peacock dancer, ending in the heroine alone with tear-filled eyes; 111 rebuilds the stage in the rain-forest with the glory lily's hands, the sky's call and the bee lute.
teaches: Moved from the kurinji hill to the mullai forest, the nature-theatre keeps its function of tormenting the lone woman but changes its occasion, from the lover seen by many in secret love to the season of a husband's promised return.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the konrai is foolish, blooming on a stray rain before the season he named; 114: the kurundham blooms before the clouds have even shed their drops, and the heroine says it has fixed the season and decreed her grief.
teaches: The premature bloom that the Kuruntokai friend waves away as a plant's mistake is, to the heroine of 114, a verdict, which shows that the consolation of untimely rain only works on someone who does not take the flower as the sign itself.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain that opened the mullai is untimely, for if this were the season he would have come; 118: the heroine says the forest has kept its season and rejects the friend's 'it is not the season'.
teaches: The Kuruntokai gives the friend's argument from his absence to the season's falseness, and 118 gives the heroine's refusal of it from the forest's evidence, so read together they show the untimely-rain consolation as one move in a dispute the heroine could win.

note: In Akananuru 388 the girl, in private, mocks the diviner whose god is said to have caused her sickness; in Thinaimalai 12 the friend tells the household to send the velan away, free the kid and recognise the man who saved her from the flood.
teaches: The long poem stops at the girl's private scorn for the rite, and the short one shows the next move, so the pair shows mockery of the velan turning into the friend's disclosure to the family, where dismissing the diviner and naming the rescuer are one act.

note: Ainkurunuru 66: the wife asks who the woman is who snatched away his coming home to his rich house when he was thinking of his toddling son with his little chariot (தேரொடு தளர்நடைப் புதல்வனை). Thinaimalai 124: before the boy appears drawing his toy chariot this way, the man has already bathed and embraced her 'sisters'.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 66 grants that the toddler with his chariot did pull the father toward home and blames a rival for stopping him, while the venba times the man's straying 'before the boy appears' and so denies the child ever had that pull, which shows the toy-chariot son working as the conventional test of a straying father's heart, passed in one poem and failed in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man of the rich town that his bard is a greater liar than he and swears many oaths (பாணன் பொய்யன் பல்சூ ளினனே). Thinaimalai 131: she tells the bard, whose lute is bent like a prawn, not to fashion words of reconciliation, since she has heard the man's lies (ஊரன்பொய்).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's in a single comparison, while Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal from the day she heard the man's own lie and so sets the bard's words aside as useless rather than worse, which shows the go-between's credit in marutham falling with his master's and not on its own.

note: Kalittokai 81: the boy moves his toy chariot by hand in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க), the father is caught coming from another woman, and the wife ends by going to the boy like a cow to the place where its calf is tied (கன்று யாத்த உழிச் செல்லும் ஆ போல்). Thinaimalai 138: in this boy's father's town the buffalo's milk runs as she thinks of her calf.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 gives the cow's pull to its calf to the mother as an open simile, while Thinaimalai 138 leaves the same yearning beast unglossed in the father's own fields, so the pair shows how the marutham poets could turn one image of parental pull from praise of the mother into a silent reproach of the father.

note: Ainkurunuru 403: watching the boy, who bears his grandfather's name, pull his little chariot with tottering steps, the man's heart grows great toward the son as well as the wife. Thinaimalai 139: the wife names the field town only as the town of the father of the boy whose chariot does not run (ஊராத்தேரான் தந்தை). On the reading that 139 speaks during the man's absence, the two claim opposite effects for the same sight.
teaches: In the mullai poem the son's toy chariot binds the father to the house, while the marutham wife uses the same child to name a man who is not there, so the pair shows the son as the household's strongest tie and, when that tie fails, the wife's way of addressing the father without speaking to him.

note: Natrinai 250: the man, come home with his son, tells the bard how his wife, seeing him approach, shrank away like a startled doe asking 'who are you?'. Thinaimalai 145: amid songs, tunes and horns he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
teaches: The Thinaimalai gives the son-bearing return from outside, as a procession fit for Indra, and the Natrinai gives it from the man's side, where the same entry ends in his wife's recoil, so together they show that the son as passport was a public spectacle whose private outcome the poets left open.

note: Akananuru 46: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its tether, raids the pond, scatters the fish and eats the lotus, and the friend says he has brought another woman home. Thinaimalai 147: the red-eyed black-horned buffalo plunges into the field pond and comes back crowned with lilies and kayal fish and carrying frogs.
teaches: The Akananuru states the situation the raiding buffalo stands for, while the Thinaimalai keeps only the image and adds the buffalo coming home dressed in the pond's spoils, which shows the image had become a sign of the straying husband that a later poet could leave unexplained and even play for comedy.

note: Ainkurunuru 95: the black-horned buffalo snaps its rope and grazes the long-eared paddy all morning; its lord gives her pain even by day. Thinaimalai 148: the dark-horned buffalo grazes the great field pond, then lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing paddy straw.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's straying buffalo is left grazing, as the husband is left away, while the Thinaimalai brings the same animal home and gives the calf as the reason, so the pairing shows the marutham buffalo could carry the wife's hope as well as her complaint: the child that draws the stray back.

note: In Natrinai 300 a suitor sets a great chariot at the gate as the price of the girl's bangles (சிறு வளை விலை); in Thinaimalai 15 the friend says no price, not the sea-girt world, could buy the girl, and she must be given to the elders who come for her.
teaches: Natrinai shows a bride price actually offered, and Thinaimalai answers the practice: by declaring her beyond any price the friend moves the marriage from purchase to gift, so the only claim the household should honour is the formal coming of the suitor's elders.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying they are soiled with ghee and smoke and smell of the new-born son, no match for the decked women of his master's street. Thinaimalai 151: the wife tells the bard her son plays in the dust before this house, not as other women's do, and his master may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
teaches: Both refuse the bard by setting the soiled household against the decked rivals, but the Natrinai turns the grime on the women of the house as mock unfitness, while the Thinaimalai turns it on the son and calls the rivals 'our younger sisters', so the same refusal could be humble or proud depending on whom the dirt is laid on.

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the lord not to embrace her body that has borne a son, since it would spoil his chest. Thinaimalai 152: do not embrace me; our son's wet mouth would wipe off the marks of breasts, jewels and leaf-paint on your chest, and my milk would spoil your garland.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's mother refuses the embrace by pretending to protect his chest from her post-partum body; the Thinaimalai keeps that pretext and names what is on the chest, another woman's marks, so the pairing shows the old formula of 'spoiling' was an accusation waiting to be made explicit.

note: Akananuru 26: the wife recalls that lately her husband held back from embracing her for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son. Thinaimalai 152: the wife herself refuses his embrace, saying her milk would spoil his garland.
teaches: In the Akananuru it is the husband who fears the milk and the wife who is hurt by his caution; in the Thinaimalai the wife takes up the same fear as her weapon, so together they show the nursing mother's milk standing on either side of the quarrel, as his excuse or as her refusal.

note: Thinaimalai 18 fears that the harvested millet ends the bond; in Akananuru 132 the millet ears are already cut and the friend tells the man to take the girl away.
teaches: Thinaimalai 18 stops at the fear that the stubble field ends the meetings, and Akananuru 132 shows what the friend does with that fear, turning it into a demand to take the girl away, so the harvest is the point at which kalavu must become marriage or flight.

note: Natrinai 13 likens the girl's red-lined eyes to the arrows millet-watchers pull out of a felled beast; Thinaimalai 22 has her eyes as two arrows that have felled the man.
teaches: The friend of Natrinai 13 gives the eyes the hunters' bloodied arrows, and the man of Thinaimalai 22 draws the consequence that he is the beast they brought down, so the two poems together show the eye-as-arrow belonging to a hunting household's daily kill.

note: In both the fallen vengai flowers look like a tiger: in Akananuru 228 a she-elephant bolts from them on the man's moonlit way home, in Thinaimalai 26 the girl will not survive his night visit.
teaches: Akananuru 228 shows the vengai's false tiger frightening a beast on the path, and Thinaimalai 26 transfers that fright to the waiting girl, which shows that the friend's case against the night visit rests on fear of a likeness rather than on any real tiger.

note: Akananuru 92 forbids the night and promises the man a day meeting by a cool fall where red glory lilies open; Thinaimalai 29 describes such a place by a forest stream in a glory-lily thicket.
teaches: Akananuru 92 gives the day tryst as the friend's offer in exchange for the dangerous night, and Thinaimalai 29 gives only the place, which shows the daytime meeting ground was a fixed set (stream, glory lilies, low shade) a four-line verse could call up without the bargain around it.

note: Akananuru 80 forbids the night swim and offers a day meeting in the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 35 forbids the night and warns that a day visit brings gossip.
teaches: Set beside Akananuru 80, where the day meeting is the friend's remedy for the night's danger, Thinaimalai 35 shows a later stage in which the day too is closed by gossip, so that the only road left is marriage.

note: Both use a shore bird that takes something else for a heron's chick: in Ainkurunuru 151 a stork treads a neythal flower going to see it; in Thinaimalai 36 a heron feeds a screwpine bud and shades it with its wings.
teaches: The same mistake of a bird taking a flower for a chick can carry opposite senses: in Ainkurunuru the error bruises the flower, which still gives off scent, like the heroine who stays tender to the man who hurt her, while in Thinaimalai it becomes devoted care held up to shame a man whose visits do not stay.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the man was there, only a heron watching for fish, on the day he took her; Thinaimalai 37: the tide knew it that day (ஓதநீர் அன்றறியும்), so marry her before the common square.
teaches: Kuruntokai's girl fears that a union witnessed only by a shore creature leaves her helpless if he lies, and Thinaimalai's friend answers that fear: a witness that cannot speak is why the union must be made public in the square.

note: Kuruntokai 163 asks the sea who has afflicted it (யாரணங் குற்றனை) since she hears it even at midnight; Thinaimalai 38 asks the sleepless sea who did this to it, 'like me'.
teaches: Kuruntokai leaves the girl's own state unsaid behind her question to the sea, while Thinaimalai 38 names it, the breast of the shore lord and a sleeplessness 'like mine', so the pair shows the later poet making explicit the projection the older poem left to the hearer.

note: In Akananuru 380 the man shows the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate and says 'this is a fine way'; in Thinaimalai 40 the girl watches a crab playing with its mate after the man has left.
teaches: The crab with its mate is the shore lover's own emblem of devotion, used by the man in Akananuru 380 to court the girl; Thinaimalai 40 shows the emblem turned against him, watched by the girl alone after he dismissed her ache and went.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish and bids him come by day to the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 44 names the grove where the girl went to drive birds from the drying fish (புட்கடிவான் புக்க).
teaches: The long poem spells out the trade behind the short one: naming the grove where the girl chases birds from the fish is the friend's way of replacing the dangerous night swim with a day meeting, which Thinaimalai 44 implies but never states.

note: In Natrinai 287 the girl says he came unafraid of the dread crocodile of the backwater; in Thinaimalai 46 the friend bars him from the night when the striking shark circles.
teaches: The night beast of the backwater counts for the girl in Natrinai 287 as the proof of his love and for the friend in Thinaimalai 46 as the reason to stop him and ask for marriage, so the same danger is read by each speaker to serve her own aim.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says he has come by night across the dark backwater of crocodiles and sharks and asks him to come by day to the grove where they guard drying fish. Thinaimalai 49: no dark at all to cross, since the pearls sweep away the midnight.
teaches: The two friends refuse the same night visit for opposite reasons, the older one because the dark hides beasts and the venba because the shore has no dark to hide him, so the convention needs only the refusal and lets the reason be turned inside out.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend tells the shore lord that they guard their father's drying fish from birds in the punnai grove and asks him to come there by day. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish in the grove.
teaches: The same chore that in Natrinai 45 marks the girls as beneath the suitor is in Akananuru 80 the cover for a daytime meeting, so the venba's bare picture of fish-watching could be either a rebuff or an invitation, which is why its sense stays open.

note: Natrinai 45: the friend tells the rich man's son that they are fishermen's daughters who drive birds from drying shark and smell of fish (புலவு நாறுதும்), so their life is no match for his. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish on the sand that reeks of it.
teaches: The venba keeps only the smell and the trade and drops the explicit 'go away, we are not your equals' of the Natrinai, which shows how far the later poet could rely on the reader supplying the refusal from the fish-smell alone.

note: Akananuru 86: the husband recalls the wedding held at a bright dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet on a faultless day. Thinaimalai 54: the friend tells the hero to call the diviners and choose a day.
teaches: The diviners' day that the friend demands in the venba is the day the older poem remembers by the moon's freedom from the planet, so the pair shows the omen-reading as the hinge that turns the secret tryst into the public rite.

note: Natrinai 303: the heroine lies sleepless at each cry of the anril joined with its mate in the palmyra of the common ground. Thinaimalai 56: the friend tells the shore lord that the anril calls from the tall palmyras of their front yard.
teaches: Natrinai 303 shows what the anril's cry does to the heroine at midnight, so when the friend in the venba points the hero to the anril in their own yard she is telling him, without saying so, what the girl hears each night he is away.

note: Kalittokai 124: the white waves ring the white dune like the blue garment worn by the milk-white elder brother of the god who measured the world. Thinaimalai 58: the dark sea and the white sand lie together like Mayavan and his elder brother.
teaches: Both neythal poets read the shore's dark and white through the two divine brothers, but Kalittokai puts both colours on the one white brother in his blue cloth, while the venba splits them between the two brothers, so the sea and the sand become kin rather than body and garment.

note: Kuruntokai 217: the friend tells the hill lord that meeting by day is possible while they guard the millet, but she fears his coming by night. Thinaimalai 59: by day the gossip is great, and by night the dangers are as great.
teaches: The Kuruntokai friend still leaves the day open and fears only the night, while the venba's friend closes both, so the pair shows the second step of the convention, where barring day and night together leaves marriage as the only way.

note: Kalittokai 33: in spring the silk-cotton flowers like fire and the pungu sheds blossom like puffed rice (எரி உரு உறழ இலவம், பொரி உரு உறழப் புன்கு), and the heroine feels the season mock the lonely. Thinaimalai 64 gives the murukku as scattered fire and the pungu as scattered puffed rice.
teaches: The pungu as puffed rice is fixed across both poems while the fire moves from silk-cotton to murukku, and the same paired images serve the heroine's complaint in Kalittokai and the friend's rebuke of open grieving in the venba, so the spring catalogue was a shared stock that either speaker could turn.

note: Akananuru 18 says that if the man suffers harm on the night ford even once, her friend will not live after it, and asks him to come by day; Thinaimalai 7 says that if he comes by night the daughter of the hill lord will not live.
teaches: Thinaimalai's flat 'she will not live' is explained by Akananuru 18: her life hangs on his safety on the path, so forbidding the night visit protects her through him, and the long poem's offer of a daytime meeting shows what the short ban leaves for him to infer.

note: Akananuru 369: the foster mother grieves that since the girl left, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and the doll gets no offering. Thinaimalai 73: the mother says the girl has given up her playmates' parrot and the pond's blue lily.
teaches: Read together they give both sides of the break: in the Akananuru the home's things go without the girl, in the venba the girl has already let go of the things her beauty was measured by, so the mother's grief covers both what the house lost and what the daughter chose.

note: Kalittokai 11: the heroine reasons that the man will return because he told her the burning forest holds a tusker that lets its mate drink the little muddy water first, a dove that fans its mate and a stag that shades its doe. Thinaimalai 78: an elephant alone finds no water in the spring and falls.
teaches: The same waterless road gives comfort in Kalittokai 11 and fear in the venba, and the difference is whether the poet gives the elephant a mate: the paired beast turns drought into proof of tenderness, the lone beast only into a measure of danger.

note: Kalittokai 11 closes its argument that the man will return with the omens at home: the lizard chirps on the good side and her lovely eye throbs on the left (உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே). Thinaimalai 80 ends on the same left-eye omen, with the same closing word இடம்.
teaches: Kalittokai 11 reaches the throbbing left eye only after a long proof from the man's own words, while the venba rests the promise of return on the omen alone, which shows the left-eye sign was a recognised closing proof that could carry a whole short poem.

note: Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the heroine not to cry: the man himself said work is life to men and men are life to women of the house, so he will put off his going. Thinaimalai 82: the friend says a man's duty makes him go for wealth, so she should not grieve. On the plain reading the two friends draw opposite conclusions from the same premise.
teaches: Both friends begin from the maxim that work belongs to men, but the Kuruntokai adds that men are women's life and concludes he will stay, while the venba stops at the man's duty and concludes he will go, so the outcome turns entirely on whether the maxim's second half is said.

note: Akananuru 375: the heroine says she would not weep if she knew he passed unharmed the waste where raw youths kill even travellers without ornaments to test their arrows. Thinaimalai 84: the same robbers who shoot travellers with no wealth are the heroine's reason he should not go at all.
teaches: The robbers who kill the penniless serve the Akananuru heroine as a fear for a man already on the road and the venba's heroine as an argument against his setting out, so one road-danger supports both the anxiety after departure and the plea before it.

note: Kalittokai 15 ends a long plea with the argument that wealth can be made any day, but asks whether it can bring back youth once it has passed (வளமையோ வைகலும் செயல் ஆகும் ... இளமையும் தருவதோ). Thinaimalai 85 builds its whole verse on the same contrast of வளமை and இளமை.
teaches: The venba condenses into four lines the closing move of a long Kalittokai paalai, keeping even the rhyme of வளமை and இளமை, which shows that the retort had become a fixed argument of the separation poem that needed no road scene to carry it.

note: Kalittokai 9: the mother asks travelling brahmins whether they saw her daughter and the youth; they say they did, and argue that as sandal, pearl and music serve others than their source, so the daughter belongs to the man she followed. Thinaimalai 89: travellers say they saw the man like the sun and the girl like the moon.
teaches: The venba keeps Kalittokai 9's frame of the mother questioning travellers and their 'we saw them' but drops the brahmins' argument that a daughter belongs to her husband, so the consolation shrinks to an image of a well-matched pair, and the mother is left with a report rather than a reason.

note: Kuruntokai 315: the heroine says the hill man is like the sun (ஞாயிறு அனையன்) and her shoulders like the nerunji flower. Thinaimalai 89: the man is like the hot sun and the girl like the cool moon.
teaches: In the Kuruntokai the man as sun makes the woman a nerunji that turns after him, while in the venba she is the moon, a second light of her own, so the same sun-image yields dependence in one poem and parity in the other.

note: Akananuru 195: the mother of the eloped girl, after picturing the other mother preparing her house for the couple, asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?). Thinaimalai 90 asks the same question in nearly the same words.
teaches: The venba keeps the Akananuru mother's question almost word for word while dropping the rival mother's preparations and her own years of nursing, which shows that by the later anthology the question to the diviner had become a fixed turn of the eloped girl's mother that could stand without its reasons.

note: Kuruntokai 148: konrai buds like the gold coins of rich children's anklets bloom with the kurunthu; if you say this is not the rainy season, is it a dream? Thinaimalai 98: the konrai blooms into anklet, golden coin, garland and more; look at it now, you and the others.
teaches: Kuruntokai uses the anklet-coin likeness to make the konrai unanswerable evidence that the season has come, and the venba expands that single likeness into a run of six ornament shapes and calls witnesses, so the flowering becomes a proof displayed to an audience.

note: Both are the friend forbidding the night visit by a path where elephants go; Akananuru 318 adds 'மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை', you may have the wedding if you want it.
teaches: The four-line verse stops at the prohibition, and the long poem shows what the prohibition is for: shutting the night road is the friend's way of pressing for marriage, which Thinaimozhi 1 leaves unsaid.

note: In Akananuru 28 the mother would replace the girl at the field if she failed to scare the parrots; in Thinaimozhi 10 the mother bars her from the field because she has learnt of the union.
teaches: The pair shows two routes to the same confinement, neglect of the field-watch and the mother's knowledge, which makes clear that the millet field is the one place the girl is allowed out, and losing it is losing him.

note: Akananuru 229: the girl answers her friend that the man who promised to come at once has not come even in young spring, when the koel calls on the budding branch. Thinaimozhi 13: the flowering season has come and the koel has made all his sworn words false.
teaches: The Akananuru lets the koel mark the date the promise failed, while the venba makes the koel the agent that turns his oath into a lie, so the four-line form compresses the long poem's reasoning into a single accusation aimed at the bird instead of the man.

note: Akananuru 375: the girl tells her friend her eyes would not weep if she knew the man who crossed the wasteland of killers would return unharmed. Thinaimozhi 15: she asks her friend whether the man who gave up grace for wealth halts on the long waste where the hawk attacks the dove.
teaches: In Akananuru 375 fear for his safety is the whole cause of her tears, but the venba puts that fear in the same sentence as the charge that he abandoned grace, showing that the heroine's worry for him survives her own accusation against him.

note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

note: Natrinai 9: the eloping man tells the white-toothed girl to go without strain, lingering at every shade, since the road they take (யாம் செல்லும் ஆறே) runs through cool groves where the koel calls. Thinaimozhi 16: he tells the girl with budding teeth that the place they go (நாம் செல்லும் இடம்) is to be desired, as maraa blooms and bees hum.
teaches: Both men answer the girl's fear of the waste by describing its blossoms, which shows a fixed speech of the eloping lover; the venba's own turn is to have the bees hum the paalai melody, turning the name of the dreaded land into the music that leads her across it.

note: Akananuru 185: her bright bangles slip as the man crosses summer hills where seed-bearing bamboo bursts with the twang of warriors' bows. Thinaimozhi 18: on the road where sun-split bamboo sheds pearls, her bangles seem ready to fall.
teaches: In the Akananuru the bursting bamboo is a sound of violence on his road, while the venba makes the same bursting shed pearls, a treasure dropped in the land where he seeks wealth, set against her bangles falling for nothing, so the image of the split bamboo is turned from danger to the waste of what is precious.

note: Akananuru 28 warns that the millet ears are bowing and stalks are showing, so the girl may soon be replaced at the field; Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the fields has ended.
teaches: Read in order the two poems give the harvest as the clock of the secret love, a warning while the ears ripen and the closed field once they are cut, so the end of the field-watch is the end of their meetings.

note: Natrinai 279: the mother asks whether the feet of her jewelled girl, her anklets removed, are weary on the sun-glittering track. Thinaimozhi 20: the mother asks a man on the road whether her daughter can bear to walk the harsh waste with a youth whose bow is like Death.
teaches: Natrinai's mother fears only the road and the girl's tender feet, but the venba's mother fears the companion too, calling him Death-like, which shows the mother's grief can doubt the very youth the girl trusted for protection.

note: Both liken the thundering rain to the drums of kings (வேந்தர் ... முரசின்). Kuruntokai 380: the friend says their lover is in a far country, not before them; how shall they bear it? Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 23: the friend says he who went will come, and the rain will be greater tomorrow.
teaches: One image, the sky beating like a king's drum, serves the friend once as proof that he is coming and once as a measure of how far away he still is, which shows that in the rains the friend's comfort is a choice of reading, not a fact the season settles.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could hold firm on the friend's repeated comfort (he will see the doe with the stag in the rain-fresh scrub, think of you and come today, இன்றே வருவர்) if only the herdsmen's harsh little flute did not torment her at evening. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 25: the friend points to the buck leaping with his doe and says he will come right now (இன்னே வருவர்).
teaches: The Thinaimozhi verse gives the friend's argument by itself, and the Akananuru heroine quotes that same argument and tells us where it breaks, at evening with the flute, so the four-line comfort is shown as one turn of a longer exchange in which it does not fully hold.

note: Kuruntokai 21: though the forest's konrai says it is the rainy season, the heroine will not believe it, for he does not lie. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 26: the friend says the thundering rain is the time he named, fitting his word.
teaches: Both trust the man's word, but they draw opposite conclusions from it: the friend reads the rain as his promise kept, the Kuruntokai woman reads his absence as proof the rain is not yet the true season, so the same faith can either confirm the season or deny it.

note: Akananuru 14: in the evening when good cows with swollen udders ooze sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற) and call to their calves, the wife asks the bard how she will be at dawn if he does not remember them; the bard then sees the chariot coming. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 30: with the herds oozing sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற), the friend asks 'will our man come?'
teaches: The same phrase of cows streaming milk carries the question of his return in both poems, and the long Akananuru supplies the answer the venba leaves open, the chariot on the road, so the milk-heavy herd going home is a fixed cue that the man too must be on his way.

note: Kalittokai 25 likens the woman's eyes, bangles and brow, bright while he is near and failing when he leaves, to the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; Thinaimozhi 33 likens the man himself, who ate her youth and moved on, to the friendship of the base.
teaches: Both poems borrow the moral figure of the false friend for a husband's desertion, but the Kalittokai sets it on the wife's changing body while the venba sets it squarely on the man, so the same ethical simile can either describe the damage or name the culprit.

note: In Natrinai 200 the friend, with the bard listening, has the potter cry through the town that women should guard against this bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; in Thinaimozhi 34 the bard is found standing in the other women's street for his own gain.
teaches: Read together the two show the bard's double standing in marutham: the man's envoy at the wife's door is, to the town and the wife, a known agent of his affairs elsewhere, and the venba adds that he profits from it.

note: Kalittokai 74 opens with a striped bee that has fed on pond flowers and backwater neythal moving on to the field lotus, and says the man joins one woman at forenoon and seeks another by afternoon; Thinaimozhi 35 likens him openly to the bee that sips fresh flowers and leaves the women only their bodies.
teaches: What the Kalittokai leaves as an opening scene to be matched with the man's day, the four-line venba states as an explicit simile with its result, the emptied body, showing the hidden image of the longer poem made plain in the later form.

note: In Kalittokai 74 the wife answers the bard who praises the man as not loveless by calling the bard, the trusting women, the man and his chariot all deluded; in Thinaimozhi 38 she stops the bard's praise of the man's goodness by pointing to the loosened hair his garland lay on.
teaches: Both wives reject the bard's praise of the husband, but the Kalittokai argues the case at length while the venba answers with a single visible sign, so the shorter form shows the refusal resting on evidence rather than rebuttal.

note: Kuruntokai 121: the heroine grants her friend that for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst (தான்குறி வாயாத் தப்பற்கு) her own shoulders have turned pale, as the branch goes down with the langur that missed its leap. Thinaimozhi 41: for the same failure she questions his nobility.
teaches: The same failed tryst draws two answers from the heroine: in the Kuruntokai she takes the fault into her own body, while the later venba turns it outward into a charge against his worth, which shows accusation as a second, sharper register of the same situation.

note: Natrinai 11: the friend tells the heroine, wilting since the tryst he set failed (அவர் செய் குறி பிழைப்ப), to drop the resentful thought that he will not come, for his charioteer is driving along the moonlit shore sparing the crabs. Thinaimozhi 41 is that resentful thought spoken: his trysts have turned false (செய்த குறியும்பொய் யாயின).
teaches: Held together the two give the complaint and its answer in one neythal exchange: the venba lets the heroine conclude from the failed tryst that his bond is false, while the older poem shows the friend refusing that inference and offering his gentleness on the road as proof.

note: Akananuru 260 lists the signs of evening on the neythal shore (the sun dimming, herons crying, the crab slipping into its hole, the waves falling quiet) before the heroine asks what will become of her. Thinaimozhi 48 gives a chariot cutting the sand, crabs scattering and the sun hurrying away as the evening comes.
teaches: The long poem shows that the neythal evening was built as a catalogue of shore signs ending in the heroine's dread, which lets the four-line venba keep only three signs and the bare 'evening will come' and still carry that dread unstated.

note: Akananuru 282: the father agrees to give the girl to the hill lord whose hunters bring ivory, gold, gems and pearls together, and the household prays for the wedding day. Thinaimozhi 50: the heroine asks whether the sea lord will come to the front yard where coral, pearls and crystal are heaped as if in praise.
teaches: Akananuru 282 makes the suitor's treasure of the land the very thing that wins the father's consent, so beside it the shore's coral, pearls and crystal piled at the heroine's door read as the bride-wealth her question 'will he come?' is waiting for.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage where the waterfall is the drum, the bamboo wind the flute and the bees the lute, with a peacock dancing; Thinaimozhi 7 compresses it to one line, the cascade sounding as lute, flute and drum.
teaches: In both the orchestra of the hill sets up an audience: in Akananuru 82 many saw him at the field, and in Thinaimozhi 7 the night visit will be known to the whole town, so the stage image carries the danger of the love being seen and heard.

note: In Akananuru 388 the young hunter asks the girls on the millet platform whether a tusker wounded by his arrow has passed by their field; in Thinaimozhi 8 the friend answers that no bleeding tusker came this way.
teaches: The long poem gives the pretext question and the short one gives only the reply, which a reader can only read as a reply because the question is a fixed form; together they show the wounded-elephant question as a standard opening the girls know how to parry.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a battle in which both kings die, their drums are abandoned (முரசு ஒழிந்தனவே) and no one is left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi Narpathu 11 describes the abandoned drums (ஒழிமுரசம்) of those whose strength failed, kicked by blinded elephants, on the field Sengan won.
teaches: The abandoned drum is the same sign in both, but whose drum it is decides what it means: when only the loser's drum is dropped it proves a victor and the field becomes his song, and when both drums fall, as in Purananuru 62, the field has no owner and the poet can only ask what the war was for.

note: Purananuru 373 (Kovur Kizhar, thurai மறக்களவழி) praises the Chola Killivalavan who made the Kongu turn their backs (கொங்கு புறம் பெற்ற) and ends among vultures on the fearful field, asking a gift; Kalavazhi Narpathu 14 names the Kongar as the enemy the lord of the river country killed (கொங்கரை அட்ட களத்து).
teaches: Read together they show that a Chola victory over the Kongu was already sung as a field-of-battle poem in the Purananuru, with the bard asking for his share; Poigaiyar keeps the enemy and the field but lets the stanza end on the field itself, turning a petition into a celebration complete without the bard's request.

note: Purananuru 369 (Paranar, thurai மறக்களவழி) builds the whole battle as a season of rain and tillage, elephants as clouds and arrows as rain on a wet field (ஈரச் செறுவயின்), ending in a request for elephants; Kalavazhi Narpathu 2 gives one farming image, blood running through burst drums like a tank's sluices after the monsoon (கார்ப்பெயல் பெய்தபின்).
teaches: Together they show how the kalavazhi theme changed form: Paranar's single sustained allegory of the farm year, made to earn a gift, becomes in Poigaiyar one quick water-and-field simile per stanza with no request, so the farming root of the genre's name survives only as a store of images.

note: Purananuru 25 praises Chezhiyan because his spear stopped short when he saw the enemy's widows beat their breasts and cut their hair; Kalavazhi 29 shows the enemy's bereaved kin wailing in all four directions and closes on the Chola's field.
teaches: Both poets put the defeated side's mourners in a victory poem, but one makes the king's restraint before them the glory and the other makes their wailing part of the spectacle of the field, so the pair shows two incompatible uses of the same grief in royal praise.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a field where both kings fell, the umbrellas shook, the famous drums were lost and no one was left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi 37 has the kings' corpses pour out blood that carries off the drums and the elephants, and the field belongs to the lord of the watered land.
teaches: The same lost drums and dead kings make a kalavazhi only because one king survives to own the field; Purananuru 62 shows the case where nobody does, and the poet must turn the praise to the heavenly guests, which marks the victor as the genre's precondition.

note: Kalavazhi 39 ends on the field where the Chola killed the Vanji king (வஞ்சிக்கோ), his white umbrella torn down and full of flesh; Purananuru 74 is a Chera king's own poem from captivity, held like a chained dog (தொடர்ப்படு ஞமலியின்) and begging water. The two are tied by the tradition that the Chera defeated in Kalavazhi was Kanaikkal Irumporai, the poet of Purananuru 74; neither text in our corpus states it.
teaches: The victor's song counts the Chera's defeat as the end of the matter, but the defeated king's poem says that being taken alive and fed by strangers is worse than the sword, so on that reading the field the Kalavazhi praises produced a fate its own frame cannot see.

note: Purananuru 19 has the cut-trunked elephants rolling on the ground like ploughs (நாஞ்சில் ஒப்ப நிலமிசைப் புரள) in a field where old mothers weep for their sons; Kalavazhi 40 has all the elephants fall as if the god of the silver plough (வெள்ளிவெண் ணாஞ்சிலான்) were ploughing the world.
teaches: The Purananuru simile sits beside the mothers' grief, while the Kalavazhi lifts the same plough image to a god's tillage and drops the mourners, showing how the battlefield-as-ploughing figure grew into a frame of pure praise once the kalavazhi became a genre of its own.

note: Purananuru 19 (lines 8 to 9) likens arrows lodged in a wounded elephant to a flock of sparrows settled on a hill (குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல); Kalavazhi Narpathu 8 says elephants hidden by arrows look like countless hills with flocks of sparrows (எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம்).
teaches: The near-identical image shows a stock battle simile passing from a Pandya victory poem to a Chola one, and the frames show it carries no fixed feeling: in Purananuru 19 it leads into mothers weeping for sons and Death fleeing in shame, while in Poigaiyar it is pure spectacle of the victor's field.

note: Purananuru 42: the Chola's army roars like the sea. Thinaimalai 52: the sea, with waves for mahouts and boats for elephants, is like a king's force rising.
teaches: The puram simile is run backwards in the neythal venba: where the war poem makes an army sound like the sea, the love poem makes the sea a mustered army, so that the shore lord is held to a king's measured conduct and the wedding becomes his orderly campaign.

note: Purananuru 312 assigns each person a கடன்: bearing the son is the mother's, making him worthy the father's, and killing elephants in battle the young man's. Thinaimalai 82 calls going to make wealth the man's கடன், repeating the word three times.
teaches: The venba carries the heroic vocabulary of duty from the battlefield to the trade road: what Purananuru 312 makes the young man's duty in war, the later akam friend makes his duty in wealth-making, and uses it to silence the wife's grief.

note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: dark clouds like oiled elephants rise on the right every day, a sight beyond doubt that he will come. Mullaippattu 4-5: the cloud drinks the cold sea and rises rightward (வலனேர்பு), just before the old women go out to seek an omen.
teaches: The idyll sets the rightward-rising cloud beside a separate omen rite, while the venba makes the cloud itself the omen 'beyond doubt', which shows the rising on the right read as a good sign for the absent man's return.

note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

note: The sages who have cast out lust and fierce anger walk first into Avinankudi; the Siddhar poet clears lust, anger and the great lie out of his heart so that it can become the Lord's bedchamber.
teaches: Driving out lust and anger is in the idyll the qualification of a class of sages to approach the god's shrine, and in the later poem the housework every devotee must do to make the heart itself the shrine.

note: The idyll's assembly of gods comes with Brahma 'in mind' and a need it does not name; the Thiruppugazh number-poem tells that Murugan imprisoned Brahma and freed him when the three gods came begging at his feet.
teaches: If the Thiruppugazh's story is the one behind lines 160 to 165, the oldest Murugan poem already assumes the episode of Brahma's imprisonment, and the later hymn only states outright what the idyll leaves as an allusion.

note: Nakkirar's Eragam is the shrine where brahmins recite the rare six-letter mantra; Arunagirinathar's Eragam is where 'the brahmins of the six letters' (ஆறெழுத்து அந்தணர்) praise his feet.
teaches: The six-letter brahmins of Eragam pass from Nakkirar's description into Arunagirinathar's epithet almost word for word, showing that the later poet read the shrine through this idyll's line 186.

note: Nakkirar defines the brahmins of Eragam by their outward order (six duties, three fires, sacred thread, wet cloth, chanting at set hours); Tirumular defines the true brahmins by meditating on the mantra and riding the chariot of love so as not to sink in maya.
teaches: The same figure of the mantra-reciting brahmin is praised by the idyll for keeping the forms and by Tirumular only for the inner love the forms should lead to, which shows the Saiva yogic tradition re-grounding a figure it inherited.

note: In the idyll, dancing on every hill with the hill women is the god's settled nature (குன்றுதொறாடலும் நின்றதன் பண்பே); in the Thiruppugazh, Kunruthoradal is the name of a shrine where the hill tribes worship him with frenzied dance (வெறியாடி).
teaches: A phrase that in the Sangam idyll describes the god's habit among the hill people became by Arunagirinathar's time the proper name of a shrine, so the idyll's description is the origin of a later place of pilgrimage.

note: The idyll finds the god in every outer place of worship, festival ground, veri ground, grove, river, crossroads and kadamba tree; Sivavakkiyar asks what use any puja is while the Lord being sought is within us. On the reading that the Siddhar rejects outer places and rites altogether, the two are incompatible.
teaches: The idyll widens the god's presence outward to every spot where he is called, and the Siddhar narrows it to the one place inside the worshipper, so the pair marks the two ends of the Tamil argument over where the divine is met.

note: The idyll says those who worship with offerings of goat's blood and red millet obtain what they ask; Sivavakkiyar says that offering goat and cock at the shrine when you are sick does not stop you wasting away. The claims about whether such offerings work are incompatible.
teaches: The Siddhar's mockery of goat and cock sacrifice is aimed at a rite the Sangam idyll describes in detail and promises results from, so his scepticism attacks a claim with a long and respected Tamil history.

note: The idyll's rite offers rice mixed with a ram's blood and spreads millet with blood, and calls it worship that brings each seeker what he sought; Tirumular says that in worship the bright flower is not killing other small lives. Read plainly, one counts a killing as part of right worship and the other counts not killing as the best offering.
teaches: Blood offering stands in the oldest Murugan poem as an ordinary part of effective worship, so Tirumular's rule that not killing is the true flower is a reform of an existing Tamil practice, not a restatement of it.

note: Nakkirar calls the god 'bull among poets of praised good speech' (புலவர் ஏறே); the Thiruppugazh says Murugan delighted in the poems of Keeran (Nakkirar) and taught him grammar.
teaches: The idyll's epithet makes the god a poet, and the later tradition turns that into a story in which the idyll's own author becomes the god's pupil, so the poem's praise of the god's speech came back as the poet's legend.

note: In the idyll the god appears in his own form to a living suppliant and says 'Fear not; I knew of your coming'; in the Thiruppugazh the poet asks that at the moment Death's servants come he appear on the peacock and end his fear.
teaches: The god's appearance and his word against fear, which the idyll promises to any suppliant who makes the journey, the later poet saves for the single hour of death, showing how the guide-poem's promise of a meeting became a plea for rescue.

note: The seeker says it is hard for living beings to know the god to his measure (நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின்); Tirumular says Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, measuring with thought, cannot conceive the Lord, who stands beyond all measuring.
teaches: The theme that the god cannot be measured, which Tirumular argues through the gods' failure, is already in the Sangam idyll as the suppliant's reason for coming to the feet, so unknowability led to approach rather than to despair from the start.

note: Nakkirar gives each of the six faces and the twelve hands a work in the world; Arunagirinathar asks to hold the same faces, arms, feet, vel and peacock in thought every day.
teaches: The list of the god's faces and arms began as a description of what he does for the world and became, in the later hymn, a sequence to meditate on, so the same inventory moved from cosmology to devotional practice.

note: The guide scripts the bard's praise of the patron (warrior of warriors, lord of the wealthy, of unceasing giving) as the way to his gifts; Arunagirinathar confesses that praising people as lotus-handed and clouds in giving, to beg from them, wounded his heart, and asks to serve Murugan instead.
teaches: The patron praise that the guide poem teaches as a craft with a sure reward is in the later hymn the very habit the poet repents, so the bard's profession that founded Tamil praise poetry became for the devotional poet the model of misplaced service.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts at a host's changed face; in the idyll the hill people take the troupe in as kin without asking who they are and speak sweet words to end the loneliness of a far country, but only after the troupe says it is the Vel's musicians.
teaches: The idyll confirms the Kural's point that a welcome lies in the manner more than the meal, but it shows the welcome opened by the patron's name rather than owed to any guest, so in the guide poem hospitality is a sign of a king's reach, not the householder's duty the Kural makes it.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; in the idyll everyone in the patron's town looks on the arriving bards sweetly and gladly before any gift is given.
teaches: The Kural makes the host's face the guest's first need inside one household; the idyll extends that glad look to a whole town, so the welcoming face becomes a public mark of the patron's realm rather than a private courtesy.

note: The Kural says giving without the misery of saying 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born; the patron, hailed as the scion of an unfailing line, will not let the bards even finish telling of their journey before he welcomes them.
teaches: One of the senses of the couplet, giving before the asker must speak of his need, is in the idyll a court scene in which the patron cuts short the suppliants' account, and the idyll ties it, as the Kural does, to the giver's lineage.

note: The Kural says nothing stands undying in the world but towering fame; the idyll sets beside the patron's choice of fame a crowd of dead rich men past counting whose names went with them.
teaches: The Kural states that fame alone survives without saying what the alternative looks like; the idyll supplies it as a number, the sands of a riverbank, so the couplet's single survivor is measured against a vast forgetting.

note: Naladiyar 2 tells those who gain wealth to share its food with many at once, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; the idyll's bard passes on to others what he received on the road, and the king, weighing the instability of the world, will not dismiss his guest.
teaches: The impermanence that the Naladiyar uses as an argument for giving is already in the idyll a motive at both ends of the gift, the bard redistributing as he goes and the king holding on to the guest, so instability argued for keeping company as well as for releasing wealth before it became a quatrain about wealth alone.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the idyll grants that in Karikalan's land, under a sceptre it has just called just, the rain can fail in great drought, and gives the harvest to the Kaveri instead.
teaches: On the idyll's reading the just king's land is not spared drought, which the Kural's couplet implies it should be, so the poet keeps the king's righteousness and the land's plenty together by moving the source of harvest from the sky, which answers to the sceptre, to the river, which does not need to.

note: The Kural likens the wealth of a man of நயன் to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town; the guide says he went to Karikalan like a bird that thinks of a fruiting tree, through a gate that bars no one in need.
teaches: The Kural states the tree from the giver's side and makes its public place the point, while the idyll shows the same tree from the hungry bird's side and supplies the condition the couplet compresses into உள்ளூர், an open gate, so the maxim's promise turns out to depend on access as much as on fruit.

note: The Kural says a ruler easy to see and not harsh of speech has his land praised above others; the idyll praises a gate never shut to bards, poets and brahmins, a glad face and freedom from fierce anger, each praised by a named class of people.
teaches: The Kural's abstract reward of praise has a concrete source in the idyll, where the people at the open gate (wise men, warriors, women and suppliants) are the ones who do the praising, so accessibility is rewarded by the very classes it admits.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbending sceptre; the bard's song praises both, the sceptre that shades the ploughmen and the spear that burns the chariot warriors.
teaches: The bard gives sceptre and spear equal places by assigning them to different people, subjects and enemies, while the Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear even in war, so the ethical book turns the praise poem's balanced pair into a hierarchy.

note: The idyll's bards wander like birds that search for fruiting trees on a hill the rain has left; the Kural likens the wealth of a man with nayan to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: The patron-as-fruit-tree image is seen from the tree's side in the Kural and from the birds' side in the idyll, and the idyll adds the condition the Kural's town tree removes: the guide poem exists because, for the wandering bard, the fruiting tree is far off and must be pointed out.

note: The idyll's warriors trade raided cattle for toddy and drink home brew all day as part of a life of valour; the Kural forbids drink, allowing it only to those who do not wish to be counted by the worthy.
teaches: The Kural's ironic concession names a class of people who do not seek the esteem of the worthy, and the idyll shows that such a class was a whole warrior community whose honour lay in the raid, not in sobriety, so the Kural's ban addresses a scale of values the older poem did not share.

note: The Kural says only those who live by their own ploughing truly live and all others bow to eat and follow behind; the idyll's bard, who lives by praise, is fed millet and beans at the farmers' village.
teaches: The idyll shows the arrangement the Kural ranks: the bard is exactly one who eats from another's plough, yet the guide poem treats being fed by farmers as the patron's honour and the bard's due, not as a lesser life, so the Kural's verdict is a moral claim against the old patronage order.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll says that in the land of Thiraiyan's just sceptre robbers are absent and thunder, snakes and beasts do no harm.
teaches: The idyll extends the Kural's claim that a just ruler's land is blessed by nature from rain and crops to the dangers of the road, so for a travelling bard the just sceptre is proved by a safe journey rather than a good harvest.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies; the idyll describes a town that has never known hunger, whose granaries grow old unopened and whose children sleep fed on milk.
teaches: What the Kural defines by absences the idyll shows by presences (unopened granaries, toy chariots, nurses, white rice and fowl for a guest), and its phrase தொல்பசி அறியா makes freedom from hunger a property of the town's history, not only of its present.

note: The Kural says the base, like sugarcane, yield only when crushed; the idyll's cane presses roar day and night and the bard is told to drink the juice as he likes.
teaches: The Kural's image of giving extracted by force uses the same press that the idyll presents as the very sound of open plenty, so the simile's sting depends on the contrast: what the base give only under crushing, the cane in a good land gives to any passing guest.

note: The guide promises the bards rice toddy brewed by fisherfolk and roasted fish until they stagger; the couplet says do not drink, or let only those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy drink.
teaches: The idyll counts drinking to the point of staggering among the best hospitality of the road, given freely by the poorest folk, while the couplet makes drink the mark of one who forfeits esteem, so the ethics book is rejecting a pleasure the oldest praise poetry offered as part of the gift.

note: In the idyll a kingfisher strikes a bathing girl's golden earring for a fish and carries it off to a sacrificial pillar; in the Naladiyar quatrain a kingfisher takes the beloved's eyes for carp but does not dive, seeing her brow as a drawn bow.
teaches: The kingfisher's mistake about a woman's ornament or feature was a set conceit: the idyll lets the bird act on its mistake as part of a port scene, while the later love quatrain stops the bird short, turning the same error into praise of the woman's brow.

note: The toddy-sellers keep a boar in a pit for many days, fed on rice flour and kept from its sow, to serve its fat to the bards; the couplet says that if no one killed to eat, no one would bring flesh for sale.
teaches: The idyll describes exactly the chain the couplet condemns, an animal fattened in confinement to be served and sold, and offers it as a reward of the road, so the Kural's argument against buying meat cuts against a hospitality the guide poems praise.

note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

note: Weighing the condition of the unlasting world, the king gives before the bard has finished asking; the couplet says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts.
teaches: The idyll turns the couplet's 'at once' into a patron's habit with its motive stated, wealth that will not stay given for fame that will, so the maxim had a heroic model in the bard's patron before it became a rule of the ethics book.

note: Kural 780: a death that fills the eyes of those who maintained one with tears is worth begging for; Mullaippattu's king remembers those who fell having made good the rice they ate (சோறுவாய்த் தொழிந்தோர் உள்ளியும்).
teaches: The Kural measures the warrior's best death by the tears of the one who fed him, and the idyll shows that patron from inside, lying awake over the men who repaid his rice with their lives, so the maxim gains a scene where the debt of food and the king's grief are both seen.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll opens on a world where the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and credits it to the rule of the patron's ancestors among truthful men.
teaches: The idyll gives the Kural's cause-and-effect rule a cosmic setting and a past: the plenty is the order of the world itself and belongs to the ancestors' rule, so a king inherits a moral weather he must keep up rather than earning it afresh, which is what the counsel later in the poem asks of him.

note: The Kural rates the worst poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; the idyll says the king, offered the treasure Vanan buried in the south, would not say 'let blame come to us', but would rather give treasure away for fame.
teaches: The idyll shows the Kural's maxim as a king's test with a named treasure and adds the alternative the Kural leaves out, giving wealth away for fame, so refusing blamed gain is tied to giving: the ruler's honour lies in both refusing and spending.

note: The idyll's sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring balance; the Kural says the vast sea itself would lose its nature if the cloud took and did not give back.
teaches: The sea's unchanging fullness was a stock figure of plenty in the city poem, and the Kural takes the same sea to show that the fullness depends on the return, which, read back into the market, makes Madurai's inexhaustible plenty the effect of continual exchange rather than a fixed store.

note: The idyll's அந்தணர் are marked by Veda, rite and high conduct, and only in passing by a loving heart; the Kural says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous because they are kind to every creature.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Kural keeping the idyll's name but moving its definition from the Veda and the rite to the one trait the idyll mentions last, kindness, so the couplet reads as a deliberate redefinition of a status the court poem took for granted.

note: The Kural's worthy man is like the balance that first levels itself and then weighs; the idyll's court is straight like the balance once it has put away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
teaches: The idyll's list says what the Kural's 'first making itself level' consists of, the clearing of five named passions before judgment, so the couplet's compressed image can be unpacked from a description of a working court.

note: The idyll names the courtesans' many deceiving lies and hidden embraces and their draining of rich young men, but lists them among the splendours of the city; the Kural likens the false embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
teaches: The deceit the Kural turns into horror was already admitted, in the same terms of lying and false embrace, by the court poet, who still counted it as part of the city's wealth, so the moralist's chapter answers a practice that praise poetry had treated as a sign of prosperity.

note: The Kural says many will live by a king who looks at people not alike but by rank (வரிசை); the idyll's king crowns warriors with the gold thumbai 'not asking who they are' but weighing their order (முறைகருதுபு), after listing the deeds that rank them.
teaches: The idyll shows a ceremony in which the king's ranking goes by deeds rather than by birth, which supports reading the Kural's வரிசை as an order of merit and shows what the couplet's 'many will live looking to it' meant in practice for a warrior following.

note: Naladiyar 6 starts from the appointed span of days and concludes: give your wealth away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; the idyll starts from the good time given within a bound and concludes: rejoice and live sweetly every day.
teaches: Both counsels rest on the same premise of a fixed span, but the idyll, after showing the king's giving, lets pleasure stand beside it as a right answer, while the ethics book allows only giving, so the later text narrows a kaanchi argument that once had room for enjoyment.

note: The Kural counts every day without a glorious wound (விழுப்புண்) as wasted; the idyll's king walks the camp at midnight in the rain to see the glorious wounds (விழுப்புண்) of the warriors who felled elephants.
teaches: The Kural makes the wound a soldier's private reckoning of his days, and the idyll shows its public side, the king coming out at night to look at each wound, so the honour the soldier counts by was conferred in person by his king's seeing it.

note: The Kural likens those fallen from their station to hair fallen from the head; the friend says broken jewels can be rejoined but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages.
teaches: The friend uses the Kural's idea that a fall in standing is beyond repair as an argument for speaking at once, not for keeping quiet: because a girl's good name cannot be restored once it is lost, the secret has to come out before gossip costs her it, so the maxim on honour drives the plot of disclosure.

note: The Kural says household life and its guarding of goods exist to care for guests; the man's oath promises a house of open doors where he and the girl will eat what is left after feeding guests.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the household exists for guests is already in the idyll the language in which a hill man pledges marriage: what he swears to give the girl is not a feeling but a guest-feeding house, so the ethic of virundhu was the content of the promise before it was a maxim.

note: The Kural says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the whole wide world; the idyll says that though the sky fails, the Kaveri does not, and the Chola fields never stop yielding. On the literal reading the claims conflict: the Kural admits no land exempt from failed rain, the idyll names one.
teaches: Read together they show that the Kural's universal law of rain met a regional boast in the poets' own geography, a river delta praised precisely as the place the warning does not reach, although the idyll's own line 6 (மலைத்தலைய) concedes that the river too begins as rain on the hills.

note: The Kural names customs (உல்கு) as one of the three kinds of the king's wealth; the idyll shows Puhar's customs men levying duty every day without shortfall and stamping the tiger seal on goods for the good king.
teaches: The Kural's single word for customs revenue is in the idyll a working institution with officers, a royal seal and a daily round at the port, so the couplet's category can be seen to name an administration the earlier poets had watched in operation.

note: The Kural says a trader's true trade is to care for others' goods as his own; the idyll's merchants weigh their own goods and others' alike (தமவும் பிறவு மொப்ப நாடி) and take no more and give no less.
teaches: The idyll's phrase is nearly the Kural's பிறவும் தமபோல், and it adds the working test of fair dealing at the scale, so the maxim appears first as the praised reputation of a real merchant class in a named port before it is stated as a rule for all traders.

note: The Kural argues that if no one killed to eat, no one would sell meat; the idyll praises a city where killing is banned and beasts crowd safely at the meat-sellers' huts, yet the same city fries fish and flesh in its toddy-shop yards (lines 176-177) and its fishermen eat prawns and tortoise (lines 63-64).
teaches: Held together they show the ban on killing in the older poem as the virtue of particular classes in a city that still ate meat, whereas the Kural's demand-side argument makes every buyer answerable, so the later ethic is stricter than the ideal the idyll praised.

note: The Kural says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; the idyll gives Karikalan both, the spear hot to his enemies and the sceptre cool to his people, and uses them as the measures of the forest's heat and the heroine's coolness.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear as the source of victory, while the idyll keeps the two as equal faces of one king, each true in its own sphere, so the pair shows the rhyme வேல் and கோல் as an older fixed figure of kingship that the Kural argued with and the akam poet borrowed for love.

note: In the idyll the forest men who have broken a hard stronghold (அருங்குறும் பெறிந்த) set aside their spoil as guest-tribute for their lord; in Akananuru 349 Nannan pours out unasked to weary bards the great wealth taken from broken strongholds (அருங்குறும்பு எறிந்த).
teaches: Read together the two poems show a chain of wealth: the spoil of forts taken by the hill people goes to Nannan as tribute and goes out again from him to the bards, so the patron's generosity praised in love poetry rests on his people's raids.

note: The idyll says Nannan brings back treasures from those whose backs he has seen and pours his gifts on poets (சுரக்கும், 71-72) and lays waste the enemy front (முனைபாழ், 59); Akananuru 349, in a heroine's lament, names a Nannan who lays waste the front, breaks forts and pours their wealth unasked (சூழாது சுரக்கும்) on bards who come with their kin.
teaches: An akam heroine can name Nannan's land by a two-line formula that the guide poem unfolds into a whole promise to a troupe, which shows the patron's praise circulated as a fixed epithet that love poets could assume their hearers knew, though the identity of the two Nannans is not certain.

note: Both describe Kuttuvan's western land by a buffalo that leaves the lotus pond to rest in jackfruit shade; Akananuru 91 says the hero will not stay for it even if he gains it, and the idyll calls even Kuttuvan's Vanji empty.
teaches: The buffalo resting in the jackfruit shade was a set emblem of the Chera land's ease, and both genres used it as the standard of plenty that is outweighed: by the heroine's beauty in the love poem and by a minor chief's giving in the guide poem.

note: The idyll's herd girl buys food with buttermilk (அளை) but will not take gold for ghee; in Kalittokai 110 the herd girl rebukes a man who thinks one easy to buy buttermilk from is easy for butter too.
teaches: The Kalittokai girl's retort turns on a real price difference that the idyll records, buttermilk as cheap daily barter and ghee as a good kept for livestock, so her wordplay about being 'easy' depends on the herding economy the guide poem describes.

note: The idyll says Thiraiyan is of the line the waves brought (திரைதரு மரபு); Akananuru 340, a shore poem, likens the girl to his Pavaththiri of many flowering seaside groves.
teaches: Read together, the two place Thiraiyan as a ruler of the coast: the praise poem's sea-born lineage and the love poem's choice of his seaside town as the measure of a neythal girl's beauty rest on the same identity, so the akam simile draws on the fame the guide poem states.

note: Both use the formula of the salt carts that proclaim their rate (கொள்ளை சாற்றி, கொடுநுக ஒழுகை); in Akananuru 159 raiding bowmen cook meat at the cold hearths the salt carters left, on the road the lover crossed.
teaches: The same stock road scene serves opposite ends: in the love poem the salt-carters' track is where raiders lurk and the woman fears for her man, while in the guide poem it is a road made safe for travellers by day under the patron, so the formula's meaning is set by whose land the road runs through.

note: In Akananuru 9 the returning husband pictures his wife at the evening when calves come home, standing at a corner of the house and praying at every chirp of the lizard; in Mullaippattu the old women seek the omen at evening, a calf supplies it, and the wife will not accept it.
